title: Shohoz under railway scrutiny over ticket scams
text:
Bangladesh Railway (BR) has sought an explanation from its ticketing contractor, Shohoz-Synesis-Vincen JV, over allegations that bots were used to secure train tickets as soon as online sales opened and resell them at higher prices.

Shohoz has submitted its explanation, company officials confirmed. Railway authorities are examining the company’s possible involvement in ticket black marketing in consultation with IT experts.

An audit of the online ticketing system by the railway has also flagged security weaknesses and identified around 169 administrator accounts. The railway is currently reviewing Shohoz’s response to the findings.

Meanwhile, the railway is taking over administrative controls held by the contractor at some stations and preparing to invite tenders for a new ticketing agency before the existing contract expires in January 2027.

Railway Director General Afzal Hossain told The Daily Star that the audit reports were received last week. Some findings concerned Shohoz, while others involved the railway’s operational and commercial departments.

Necessary action will be taken after reviewing the explanations, he said.

An internal document dated October 11 recommended asking the joint venture’s managing director to respond within three working days.

It alleged that bots operating through an unauthorised website -- bookmyrailbd.com -- were holding large numbers of tickets for resale at inflated prices. It also referred to the contractor’s security obligations under the integrated ticketing contract.

The audit found that the administrator dashboard could allow tickets to be held several days before sales opened.

It warned of possible black marketing through collusion between contractor representatives and railway booking assistants using administrator accounts operated by Shohoz employees.

Afzal said Shohoz retained administrator privileges at certain stations to add or remove coaches and update seat information. Some accounts were also registered in stationmasters’ names.

“These functions are now being brought under the railway’s operational and commercial departments,” he said.

Asked whether Shohoz was involved in ticket black marketing, Afzal said the possibility could not be ruled out, and the railway had found evidence relating to several issues. Further consultations with IT experts would help determine the next steps.

Shohoz Limited CEO Lt Col (retd) Aminul Haque, in a written statement sent to The Daily Star through public relations agency Benchmark, said the company had submitted responses and supporting documents to the authorities following observations by the Transport Audit Directorate.

“The issues raised in the audit relate to contractual terms, technological infrastructure, data management and operational processes. The evidence and information submitted to the relevant authorities are under review. Therefore, it would not be appropriate to provide a detailed explanation or comment at this stage,” the statement said.

Shohoz said it would continue cooperating with the audit and working with the relevant parties to ensure passenger service, data security, transparency, and accountability.

To curb black marketing, the railway has blocked nearly 10,000 suspicious mobile phone numbers and national identity card numbers, DG Afzal said.

The railway has also asked the Bangladesh Telecommunication Regulatory Commission to shut down bookmyrailbd.com. On October 8, it ordered action to close the website and strengthen ticketing-system security.

An audit covering fiscal years 2021-22 to 2025-26 also flagged alleged financial irregularities, including a shortfall in deposits to the government treasury against revenue from online ticket sales. It cited Tk 1,39,88,000 in fines that had not been recovered from Shohoz.

The Transport Audit Directorate sent 22 audit memos to the railway director general on August 16, seeking action.

Afzal said the contractor had previously been warned and fined several times over slow servers, outages and other system faults. The fines were adjusted against payments due to the company rather than paid directly, he said.

Meanwhile, the railway is preparing to appoint a new ticketing service provider before the joint venture’s five-year contract, awarded in February 2022, expires in January 2027.

Afzal said the tender documents were ready and tenders would be invited next week, though the notice had not yet been published.

He did not specify whether the decision to appoint a new agency was linked to the allegations against Shohoz but said the railway had to engage another provider before the existing contract expired.

title: Bangladesh’s storytellers bask in the spotlight
text:
Some stories stay with viewers long after the screen goes dark. A memorable performance, a line of dialogue, a haunting melody or a scene that refuses to fade. Behind each are the creative minds who bring these stories to life.

Yesterday, it was their turn to take centre stage.

Image

Actors, filmmakers, musicians and digital content creators gathered at the Bangladesh-China Friendship Conference Centre in Agargaon for the fifth Blender’s Choice-The Daily Star OTT & Digital Content Awards, celebrating the best of Bangladesh’s OTT and digital productions of 2025.

Nuhash Humayun’s “Dui Shaw” dominated the evening with nine Critics’ Choice awards, including Best Actor (Male) for Mosharraf Karim, Best Director, Best Screenplay and six technical honours. Afran Nisho and Mehazabien Chowdhury won the top Popular Choice acting awards.

Image

Organised by The Daily Star with support from Ispahani Tea Limited, the ceremony honoured productions released between January and December 2025 across 28 categories. It began around 6:30pm with the national anthem, followed by a performance by Alifia Squad and Sarika Sabah.

In his welcome address, Ispahani Group Chairman Mirza Salman Ispahani said the growing volume of quality digital content made selecting winners increasingly difficult.

Image

“It’s becoming increasingly difficult to choose the right awardees because there is so much good content available,” he said.

He thanked the jury for ensuring fair and transparent selections, congratulated the winners and encouraged other nominees to keep striving.

Mahfuz Anam, editor and publisher of The Daily Star, called for greater recognition of artistes, writers and technicians whose work enriches lives and contributes to cultural development.

Image

Reflecting on his career in journalism, he said much of his work involved confronting political and social problems, making evenings celebrating creativity a welcome change.

“On evenings like this, I really get into the world of art, the world of creativity.”

Image

He praised OTT platforms for bringing new dimensions to literature and storytelling.

“OTT has added so many beautiful dimensions to our lives,” Anam said, praising scriptwriters, cinematographers and professionals working in lighting, sound and production for their contributions.

Image

“The world of art is just as important to our lives as the economy, our professions and our skills.”

He said memorable films and dialogue could leave lasting impressions. “This evening is not only a celebration of great performances; it is a celebration of our consciousness.”

The Star editor urged artistes to embrace technological change while preserving Bangladesh’s history and traditions, and thanked the Ispahani family for supporting the event for five years.

In the Popular Choice categories, Afran Nisho won Best Actor (Male) for “AKA” and Mehazabien Chowdhury Best Actor (Female) for “Neel Shukh”.

Image

Mehazabien said she had been so preoccupied with her dance performance that she had no time to prepare an acceptance speech. Thanking the production team, fellow artistes and her family, she dedicated the award to director Vicky Zahed and expressed excitement over his move into filmmaking.

Asked whether audiences could expect to see them collaborate on the big screen, she teased, “Something is cooking.”

Nisho thanked viewers for voting for him, along with director Vicky Zahed, the producers and his family. He said the recognition meant a great deal but did not diminish the achievements of his fellow nominees, all of whom deserved appreciation.

Image

He dedicated the award to the late actor Humayun Faridi, whom he considered his mentor.

Vicky Zahed won Best Director (Drama/Series) for “AKA”, thanking producer Shahriar Shakil and the entire team for believing in its challenging storyline. Describing “AKA” as his third OTT film, he said bringing such a story to the screen required considerable courage.

Raihan Rafi won Best Director (Film) for “Amalnama”. He said he had long wanted to explore a taboo subject and thanked Chorki for giving him the creative freedom to realise his vision.

Image

He described the production as risky because of its sensitive subject matter but said he enjoyed taking such risks. He also urged audiences to support Bangladeshi cinema by watching films in theatres.

Manoj Pramanik won Best Supporting Actor (Male) for “Omimangshito” and Runa Khan Best Supporting Actor (Female) for “Bohemian Ghora”.

Runa thanked viewers for their love and support for her portrayal of Ambia, as well as director Amitabh Reza Chowdhury, Hoichoi and the entire production team.

Hoichoi’s “Bohemian Ghora” was named Best Drama/Series, while Chorki’s “Ghumpori” won Best Film. “Daagi” received the People’s Choice award.

Image

In the Critics’ Choice categories, Mosharraf Karim won Best Actor (Male) for “Dui Shaw”, Tama Mirza Best Actor (Female) for “Amalnama”, and Chorki’s “Feu” Best Film/Drama/Series.

Accepting the award on Karim’s behalf, Nuhash called him “a national treasure” and praised his generosity towards fellow artistes.

Tama said she had not expected to win against so many accomplished nominees. Describing her mother, who attended the ceremony, as her lucky charm, she thanked Chorki and director Raihan Rafi for the opportunities that helped shape her career.

Nuhash accepted the Best Director (Film/Drama/Series) and Best Screenplay awards for “Dui Shaw” alongside his mother, Gultekin Khan.

Image

“I am dedicating this to my mom and to my whole Dui Shaw team,” he said, thanking the crew for bringing his script to life. He added that recognition in his own country made the awards particularly special.

“Dui Shaw” also won Best Cinematographer for Joaher Musavvir Jyoti and Abdul Mamun; Best Makeup Artist for Md Emon Hossen and Sworna Bhoumick; Best Editing for Fuad Shourav; Best Art Director for Rainirr Borshon; and Best Costume Designer for Edila Farid Turin. Rajesh Saha, Sajib Ranjan Biswas and Rasheed Sharif Shoaib shared Best Sound Design.

In the music categories, “Premeri Jokhom” from “Ghumpori” won three awards: Best Lyricist for Jahid Preetom, Best Singer for Mahtim Shakib and Shithi Saha, and Best Music Composer for Jahid Nirob. Nirob thanked the singers for bringing the song to life.

Image

Ishaan Mozumder won Best Music (Digital Platforms) for “Gulbahar”, while Ruslan Rehman won the Critics’ Choice award for Best Background Score for “Gulmohor”.

Ruslan said awards made his otherwise ordinary life feel extraordinary for a few days, bringing particular joy to his mother and elder brother. He thanked the organisers for recognising background scoring, saying such honours helped music directors overcome the social anxiety associated with working largely behind the scenes. He also thanked his colleagues and the “Gulmohor” team.

In the Individual Content categories, Sunehra Tasnim won Best Content Creator of the Year under Popular Choice, while Syed Rashad Imam Tanmoy took the Critics’ Choice honour.

Image

“Awards have never been my primary motivation. It’s my audience, their love and the work that I get to create that keep me going,” Sunehra said.

Tanmoy recalled how a rickshaw puller once recognised his cartoons, convincing him that videos could take his drawings to audiences he had been unable to reach through newspapers over 15 years.

Nadir On The Go won Best Content Creator (Food & Recipe/Travel), while Sameerscane won Best Content Creator (Infotainment/Podcast).

Image

Sameerscane, who said he had previously attended the ceremony only to support friends, thanked his family.

“I just want to thank my parents for always allowing me to pursue content creation,” he said.

The evening also featured performances by Sunerah Binte Kamal and Irfan Sajjad, as well as Mehazabien Chowdhury. Musician Emon Chowdhury’s band -- Bengal Symphony -- also took the stage.

Rafsan Sabab and Afsan Ara Bindu hosted the ceremony.

title: Tigers’ spin dilemma in Mirpur
text:
Bangladesh head into today’s crucial first Test against West Indies in Mirpur uncertain about the conditions they will encounter. Pace has been a strength for the Tigers in the current World Test Championship (WTC) cycle, but the visitors also boast a formidable pace attack for the two-match series.

Statistics, however, suggest that relying heavily on spin against stronger opposition at the Sher-e-Bangla National Cricket Stadium has rarely paid off for Bangladesh.

There has been speculation that the team management has requested a spin-friendly pitch in Mirpur. But after the venue recently produced more sporting surfaces, a shift towards a turning track would mean moving away from Bangladesh’s pace strength while exposing their batters to the challenges posed by Mirpur’s turners.

Bangladesh have played nine Tests in Mirpur over the past five years, six of them against top opposition. Since December 2021, they have hosted Pakistan, Sri Lanka, India, New Zealand, South Africa and Pakistan again at the venue. Their only win in those six matches came against Pakistan this year, while the other five ended in defeats.

Bangladesh earned plaudits after that victory, particularly for the balance between pace and spin. Nahid Rana made the difference on the final day, with reverse swing from the old ball working in the Tigers’ favour.

The pace attack had also developed well, aided by some assistance from the surface. The Mirpur pitch looked green in the days leading up to the match, but appeared more barren as the Test approached.

“I still think they're going to probably shave down some grass [from the wicket] or have a little more preparation,” West Indies skipper Roston Chase said at Tuesday’s press conference.

“Obviously, with the amount of grass, you would think that it may be more spin-friendly, but looking at it, it still looks a bit dry underneath. And it's Bangladesh. Bangladesh is really known for mainly spin, so we think that it will get some spin also,” he added.

Exactly how much turn the surface will offer remains to be seen. However, Bangladesh’s recent record in Mirpur suggests that spin has often been a double-edged sword. Over the past five years, spinners have taken 80 wickets against Bangladesh at the venue, compared with 73 for pace bowlers.

In 2021, Bangladesh lost to Pakistan by an innings and eight runs despite nearly two days being lost to rain. Off-spinner Sajid Khan claimed 12 wickets across the two innings, including eight for 42.

A year later, Ravichandran Ashwin and Axar Patel combined to take nine wickets as India edged Bangladesh out on a surface that offered little assistance to the pacers.

In 2023, New Zealand’s spin trio of Ajaz Patel, Mitchell Santner and Glenn Phillips dominated their Bangladesh counterparts, taking 17 wickets between them in the Mirpur Test. The home side’s spin-heavy approach backfired badly.

With Bangladesh still harbouring hopes of reaching the WTC final, their pace resources offer a strong alternative. Captain Najmul Hossain Shanto indicated that the quicks were ready to deliver.

“Our pacers are very clear about what conditions they will play in, and preparation-wise, they are all in a good position. That’s a positive, as I can pick them for any match,” Shanto said when asked about the pace attack.

With West Indies also armed with a formidable pace unit, the surface could prove decisive. Whether Bangladesh stick to their strengths or put their faith in spin remains to be seen -- as does whether a turning track will work in their favour or backfire once again.

title: Israeli exit polls show deadlock in apparent setback for Netanyahu
text:
Israel's wartime election was deadlocked on Tuesday, exit polls showed, with two major television networks giving Gadi Eisenkot's opposition bloc a narrow lead over Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's camp and a third showing them tied, leaving neither side with a clear path to power.

If the projections hold, the result would mark a major setback for Netanyahu's coalition, which entered the election with 68 seats, though the deadlock could allow Israel's longest-serving prime minister to remain in power as caretaker during coalition negotiations.

Turnout was 77.7%, Israel's Central Elections Committee said, the highest in more than two decades and around 7 percentage points higher than in 2022.

Two of Israel's three major television networks gave Eisenkot's bloc a narrow edge over Netanyahu's Likud-led camp in updated exit polls, while Channel 13 put the two blocs level at 51 seats each.

None of the projections gave either camp the 61 seats needed for a majority in the 120-seat Knesset. Far-right religious parties led by Itamar Ben-Gvir and Bezalel Smotrich were projected to take a combined 13 seats within Netanyahu's bloc.

Arab parties outside the two main blocs could hold the balance of power. But Eisenkot, leader of the Yashar party and a former military chief, has all but ruled out forming a government with them, complicating his path to power even in projections where his bloc finishes ahead.

Final results could take days, and Israel's fragmented political system leaves smaller parties potential kingmakers. No single party has ever won 61 seats outright in the 120-seat Knesset, making coalitions the norm.

It was the first election since the Hamas-led attacks of October 7, 2023, and the ensuing wars in Gaza, Lebanon and Iran.

Yohanan Plesner, president of the Israel Democracy Institute, called the exit polls a major defeat for Netanyahu's coalition, which was projected far below its 68 seats in the outgoing Knesset, while cautioning that Eisenkot had not emerged as a clear winner and much could change as votes were counted.

NETANYAHU SETBACK, NO CLEAR WINNER

Opposition leader Yair Lapid said in a statement: “Don’t let anyone confuse you: the Netanyahu bloc has suffered a crushing defeat. This is a total collapse and the public has told them to go home.”

Eisenkot, 66, who lost a son and two nephews in the Gaza war, emerged as Netanyahu's strongest challenger, stressing his security credentials while positioning himself as a centrist domestically.

He entered politics only four years ago and joined Netanyahu's war cabinet after the 2023 Hamas attack, but quit eight months later, criticising the prime minister's leadership.

Eisenkot offers a break with Netanyahu's leadership and far-right allies, but not with the hardline approach to security that has become more entrenched since the 2023 Hamas attack. He opposes Palestinian statehood and says Hamas' military wing must be destroyed or dismantled.

Eisenkot says Israel's response — a war that has killed more than 74,000 Palestinians, according to Gaza health authorities — was a failure because Hamas remains in charge.

"Dear Democrats, a decision was made," Yair Golan, leader of the Democrats party and a Netanyahu rival, said at a party rally after polls closed. "The nation has given us a sacred duty: to translate the trust they have placed in us into action, to fortify democracy, to save Israel and to provide true defense for the state."

The headquarters of the Joint List, an alliance of several Arab parties, burst into whistles and applause when exit polls were released, on a historic night for turnout among Palestinian citizens of Israel.

“We refuse the occupation and racism, and we will remain here,” said Faten Gattas, a candidate in the Joint List, in a speech at the alliance’s headquarters in Nazareth. Candidates hoped that high Arab voter participation would allow them to play a decisive role in preventing Netanyahu’s coalition – the most far-right in Israel's history – from returning to power.

A WARTIME VERDICT

Voters grappled with the trauma of Israel's deadliest day, when Hamas killed 1,200 people and took 251 hostages, and the wars in Gaza and with Lebanon's Hezbollah and Iran that followed.

While Netanyahu was criticised for the country's biggest security failure, he argued that he had made Israel and the world safer by assassinating top leaders of Hamas, Hezbollah and Iran.

The policies of Netanyahu's right-wing coalition have been divisive at home and deepened Israel's international isolation, but he has portrayed himself as the leader with the mettle to face down Israel's foes.

Netanyahu, 77, has served as prime minister for nearly 19 of the past 30 years and has repeatedly survived political crises. His opponents have managed to wrest the premiership from him only once since 2009, after four inconclusive elections in two years. Eighteen months later, he was back.

He entered the election facing longstanding corruption charges, which he denies, and criticism over intelligence failures that allowed Hamas-led militants to carry out their attack.

Netanyahu campaigned on an endorsement from US President Donald Trump, his ally in the war against Iran.

title: FIFA to visit potential 2030 World Cup host cities in November and December
text:
FIFA will carry out a series of visits to candidate host cities in Spain, Portugal and Morocco in November and December as part of the venue selection process for the 2030 World Cup, world football's governing body said on Tuesday.

A FIFA delegation will visit candidate cities and stadiums in all three host countries to assess their suitability to host games.

FIFA has yet to confirm which venues will be included, and has not announced where the World Cup final will be held, with Spain and Morocco battling to hold football's biggest match.

Visits are planned for Agadir, Casablanca, Fez, Marrakech, Rabat and Tangier in Morocco; Lisbon and Porto in Portugal; and Barcelona, Bilbao, Las Palmas, Madrid, San Sebastian, Seville and Zaragoza in Spain. FIFA said it may also conduct visits to additional venues during the selection process.

The governing body added that the allocation of matches and the type of games to be staged at each venue would only be determined after the final list of host cities is confirmed and work on the tournament match schedule progresses.

The first three games of the 2030 World Cup will be held in Argentina, Uruguay and Paraguay, in tribute to the centenary of the competition, which was first staged in 1930 in Uruguay.

title: Master out of sight, Messi orbits beyond the glare
text:
Watching a legend step aside carries a heavy, profound weight. For nearly two decades, Lionel Messi owned football. He turned the green pitch into his personal canvas, rendering the extraordinary utterly routine. Now, sitting fifth in the 2026 Ballon d’Or voting at 39, he watches the sport stride toward its next chapter.

While Harry Kane soaked in a well-earned spotlight under the London stage lights yesterday, a secondary storyline hovered in the shadows. Messi chose to remain absent. Thursday at 5:30 am Bangladesh time, while the glitz of London settles, he will simply put on his boots for Inter Miami in another MLS fixture, carrying on with business as usual while letting the new generation take their bows.

Naturally, the terraces argue whether his fifth-place spot rests on the weight of memory or current form. Critics point quickly to his current surroundings: playing under warm Florida skies puts him outside Europe's weekly meat-grinder. But look at his 2026 World Cup run. Driven by instinct, vision, and pure brilliance, he dragged Argentina to another final with eight goals and four assists, falling only to a ruthless Spanish side. He achieved that at 39 before calling time on his international career. Most of his generation had already hung up their boots.

Monday night merely mirrored a reality long since accepted. In 2006, a long-haired kid from Rosario took 20th place on the ballot. That was the spark before the fire. Eight golden balls followed, along with endless records and the holy grail in Qatar.

Twenty years on, the ongoing shift completes another turn. The torch remains firmly with Kane, Kylian Mbappe, and Lamine Yamal, making Messi’s empty chair feel more like a conductor quietly stepping into the dark while the hall still echoed with his music.

Monday night merely mirrored a reality long since accepted. In 2006, a long-haired kid from Rosario took 20th place on the ballot. That was the spark before the fire. Eight golden balls followed, along with endless records and the holy grail in Qatar.

Toni Kroos offered a similar exit in 2024, walking away at the summit while the applause was deafening. But Messi’s curtain call carries a different gravity. His decade-long rivalry with Cristiano Ronaldo defined an era. It elevated football to mythic heights. Watching those final pages turn brings a bittersweet reality: the golden age we lived through is now history.

A ninth Ballon d’Or would have been the cataclysmic detonation of a supernova, a blinding, explosive spectacle forcing the universe to pause. Instead, a fifth-place finish feels akin to a star taking a far more fascinating evolutionary path. It has shed its violent outer shell, collapsing into a white dwarf: super-dense, intensely bright, and radiating warmth long after its primary fuel has spent itself.

Whether fifth place was precise math or pure tribute hardly matters. The real image remains fixed. A titan who made miracles look easy is gracefully letting the game walk ahead of him, all while continuing to play the sport he loves on his own terms. Lionel Andres Messi Cuccittini leaves behind a stage he forever changed. The main auditorium may have shifted its spotlight to the next act, but out on the field, the steady, white-hot glow of the master still burns bright.

title: Bangladesh vs West Indies: Head-to-head record, key stats and more
text:
Bangladesh will be desperate to put their disappointing UAE tour behind them when they take on West Indies in the first of two Tests at the Sher-e-Bangla National Cricket Stadium today.

After a frustrating draw in a one-off Test against Afghanistan, the Tigers lost both their matches in the ODI tri-series against Zimbabwe and the Afghans by considerable margins.

Despite those recent stumbles, the tantalising prospect of reaching the World Test Championship (WTC) final offers a massive beacon of hope for the country's cricketing faithful. Hence the Windies Test series offers more than a chance to bounce back.

Bangladesh are fourth in the World Test Championship (WTC) standings, and while a top-two finish remains a long shot, winning all four of their remaining Tests would keep their hopes alive. Their campaign has already been their best across the four WTC cycles, with home victories over Pakistan and a remarkable 1-1 series draw in Australia providing reasons for optimism despite the recent setbacks.

Here’s a look at the key stats ahead of the first Test against West Indies:

Series history: In 11 two-Test series between the sides, Bangladesh have won just two -- both by 2-0 margins, away in 2009 and at home in 2018.

Last series: The most recent series in 2024 ended in a 1-1 draw, the only drawn series between them. West Indies won the first Test by 201 runs in Antigua before Bangladesh hit back with a 101-run victory in Jamaica.

Overall head-to-head: Bangladesh have won five of 22 Tests against West Indies, losing 15 and drawing two. Interestingly, three of their five wins came in the Caribbean, compared with two at home -- both in 2018, in Chattogram and Dhaka.

Windies' form: West Indies are unbeaten in Test series in 2026, having beaten Sri Lanka before drawing against Pakistan.

Mushfiqur's milestones: Bangladesh's leading Test run-scorer is 43 runs short of 7,000. Amongst active players, he has scored the most runs in Bangladesh-West Indies matches, amassing 782 runs in 14 matches at an average of 31.28 (including three fifties and a century). Since becoming the country's first 100-Test player, he has averaged 44.7 across six matches.

Roach's Bangladesh record: Kemar Roach averages 19.73 against Bangladesh -- his best against any Test opponent -- with 53 wickets in 13 matches, also the highest tally by a player in Bangladesh-West Indies matches. Twenty-one of those scalps have been left-handers, accounting for almost 40 percent of his victims.

Mominul vs Roach: Mominul Haque has fallen to Roach five times, joint-most among Bangladesh players alongside Shakib Al Hasan. Mominul also has the most ducks (5) to his name in Bangladesh-West Indies matches. Roach is second on the list with four scores of nought.

Roach's recent form: The veteran pacer has taken 10 wickets at an average of 22.4 in 2026, including figures of 4-51 against Sri Lanka.

Shadman stands firm: Bangladesh opener Shadman Islam has yet to fall to Roach, having faced 80 balls from the pacer across four Test innings.

title: 'A reset at lunch': Starc takes six as Australia fight back in South Africa decider
text:
Mitchell Starc said a "reset at lunch" led to an Australian fightback after South Africa made a flying start on the first day of the third Test at Newlands on Tuesday.

Starc finished with six for 72 as South Africa were bowled out for 329 shortly before the close in a match which will decide a series between the two leading Test nations.

It was a performance which looked unlikely as South Africa raced to 140 without loss at lunch after being sent in.

Starc was one of the bowlers punished, with the tall left-arm pacer conceding 39 runs in seven overs, including four successive boundaries by Marques Ackerman, who went on to score a rapid 95.

"We probably expected more out of the wicket," said Starc. "It was quite slow, with tennis ball bounce. They came at us hard.

"We didn't have our best stuff in the first two hours but the last two sessions were right up there. It's what we expect from this group. We had a reset at lunch and just tried to change the momentum in the field."

Ackerman, playing in his second Test, took the fight to the Australian bowlers with some dazzling strokes.

The slightly-built left-hander was on 82 not out at lunch, scored off just 75 balls.

He attacked veteran off-spinner Nathan Lyon, dancing down the pitch and hitting him over the stand at midwicket for six. But he tried one shot too many after lunch and was stranded when Lyon pushed the ball wider, giving Alex Carey an easy stumping.

Ackerman, 30, said South Africa would probably have been happy if they had been offered a total of 329 before play.

But he admitted: "We probably left a few runs out there."

Ackerman, who won a place in the side through strong domestic performances and some big scores for South Africa A, including 256 against Bangladesh A in August, is not normally an opening batsman but said he was not troubled by the adjustment.

"I have quite often had to face a new ball in my career and playing against our own fast bowlers in the nets has been good preparation," he said.

title: 13-0 defeat: Bangladesh concede 10-plus goals against India for third straight game
text:
Bangladesh began their Hero Asian Champions Trophy campaign on a disappointing note, suffering a massive 13-0 defeat to hosts India in their opening match at the Olympian Surjit Singh Hockey Stadium in Punjab, India, on Tuesday.

It was the third consecutive match in which Bangladesh conceded more than 10 goals against India. The men in red and green suffered a 10-0 defeat to the same opponents at the Asian Games in Japan last September, following a 12-0 drubbing at the 2023 Asian Games in China.

India opened the floodgates in the second minute and ended the first quarter with a 4-0 lead before adding two more goals ahead of the break. The five-time champions struck three times in the third quarter before adding four more goals in the final quarter to complete the rout, with Mandeep Singh scoring a hattrick.

title: Bangladesh’s fish future is at risk. Are we paying attention?
text:
For centuries, the culture and food traditions of Bangladesh have been closely tied to its rivers, wetlands and floodplains. The proverb “Machhe-Bhate Bangali” (fish and rice make a Bengali) sums up this bond. The connection is practical as well as cultural: fish underpin the country’s food security, rural livelihoods and economy.

Bangladesh is among the world’s top fish producers. In 2023–24, it produced 5.02 million metric tonnes of fish, worth BDT 250,900 crore (USD 20.44 billion). The fisheries sector accounts for 2.43% to 2.53% of GDP and over 22% of agricultural GDP. It provides nearly 60% of the animal protein Bangladeshis consume each day and supports the livelihoods of 19 to 20 million people, directly and indirectly.

Bangladesh ranks first in the world in hilsa production, third in inland open-water capture fisheries, fourth in tilapia production and fifth in aquaculture overall.

Image A fisherman catches fish in a pond in Dhirasram, Gazipur. While pond-based aquaculture accounts for a major share of Bangladesh’s fish production, it cannot replace the biodiversity and ecological functions of natural rivers and wetlands. Photo: Amran Hossain

The shift to pond farming and the loss of water bodies

Behind these figures lies a growing ecological crisis. Over the past four decades, the structure of Bangladesh’s fisheries sector has been transformed. Before 1971, capture fisheries in our open waters (rivers, beels, haors and canals) supplied nearly 90% of the country’s fish. Today, closed-water aquaculture (pond farming) accounts for 60.6% (3.14 million metric tonnes) of national output. Inland open-water capture fisheries have declined to 26.4%–28.1% (1.36 million metric tonnes), while marine fisheries supply the remaining 12.5%–13%.

The aquaculture boom has helped prevent a national protein deficit. It has been driven by advances in hatchery technology, the development of high-yielding strains such as GIFT tilapia, improved rohu and catfish, and private investment. However, farmed fish alone cannot sustain the sector’s future.

Aquaculture faces growing problems of its own: genetic deterioration of broodstock, rising feed costs, disease outbreaks and heatwaves brought on by climate change. More importantly, pond farming cannot replace the biodiversity and ecological services provided by healthy, free-flowing rivers and wetlands.

The core vulnerability of our fisheries system is the degradation and physical disappearance of natural aquatic habitats. In the 21 years from 2001–02 to 2022–23, Bangladesh lost over 1.05 million hectares of inland open water, a 21.52% reduction in water surface area. That shrinkage costs the country nearly 380,000 metric tonnes of potential wild fish production a year, worth an estimated BDT 22,763 crore.

Had this inland open water not been lost or degraded, Bangladesh would now rank second, if not first, in the world for inland capture fisheries production.

Three forces are destroying these water bodies:

Rivers, canals and beels are silting up or being illegally filled for real estate development, industrial infrastructure and other commercial uses.

Untreated effluent from textile mills and tanneries, urban sewage and agricultural chemicals have left many waterways toxic and biologically dead.

Fine-mesh monofilament nets (current jal) and other illegal fishing gear continue to kill juvenile fish, including jatka, and native broodstock.

This degradation threatens aquatic biodiversity, the cost-free protein safety net for rural communities and the country’s long-term economic resilience.

Image A fisherman casts his net near discoloured wastewater in the Shitalakshya River. Pollution from industrial waste and untreated sewage continues to threaten Bangladesh’s natural fishing grounds, aquatic biodiversity and freshwater fish stocks. Photo: Anisur Rahman

Conserve water bodies first, and fish production will follow

If Bangladesh is to maintain food security for its growing population, we must adopt a fundamental guiding philosophy: conserve water bodies first, then prioritise fish production.

To achieve a sustainable 5% annual growth rate in wild capture fisheries, Bangladesh urgently needs a coordinated national response built on the following pillars.

Figure 1. Strategic framework for restoring inland water bodies

Image

Table 1. Strategic action plan and policy framework

Strategic pillar Core actions Implementation mechanism Expected outcome Pillar 1: Habitat-first environmental policy Mark out and protect the boundaries of natural water bodies

Prioritise ecosystem integrity before fish production Legal enforcement; integrated ecological impact assessments Long-term restoration of natural hydrological regimes and breeding grounds Pillar 2: Sanctuary network expansion Establish permanent sanctuaries in critical wetland basins (haors, baors, rivers)

Impose seasonal fishing bans during peak spawning Co-management committees; Department of Fisheries (DoF) oversight Recovery of indigenous broodstock and richer biodiversity Pillar 3: Community-based management Empower local fisher co-operatives

End the exploitation of open waters by leaseholders Legal models for community-based fisheries management (CBFM) Equitable access to resources, less destructive fishing, and sustainable management Pillar 4: Integrated pollution control and restoration Enforce ETP compliance in industry

Dredge silted river channels where needed most Inter-ministerial task force (Environment, Fisheries, Water Resources) Better water quality, connected habitats, and more resilient aquatic ecosystems

1. Launch a nationwide programme to restore water bodies

Establish a permanent, nationwide habitat restoration programme under the Department of Fisheries to routinely re-excavate silted rivers, canals and beels.

Re-excavate and rehabilitate at least one major water body in each union or upazila every year.

Allocate a dedicated annual Blue Revenue Budget of BDT 10,000 crore for open-water habitat restoration.

2. Zero tolerance for wetland encroachment and conversion

Ban any alteration of natural beels and seasonal wetlands, as well as any commercial construction within them. These water bodies must be preserved to allow fish to breed and water to flow freely.

Impose heavy fines, legal liability and prison sentences for illegal landfilling, industrial dumping and the conversion of wetlands to other uses. Read more Where have Bangladesh’s hilsa gone?

3. Reclaim, restore and return stolen wetlands

Launch state-led drives without delay to identify public water bodies that have been illegally occupied, converted or filled, recover them from encroachers and restore community access.

Before handing over management, use state funds to re-excavate and ecologically restore reclaimed water bodies so that they can produce fish again.

Then hand over the restored water bodies to local fishing communities to be managed under scientific guidelines, ensuring that they serve community livelihoods rather than private interests.

4. Protect breeding seasons and support fishers

Enforce fishing bans in critical inland waters during the peak breeding season (April–July) so that native fish species can spawn safely.

Replicate the successful hilsa conservation model by providing alternative income support and food assistance through the Vulnerable Group Feeding (VGF) programme to vulnerable fishing families during fishing ban periods.

5. Empower local communities and safeguard biodiversity

Transfer the management of local beels and haors from short-term commercial leaseholders to local fisher co-operatives.

Expand fish sanctuaries in ecologically critical areas, such as the haor basin, to safeguard small indigenous fish species (SIS) that cannot easily be farmed in ponds.

6. Clean up industrial and agrochemical runoff

Make effluent treatment plants (ETPs) mandatory in all industrial units and ensure that they operate continuously.

Carry out routine water quality testing across major river networks.

Plant native riparian trees, such as hijol and koroch, along wetland dykes to prevent soil erosion and create naturally shaded habitats for aquatic life.

The way forward

Bangladesh has repeatedly demonstrated its capacity for agricultural innovation. Our scientists have developed climate-resilient fish strains, and our farmers have made the country the world’s fifth-largest aquaculture producer. But our continued failure to protect inland open waters has cost us wild fish stocks and capture fisheries production. Habitat loss, environmental degradation and illegal fishing have left 64 freshwater fish species threatened with extinction (IUCN, 2015).

Image Fishers prepare their nets on the Surma River, where declining fish stocks have made it increasingly difficult to earn a living. The depletion of natural fish stocks poses a growing threat to communities dependent on inland waterways. Photo: Sheikh Nasir

Farmed fish alone cannot meet our nutritional needs or preserve our natural heritage. The survival of Bangladesh’s fisheries depends on the health of its natural water systems. If it stops industrial pollution and wetland destruction, revives inland capture fisheries and combines modern technology with community-based management, Bangladesh can secure affordable protein for all and leave clean, living rivers for future generations.

Focusing on fish farming alone, while inland capture fisheries are neglected, will put aquatic ecosystems at further risk, worsen water scarcity and destabilise agriculture more widely. In the end, it could cause serious damage to the national economy.

Dr M.A. Mazid is a former director general of the Bangladesh Fisheries Research Institute and a recipient of the Ekushey Padak.

title: Marble Correspondence: A missionary letter that challenged America’s view of 1971
text:
An aerogramme written from India in January 1972 by a missionary couple, Reverend R V Marble and Martha Marble, reveals interesting facts about the 1971 Liberation War of Bangladesh and its aftermath. More than fifty years later, the letter survives as a witness to one of the most defining moments in our history and South Asian politics.



Finding the Marble letter

Letters from the past are often considered important sources of information by historians. They serve not only as windows into times gone by, but, by analysing their contents, it is often possible to reconstruct the thought processes of the writers, their psychology, and the effects of the prevailing circumstances on the collective psyche of the people.



For students of social philately, the branch of stamp collecting that deals with postal ephemera and their connections to society, letters with interesting contents are eagerly sought after.



The aerogramme featured in this article was acquired a few months ago when it was offered for sale at an online philatelic auction. As a collector of memorabilia related to the 1971 war, my primary interest in this item was the Indian “Refugee Relief Tax” stamp affixed to it. Burdened by the mass migration of 1971, the Indian government had imposed a five-paisa tax on almost all letters, with a few exceptions. However, once I received it a few weeks later, the joy of acquiring it became even greater.



The letter was addressed to Mr and Mrs J W Jacobs Jr, of South Main, Fayette, Missouri, USA, and was written by the Marbles.



Initially, I could not find any trace of a priest named “R V Marble” living in Delhi around 1972 through readily searchable online records. The search results mostly returned unrelated modern businesses and legal references rather than information about a person. The name Jacobs yielded no significant search results either.



So, I decided to delve deeper into the material. I contacted the United Methodist Church in the USA and requested information about the Marble couple. This finally revealed a deep-rooted connection between the writer, the Liberation War of Bangladesh, and South Asian politics.



Image An aerogramme sent from Delhi, India, to Fayette, Missouri, USA, in January 1972 by missionaries R V Marble and Martha Marble. It bears an Indian Refugee Relief Tax stamp introduced during the 1971 refugee crisis.



The missionaries



My research revealed that Reverend Robert V Marble was born in Conway, Arkansas. He grew up in Neosho, Missouri, received his higher education at Central College in Fayette, Missouri, and completed his divinity studies at the prestigious Yale Divinity School.



Martha Marble, his wife, was also a graduate of Central College. She was from Salisbury, Missouri, received a Master of Arts degree from Scarritt College in Nashville, Tennessee, and later became a missionary.



It is not clear when they married or moved to the subcontinent, but records show that between 1945 and 1966, the couple worked among tribal communities in villages across Central India. During that period, they were deeply involved in running mission schools, boys’ hostels and mission farms, and also conducted church services in villages.



After 1966, the nature of their work changed somewhat. Until 1982, Rev R V Marble directed the work of the United Methodist Committee on Relief (UMCOR) in India. Working with other organisations, including government agencies, his responsibilities involved disaster relief programmes and development projects. It was during this tenure that the Liberation War of Bangladesh broke out.



Image The reverse of the aerogramme, showing the sender’s name, R V Marble, and address at 40 Battery Lane, Delhi, India.

Before the Second World War, missionary letters from India generally focused solely on matters concerning the church . They provided details about schools, orphanages and hospitals, and missionary writers often acted as narrators of Indian social customs for a foreign audience.Following the Second World War, several global developments changed missionary thinking. As the war ended, nations were gaining independence from their colonial rulers, and missionaries found themselves confronted with growing feelings of nationalism and post-colonial identity. Thus, some of them became sympathetic to the newly emerging political spirit of these nations, and their routine letters reflected that change.Rather than being merely letters romanticising the lives of the people whom evangelists helped, church correspondence from the 1960s and 1970s served a multitude of purposes. These letters were now addressed to individual donors, family members, friends and missionary societies. They sought financial support by demonstrating that funds were being used effectively, while also helping to build emotional and spiritual connections between missionaries and their supporters.The Marble letter belongs to this newer generation of correspondence. Written in January 1972, it is particularly interesting not only because it offers a glimpse into the circumstances of the time, but also because it presents the emergence of Bangladesh from a fresh perspective.



The contents of the letter



Delhi

January 1972

Dear Friends:

Many friends from USA have asked questions about the conflict between India and Pakistan and about the deteriorating relations between the USA and India. For that reason I felt I should write something to all of you. I hope it is helpful.



Background



1. Partition of India into Pakistan and India in 1947 was a mistake. The present conflict is the result of that mistake, The mistake could not stand—has collapsed.

2. Pakistan, an Islamic state, has never been able to establish a secular democracy.

3. Early tension over Kashmere. USA early took a pro-Pakistan position.

4. USA has never Officially respected the desire of India to be independent of the great powers—even though USA maintained such a position herself for most of her history.

5. USA became more pro-Pakistan when the latter allowed her to build military bases there—which India would not permit.

6. Pakistan in recent years has:

(a) Failed to establish a democracy,

(b) Persecuted Hindus,

(c) Carried on a bitter hate campaign against India in which India did not indulge,

(d) Tried to cover up internal stresses by accusing India of interference.



Facts of present



1. The military dictatorship of Pakistan, in order to kill the democratic aspirations of its citizens, has killed hundreds of thousands of its citizens and imprisoned Mujibur Rehman—the man with the largest number of democratic votes in Pakistan history.

2. India received the intolerable burden of ten million refugees who fled in terror from East Pakistan—both Hindus and Muslims. India has had to spend over three million dollars a day for their care.

3. Mrs. Indira Gandhi and her government have shown remarkable restraint in the impossible predicament. Mrs. Gandhi went to all major countries and tried to get the world to do something. They did nothing about a solution. They did not condemn the genocide.

4. India did not start this war. Pakistan attacked by air on eight Indian cities and airports on December 3. This started it. President Nixon has placed the blame on India. He is ridiculously wrong.

5. India the Great Democracy of Asia had no territorial ambitions in the struggle. President Nixon said the opposite. He was wrong.

6. India called for a cease-fire when Bangla Desh was freed from Pakistan military rule and brutality. Mr. Nixon gets no credit for that. He committed a blunder in sending the Seventh Fleet here. He has illusions of what USA military might can do in Asia in spite of Vietnam.



What should USA do?



1. Reassess the whole situation and listen to such Senators as Kennedy, Church, Saxbe, Symington, Muskie, McGovern or listen to Chester Bowles or Galbraeth (former ambassadors to India).

2. Recognise Bangla Desh.

3. Help with funds in rehabilitation of 10 million refugees and development of war torn Bangla Desh.

4. Admit the error of past policies and form new ones that will support Democracy and Liberty in Asia.



The above is very sketchy. To fill it in properly would require a book. I have tried to say it briefly.



Is this a proper missionary letter? It is a voice crying out of the midst of the greatest single tragedy in humanity history. To remain quiet would be to invite the very rocks to cry out. In the name of humanity let USA policies become more enlightened about the creative forces at work in Asia. I believe creative forces represent the hand of God at work. May be it is a proper missionary letter after all!

Sincerely yours

R. V. and Martha Marble



Image The January 1972 letter written by R V Marble and Martha Marble from Delhi, challenging US policy towards the 1971 Liberation War and calling for the recognition of Bangladesh and assistance with postwar rehabilitation.



An analysis



The letter begins with “Many friends from the USA have asked questions...”, a classic opening sentence in missionary correspondence.

The letter was written only weeks after Pakistan's military surrender in Dhaka on 16 December 1971 and the emergence of Bangladesh as an independent nation. At the time of writing, the world was still debating the meaning and profound consequences of that historic event.

The Marbles were writing at a time when the historical narrative of the war was still being contested in the West. While India had emerged militarily victorious and was bearing the economic burden of hosting millions of refugees, the United States and many other countries had yet to formally recognise Bangladesh.



Besides setting the backdrop to the prevailing political situation in South Asia in January 1972, the letter makes some interesting observations.





One of its central arguments is that the Bangladesh crisis was not fundamentally a war between India and Pakistan. The Marble letter presents it as a democratic struggle by the people of East Pakistan, which was tragically crushed by the Pakistani military dictatorship.

Image A woman refugee at a camp in Kolkata holds a placard reading, “They are human beings. Democracy or demockery??” during the 1971 Liberation War. Photo courtesy: Muktijuddha Smriti Trust

One of its central arguments is that the Bangladesh crisis was not fundamentally a war between India and Pakistan. The Marble letter presents it as a democratic struggle by the people of East Pakistan, which was tragically crushed by the Pakistani military dictatorship.The Marbles’ focus on the 1970 Pakistani general election, the electoral victory of Sheikh Mujibur Rahman , the refusal of West Pakistani elites to transfer power, and the subsequent military crackdown is also noteworthy.By describing Bangabandhu Sheikh Mujibur Rahman as “the man with the largest number of democratic votes in Pakistan's history”, the writers frame the conflict in democratic terms. This was a powerful statement during the Cold War because it challenged the notion that supporting Pakistan meant supporting stability and democracy.Another striking feature of the document is that it fundamentally challenges the official American interpretation of the conflict. At that time, US President Richard Nixon and his National Security Adviser, Henry Kissinger, viewed Pakistan as strategically indispensable, as it served several American interests.The Marbles reject this entire framework and argue that American policy had been shaped by political interests and military alliances rather than democratic values. The letter also seeks to refute another dominant Western narrative: many Americans feared that India intended to destroy Pakistan or dominate South Asia.The Marbles also object to this idea and emphasise that India's intervention was primarily driven by the fact that Pakistan's internal conflict had become an international humanitarian crisis. Whether one accepts this interpretation entirely or not, it accurately reflects how many Indians and their supporters viewed the conflict of 1971, both at the time and in subsequent years.



As first-hand witnesses to the crisis, the Marbles knew that the figure of ten million refugees was not an exaggeration. India had received millions of displaced people from East Pakistan during 1971, and this was, at the time, one of the largest population displacements since the Second World War.



The writers’ emphasis on rehabilitation and reconstruction shows that they were already looking beyond military victory towards the practical challenges of building Bangladesh. As many missionaries and aid workers active on the ground understood, the refugee crisis transformed the conflict from a regional political dispute into a moral issue.



The final paragraph of the letter reveals why this document is especially valuable. The authors ask: “Is this a proper missionary letter?”

Moving beyond church activities, the Marbles felt obliged to discuss genocide, refugees, democracy and foreign policy. Through the letter, they expressed a theological perspective in which Bangladesh's liberation was interpreted as part of a moral and historical process rather than merely a political event.



Afterthought



The Marble correspondence is not merely an expression of personal opinion, but also offers a glimpse into a broader network of political criticism that maintained that the birth of Bangladesh exposed the moral shortcomings of Cold War diplomacy. It represented the triumph of democratic aspirations over military authoritarianism. For historians of 1971, this makes it a particularly valuable contemporary source, and for a philatelist, a cherished addition to a collection.

Mannan Mashhur Zarif is a journalist and a philatelist.

title: What’s Rotten in the Republic of France?
text:
« La France est une République indivisible, laïque, démocratique et sociale. »

“France is an indivisible, secular, democratic and social Republic.”

— Article 1, Constitution of the French Republic

Something is rotten in the Republic of France. Shakespeare’s Hamlet offers more than a literary echo of the corruption in the state of Denmark; it provides a vantage point from which to examine the predicament of citizens confronting what seems an overwhelming sea of troubles. In his celebrated soliloquy, Hamlet weighs the endurance of suffering against the prospect of “taking arms against a sea of troubles,” exposing the tension between resignation and resistance, endurance and action. The analogy with contemporary France is not literal: an individual’s existential dilemma is not the same as collective political protest. Yet Hamlet’s predicament acquires contemporary resonance when citizens take to the streets, not merely to oppose particular policies, but to give voice to accumulated grievances over economic insecurity, political exclusion and the feeling of being governed without being heard. Protest makes visible the distance between political authority and lived experience. Whether it can compel institutions to respond—and restore the connection between representation and consent on which democratic legitimacy depends—is a question that reaches beyond any single protest or government.

That distance lies at the heart of France’s present predicament. Emmanuel Macron’s presidency, after years of mounting disaffection, appears to have outstayed its political welcome. Yet the crisis cannot be reduced to his personality or political fortunes. It exposes a deeper tension within the Fifth Republic: a constitutional system designed to secure executive stability can become a source of political deadlock when presidential authority persists but the parliamentary support and public confidence needed to exercise it effectively erode. The question is why institutions built to overcome governmental paralysis have proved vulnerable to a crisis of representation—and whether the Republic can renew the relationship between the authority to govern and the consent of the governed.

The paradox of a powerful presidency

Established in 1958 amid governmental instability and the unresolved conflict over Algeria, the Fifth Republic strengthened the executive. The introduction of direct presidential elections in 1962 further elevated the presidency as the principal focus of national political authority. This settlement sought to reconcile democratic legitimacy with governmental effectiveness. Its durability, however, has depended not only on the powers conferred by the Constitution but also on the political conditions that make those powers workable.

Macron’s decision to dissolve the National Assembly in June 2024 exposed the vulnerability of this arrangement. Rather than securing a more coherent parliamentary majority, the subsequent election produced a fragmented legislature and made the formation of a stable governing coalition more difficult. The presidency retained its constitutional authority, but the political circumstances required to exercise that authority effectively had deteriorated. Possessing the power to govern is not the same as possessing the political means to secure agreement.

A September 2026 analysis in Le Monde, discussing France’s crisis of presidentialism, places this predicament within a wider institutional problem. The question is whether a system that places such symbolic and practical weight on the presidency can adequately mediate conflict when presidential authority no longer commands broad political confidence. The dissolution of the Assembly did not create every division in French society, but it intensified the difficulty of governing through a legislature divided among competing political forces.

Image A general view of the Place de la République in Paris as demonstrators gather to protest against the French government's pension reform plan during a day of national strikes and rallies, 19 January 2023. Photo: REUTERS





Alexis de Tocqueville’s The Old Regime and the Revolution offers a historical perspective on this problem. Tocqueville argued that administrative centralisation in France had roots extending back before the Revolution, and that revolutionary change did not simply abolish the structures inherited from the monarchy. His analysis complicates any straightforward opposition between an authoritarian past and a democratic present: political regimes may transform their sources of legitimacy while retaining administrative habits and institutional arrangements that limit local initiative.

Applied to contemporary France, Tocqueville’s argument suggests a tension, not a direct historical equivalence. Administrative centralisation can coexist with democratic elections, constitutional protections and universal citizenship. Yet when decision-making is concentrated at the centre, citizens may experience political participation as episodic: they are invited to choose representatives but may feel they have little influence over consequential decisions between elections. Tocqueville did not analyse Macron’s presidency. His work instead helps illuminate whether the concentration of administrative and political authority can weaken the civic agency on which democratic life depends.

Legality, legitimacy and the social contract

The controversy surrounding pension reform in 2023 brought the distinction between legal authority and political legitimacy into sharp relief. The government’s use of Article 49.3 of the Constitution enabled it to advance the reform without a conventional final vote on the bill, subject to the constitutional procedure’s provisions for a no-confidence motion. The mechanism was not, in itself, unconstitutional. Yet its legality did not settle the wider dispute over the reform or the manner in which it was imposed.

Constitutional rules establish how decisions may lawfully be made; they do not guarantee that those decisions will command public acceptance. Nor can popular opposition automatically invalidate every policy adopted through lawful procedures. The harder question is how democratic institutions respond when a government’s formal authority and the public’s sense of political ownership diverge.

Jean-Jacques Rousseau’s The Social Contract is pertinent here, provided his argument is not reduced to the proposition that the majority is always right. For Rousseau, sovereignty resides in the people, and legitimate political authority must be understood in relation to their status as citizens participating in a collective order. The general will is not simply the sum of private preferences, nor is it interchangeable with the wishes of a temporary majority. It concerns the common terms under which people can recognise themselves as members of a political community.

Following constitutional rules is essential, but legality alone does not make a political decision legitimate in the eyes of the public. Citizens must also feel that their voices matter, that the government listens to their concerns, and that the burdens imposed on them are fair and justified. Article 49.3 therefore raises a question that goes beyond whether the government acted within the law: when a government repeatedly uses its formal powers despite strong public opposition, how long can it maintain the public trust on which effective democratic government depends?

Montesquieu’s The Spirit of the Laws provides a complementary perspective. His account of the distribution of political power emphasises that liberty depends not on the virtue of officeholders alone but on institutional arrangements that prevent power from becoming unchecked. Montesquieu did not prescribe France’s present parliamentary arrangements or offer a ready-made solution to presidentialism. His continuing relevance lies in the principle that institutions must provide meaningful opportunities to contest, revise and restrain decisions.

Parliamentary scrutiny, negotiation with political opponents and public deliberation are therefore not merely obstacles to executive efficiency. They are means through which disagreement can be incorporated into democratic government rather than displaced into sustained confrontation. When these forms of mediation appear ineffective, constitutional power may remain legally secure while its capacity to command acceptance diminishes.

Image Cover of The Old Regime and the Revolution by Alexis de Tocqueville, first published in 1856

Fiscal pressure and the social contract

More to the point, France’s present political difficulties are compounded by a serious fiscal challenge. On 19 September 2026, Reuters reported that the French finance ministry projected public debt at 119.3 per cent of GDP in 2026 and a budget deficit of 5.4 per cent. The ministry also projected a debt ratio of 121.7 per cent in 2027. These are government forecasts, not final outturns, and should not be confused with estimates prepared by international institutions.

The International Monetary Fund’s July 2026 Article IV consultation similarly identified high deficits, modest growth and rising spending pressures as significant challenges. Its baseline projections put public debt on a rising path, reaching approximately 121.8 per cent of GDP by 2030. The IMF also stressed the need for a credible medium-term fiscal strategy while protecting vulnerable groups and preserving the conditions for inclusive growth. These projections are not inevitable outcomes: they depend on economic developments, policy choices and the implementation of fiscal measures.

The figures illustrate the constraints facing France’s next government. Debt servicing, public investment, social protection and the costs associated with an ageing population compete for fiscal room. A divided parliament makes agreement over these priorities more difficult, while measures intended to restore fiscal credibility can deepen public dissatisfaction when their burdens are perceived as unfairly distributed.

The political question is not whether fiscal constraints exist, but how they are interpreted and addressed. Fiscal consolidation presented as a technical necessity still has distributive consequences. Citizens who experience declining public services, rising living costs or diminished economic security may reasonably ask why they should bear additional burdens and whether those with greater resources will contribute proportionately. Debt ratios alone cannot answer such questions.

Rousseau’s social contract is relevant here not because it supplies a fiscal programme, but because it directs attention to the terms on which citizens accept common obligations. A sustainable settlement requires governments to explain the purpose of sacrifice, demonstrate that burdens are fairly shared and preserve confidence that collective resources serve a common good.

Fiscal pressure, however, should not be treated as the sole cause of France’s political unrest. Economic insecurity intersects with longer-standing disputes over representation, public services, inequality and institutional responsiveness. Fiscal constraints narrow the choices available to governments; they do not determine how those choices must be made or whose interests they should serve.

Image A masked demonstrator raises a French flag as police deploy water cannon during clashes in Paris, amid nationwide protests by high school and university students, supported by teachers, parents, and trade unions, demanding improved educational conditions, 13 October 2026. Photo: REUTERS

Political fragmentation and the crisis of representation

France’s political fragmentation reflects more than temporary parliamentary arithmetic. Competing political forces articulate different, often incompatible understandings of national identity, economic justice, public order and the future of the Republic. The National Rally has drawn support from voters who feel alienated from established political elites, while the radical left has mobilised constituencies angered by inequality, economic insecurity and what they regard as the exclusion of ordinary citizens from consequential decisions. These constituencies are not interchangeable, and their grievances should not be collapsed into a single narrative of popular discontent.

What connects them, in different ways, is the challenge they pose to the established political centre. Traditional parties and governing coalitions have struggled to maintain the authority that once made them effective intermediaries between voters and the state. Macron’s political difficulties have both reflected and intensified this transformation. The weakening of established political loyalties has made stable majorities harder to assemble, while the prominence of the presidency has encouraged the expectation that the president should answer for problems no individual officeholder can resolve alone.

The presidential election scheduled for 2027 may reorder political alignments, but an election cannot by itself repair the institutional relationships on which democratic government depends. A new president could possess a stronger mandate yet encounter similar difficulties if parliamentary fragmentation, distrust of governing institutions and competing demands over public resources remain unresolved. Conversely, a divided legislature need not make government impossible if political actors can negotiate durable agreements and recognise opposition as a legitimate part of democratic life.

The challenge is to restore credible channels through which conflicting interests can be represented, debated and reconciled. Representation loses substance when citizens see elections as the only meaningful occasion for political participation, or when parliamentary debate appears incapable of affecting decisions already settled by the executive. Participation must be capable of making a difference, even though no government can meet every demand.

Public order and the limits of power

The unrest reported in France in October 2026 further exposed the fragility of the relationship between public authority and civic trust. Reuters coverage described a volatile situation in which protests and public anger coexisted with incidents of violence and disorder. The reporting also pointed to concerns about the cost of living, public services and wider political frustration. These developments should be understood neither as grounds for a romantic celebration of protest nor as evidence of undifferentiated lawlessness.

The distinction between peaceful dissent and violence is essential. Citizens have a democratic right to demonstrate, criticise the government and demand change. That right does not confer immunity for assaults, arson or attacks on others. Equally, violence committed by some participants does not erase the legitimacy of peaceful protest or establish that demonstrators’ grievances are without foundation. A government that conflates these categories risks turning a problem of political legitimacy into a narrower problem of public order.

The state has both the authority and the responsibility to protect public safety. Yet the exercise of that authority can reinforce or weaken democratic confidence, depending on its proportionality, accountability and consistency. Treating all opposition as a threat may secure temporary compliance while deepening the alienation that made confrontation more likely. The alternative is not governmental passivity, but the disciplined use of power within legal and democratic limits.

Image Cover of The Rebel by Albert Camus, first published in 1951

Albert Camus’s The Rebel offers an ethical lens through which to consider this dilemma. Camus explores the point at which resistance to injustice can become a new form of domination, insisting on the moral limits of political action. His argument is neither a policing manual nor a programme for constitutional reform. Its relevance lies in the warning that neither the state nor those who oppose it can justify every action by appealing to a supposedly higher cause. Political ends do not make present abuses morally inconsequential.

The state cannot invoke order to place its actions beyond scrutiny, just as protesters cannot invoke injustice to excuse violence against others. Democratic legitimacy depends on holding both propositions together: public authority must protect citizens while remaining answerable to them.

Can the Republic renew itself?

France’s present predicament should not be mistaken for the exhaustion of republicanism. The Republic’s commitments to citizenship, equality before the law and popular sovereignty remain standards by which its institutions can be judged. The crisis arises partly because citizens continue to appeal to those commitments while questioning whether existing political practices adequately realise them.

Renewal requires more than a change of personnel or a tactical reconfiguration of parliamentary alliances. It calls for reconsideration of how executive power is exercised, how parliamentary institutions mediate disagreement and how public decisions are explained and justified. Constitutional reform may be part of that discussion, but no institutional redesign can substitute for political practices that take opposition seriously and treat public consent as something to be sustained rather than presumed.

Tocqueville helps illuminate the need to strengthen civic agency alongside central administration. Rousseau directs attention to the relationship between collective obligations and popular sovereignty. Montesquieu reminds us that liberty depends on the distribution and restraint of power, not merely on the intentions of those who exercise it. Camus adds an ethical warning: neither authority nor resistance should turn its ends into an unlimited licence. These thinkers offer different arguments, not a single doctrine, and none can simply be transferred from his historical context to contemporary France. Read together, they help frame the questions democratic renewal must confront.

Governments must make the reasons for difficult decisions publicly intelligible, distribute the burdens of adjustment fairly and leave genuine room for parliamentary negotiation. Opposition parties, in turn, must do more than denounce the failures of their rivals: they must show how competing demands can be reconciled within a workable political settlement. The responsibilities are not identical. The government exercises state power and bears particular obligations, but no democratic system can function indefinitely if every institution treats compromise as capitulation.

The aim is not to eliminate conflict. Democratic politics exists because citizens differ over priorities, values and the distribution of resources. The task is to ensure that disagreement can alter decisions, expose abuses and generate alternatives without making institutions appear incapable of governing.

Image Cover of The Spirit of the Laws by Montesquieu, first published in 1748

What is rotten in the state?

The rot, if Shakespeare’s phrase is to be retained, lies not in France as a nation, nor in the republican ideal, but in the weakening relationships that should connect constitutional authority to democratic consent. A powerful presidency can provide stability yet become a source of paralysis when the political means of governing fall away. A legally valid decision can remain democratically contested. Fiscal discipline can be necessary yet lose legitimacy if its costs are experienced as arbitrary or inequitable. Public order can be indispensable yet become counterproductive when the state fails to distinguish dissent from violence.

These failures reinforce one another. Institutional centralisation can intensify the sense that citizens have little influence; exclusion can deepen political fragmentation; fragmentation can obstruct agreement over fiscal and social priorities; and deadlock can encourage the executive to rely more heavily on formal powers. Each turn of this cycle makes the next more difficult to break.

The way forward is neither to abandon the Fifth Republic’s institutions at the first sign of crisis nor to defend them as though constitutional legality were sufficient proof of democratic health. It is to reconnect authority with accountability, collective obligations with fair treatment, and political disagreement with the possibility of negotiated agreement.

The question facing France is therefore larger than whether Macron has outstayed his political welcome or which party will prevail in 2027. It is whether the Republic can make its institutions responsive enough to command consent without sacrificing the capacity to govern. France’s democratic inheritance remains a resource for that task, not a guarantee of its success. What is at stake is not the survival of the Republic as a constitutional form, but its ability to make republican government meaningful to the citizens in whose name it acts.

Dr. Faridul Alam, a former academic, writes from New York City.
