title: Mud marvels of Bengal: The living heritage behind pottery and terracotta
text:
A clay pot can be placed in a museum. A terracotta plaque can be preserved behind glass. The façade of a historic temple can be documented through photographs and measured drawings. But where does the heritage reside when the potter’s knowledge disappears, the artisan’s workshop falls silent, or the generations who once maintained an earthen house no longer know how it was made?

This question lies at the heart of Bengal’s relationship with clay.

Across the delta, earth has served as a material for everyday survival and an extraordinary medium of artistic expression. It has been shaped into vessels for cooking and storage, figurines for domestic and ritual purposes, bricks for monumental architecture, and the walls and floors of rural homes. Through these transformations, clay has connected the practical requirements of life with the creative imagination of communities.

Image Pottery and earthenware from Mahasthangarh. Illustration: Sajid Bin Doza



The material evidence of this relationship is visible in archaeological settlements such as Mahasthangarh, the monumental remains of Somapura Mahavihara at Paharpur, the richly ornamented temples of Bengal, and historic brick-built mosques. Its living dimensions remain present in pottery workshops, traditional craft communities, and vernacular settlements where knowledge is still transmitted through the act of making.

UNESCO’s 2003 Convention for the Safeguarding of the Intangible Cultural Heritage recognises traditional craftsmanship, knowledge concerning nature and the universe, social practices, rituals, and oral traditions as domains of living heritage. Crucially, this heritage is transmitted from generation to generation while being continually recreated in response to changing environments and social circumstances (UNESCO, 2003).

This understanding offers a compelling way to interpret Bengal’s clay traditions. The pot is not simply an object; it embodies the knowledge that produced it. A terracotta façade is not merely an architectural surface; it bears traces of the skills, labour, and cultural imagination that brought it into being. An earthen house is not only a structure; it may also embody generations of environmental knowledge, domestic practices, and community relationships.

The distinction matters. Tangible heritage gives us the physical evidence of the past, while intangible heritage helps explain the knowledge and practices through which people create, maintain, and understand that evidence.

Image Fragile legacy of Bengal’s clay craftsmanship. Illustration: Sajid Bin Doza





Mud as strength: Learning from the delta

Bengal’s clay traditions are inseparable from its landscape. Rivers, floods, and the deposition of alluvial sediments have shaped the region’s soils and settlement patterns over long periods. Communities have developed building and craft practices using locally available earth, adapting their techniques to different environmental and material conditions.

Mud became an important resource for walls, floors, and domestic construction. Clay was also processed into sun-dried objects and fired pottery, bricks, and terracotta. Where stone was scarce or difficult to obtain, brick and clay offered alternative ways of creating durable buildings and expressive architectural surfaces.

Traditional earthen construction required considerable practical knowledge. Soil had to be selected according to its suitability; clay mixtures needed appropriate preparation; walls required protection from prolonged moisture; and roofs, foundations, and drainage had to respond to local conditions. The maintenance of an earthen house was not an incidental task but part of the knowledge system that sustained it.

Such knowledge was usually acquired through participation rather than formal instruction. Younger members of a household observed experienced builders, helped prepare materials, and gradually acquired the ability to recognise suitable soil, understand construction sequences, and carry out repairs. The knowledge was embodied in practice, in the hand as much as in memory.

Image Traditional earthen construction in Bengal. Illustration: Sajid Bin Doza (2020)



Traditional construction should not, however, be romanticised as universally durable or environmentally harmless. Earthen buildings can be vulnerable to flooding, erosion, and inappropriate repairs. Their performance depends on the materials, design, workmanship, and maintenance. Contemporary approaches can learn from traditional systems while subjecting them to appropriate technical assessment.

Mahasthangarh: Reading everyday life through clay

At Mahasthangarh, the ancient urban centre associated with Pundranagar, archaeological remains provide a window into the long history of settlement in northern Bengal. Excavations have uncovered structural remains, pottery, terracotta objects, and other artefacts that illuminate different dimensions of the region’s material culture. Recent research has also examined the relationship between the site, the Karatoya River, and the changing alluvial landscape.

As Rafa and Bishwas observe in their review of archaeological pottery research in Bangladesh, pottery is among the most frequently recovered categories of archaeological material, yet important questions about its scientific study remain. The interpretation of individual objects therefore requires careful attention to archaeological context, material characteristics, and comparative evidence.

Image Terracotta objects and pottery at Mahasthangarh Site Museum. Photo: Collected



My sketch of pottery from Mahasthangarh approaches these objects through architectural illustration and close visual observation. The vessels appear together, their profiles and surfaces revealing differences in proportion, construction, and use. Drawing encourages us to look beyond the object as a chronological specimen and consider the human decisions embedded in its making.

The value of such objects extends beyond their physical form. Each vessel is the outcome of a sequence of activities: selecting and preparing clay, shaping the body, finishing the surface, drying, firing, and determining the object’s intended use. Archaeological pottery preserves evidence of some of these processes, although it cannot independently reconstruct every aspect of the original craft tradition.

This is where archaeology and living craftsmanship can inform one another. Contemporary pottery practices provide comparative insights into the relationship between material, technique, and function. Such comparisons must be made cautiously because modern practices cannot simply be projected backwards onto ancient communities. Nevertheless, they can help researchers formulate questions about production and technological choices.

The potter’s knowledge: A living tradition

The making of pottery is not merely a technical operation. It is a learned relationship between the human body, clay, tools, water, heat, and the environment.

A potter must recognise the qualities of suitable clay, understand how it responds to pressure, judge the moisture required for shaping, and anticipate how the vessel will behave during drying and firing. The timing of these stages can determine whether the finished object succeeds or fails. These decisions often depend on experience that cannot be fully communicated through written instructions alone.

The potter’s workshop is also a social space. Work may involve family members, apprentices, suppliers, traders, and customers. The circulation of clay products connects craft production to household economies, local markets, and ritual occasions. Knowledge is sustained not only by the individual artisan but also by the relationships that make continued practice possible.

Image Traditional pottery and terracotta craftsmanship in rural Bengal. Illustration: Sajid Bin Doza





The living character of pottery becomes particularly clear when we consider how artisans respond to changing circumstances. New materials, changing consumer preferences, rising production costs, and shifts in domestic use can influence the forms they produce. Some traditional objects become less commercially viable, while others are adapted for decorative, commemorative, or contemporary purposes.

Such changes do not automatically destroy authenticity. Intangible heritage is not a fixed collection of techniques preserved without alteration. It remains alive because communities continue to practise and reinterpret it. The central question is whether artisans retain meaningful control over their knowledge, whether the practice remains socially relevant, and whether the next generation has opportunities to learn it.

Safeguarding pottery therefore requires more than collecting beautiful objects. It requires supporting the people who make them, recognising their knowledge, and creating conditions in which the craft can continue to evolve.

Image Terracotta plaques and architectural remains at Somapura Mahavihara, Paharpur.





Terracotta: From craft knowledge to architectural expression

Terracotta represents one of Bengal’s most distinctive achievements in the transformation of clay into art and architecture. Its significance extends from small figurines and domestic objects to the elaborate plaques and reliefs that adorn the façades of historic religious buildings.

At Somapura Mahavihara in Paharpur, the monumental brick complex and its terracotta plaques reveal the artistic achievements of Buddhist Bengal. The site, recognised as a UNESCO World Heritage, contains evidence of a major religious and intellectual centre whose architectural influence extended beyond the region.

The terracotta plaques were not incidental additions to an otherwise complete building. They formed part of the architectural composition, contributing to its visual articulation and cultural meaning. Their production required the coordination of material preparation, modelling, moulding, firing, and placement within the building fabric. They also reminds us that monumental art was produced through collective labour, not through artistic imagination alone.

The terracotta façades of Bengal’s temples offer an especially rich example of architecture functioning as a visual narrative. At Kantajew Temple in Dinajpur, elaborate panels depict religious stories, human figures, animals, vegetation and scenes associated with social life. The temple tradition reveals how architectural surfaces became spaces in which sacred narratives and representations of the wider world could coexist.

Image Terracotta narratives on the façade of Kantajew Temple, Dinajpur. Photo: Sajid Bin Doza



The UNESCO Tentative List entry on Mughal and colonial temples of Bangladesh describes the importance of terracotta plaques in communicating religious and secular themes, including narratives from the epics and scenes reflecting contemporary.

The plaques can be read as works of art, but they also preserve evidence of the craft knowledge through which complex compositions were created and integrated into architecture. Their repetition, scale, relief and placement demonstrate the relationship between individual artistic elements and the larger building.

Bengal’s historic mosques reveal another dimension of this relationship. Brick construction, terracotta ornament, stucco and other decorative treatments contributed to the distinctive character of Islamic architecture in the region. The decorative vocabulary varies according to period, patronage and monument, but the use of locally available materials formed an important part of the region’s architectural history.

The religious traditions represented by Buddhist monasteries, Hindu temples and Islamic mosques should not be collapsed into a single narrative. Their forms, iconography and functions emerged from distinct historical and theological contexts. Their significance lies not in being interchangeable but in showing how communities across different periods developed architectural expressions through the materials and skills available to them.

Image Brick and terracotta ornamentation at Darasbari Mosque. Photo: Sajid Bin Doza





Santal homesteads: The living artistry of painted earth

The connection between clay and living cultural practice is especially visible in the homesteads of Santal communities in northern Bengal. Here, the earthen house is not simply a shelter; it can also be a carefully composed work of vernacular art, shaped by an intimate understanding of material, colour, pattern and domestic space.

In the Santal settlements of the Barind region, mud walls may be finished with remarkable care and decorated with painted bands, geometric borders, floral motifs and rhythmic patterns. The surfaces are often organised with a meticulousness that reflects both practical knowledge and artistic judgement. Doorways, windows, wall divisions and plinths become parts of a larger visual composition in which colour and pattern establish a distinctive character for the home.

My sketches and photographs of Santal homesteads around Tanore record this understated yet sophisticated artistic practice. In one drawing, a window is framed by repeated arches and carefully arranged bands of red, ochre, white and dark pigment. In another, an open doorway is surrounded by delicate floral motifs, while a hanging earthen vessel and the carefully finished wall contribute to the atmosphere of everyday domestic life. These are not monumental artworks separated from ordinary experience. Their artistic significance emerges from the way they are integrated into the architecture of the home.

The visual order of these houses suggests a deep familiarity with the behaviour of earthen surfaces and the practical demands of maintaining them. Preparing a wall, achieving an even finish, choosing suitable pigments and applying repeated motifs require patience and experience. Where these practices are transmitted through family and community life, they also become a means of passing artistic knowledge between generations.

Image Painted wall and window of a Santal homestead in Tanore, Rajshahi. Illustration: Sajid Bin Doza (2025)



Such knowledge should not be treated as an anonymous folk technique. The people who design, prepare and maintain these surfaces are practitioners whose individual choices and skills deserve recognition. Their work may reflect shared conventions, but each house also bears the decisions of its occupants and makers.

The painted Santal homestead therefore brings the tangible and intangible dimensions of heritage into close relationship. The wall and its pigments are physical; the knowledge of preparing, decorating and renewing them is living. The visual composition can be documented in a drawing, but the full heritage also includes the gestures, observations, memories and social relationships through which the work is carried out.

These traditions should not be assumed to be uniform across all Santal communities, nor should individual motifs be assigned fixed ritual meanings without evidence from their makers. Their significance must be understood through careful observation and, above all, through conversations with the people who sustain them.

The conservation of Santal homesteads consequently requires more than photographing attractive façades. It calls for documenting building techniques, recording practitioners’ accounts, understanding the role of domestic maintenance and recognising the community’s own priorities. Any safeguarding initiative should respect the right of households to adapt their homes to changing needs.

For me, drawing these houses is a way of paying close attention to the artistic intelligence embedded in everyday architecture. It reveals that the history of Bengal’s material culture does not belong exclusively to archaeological sites and monumental buildings. It also lives in the precise lines of a painted wall, the framing of a doorway and the knowledge through which a home is continually renewed.

Image Painted doorway of a Santal homestead in the Barind region. Illustration: Sajid Bin Doza (2026)



What is lost when the craft falls silent?

The disappearance of a clay object or an old building is a visible loss. The disappearance of the knowledge behind it can be more difficult to recognise.

When a pottery workshop closes, the loss may extend beyond its products. Knowledge of local clay, firing methods, tool use and the timing of production may disappear with the practitioners. When an earthen house is replaced without documentation, construction details and maintenance practices can be lost. When terracotta fragments are removed from their architectural context, their relationship to the building and knowledge of their original placement become harder to reconstruct.

These losses are not inevitable, but they require attention. Traditional craftsmanship depends on more than appreciation from outside the community. It needs opportunities for learning, viable livelihoods, access to materials, spaces for production and recognition of artisans as knowledge holders.

Safeguarding should therefore connect conservation with social and economic realities. Documentation can record techniques, tools, vocabulary and production sequences, but it should be undertaken with the participation and consent of practitioners. Oral histories can preserve accounts of training and family traditions. Workshops and apprenticeships can create opportunities for younger generations to learn directly from experienced artisans.

Museums can contribute by interpreting objects alongside the processes that produced them. Architectural conservation projects can work with skilled craftspeople where appropriate. Universities can support research into materials and construction techniques, while public programmes can introduce audiences to the people behind the objects they admire.

The goal is not to turn living crafts into performances staged for visitors. Nor should safeguarding require communities to continue practices that no longer meet their needs. The aim is to protect the conditions under which knowledge can be transmitted, adapted and valued.

Safeguarding a living legacy

A meaningful approach to Bengal’s clay heritage must bring together archaeology, architectural conservation and the living practices of craft communities.

Image Fragile legacy of Bengal’s clay craftsmanship. Illustration: Sajid Bin Doza





First, documentation should connect objects with their makers, uses and contexts wherever this information is available. A photograph of a pot is more informative when accompanied by the artisan’s account of its production, the source of its clay and its intended use. A terracotta plaque becomes easier to interpret when its architectural location, material condition and historical context are recorded.

Second, the transmission of knowledge must remain central. Training opportunities, apprenticeships and intergenerational workshops can support traditional craftsmanship without requiring every practitioner to reproduce an identical historical form. Such programmes should be developed in collaboration with artisans rather than imposed upon them.

Third, heritage institutions should recognise that conservation and contemporary life are not opposing goals. Traditional materials and techniques may contribute to repair and new design, provided they are used appropriately and assessed for performance. Equally, craft traditions may evolve into new forms of production while retaining important knowledge and community connections.

Finally, heritage policy must acknowledge the people who sustain these practices. Artisans should be recognised not simply as labourers who execute a design but as bearers of technical and cultural knowledge. Their voices and priorities must inform decisions about documentation, interpretation and the future of their crafts.

UNESCO’s framework emphasises that intangible heritage is continually recreated by communities in response to their environment and history. This principle is especially relevant to Bengal, where the relationship between people and clay has developed through changing landscapes, livelihoods, technologies and cultural practices.

Safeguarding does not mean freezing tradition in time. It means ensuring that knowledge remains available to be practised, understood and reinterpreted by future generations.

Image

Conclusion: The heritage lives in the hands

Bengal’s clay traditions connect the material evidence of ancient civilisation with the living practices of rural communities. The pottery of Mahasthangarh, the terracotta plaques of Paharpur, the narrative façades of Kantajew Temple, the brick ornamentation of historic mosques and the painted earthen homes of Santal communities belong to different historical and cultural contexts. Together, however, they demonstrate the extraordinary range of ways in which clay has shaped the region’s artistic and architectural identity.

Their significance cannot be understood through physical objects alone. Behind every vessel lies a process of making; behind every terracotta façade lies a history of craft knowledge and collective labour; behind every painted wall lies a practice sustained through observation, memory and participation.

The objects are precious because they preserve material evidence of the past. The knowledge is equally precious because it allows people to continue creating, maintaining and interpreting their cultural world.

As an architectural historian and heritage illustrator, I find that drawing these objects and buildings offers a way to observe their forms closely and make their details visible to a wider audience. Yet illustration also reminds me of its limitations. A drawing can record a vessel’s shape or a façade’s ornament, but it cannot fully capture the potter’s movements, the conversations within a workshop or the relationships through which knowledge passes from one generation to another.

That living dimension must be understood through people, practice and participation.

The future of Bengal’s clay heritage therefore depends on a broader understanding of what we seek to preserve. We must protect archaeological objects and historic buildings, but we must also recognise artisans, document their knowledge, support their livelihoods and create opportunities for younger generations to learn.

Dr Sajid Bin Doza is an associate professor of art and architectural history in the Department of Architecture at BRAC University. He is also a heritage illustrator and cultural historian. He can be reached at [email protected].

title: Harry no wizard, but he broke the curse
text:
Harry Kane needed a moment to take it all in as his name was announced as the men’s Ballon d’Or winner at the London Palladium yesterday. The England captain sat absorbing the moment, with Lamine Yamal and Rodri applauding beside him. After years of doubt, heartbreak and relentless pursuit, Kane had reached the summit of world football.

The boy Arsenal reportedly rejected as too ‘chubby’ was now the best footballer in the world.

Image

Football has its wizards, the likes of Kylian Mbappe and Lamine Yamal, whose extraordinary talent marked them out for greatness from an early age. Kane’s rise was different. There was no teenage explosion or overnight sensation, but a slower, harder journey shaped by setbacks and closed doors. For him, reaching the top took years of hard work, not spells.

Football has its wizards, the likes of Kylian Mbappe and Lamine Yamal, whose extraordinary talent marked them out for greatness from an early age. Kane’s rise was different.

Leyton Orient, Millwall, Norwich City and Leicester City offered no guarantees. At Norwich, opportunities were scarce before a foot injury stalled his progress. At Leicester, he was a substitute in the 2013 Championship play-off defeat to Watford.

“If I can’t play for Norwich or for Leicester, even in the Championship, then how am I going to get back and play for Tottenham?” he later recalled thinking.

When you realise that you really won the 2026 Ballon d'Or! 🌟 https://t.co/J6Z9EIUEue — Ballon d'Or (@ballondor) October 27, 2026

He returned to Spurs to become their record goalscorer, with 280 goals in 435 appearances, and England’s all-time leading scorer with 91 international goals.

But one curse refused to loosen its grip.

For all the records and individual accolades, Kane’s lack of major trophies became a punchline. At Tottenham, silverware remained elusive. With England, he endured the agony of losing European Championship finals in 2021 and 2024.

It was painful to watch him come so close, only to fall short. He had given the country so many reasons to believe, yet the biggest prizes remained out of reach.

His move to Bayern Munich in 2023 was supposed to change that. Instead, his first season in Germany ended without a trophy, prolonging a narrative that seemed almost impossible to escape.

Then came the breakthrough.

Kane began winning silverware with Bayern and took his performances to extraordinary heights. His 73 goals in 65 appearances for club and country in 2025-26 underlined his remarkable consistency. No longer just a ruthless finisher, he had become a complete forward, capable of creating chances, dictating play and making those around him better.

His Ballon d’Or triumph carried significance beyond personal glory. He ended Bayern Munich’s 45-year wait for another winner, following Karl-Heinz Rummenigge’s victories in 1980 and 1981, and ended England’s 25-year drought. For a player who had spent years chasing silverware, Kane was now breaking curses for club and country alike.

His Ballon d’Or triumph carried significance beyond personal glory. He ended Bayern Munich’s 45-year wait for another winner, following Karl-Heinz Rummenigge’s victories in 1980 and 1981, and ended England’s 25-year drought.

Yet the most revealing part of his coronation was his humility. There was no grandstanding or attempt to settle scores with his doubters. His acceptance speech reflected a player who understood the work behind the glory and the people who had helped him along the way.

Soon after the ceremony, he posted: “Work hard in silence. Let success make your noise.”

He let his success do the talking, just as he always had.

For England supporters, his triumph feels personal. He has spent years carrying the nation’s hopes, enduring its heartbreak and giving it reasons to believe again. In his own way, he has been a Wonderwall for those who followed him through the near-misses and disappointments.

Harry, it's not just a dream! #ballondor https://t.co/5SBrrcN826 — Ballon d'Or (@ballondor) October 27, 2026

Harry is no wizard. He never needed a magic wand. He needed patience, perseverance and an unshakeable belief in what he could become.

In 2017, it was a dream to be the best player in the world. Now, he is living it.

title: In China, the AI bubble has already burst
text:
While global tech stocks teeter, in China they have already crashed as lofty valuations collapse under worries about AI demand and curbs on Chinese exports.

The meltdown, tanking the mainland STAR50 index of AI and semiconductor leaders ​by 40 percent in less than four months and vaporising some $480 billion in market value, is an ill omen for wobbly world markets and a dampener on China’s efforts ‌at encouraging its savers into stocks to fund the AI boom.

It has also slammed the brakes on a rally running two years, since economic stimulus promises sent shares soaring, and has stalled Beijing’s push to break with a long boom-bust pattern and drive a “slow bull” market that delivers reliable performance. China’s broad blue-chip index has dropped about 20 percent from highs made in June.

“The stock market later evolved into a speculative crazy bull,” said Beijing-based fund manager Dong Baozhen. “And now we see ​the bubble bursting.”

The reversal reflects a rally that ran to higher heights than markets in the West or elsewhere in Asia, and compares with a mere prick to US AI stocks, which ​have led a 6 percent drawdown in the Nasdaq from a record high scaled three weeks ago.

There has been no obvious selling trigger in China, although traders said high prices, tax bills and the threat of the US or other nations banning Chinese equipment in data centres all contributed.

With AI stocks running to 42 percent of China’s market capitalisation and 57 percent of ​turnover across mainland-listed A-shares and Hong Kong’s H-shares, according to Goldman Sachs, few in a market dominated by small investors have escaped pain.

Shares in robot-maker Unitree 8,000 times oversubscribed by retail buyers at ​listing, have halved since they started trading in August, and chipmaker CXMT has lost more than a quarter of its value in the past month.

Chipmakers MetaX Integrated Circuits and Moore Threads Technology, which leapt 700 percent and 400 percent respectively on their market debuts last year, have also halved in value since July.

Across the river is Kaepung County in North Korea.

Chen Wensheng, a small business owner and investor from China’s southern Hainan, said he bought into the rally emboldened by what he felt was official support for the likes of ​Unitree, which counted state-backed funds as investors. But Chen and his friends are now nursing losses.

Frustration that an investment theme backed by Beijing has ended so badly has driven many investors into defensive assets ​and is likely to slow equity fundraising by tech firms.

Shares in optical parts makers Zhongji Innolight and Eoptolink Technology are down roughly 60 percent from highs in June and July, in part as Washington moves towards banning the one-time ‌darlings from supplying US data centres.

With the STAR50 index still at around 100 times trailing earnings, albeit down from a high of nearly 250, investors compare the Nasdaq 100’s multiple of 30 and worry the selloff could get worse before it gets better.

“What’s happening is now going to put a stop for many of the companies trying to get themselves listed,” said Hong Hao, managing partner and chief investment officer at Lotus Asset Management in Hong Kong.

‘ALL BUBBLES INEVITABLY BURST’

The frenzy and its fallout contrast with a push by authorities to improve returns and dampen volatility by cracking down on leverage and high-frequency trading. State-backed investors were sellers into rallies ​to keep gains in check.

China’s market regulator, the China ​Securities Regulatory Commission, did not immediately reply to ⁠questions faxed by Reuters last week.

CRSC Chairman Wu Qing met with market participants earlier this month to hear suggestions on improving capital markets, the regulator said on its website, and some in the investment community say the boom has been bad for the market’s structure.

“Overemphasising the ‘technology content’ — that is, the weighting of ​tech companies by market value in major indexes — leads to a deviation, even a distortion, in capital behaviour,” said Leo Wang, partner at Beijing-based Qianchuang ​Capital.

“This created a severe bubble ⁠in certain sectors and a serious drain on others.”

Some see value in the selloff, saying it is neither surprising nor detrimental to market reforms that are geared for the long term and have gained traction in driving up returns, particularly income, in recent years.

Although they have been sellers over the past three months, Asia funds in general are overweight on China, according to HSBC research.

Goldman Sachs has Innolight and CXMT among dozens of Chinese ⁠AI stocks on ​a revamped recommendation list it published earlier this month, and BNP Paribas Securities strategist William Bratton has said the market ​offers buying opportunities for the careful.

Still, on the mainland many are looking at other sectors or for even lower valuations before they turn buyers.

“Just like all other Chinese manufacturers, (chipmakers and AI suppliers) will eventually end up in a price war,” said fund manager Wang ​Zhuo, partner at Shanghai Zhuozhu Investment Management.

“There’s no exception,” he said. “All bubbles inevitably burst.”

title: Skeletal remains of ‘missing teacher’ found after 10 days
text:
Another set of burnt skeletal remains was recovered from the debris of TupTup Resort in Ukhiya, Cox’s Bazar yesterday, 10 days after a fire broke out there.

The remains are believed to be those of missing schoolteacher Nasrin Akter Mukta, 27, but DNA testing is needed to confirm the identity, officials said.

Fire service personnel recovered the remains around 2:30pm from a spot identified by Mukta’s relatives, said Ukhiya Upazila Nirbahi Officer Panna Akter. Her husband, Faisal Dewan, said he recognised a gold chain and locket found around the remains.

Ten bodies were recovered after the October 17 fire. The Criminal Investigation Department confirmed the identities of all 10 victims through DNA tests on Monday. Mukta, a teacher at Swapnabilash Niribili School in Ashulia, had remained unaccounted for.

Police filed a case against 23 people over alleged negligence. Resort owner Mohammad Tanvir Sultan Mia remains absconding, while assistant manager Mohammad Zahid Hossain has been arrested.

title: Turning local banking access into business finance
text:
Success should be measured not only by transactions and deposits, but also by sustainable business growth and financial inclusion. Faisal Rahman Chief Executive Officer Prime Bank PLC

For small businesses, a nearby banking outlet can make transactions easier, but securing finance requires a closer assessment of income, records and repayment capacity. In a conversation with The Daily Star, Faisal Rahman, chief executive officer of Prime Bank PLC, discusses how agents and lending teams can work together to support local enterprise.

The Daily Star (TDS): How is agent banking evolving beyond savings, remittances and everyday transactions?

Faisal Rahman (FR): Customers initially relied on agents for deposits, withdrawals, remittances and everyday banking. The opportunity now is to connect them with financial services that support livelihoods and enterprise. Small traders, agricultural input sellers, farmers and micro-business owners need working capital, convenient payments and financing suited to their business cycles.

Remittances can provide seed capital for enterprises and agriculture alongside household income. Convenient access to savings and formal financial services can also help women build financial independence and explore entrepreneurship.

As familiarity with digital banking grows, customers expect faster services and solutions suited to their needs. Our aim is to combine digital services, financial literacy and responsible financing to help local businesses grow. The next phase should turn financial access into productive engagement with the banking system.

TDS: What services can entrepreneurs access, and where does an agent’s responsibility end?

FR: Entrepreneurs can access account opening, subject to regulatory requirements, deposits, withdrawals, domestic remittance services and other authorised transactions. These help them manage sales proceeds, maintain savings and transact closer to home or work. Depending on approved arrangements, agents may facilitate digital banking access, explain financial products and guide customers through loan application procedures.

Agents provide a local access point and help with documentation, but must operate within prescribed policies and regulatory guidelines. Credit approval, risk assessment and decisions requiring professional banking judgement remain with authorised bank personnel.

When a trader seeks expansion finance, the agent may facilitate the application and document submission. The branch or lending team assesses the business, cash flow, repayment capacity, credit history and risks before deciding. Local familiarity complements formal assessment; it does not replace it.

TDS: What does the financing application process involve, and what determines processing time?

FR: The entrepreneur first explains the business, financing requirement and intended use of funds at the outlet. The agent provides preliminary product and eligibility information and guides the customer to the designated branch or lending team.

That team receives the formal application, checks documents and assesses business viability, cash flow, repayment capacity, existing liabilities, credit history and any applicable collateral or guarantees. Business visits and other checks may follow. The authorised approving authority makes the decision, after which legal documentation and security formalities must be completed before disbursement.

Applicants should generally prepare their national identity card, valid trade licence, e-TIN and relevant tax documents, business address details, bank statements, sales and expense records, financial information and details of existing borrowings. Partnership or company documents, guarantor information and collateral papers may also be needed, depending on the business and product.

Processing time depends on application completeness, the quality of records, verification, collateral formalities and the approval level required.

TDS: How do you assess businesses with limited formal accounts or collateral?

FR: We assess actual business performance and repayment capacity while maintaining prudent credit standards. This means examining daily sales, purchasing patterns, operating expenses, inventory turnover, seasonal variations and existing obligations. Business visits and discussions with entrepreneurs help us understand their operations.

Regular savings may indicate financial discipline. Remittance receipts can demonstrate supplementary income where it is reliably available for repayment. Deposits of business proceeds and supplier payments can help establish transaction patterns and estimate cash flow, but these indicators require verification and assessment.

Where approved products and risk policies permit, alternative financing arrangements may help eligible businesses without conventional collateral.

TDS: How should financing accommodate seasonal or uneven business income?

FR: Retailers need working capital for inventory, agricultural businesses need funds linked to production cycles, and cottage industries or women-led enterprises may need equipment, raw materials or expansion finance.

Loan sizes should reflect genuine funding needs and repayment capacity. Where the approved product permits, repayment schedules should align with business cycles and expected revenue.

We communicate applicable interest rates, fees, charges and repayment obligations so customers understand the total borrowing cost.

TDS: What would strengthen agent banking’s contribution to local enterprise?

FR: Priorities include identifying viable businesses, strengthening referrals between agents and lending teams, and developing financing that reflects entrepreneurs’ cash flows. Success should be measured not only by transactions and deposits, but also by sustainable business growth and financial inclusion.

Md Zafar Khan, a farmer from Ramdirgati, Magura, uses a nearby outlet for transactions and needs funds for seeds, fertilisers and other inputs as his farming activities expand. Informal records, seasonal income and limited conventional collateral complicate assessment.

Agent support can connect him with the branch’s lending team for a business visit, cash-flow assessment and explanations of documentation and repayment obligations. Financing remains subject to assessment and approval by the competent authority.

title: Dengue death toll now 400
text:
At least 11 dengue patients died yesterday, taking this year’s death toll to 400, as health experts warned of delayed diagnosis and hospitalisation, inadequate treatment and gaps in dengue management.

So far, 128,237 dengue patients have been hospitalised nationwide this year, according to the Directorate General of Health Services.

Dengue admissions have started to decline compared with previous weeks, but a larger proportion of patients arriving at hospitals are critically ill, said HM Nazmul Ahsan, associate professor at Shaheed Suhrawardy Medical College Hospital.

“We are seeing a significant number of patients arriving in shock, with undetectable blood pressure and falling oxygen saturation.”

Patients suffering from dengue shock have a much better chance of recovery if they receive treatment early.

Delays, however, could cause irreversible damage to vital organs and significantly increase the risk of death.

Patients sometimes lose valuable time during transportation, emergency assessment and admission procedures, allowing their conditions to deteriorate before they receive appropriate care.

He also identified elderly people, patients with underlying health conditions and those who are obese as particularly vulnerable to severe dengue outcomes.

Ahsan stressed that timely, appropriate use of intravenous fluids, blood products and other treatments is crucial for critically ill patients.

He has also observed severe complications, including liver failure, kidney failure, respiratory failure, heart failure and myocarditis, or inflammation of the heart muscle, among dengue patients this year.

Such complications appeared to be more common than in previous years, although further studies are needed to establish the reasons behind the increase in severe cases and deaths.

The circulation of dengue virus serotype 3 (DENV-3) could be another contributing factor, Ahsan said, adding that variations within a serotype might influence disease severity.

Repeat dengue infections and delays in diagnosis and treatment are among the key factors contributing to the rising number of deaths, said ABM Abdullah, medicine specialist at Central Hospital.

Many patients who died might have been infected with dengue previously, potentially increasing their vulnerability to complications from subsequent infections.

He urged people to seek medical advice and get tested for dengue if they develop symptoms such as fever, body aches or other signs of illness, rather than waiting for their conditions to worsen.

He also advised patients with suspected dengue to drink sufficient fluids, including water and oral rehydration solution (ORS), to prevent dehydration.

Paracetamol may help control fever under appropriate medical guidance, but patients should avoid other painkillers unless prescribed by a doctor.

“If a patient cannot take fluids orally, staying at home is not advisable. They need to be taken to hospital for proper assessment and treatment,” he said.

Public health expert Mushtuq Hussain suggested piloting free dengue testing at existing primary healthcare facilities and referring vulnerable patients to hospitals when necessary.

Reducing dengue deaths required a comprehensive approach involving community-level prevention, affordable early testing, timely referrals and proper hospital management, rather than relying solely on tertiary hospitals.

title: Karnaphuli Garden City shuts as old shopping malls struggle
text:
For many Dhaka residents now in their 30s, Karnaphuli Garden City Shopping Complex in Kakrail evokes memories of a bustling retail hub that drew shoppers from different income groups.

Opened in 1998, the complex shut down on October 1 after years of dwindling business, with only 25 of its 198 shops operational before the closure, according to its owners’ association.

Its closure highlights the challenges facing Dhaka’s older shopping destinations, as changing shopping habits, intensifying competition and falling sales erode their business.

At least 10 other older shopping complexes in the capital are also facing the prospect of closure amid dwindling customer numbers and a prolonged business slump, according to information gathered for this report.

The owners of Karnaphuli Garden City have decided to sell the property, with a hospital, diagnostic centre or office space among the possible future uses.

The development raises questions about whether other established shopping complexes can adapt to changing market conditions and remain viable.

FROM BUSTLING HUB TO CLOSURE

Developed by Karnaphuli Group, the complex occupied the basement and first four floors of a 20-storey building, with residential apartments above. Its shops sold ready-made garments, shoes, cosmetics, jewellery and other goods, alongside a food court.

AKM Iqbal, president of the Karnaphuli Garden City Shop Owners’ Association, told The Daily Star that the owners had unanimously decided to sell the property.

“We are selling it. All the owners are making this decision together. It could become a hospital, a diagnostic centre, a television centre or any other type of office,” he said.

The main complex has shut down, although a handful of shops near the entrance remain open to generate rental income to cover essential expenses, including security guards’ and a manager’s salaries. The owners are even borrowing money to meet these costs, Iqbal said.

The closure does not affect the residential apartments on the upper floors, according to the authorities.

Concord Twin Tower in nearby Shantinagar is also grappling with sluggish business. Although reports suggested the complex might close, its owners later backed away from the decision.

Syed Sharif Uddin, joint secretary of the Concord Twin Tower Owners’ Association, said there were no plans to shut down the complex.

“Our business is not doing well. However, no decision has been taken to close the complex. We are trying to attract customers,” he said.

CHANGING SHOPPING HABITS

Iqbal said Dhaka’s retail market had changed significantly, with new malls, branded outlets and online shopping giving customers more choices.

“Customers can now compare prices and product quality across shops and online platforms. They do not always need to visit traditional shopping complexes,” he said.

Declining footfall has made it harder for shop owners to cover rent, service charges, staff salaries and electricity bills, he added.

Md Helal Uddin, president of the Bangladesh Dokan Malik Samity, said shopping markets had been facing a severe downturn for nearly two to two and a half years. Some shopkeepers go three to five consecutive days without making a sale, he said.

Many businesses can no longer pay staff from their earnings and are dipping into their capital to meet payroll costs. Even those willing to sell goods without making a profit are struggling to stay afloat.

Helal Uddin warned that two or three more markets could close within the next two to three months if the situation did not improve. Representatives of two markets, each with around 300 shops, had recently told him they could no longer sustain their businesses.

He said small and medium-sized businesses had received little government support during the downturn, claiming they had not benefited from taxpayer-funded relief measures since the Covid-19 pandemic.

Closures could wipe out investments worth hundreds of crores of taka and leave thousands of workers unemployed, with few alternative job opportunities, he warned.

Citing Karnaphuli Market, he said the four-floor commercial centre had employed around 3,000 workers and attracted shoppers with its shopping environment and competitive prices.

The association also identified Molla Tower in Rampura, opposite the Television Center, and Bishal Centre in Maghbazar as struggling.

It estimated that another 10 to 12 shopping centres in Dhaka faced a serious risk of closure but declined to identify them.

title: Connecting local savings with enterprise finance
text:
Our objective is to ensure that finance supports the business’s cash flow rather than becoming a pressure on it. Md Altaf Hossain Managing Director (Acting) Islami Bank Bangladesh PLC

Agent outlets can help rural customers turn regular banking activity into a foundation for business finance. In a conversation with The Daily Star, Md Altaf Hossain, acting managing director of Islami Bank Bangladesh PLC, discusses investment assessment, repayment arrangements and the role of the bank’s RDS programme in reaching women.

The Daily Star (TDS): How is agent banking supporting local enterprise, and what services are available?

Md Altaf Hossain (MAH): Rural customers are becoming more financially active, using formal channels to turn savings and remittance income into working capital and investment.

Entrepreneurs can open accounts, deposit and withdraw money, transfer funds, receive remittances, pay bills and obtain statements. Eligible customers can also access collateral-free investment facilities under RDS. Agents assist with transactions and documentation; branches and investment teams handle appraisal, risk assessment, eligibility verification and final approval.

TDS: What must applicants prepare, and how are businesses with limited records assessed?

MAH: For larger investment requests, agents help with initial applications and refer customers to the relevant branch or investment team. Documents may include national identity cards, photographs, business and income information, transaction records and relevant trade documents. Processing time depends on completeness, business complexity and due diligence.

We assess business activity, cash flow, repayment capacity and financial behaviour. Savings, remittances and transaction histories provide evidence of income patterns and repayment capacity when formal records are limited.

TDS: How do investment terms accommodate seasonal or uneven income?

MAH: Eligible micro and small businesses can access RDS, while more structured financing can be processed through branches. Investment size and repayment arrangements reflect the business’s nature, scale and cash-flow cycle.

Where appropriate, repayments can align with income cycles. Costs follow applicable Shariah-based products and regulatory frameworks. Our objective is to ensure that finance supports the business’s cash flow rather than becoming a pressure on it.

TDS: What barriers do women entrepreneurs face?

MAH: Limited collateral, business records, mobility and financial information can restrict access. Our agent network brings services closer, while RDS offers collateral-free investment. Women account for around 94 percent of RDS members. We are also focusing on financial literacy and digital capability. Better access to markets, technology and formal documentation requires further collective effort.

TDS: How can customers verify terms or raise complaints?

MAH: Agents and official channels explain charges, investment terms, required documents and application status. Branches and relevant teams oversee investment matters. Customers can verify information and report misleading statements, unauthorised charges or service problems through branches, the contact centre and designated grievance channels.

title: Indian media groups decry Modi’s privacy law in court
text:
The Indian government’s privacy law, which would require journalists to seek consent from people they write about, amounted to pre-censorship and could lead to newsrooms shutting down, media groups told the Supreme Court yesterday, starting the most high-profile challenge against the legislation.

The lawsuit comes amid accusations of declining press freedom in India since Prime Minister Narendra Modi ​took office in 2014.

Critics say many mainstream media outlets have not done enough to scrutinise Modi’s government, which has denied such allegations and says it respects press freedom.

A group of 21 news publishers, including companies owned by billionaires Mukesh Ambani and Gautam Adani, has challenged the privacy law, arguing it would trample upon investigative work and allow New Delhi to identify journalists’ sources.

title: 174 Bangladeshis return from Libya
text:
Forty-one of the 174 Bangladeshis repatriated from Libya early yesterday were physically ill, while 36 had been held at a detention centre in Tripoli after being intercepted at sea, said Bangladesh embassy in Libya.

The returnees arrived in Dhaka at 5:40am via Buraq Air flight UZ-222, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs said in a statement.

Of the 174 returnees, 36 had been detained at the Tajoura detention centre in Tripoli after being intercepted at sea. The remaining 138 returned home voluntarily amid dangerous conditions in the Libyan capital, according to the embassy.

Most of the returnees had reportedly entered Libya with the help of human traffickers, intending to reach Europe across the Mediterranean Sea, the foreign ministry said. Some alleged that they had been abducted and tortured during their stay in Libya.

Bangladesh Ambassador to Libya Major General Md Habib Ullah met the returnees at the embassy before their departure and warned them about the risks of irregular migration.

title: Bangladesh, Malaysia target FTA by 2027
text:
The government began formal negotiations with Malaysia for a free trade agreement (FTA) in Dhaka yesterday, targeting a deal by 2027 to expand bilateral trade and investment as Bangladesh prepares to graduate from least developed country status.

At the opening of the three-day first round of talks at the Pan Pacific Sonargaon Dhaka, the two sides signed the terms of reference (ToR), setting out the framework and scope of the negotiations, according to a statement from the commerce ministry.

The talks will continue until October 29.

Additional Commerce Secretary Khadiza Nazneen led the Bangladesh team, while Malaysia’s 31-member delegation was headed by Rashidi Said, a senior director of the Bilateral Economic and Trade Relations Division at the country’s Ministry of Investment, Trade and Industry.

The negotiations will cover trade in goods and services, rules of origin and customs procedures, with the two sides seeking to improve market access and reduce trade barriers while safeguarding their respective interests, Khadiza said.

She said the FTA would create opportunities for investment and employment by easing market access and reducing trade barriers.

Commerce Secretary Sharf Uddin Ahmed Choudhury noted that an FTA was critical for Bangladesh to address the challenges of LDC graduation and maintain its competitiveness in international markets.

Although trade relations between the two countries were promising, opportunities to diversify trade and expand investment remained largely untapped, he said.

There are opportunities for joint investments in the halal industry, semiconductor skill development, digital trade, logistics, and special economic zones, he added.

Sharaf also mentioned that Prime Minister Tarique Rahman and his Malaysian counterpart Anwar Ibrahim had discussed concluding a sustainable and mutually beneficial FTA by 2027 during the premier’s visit to Malaysia in June.

He also thanked Malaysia for supporting Bangladesh’s aspiration to join the Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership (RCEP), a regional trade agreement.

Meanwhile, Rashidi said the proposed FTA was intended to establish a long-term economic partnership rather than simply reduce tariffs.

Bilateral trade between the two countries reached around $2.84 billion in 2025, he said, adding that the agreement could open up further opportunities for trade, industrialisation and investment.

He expressed optimism that the negotiations would conclude by 2027 through mutual understanding, flexibility and a practical action plan. A planned visit to Bangladesh by the Malaysian prime minister could help advance the process, he added.

title: Bank Asia holds breast cancer awareness session
text:
Bank Asia PLC organised a Breast Cancer Awareness Session for its female employees on Monday, marking Breast Cancer Awareness Month, said a press release.

The session, held at Bank Asia Tower in Dhaka’s Karwan Bazar, was conducted by Dr Shifat Tanjila of Asgar Ali Hospital.

Dr Shifat shared insights on breast cancer awareness, importance of early detection, preventive measures and the need for timely medical consultation.

Bank Asia AMD and COO Md Sabbir Hossain was present among others.

The initiative reflects the organisation’s commitment to promoting employee well-being, raising health awareness and fostering a supportive and inclusive workplace as integral parts of its organisational culture.

title: Trump offers $1m reward for info about voter fraud
text:
US President Donald Trump on Monday announced a $1 million reward for information about voter fraud, in a fresh bid to sow doubt ahead of the US midterms and push his false claim about winning the 2020 election.

“Anybody reporting Voter Fraud in the past Elections, or the upcoming 2026 Midterm Election, will be paid $1,000,000 upon the arrest and conviction of those that created the Fraud!” Trump wrote on his Truth Social network.

The president gave no details of how the reward would be funded.

With the November 3 elections just eight days away, polls show Democrats pulling ahead as Republicans fight to retain control of both chambers of Congress. A Democratic victory would threaten to expose his administration to congressional investigations.

title: CPB demands justice after alleging attack on party office
text:
The Communist Party of Bangladesh (CPB) and several left-leaning political organisations yesterday condemned what they described as an attack on the party’s central office, Mukti Bhaban, in the capital’s Purana Paltan, though police said no such incident had taken place.

In a statement, CPB President Kazi Sajjad Zahir Chandan and General Secretary Abdullah Kafi Ratan said attacks carried out on the basis of false accusations against people holding different political views undermine democracy, political coexistence and the right to engage in political activities freely.

They also demanded that those responsible for the attack be identified and brought to justice.

According to the statement, a group of people carrying sticks gathered in front of Mukti Bhaban on Monday night and attempted to force their way into the building by breaking its main gate.

The group identified itself as activists of the ruling party and alleged that members of a banned political organisation were staying inside the CPB office, the statement said.

When CPB leaders and activists tried to prevent them from entering, the group turned violent, leaving several people injured, it added.

The statement further alleged that the group continued to surround the building even after police arrived and took charge of its security. They also demanded that the alleged members of the banned organisation be handed over to them.

However, Shafiqul Islam, investigation inspector of Paltan Police Station, denied that any such attack had occurred.

Speaking to The Daily Star around 6:00pm yesterday, he said, “They [CPB] did not file any written complaint. There was no attack or vandalism.”

Dhaka South BNP Member Secretary Tanvir Ahmed Robin also questioned the allegations.

“It should first be verified whether the incident actually took place. If it did, we need to determine who was involved. But allegations against the BNP should not be made hastily. I do not even know whether such an incident occurred,” he said.

“They have not made any specific allegation either, which makes the matter confusing.”

In their statement, the CPB leaders noted that the party had participated in every democratic movement in Bangladesh and that many of its leaders and activists had sacrificed their lives in those struggles. They also said Mukti Bhaban had served as an important centre during the 2024 mass uprising.

Regardless of the political identity of those involved, such actions constitute an attack on democracy, democratic rights and freedom of political activity, they said.

The CPB leaders added that threats and attacks would not deter people’s aspirations for democracy. They said the public would assess the government’s commitment to democratic values based on whether those responsible were identified and brought to justice.

The Jatiya Samajtantrik Dal (JaSod) also condemned the alleged attack and the assault on CPB leaders and activists.

In a statement, JaSod described mob violence as a “national curse” and called for a united national resistance against such acts.

The party also alleged that police had wrongfully detained Dhaka Metropolitan North Jubo Union President Iran Mollah and General Secretary Sohel Fakir during the incident and demanded their immediate and unconditional release.

The left alliance, the Ganatantrik Jukta Front, staged a protest rally and procession over the incident. Senior alliance leaders joined a march in front of the National Press Club yesterday afternoon.

The alliance leaders called for an impartial investigation into the attack on the CPB office, the identification and trial of those involved, and adequate security for the offices of political parties and democratic organisations.

Meanwhile, Prime Minister’s Information Adviser Zahed Ur Rahman said the government would look into the alleged attack on the CPB office.

He made the remarks while responding to journalists’ questions during a briefing on government activities at the Secretariat yesterday.

title: Ramadan essentials see rise in imports, LC openings
text:
Imports of major essentials, including edible oil, sugar, chickpeas, red lentils and dates, have increased in the first four months of the current fiscal year, improving the supply outlook ahead of Ramadan.

Import commitments have also increased for several items, suggesting that supplies could receive further support from upcoming shipments, although international prices, import costs and domestic market conditions will remain crucial to keeping prices stable.

Data from the Bangladesh Trade and Tariff Commission (BTTC), presented at a review of the market situation for essential commodities on Monday, showed that imports of the five items rose between July 1 and October 25 compared with the same period a year earlier.

Edible oil imports rose to 8.23 lakh tonnes during the period from 7.05 lakh tonnes a year ago. Letters of credit (LCs) opened for the commodity also increased, reaching 8.05 lakh tonnes, up 1.31 lakh tonnes year-on-year.

Imports of soybean seed, used to produce soybean oil, reached 5.01 lakh tonnes, an increase of 1.13 lakh tonnes from the same period last year.

Sugar imports rose to 6.87 lakh tonnes, up 1.53 lakh tonnes year-on-year, while LCs opened for the commodity stood at 8.10 lakh tonnes, indicating further import commitments.

Chickpea imports, particularly important during Ramadan for preparing iftar items, increased to 82,000 tonnes from 12,000 tonnes a year earlier.

LCs opened for chickpeas reached 1.38 lakh tonnes, substantially exceeding the volume imported so far in the current fiscal year.

Red lentil imports rose to 1.22 lakh tonnes, up 64,000 tonnes from the same period last year. LCs opened for the pulses stood at 1.14 lakh tonnes.

Date imports also increased, reaching 11,000 tonnes compared with 4,000 tonnes a year earlier.

The higher import volumes and LC openings have improved the supply outlook, but they do not necessarily guarantee lower retail prices, as the cost of imports and the pace at which shipments reach the market also influence domestic prices.

The BTTC review noted that international prices of edible oil and chickpeas had remained somewhat elevated, while red lentil prices had declined.

It called for close monitoring of global market trends, import costs and domestic supply conditions.

The commission also noted that chickpeas and lentils currently faced no import duties or taxes. A review and rational adjustment of the existing tariff structure for sugar and fruit imports could help keep market prices at tolerable levels, it said.

Mostafa Kamal, chairman of Meghna Group of Industries, one of the country’s major commodity importers, said importers had stepped up efforts to ensure adequate supplies and prevent shortages, aided by Bangladesh Bank’s simplified LC procedures for essential commodities.

The overall supply situation remained stable, with no major shortages, he said.

However, volatility in international markets, particularly rising oil prices amid ongoing global conflicts, remained a concern, he added.

Imports were continuing through regular shipments and new LCs ahead of Ramadan, he said, adding that future market conditions would depend on developments in the global economy and geopolitical situation.

title: Helping local businesses build a financial record
text:
Regular savings, remittance receipts and banking transaction histories can provide useful insights into a customer’s financial activity and cash flow. Imtiaz U Ahmed Managing Director Midland Bank PLC

Regular banking transactions can help small businesses establish financial records, but incomplete documentation and uneven income still complicate access to credit. In a conversation with The Daily Star, Imtiaz U Ahmed, managing director and CEO of Midland Bank PLC, discusses how agent outlets, credit assessment and support for women entrepreneurs can help.

The Daily Star (TDS): How are customers using agent banking, and what services can entrepreneurs access?

Imtiaz U Ahmed (IUA): Customers increasingly see outlets as access points to formal banking, beyond deposits and withdrawals. Regular use can help them establish transaction histories and manage business finances.

Services include account opening, deposits, withdrawals, transfers, inward remittances, utility bill payments and balance enquiries. Agents guide customers and assist with initial documentation, but do not assess or approve loans. Financing applications go to branches or lending teams for verification, assessment and approval.

TDS: What should applicants prepare, and how are businesses with limited records assessed?

IUA: Documents generally include identification, photographs, ownership details, a trade licence where applicable, bank statements and income and expense records. Tax, liability and security documents may also be required. Processing time depends on application completeness, business type, financing amount and verification.

We consider income patterns, existing obligations and repayment capacity under our credit policies. Savings, remittance receipts and transaction histories offer additional insights but cannot replace proper assessment.

TDS: How should financing accommodate different business cycles?

IUA: Short-term loans, working-capital facilities, SME term loans and agricultural finance serve different needs. Eligible customers may benefit from applicable Bangladesh Bank refinance schemes.

Amounts, repayment periods and instalments should reflect actual cash flow. Agricultural repayments may need to follow harvests, while traders need working capital aligned with business cycles. Decisions and costs remain subject to bank policies and product terms.

TDS: How are you addressing barriers facing women entrepreneurs?

IUA: Limited collateral, incomplete documentation, insufficient records and low awareness of financing options create difficulties. Support includes branch-level service desks, products such as MDB Nari Uddog and participation in applicable refinance schemes.

Agent outlets bring services closer to women who struggle to visit branches. Gaps remain in larger loans, financial literacy and reliable business records, requiring continued education and appropriate financing support.

TDS: How can customers understand charges and report problems?

IUA: We explain charges, repayment schedules, instalments and other key terms. Outlets must display approved charges and authorised services; records and inspections support accountability.

Customers can report misleading information, unauthorised charges or service problems through branches, the contact centre or designated complaint channels.

title: French edn measures to quell protests fall short
text:
French teachers said yesterday that education reforms aimed at ending weeks of protests were insufficient and would not be enough to quell students’ anger.

The French government on Monday announced a raft of proposals, including capping some class sizes at 28, billions of euros in loans for building renovation and a revamp of the university admissions system, to try to ease popular anger.

But Sophie Venetitay, the secretary general for teachers’ union SNES-FSU, told reporters that the measures did not go far enough, saying the size of more classes should be capped and more people should be hired to improve learning conditions for students.

“Today, what the ministry has said is only the beginning of a response,” she said. “It will not be enough to extinguish the anger.”

High school students initially blockaded their schools to protest against inadequate staffing and resources, in a movement that has since broadened to encompass general trade unions and the so-called “Yellow Vests” to express anger about weakening public services and cost-of-living increases.

Student leaders also said the government’s concessions were a good first step, but vowed to continue demonstrations, on Saturday and on November 5.

title: 3 Hindu homes vandalised, looted over FB post
text:
Three homes belonging to Hindu families were vandalised and looted in Rangpur’s Pirganj upazila on Monday night over a Facebook post that allegedly hurt the religious sentiments of Muslims, police said.

The owner of the affected houses are Bishu Chandra Mohanta, 50; his elder brother Jagadish Chandra Mohanta, 60; and their younger brother Dinesh Chandra Mohanta, 46 -- all residents of Chak Karimpur village.

According to police, Bishu’s son, Saurav Chandra Mohanta, 22, who works at a garment factory in Gazipur, shared a video on Facebook several months ago that allegedly hurt the religious sentiments of local Muslims.

Although Saurav later deleted the post, its screenshots resurfaced on Sunday, triggering tension in the area and leading to the attack, said Nazmul Haque, officer-in-charge of Pirganj Police Station.

Law enforcers detained Saurav early yesterday in Kichak Bela village of Bogura’s Shibganj upazila. He was later formally arrested in a case filed by local resident Aminul Islam on allegations of hurting religious sentiments, the OC said.

Separately, Bishu filed a case with Pirganj Police Station the same day over the vandalism and looting.

Eight people were named in the case, while 60 to 70 unidentified individuals were also accused. Police arrested one of the named accused, Shafiqul Islam Arif, 30, in connection with the case, the OC said.

According to eyewitnesses and the victim families, 50 to 60 people armed with sticks, iron rods and locally made weapons attacked the houses around 7:00pm on Monday.

The assault lasted about an hour, during which the homes and furniture of the three families were vandalised. Some attackers also looted livestock and other belongings.

Bishu told The Daily Star that his son had married about a year and a half ago and had not maintained contact with the family since.

“I don’t even have his mobile phone number. If he has committed an offence, why should we be punished?” he said.

He said the attackers damaged a television, furniture, walls and doors of his house and took away two goats.

“We are poor people. Everything we had has been damaged. We cannot afford to repair the house or buy new furniture,” said Saurav’s mother, Taru Rani Mohanta, 45.

Jagadish and Dinesh said their houses, doors, fences and furniture were vandalised, while televisions and other valuables were looted.

Jagadish’s wife, Arati Rani, said she fled her home to save herself.

“When the attackers stormed our house, we pleaded with them to stop. But they threatened to kill me,” she said.

After the attack, fear has gripped the village, where about 65 Hindu families live, residents said.

Members of the community also said they identified some of the attackers as residents of adjacent villages.

“Police have been deployed in the area to prevent further untoward incidents. Operations are underway to arrest the remaining accused,” the OC said.

Pirganj Upazila Nirbahi Officer Abdullah Al Bakiul Bari said the affected families would receive financial assistance.

title: Govt eyes 1m digital jobs in five years
text:
The government aims to create one million jobs in the digital sector over the next five years and turn Bangladesh into a regional hub for information technology and artificial intelligence, ICT Minister Faqir Mahbub Anam said yesterday.

The minister was speaking as the chief guest at Bangladesh TechConnect 2026, jointly organised by the Posts and Telecommunications Division and Huawei, at the Bangladesh-China Friendship Exhibition Center in Dhaka.

He said the government was committed to building a modern, technology-driven and knowledge-based country under its “Bangladesh First” policy.

The minister stressed the need to ensure reliable, secure, high-speed and affordable internet connectivity across the country. He said modern telecommunications infrastructure, digital skills development, investment and support for local innovation would be essential to achieving the government’s goals.

“Effective use of AI and digital technologies would boost productivity, create new jobs and accelerate economic growth,” he said.

He also called for stronger cybersecurity, better protection of personal data and responsible use of technology.

Emphasising cooperation between the public and private sectors, the minister said joint efforts by the government, local businesses and international technology partners could help build an inclusive and competitive digital economy.

Md Kamruzzaman, secretary of the Posts and Telecommunications Division, said Bangladesh TechConnect had become a national platform bringing together the government, businesses, educational institutions, development partners and the media.

The conference offered an opportunity to strengthen cooperation between policymakers and industry, he said, adding that digital infrastructure was no longer a luxury but a key foundation for a prosperous, investment-driven and knowledge-based economy.

Md Mamunur Rashid Bhuiyan, secretary of the Information and Communication Technology (ICT) Division, said the government had identified five priorities to accelerate the country’s digital transformation.

These are a strong legal and policy framework, reliable connectivity, digital public infrastructure, AI and cybersecurity, and domestic manufacturing.

Work had begun on a national AI policy, which the government expected to complete within the next three to four months, he said.

Jason Wu, president of Huawei’s South Asia region, said the company was committed to working with the government and industry partners to develop digital infrastructure and expand technology adoption in Bangladesh.

Drawing on its expertise in connectivity, cloud computing and AI, Huawei aims to help local industries improve efficiency, develop new services and support the country’s long-term digital growth, he added.

The event featured three panel discussions on “Future Technologies and Connectivity”, “The Role of Technology in Enhancing Industrial Efficiency” and “Artificial Intelligence: Global Trends, Impact and Bangladesh’s Readiness”.

The sessions were moderated by Iqbal Ahmed, commissioner of the Bangladesh Telecommunication Regulatory Commission (BTRC); Syeda Naushin Parnini, additional secretary at the Ministry of Science and Technology; and Md Taibur Rahman, director general of the National Cyber Security Agency, respectively.

Panellists discussed the development of 5G and connectivity infrastructure, ways to improve industrial efficiency through technology, and Bangladesh’s readiness to adopt AI.

They also examined the commercial potential of 5G, fixed wireless access and enterprise connectivity in sectors such as readymade garments, ports, agriculture and healthcare.

Meanwhile, Shahed Alam, chief corporate and regulatory affairs officer of Robi, said infrastructure-sharing guidelines had failed to deliver results over the past 15 years because of weak enforcement.

“Without mandatory implementation and proper enforcement, infrastructure sharing will not work effectively. Investment costs are rising, and smaller operators are struggling to expand their networks. As a result, network duplication is not being avoided,” he said.

“In a small country like Bangladesh, if every operator has to install its own towers, space constraints will become a major problem. Ultimately, customers will suffer,” he added.

title: Telcos seek deeper cuts in spectrum renewal prices
text:
Mobile phone operators have urged the telecom regulator to further cut spectrum renewal prices and allow payments in 20 equal annual instalments instead of 12.

In a letter to Bangladesh Telecommunication Regulatory Commission (BTRC) Chairman Md Emdad Ul Bari on October 25, the Association of Mobile Telecom Operators of Bangladesh (AMTOB) welcomed the commission’s proposal to extend the spectrum renewal tenure to 20 years, calling it a progressive measure aligned with international practice.

Moreover, the regulator proposed payment in 12 instalments, up from the eight instalments proposed earlier.

The proposed tenure was previously 12 years and four months.

AMTOB also sought the withdrawal of the annual spectrum charge and an urgent meeting between the regulator’s top leadership and the heads of mobile operators.

The letter, signed by AMTOB Secretary General Lt Col Mohammad Zulfikar (retd), covers the 900MHz, 1800MHz and 2100MHz bands held by Grameenphone, Robi and Banglalink.

Their existing spectrum licences expire on November 10.

While welcoming the proposed extension, AMTOB expressed surprise at the pricing, saying the fees appeared to have been calculated by mechanically extending the rates proposed for the shorter tenure in the regulator’s October 19 letter.

“Spectrum valuation and spectrum renewal pricing are not typically determined through a simple linear extrapolation,” the association said, citing factors such as discounted cash flow, inflation, technological change and investment risk.

AMTOB said operators had not expected their request for a 20-year renewal to result in a straightforward scaling up of the earlier valuation. Instead, they expected the regulator to apply its “prevailing reference pricing framework” to determine fees for the longer tenure.

The operators cited the GSMA, the global body representing mobile operators, which maintains that longer spectrum validity and certainty over renewal encourage investment. They also referred to the UK regulator Ofcom, which they said had recently reduced spectrum fees based on forward-looking valuations.

AMTOB questioned the transparency of the valuation process, saying public reports indicated that a consultant’s study had produced a range of values using economic, engineering and international benchmarking methods. However, the industry had not been given access to the study’s assumptions or findings.

Available information suggested that the final prices reflected neither the lower end of the valuation range nor its average, the association said.

AMTOB called for further cuts to the base prices proposed on October 19, a 20-year renewal period with fees paid in 20 equal annual instalments without any upward revision for the longer tenure, and withdrawal of the annual spectrum charge.
