“Spectrum pricing should be viewed not merely as a revenue consideration but also as a strategic enabler,” the letter said, warning that excessive costs could constrain investment, delay network expansion and undermine service quality and affordability.

On October 15, the BTRC sent the Posts and Telecommunications Division a proposal to cut spectrum prices by 10 to 30 percent across the three bands, covering a total of 79.2MHz.

Under that proposal, spectrum renewal would cost around Tk 13,100.5 crore, or $1.07 billion, compared with Tk 16,845.2 crore, or $1.37 billion, at existing rates.

The proposed cuts would reduce potential government revenue by Tk 3,744.7 crore, equivalent to about $304 million.

The proposed rates covered a period ending March 10, 2039, or approximately 12 years and four months. Taxes, VAT and other fees would be charged separately.

The prices were based on a consultant’s study that used four valuation methods.

BTRC Chairman Md Emdad Ul Bari has defended the proposed rates, saying they were based on the study and that the regulator aimed to sell at least 80 percent of the spectrum available for renewal.

With the existing licences due to expire on November 10, AMTOB said a direct meeting between the regulator and industry representatives could “quickly resolve any misunderstandings” and help settle the outstanding issues within the limited time available.

title: Turning transaction histories into opportunities for enterprise
text:
Transaction data can make the financially invisible visible. Mashrur Arefin Managing Director and CEO City Bank PLC

Agent banking can help small businesses access finance, but local reach must be supported by sound assessment and customer protection. In a conversation with The Daily Star, Mashrur Arefin, Managing Director and CEO of City Bank PLC, discusses cash-flow-based lending, support for women entrepreneurs and the role of agents in developing local enterprise.

The Daily Star (TDS): How is agent banking evolving into a platform for local enterprise development?

Mashrur Arefin (MA): Our network serves around six lakh customers through 500 outlets, with deposits exceeding Tk 1,800 crore and loan disbursements of around Tk 4,500 crore. Our ambition extends beyond deposits to access to finance, financial literacy and economic inclusion.

By integrating agent banking with our Small & Microfinance business, we are helping customers move from savings and remittances towards productive credit and entrepreneurship. We are beginning to see that shift across the network, particularly where branches and sub-branches are absent. Agents provide a link between the bank and customers who would otherwise struggle to reach formal services.

TDS: What services can entrepreneurs access, and where does the agent’s responsibility end?

MA: Agents facilitate account opening, deposits, withdrawals, transfers and remittances. They also connect entrepreneurs with our Small & Microfinance unit for financing, including loans for small businesses, women entrepreneurs and remittance beneficiaries, and eligible facilities under refinance, pre-finance and credit guarantee schemes. Agents identify needs and facilitate access. The bank’s authorised business and credit risk teams conduct assessment and approval, maintaining credit discipline while bringing services closer to customers.

TDS: How does an entrepreneur apply for finance?

MA: The agent connects the applicant to our Small Business team. SME relationship officers are stationed at selected outlets in areas with strong business potential, making sourcing and service more convenient.

Applicants generally need a national identity document, a valid trade licence where applicable, business and bank transaction records, and documents specific to the facility. The bank assesses business cash flow, repayment capacity, credit history and regulatory requirements. Processing time depends on document completeness, verification needs and the facility’s complexity.

TDS: How do you assess businesses with limited formal accounts or collateral?

MA: We should examine what a business generates alongside what an entrepreneur owns. Savings patterns, remittance receipts, account transactions, business cash flows and repayment behaviour help build a financial profile. Alongside conventional credit assessment, these provide a clearer understanding of small borrowers’ repayment capacity. Transaction data can make the financially invisible visible. It cannot replace sound credit assessment, but it can support better-informed decisions and expand responsible access to finance.

TDS: Which financing options suit local businesses with seasonal or uneven cash flows?

MA: We facilitate cottage, small and micro-enterprise loans, women entrepreneur financing, remittance beneficiary loans, agribusiness and farmer financing, and eligible facilities under refinance, pre-finance and credit guarantee schemes. We also disburse short-term digital agricultural loans to smallholder farmers through agent banking, working with farmer associations, agricultural fintech firms and aggregator or supply networks.

Loan amounts and repayment schedules should reflect the financing purpose, business cash flow and repayment capacity. Seasonal enterprises and farmers may need arrangements aligned with their operating cycles, within approved products and credit policies. The aim is to provide finance for a clear purpose, with sustainable repayment terms.

TDS: What barriers do women entrepreneurs face, and how are you addressing them?

MA: Mobility, financial literacy, documentation, digital confidence and limited credit histories remain barriers. Agent banking brings services closer to homes and workplaces, while SME relationship officers at many agent points improve access.

The harder challenge is helping women develop the confidence and capabilities to start, sustain and grow businesses. Our City Alo platform works with agent banking to train rural women entrepreneurs, build business skills and financial awareness, and support access to appropriate financing. We also offer tailored products and, in some cases, relaxed underwriting policies to these segments.

TDS: How do you ensure transparency and protect customers at agent outlets?

MA: Customers must understand charges, financing costs, repayment obligations and application status. We emphasise transparent disclosure, transaction documentation, authentication, agent monitoring and compliance with bank policies and regulatory requirements. Concerns can be raised through our official customer-service and complaint-resolution channels. Agents cannot promise unapproved loans, misrepresent financing terms or charge unauthorised fees.

TDS: What would strengthen agent banking’s contribution to enterprise development?

MA: With training and appropriate incentives, agents can identify potential borrowers, connect them with our Small Business teams and support follow-up and repayment monitoring. Transparent, performance-based commissions should reward genuine referrals, quality borrower selection and repayment support, subject to regulation and credit policies. Customers should never face undisclosed interest or charges to fund these commissions.

As an illustration, a rural farmer borrowing informally could be connected through an agent to our Small Business team and assessed for suitable finance, including under an eligible Bangladesh Bank credit guarantee scheme. The agent could help verify business activity and facilitate repayment follow-up, while the bank retains responsibility for credit assessment and approval. This could give the borrower access to more affordable formal finance, allow the agent to earn legitimate commission and help the bank extend responsible lending into underserved communities.

title: India orders evacuations as Arnab looms
text:
Indian authorities ordered nearly 100,000 people to evacuate homes in Andhra Pradesh and Odisha, ahead of a severe cyclone the national weather office expects to make landfall today.

Neighbouring Nepal and Sri Lanka have also issued weather warnings.

Cyclone Arnab is forecast to hit India’s southwestern Andhra Pradesh coast as a “very severe cyclonic storm”, with gusts of up to 150 kilometres (93 miles) per hour on Wednesday morning at 6:00am GMT (11:30am Indian Standard Time), the India Meteorological Department (IMD) said in a bulletin.

Torrential rain lashed the coast in the port city of Kakinda as heavy waves crashed on shore.

“I’ve never seen anything like this before,” Kotesh Kumar, 35, told AFP, adding the government warned people to stock up on groceries.

“There was a cyclone here three years ago, but the water didn’t rise this much.”

Cyclones, called hurricanes in the North Atlantic and typhoons in the Pacific, are a regular menace in the Bay of Bengal and northern Indian Ocean.

The storm season, however, has been turbocharged by the El Nino weather phenomenon that has caused unprecedented warming.

Neighbouring Sri Lanka, meanwhile, closed schools with warnings of torrential rain, with the island’s Department of Meteorology warning storms could trigger flash floods and mudslides.

The military has been placed on alert, Colombo’s Disaster Management Centre said.

Indian media reported that as many as 50,000 people have been told to move to safe areas in Andhra Pradesh, and 48,000 in Odisha.

Nepal’s disaster authority issued a warning yesterday, saying that as the storm travels inland towards the Himalayas -- likely overnight Thursday -- it will bring heavy rainfall as well as “a high risk of heavy snowfall, snowstorms and avalanches”.

It called on tourists to avoid travelling to high mountain areas and advised those already there to remain in safe locations.

Nepal is still recovering from a catastrophic August 26 flood sparked by a glacial mountain collapse, which swept away more than 1,400 people and left over 5,000 missing.

India’s weather bureau said it expects the cyclone to result in “total destruction” of thatched houses and create localised flooding, uprooting of power and communication poles, and “widespread damage” to standing crops.

In Kakinada, police barricaded roads leading to the sea.

Andhra Pradesh State Chief Minister Nara Chandrababu Naidu ordered the storm to be “constantly monitored and advance precautions taken”, his office said in a statement on Monday.

“Adequate shelters and evacuation arrangements have been made,” New Delhi’s Cabinet Secretariat said in a statement.

The neighbouring Indian state of Odisha opened 1,735 cyclone shelters and imposed restrictions on movement in landslide-prone zone areas, the state’s information office said.

Local media reported that Andhra Pradesh authorities ordered evacuations in key, low-lying areas and shut “all educational institutions” in some districts from Tuesday until Saturday.

Over 4,700 pregnant women residing in potentially dangerous sites were moved to hospitals, according to The Indian Express newspaper.

title: Ex-FBI chief, Trump critic Comey hit with fresh charges
text:
Former FBI director James Comey has been charged with allegedly disclosing national defense information, the third criminal case brought against the outspoken critic of US President Donald Trump.

In a criminal complaint unsealed on Monday, Comey is accused of communicating the information in October 2016, when he was head of the Federal Bureau of Investigation, to a “person not entitled to receive it.”

Comey was charged in September 2025 with making false statements to Congress and obstructing a congressional proceeding in what was widely seen as retribution by the Republican president against a political opponent.

A federal judge threw out the case on the grounds that the US attorney handpicked by Trump who brought the charges had been unlawfully appointed.

Comey was indicted again in April, this time for allegedly threatening Trump’s life in an Instagram post that showed the numbers “86 47” spelled out in sea shells.

The Trump administration’s Justice Department has claimed that “86 47” constitutes a threat to the president -- “86” meaning to kill and “47” a reference to Trump being the 47th president.

Comey has denied threatening the president’s life.

In the latest case, Comey is accused of directing an unidentified individual to “disclose national defense information to a reporter for a national news publication.”

“They’re back again,” Comey said in a video posted on his Substack in response to the latest charges.

“It would almost be funny if it weren’t such an appalling abuse of the Department of Justice,” he said. “I’m still innocent. I’m still not afraid of these people, and I still believe in the independent federal judiciary.”

In a statement to US media, Comey’s attorney, Patrick Fitzgerald, said the charges in the latest case had been investigated by prosecutors during the first Trump administration and “the Government determined that no charges should be brought against anyone.”

“Mr Comey steadfastly maintains his innocence,” Fitzgerald said.

The unsealing of the court documents came just hours after a US federal judge ruled that the July 2025 firing of Comey’s daughter, Maurene Comey, a former federal prosecutor in New York, was unlawful.

Maurene Comey filed suit against the Department of Justice claiming she had been dismissed “solely or substantially” because of her father’s criticism of Trump or “because of her perceived political affiliation and beliefs.”

In ruling against the Department of Justice, District Judge Jesse Furman said the younger Comey had been deprived of her due process rights and ordered that she be reinstated.

Since taking office, Trump has taken a number of punitive measures against his perceived enemies, purging government officials deemed to be disloyal, targeting law firms involved in past cases against him and pulling federal funding from universities.

title: Shanta Life opens regional office in Ctg
text:
Shanta Life Insurance PLC yesterday opened its regional office in Chattogram to make its life insurance services more accessible to customers in the country’s commercial hub.

The new office, located in the Muradpur area, is expected to bring Shanta Life’s insurance solutions closer to individuals and families in Chattogram and its surrounding areas, company officials said. Nafis A Ahmed, chief executive officer of the life insurer, inaugurated the office as the chief guest.

Addressing the event, Nafis said the company was a new entrant in the country’s insurance sector, which comprises 36 companies, but stood out for its values, including trust, transparency and the delivery of high-quality services in a simple manner.

The company was working to digitalise the entire insurance process, including claim settlements, to build customer trust, the CEO said. He added that customers would be able to purchase policies and access other services through the company’s mobile app.

Claiming that the company settles 99 percent of insurance claims within five days, setting a new standard in the sector, the CEO said the insurer was also focusing on cashless operations.

Jane Alam Romel, chief marketing officer of the insurer, was also present at the event, along with other senior company officials and corporate representatives from various organisations in Chattogram.

title: Indian firm L&T wins $1b Dhaka Metro contracts
text:
India’s infrastructure major Larsen & Toubro (L&T) has secured contracts worth up to $1 billion to design and build two key system packages for Dhaka Metro Rail Line 1.

The contracts cover track works, electrical systems, signalling, telecommunications and platform screen doors, the company said in a stock exchange disclosure.

Dhaka Metro Rail Line 1 is Bangladesh’s first underground metro rail project. It will connect Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport (HSIA) to Kamalapur, passing through Rampura, Malibagh and Rajarbagh, before branching towards Purbachal.

L&T is an engineering, procurement and construction (EPC) and high-tech manufacturing conglomerate.

The company said the awards build on its previous work in Bangladesh, where it won and delivered the integrated railway systems package for Dhaka Metro Line 6, the country’s first metro rail corridor.

The announcement follows the Cabinet Committee on Government Purchase approval of eight construction packages for Metro Rail Line 1 and Line 5 (Northern Route), worth about Tk 58,500 crore.

L&T classified the combined contracts as a “major” order under its standardised reporting framework, which defines such orders as those valued between ₹5,000 crore and ₹10,000 crore.

Apart from the Indian firm, contractors from Japan, China and Bangladesh have also secured work on the two metro lines. The projects are funded by the Japan International Cooperation Agency (JICA).

Dhaka Metro Line 1 will span about 31km across two routes: an underground section from HSIA to Kamalapur and an elevated section from Natun Bazar to Purbachal Terminal. The line will have 19 stations and a depot at Pitalganj.

The 20km Metro Rail Line 5 (Northern Route) will run from Hemayetpur in Savar through Gabtoli, Mirpur-14 and Natun Bazar to Vatara.

title: What can you actually do at an agent banking outlet?
text:
A shopkeeper wants to deposit the day’s earnings. A family needs to collect money sent from abroad. A small entrepreneur wants to enquire about a loan. An agent banking outlet can be a starting point for all three, although the services available depend on the bank and its arrangement with the agent.

These outlets provide selected banking services on behalf of a bank. Knowing what they are allowed to offer and which decisions remain with the bank can help customers avoid an unnecessary trip to a branch.

Open an account and build savings

Customers can begin the account-opening process at an outlet by submitting forms and supporting documents. The agent helps collect the information, while the bank verifies it and approves the account. Before visiting, ask which identification documents, photographs and nominee details are required.

Some banks also offer monthly savings schemes and fixed deposits through their agent banking channels. Dutch-Bangla Bank, for example, lists both among its services. Customers should check the deposit amount, tenure, applicable return and early-withdrawal conditions before choosing a product.

Deposit, withdraw and transfer money

Cash deposits and withdrawals are core services. Customers can also check their balance, obtain a mini statement and transfer funds through the channels supported by their bank. Before sending money, confirm whether the outlet can transfer it to the intended account and what charges apply.

Transaction limits apply, and a larger withdrawal may require advance arrangements. Checking with the outlet beforehand can help establish whether the requested amount can be handled during the visit.

Receive remittances and make payments

Participating outlets disburse inward foreign remittances, allowing recipients to collect money sent through supported channels. This does not mean the agent operates a foreign currency exchange counter: receiving a remittance and buying or selling foreign currency are different services.

Utility bill payments are another available service, although customers should confirm that their particular biller is supported. Depending on the bank’s arrangements, outlets may also handle insurance premiums and payments under social safety-net programmes. Bank Asia lists these among its agent banking services.

Start a loan application

An outlet can provide a local point of contact for submitting a loan application and supporting documents. Bank Asia, for instance, lists SME and agricultural loan processing among its services.

However, submitting an application to an agent does not guarantee financing. Assessment and approval remain with the bank. Authorised outlets may also facilitate disbursement and collect repayments after a loan has been sanctioned.

Check before completing a transaction

Ask about the bank’s prescribed charges and retain the transaction receipt or acknowledgement. Check the amount and account details, and review any SMS confirmation received. Dutch-Bangla Bank’s published deposit procedure, for example, includes a receipt and an SMS where a mobile number is provided.

If the system is unavailable or cannot generate an acknowledgement, do not leave money to be processed later. An agent’s familiarity with the neighbourhood is useful, but each transaction still needs to pass through the bank’s authorised system.

title: Gambia students protest over study conditions
text:
Hundreds of Gambian students demonstrated on Monday to protest deteriorating studying conditions as well as issues with food and internet access, AFP journalists reported, echoing demands by students across Europe.

The protests at the University of The Gambia (UTG) in the capital Banjul, the country’s leading higher education institution, come weeks after demonstrations sparked by persistent power cuts in the West African country whose President Adama Barrow is seeking a third term in an election scheduled for 5 December.

“We’re fed up,” the protesters chanted, a day after their student union had stated that “students continue to endure inadequate transport, limited access to drinking water, the closure of a canteen, unreliable internet and disruptions to academic activities.”

The Ministry of Higher Education stated it had “taken note of the concerns raised by the students”.

The ministry called for “constructive dialogue” and conceded their demands “require ongoing attention, effective coordination and practical solutions.”

On Saturday, the government announced several measures in response to the students’ demands, including the resumption of catering services from Monday, the deployment of additional water dispensers, better transport services and improved internet connectivity.

But the student union called a mass mobilisation, while urging participants to remain peaceful.

Over the past weeks, high-school students in France, Italy and Belgium have protested for better conditions, with some demonstrations turning violent.

title: World to add less clean energy capacity this year
text:
The world will add less clean energy capacity in 2026 for the first time in five years due to inadequate ​transmission networks and trade barriers, the chief of the International ‌Renewable Energy Agency (IRENA) said.

Growth in solar and wind capacity has been accelerating every year since 2021, when the coronavirus pandemic disrupted global supply chains. Clean power installations including ​hydropower surged a record 692 gigawatts, or 15.5 percent, to 5,149 GW ​in 2025 — representing half the world’s power capacity.

Clean power installations including ​hydropower surged a record 692 gigawatts, or 15.5 percent, to 5,149 GW ​in 2025 — representing half the world’s power capacity.

Governments have pledged to boost clean energy use to ensure reliable power supply and cut ​costs, particularly after the US-Israeli war with Iran choked energy supplies and inflated ​prices. But IRENA Director-General Francesco La Camera noted that there has been a slowdown in renewables deployment in China due to curtailment — or rejection of clean power when a ​grid hits its limits.

“The main cause of a lack of new record ​in additions this year is the mismatch between generation capacity and the capacity to ‌distribute and transmit electricity,” he told Reuters on the sidelines of the Singapore International Energy Week conference.

China, the world’s biggest renewable energy producer, turned away enough clean energy to power Mexico for a year in the first half of ​2026, while networks ​in nations such as Australia and Japan also failed to keep pace with a surging renewables buildout.

“The amount of the (capacity) increase in ​the other parts of the world this year, I ​don’t think it will offset the slowing down in China,” La Camera said. He declined to provide a numerical forecast for expected growth in clean energy additions this year.

Renewable ​energy additions are crucial to reducing global ​emissions, and the United Nations said in a report last week that “urgent and stringent” emission cuts ​were required to slow global warming.

title: RMG wage board gazette to be published soon: minister
text:
The government will soon form the minimum wage board for garment workers, Labour and Employment Minister Ariful Haque Choudhury said yesterday.

The list of representatives from the employers’ side has already been received, and the gazette notification for the formation of the wage board will be published as soon as the list from the workers’ side arrives, according to a statement from the labour ministry.

The six-member wage board for garment workers consists of employer, worker, government and independent representatives.

The minister shared the information at the 96th meeting of the Tripartite Consultative Council (TCC) and the 25th meeting of the RMG Tripartite Consultative Council (RMG TCC), organised by the ministry at the CIRDAP Conference Centre in Dhaka.

Regarding the ongoing labour unrest and protests, the minister said he had urged employers to clear workers’ outstanding wages by the seventh of every month.

“At the same time, I would tell protesting workers not to cause public suffering by blocking roads in the name of a movement.”

Any problem should be resolved internally through discussions between employers and workers within the factories, he said.

He further warned that if anyone tried to put the government in an embarrassing situation or pursued any other malicious intent, neither the government, nor the employers, nor the worker representatives would tolerate it.

“I am directing law enforcement agencies and intelligence organisations to swiftly bring to justice those who are instigating unrest from outside the actual labour leadership and turning non-issues into issues. No third party will be allowed to create chaos in the industrial sector at any cost,” he added.

At the meeting, Nazma Akter, president of Sommilito Garments Sramik Federation, talked about recent incidents of labour unrest in various industrial areas, including Gazipur.

She stated that the government, employers and worker representatives were working jointly to clear outstanding wages quickly, and efforts were underway to resolve the issues with the help of the industrial police and local administration.

She noted that initiatives had been taken to complete the process of forming the wage board within the month.

Furthermore, discussions were ongoing with the government regarding increasing workers’ wages, controlling house rent, reducing the prices of daily essentials, and resolving gas and energy crises.

Razekuzzaman Ratan, assistant general secretary of Bangladesher Samajtantrik Dal, said that a policy decision on forming the wage board had been made at the TCC meeting, and he expressed optimism that it would be implemented swiftly.

Rezwan Selim, vice-president of the Bangladesh Garment Manufacturers and Exporters Association, expressed concern over the ongoing protests in Gazipur and Kaliakair and called for a quick and sustainable solution.

Mohammad Hatem, president of the Bangladesh Knitwear Manufacturers and Exporters Association (BKMEA), said the government was highly committed to increasing workers’ wages.

If employers and workers shared the same mindset, there would be no need for fresh protests, he said.

The BKMEA president urged workers not to damage industrial factories or embarrass the government.

Md Abdur Rahman Tarfder, secretary to the labour and employment ministry, also spoke.

title: Lakshmipur betel nut sales likely to hit Tk 700 crore
text:
Favourable weather and suitable soil have helped produce a bumper betel nut crop in Lakshmipur this season, with sales expected to reach around Tk 700 crore.

One of the country’s leading betel nut-producing districts, Lakshmipur has seen bustling activity at more than 50 wholesale markets across its five upazilas as harvesting and marketing gather pace.

According to the Department of Agricultural Extension (DAE), around 42,000 tonnes of betel nuts were produced on 7,250 hectares of land in Ramganj, Raipur, Lakshmipur Sadar, Kamalnagar and Ramgati this season.

Last year, the district produced 42,270 tonnes on 7,245 hectares. Despite a slight decline in output, farmers are satisfied with prevailing prices and strong demand.

Raipur accounts for the largest share of production, followed by Lakshmipur Sadar, agriculture officials said.

Harvesting peaks during the Bengali months of Kartik and Agrahayan, bringing major markets in Raipur, Ramganj and Lakshmipur town to life. Uttar Tehmani Bazar in Lakshmipur town holds its betel nut market twice a week, attracting wholesalers from different areas.

Growers and traders said betel nuts are sold in three forms: ripe, water-cured and dried. Ripe betel nuts currently sell for Tk 160-170 per pon (80 pieces), while a kaon (1,280 pieces) costs Tk 2,400-2,700. Dried nuts with husks are sold by the maund, equivalent to 63kg.

Around 60 percent of the district’s betel nuts are water-cured, while the rest are sold ripe or sun-dried. Demand and prices for water-cured nuts typically rise sharply between January and March.

Several thousand workers and more than 200 major traders are involved in harvesting, sorting, transporting, soaking and drying the nuts.

Zakir Hossain, a worker from Keroa in Raipur, said he earns Tk 2,500-3,000 a day by climbing 250-300 trees to harvest the nuts.

Mokhlesur Rahman, a trader in Raipur, said he deals in betel nuts worth Tk 20-25 crore annually.

Growers and officials said the district’s soil and climate favour cultivation. A mature tree can remain productive for around 30 years under suitable conditions, providing farmers with a long-term source of income.

Known for their quality and distinctive taste, Lakshmipur’s betel nuts enjoy strong demand at home and abroad.

DAE Deputy Director Zahir Ahmed said the bumper harvest had boosted the rural economy, benefiting growers, traders and labourers.

“More than half of the betel nuts produced in Lakshmipur come from Raipur upazila, followed by Lakshmipur Sadar. According to our calculations, this season’s yield is worth approximately Tk 700 crore,” he added.

title: US-brokered truce starts in Ukrainian town facing starvation
text:
A ceasefire began around the Ukrainian town of Oleshky yesterday after more than four years of Russian occupation which have left trapped and starving residents desperate for food, water and medicine.

The local ceasefire, brokered by US first lady Melania Trump with the involvement of Pope Leo, is intended to allow aid into Oleshky and enable those who want to leave to do so. Some residents say they have survived on a cup of rice or buckwheat a day, sometimes with a tomato, cucumber or wild weed added.

Russia and Ukraine both said they were abiding by the local ceasefire around the frontline city, which went into force at 3:00 am Ukrainian time as part of stuttering US efforts to end Russia’s war in Ukraine and is due to last until November 1.

The ceasefire does not apply elsewhere, and Russian forces again pounded the Ukrainian capital Kyiv with ballistic missiles overnight, killing at least one person, local officials said.

Oleshky lies on the eastern bank of the Dnipro River in Ukraine’s southern Kherson region, opposite Kherson city, which is held by Ukrainian forces. Russian troops seized Oleshky during the first days of their full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022 and have controlled it ever since.

Kyiv residents said they hoped the Oleshky ceasefire would finally bring some relief to locals, but optimism was tinged with concerns that Russia would not abide by the terms of the agreement.

“I want to hope that things will indeed work out this way, that the agreement will actually be implemented, and that the Russian side will keep its word,” Olha Haiduk, 59, told Reuters.

The head of President Volodymyr Zelensky’s ruling faction in parliament, David Arakhamia, called it the “biggest de-escalation since 2022.”

Oleshky has suffered extensive war damage and was hit hard by flooding after the destruction of the nearby Kakhovka dam in 2023.

The US has said only a few thousand people remain in the town from a prewar population of 24,000. Residents and officials have reported severe shortages of food, medicine and other basic supplies, and Oleshky has been largely cut off from running water, electricity, gas and central heating. Residents have offered harrowing accounts of risking their lives travelling along mine-strewn roads just to access food and water.

title: Japan to invest $6.35b, create 2 lakh jobs in 5yrs
text:
Japan projects up to one trillion yen ($6.35 billion) in private investment in Bangladesh over the next five years, with the investment expected to create 2 lakh jobs.

The projection was welcomed by Prime Minister Tarique Rahman and his Japanese counterpart Sanae Takaichi at their bilateral summit in Tokyo yesterday, according to a joint statement issued after the meeting. Dhaka and Tokyo agreed to deepen economic cooperation, strengthen supply chains, and expand strategic ties.

Image

The two leaders also agreed to upgrade their flagship bilateral initiative, the Bay of Bengal Industrial Growth Belt (BIG-B), to “BIG-B for Shared Prosperity”, with the aim of developing the Matarbari-Maheshkhali area into a major hub for logistics, energy, and industry centred on the Matarbari Deep Sea Port.

The two countries also shared a vision of developing resilient supply chains in manufacturing, food and agriculture, information and communication technology, and pharmaceuticals.

According to Japan’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs website, the two countries signed six instruments: four memorandums of cooperation (MoCs), a letter of intent (LoI), and a letter concerning grant aid.

The MoCs cover economic relations and improvement of the business environment; cooperation in agriculture; and cooperation in fisheries and livestock. The two agriculture-related areas are intended to strengthen business ties and attract investment. The LoI concerns climate change cooperation, while the grant-aid letter provides for up to 2.12 billion yen ($13 million) for a maritime security capacity-building project.

Tarique reached Tokyo on Monday on a four-day official visit at the invitation of his Japanese counterpart. The two leaders yesterday held a summit meeting, followed by a joint press appearance and lunch.

At the start of the meeting, Takaichi said Japan strongly supported Bangladesh’s ability to make its own decisions and strengthen its resilience under Japan’s updated Free and Open Indo-Pacific (FOIP) vision. She said Japan wanted to further develop bilateral relations under the Strategic Partnership and contribute to regional peace and prosperity.

Tarique said the two leaders had held fruitful discussions on a broad range of bilateral, regional, and international issues.

“Reaffirming our long-standing friendship, we expressed our shared commitment to further strengthening our partnership through enhanced cooperation in energy, ICT, rail, and infrastructure, deep-sea ports, and foreign direct investment,” he said.

“Our ambition is clear: to turn this friendship between our two nations into a powerful engine of economic opportunity and shared prosperity.”

INVESTMENT, TRADE

Takaichi commended the efforts of Tarique’s administration to promote foreign direct investment and stressed the need to improve Bangladesh’s investment environment.

She expressed the expectation that Tarique’s leadership would help create conditions conducive to Japanese business activities and promote public-private cooperation. Tarique said Bangladesh would work towards that goal transparently.

The two leaders welcomed a memorandum of cooperation between Japan’s Ministry of Economy, Trade and Industry and Bangladesh’s Economic Relations Division on economic relations and improving the business environment. They also welcomed two separate MoCs covering agriculture and fisheries and livestock.

The joint statement said the two countries would promote resilient supply chains and explore further cooperation in digital transformation, the development of skilled ICT professionals, and secure digital connectivity.

Takaichi also said Japan looked forward to further discussions on Bangladesh’s request to accede to the Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership (RCEP) Agreement.

The two prime ministers welcomed the signing of the Bangladesh-Japan Economic Partnership Agreement (EPA) and reaffirmed their commitment to its early entry into force. They said the agreement would help expand trade and investment, promote industrial diversification, and support Bangladesh’s smooth and sustainable graduation from least developed country status.

ENERGY SECURITY

Japan will provide a 50-billion-yen loan, equivalent to around $317 million, under the “Emergency Support Loan for Enhancing Economic Resilience and Stable Energy Supply”.

The loan is the first yen-loan project under Japan’s Partnership on Wide Energy and Resources Resilience Asia (POWERR Asia) initiative.

Recognising volatility in global energy markets and rising energy prices, the two leaders stressed the importance of international cooperation to strengthen oil stockpiles and improve coordination between energy-producing and consuming countries.

Takaichi promised Japan’s continued support for Bangladesh’s energy infrastructure to help bridge the gap between energy supply and demand.

The two countries also agreed to deepen cooperation on climate change, energy efficiency, and renewable energy.

CONNECTIVITY, SECURITY

Under the upgraded BIG-B framework, the two countries will work to strengthen regional connectivity, improve resilience against natural disasters and geopolitical uncertainties, promote public-private partnerships, and step up cooperation for peace and stability.

They agreed to advance preparatory work for the early operationalisation of the third terminal of the Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport in Dhaka.

They also expressed their aspiration to move forward with the early construction of Dhaka metro rail lines and discuss future cooperation on the operation and management of Matarbari Deep Seaport.

According to the statement, the two leaders reaffirmed their commitment to work towards upholding international order, which is free, open, and based on the rule of law. To this end, Tarique noted the importance of Takaichi’s initiative of the “Free and Open Indo-Pacific (FOIP)”.

The statement further welcomed a pledge for a yen-loan programme for the second phase of the Upazila Governance and Development Project, aimed at strengthening the administrative and fiscal capacities of local governments.

The two leaders also reaffirmed their commitment to cooperation in education, skills development, public health, disaster management, and sustainable local governance.

Following the bilateral meeting, Tarique visited the onshore liquefied natural gas (LNG) terminal and power plant of JERA, a major Japanese energy company, in Futtsu city in Japan’s Chiba Prefecture. He also visited the Nittsu logistics hub.

Besides, Tarique will today call on the governor of the Japan Bank for International Cooperation (JBIC), visit UNIQLO’s Ariake office, and meet the president of the Japan External Trade Organization (JETRO).

He is also scheduled to meet representatives of Mitsui & Co, Sumitomo Corp and JERA, and attend the Bangladesh-Japan Economic Forum, where MoUs on education and human resource development are expected to be inked.

On the final day of his tour, the PM will visit a Toyota factory before departing for Dhaka.

title: India seeks bigger share of diesel exports on refining capacity boom
text:
India’s ​diesel exports are set to surge from 2027, giving the South Asian nation a bigger role ‌in global markets, as state-run companies boost refining capacity, industry officials said on Tuesday.

That will bolster India’s position as a swing supplier of refined products in an already tight global market buffeted by the US-Iran and Ukraine-Russia wars that have disrupted trade flows and boosted ​freight rates worldwide.

“We will be in a happy situation of not only refining for ourselves but for the ​world,” said Oil Minister Hardeep Singh Puri.

India is becoming a global refining hub as it prepares to boost refining capacity to 300 million tons per year by 2030, and increasing further to 400 ​million tpy later.

Amid unprecedented disruption to global refining from conflict and plant closures, with operating refineries running at historic utilisation rates ​to ease fuel shortages, India has emerged as the second-largest exporter of seaborne diesel this year, behind only the US, ship-tracking data from Kpler shows.

In 2027, Indian state refiners will together increase their diesel production capacity by 16.5 million tons as they boost capacity ​of existing refineries, officials said.

“We will be exporting diesel due to refinery expansion,” said A S Sahney, chairman of ​Indian Oil Corp, the country’s largest refiner, which aims to add about 18 million tons of annual capacity, to produce about 8 ‌million tpy of additional diesel.

Hindustan Petroleum Corp’s new 9-million-tpy refinery in the western state of Rajasthan will turn out 3 million tpy of diesel next year, once the refinery stabilises, said Chairman Vikas Kaushal.

Bharat Petroleum Corp plans to produce 1.5 million tpy extra diesel from next year, its chairman, Sanjay Khanna, said.

Oil India’s subsidiary Numaligarh refinery in the eastern region, which will ​be expanded to 9 million ​tpy in March next year, will add 3 million tpy of diesel production.

Some refiners, such as HPCL, buy refined products from private companies for sale by their retail outlets. The expansion will limit ​their purchases from other companies for local sales, and free up volumes for exports, ​officials said.

Additionally, India’s expanding refining capacity is designed to process a broad range of crude grades and flexible petrochemical feedstocks, letting companies capitalise on price arbitrage and produce higher-value products.

Private refiners Reliance and Nayara now export refined fuels while state companies mainly meet domestic demand.

US Secretary ​of State Marco Rubio described India as a refining “superpower” during a ​recent visit to Reliance’s massive refining complex in the port city of Jamnagar.

Puri said India aimed to become a global refining hub with fuel ​demand expected to rise to drive its economic expansion.

title: BB lets UCB offer up to 30% stake to an investor
text:
The Bangladesh Bank has relaxed the shareholding ceiling for United Commercial Bank PLC (UCB), allowing a single investor or family to hold up to 30 percent of the lender’s paid-up capital as the bank seeks fresh investment to strengthen its capital base.

In a circular issued on Tuesday, the central bank exempted UCB from Section 14 (Ka) of the Bank Company Act, 1991, which generally bars any individual, institution, company or family from holding more than 10 percent of a bank’s shares.

The exemption was granted under Section 121, which empowers Bangladesh Bank, in consultation with the government, to exempt a specific bank from provisions of the law through a gazette notification, either generally or for a specified period.

The move could widen the scope for large investors to enter the bank at a time when a substantial portion of its shares is blocked by a High Court order, according to a Bangladesh Bank official

The move could widen the scope for large investors to enter the bank at a time when a substantial portion of its shares is blocked by a High Court order, according to a Bangladesh Bank official.

The circular said the decision was taken “to strengthen the capital base” of the bank. It did not name any prospective investor or specify how much capital UCB intended to raise.

A BB official, requesting anonymity, said the shares blocked by the court order belonged to former land minister Saifuzzaman Chowdhury, also a former director of UCB.

The relaxation is intended to create an opportunity for the bank to raise capital, the official said.

Following the fall of the Awami League regime in the face of a mass uprising in August 2024, the BB dissolved UCB’s 18-member board, which was dominated by members of the family of Saifuzzaman.

His wife, Rukhmila Zaman, was the bank’s chairman, while his sister Roxana Zaman Chaudhury and relatives Anisuzzaman Chowdhury and Asifuzzaman Chowdhury also served on the board.

UCB has been seeking to strengthen its finances through regulatory-approved fundraising initiatives. The bank has received approval for a Tk 775 crore rights share issue and an Tk 800 crore subordinated bond issue.

It now wants to bring in financially capable strategic investors from Bangladesh and abroad, according to a statement from the bank. Shareholders approved the plan at its last annual general meeting.

UCB said the new investors could contribute not only capital but also advanced technology, international experience, stronger governance and a long-term commitment to the bank’s development.

In its statement, UCB described the central bank’s decision as a significant step towards removing a legal barrier to large share investments.

It said stronger capital, transparency and good governance were priorities as it sought to build a more reliable and customer-friendly bank.

title: Judgment in case against Hanif tomorrow
text:
The International Crimes Tribunal-2 will deliver its verdict tomorrow in a crimes against humanity case against Awami League Joint General Secretary Mahbubul Alam Hanif and three other party leaders over the killing of six people in Kushtia during the 2024 July uprising.

The three-member tribunal, headed by Justice Nozrul Islam Chowdhury, announced the date yesterday.

The other accused are Kushtia district AL president Sadruddin Khan, general secretary Azgar Ali, and Kushtia city AL general secretary Ataur Rahman Ata.

All four accused are absconding.

Earlier on October 5, the prosecution concluded its arguments and sought the maximum punishment for all four accused, while defence argued that their clients are innocent.

ICT-2 framed three charges against them on November 2, 2025.

The charges include endorsing provocative statements by AL General Secretary Obaidul Quader during the uprising, encouraging and facilitating the use of lethal weapons against protesters, directing party activists to suppress the protesters using force and open fire that led to the death of six protesters on August 5.

Investigation into the case began on March 25, and the report was submitted to the prosecution on September 11 last year.

The prosecution produced 19 witnesses, and submitted 36 series of documents and five material exhibits after it began opening statement on December 8, 2025.

title: Connecting grassroots businesses with credit and digital payments
text:
Around 50 percent of our agent banking customers belong to the cottage, small and medium enterprise segment. Nazmur Rahim Deputy Managing Director and Head of Alternate Banking Channels BRAC Bank

Agent outlets can connect small businesses with credit, digital payments and banking closer to home. In a conversation with The Daily Star, Nazmur Rahim, deputy managing director and head of alternate banking channels at BRAC Bank PLC, discusses lending referrals, support for women entrepreneurs and digital services.

The Daily Star (TDS): How is agent banking supporting local enterprise?

Nazmur Rahim (NR): Around 50 percent of our agent banking customers belong to the cottage, small and medium enterprise segment. Outlets offer account and term deposit opening, cash transactions, transfers, remittances, bill payments, loan disbursements and repayments.

Agents also promote Bangla QR for merchants’ digital payment collection, while customers can manage finances through the Astha app.

TDS: How do entrepreneurs apply for finance, particularly with limited records or collateral?

NR: Agents gather basic business information and refer eligible prospects to our SME Banking Team. They do not assess or approve credit. The team collects documents and evaluates viability, cash flow and repayment capacity. Documents may include a national identity card, trade licence, bank statements, tax returns and evidence of operations.

Assessment considers business experience, sales, expenses, liabilities, repayment history and financial health. Savings, remittances and transaction histories provide additional insights. We also offer dedicated loans linked to inward remittances credited to customers’ accounts, helping migrant workers’ families start or expand businesses.

Agricultural financing amounts and repayments reflect the activity, seasonal cash flows and repayment capacity, with eligible customers able to access applicable refinancing schemes.

TDS: How are you addressing barriers facing women entrepreneurs?

NR: Limited financial and digital literacy, mobility, inadequate records, collateral requirements and limited credit histories can restrict access.

TARA offers tailored SME financing, dedicated desks and documentation support. Our women-led TARA Agent Banking initiative extends access in underserved communities. Uddokta 101 and TARA Uddokta Mela help entrepreneurs develop management skills, showcase products, build networks and reach customers.

TDS: How can customers check charges and raise complaints?

NR: Each outlet displays the Schedule of Charges and a Customer Grievance poster with relevant contact details, alongside a complaint box. Complaints are recorded, investigated and addressed through a structured process to protect customers against misleading information, unauthorised charges and unfair treatment.

TDS: What changes would strengthen agent banking’s contribution?

NR: Priorities are interoperability, digital lending and a change in perceptions. Interoperability would enable transactions across institutions. Digital lending could help assess cash flows and transaction histories to provide timely finance to eligible entrepreneurs. Agent banking should be recognised as an extension of the bank’s service network, beyond cash deposits and withdrawals.

title: Good start, but delivery will make the difference
text:
Prime Minister Tarique Rahman’s visit to a G7 country within eight months of his taking power should in itself be seen as a positive and major step. Continuation of the traditional bilateral relations with the Asian giant is both desirable and beneficial for Bangladesh, especially in these challenging times.

While the joint statement of the two prime ministers highlights cooperation in infrastructure, energy, human resource, trade, and investment under a ‘strategic partnership’, it dampens hope for a visible elevation of bilateral relations with new terminology or for more robust budgetary support.

There are a few promises of loans, along with the commitments for three substantial projects: Dhaka airport’s third terminal, another MRT line in Dhaka, and the Matarbari port, which is part of an old initiative.

Envisioned as the centrepiece of Japan and Bangladesh’s cooperation, the Bay of Bengal Industrial Growth Belt, BIG-B for Shared Prosperity as it will now be called, is an ‘update’ of an older project that had begun in 2014.

In its new form, this initiative includes the Moheshkhali-Matarbari Integrated Infrastructure Development Initiative (MIDI) that will lead towards a bustling regional hub, a node of international maritime traffic connecting South Asia and countries further west with South East Asia and the far east.

Although mentioned as an exclusive project, the Japan-Bangladesh project, observers say that the BIG-B is meant to be a ‘logistical hub’ for the region, which may include other countries of the region too.

The country representative of Japan External Trade Organization Kazuiki Kataoka, who is also the president of the Japan Bangladesh Chamber of Commerce and Industries, also thought Matarbari was envisioned as a crucial regional node. “It can become a logistical hub between South Asia and East Asia, connecting not just the seven sisters [eastern provinces of India] but also Nepal and Bhutan.”

Taken together with the Free and Open Indo-Pacific, the joint statement suggests that Bangladesh, wedged between India and South East Asia on top of the Bay of Bengal, is key to Sanae Takaichi’s vision of a peaceful and prosperous Indo-Pacific.

The statement reads, “Prime Minister Rahman noted the importance of Prime Minister Takaichi’s initiative of the ‘Free and Open Indo-Pacific (FOIP)’ in ensuring peace, stability and prosperity for all.”

Other than a commitment of about 50 billion yen, worth almost $317 million for fuel purchase, the joint statement projects a private investment of about $6.33 billion over five years, creating two lakh jobs. While there is naturally no guarantee, Kataoka says with conviction that “it is very realistic”. There is also mention of a Japanese business delegation visiting Bangladesh soon, perhaps to further explore possibilities. A loan for a project to improve the investment environment as mentioned in the statement, without any specific figures also appears to be a rational decision.

The two prime ministers agreed on reform of the UN Security Council, including expansion of both permanent and non-permanent categories of membership. But there was nothing significant or forthcoming from Japan as regards the Rohingyas are concerned as joint statement expressed concern over the worsening crisis in Myanmar. The statement called for immediate cessation of violence, release of those detained, conducive environment for humanitarian assistance; “and dialogue between all parties and affected groups, including the Rohingyas”.

Although there had been reports of both countries working on the language to signify an elevation of relations from “strategic partnership” to “comprehensive strategic partnership”, it did not materialise. There was also an expectation, based on reports, that this visit would result in loans and financial support worth around $2 billion dollars. That does not seem to have materialised either. However, a full assessment of the complete package of assistance can only be done once the details of the deals signed during the visit become clearer.

title: Tourism fair opens tomorrow, focusing on AI, sustainability
text:
The three-day Bangladesh Travel and Tourism Fair (BTTF) 2026 will begin in Dhaka tomorrow, bringing together local and international tourism businesses to explore new opportunities in technology, investment and sustainable travel.

The 14th edition of the international fair, organised by the Tour Operators Association of Bangladesh (TOAB), will run until Saturday at the Bangladesh-China Friendship Conference Center under the theme “AI-Powered Tourism, Sustainable Destination”.

TOAB President Mohammad Hanif announced the details at a press conference at Crowne Plaza Dhaka Airport yesterday.

“The fair aims to accelerate tourism development in Bangladesh by integrating modern technology and AI into tourism services, promoting environmentally responsible travel and strengthening international connectivity,” he said.

Tourism organisations, airlines, hotels and other industry representatives from more than 20 countries are expected to participate. These include Nepal, India, Singapore, the Maldives, the Philippines, Turkey, the United Arab Emirates, China, Sri Lanka, Pakistan, Thailand, Brunei, Saudi Arabia, Malaysia and Azerbaijan.

The fair will feature more than 200 booths and stalls, over 220 exhibitors and more than 250 qualified buyers. Around 2,500 trade visitors and more than 60,000 members of the public are expected to attend.

More than 200 airlines, hotels and tour operators will showcase their offerings across four themed exhibition halls.

The event will give local and international businesses a platform to display their products, explore investment opportunities, build partnerships and establish business-to-business (B2B) connections.

Hanif said BTTF had grown into one of South Asia’s leading tourism platforms over its 13 previous editions.

He said the fair would help promote Bangladesh’s tourism potential internationally, connect local operators with global tourism brands and create new business opportunities.

Artificial intelligence is taking on a growing role in the global travel industry, and the organisers hope the fair will encourage businesses to adopt digital tools to improve services, market destinations and connect travellers with service providers.

The focus on sustainable tourism also aims to encourage environmentally responsible travel and support the long-term development of Bangladesh’s tourism resources.

The fair is expected to help local tour operators establish direct links with international buyers, travel agencies, airlines and hospitality businesses.

US-Bangla Airlines is the title sponsor, while Biman Bangladesh Airlines is the airline partner.

The event is being organised with support from the Ministry of Civil Aviation and Tourism, the Ministry of Cultural Affairs, the National Skills Development Authority, Bangladesh Parjatan Corporation, the Bangladesh Tourism Board, the Bangladesh Tourist Police and the Federation of Bangladesh Chambers of Commerce and Industry.

TOAB expects the fair to strengthen Bangladesh’s position in the global tourism market by showcasing the country’s diverse attractions and connecting local businesses with international partners. It also aims to encourage innovation and support a more competitive and sustainable tourism industry.

title: Bringing small business lending closer to rural customers
text:
Not having a bank account does not automatically make an applicant ineligible. A customer may still qualify, subject to the bank’s requirements. Mohammad Ridwanul Hoque Deputy Managing Director United Commercial Bank PLC

Agent banking has brought deposits and everyday transactions closer to rural customers, but expanding access to business finance remains a challenge. In a conversation with The Daily Star, Mohammad Ridwanul Hoque, deputy managing director of United Commercial Bank PLC, discusses the bank’s expansion plans, proposed digital lending and support for agents and women entrepreneurs.

The Daily Star (TDS): How is agent banking changing, and what are your expansion plans?

Mohammad Ridwanul Hoque (MRH): Agent banking is becoming a local financial hub where trusted agents support small businesses. Customers are moving from occasional cash transactions to regular banking close to home. More women and rural households are joining the formal system, while confidence in digital methods is spreading through word of mouth.

Our network has more than 630 outlets serving underserved and unbanked communities. Alongside banking services, we conduct financial literacy campaigns and support women entrepreneurs and small businesses in accessing the formal financial system.

We aim to reach 400 upazilas by the end of 2026 and achieve coverage of every upazila by 2027.

TDS: What can entrepreneurs do at an outlet, and who handles loan decisions?

MRH: Entrepreneurs can open accounts, deposit and withdraw money, receive remittances, transfer funds, check balances and open savings schemes. Outlets also offer utility bill payments and access to digital banking.

They serve as channels for loan applications, collecting documents and forwarding them to the respective branches for verification, approval and disbursement. Where required, agents assist with collecting loan instalments.

When an entrepreneur enquires about a loan, the outlet checks basic eligibility and the source of income before referring the applicant to a branch. Agents facilitate access and documentation; the bank retains responsibility for credit assessment and approval.

TDS: What financing is available, and what will change under your digital lending plans?

MRH: Our agent banking channel currently offers secured overdraft and agricultural loan facilities. From 2027, we plan to introduce digitally enabled SME, micro and cottage industry loans of up to Tk 10 lakh, targeting disbursement within one working day, subject to eligibility and credit assessment.

The plan involves simpler digital applications, faster assessment and streamlined approvals to improve access for small businesses and rural entrepreneurs.

Our collateral-free products supporting local enterprises include Suchana, offering Tk 1–6 lakh for new and micro entrepreneurs; Pragati, offering up to Tk 10 lakh for established businesses; and ARFL, offering up to Tk 10 lakh for agriculture and rural livelihoods.

Interest rates depend on the customer’s banking relationship and applicable loan terms. In some cases, rates may be below 7 percent, subject to the availability of Bangladesh Bank refinancing facilities.

TDS: How do you assess small businesses with limited formal records or collateral?

MRH: We examine whether applicants are local residents, whether they have an existing business and how they operate it. The main considerations are business activities, income and the ability to repay. Not having a bank account does not automatically make an applicant ineligible. A customer may still qualify, subject to the bank’s requirements.

TDS: How do you support women customers and entrepreneurs?

MRH: Around 47 percent of our agent banking customers are women, and we have more than 100 female agents. Their presence helps women access services comfortably and conveniently.

In remote rural areas, limited literacy and financial knowledge can make formal banking difficult to navigate. We seek to bring more women into the financial system through awareness and inclusion initiatives.

We also offer dedicated loan products for women entrepreneurs. Before financing, we arrange training in business management and financial matters to help them develop their enterprises and use borrowed funds more effectively.

TDS: How are you helping agents build viable businesses?

MRH: Outlets offer products and services from UCB subsidiaries, including Upay, UCB Asset Management, UCB Stock Brokerage and UCB Investment. These provide additional revenue opportunities and diversify agents’ income. We also introduce utility bill payment services to broaden their offerings.

Quarterly agent meetings, held in person and online, allow us to hear about operational challenges, business needs and earning opportunities. We use this feedback to make improvements before the next meeting. Supporting agents’ business growth helps sustain the network serving local communities.

TDS: What safeguards help customers understand charges and report problems?

MRH: Prescribed schedules of charges are displayed prominently at outlets and published on our website. We regularly train agents and their staff on charges, fees and service terms.

Each outlet displays contact numbers for the call centre, linked branch manager, operations manager, area manager and outlet in-charge. Customers can use these channels to clarify information, complain or report irregularities.

Head office also monitors customer transactions through telephone calls. Physical outreach and social media campaigns promote safe banking practices, fraud awareness and secure use of agent services, alongside compliance with Bangladesh Bank requirements.

TDS: What would help agent banking contribute more to local enterprise?

MRH: Lending has not expanded at the same pace as deposit mobilisation. Banks should introduce simpler, small-value loans through outlets. Agents can identify potential borrowers, facilitate documentation and monitor businesses and repayments, while banks retain credit assessment and approval responsibilities. Simplified procedures, digital assessment and faster disbursement could strengthen agent banking’s contribution to rural entrepreneurship and employment.

title: Looking beyond formal records to assess small businesses
text:
We believe financial empowerment begins with awareness and trust. Syed Mizanur Rahman Managing Director Meghna Bank PLC

Many small businesses operate mainly in cash, making formal financial records difficult to produce when seeking credit. In a conversation with The Daily Star, Syed Mizanur Rahman, managing director of Meghna Bank PLC, discusses how agent outlets can connect these enterprises with finance while building customer trust and supporting women’s participation.

The Daily Star (TDS): What services can entrepreneurs access, and where does an agent’s responsibility end?

Syed Mizanur Rahman (SMR): Outlets offer account opening, deposits, withdrawals, transfers, remittance disbursement, utility bill payments and government payments through A-Challan.

Agents identify prospective borrowers, collect applications and check initial documentation. The bank handles credit assessment, approval and disbursement. Agents also maintain contact with borrowers and facilitate repayments, combining local knowledge with bank oversight.

TDS: What should applicants prepare, and how long can financing take?

SMR: Applicants generally need a national identity card, photographs, trade licence, TIN where applicable, bank statements and relevant business documents. Credit teams review turnover, cash flow, inventory, liabilities and credit history.

A straightforward unsecured application may take approximately three to five working days, subject to complete documentation and satisfactory assessment. Secured financing may need additional time for valuation, legal checks and higher-level approvals. Loan amounts and repayment schedules reflect business needs, cash flow and repayment capacity.

TDS: Can businesses without formal bank statements be considered?

SMR: We consider proposals without formal bank statements where the business is legitimate and its existence, operations, cash flow and repayment capacity can be verified. Where applicable, mobile financial services transaction records provide supporting evidence.

The aim is to assess the actual business and its financial capacity while maintaining appropriate credit standards. Small business financing through our outlets also includes facilities under Bangladesh Bank-supported refinance schemes.

TDS: How are you addressing barriers facing women entrepreneurs?

SMR: Financial literacy programmes, community workshops and courtyard meetings help explain services, savings, financial security and responsible borrowing. Gaps remain in digital awareness and documentation. Building confidence in banking is an essential first step.

TDS: How do you protect customers and maintain trust?

SMR: Outlets display approved charges and service contacts. Customers receive information through SMS, branches, representatives and our round-the-clock toll-free contact centre. We explain biometric authentication, system-generated receipts and official SMS alerts, and warn against sharing PINs or passwords. Complaints can be reported through branches or the contact centre.

Reliable, financially capable agents and sustainable outlet businesses are essential. Misconduct or service failures can undermine wider banking confidence.

title: When does non-payment amount to cheating?
text:
This week, Your Advocate is Barrister Omar H. Khan, Advocate of the Supreme Court of Bangladesh. He heads the chambers of the renowned law firm ‘Legal Counsel,’ a full-service corporate practice in Bangladesh with extensive expertise in commercial, family, labour, land, constitutional and criminal law, as well as dispute resolution.

Query

Hello, I run a small business in Bangladesh. A few months ago, another company approached me to purchase goods on credit. Before supplying the goods, they assured me they could pay within the agreed time and provided various business documents and information to support their claims. We agreed that they would pay within 30 days of delivery. Relying on these assurances, I supplied the goods.

However, after receiving the goods, they failed to make payment despite repeated reminders. On top of that, I have now come across information suggesting that some of the statements and documents provided by them may not have been genuine. I suspect that they may have misled me from the beginning to obtain goods without any intention of paying.

I believe I have been cheated. Can I file a criminal case against them? What legal steps should I take, and where should I file a complaint?

Sefina Hossian

Response

Thank you for your query. When a buyer fails to pay, a business owner may wonder whether the matter is a civil dispute or a criminal offence. I understand that such situations can affect a business financially and leave business owners uncertain and concerned about what steps to take next.

The answer depends on the facts of each case. Not every failure to pay amounts to a criminal offence. For instance, if a buyer intended to pay but later became unable to do so because of financial difficulties or business losses, the matter will only be a civil dispute.

However, the situation is different when a person never intended to pay from the beginning and used false information, misleading representations, or fake documents to persuade another person to deliver goods. In such circumstances, the conduct may amount to the criminal offence of cheating.

Since cheating can be cognisable or non-cognisable depending on the section that applies, the first step varies. You may approach the police station having jurisdiction over the place where the alleged offence occurred. If the information you provide discloses a cognisable offence, section 154 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898 requires the police to record your complaint in writing (if it is made orally), read it back to you, obtain your signature and enter it in the prescribed register.

Section 415 of the Penal Code, 1860 defines cheating. It defines it as deceiving a person to dishonestly or fraudulently induce them to deliver property, or to consent that any person shall retain any property, or intentionally induce a person to do or omit to do something they would not otherwise have done. The conduct must cause, or be likely to cause, harm to the person’s body, mind, reputation or property. Under section 417, cheating is punishable with imprisonment for up to one year, a fine, or both. Where such deception results in the delivery of property, section 420 of the Penal Code 1860 may apply. A person convicted under section 420 may be punished with imprisonment for up to seven years and shall also be liable to a fine.

The key question, therefore, is whether the other party intended to deceive you from the very beginning. An honestly made promise that is later broken is not necessarily cheating. However, if the promise to pay was made only to convince you to supply goods when there was no intention of making payment, criminal liability can arise.

Since cheating can be cognisable or non-cognisable depending on the section that applies, the first step varies. You may approach the police station having jurisdiction over the place where the alleged offence occurred. If the information you provide discloses a cognisable offence, section 154 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898 requires the police to record your complaint in writing (if it is made orally), read it back to you, obtain your signature and enter it in the prescribed register.

After receiving the information, the police may investigate the matter. During the investigation, they may collect relevant evidence, examine witnesses and take other steps permitted by law. Once the investigation is completed, the police may submit a report before the court under section 173 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898. If the offence is non-cognisable or if the police do not take action despite the complaint disclosing a cognizable offence, you can approach the Magistrate. Under section 190 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898, a Magistrate may take cognisance of an offence upon receiving a complaint and proceed in accordance with the law.

It is also important to assess whether the amount justifies filing a case. A criminal case does not deal with recovery of money; rather, it is concerned with punishment for a crime. However, practically, it is sometimes seen that the perpetrator comes forward to pay the amount in order to settle the case. I would advise you to formally write to them and demand payment. If they do not pay, you may decide to serve a legal notice to them through a lawyer. Only after that should you consider filing a case.

title: Another round of LPG price hike likely
text:
LPG consumers can brace for another round of price hike as the Bangladesh Energy Regulatory Commission (BERC) kickstarts a process for revising the rates and charges tomorrow.

The commission will hold a public hearing, its first since introducing the monthly LPG price-fixing mechanism in April 2021.

The hearing, which comes after industry players asked for increasing their charges, is taking place at a time when consumers are paying more than the commission-fixed price for more than a month now, according to market participants and consumers interviewed by The Daily Star.

When the BERC rate was Tk 1,585, consumers paid Tk 2,500 for the 12kg cylinder amid a supply crunch. Then on October 4, the BERC raised the price to Tk 1,837, but the retail prices remained above Tk 2,200.

Subsequently, more than one crore LPG users continue to pay between Tk 2,200 and Tk 2,400 for a cylinder, The Daily Star learnt from discussions with at least 10 consumers, six retailers, two distributors and two importers.

Under the announced pricing structure, distributors are supposed to receive a 12kg cylinder from importers and bottlers at Tk 1,752. With a distribution charge of Tk 50 per cylinder, distributors are supposed to sell it to retailers at Tk 1,802.

The prescribed retail charge is Tk 45 per 12kg cylinder, which brings the final price to Tk 1,847.

In contrast, The Daily Star found that distributors are paying more than Tk 1,850 per cylinder and charging retailers substantially more than the prescribed distribution charge, resulting in retailers paying at least Tk 2,100 per cylinder.

Against the fixed retail charge of Tk 45 per cylinder, retailers are charging an additional Tk 200-300, pushing the price further above the official rate.

Amid this backdrop, four distributors from Dhaka, Cumilla, Chattogram and Gazipur on October 13 applied to the BERC for an increase in distribution and retail charges as fuel costs, licence fees and other expenses increased.

All four sought an increase in the distribution charge from Tk 50 to Tk 150 per cylinder and the retail charge from Tk 45 to Tk 70.

The applications, which had similar wording, said that importers and bottling companies were adjusting their prices more than once a month bypassing the rates fixed by BERC.

The distribution charge fixed by the BERC is insufficient to cover operating costs, said an LPG distributor in the Tejgaon area.

Companies did not deliver cylinders to distributors’ warehouses as per the BERC rules, forcing distributors to arrange their own transport.

“Some companies supply LPG cylinders at Tk 1,742 each, but we have to spend another Tk 40-50 per cylinder to bring them to our warehouses. We often have to wait two to three days to collect the cylinders.”

Loading, unloading, labour, transport and other operating expenses further increased costs, leaving distributors unable to operate profitably within the prescribed charges, he said.

According to the distributor, companies including Omera, BM, Total and Aygaz are supplying cylinders at the fixed rate, while the others are charging between Tk 2,000 and Tk 2,080.

The wider market is influenced by the rates charged by some major suppliers, he said, while acknowledging that distributors were charging high prices.

Distributors have stopped providing receipts for months, said a retailer in the Moghbazar area.

“If we ask for a receipt, they tell us they will stop our supply. We have to collect a cylinder from them at Tk 2,100 or Tk 2,200. How can we sell it at the official rate?” he said.

LPG importers have also sought an increase in storage and bottling charges to Tk 25 per kilogram from Tk 16.74, citing higher financing costs for working capital and project loans, as well as expenses related to compliance with safety standards.

In its proposal, the LPG Operators Association of Bangladesh said that operators, distributors and retailers respected the BERC-announced prices but cannot always comply because the rates are not adjusted quickly enough to reflect changing market conditions.

Several LPG companies have created an artificial shortage by stockpiling cylinders, said M Shamsul Alam, energy adviser to the Consumers Association of Bangladesh.

“Consumers are being held hostage in a market dominated by profiteering, while BERC remains inactive. Now another public hearing is being held to increase prices.”

He called for a judicial investigation to identify and punish those involved in stockpiling. The licences of companies found responsible should be cancelled, he said.

The private sector accounts for around 99 percent of the country’s LPG market.

title: UCB launches sticker payment card with Mastercard, GP
text:
United Commercial Bank PLC (UCB) yesterday launched a co-branded sticker payment card with Mastercard and Grameenphone Limited (GP), offering contactless payments alongside cashback, rewards and lifestyle benefits.

Brent T Christensen, the US ambassador to Bangladesh, inaugurated the card as the chief guest, according to a press release.

The prepaid sticker can be attached to a smartphone or another suitable item, allowing users to make payments by tapping it on a contactless-enabled point-of-sale (POS) terminal without carrying a conventional payment card.

The card combines UCB’s banking services, Mastercard’s payment technology and GP’s MyGP digital ecosystem. Sharif Zahir, chairman of UCB, said the collaboration reflected the bank’s commitment to innovative financial solutions that meet customers’ evolving needs.

Solaiman Alam, chief product officer of GP, said the card brought payments closer to the digital experiences customers already use through MyGP.

Gautam Aggarwal, division president for India and South Asia at Mastercard, said the initiative expanded consumer choice while supporting the growth of contactless payments in Bangladesh.

The card offers a first-year fee waiver. The annual fee will also be waived for cardholders spending Tk 1 lakh or more in a calendar year.

Benefits include 10 percent cashback on eligible OTT services and bundle purchases through MyGP, MyGP Shop transactions and learning courses, as well as 3 percent cashback on eligible GP Fi subscriptions.

Cardholders will also receive Tk 50 cashback on eligible roaming pack purchases, exclusive offers at GPStar and Mastercard partner merchants, and additional MyGP Points on qualifying transactions. All cashback offers are subject to applicable terms and conditions.
