Mohammad Mamdudur Rashid, chief executive officer of UCB; Sandun Hapugoda, country manager for Sri Lanka, the Maldives, Bangladesh, Bhutan and Nepal at Mastercard; and Zakia Sultana, country manager for Bangladesh at Mastercard, attended the event.

title: Gas crisis slows machinery imports
text:
Businesses ordered fewer machines from abroad and paid for less equipment already shipped in the July-September quarter than a year earlier, as a severe LNG and power crisis brought production lines in key industrial areas across the country to a standstill.

In the first quarter of the fiscal year 2026-27, fresh letters of credit (LCs) openings for capital machinery fell by 3.58 percent to $515 million from $534 million a year earlier, according to Bangladesh Bank data.

Similarly, LC settlements for manufacturing equipment declined by 2.56 percent to $433 million from $444 million a year ago.

The fall contrasted with a rebound in LC openings for capital machinery in the July-December period last year. In the first six months of FY2025-26, new LC openings rose 24 percent to more than $1 billion.

Besides, this slowdown came at a time when LC openings and settlements for overall import activities were resurging.

LC openings for capital machinery show how willing businesses are to invest and expand, while settlements show how much of that investment has become actual imports and payments. Rises in both can signal stronger business confidence, while falls may point to cautious investment.

In July, a technical fault at a floating liquefied natural gas (LNG) terminal in Cox’s Bazar set off a worsening gas crisis and, in turn, a power crisis that lasted until mid-September.

The energy shortage eased in late September, but the continuing conflict in the Middle East threatens the country’s overall energy security and its exports to Western markets.

Taskeen Ahmed, president of the Dhaka Chamber of Commerce and Industry (DCCI), said businesses are holding back on new machinery purchases because expansion has become increasingly risky amid economic uncertainty at home and abroad.

He said the conflict in the Middle East and disruption to global shipping have pushed up fuel and freight costs, while weaker demand in Europe, Bangladesh’s largest export market, has left factories with fewer orders.

“With interest rates high and access to finance and reliable utilities still uncertain, entrepreneurs are reluctant to make large investments,” said Taskeen.

“Businesses are choosing to preserve cash flow rather than take on costly debt to expand,” he added.

The DCCI president urged the government to draw up a clear industrial roadmap that ensures reliable utility supplies and affordable financing.

He said that such measures would help promote import substitution, conserve foreign exchange and safeguard domestic manufacturing.

UNEVEN SLOWDOWN ACROSS INDUSTRIES

In the first quarter of FY27, the LC for capital machinery slowdown was not uniform. Some sectors recorded increases in fresh LC openings even as settlements declined.

Fresh LC openings for textile machinery more than doubled, rising 120 percent to $33 million in the July-September quarter from $15 million a year earlier. Settlements, however, fell 29 percent to $24 million from $33 million, according to Bangladesh Bank data.

In the garment industry, fresh LC openings rose 11.59 percent to $73 million, while settlements fell 8.90 percent to $86 million.

Drugmakers also committed to more machinery imports, with fresh LC openings up 31.25 percent at $27 million. However, settlements in the pharmaceutical sector dropped 10.88 percent to $18 million.

The picture was different in the “other industry” category, where fresh LC openings fell by 11.58 percent to $381 million. Settlements in the segment rose 2.96 percent to $303 million.

The mixed results suggest demand for imported machinery varied across industries, with gains in some sectors failing to offset losses in others.

‘A REFLECTION OF WEAKENING INVESTOR CONFIDENCE’

M Masrur Reaz, chairman of Policy Exchange Bangladesh, a local think tank, said the year-on-year fall in both LC openings and settlements for capital machinery in the first quarter of the current fiscal year reflects a broader economic slowdown and weaker investor confidence.

The economist said prolonged energy shortages, sluggish domestic demand amid high inflation and persistent law and order concerns all played a part.

Investors expected law and order to improve largely after the new government took office in February, he said, but those hopes have yet to be fully realised. As a result, many businesses have put plans for new factories and capacity expansion on hold, cutting capital machinery imports.

On the overall rise in LC openings and settlements, Masrur said higher petroleum import costs, driven by global price increases, were probably a major factor.

Imports of intermediate goods and raw materials had also risen somewhat, he added.

Md Fazlul Hoque, administrator of the Federation of Bangladesh Chambers of Commerce and Industry (FBCCI), said the energy crisis in the past few months created confusion among investors. This led to a fall in capital machinery imports.

Fazlul, also a former president of the Bangladesh Knitwear Manufacturers and Exporters Association (BKMEA), said factories need energy to run imported machinery, and when the energy crisis prevails, it creates a burden.

Now, LC openings for capital machinery would improve as the energy crunch eased, he said. “But there is little prospect of the industrial sector gaining significant momentum soon.”

title: From Law to Practice: Building Workplaces Free from Sexual Harassment
text:
Bangladesh has taken important steps towards addressing sexual harassment at work. The Labour Act has been strengthened, sexual harassment is now addressed in legislation, and Bangladesh has ratified ILO Convention No.190 (C190) on Violence and Harassment. With the Labour Rules now under review, the opportunity before us is to turn these commitments into a system that works in practice.

The question is no longer whether sexual harassment should be addressed. It is how Bangladesh can create a framework that people in the world of work can trust, organisations can operate, and regulators can enforce.

This is first a matter of rights. No one should have to trade dignity, safety or equality for work. When harassment occurs, and there is no effective response, inaction can allow a rights violation to continue. C190 recognises the right to a world of work free from violence and harassment and calls for prevention, protection, enforcement, remedies and effective investigation.

It is worth noting that poorly handled complaints can turn workplace problems into prolonged disputes, loss of trust, reputational damage and organisational disruption. For organisations, prevention and effective response are therefore not simply compliance costs; they are part of good governance, risk management and institutional performance.

For government, this is fundamentally about giving practical effect to Bangladesh’s international and national commitments. Bangladesh ratified C190 in November 2025, and the Convention enters into force for Bangladesh on 20 November 2026. C190 calls for an inclusive, integrated and gender-responsive approach to preventing and addressing violence and harassment, including prevention, enforcement, remedies, investigation, training and social dialogue.

The current reform of the Labour Rules therefore provides an important opportunity to ensure that Bangladesh’s domestic framework can give practical effect to these commitments. The next stage should not simply be to add more requirements to the Rules. It should be to ensure that the Labour Act and the Rules operate as one coherent system.

First, the relationship between Sections 23, 24, 332 and 332A needs to be clarified. Sections 23 and 24 provide the misconduct and disciplinary framework, while Sections 332 and 332A address prevention of violence and harassment and establish the complaints committee. The legal framework should clearly explain how an investigation into sexual harassment connects with the disciplinary process when misconduct is established, who initiates disciplinary proceedings, who makes the final decision, and what safeguards apply to all parties.

The objective is not to prejudge a complaint or to make the complaints committee a substitute for disciplinary authority. It is to establish a clear pathway from complaint, investigation and findings to disciplinary decision-making and remedy. If the Act does not provide a sufficient legal basis for that pathway, the relevant provisions of the Act may need amendment; the Rules alone cannot create substantive legal duties or consequences that the Act does not support.

Second, Section 332 needs to be operationalised through the Rules. The amended provision places responsibilities on employers and authorities to prevent violence and harassment and to establish preventive measures. The Rules should translate these broad duties into practical requirements covering workplace policies, risk assessment, awareness and training, reporting, protection and prevention.

Third, Section 332A needs clear procedural and institutional rules. The Act establishes a five-member complaints committee, with a majority of women, a woman chair and two members from organisations working on gender and sexual violence. The committee is expressly responsible for investigating complaints. The Rules should clarify its mandate, competence, independence, timelines, confidentiality, reporting lines and safeguards against interference. They should also clarify how its investigation and findings connect with the formal disciplinary process and the authority responsible for the final decision.

Fourth, the Rules should establish a clear end-to-end process: how a concern is received; how immediate safety is assessed; when a matter proceeds to formal investigation; who investigates; how conflicts of interest are managed; how evidence is assessed; who initiates any disciplinary or other action; who makes the final decision; how the parties are informed; and what remedies and avenues for review are available.

The framework should also recognise that sexual harassment is not always worker-to-worker conduct. It may involve supervisors, managers, contractors, clients, service providers or others connected with the workplace. The system should therefore ensure that a complaint does not fall outside the protection of the framework simply because the complainant or respondent does not fit a narrow statutory category.

Fifth, there must be effective protection against retaliation and victimisation, alongside confidentiality and safe reporting. Protection should extend, where appropriate, to complainants, witnesses, committee members and others participating in a process. At the same time, confidentiality must be balanced with the requirements of a fair investigation and the respondent’s right to know and respond to the relevant allegations.

Finally, the Rules need to be workable across different sectors and organisational sizes. A multinational, a large factory, an NGO and a smaller enterprise may require different operational arrangements, but all should be capable of meeting the same core principles of prevention, safe reporting, fair investigation, accountability and remedy.

This distinction between law and Rules matters. The Act should establish substantive rights, duties, misconduct and protections. The Rules should provide the practical machinery through which those rights and duties can be exercised and enforced. Rules can operationalise the law; they cannot substitute for substantive gaps in the Act.

Why does this matter?

For people in the world of work, a credible system means that speaking up does not have to mean risking their livelihood, dignity, safety or professional standing.

For organisations, it provides clarity, consistency and a defensible process for managing workplace risk. It also helps address problems before they become entrenched disputes, turnover, absenteeism or wider disruption.

For workers’ organisations and trade unions, it provides greater confidence that workers can raise concerns and exercise their rights without retaliation. For employers’ organisations and industry associations, a clear and workable framework provides a more level playing field and reduces uncertainty about how cases should be handled.

Poorly handled complaints can turn workplace problems into prolonged disputes, loss of trust, reputational damage and organisational disruption. For organisations, prevention and effective response are therefore not simply compliance costs; they are part of good governance, risk management and institutional performance.

For government, it demonstrates that Bangladesh’s international commitments are being translated into domestic practice rather than remaining commitments on paper. For the development sector, credible PSEAH and safeguarding systems are increasingly important to maintaining donor and partner confidence. For business, the issue extends beyond the workplace itself. Responsible-business expectations increasingly reach into supply chains. Buyers want evidence that labour rights, worker voice, grievance mechanisms, investigation and remedy are functioning in practice, not simply that a policy exists.

There is also a wider market-access dimension. The European Union is Bangladesh’s largest trading partner, and textiles account for the overwhelming majority of EU imports from Bangladesh. Bangladesh currently benefits from the EU’s Everything but Arms arrangement. Following LDC graduation, Bangladesh will continue to receive EBA preferences for at least three years and has the possibility of seeking GSP+, subject to its conditions. The EU’s revised GSP framework, applying from 1 January 2027, places continued emphasis on human rights, labour rights, sustainable development and good governance.

The supply-chain implications are also becoming more significant. From 14 December 2027, the EU Forced Labour Regulation will prohibit products made with forced labour from being placed on, made available on, or exported from the EU market. Sexual harassment should not be equated with forced labour. However, violence, intimidation, abuse of vulnerability and other coercive practices can be relevant to wider labour-rights and forced-labour risks. For businesses and supply chains, credible worker voice, grievance, investigation and remedy mechanisms are therefore increasingly part of responsible risk management.

This matters for Bangladesh’s export-oriented economy. Market access is no longer determined only by price, quality and delivery. Increasingly, buyers, regulators and consumers want confidence that labour rights and responsible-business commitments are implemented in practice.

The case is therefore not simply about compliance. It is about good governance and good business. A credible system can protect rights, reduce avoidable productivity losses, strengthen trust across the workplace, support responsible supply chains, meet Bangladesh’s international commitments, strengthen donor confidence and contribute to continued access to important markets. These are not competing interests. People in the world of work need protection and remedy. Organisations need clarity and workable processes. Government needs an enforceable framework. Trade unions need confidence in workers’ rights. Development partners need credible safeguarding systems. Industry needs a level playing field. Buyers need confidence in responsible supply chains.

They all point towards the same objective: a workplace system that works in practice.

The writer is a Barrister-at-Law and Principal of Jenefa Jabbar Consultancy.

title: Govt distances itself from IGP’s comments
text:
Home Minister Salahuddin Ahmed has said Inspector General of Police (IGP) Ali Hossain Fakir’s remarks do not reflect the government’s position.

“The government is firmly opposed to extrajudicial killings, enforced disappearances and custodial deaths,” he told The Daily Star yesterday.

“The government is firmly opposed to extrajudicial killings, enforced disappearances and custodial deaths.” Home Minister Salahuddin Ahmed

Noting that the July uprising, which led to the fall of the Awami League regime, was aimed at establishing the rule of law, the minister said upholding that principle remained one of the government’s key commitments to the people.

Speaking at a programme on Monday, IGP Fakir said, “Wherever crossfire is necessary, if the government allows it, we will do that.”

The Police Headquarters later issued a clarification, saying the IGP had not intended to endorse extrajudicial killings. It said he had used the term “crossfire” in its “literal sense” while stressing firm action against drug traffickers, terrorists, extortionists and other criminals threatening public safety.

BNP acting Secretary General Ruhul Kabir Rizvi said the IGP’s remarks were “embarrassing” for the government and expressed concern that such comments were made at a time when the BNP, which had long opposed enforced disappearances and extrajudicial killings, was in power.

Rizvi, who also serves as the prime minister’s political adviser, made the comments while inaugurating a free medical camp outside the BNP’s central office in Nayapaltan, marking the 48th founding anniversary of Jubo Dal.

Asked why no action had been taken against the IGP, Prime Minister’s Adviser on Information and Cultural Affairs Zahed Ur Rahman said Tarique Rahman, who is currently abroad, would decide the matter upon his return from Japan.

“The prime minister is not in the country. He will consider the matter himself. The government’s final position on this issue will be determined by the prime minister, perhaps after he completes his visit,” Zahed told reporters at the weekly press briefing at the Secretariat.

Meanwhile, the Bangladesh Police Service Association (BPSA) has defended the IGP, saying an unfortunate choice of words can occur in public remarks but should not be construed as support for extrajudicial killings.

In a statement, the BPSA said Bangladesh Police conducts its activities in accordance with the constitution and the law, and that performing duties with firmness, impartiality and professionalism, without exceeding legal limits, is essential for maintaining public confidence.

It added that the IGP’s remarks could be seen as a call for the strict and uncompromising enforcement of existing laws, the proper exercise of police authority and a stronger role in combating crime and protecting public safety.

Speaking on the association’s defence, BPSA General Secretary Shamima Pervin, superintendent of police, Dhaka, said a poor choice of words can occur while speaking and should not be interpreted as support for extrajudicial killings.

“Our position is that police must act within the law to protect people’s lives and property,” she said. “Neither our statement nor the association endorses any action outside the law.”

title: Jamuna Bank opens 116th sub-branch in Savar
text:
Jamuna Bank PLC has opened a new sub-branch at Nama Bazar in Savar, Dhaka aimed at providing modern, innovative banking services and secure investment opportunities.

This is the bank’s 116th sub-branch, according to a press release.

Md Belal Hossain, chairman of the bank, inaugurated the sub-branch as the chief guest.

The event was presided over by Mirza Elias Uddin Ahmed, managing director and CEO of the bank.

The new sub-branch is expected to make banking services more accessible, convenient and efficient for the local community.

Local businesspeople, dignitaries, senior officials from the bank’s head office and a large number of customers, were also present at the inauguration ceremony.

title: A surge in gun violence rattles Khulna
text:
At least three people were shot and injured in separate incidents in Khulna yesterday, amid growing concerns over gun violence in the district.

Meanwhile, a total of 71 people were killed across the district in nearly 10 months, with 23 of those cases involving shootings.

Ahidul Islam Badal, 35, a former Jubo Dal leader, was shot at Chakrakhali Bazar in Batiaghata upazila around 5:45pm yesterday. The attackers arrived on a motorcycle, opened fire and fled. Locals took him to Khulna Medical College Hospital (KMCH).

According to district police, Badal is a former president of Ward 9 Jubo Dal in Jalma union and faces eight cases, including a murder case.

Khulna Superintendent of Police Sarker Omar Faroque said the motive behind the attack was not immediately known.

In another incident, Salman, 25, a private company employee, was shot and his laptop bag snatched by five assailants on two motorcycles in Nirala Residential Area around 11:15am, police said.

His colleagues took him to KMCH, where he was declared out of danger.

Earlier, around 12:30am, Sohail Sheikh, 34, another former Jubo Dal leader, was shot in front of a government primary school in Boro Karia village of Batiaghata. He was sent to Dhaka for advanced treatment.

The shootings reflect a wider pattern of armed violence in Khulna, where firearms are used in killings, robberies, intimidation and criminal rivalries.

Police records show that 71 people were killed between January and October 26. A total of 69 cases have been filed over the 71 murders.

Of the cases, 34 were recorded by eight police stations under the Khulna Metropolitan Police (KMP) and 35 by nine district police stations.

Of the 34 murder cases recorded by KMP, 14 involved shootings. District police recorded nine firearm-related killings among 35 murder cases.

Police and local sources link much of the violence to disputes over drugs, extortion and territorial control, as well as personal enmity and other criminal conflicts.

On October 24, Ramim Biswas, 32, a Jubo Dal leader in Terokhada upazila, and grocery shop owner Dhananjay Kundu, 45, were shot in separate incidents.

Two days earlier, Tawhidul Islam was shot dead in Purba Baniakhhamar, while housewife Khushi Akter was killed near her home in Jinnahpara. Police suspect drug-related disputes in both cases and are investigating possible links.

Khulna civil society member L Kudrat-e-Khuda blamed policing shortcomings for the deteriorating law and order situation, saying rival groups continued to fight for control of the drug trade despite political changes.

KMP Detective Branch Deputy Commissioner Mohammad Ahaduzzaman Mia said drug-related disputes were behind most killings.

Some criminals resumed their activities after securing bail, while public reluctance to speak against them hampered efforts to curb violence, he added.

Meanwhile, amid the violence, Khulna police were instructed not to move alone at night in a letter issued on October 23.

SP Faroque said the measure was intended to ensure police personnel’s safety, not to signal a breakdown in law and order.

KMP Commissioner Md Sazzadur Rahman said the shootings had various motives, including personal disputes, robbery, drugs, extortion and criminal rivalries.

title: ‘Police can’t carry out crossfire even if govt orders it’
text:
The government cannot order police to carry out “crossfire”, and even if it does, officers cannot execute such an order because public servants are not obliged to obey “unlawful instructions”, said Prime Minister’s Adviser on Information and Cultural Affairs Zahed Ur Rahman yesterday.

He was holding weekly press briefing at the Secretariat.

Referring to IGP Ali Hossain Fakir’s recent remarks that police would resort to crossfire if necessary and if permitted, Zahed said the police chief had subsequently acknowledged the problem with his statement and stepped back from that position.

Zahed further said the PM is currently visiting Japan and will consider the government’s final position after returning to Bangladesh.

He questioned whether the IGP should be treated too harshly after retracting his position. “When someone does not stick to their stance, are we being a bit too unkind to him?” he said.

Asked whether an explanation was enough to absolve someone of responsibility for such remarks, Zahed replied that he believed it could be, as the IGP had not maintained his original position.

title: Service quality must keep pace with agent banking expansion
text:
Expansion must be supported by capable agents, adequate liquidity and consistent service quality. Mati Ul Hasan Managing Director Mercantile Bank PLC

As small businesses increasingly use agent outlets to manage their finances, service quality and customer protection become more important. In a conversation with The Daily Star, Mati Ul Hasan, managing director of Mercantile Bank PLC, discusses agent selection, barriers facing women and the practical requirements for supporting local enterprise.

The Daily Star (TDS): How are entrepreneurs using agent banking, and what support can outlets provide?

Mati Ul Hasan (MUH): Small entrepreneurs increasingly use agent banking to manage business transactions, facilitate salary disbursements and build financial records, alongside savings and remittances.

Our outlets offer account opening, deposits, withdrawals, fund transfers and inward remittance disbursement. Agents assist with documentation and authorised transactions. Financing enquiries requiring detailed assessment go to designated lending teams, while services beyond an outlet’s authority are referred to branches.

TDS: How do you attract and select agents while maintaining standards?

MUH: We require no security deposit, reducing agents’ initial financial burden, and offer competitive commissions. Selection considers credibility, financial capability, business experience, local reputation and the ability to serve customers responsibly. Monitoring, regulatory compliance and customer service standards are central to maintaining trust. Expansion must be supported by capable agents, adequate liquidity and consistent service quality.

TDS: What barriers do women face, and how are you responding?

MUH: Women may lack collateral, trade licences for home-based businesses and financial or digital literacy. Restricted mobility, concerns about hidden costs and dependence on male intermediaries also create barriers.

We encourage suitable sanitation facilities, female tellers and staff, and local outreach. Women own 12 percent of our agencies; we aim to raise this to 50 percent. Broader social and economic barriers require collaboration beyond banks.

TDS: How are customers informed about charges and protected against misconduct?

MUH: Outlets display the Citizen’s Charter and Schedule of Charges. Transaction receipts, relevant SMS alerts and biometric authentication for applicable services provide safeguards. Agents cannot collect unauthorised fees.

Customers can complain through our call centre, responsible branch or controlling office, and escalate complaints to Bangladesh Bank’s Customer Interest Protection Center.

TDS: What would help agent banking contribute more to local enterprise?

MUH: Agents need training, reliable connectivity and sufficient cash. Incentives should recognise service quality and customers’ needs. Financial literacy can help entrepreneurs maintain records and explore financing.

A grocery shop owner depositing sales proceeds through an outlet can build transaction records. However, transaction history alone may not establish profitability or financing eligibility; additional business information may still be needed.

title: JCD leader killing: Natore-4 MP’s son on 3-day remand
text:
Nooruzzaman, son of Natore-4 BNP lawmaker Abdul Aziz, has been placed on a three-day remand in a case filed over the killing of Jatiyatabadi Chhatra Dal (JCD) leader Shakil Islam.

District Senior Judicial Magistrate’s Court passed the order yesterday afternoon after police sought 10 days to interrogate Nooruzzaman, showing him arrested in the case.

Nooruzzaman was taken into police custody late Monday and first brought to Gurudaspur Police Station before being transferred to the Detective Branch (DB) office in Natore town. DB officials questioned him until yesterday afternoon before producing him before the court.

Asked why the lawmaker’s son was being interrogated, Natore DB Officer-in-Charge Nazrul Islam said Nooruzzaman’s name had surfaced during the investigation into the murder. He declined to provide further details, citing the interests of the investigation.

Shakil Islam, 30, joint general secretary of JCD’s Gurudaspur upazila unit, died at a hospital on Monday night, 12 days after he was attacked by a group of assailants.

Police said a group of helmeted attackers hacked Shakil with sharp weapons in the Chachkoir Bazarpara area on October 14.

He was initially taken to Gurudaspur Upazila Health Complex and later shifted to Rajshahi Medical College Hospital before being referred to Dhaka for advanced treatment.

On October 19, the victim’s father filed a case with Gurudaspur Police Station against eight to 10 unidentified people.

Locals alleged that Aziz’s two sons, Nooruzzaman, also known as Mintu, and his younger brother, Mahamuduzzaman, had long been engaged in a rivalry for political influence in the area and that the killing might have been linked to the dispute.

Denying the allegation, Aziz said the disagreement between his sons was a “family matter” and had no connection to Shakil’s death.

“The loss of Shakil feels like losing my own child. I want those responsible for his killing punished, even if it is my own son,” Aziz said, adding that he had fully cooperated with police when they came to take Nooruzzaman into custody.

“I will not seek bail for my son unless his innocence is proven,” he added, calling for a thorough investigation to identify those responsible.

Shakil’s death triggered protests among local BNP and JCD activists in Gurudaspur. Chhatra Dal leaders and activists brought out a procession demanding exemplary punishment for those involved in the attack.

Md Kamruzzaman Bepari, general secretary of the Natore district unit of JCD, told The Daily Star that the perpetrators must face exemplary punishment.

“Shakil was a dedicated Chhatra Dal leader. He was always vocal against drugs and irregularities. He was brutally killed by criminals. We want a proper investigation to identify the real culprits and bring them to justice,” he said.

title: Bank Asia clients to get home loan for JCX flat purchases
text:
Bank Asia PLC has signed a memorandum of understanding (MoU) with Dhaka-based real estate developer JCX Developments Limited to offer convenient and accessible home loan facilities to buyers of apartments across the developer’s projects.

Under the agreement, the two organisations will also undertake joint marketing initiatives, customer engagement programmes and promotional activities to raise awareness of and improve access to home financing.

Md Zahed Chowdhury, executive vice-president and head of the assets section of the bank’s retail banking division, and M Tareq Hosen Mozumder, chief executive officer of JCX Developments, signed the agreement at the developer’s corporate office in Bashundhara, Dhaka, recently, according to a press release. The partnership aims to make purchasing an apartment in JCX projects more affordable and accessible, helping buyers move closer to owning a home.

The collaboration is also expected to strengthen ties between the two organisations and contribute to the development of Bangladesh’s housing and financial services sectors.

title: Two violence cases: Expelled leader of Swechchhasebak Dal sent to jail
text:
Wakil Hossain Boga, also known as Bihari Boga, an alleged criminal and expelled leader of Chattogram city’s Swechchhasebak Dal, and 12 of his followers were sent to jail yesterday after they surrendered before a court in two cases filed with Khulshi Police Station.

AGM Monirul Hasan Sarkar, chief metropolitan magistrate, rejected their bail petitions, said Assistant Public Prosecutor Raihanul Wazed Chowdhury.

Boga and his followers surrendered seeking bail in the cases, which involve allegations of attacking police, vandalism and obstructing police from performing their duties, among other charges, he said.

Boga was brought to court under tight security.

He had earlier surrendered before another court on October 18 and was sent to jail.

Boga was expelled from the party on June 8, 2025, following a shooting incident over the occupation of government land. He faces more than 23 cases involving allegations of extortion, drug-related offences, assault, attacks on police, vandalism and explosives-related offences.

title: HSC results deferred to Oct 31
text:
The results of this year’s HSC and equivalent examinations will be published on October 31, two days later than previously announced. The results were initially scheduled for October 29.

The Bangladesh Inter-Education Board Coordination Committee announced the revised date in a notice issued yesterday.

The results will be announced at 11:00am at the International Mother Language Institute in Dhaka and made available simultaneously at educational institutions and online.

The notice was signed by committee president Prof Syed Akhtaruzzaman, also chairman of the Dhaka Education Board.

Students can check their results through their respective education boards’ websites or from their institutions. Results will also be available via SMS.

Applications for re-scrutiny will be accepted online from November 1 to 7, with details available on the education boards’ websites.

A total of 12,70,583 candidates registered for this year’s HSC and equivalent examinations under 11 education boards.

title: Local enterprise needs more than access to credit
text:
More flexible repayment arrangements, alongside training in bookkeeping and financial management, can also help small businesses grow sustainably. Sohail R K Hussain Managing Director Bank Asia PLC

Access to a nearby banking outlet can help small businesses save, transact and seek finance, but documentation and repayment remain challenges. Sohail R K Hussain, managing director of Bank Asia PLC, discusses how agent banking can support local enterprise, the bank’s lending process and the gaps that remain, in a conversation with The Daily Star.

The Daily Star (TDS): How is agent banking moving beyond everyday transactions to support local enterprise?

Sohail R K Hussain (SRKH): Bank Asia initially focused on bringing unbanked and marginalised people into formal banking. Through more than 5,000 agent outlets, we open around 40,000 accounts monthly, over 80 percent of them for first-time banking customers.

We now combine financial literacy with access to finance to help farmers, small traders and women entrepreneurs invest in productive activities. Over the past five years, we have extended Tk 1,300 crore in financial support to approximately 100,000 customers and supported more than 8,000 women entrepreneurs in starting and growing their businesses.

TDS: What services can entrepreneurs access, and where does an agent’s responsibility end?

SRKH: Entrepreneurs can access deposits, withdrawals, remittances, fund transfers, account-opening support and bill payments. Agents also assist with SME and agricultural loan applications, disbursements and repayments within their authorised scope.

Credit appraisal, due diligence and loan approval remain with the bank’s designated lending teams. Our Online Credit Approval System (OCAS) helps speed up processing. The model combines local access with the bank’s formal risk management framework.

TDS: What does applying for business finance involve, and how long does it take?

SRKH: Entrepreneurs can approach an outlet for guidance on suitable products and application procedures. They usually need their national identity card, photograph, trade licence, business bank statements and income records.

The lending team verifies the business, assesses repayment capacity and makes the credit decision. Disbursement generally takes three to five working days after all required documents are submitted, subject to verification and fulfilment of the bank’s requirements. Agents facilitate the application; assessment and approval remain with the bank.

TDS: How do you assess businesses with limited formal accounts or collateral?

SRKH: We consider actual business performance, income patterns and overall creditworthiness rather than relying solely on formal accounts or collateral. Savings patterns, remittance receipts and transaction histories offer insights into financial behaviour and repayment capacity.

Field verification, Credit Information Bureau reports, guarantor assessments and market reputation also inform appraisal. Local agents provide insights into customers and their businesses. Lending decisions must comply with our credit policies and Bangladesh Bank guidelines, balancing wider access with prudent risk management.

TDS: What financing is available for businesses with seasonal or uneven cash flows?

SRKH: We offer cottage, micro, small and medium enterprise (CMSME) and agricultural financing, including working capital, term loans and seasonal finance. Loan amounts range from Tk 30,000 to Tk 50 lakh, depending on the product and borrower’s eligibility.

Repayment schedules and financing costs depend on the business, its cash-flow patterns and the approved facility. Seasonal financing helps enterprises build inventory and meet peak demand, with repayment terms structured around their financial capacity.

TDS: What barriers do women entrepreneurs face, and how are you addressing them?

SRKH: Limited collateral, inadequate documentation, low financial literacy, mobility constraints and social barriers can restrict women’s access to finance. We respond through financial literacy and capacity-building programmes, alongside SME and agricultural financing.

Women represent 64 percent of our agent banking customers. Over the past four years, more than 100 physical capacity-building events have reached around 6,000 women entrepreneurs, alongside virtual programmes. Our network includes 527 women agents and around 1,700 women micro-merchants.

We have disbursed approximately Tk 150 crore to women entrepreneurs. Gaps nevertheless remain in collateral, formal documentation and business development support, requiring targeted finance, partnerships and training.

TDS: How do customers learn about charges and terms, and raise complaints?

SRKH: We communicate charges, financing terms and application updates through outlets, SMS alerts, customer support and written receipts, using simple Bengali where appropriate. Agents are trained to explain terms clearly.

More than 90 percent of loan applications are initiated through OCAS, allowing credit officers to track them in real time. Customers can complain through our hotline, branches or agent outlets. Complaints are recorded in our Complaint Management System and monitored by designated officers for timely resolution.

TDS: What would strengthen agent banking’s contribution to enterprise development?

SRKH: More varied financing products, simpler documentation, stronger digital and financial literacy, and better access to markets and business support are needed. More flexible repayment arrangements, alongside training in bookkeeping and financial management, can also help small businesses grow sustainably. Coordination among banks, government agencies and development partners would help.

Shikah Moni Hosiary in Narayanganj illustrates the opportunity and challenges. The business accessed a Tk 3 lakh CMSME loan to expand inventory before winter. The entrepreneur’s savings and previous loan history supported eligibility without formal collateral. Sales increased significantly during the festival season, but uneven cash flows and limited bookkeeping made repayments difficult to manage. Finance therefore needs complementary support in financial management and business development.

title: Police map teen gangs; legal action remains tricky
text:
Police are preparing coordinated drives against teen gangs and their patrons but face a tougher task beyond identifying and detaining suspects: taking action without specific allegations.

Amid growing concerns over juvenile involvement in organised violence, extortion, drug dealing, and other crimes, Police Headquarters (PHQ) has directed all police units to identify active gangs, their members, and influential people who allegedly organise, finance or protect them.

“We issued a directive to all police units across the country eight to 10 days ago and expect to receive the lists shortly,” Md Sayedur Rahman, additional inspector general (Crimes and Operations) at the PHQ, told The Daily Star on October 17.

Police will hold meetings after receiving the lists and draw up a detailed plan for coordinated drives in areas where juvenile delinquency is prevalent, he said.

Asked yesterday what action would be taken against those with no criminal records, Sayedur said they would not be included in the list.

“The action will target those who threaten public safety and violate the laws of the state,” he added.

The directive covers all units, including the Special Branch, Dhaka Metropolitan Police (DMP), Special Response Battalion (SRB), formerly the Rapid Action Battalion, and district police.

An SRB official said the force had completed preliminary mapping of 1,333 juvenile groups, 213 organisers or leaders, and 27 alleged patrons.

The lists were undergoing final departmental verification before submission to the PHQ.

The official, speaking on condition of anonymity, said the SRB had detained 174 suspected gang members since February 12.

However, police acknowledge that identifying and detaining suspected gang members is easier than taking further legal action when no specific offence can be established against them.

Additional IGP Sayedur Rahman and SRB Director General Md Ahsan Habib said the difficulty often lay in proceeding against suspected gang members and alleged patrons without specific criminal allegations.

Sayedur said the police had to act within the law while addressing the problem.

“If we arrest juveniles under the Special Powers Act, it will not be a good practice. We can be strict but cannot be cruel,” he said.

He added that investigators would also examine whether politically influential people were patronising juvenile gangs.

According to police officials, adult criminals often use teenagers to commit offences for personal gain, exploiting their vulnerability and the comparatively lenient treatment juveniles may receive under the law.

Teenagers can also be easier to influence and recruit into criminal activities, they said.

OUTDATED LISTS

The planned nationwide initiative also highlights the absence of a comprehensive, up-to-date database of juvenile gangs. Different police units maintain their own lists, many of which are outdated and may not reflect the situation on the ground.

Existing PHQ data list 307 teen gangs nationwide, including 93 under Chattogram Metropolitan Police, 78 under Dhaka Range and 54 under Chattogram Range.

The DMP list contains 41 gangs, while Khulna Metropolitan Police has 13, Rajshahi Metropolitan Police 12, Sylhet Metropolitan Police five, Barishal Metropolitan Police three and Khulna Range four.

No gangs are listed under Gazipur Metropolitan Police, Rangpur Metropolitan Police, Rajshahi Range or Barishal Range.

PHQ data further show that 270 members of 48 gangs faced 69 criminal cases during the first nine months of this year. Of those cases, 21, or 30.4 percent, were linked to gang clashes.

The 48 gangs had 577 listed members, according to the data.

CUMILLA DRIVES

The nationwide plan comes amid intensified police action in Cumilla following the September 18 killing of Ishayat Shahriar Oprotim, a Class VII student and son of Nahida Begum, an associate professor of Bangla at Comilla University.

Police launched coordinated anti-gang drives on September 23, involving all 18 police stations in the district and the Detective Branch.

The alleged involvement of teen gang members in the killing fuelled demands for stronger action against juvenile crime.

By October 15, police had detained 2,811 suspected teen gang members in Cumilla alone. Many were subsequently released on bonds furnished by their families.

The scale of the detentions raises questions about how police distinguish between those suspected of specific crimes and teenagers identified through gang mapping.

Separately, a young man was stabbed in the abdomen and his father was shot in the leg when six masked assailants attacked them in Mohammadpur on October 15. Police suspect the attack stemmed from a longstanding rivalry between two criminal gangs, identified as the Patali and Sazzad groups.

Police and local residents described the groups as juvenile gangs allegedly involved in drug dealing, snatching, and extortion, with older youths directing their activities. Their operations reportedly extend across several parts of Mohammadpur, where gang-related crime remains a persistent concern.

ARRESTS ALONE WON’T DO

Md Omar Faruk, a professor of criminology and police science at Mawlana Bhashani Science and Technology University, said arresting or detaining juveniles alone would not solve the problem.

He said teen gangs often operate under the patronage of politically backed individuals who use them to commit crimes. Law enforcers should target these patrons, he added.

“Bringing their political patrons to justice would significantly reduce teen gang culture and related crimes,” he said.

Many gang members, he said, are rootless, beyond parental control and addicted to drugs. Those already involved in gangs need close monitoring, care, and counselling.

“Every part of society must be involved in tackling this problem. The police alone cannot do it,” he said.

title: Russia could build wheat silo at Payra port
text:
Food Minister Afroza Khanam has proposed that Russia build a wheat silo using its own funds on unused land at Payra sea port in Patuakhali.

The proposal followed a suggestion by Russian Ambassador to Bangladesh Alexander Khozin to finance a wheat silo at Moheshkhali in Cox’s Bazar. He made the proposal during a courtesy call on the food minister at the Ministry of Food yesterday.

The ambassador also proposed exporting wheat to Bangladesh on a government-to-government basis.

Responding to the Moheshkhali proposal, the minister said finding suitable land for such a large infrastructure project in the area could be difficult because of a shortage of land.

She suggested Payra sea port as an alternative location, saying it has the necessary port infrastructure and communication facilities to accommodate a large-capacity wheat silo.

The silo could initially have a storage capacity of 200,000 tonnes, which could gradually be increased to 500,000 tonnes, she said.

A silo at Payra would facilitate the transportation of wheat to key distribution and supply hubs across the country, including Narayanganj and Baghabari in Sirajganj, she added.

The minister invited the Russian ambassador to visit Payra sea port to assess the feasibility of the proposal. An on-site visit would help identify a suitable location, assess the available infrastructure and determine how the project could be implemented, she said.

The ambassador welcomed the proposal and expressed interest in it.

A wheat silo is a specialised structure designed to store large quantities of wheat in a controlled environment, protecting the grain from weather and other external factors.

According to food ministry data, Bangladesh currently has 12 silos, of which 10 are operational. Work on the remaining two has yet to be completed. Of the 10 operational silos, six are used for wheat and four for rice. The wheat silos have a combined storage capacity of 350,000 tonnes.

title: Man gets life term for murder
text:
A court in Chattogram yesterday sentenced an expatriate, Md Jahangir Alam, to life-term imprisonment on the charge of killing a boy in Sandwip upazila.

The court of Chattogram District and Sessions Judge Kazi Abdul Hannan handed down the verdict after the court found the accused guilty beyond a doubt, examining all the records and witnesses. District and Sessions Judge Court’s Administrative Officer Gias Uddin Chowdhury confirmed the matter.

After the verdict, the court sent him to jail.

According to the case statement, five-year-old Ali Hossen had died on the way to the CMCH after Jahangir, a neighbour of the deceased, slammed him to the ground over a family dispute. Following the incident, locals had caught Jahangir and handed him over to the police.

title: Building banking relationships that support local enterprise
text:
Turning financial access into productive enterprise growth requires sustained engagement and responsible lending. S M Mainul Kabir Managing Director and CEO SBAC Bank PLC

Opening an account can give an entrepreneur a foothold in formal banking, but accessing finance requires reliable records and repayment capacity. In a conversation with The Daily Star, S M Mainul Kabir, managing director and CEO of South Bangla Agriculture and Commerce Bank PLC (SBAC), discusses how agent banking can help customers make that transition.

The Daily Star (TDS): How is agent banking supporting local enterprise?

S M Mainul Kabir (SMMK): Beyond transactions, agent banking can help entrepreneurs build financial records, develop savings discipline and establish banking relationships. Previously unbanked people in rural and underserved areas are entering the formal system.

Our outlet in Dhankhali, near the Sundarbans in Shyamnagar, Satkhira, illustrates this potential. People who never held accounts are accessing banking.

TDS: What can entrepreneurs do at outlets, and how do they apply for finance?

SMMK: Available services include account opening, deposits, withdrawals, remittance receipts and routine transactions, subject to regulations. Agents provide initial guidance and refer prospective borrowers to branches or lending teams; credit assessment and approval follow authorised bank processes.

Applicants select a suitable product and submit documents that may include a national identity card, trade licence, business records, bank statements, income evidence and applicable security papers. Processing time depends on application completeness, business viability, verification, risk assessment and approval procedures.

TDS: How do you assess enterprises with limited records and match finance to their needs?

SMMK: Limited documentation should not automatically prevent consideration of a viable enterprise. Where product and regulatory frameworks permit, assessment may consider cash flow, operating history, repayment capacity, market prospects and risk. Savings behaviour, remittances and transaction histories provide supplementary evidence.

Working capital may support inventory and operating expenses; term finance may fund equipment or expansion. Loan sizes and repayments should reflect verified cash flows, seasonality and product terms.

TDS: What would improve women entrepreneurs’ access?

SMMK: Barriers include limited financial literacy, inadequate records, lack of acceptable collateral, mobility constraints and low awareness of financing options. Progress requires awareness-building, customer guidance, better documentation and fair, transparent assessment, alongside financing suited to viable women-led enterprises.

TDS: How should customers be protected?

SMMK: Customers should receive clear information on charges, financing terms, eligibility and application status through authorised channels. Monitoring, compliance checks and risk-based supervision help identify irregularities. Misleading information, unauthorised charges or service problems should be reported promptly through official complaint channels or the responsible branch.

title: Local savings to local enterprise
text:
For Rehana Begum, banking is available just across from her home in Munshiganj. Through a Bank Asia agent outlet, she maintains savings, receives money from her son in Kuwait and has accessed financing for the grocery shop she runs with her husband, Mosharraf Hossain.

She says she borrowed Tk 10 lakh against two DPS savings accounts to support the business. Stocking rice, cooking oil and other essentials requires substantial working capital, particularly when customers buy on credit and the next consignment must arrive before those dues are collected.

The financing took about 10 to 15 days, she recalls. The money was disbursed through the local outlet, but she visited the bank’s Nimtala branch to sign documents. Obtaining a chequebook took about a week.

Both describe the banking service positively. Their reservations concern the time and expense of arranging documents, including guarantors’ trade licences and an affidavit. For a shop operating on limited margins, Mosharraf says, those expenses matter.

Their experience captures a question facing agent banking: how effectively can a familiar place for savings and withdrawals help a small business obtain suitable finance?

A counter closer to home

The convenience of nearby banking is considerable. Md Moffazel Hossain, who operates a Bank Asia agent outlet in Shawli Bazar, recalls that residents previously travelled nearly two hours to Bogura for banking services. His outlet opened in 2015.

For traders, such journeys mean transport costs and time away from the shop. For households receiving remittances, a local outlet provides a convenient place to collect money and maintain savings.

Bangladesh Bank’s April–June 2026 report, records 30 banks providing agent banking services through 20,597 outlets. Accounts numbered approximately 2.72 crore, around 85 percent belonging to rural customers. Deposits stood at approximately Tk 51,907 crore.

However, the network’s reach does not tell the whole story of access to finance. A March 2026 International Growth Centre policy brief, drawing on Policy Research Institute research, found that about two-thirds of agent banking outlets had no outstanding loans as of December 2024. This does not establish that they had never facilitated lending, but it shows how much of the network’s activity remains centred on transactions and deposits.

From enquiry to application

When a customer needs business finance, the outlet’s role changes. Beyond handling transactions, it may explain available products, help arrange documents and connect the applicant with a branch or lending team.

The agent does not decide whether the business receives a loan. That responsibility remains with the bank, which assesses the application, checks repayment capacity and completes the necessary approval and legal procedures.

Rehana’s experience makes this division tangible. Her local outlet provided access to the money, while signing took place at the branch. Her savings also served as security: this was borrowing against existing deposits, rather than financing granted solely on the strength of the grocery business.

Applicants may need identification, a trade licence, business and income information, bank statements and details of existing borrowing. Guarantors or collateral documents may also be required, depending on the product.

The practical difficulty is often assembling these requirements. A customer accustomed to withdrawing money with fingerprint verification may not already have a chequebook, as Rehana discovered. Obtaining another person’s documents can involve additional visits and expense.

Clear guidance at the outset can help applicants understand what they need, which steps require a branch visit and where their application stands.

Image

Showing how a business earns

A busy shop does not necessarily keep detailed accounts. Rehana describes a continuous cycle of buying stock and making sales, without calculating precise profit figures.

That leaves a bank with questions that transaction records alone cannot answer. How much of the money entering an account comes from sales? How much must go towards suppliers, rent or household expenses? What remains available for repayments?

In their responses for this supplement, Prime Bank and Islami Bank describe considering cash flow and business activity alongside savings and transaction histories. Business visits and verification help put those records in context.

Regular use of an account can therefore support an application, but deposits are not the same as profit. Remittances may supplement household income without necessarily being available to repay a business loan.

Simple records of sales, purchases, expenses and customer dues can make a small enterprise easier to assess. They can also help the owner judge how much borrowing the business can manage.

When the amount matters

In Malumghat, Cox’s Bazar, Farbeen Akter makes crochet toys and accessories under the name Papiya Fashion House. Producing an order requires cash for yarn and other materials before payment arrives from the buyer.

She says buyers may pay 15 to 20 days after delivery. Purchasing materials in bulk can reduce costs, but requires more money upfront.

Farbeen recalls requesting Tk 50,000 through a local banking outlet and receiving Tk 25,000. She used the financing to buy materials in smaller batches than planned. The agent helped scan documents and coordinate with branch staff, although she still needed two guarantors and a branch visit.

Her account shows why receiving finance and receiving enough suitable finance are different experiences. A smaller amount may help fulfil orders while leaving the business unable to obtain the savings available through bulk purchases.

Timing matters too. A loan arriving after an order’s deadline may be less useful, while repayments falling before customers settle their bills can put pressure on working capital.

The amount, duration, repayment frequency and total borrowing cost all shape what an entrepreneur can do with the money. These terms need to be understood before the commitment is made.

Women and the paperwork barrier

Women held approximately half of agent banking accounts at the end of June 2026, but received 12.72 percent of cumulative loan disbursements by value. This measures their share of money disbursed, rather than the proportion of women who obtained loans.

Farbeen’s experience illustrates one complication behind an application. Her trade licence was in her own name, but the family home housing her workshop was not. She says she obtained local verification of her right to use the premises.

Mercantile Bank’s responses identify similar barriers, including limited collateral ownership, missing licences for home businesses, restricted mobility and dependence on male intermediaries. UCB points to financial and business training as part of its support for women entrepreneurs.

Nearby service can reduce travel, but it cannot by itself resolve ownership and documentation difficulties. Applicants still need a workable route through requirements that may involve family members, guarantors and local authorities.

Beyond the first transaction

The outlet must also function reliably. Cash availability, connectivity, staff knowledge and clear information about charges affect customers’ experience before borrowing even enters the picture.

For financing enquiries, useful assistance means explaining eligibility and documents accurately, making effective referrals and helping customers obtain updates. Displayed charges, receipts and accessible complaint channels also give customers a way to check what they are paying.

The borrowers’ accounts show that satisfaction and frustration can coexist. Rehana values the service while her husband questions paperwork expenses. Farbeen would consider using the channel again, but wants financing better matched to her production needs.

For these businesses, progress will be felt in practical ways: fewer avoidable visits, understandable requirements, timely decisions and repayments that fit their earnings. The nearby counter has already become part of their financial lives. What happens after they ask for finance will determine its role in their businesses.

title: ‘Oh, my son! Where have you gone?’
text:
“Oh, my son! Oh, Rakib, where are you? Where have you gone?” cried Azharul Islam.

With both legs bandaged, he lay on the floor outside the emergency department of Chittagong Medical College Hospital (CMCH), crying inconsolably over the death of his six-year-old son.

Beside him sat his wife, Fatema Aktar, with visible injuries on her face and hands. She stared blankly ahead, too shocked and grief-stricken to speak.

The couple’s journey home turned tragic early yesterday when a speeding lorry ploughed into a group of passengers standing beside their broken-down bus on the Dhaka–Chittagong highway in Sitakunda.

Three people died on the spot, while eight others, including Azharul and his family, were injured and taken to hospital, police said. Two of the injured, including Rakib, later died while undergoing treatment at CMCH.

The other deceased were identified as Fatema Akter, 38, daughter of Md Abdul Hai, from Mohammad Nagar in Chattogram; Absa, 44, daughter of Abdul Hashim; and Swapna Akter, 30, daughter of Nizam Uddin, both from Kishoreganj. The fifth victim was an unidentified man, aged around 49.

Speaking to The Daily Star hours after the crash, Azharul, a farmer, said he had travelled to Chattogram city to bring his wife and Rakib, the younger of their two sons, back to their village home in Madan upazila of Netrokona.

His wife Fatema works at a readymade garment factory in the Karnaphuli Export Processing Zone and had been living in a rented house in the Narikeltola area under Patenga Police Station.

Azharul’s brother, Anwar Hossain, said the family boarded a Netrokona-bound Shapla Paribahan bus from Narikeltola around 12:30am.

Around 1:00am, the bus broke down in Sitakunda. As the driver and his assistant tried to repair it, the heat inside became unbearable, prompting some passengers, including Azharul and his family, to get off.

“We were standing beside the bus with around 20 other passengers. I could hear the driver talking to the bus owner over the phone.

“My son was just two yards away from me. Suddenly, a tank lorry trying to overtake another vehicle ploughed into the passengers standing beside the bus.”

Azharul said he saw his son lying in a pool of blood.

“Both my legs were injured, but I didn’t feel any pain. All I could see was my son. I shouted for help to save him. Locals rushed to our rescue and took us to CMCH, but my son could not be saved,” he said, breaking down in tears.

The accident took place near Royal Cement Gate in the Chhota Kumira area of Sitakunda upazila in Chattogram, said Sitakunda Police Station OC Mohinul Islam.

Inspector Shamim Ahmed, officer-in-charge of Baro Awlia Highway Police Station, said at least five people, including three women and a child, were killed in the collision. Six injured passengers were receiving treatment at CMCH.

“While the Dhaka-bound bus was being repaired, the passengers got off and stood by the roadside. Suddenly, a speeding Dhaka-bound lorry ploughed into them,” he said.

Police seized the lorry, but its driver fled the scene, he added.

The injured were admitted to different hospital wards, with several in critical condition, said Nurul Alam, in-charge of the CMCH Police Camp.

title: GP revenue, profit fall in Jan-Sept
text:
Grameenphone Ltd’s (GP) revenue and profit declined in the first nine months of 2026, as business performance remained weak despite marginal growth in third-quarter revenue.

The country’s largest mobile operator reported revenue of Tk 11,756 crore in January-September, down 1.6 percent year-on-year, according to its unaudited interim financial statements published recently.

Net profit fell 4 percent to Tk 2,172 crore from Tk 2,264 crore in the same period last year. Earnings per share (EPS) also declined.

However, third-quarter revenue edged up to Tk 4,017 crore in July-September from Tk 4,010 crore a year earlier.

Net profit stood at Tk 751 crore, almost unchanged from the same quarter last year, while EPS remained at Tk 5.56 during the period.

The company’s operating cash flow, however, rose 9.2 percent year-on-year to Tk 5,683 crore in January-September from Tk 5,205 crore.

During the period, Grameenphone spent Tk 1,661 crore on property, plant and equipment, right-of-use assets and intangible assets, up from Tk 1,147 crore a year earlier.

Shares of Grameenphone fell to Tk 237 on the Dhaka Stock Exchange yesterday.

title: Business finance needs more than transaction records
text:
Limited formal records should not automatically exclude a viable entrepreneur from consideration for financing. Md Ahteshamul Haque Khan Managing Director and CEO Dutch-Bangla Bank PLC

Agent banking can connect local businesses with finance, but account activity alone cannot establish repayment capacity. In a conversation with The Daily Star, Md Ahteshamul Haque Khan, managing director and CEO of Dutch-Bangla Bank PLC, discusses credit assessment, barriers facing women entrepreneurs and the safeguards needed to protect customers.

The Daily Star (TDS): How can agent banking support enterprise, and where does an agent’s responsibility end?

Md Ahteshamul Haque Khan (AHK): Rural customers who once relied solely on remittance withdrawals are now engaging in business financing. Stronger coordination among outlets, branches and lending teams can support this shift. Outlets offer account opening, deposits, withdrawals, transfers, remittances and other approved transactions. Agents provide guidance and referrals, while credit appraisal, lending decisions and approval remain with authorised bank officials.

TDS: What should applicants prepare, and how are businesses with limited records assessed?

AHK: Applicants generally need identification, a trade licence where applicable, bank statements, business information and details of existing liabilities. Collateral or guarantor documents may also be required. Processing time depends on document completeness, loan complexity and verification.

Limited formal records should not automatically exclude a viable entrepreneur from consideration for financing. We can examine sales, expenses, stock, supplier relationships, liabilities and business experience, supported by visits and independent checks. Savings and transaction histories provide additional insights. Remittances must be distinguished from business income as well.

TDS: How should financing reflect business needs and cash flows?

AHK: Working capital can fund inventory and raw materials, while term loans may support equipment or expansion. Agricultural and women-focused facilities can address other needs, subject to eligibility and lending conditions.

Loan amounts should reflect verified cash flow, business needs and repayment capacity. Agricultural repayments may be aligned with harvesting and sales where product terms permit.

TDS: What barriers do women entrepreneurs face?

AHK: Distance, limited collateral, inadequate records, restricted mobility and limited market information can impede access. Family responsibilities and social expectations add difficulties.Opportunities for support include identifying potential entrepreneurs, financial literacy sessions, application guidance and coordination with lending teams.

TDS: What safeguards should protect customers at agent outlets?

AHK: Customers should receive clear information on charges, financing terms, eligibility, repayment obligations and application status, alongside transaction evidence. They must never disclose PINs or confidential authentication credentials to agents or unauthorised persons. Problems should be reported through designated branches and official customer service channels. Complaints about misleading information, unauthorised charges or suspected fraud should be documented and investigated promptly.

title: Urban slum children face rising climate risks: speakers
text:
Children in urban slums face growing health risks from climate change, including heatwaves, waterlogging, and mosquito-borne diseases, compounded by poor housing, unsafe water, and inadequate sanitation, speakers said at a seminar yesterday.

The seminar, titled “Urban Child Health at Risk from Climate Change: Challenges and Solutions”, was organised by Children Watch Foundation at The Daily Star Centre in the capital.

Poor housing, unsafe drinking water, and inadequate sanitation further increase children’s vulnerability. Shah Israt Azmery Chairman of Children Watch Foundation

Delivering the keynote, Shah Israt Azmery, chairman of Children Watch Foundation, highlighted findings from a 2025 survey conducted in selected slums in Dhaka, Rajshahi and Satkhira.

The survey found that 54.5 percent of households considered children the family members most affected by climate-related risks.

Heatwaves were identified as a major stressor by 51.87 percent of respondents, while 30.48 percent reported waterlogging. Dengue and chikungunya were the leading health concerns, cited by 69 percent.

Poor housing, unsafe drinking water, and inadequate sanitation further increase children’s vulnerability, she said.

The survey found that 43.5 percent of households live in tin-shed houses and 64.5 percent use shared toilets.

The study recommended strengthening climate-resilient healthcare, improving drainage and sanitation, expanding early-warning systems, and raising community awareness.

At the event, Dr MA Muhit, state minister for Health and Family Welfare, said the government had pledged free primary healthcare for all citizens and planned to recruit 100,000 additional health workers.

Young volunteers had been mobilised for dengue prevention, while 2,000 doctors had received refresher training in dengue patient management, he said. “These efforts had helped reduce the mortality rate by around 40 percent.”

The government also planned to equip health workers with modern tools, he added.

Muhit said more than 300 children with severe disabilities had been identified in Korail slum within a month, but bureaucratic complications had delayed initiatives to support them.

He urged the media and civil society to ensure transparency in healthcare spending, saying not a single taka of the Tk 16,000 crore expected to be spent on healthcare tenders should be lost to corruption or waste.

Sanaul Islam, professor of Soil, Water and Environment at Khulna University, said the loss of rivers, canals, wetlands and ponds, alongside expanding concrete structures, is worsening urban heat.

He called for restoring water bodies, preserving forests and rethinking urban development to build a sustainable, climate-resilient environment.

MP Anisur Rahman Khokon said the government is committed to environmental protection and safeguarding people’s fundamental rights.

Prof Md Nurunnabi, director of Centre for Sustainability and Climate; Anowar Hossain, deputy programme manager of Climate Change Adaptation and Disaster Resilience; Syed Mahbubul Alam, secretary of the Centre for Law and Policy Affairs; and Md Ferdous, director of the Cell for Adaptation, Resilience, Security and Disaster Resilience at Islamic Relief Bangladesh, were present, among others.

title: Grid glitch disrupts power to parts of Dhaka, Ctg
text:
A technical fault in the national grid disrupted electricity supply in parts of Dhaka and Chattogram yesterday, leaving several areas without power.

The affected areas in Dhaka include Gulshan, Rampura, Ulan and Motijheel, as well as Bhulta, Haripur and Siddhirganj in Narayanganj, state-owned Power Grid Bangladesh PLC said in an emergency statement.

The Secretariat reportedly remained without electricity for nearly an hour, it said.

The outage began at 12:43pm after a fault developed in the Meghnaghat-Haripur national grid line, according to multiple officials at the Power Division.

Power Grid Bangladesh said efforts were underway to restore electricity supply to the affected areas.

“Power connections have already been restored in most affected areas. We hope to ensure electricity supply to the remaining areas within a short time,” the statement said.

The company apologised to customers for the temporary inconvenience.

Power supply in northern Bangladesh and other unaffected areas remained normal, according to the statement.

title: HSBC net profit jumps in Q3 but misses forecasts
text:
Banking giant HSBC said Tuesday that net profit in the third quarter rose less than expected, as it carries out sweeping job cuts and an AI expansion.

Profit attributable to shareholders rose 45.5 percent year-on-year to US$7 billion from July to September, the bank said in a filing to the Hong Kong stock exchange. That figure was up from US$4.87 billion a year earlier, but fell short of the US$7.3 billion market estimate.

HSBC has been carrying out job cuts and a global restructuring since CEO Georges Elhedery took the helm two years ago, turning the London-headquartered bank’s focus to core Asian markets.

Pre-tax profit in the third quarter grew 32 percent to US$9.6 billion, with revenue increasing by US$800 million to US$18.6 billion, the filing said.

HSBC also approved a third interim dividend of US$0.10 per share, and announced a second US$1 billion buyback after completing one in the previous three months.

“As we simplify HSBC, we are creating greater capacity to invest, grow and deliver strong returns for our shareholders,” Elhedery said in the filing.

The third quarter performance “shows that in a more complex world, clients continue to turn to us to navigate uncertainty and seize new opportunities”, he added. However, Tuesday’s results left investors disappointed.

Shares in Hong Kong plunged more than 6 percent, at around HK$133.5 apiece, during afternoon trading, wiping out the morning’s gains.

Restructuring and cost-saving actions, which include selling off a series of business units this year, have saved the bank US$1.4 billion since 2025, according to its report.

HSBC has also been increasingly adopting artificial intelligence in its operations, which Elhedery has said “will change how work is done across industries, impacting some jobs, transforming others.”

The lender told AFP this month that it was “in a consultation period” after the Financial Times reported it was planning sweeping cuts to its UK wealth management business, which is estimated to employ hundreds of relationship managers.

The cuts are “part of a push to use AI to help serve wealthy clients”, the FT said.

Citing “people familiar with the plans”, the newspaper said “about half of the business’s management and specialist roles are expected to go, while the reduction in the ranks of financial advisers will be closer to 70 percent”.

The bank said in Tuesday’s filing that it remained “confident in achieving the targets” set out this year, including a return on tangible equity of 17 percent or better through 2028.

“We continue to target year-on-year growth in revenue from 2026 to 2028, rising to five percent growth in 2028 compared with 2027,” it said.

It expects banking net interest income of at least US$46 billion for 2025.

title: Truck driver stabbed to death
text:
A truck driver was stabbed to death, allegedly by another driver, inside a cement factory in Chattogram city’s Patenga area on Monday night.

The deceased, Ezhar Mia Shuvo, 35, was a driver at NGS Cement Factory in Patenga.

Security personnel caught the alleged killer, Shahedul Islam Rony, 36, and handed him over to the police later, said police.

“Shuvo and Rony were colleagues. They had an altercation around 11:00pm inside the cement factory. At a point, Rony stabbed Shuvo multiple times, leaving him critically injured,” said Parvez Ali, officer-in-charge of Patenga Police Station.

“He was rushed to Chattogram Medical College Hospital (CMCH), where he succumbed to his injuries at around 12:30am,” the OC said.

“The body has been sent to the CMCH morgue for an autopsy. A case has been filed in this connection,” OC Parvez added.

title: Migrants from 29 countries lured into Russia’s war: UN
text:
Bangladeshis were among nationals of several countries trafficked into the Russian armed forces through deception or coercion, a United Nations investigation has found.

Lured to Russia with promises of well-paid civilian jobs, men from at least 29 countries were instead made to sign military contracts in Russian, a language most did not understand, before being sent to the front lines in Ukraine.

Many of the recruits were reportedly killed or went missing, leaving their families struggling to find out what happened to them.

The Independent International Commission of Inquiry on Ukraine also obtained copies of business visas issued to Bangladeshi recruits, showing that a civilian company in Russia had invited them for civilian work.

The findings were presented to the UN General Assembly’s Third Committee on Monday. The report, however, did not specify how many Bangladeshis had been trafficked, killed or reported missing.

According to the Bureau of Manpower, Employment and Training’s Overseas Employment Platform, 7,949 employment clearances were issued for Russia between January 1, 2025, and October 27, 2026. The figure, however, does not establish how many people actually travelled to Russia or were trafficked.

A joint investigation by Fortify Rights and Truth Hounds, reported in March, identified at least 104 Bangladeshis recruited into the Russian military, of whom at least 34 were reportedly killed.

On October 14, the Special Response Battalion said 20 of 30 Bangladeshis sent to Russia with promises of construction jobs had been killed. The workers had paid an average of Tk 10 lakh each and undergone 21 days of training, it said.

The probe examined recruitment involving 48 countries, drawing on 245 testimonies, travel records and Russian military contracts. It found close coordination between recruiters and Russian authorities. Men from at least 29 of those countries were identified as trafficking victims.

Russian officials have publicly denied illegal recruitment, the report noted.

According to the report, recruiters offered jobs as drivers, security guards, electricians and construction workers, arranged travel and then handed recruits over to the Russian military. Their passports and phones were often confiscated, while military training ranged from 20 minutes to a month.

Shariful Islam Hasan, associate director of BRAC’s Migration Programme, said BRAC had warned about the practice last year.

“Many Bangladeshis were lured to Russia with promises of jobs but were later recruited into the war. Some travelled on work visas, while others went on tourist visas.”

He urged the government to trace around 8,500 Bangladeshis who had travelled legally to Russia over the past two years and determine how many were working, fighting, missing or dead.

He also called for figures on visas issued by the Russian embassy.

The commission urged Russia to release trafficking victims and investigate recruiters. It said captured recruits were entitled to prisoner-of-war protections and urged their home countries not to prosecute the victims.

title: Making merchant solar work for Bangladesh’s industry
text:
For Bangladesh's garment industry, reliable and competitively priced electricity is fundamental to manufacturing.
