Increasingly, access to verifiable renewable electricity is also becoming essential to export competitiveness. Inditex, owner of Zara, targets a 53 percent reduction in greenhouse-gas emissions by 2030, compared with 2018, and net-zero emissions by 2040. Under its 2024–2027 Supply Chain Transformation Plan, manufacturing facilities are expected to adopt measures including renewable electricity procurement, lower-impact technologies and emissions reductions.

Vietnam, a major competitor in garment exports, demonstrates the urgency. Vietnam introduced its Direct Power Purchase Agreement (DPPA) framework in 2024 allowing large industrial consumers to contract renewable electricity directly from private generators through dedicated connections or the national grid. In June 2026, Samsung Electronics Vietnam became the first corporate consumer to procure electricity through the grid-connected DPPA mechanism, contracting approximately 70 million kWh of solar electricity annually.

The Government's rooftop solar initiative is an important step towards expanding renewable electricity generation. However, limited roof space in manufacturing clusters makes merchant solar a valuable complement, enabling manufacturers to procure renewable electricity from larger projects located elsewhere.

The regulatory foundation for this is already in place. The 2025 merchant renewable-power policy permits private developers to sell electricity directly to large industrial consumers through negotiated Merchant Power Purchase Agreements (MPPAs), with open access to transmission and distribution networks and procurement from multiple generators. More recently, BERC has established transmission, distribution and settlement charges for merchant renewable power, together with tariffs of Tk 6.98–7.11 per kWh applicable to Bangladesh Power Development Board (BPDB) purchases of up to 20 percent of eligible merchant renewable generation.

Consider a garment manufacturer in Dhaka consuming 4 million kWh annually. Inditex also targets 50 percent renewable electricity across its supply-chain manufacturing processes by 2030, rising to 100 percent by 2040. Although this is an aggregate target, a manufacturer choosing to target 50 percent renewable electricity would need 2 million kWh from renewable sources. If rooftop solar provides 0.6 million kWh annually, requiring approximately 3,000 sqm of suitable roof space, the remaining 1.4 million kWh could be contracted through a 15-year MPPA with a 50 MW solar plant near Chattogram supplying multiple industrial customers. The manufacturer’s contracted allocation would correspond to approximately 1 MWp of solar capacity. The solar plant would inject electricity into the national grid, while the factory continues receiving power through its local distribution network, with generation and consumption reconciled through metering and settlement. At an illustrative negotiated solar tariff of Tk 6 per kWh, plus approximately Tk 1.60 in assumed transmission, distribution and settlement charges, the indicative cost would be Tk 7.60 per kWh before network losses, renewable-energy certificates, taxes and other applicable charges.

Three areas require attention.

First is settlement and risk allocation during grid constraints. BERC has established open-access charges and an energy management and settlement framework, but commercial arrangements must clearly address grid curtailment and differences between contracted generation and consumption. If the Chattogram plant generates electricity while the Dhaka factory experiences load shedding, how is the contracted generation accounted for, and who bears the resulting financial consequences? Can unmatched generation be allocated to another customer or sold to BPDB, subject to the applicable rules and contractual arrangements? BERC should ensure its framework provides clear, enforceable provisions for settlement, treatment of unmatched generation and allocation of financial risks, which can be reflected in standard MPPAs. Industrial consumers will continue relying on utilities when solar generation is unavailable. BERC should therefore ensure that network and backup supply charges fairly reflect the costs of maintaining reliable service, while addressing the financial impact on utilities without undermining the competitiveness of merchant solar.

Second is bankability. Unlike conventional power projects selling to BPDB, merchant projects depend on private industrial buyers. Standard MPPAs should incorporate payment security through revolving letters of credit or bank guarantees, enforceable default provisions, lender step-in rights and the ability to replace defaulting customers. Larger projects should be able to contract multiple industrial consumers to diversify credit risk. Recent Government–ADB discussions on several hundred million dollars in proposed renewable-energy financing offer an opportunity to engage other development finance institutions (DFIs) in establishing a merchant-power credit-enhancement facility, potentially through IDCOL.

Partial credit guarantees and risk-sharing arrangements for qualifying industrial buyers could strengthen payment security, improve project bankability and help commercial banks finance merchant solar projects, thereby mobilising greater private investment.

Third is verification of renewable electricity for international buyers. As electricity from different sources mixes within the national grid, renewable-electricity procurement can be substantiated through internationally recognised Energy Attribute Certificates (EACs). Under the I-REC(E) system, each certificate represents one megawatt-hour (1,000 kWh) of verified renewable electricity generation.

In the Dhaka–Chattogram example, verified generation from the solar plant could support the issuance of corresponding renewable-energy certificates, which would be transferred and redeemed on behalf of the garment manufacturer under the MPPA. The manufacturer would contract for both electricity and its renewable attributes, with certificate costs included in the negotiated tariff or priced separately. This would provide recognised evidence of renewable-electricity procurement. Standard MPPAs should therefore clearly establish certificate ownership, transfer and redemption to prevent double counting.

Addressing these three areas requires coordinated implementation. The Power Division should coordinate the development of standardised MPPAs in consultation with BERC, developers, industrial buyers and lenders. Power Grid Bangladesh, through its National Load Dispatch Centre, should coordinate scheduling and dispatch, while distribution utilities establish consistent metering, billing and settlement procedures. BPDB's arrangements for eligible surplus generation should also be clearly defined.

Rooftop solar remains essential for manufacturers seeking to strengthen energy security and reduce operating costs. Merchant solar complements this by enabling factories to procure additional renewable electricity from larger projects through the national grid, helping meet international buyers' decarbonisation requirements. Together, these approaches can support industrial production and strengthen Bangladesh's export competitiveness. Making merchant solar bankable is therefore an important part of the country's broader industrial and energy strategy.

The author is a strategic consultant across technology, media and infrastructure industries

title: Ports asked to hoist cautionary signal No 3
text:
The maritime ports of Chattogram, Cox’s Bazar, Mongla and Payra have been advised to keep local cautionary signal No 3 hoisted as the very severe cyclonic storm “Arnab” moved west-northwestward over Westcentral Bay and adjoining areas.

It was over the same area at 6:00am yesterday, about 1,040km southwest of Chattogram, 995km southwest of Cox’s Bazar, 895km southwest of Mongla and 905km southwest of Payra.

It is likely to move west-northwestwards further and cross Andhra Pradesh coasts by noon today.

Maximum sustained wind speed within 64km of the severe cyclonic storm centre is about 120kph, rising to 140kph in gusts or squalls.

Sea levels will remain very high near the very severe cyclonic storm.

All fishing boats and trawlers over North Bay have been advised to remain close to the coast and proceed with caution till further notice.

title: Proposed cyber law focuses on gagging online voices
text:
Prominent citizens, lawyers, and politicians yesterday criticised the proposed Cyber Protection (Amendment) Act, terming it a “government protection law” designed to gag citizens.

Rather than curbing cybercrimes such as hacking and cyberterrorism, the amendment aims to restrict free expression online and make it easier to arrest government critics, they said at a citizens’ dialogue at BDBL Bhaban in Karwan Bazar yesterday.

The event, titled “Cyber Protection, or Gagging? In Whose Interest Are New Limits on Free Expression and Law Amendments Being Set?”, was jointly organised by Voice for Reform, Nagorik Coalition, Human Rights Support Society (HRSS), ZRF, DSA Victims Network and Bangladesh America Alliance.

63 % of those arrested over Facebook posts since the election had been detained for making “so-called derogatory remarks” or harshly criticising the PM, ministers, or their associates.

Nabila Idris, Rights activist

Presenting data related to the act, rights activist Nabila Idris said 63 percent of those arrested over Facebook posts since the national election had been detained for making “so-called derogatory remarks” or harshly criticising the prime minister, ministers, or their associates.

“Currently, half of these cases are filed under the existing Cyber Protection Act, while the remaining 50 percent have to rely on other laws. They are introducing the new amendment to solve this very problem so that arresting critics gets easier,” she added.

Joining virtually, Kamal Ahmed, former chief of Media Reform Commission, said the draft conflates political criticism and free expression with offences such as online gambling, fraud, and sexual harassment.

He cited a case in Mymensingh in which a woman was arrested and jailed for saying on Facebook Live that she had made a mistake by voting for the BNP in the election.

He also criticised the proposed National Cybersecurity Council to be formed under the act, saying the draft law would grant it powers similar to those of an executive body.

He also questioned the inclusion of a retired judge nominated by the chief justice, arguing that it would draw the chief justice into the council’s work.

“If a citizen is harmed by any decision of this council, where will they seek justice? Will they go to the very court whose chief justice is a part of this process?” he asked.

Kamal, also the consulting editor at The Daily Star, recommended making prior court approval mandatory for arrests and searches and treating defamation as a civil rather than criminal offence, punishable through hefty fines.

Barrister Priya Ahsan Chowdhury of Bangladesh Legal Aid and Services Trust (BLAST) said the power to block content is being extended beyond the Cyber Protection Agency to the information and broadcasting ministry and any government-authorised agency.

She also criticised the removal of certain safeguards from the current act, including the requirement for Cyber Tribunal approval within three days of blocking content, failing which the content must be unblocked. The draft also removes the requirement to publish a transparent list of blocked content, she said.

Chairing the discussion, photographer and rights activist Shahidul Alam said the proposed amendment made no changes to provisions concerning hacking, malware or attacks on critical information infrastructure, focusing instead on controlling what people say and share online.

“This is not a cyber protection law; it is a law to gag voices,” he said.

National Citizen Party lawmaker Akhter Hossen, Daily Waadaa Editor Shafiqul Alam, and Alternatives organiser Dr Tajnuva Jabeen also spoke at the event, among others.

The discussion was moderated by Voice for Reform co-convenor Fahim Mashroor.

title: Israeli polls: Netanyahu faces tough test, turnout record high
text:
Israelis streamed to the polls yesterday in record numbers to pass wartime judgement on Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in what some described as the most consequential election in the nation’s history.

Long lines formed outside polling stations for the first election since the Hamas-led attacks on October 7, 2023, as voters grappled with the trauma of Israel’s deadliest day and its ensuing wars in Gaza, Lebanon and Iran.

The Central Elections Committee reported the turnout at 6:00pm (1600 GMT) at 66.7%, a record at that point of the day. With four hours left to go, more people had voted than in the entire previous election.

The policies of Netanyahu’s right-wing coalition have been divisive at home and have deepened Israel’s international isolation. But he has portrayed himself as the only leader with the mettle to face down Israel’s foes.

Netanyahu, Israel’s longest-serving leader with 19 years in office, is an unmatched political survivor, and his nationalist politics are increasingly entrenched. Israel’s fragmented system makes it difficult for an array of opponents to force out his coalition of right-wing, far-right and ultra-Orthodox parties.

His main rival Gadi Eisenkot, a military ex-chief of staff and security hawk, aims to unseat him with the support of parties on the right and centre, as well as the rump of an increasingly marginalised left. Opinion polls show a close race, giving neither man an easy path to power.

Forecasters were hesitant to guess what impact the strong turnout might have on the result. A surge in votes from Israelis of Palestinian heritage could limit gains for Netanyahu’s right-wing coalition and make it more likely that any government formed to oust him would require Arab parties’ support, a contentious prospect among Jewish party leaders.

Netanyahu urged supporters to come out to vote to balance high turnout among his opponents on the left and Arab Israelis. “You all need to stream to the polls,” he said. “This is a fateful moment.”

“I think these elections are the most important of all the ones I’ve known,” said Ruth Epstein, an 81-year-old longtime left-wing voter in Ramat Gan near Tel Aviv, who voted for the opposition Democrats.

Netanyahu has campaigned on an endorsement from US President Donald Trump, his ally in the war against Iran, who has said they should “finish the job”.

If neither Netanyahu nor Eisenkot can form a governing coalition in the 120-seat parliament, Netanyahu could stay on as caretaker until another election is held.

His opponents have managed to wrest the premiership from him only once since 2009, and that took four inconclusive elections in two years. Eighteen months later, he was back.

For many of Netanyahu’s opponents, the election turns on accountability for the security failures of October 7. Opposition groups have promised to hold a national inquiry, which Netanyahu has resisted.

“I am convinced that by the end of today, we will see a change — a new spirit for the State of Israel — that will serve as a rectification for the past three years and for that terrible day,” Eisenkot said during a visit to kibbutz Nir Oz in southern Israel, among those attacked on October 7.

He walked to the polls with Gadi Mozes, one of 251 people kidnapped by Hamas and taken to Gaza during the assault, which killed 1,200 people.

Eisenkot says Israel’s response — a war that has killed more than 74,000 Palestinians, according to Gaza health authorities — was a failure because Hamas remains in charge. He repeated his commitment to dismantle or destroy Hamas’ military and administrative power in Gaza within 18 months of forming a government.

Itamar Ben-Gvir, leader of a far-right party in Netanyahu’s coalition, cast his vote in the Kiryat Arba settlement in the occupied West Bank early on Tuesday. He predicted Netanyahu would return as prime minister and his own party would serve as the right-wing anchor of the government.

Ahmed Tibi, a candidate from an Arab party, said record turnout from Israel’s Arab minority would “pave the way for an alternative government and change the grave reality”.

Eisenkot has ruled out partnering with Arab parties, although in some scenarios he could rely on them to propup a minority government that keeps Netanyahu out.

Netanyahu has repeatedly described Arab Israelis, a fifth of the population, as a threat, in language that his opponents say crosses into racism. He posted an image on X on Tuesday showing a queue of Arab women, in niqabs or with angry expressions, purportedly at a polling station. According to OpenAI’s verification website, the image was prepared using its AI tools.

Cars bearing the flag of Netanyahu’s Likud Party drove through Jerusalem’s streets with loudspeakers blaring the Islamic call to prayer and urging, “Get out of your houses now! Arabs are voting!”

Like nearly all Jewish party leaders in Israel, Eisenkot opposes the two-state solution that once underpinned decades of peace negotiations with the Palestinians.

But he has criticised Jewish settler violence against Palestinians in the Israeli-occupied West Bank, which has surged since 2023 and strained Israel’s ties with Western states. And he opposes Netanyahu’s far-right coalition partners.

title: Netanyahu or Eisenkot: Why Israel's election may change little for Palestinians
text:
Although the two frontrunners in the Israeli elections could not be more different, neither would mean much of a difference for Palestine.

Incumbent Benjamin Netanyahu, despite his privileged upbringing in a well-to-do Jerusalem neighbourhood, has for long passed himself as the champion of the working man. Netanyahu’s American English and engaging oratory have contributed to his charm.

Netanyahu’s top challenger, Gadi Eisenkot, who served as his army chief and then in his war cabinet, grew up in the working-class township of Eilat that people of modest background actually identify with. Eisenkot joined the Golani Brigade, which could be said to be the heart of Israel’s infantry with deep roots in the land. He rose through its ranks to head the military. He is not sophisticated. Nor is he a great speaker. But he is a down to earth man who every working man can relate to.

Netanyahu is an Ashkenazi jew, meaning he is of European descent. Eisenkot is a Mizrahi -- those who are of Middle Eastern or oriental descent -- with parents from Morocco. Israel has never had a Mizrahi PM.

Netanyahu’s sons have made very little contribution to the ongoing genocide in Gaza, that Israelis appear to perceive as an existential war. In fact one of his sons has been hanging out in Miami for three years with state security at his disposal and is known for trolling political opponents of his father.

Eisenkot had driven his son to the reservists’ assembly point on October 7 when Hamas attacked Israel. A medic in the army, Eisenkot’s son died in December 2023 when he stepped on an IED. Eisenkot lost two nephews in this war too.

Both Netanyahu and Eisenkot have criticised each other for being too "soft" on Palestinians. Netanyahu, who has overseen the killing of 74,000 people in Gaza since October 2023, is "soft" on Palestine, says Eisenkot, who is credited with the "Dahiya Doctrine", which calls for disproportionate force and destruction of civilian infrastructure. The term is derived from the densely populated eponymous Beirut suburb which was a stronghold of Hezbollah. It suffered extensive bombardment in 2006.

Eisenkot has criticised Netanyahu for not caring about Israeli hostages and pulverising Gaza only to keep his far-right coalition intact. While Netanyahu continues to exempt the ultra-orthodox Jews from reserve duty and provides them government benefits, Eisenkot is of the view that everyone should share the burden of serving in the army. Although exemption for the orthodox Jews had been suspended in 2024, Netanyahu continues to overlook it, and in all likelihood, will continue to do so should he win.

Eisenkot’s alliance -- Israel has never had any single party carry the election -- is projected to take up to 54 seats in the 120-seat Knesset. Netanyahu’s coalition is projected to get about 50. It appears that Arab support could turn out to be the deciding factor. Arab parties have indicated that they might be ready to lend their support for an opposition alliance to remove Netanyahu from office.

But full results take time to come out and forming government is almost invariably a complicated affair often leading to inconclusive elections, necessitating further rounds of elections.

Since Israel’s electoral system is based on proportional representation, turn out really matters and this time there has been a record. Haaretz is reporting that Netanyahu has been railing against the Arabs for trying to "steal" the election by turning out in droves. The threshold for a party to get into the Knesset is 3.25% of the popular vote. Any party securing that percentage gets four seats.

About 15 million people live in areas under Israeli control. Just over 7 million Jewish Israelis and 1.7 million Palestinian citizens of Israel who live within what is called the green line (Israel’s pre-1967 borders) have voting rights.

Over 500,000 Israeli settlers who live in the occupied West Bank have voting rights. But the 3.1 million Palestinians do not. Similarly in occupied East Jerusalem, more than 230,000 Israelis have voting rights but about 350,000 Palestinians living there cannot.

Exit polls, due in about a few hours, may provide the first indications over who will preside over the next Israeli government but it will take a few days still for that to pan out.

title: Jamaat orders probe into alleged obstruction of freedom fighter Manik Pashari's burial
text:
Bangladesh Jamaat-e-Islami has formed a two-member committee to investigate allegations that its leaders and activists obstructed the janaza and burial of freedom fighter Manik Pashari in Pirojpur.

The committee has been asked to submit its report within three days.

The decision was taken at a special meeting of Jamaat’s Central Executive Council at the party’s central office on Tuesday evening. Leader of the Opposition and Jamaat Ameer Shafiqur Rahman chaired the meeting.

The committee comprises Jamaat MPs Saiful Alam Khan Milon and Nurul Islam Bulbul.

A press release issued after the meeting said the recent incident in Pirojpur was discussed in detail. The committee will conduct a fair and impartial investigation to determine whether anyone associated with the party was involved. The party’s local unit has been instructed to provide full cooperation to the investigation team.

On Saturday, relatives of Manik Pashari alleged that Jamaat leaders and activists obstructed the provision of state honours to the freedom fighter and his burial in Pirojpur. Pashari was a witness in the crimes against humanity case against Jamaat leader Delwar Hossain Sayeedi.

With assistance from Pirojpur district police, the body was later taken to the police lines, where a guard of honour was given at around 5:00pm. The body was subsequently kept under security before being buried in his village at around 2:00am on Sunday under police escort.

There were also allegations that the deceased’s female relatives were forced to dig the grave because of the obstruction.

title: Bonna reaches second final, Saima springs surprise
text:
Bonna Akter secured her second final berth at the Asia Cup Archery Stage-2 after edging compatriot Kulsum Akhter Mone in the women’s compound individual event in Sulaymaniyah, Iraq on Tuesday.

Having already reached the compound mixed team final, Bonna pulled off a nail-biting 142-141 victory over Mone to set up a gold-medal clash against Kazakhstan’s Burleva Milana on November 29.

Meanwhile, unheralded Saima Salah Uddin produced a stellar performance to advance to the final of the women’s recurve event. Saima handed Alexandra Zemlyanova a 6-4 defeat in the semifinals, booking a title showdown against Iran’s Fallah Mobina, also scheduled for November 29.

Despite the narrow semifinal heartbreak against Bonna, Mone will still have a chance to claim a podium finish when she competes in the bronze-medal match.

It will be a busy day for Bangladesh in the third-place playoffs, as Abdur Rahman Alif and Newas Ahmed Rakib will also fight for bronze medals in their respective recurve and compound events following their semifinal defeats on Tuesday.

title: Private ambulance owners strike at DMCH over parking facilities
text:
Private ambulance owners at Dhaka Medical College Hospital (DMCH) went on strike on Tuesday, demanding parking facilities on the hospital premises.

Mohammad Emon Ali, general secretary of the hospital unit of the Private Ambulance Owners Welfare Association, said ambulance owners had long been providing services to patients by parking their vehicles on the hospital premises.

Since the parking facilities were discontinued without any alternative arrangements, ambulance drivers have had to park on nearby roads, leaving them vulnerable to traffic congestion and cases filed by traffic police, he said.

“We will continue our strike until parking facilities are restored as they were before,” Emon Ali said.

However, DMCH Director Brigadier General AKM Farhad Hossain ruled out permanent parking facilities for private ambulances on the hospital premises.

“Our hospital has a shortage of space. How can we arrange parking for them?” he said.

The director said the hospital authorities had discussed the matter with law enforcement agencies. He warned that ambulance owners would face legal action if they continued the strike and held patients hostage while illegally parking their vehicles on nearby roads.

The authorities have also closed a room temporarily allocated to the private ambulance owners’ association near the emergency department. The room will instead be converted into a seating area for patients’ relatives, Farhad said.

Private ambulances will have to leave the hospital premises after dropping off patients and return only when needed to transport patients, he added.

“Most of our patients are poor and disadvantaged people who come here for treatment from remote parts of the country. Many of them are unfamiliar with the surrounding areas. Due to the shortage of space, we are unable to provide them with adequate seating facilities. While wandering outside the hospital, many fall victim to fraud,” he added.

Earlier on Monday, a large section of the hospital unit of the Private Ambulance Owners Welfare Association held a human chain at the hospital’s Garden Gate, demanding several measures, including permanent parking facilities and fixed ambulance fares.

title: Karnaphuli Garden City shuts down as old shopping malls struggle
text:
For many Dhaka residents now in their 30s, Karnaphuli Garden City Shopping Complex in Kakrail evokes memories of a bustling retail hub that drew shoppers from different income groups.

Opened in 1998, the complex shut down on October 1 after years of dwindling business, with only 25 of its 198 shops operational before the closure, according to its owners’ association.

Its closure highlights the challenges facing Dhaka’s older shopping destinations, as changing shopping habits, intensifying competition and falling sales erode their business.

At least 10 other older shopping complexes in the capital are also facing the prospect of closure amid dwindling customer numbers and a prolonged business slump, according to information gathered for this report.

The owners of Karnaphuli Garden City have decided to sell the property, with a hospital, diagnostic centre or office space among the possible future uses.

The development raises questions about whether other established shopping complexes can adapt to changing market conditions and remain viable.

FROM BUSTLING HUB TO CLOSURE

Developed by Karnaphuli Group, the complex occupied the basement and first four floors of a 20-storey building, with residential apartments above. Its shops sold ready-made garments, shoes, cosmetics, jewellery and other goods, alongside a food court.

AKM Iqbal, president of the Karnaphuli Garden City Shop Owners’ Association, told The Daily Star that the owners had unanimously decided to sell the property.

Image Photo: Mehedi Hasan/Star

“We are selling it. All the owners are making this decision together. It could become a hospital, a diagnostic centre, a television centre or any other type of office,” he said.

The main complex has shut down, although a handful of shops near the entrance remain open to generate rental income to cover essential expenses, including security guards’ and a manager’s salaries. The owners are even borrowing money to meet these costs, Iqbal said.

The closure does not affect the residential apartments on the upper floors, according to the authorities.

Concord Twin Tower in nearby Shantinagar is also grappling with sluggish business. Although reports suggested the complex might close, its owners later backed away from the decision.

Syed Sharif Uddin, joint secretary of the Concord Twin Tower Owners’ Association, said there were no plans to shut down the complex.

“Our business is not doing well. However, no decision has been taken to close the complex. We are trying to attract customers,” he said.

CHANGING SHOPPING HABITS

Iqbal said Dhaka’s retail market had changed significantly, with new malls, branded outlets and online shopping giving customers more choices.

“Customers can now compare prices and product quality across shops and online platforms. They do not always need to visit traditional shopping complexes,” he said.

Declining footfall has made it harder for shop owners to cover rent, service charges, staff salaries and electricity bills, he added.

Md Helal Uddin, president of the Bangladesh Dokan Malik Samity, said shopping markets had been facing a severe downturn for nearly two to two and a half years. Some shopkeepers go three to five consecutive days without making a sale, he said.

Many businesses can no longer pay staff from their earnings and are dipping into their capital to meet payroll costs. Even those willing to sell goods without making a profit are struggling to stay afloat.

Helal Uddin warned that two or three more markets could close within the next two to three months if the situation did not improve. Representatives of two markets, each with around 300 shops, had recently told him they could no longer sustain their businesses.

He said small and medium-sized businesses had received little government support during the downturn, claiming they had not benefited from taxpayer-funded relief measures since the Covid-19 pandemic.

Closures could wipe out investments worth hundreds of crores of taka and leave thousands of workers unemployed, with few alternative job opportunities, he warned.

Citing Karnaphuli Market, he said the four-floor commercial centre had employed around 3,000 workers and attracted shoppers with its shopping environment and competitive prices.

The association also identified Molla Tower in Rampura, opposite the Television Center, and Bishal Centre in Maghbazar as struggling. It estimated that another 10 to 12 shopping centres in Dhaka faced a serious risk of closure but declined to identify them.

title: Israelis shatter turnout records to pass wartime judgment on Netanyahu
text:
Israelis surged to the polls on Tuesday at a pace that shattered records, to pass wartime ​judgment on Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in what voters described as the most consequential election in the nation's history.

Long lines formed outside polling stations for the first election since the October 7, 2023, Hamas-led ‌attacks, with voters passionately engaged over the trauma of the country's deadliest day and the ensuing wars in Gaza, Lebanon and Iran.

The Central Elections Committee reported that 44.9% of eligible voters had already cast their ballots within the first seven hours of voting, with eight more hours to go. That "broke all records", it said.

Policies of Netanyahu's right-wing coalition have been divisive at home and have deepened Israel's international isolation, while he has defended his record, calling himself the only leader with the mettle to face down Israel's foes.

Netanyahu, Israel's longest-serving leader with 19 years in office, is an ​unmatched political survivor, and his nationalist politics are increasingly entrenched. Israel's fragmented system makes it difficult for an array of opponents to force out his coalition of right-wing, far-right and ultra-Orthodox parties.

His main rival Gadi Eisenkot, a military ​ex-chief of staff and security hawk, aims to unseat him with the support of parties on the right and centre, as well as the rump of an increasingly marginalised left. Opinion polls ⁠show a close race, with neither leader facing an easy path to power.

Forecasters were hesitant to guess what impact the unprecedented turnout might have on the result. A surge in votes from Israelis of Palestinian heritage could limit gains for Netanyahu's ​right-wing coalition, while increasing the odds that any government formed to oust him would require Arab parties' support, a contentious prospect among Jewish party leaders.

In a message to supporters more than five hours after polls opened, Netanyahu urged them to vote, saying turnout ​was high among his opponents on the left and among Israelis of Arab heritage, around a fifth of the country.

"We need it to be high too. You all need to stream to the polls," he said. "This is a fateful moment."

VOTER SEES ELECTION AS MOST IMPORTANT SHE'S KNOWN

"I think these elections are the most important of all the ones I’ve known," said Ruth Epstein, an 81-year-old longtime left-wing voter in Ramat Gan near Tel Aviv, who voted for the opposition Democrats.

"I’m really scared about what will be here."

Netanyahu has campaigned on an endorsement from US President Donald Trump, ​his ally in war against Iran, who has said they should "finish the job".

If neither Netanyahu nor Eisenkot can form a governing coalition in the 120-seat parliament, Netanyahu could stay on as caretaker until another election is held.

His opponents have managed to wrest him ​from the premiership only once since 2009, and that took four inconclusive elections in two years. He was back 18 months later.

EISENKOT SEES 'NEW SPIRIT'

For many of Netanyahu's opponents, the election turns on accountability for the security failures of October 7, Israel's deadliest day. Opposition groups have promised ‌to hold a ⁠national inquiry, which Netanyahu's government has resisted.

"I am convinced that by the end of today, we will see a change — a new spirit for the State of Israel — that will serve as a rectification for the past three years and for that terrible day," Eisenkot said during a visit to kibbutz Nir Oz in southern Israel, targeted in the October 7 attacks.

He walked to the polls with Gadi Mozes, one of 251 people kidnapped by Hamas and taken to Gaza during the attack that killed 1,200 people.

Eisenkot says Israel's response — a war which health authorities say killed more than 74,000 Palestinians — was a failure because Hamas remains in charge. He repeated his commitment to dismantle or destroy Hamas' military and governing power in Gaza within 18 months of forming ​a government.

Itamar Ben-Gvir, leader of a far-right party in Netanyahu's ​coalition, cast his vote in the Kiryat Arba settlement ⁠in the occupied West Bank early on Tuesday. He predicted Netanyahu would return as prime minister and his own party would serve as the right-wing anchor of the government.

ARAB TURNOUT COULD BE KEY

Ahmed Tibi, a candidate from an Arab party, said the record turnout from Israel's Arab minority would "pave the way for an alternative government and change the grave reality".

Eisenkot has ruled out partnering with ​Arab parties, citing a lack of shared values, although some possible scenarios envision them propping up a minority government to topple Netanyahu.

Netanyahu has repeatedly described Arab-Israeli voters as a threat in language his ​opponents say crosses into racism. He posted ⁠an AI-generated image on X on Tuesday showing Arabs including women in niqabs queuing at a polling station, and told his supporters they were in a battle for the country's future.

Cars with flags of Netanyahu's Likud Party drove through the Jerusalem streets with loudspeakers blaring the Islamic call to prayer and saying: "Get out of your houses now. Arabs are voting."

Like nearly all Jewish party leaders in Israel, Eisenkot opposes the two-state solution that once underpinned decades of peace negotiations with the Palestinians.

But he has criticised Jewish settler violence against Palestinians ⁠in the Israeli-occupied ​West Bank, which has surged since 2023 and strained Israel's ties with Western states. And he opposes Netanyahu's far-right coalition partners.

Israel flattened much of Gaza ​in the offensive launched after October 7, and now occupies around two-thirds of the enclave under a year-old US-brokered ceasefire. Negotiations for Hamas to disarm and Israel to withdraw have stalled.

Israel also dealt heavy blows to Iran-backed Hezbollah in Lebanon, where it now occupies a swathe of territory, and traded strikes ​with Iran, leading to a 12-day air campaign in 2025 and this year's joint US-Israeli war.

title: Indian firm L&T wins up to $1b Dhaka Metro Rail contracts
text:
India’s infrastructure major Larsen & Toubro (L&T) has secured contracts worth up to $1 billion to design and build two key system packages for Dhaka Metro Rail Line 1.

The contracts cover track works, electrical systems, signalling, telecommunications and platform screen doors, the company said in a stock exchange disclosure.

Dhaka Metro Rail Line 1 is Bangladesh’s first underground metro rail project. It will connect Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport (HSIA) to Kamalapur, passing through Rampura, Malibagh and Rajarbag, before branching towards Purbachal.

L&T is an engineering, procurement and construction (EPC) and high-tech manufacturing conglomerate.

The company said the awards build on its previous work in Bangladesh, where it won and delivered the integrated railway systems package for Dhaka Metro Line 6, the country’s first metro rail corridor.

The announcement follows the Cabinet Committee on Government Purchase approval of eight construction packages for Metro Rail Line 1 and Line 5 (Northern Route), worth about Tk 58,500 crore.

L&T classified the combined contracts as a “major” order under its standardised reporting framework, which defines such orders as those valued between ₹5,000 crore and ₹10,000 crore.

Apart from the Indian firm, contractors from Japan, China and Bangladesh have also secured work on the two metro lines. The projects are funded by the Japan International Cooperation Agency (JICA).

Dhaka Metro Line 1 will span about 31km across two routes: an underground section from HSIA to Kamalapur and an elevated section from Natun Bazar to Purbachal Terminal. The line will have 19 stations and a depot at Pitalganj.

The 20km Metro Rail Line 5 (Northern Route) will run from Hemayetpur in Savar through Gabtoli, Mirpur-14 and Natun Bazar to Vatara.

title: UN probe says Bangladeshis among nationals of 29 countries trafficked into Russian army
text:
Bangladeshis were among nationals of 29 countries trafficked into the Russian armed forces through deception or coercion, with many lured by promises of well-paid civilian jobs before being sent to fight in Ukraine, a United Nations investigation has found.

Recruits were often forced to sign military contracts written in Russian, a language most could not understand; many were killed or went missing, leaving their families struggling to establish their fate, it added.

UN's Independent International Commission of Inquiry on Ukraine also obtained copies of business visas issued to Bangladeshi recruits, showing that a civilian company in Russia had invited them.

The findings, presented to the UN General Assembly's Third Committee yesterday, come amid growing concerns over Bangladeshis seeking jobs in Russia and reports of workers being forced into combat, killed or captured.

Despite the risks, data from the Bureau of Manpower, Employment and Training's (BMET) Overseas Employment Platform show that 7,949 employment clearances were issued for Russia from Bangladesh between January 1, 2025, and October 27, 2026.

A joint investigation by Fortify Rights and Truth Hounds in March this year identified at least 104 Bangladeshis recruited into the Russian military, at least 34 of whom were reportedly killed. Families of several victims were still struggling to confirm their deaths or bring their bodies home.

The UN report did not specify how many Bangladeshis had been trafficked, killed or reported missing.

The commission investigated recruitment involving nationals of 48 countries and found evidence of deceptive or coercive practices involving people from 29 countries, including Bangladesh, India, Sri Lanka, the Philippines, Kenya, Nigeria and Uzbekistan.

Its findings were based on 245 testimonies from recruits, their families and other sources, as well as documents including employment invitations, visas, travel records and contracts with the Russian Ministry of Defence.

The commission concluded that Russian authorities, working with recruitment agents in various countries, had committed human trafficking and other human rights violations.

Recruitment agents advertised lucrative civilian jobs in Russia as security guards, drivers, mechanics, electricians, construction workers and technicians. Some also promised Russian citizenship, comfortable accommodation, pensions and other benefits.

The offers appeared credible, particularly to people from poor economic backgrounds with little or no military experience. Agents arranged visas, air tickets and accommodation, sometimes accompanying recruits on their journeys.

After arriving in Russia, however, the men were taken to temporary accommodation and handed over to the military. Many were compelled to sign one-year contracts with the Russian Ministry of Defence, written only in Russian.

Their passports and mobile phones were often confiscated, restricting communication and attempts to escape. Some were threatened with violence when they refused to sign.

Military training lasted anywhere from 20 minutes to a few days or up to a month before deployment.

On the frontlines in Ukraine, recruits were assigned dangerous tasks, including advancing towards enemy positions, digging trenches and collecting the bodies of fallen soldiers. Many were killed, injured or went missing soon after deployment, the report said.

In one case documented by the commission, a civilian company gave 30 recruits written assurances that they would not be sent to the Russia-Ukraine war. Yet 17 were subsequently killed on the frontline, five went missing and one returned injured. The commission did not identify their nationalities.

Investigators also found that recruitment agents and military personnel sometimes diverted promised salaries and bonuses, leaving victims and their families in financial distress.

Bangladeshis caught in the war

The Daily Star had earlier reported allegations that Bangladeshis lured to Russia with promises of civilian jobs were forced into military service and sent to fight in Ukraine.

In April last year, the Criminal Investigation Department's Human Trafficking Cell found that Dhaka-based Dream Home Travel had trafficked around 20 Bangladeshis to Russia with promises of civilian jobs paying Tk 2 lakh to Tk 2.5 lakh a month. At least three were reportedly killed after allegedly being forced into combat.

On October 14, the Special Response Battalion (SRB) said 20 of a group of 30 Bangladeshis sent to Russia with promises of construction jobs had been killed in the war. Seventeen reportedly died in drone strikes on their first day on the frontline, while three others died later.

According to the SRB, the workers travelled to Russia on May 7 through three recruitment agencies, paying an average of Tk 10 lakh each. Instead of receiving construction jobs, they were handed over to the Russian military and deployed after just 21 days of training.

The elite force arrested two alleged members of the trafficking network on October 13.

Shariful Islam Hasan, associate director of BRAC’s Migration Programme, said the organisation had published a report last year on the recruitment of Bangladeshis into the Russian military and warned about the risks at the time.

He said the government must take urgent steps to prevent more Bangladeshis from becoming involved in the war.

“It is equally important to trace the whereabouts of around 8,500 Bangladeshis who travelled legally to Russia over the last two years. The government needs to find out how many are still working there, how many have become involved in the war and how many are still alive,” he added.

He also called for an investigation into Bangladeshis who travelled to Russia on tourist visas, in light of the UN commission’s findings.

The UN commission said that recruiting foreign nationals through deception and coercion constituted human trafficking and called on Russia to immediately release victims still serving in its armed forces. It also recommended investigating and prosecuting those involved in the recruitment networks.

It stressed that victims trafficked into the Russian military should not be treated as mercenaries. Those who were captured or surrendered were entitled to protection as prisoners of war under the Third Geneva Convention, it added.

title: Tarique Rahman’s Japan visit: Japan’s bet on Bangladesh is really about the Bay of Bengal
text:
Prime Minister Tarique Rahman’s October 26–29 visit to Japan is framed around strengthening the strategic partnership and coordinating on Japan’s updated Free and Open Indo-Pacific (FOIP) vision. Japan does not view Dhaka merely as an aid partner, a market or a stop on a diplomatic itinerary. It sees a strategically located country on the Bay of Bengal that can connect maritime routes, supply chains and markets across South and Southeast Asia. Bangladesh, in turn, should see the visit as a negotiation over the terms of that connection. Tokyo’s core interest is a predictable and open regional environment. Dhaka’s interest is to turn that preference into national capabilities, economic value and greater foreign-policy options.

The relationship has already moved beyond development assistance. In 2023, the two governments elevated their ties to a strategic partnership. Their joint statement brought together freedom of navigation, regional connectivity, quality infrastructure, supply-chain resilience and maritime cooperation. That combination is revealing. Japan’s approach links economic integration to regional order: ports and roads move goods, but they also embed financing terms, technical standards, commercial networks and security arrangements. Bangladesh’s challenge is to shape those connections so that they expand its choices rather than simply make it a corridor through which other countries’ interests pass.

The Bay is more than a shipping map

Japan’s primary interest is maritime. Its foreign ministry has described the Bay of Bengal as lying along vital sea lanes for Japan. The point is not that Bangladesh controls those routes; it does not. Rather, the Bay’s stability affects the wider maritime system on which Japan’s trade depends. Safe passage, reliable information about activities at sea and the ability to respond to disasters are therefore strategic concerns for Tokyo. For Dhaka, the same conditions matter for trade, fisheries, coastal livelihoods, disaster response and any credible plan to develop a blue economy. The overlap creates room for cooperation, but the two countries approach it from different geographical positions and with different capabilities.

The clearest recent signal is Japan’s Official Security Assistance (OSA). In July 2026, Japan handed over five patrol boats to the Bangladesh Navy. Tokyo said the boats were intended to improve monitoring, surveillance and disaster-relief operations in the Bay. Its explanation of OSA is also unusually direct: the programme is designed to strengthen partner countries’ security capabilities, deepen security cooperation and help create a desirable security environment for Japan. That statement identifies both sides of the transaction. The equipment can help Bangladesh perform practical tasks, while the relationship also gives Japan a deeper role in the region’s maritime security landscape.

Image Prime Minister Tarique Rahman meets a Japanese parliamentary delegation led by former Prime Minister Taro Aso in Tokyo on 26 October 2026. During the meeting, he sought Japan’s support for the safe and voluntary repatriation of Rohingya refugees. Photo: PMO

That dual purpose should be discussed openly, not treated as evidence of a hidden alliance. A patrol boat is not a treaty commitment, and Bangladesh should not turn a limited capability-building project into a promise of geopolitical alignment. At the same time, acknowledging that Japan has its own strategic interests makes cooperation easier to negotiate honestly. Dhaka can ask what the assistance enables, how maintenance and training will be funded, which agencies will use the information gathered and what safeguards apply to operational data. Such questions make the partnership more durable because they define responsibilities before a crisis tests them.

Bangladesh also has concrete reasons to improve its maritime capacity. The Bay is a source of livelihoods and a route for commerce, but it is also exposed to cyclones, accidents, smuggling and other risks that do not stop at national boundaries. Boats alone cannot provide maritime awareness. They need trained crews, reliable communications, maintenance budgets, legal procedures and coordination among the Navy, Coast Guard, ports and disaster management agencies. Japan’s contribution will matter most if it helps build that system over time. For Tokyo, deeper day-to-day cooperation can strengthen confidence in the region’s security environment. For Bangladesh, the test is whether each new capability remains under clear national command and addresses an identified national need.

Connectivity is a form of influence

Japan’s second core interest is economic connectivity. The 2023 statement described Bangladesh as a potential bridge between the large markets of South and Southeast Asia. Japan’s Diplomatic Bluebook links the Bay of Bengal Industrial Growth Belt (BIG-B) with a broader industrial value chain extending towards India’s northeast. This is more than a plan to move containers faster. If roads, railways, ports and industrial zones connect across borders, they can influence where firms locate, which suppliers secure contracts and which technical standards become standard practice. Connectivity changes the geography of production as well as that of transport.

That is why Japan’s interest in infrastructure has a geopolitical dimension, even when a project is described in commercial or developmental terms. A long-term infrastructure network creates enduring relationships among lenders, contractors, regulators, operators and businesses. It can reduce logistical costs and make production more resilient, but it can also shape future choices through the standards and financing arrangements attached to it. Japan has promoted “quality infrastructure” alongside transparency, life-cycle costs and debt sustainability. Those principles are not merely decorative. They are part of the rules Japan wants to normalise across the region, and they matter to Bangladesh because the cost of a poorly chosen project can outlast the government that approved it.

Image Prime Minister Tarique Rahman is briefed on the layout plan of Matarbari Deep Sea Port during an inspection of the project site in Maheshkhali, Cox’s Bazar, on 9 August 2026. Photo: PID

The distinction between being a bridge and being a hub is equally important. A bridge carries traffic between places; a hub captures some of the value created by that traffic. Bangladesh cannot become a regional production centre merely by sitting between markets or allowing goods to cross its territory. It needs reliable links between ports and factories, predictable customs procedures, power and logistics services, skilled workers and local firms capable of supplying larger production networks. If those elements are missing, the country may bear the land, financing and environmental costs of connectivity while firms elsewhere capture most of the gains. Japan’s interest in a connected Bay can serve Bangladesh’s development, but only if Dhaka negotiates for domestic value creation rather than treating connectivity itself as the outcome.

The Economic Partnership Agreement (EPA), signed in February 2026, gives the relationship a rule-making dimension. Its official text and related documents establish a framework for closer trade and investment ties; they do not, by themselves, generate new exports or employment. The full agreement text also covers customs, product standards, services, investment, e-commerce, procurement, labour, the environment and transparency. Businesses need to understand the rules, meet standards and find buyers. Public agencies need to ensure that customs procedures, certification and implementation are predictable. Japanese firms need a stable commercial environment, while Bangladeshi producers need practical support to enter supply chains. The EPA’s geopolitical value will depend on whether both sides use it to generate reciprocal economic activity, rather than treating its signing as proof that the hard work is finished.

Why Japan matters to Dhaka’s foreign policy

Japan matters to Bangladesh because it can expand the country’s foreign-policy options. Japan’s own evaluation of its development assistance describes it as Bangladesh’s largest bilateral development partner and recognises its long record of support in infrastructure, power, transport, health and education. That record has built trust, but the relationship cannot rely indefinitely on the donor-recipient model. Bangladesh needs investment, technology, market access and skills that support a more diversified economy. Japan needs credible partners and stable regional networks. A strategic relationship is valuable precisely when both sides have something to gain and the terms are clear.

For Dhaka, a closer relationship with Tokyo can also reduce the risk of relying too heavily on any single external partner. This should not be presented as a choice between Japan and China, or between Japan and India. Bangladesh has substantial relations with its neighbours and other major economies; its geographical and economic realities make those relationships unavoidable. The foreign-policy objective is not to keep every partner at an identical distance. It is to retain the capacity to make decisions on an issue-by-issue basis, compare offers and reject terms that do not serve national priorities. Diversification creates that capacity only when Bangladesh’s institutions can assess projects, negotiate contracts and enforce agreed rules.

Image Prime Minister’s Defence Adviser Brig Gen (retd) Dr AKM Shamsul Islam and Japan’s Parliamentary Vice-Minister for Foreign Affairs Shimada Tomoaki pose with senior officials following the formal handover of five patrol boats to the Bangladesh Navy under Japan’s Official Security Assistance (OSA) programme in Chattogram on 2 July 2026. Photo: ISPR

Strategic autonomy is sometimes mistaken for silence or equidistance. In practice, it means having sufficient economic and diplomatic room to make decisions without any one partner becoming indispensable. Bangladesh’s own Indo-Pacific Outlook describes its regional vision as free, open, peaceful, secure and inclusive, while grounding engagement in sovereignty, international law and the UN Charter. That formulation gives Dhaka a useful foundation: it can support freedom of navigation, peaceful dispute settlement and resilient trade without adopting every aspect of another government’s strategy. Japan’s FOIP is a Japanese policy framework, not an obligation for Bangladesh to adopt it wholesale.

Nor should Bangladesh assume that Japan’s approach is politically neutral. Tokyo’s development policy explicitly treats cooperation as an important tool of diplomacy, and its regional strategy seeks to strengthen a rules-based order in which Japan has influence. The question is not whether Japan has strategic interests; every major international partner does. The question is whether those interests can be reconciled with Bangladesh’s priorities through transparent terms and reciprocal commitments. That distinction is especially important as security cooperation grows. If Dhaka explains each step in terms of specific capabilities and public benefits, it is less likely to be perceived as joining a bloc. If it leaves the terms vague, other governments may define their meaning for it.

What the Tokyo visit should test

The visit should therefore be judged by the quality of the arrangements it initiates, not by the number of agreements, the status of a new partnership label or the warmth of the photographs.

On maritime cooperation, the two sides could set out practical next steps for training, maintenance, disaster response and information-sharing. Data access and command authority should be agreed upon in advance. Bangladesh should identify which agencies will use the new capabilities and how they will coordinate. These details may attract less attention than a headline about new equipment, but they determine whether cooperation improves public safety and strengthens Bangladesh’s own institutions.

On the economic side, a useful agenda would link the EPA to the readiness of firms and public agencies. That means making rules understandable to exporters, helping smaller suppliers meet certification requirements and aligning infrastructure decisions with sectors that can create local production and jobs. Major connectivity proposals should be assessed for commercial demand, public costs, debt exposure, environmental effects and the distribution of benefits. Publishing the reasoning behind those decisions would help build confidence at home and abroad. Japan’s emphasis on quality and transparency is most valuable when Bangladesh applies those principles to projects it chooses for itself.

Image Prime Minister Tarique Rahman arrives in Tokyo on 26 October 2026 for a four-day official visit aimed at strengthening bilateral ties, attracting investment and expanding economic cooperation. Photo: BNP Media Cell

The leaders should also treat regional diplomacy as part of the economic relationship. The Bay’s stability cannot be separated from developments in Myanmar, the Rohingya displacement crisis, climate shocks or the interests of India and Southeast Asian states. Japan has experience and diplomatic reach that can support dialogue and humanitarian cooperation, while Bangladesh has direct knowledge of the costs of regional instability. Neither country can resolve these problems alone. Regular consultations can help them coordinate their positions without requiring Bangladesh to endorse every Japanese assessment or turning bilateral cooperation into a substitute for regional institutions.

A final measure of success is whether the relationship becomes more institutionalised and less dependent on individual visits. Targets, responsible agencies, review dates and public reporting can turn political intent into accountable action. This is not merely bureaucratic detail. It is how Bangladesh ensures that an agreement serves national development after the visiting delegations leave. It is also how Japan can be confident that commitments will survive changes in government and translate into reliable partnerships.

Japan’s interest in Bangladesh is neither charity nor a single security transaction. It is a bet on a stable, connected Bay of Bengal and on Bangladesh’s ability to participate in the regional order taking shape around it. Bangladesh should welcome the opportunity while resisting the temptation to define its value solely through geography. A bridge without local production is a passageway; a strategic partnership without domestic capacity is merely a label. Tarique Rahman’s Tokyo visit can lay the groundwork for a more balanced relationship if Dhaka uses Japan’s interest to build capabilities, broaden its economic choices and preserve the freedom to make its own decisions. The Bay may give Bangladesh strategic relevance. Only deliberate policy can turn that relevance into power.

Mohd Amdadul Haque is a doctoral candidate in the Department of International Politics at Shandong University and an assistant professor in the Department of Political Science at Gopalganj Science and Technology University. He can be reached at [email protected].

title: How Fazlul Huq's Krishak Praja Party reshaped peasant politics in Bengal
text:
In colonial Bengal, debt was not an event but a condition of existence. For generations, peasant families in eastern Bengal were born into debt, and this burden shaped their lives. When they died, the financial burden passed to their offspring as an unwelcome inheritance. Debt was more than a financial obligation. For many cultivators, it structured social relations, constrained economic choices, and defined the limits of autonomy. The majority of lenders and creditors were Hindus. The debts owed to them were more than mere financial liabilities. They created a system of dependence that trapped cultivators in unequal power relations. In this sense, debt functioned as the quiet architecture of rural life, a pervasive and enduring condition from which escape was often impossible. It was within this landscape of chronic indebtedness that A. K. Fazlul Huq and the Krishak Praja Party (KPP) developed a powerful political appeal, presenting legal reform and debt relief as instruments of both economic justice and rural emancipation.

Historical background

The Mughal land system represented a distinctive arrangement of rights and obligations. Rather than a single hierarchy of ownership, it was characterised by overlapping claims among the peasant, the zamindar, and the state. The peasant, as the actual cultivator, had the most fundamental claim: a hereditary right of possession, officially recognised as proprietary. Ordinary cultivators were referred to as owners and landholders, while administrative records protested against the sale of peasants’ “proprietary and hereditary lands”, confirming that such rights were understood as genuine property. This right was individual rather than communal. Zamindars in Bengal enjoyed considerable power and autonomy compared with their counterparts in many other parts of the Mughal Empire, partly because of the state's limited administrative penetration into the Bengal countryside. Even during Aurangzeb's reign, only about 1.5 percent of Bengal's villages had been measured for revenue assessment, compared with approximately 49 percent across the Mughal Empire.



Image Sher-e-Bangla A. K. Fazlul Huq at his residence on Eid Day, 1954. Photograph by James Burke. Courtesy of LIFE magazine.

After 1765, the East India Company’s main priority became securing a steady revenue stream, yet annual settlements yielded poor results. Successive experiments dispossessed zamindars or forced them to accept unfavourable conditions, causing widespread financial ruin. By 1775, zamindars had accumulated enormous debts and lost much of their former prestige and influence. This decline threatened the very structure of rural governance, while agricultural cultivation also declined. In 1786, the Board of Directors directed that a permanent settlement be established with zamindars recognised as proprietors and land revenue fixed in perpetuity. The British East India Company introduced the Permanent Settlement, also known as the Zamindari Settlement, in 1793. This revenue system was primarily implemented in Bengal, Bihar, and Orissa, and later extended to parts of Madras and the Varanasi region. Willem van Schendel, in his book A History of Bangladesh, argues that the Permanent Settlement formed the nucleus of the colonial system of control; other branches of administration, such as the executive, judiciary and police, were organised to ensure its effective functioning.

The colonial land revenue system and the unequal agrarian relations that developed under it gradually entrenched rural indebtedness, leaving Bengal's peasantry particularly vulnerable to economic shocks. The Great Depression of the 1930s further aggravated these conditions by severely restricting access to credit, with disastrous consequences for sharecroppers and marginal peasants. The indebtedness of Bengal’s rural poor was not simply a consequence of individual misfortune or isolated crop failures. Rather, it was an inherent feature of an agrarian system designed to concentrate power and wealth. As illustrated by Sugata Bose’s influential classification, risks were determined by one’s position in the social hierarchy; landless sharecroppers, known as bargadars, and marginal peasants were structurally vulnerable. This vulnerability was ruthlessly exploited by the jotedar class, which, as Ratnalekha Ray points out, established an “economic empire” combining the roles of landowner, grain merchant, and moneylender. Taj Hashmi reports that Muslim farmers clearly articulated the relationship between their personal identities and their indebtedness. One cultivator from Mymensingh complained:

“My father, sir, was born in debt, grew in debt and died in debt. I have inherited my father’s debt, and my son will inherit mine” (quoted in Taj Hashmi’s Pakistan as a Peasant Utopia: The Communalization of Class Politics in East Bengal, 1920–1947, 1992, p. 44).



The 1928 Tenancy Amendment: Legal gains and limits

The Bengal Tenancy Amendment Act of 1928 was a crucial element of Huq's legislative strategy, and he was among its strongest supporters in the Bengal Legislative Council, arguing vigorously on behalf of the peasants. The Bengal Tenancy Act of 1885 provided safeguards for peasants, but these proved ineffective. By the 1920s, peasants in East Bengal faced persistent losses of land. The 1885 Act made it difficult to acquire occupancy rights, requiring 12 years of continuous cultivation. Moneylenders exploited legal mechanisms to acquire land, a process that Iftekhar Iqbal describes as "depeasantisation".

When the 1928 Bill was introduced, Huq spoke on behalf of the raiyat, especially the under-raiyat, and encountered significant resistance from a coalition aligned with the zamindars. The Bill permitted a rent increase of up to four annas per rupee for an under-raiyat. Huq sought to limit this increase to two annas per rupee, but his proposal was defeated, with 27 votes in favour and 39 against. Ekramul Huq proposed another amendment to restrict evictions, but the motion was overwhelmingly defeated, with only 17 votes in favour and 59 against.

The 1928 Amendment failed to provide comprehensive protection, yet the debate strengthened his legislative agenda. It established a public record of his advocacy on behalf of peasants. However, A. K. Fazlul Huq understood that reforming tenancy alone would not suffice. The credit system also needed to be regulated. That would require new legislation, the Bengal Agricultural Debtors Act of 1935. These developments laid the groundwork for his subsequent political activities.



Image A massive crowd gathered on the seashore of Sandwip, c. 1937, to listen to Sher-e-Bangla A. K. Fazlul Huq’s speech, delivered from a launch offshore. Many stood in the water to hear their beloved leader. Courtesy: Bangladesh on Record.

The 1935 Debtors Act as Fazlul Huq's institutional weapon

The 1928 Bengal Tenancy Amendment Act gave farmers greater ownership rights over their land. However, it had no effect on the credit system. With no effective regulations governing debt and no legal ceiling on interest rates, a moneylender could still cause a peasant to lose everything, while even a manifestly unjust loan agreement could be legally enforced. There were no adequate legal safeguards for borrowers. This was the problem the Bengal Agricultural Debtors Act of 1935 (enacted as Bengal Act VII of 1936) sought to address. The 1928 legislation focused on peasants and landowners; by contrast, the 1935 Act addressed creditors and debtors, allowing the state to intervene in loan agreements and reduce excessive financial burdens. It aimed to protect a debtor's basic means of subsistence.

Before 1935, no law effectively regulated interest rates. The courts enforced loan agreements without examining the fairness of the interest charged; consequently, creditors generally prevailed, while debtors had little protection. Cooperative credit societies were intended to provide a solution to exploitation by moneylenders. However, this approach proved ineffective. Even by the early 1940s, only 10.6 percent of borrowing families in Bengal could obtain loans from cooperatives. In the period immediately preceding the 1935 Act, coverage was only 6.6 percent. More than 90 percent of peasants had little alternative but to depend on private lenders.



Although the Great Depression exacerbated this problem, its underlying causes were legal and institutional. By the mid-1930s, voluntary initiatives and cooperatives could no longer adequately address the problem. New legislation was needed to regulate interest rates and protect borrowers from dispossession. This legislation was the Bengal Agricultural Debtors Act of 1935. The Bill was introduced by Sir John Anderson's administration. However, the law's real impact became apparent after A. K. Fazlul Huq assumed power in 1937. Huq regarded this Act as more than a legal instrument. It formed the foundation of his promise to the Muslim peasantry.

Evidence of this commitment could be found in Huq's election manifesto. The KPP's 14-point manifesto called for the establishment of Debt Settlement Boards and the abolition of zamindari without compensation. Huq had promised such relief in his election manifesto, and the Boards became one of his most visible achievements. Consequently, his government instructed district officials to establish Debt Settlement Boards throughout Bengal. The results were tangible. By December 1938, the Boards had examined creditors' claims worth Rs 367 lakh and reduced them to Rs 179 lakh. The Act did not eliminate rural poverty, yet it initiated a significant transformation. It changed how peasants perceived the state and their own indebtedness.

Party strategy: Mobilising the new peasant stakeholders

The legal reforms discussed above did not automatically translate into political power. The 1928 Tenancy Amendment Act and the 1935 Debtors Act created new interests in land and credit, but they did not organise voters. The Krishak Praja Party represented Huq’s attempt to transform these divergent interests into a unified political movement.

The 1928 Tenancy Amendment marked a major change in Bengal, yet it did not benefit everyone equally. Most under-raiyats acquired occupancy rights, but the bargadars (sharecroppers) were excluded and classified as “labourers” rather than tenants, leaving them without legal protection. The principal beneficiaries were the jotedars, wealthier peasants who leased land directly from zamindars. They could now seek legal recourse and resist eviction. These jotedars wanted to weaken the power of Hindu zamindars, not abolish landlordism entirely; they aspired to become the new landlords themselves.



Image Sher-e-Bangla A. K. Fazlul Huq with his cabinet after becoming the first Premier of Bengal under provincial autonomy in 1937.

Laws established rights, but they did not organise voters. Before the 1930s, Muslim peasants in East Bengal had no political party of their own. The Indian National Congress was dominated by Hindu lawyers and zamindars, while the Muslim League remained under the influence of wealthy landlords and nawabs. Neither represented the interests of indebted Muslim peasants. Peasants were also divided by geography and class: a peasant from Mymensingh had little connection with one from Faridpur, while a jotedar had different interests from a bargadar. Patron-client relationships deepened these divisions, as poor peasants depended on their jotedars for land and loans, making it difficult for them to join movements against their patrons. Hashmi argues that peasants bound by strong patronage relationships need trusted leaders; without them, they remain loyal to local patrons rather than uniting. Several Krishak Samitis emerged in the jute-growing regions during the early 1930s, but they remained fragmented and confined to local areas. The colonial government banned some as sources of unrest, while the violence in Pabna in 1926, followed by British accusations that Muslim mobs had attacked Hindu property, further undermined the movement’s legitimacy. The Samitis therefore needed a clear vision and a united platform; without a collective voice, they could not effectively challenge the zamindars, moneylenders or colonial government.

Huq had been mobilising peasants since the 1920s. In 1929, he helped establish the Nikhil Banga Praja Samity, or All-Bengal Tenants Association, which promoted the principle that land should belong to those who cultivated it. The Samity was divided between eastern and western Bengal. In 1935, Huq became its president. In July 1936, a gathering in Dhaka renamed it the Krishak Praja Party. In Bengali, “krishak” means peasant and “praja” means tenant. Huq wanted the party to represent not only tenants but also those who actually cultivated the land, a calculated decision to broaden its support ahead of the 1937 elections.



The KPP served as Huq’s umbrella organisation, bringing together three groups: jotedars who had benefited from the 1928 Tenancy Amendment, indebted peasants seeking relief under the 1935 Debtors Act, and landless cultivators seeking access to land. Critics described it as a “jotedar party”, and Huq’s associate Abul Mansur Ahmed acknowledged that this criticism was partly justified. Yet Ahmed defended the movement as “an authentic and organic people’s uprising, fitting the demands of the period.” Huq included jotedars because of their financial resources and ability to contest elections, while also advocating debt relief and the abolition of zamindari for the poorest peasants. His political achievement lay in bringing these competing interests together under one banner. The KPP’s 14-point manifesto demanded the abolition of zamindari without compensation, the establishment of Debt Settlement Boards, free primary education, and a reduction in ministers’ salaries to Rs 1,000 per month. In 1937, the KPP won 36 seats and secured nearly one-third of the Muslim electorate’s votes; Huq defeated Khwaja Nazimuddin, a prominent Muslim League leader and member of the Dhaka Nawab family, in the Patuakhali constituency. Thus, Huq transformed legislative advocacy and fragmented peasant grievances into a unified and organised electoral force.

Conclusion

In colonial Bengal, debt was an enduring condition of life, passed from one generation to the next. A. K. Fazlul Huq transformed this hereditary bondage into organised political power through legislation, party organisation and political rhetoric. The 1928 Tenancy Amendment strengthened peasants' occupancy rights, while the 1935 Bengal Agricultural Debtors Act provided for the establishment of Debt Settlement Boards. Huq subsequently formed the Krishak Praja Party, a coalition of jotedars, small farmers and landless peasants united in opposition to landlords and moneylenders and sharing the hope of debt relief. Following the 1937 election, in which the KPP won 36 seats and secured nearly one-third of the Muslim electorate’s votes, Huq's government established these Boards to reduce creditors' claims and protect peasant landholdings. Earlier methods of elite patronage and violence, as Broomfield demonstrated, had exhausted themselves by 1918. Huq channelled this popular energy into lasting institutions, the KPP and the Debt Settlement Boards, redirecting peasant discontent towards legal and electoral avenues.

Mehrab Islam Sakib holds an MA in History and Asian Studies from the Department of History and Philosophy at North South University, Dhaka.
