title: What Lula’s victory over the right means for democracy beyond Brazil
text:
Three weeks ago, Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva’s political obituaries had all been written.

The far-right presidential candidate, Flávio Bolsonaro, son of the jailed former President Jair Bolsonaro, had come out of the first round of the presidential election with a lead that looked impossible to overcome.

At 80 years old, Lula seemed headed for a quiet exit after four decades at the centre of Brazilian political life.

On Sunday, however, Lula proved everyone wrong. He won the runoff and secured a fourth non-consecutive term as Brazil’s president.

A night of firsts

The election result is unprecedented in Brazilian politics in at least three ways.

First, no Brazilian presidential candidate had ever won the first round and then lost the runoff. Since the two-round system was adopted by the 1988 Brazilian Constitution, the first-round leader had always gone on to win.

Lula broke that pattern by turning a defeat of around 2.2 million votes in the first round into a solid victory, in three weeks.

Second, no Brazilian president has ever been elected to four terms. When his new term ends, Lula will have governed Brazil for 16 (non-consecutive) years – the longest democratically elected tenure in the country’s history.

Only Getúlio Vargas governed longer. He held power for almost two decades through a revolution, dictatorship and democratic election from the 1930–50s, and is widely considered Brazil’s most consequential president.



Third, no runoff campaign in Brazil has ever brought so many people to the streets and onto social media, supporting both sides.

Unlike the first round, the second round was not quiet, nor was it decided by television ads. Brazil saw a mass mobilization of voters, and it was ferocious.

The Brazilian left fought an uphill battle against social media platforms, economic elites, and a Supreme Electoral Court whose president was accused of trying to tip the balance to favour Bolsonaro.

Lula has a long record of political miracles, and he has added another one to the list.



Image A supporter of Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva holds a flag reading ‘Lula’ as he celebrates in Brasilia, Brazil. Source: REUTERS

An election result that matters beyond Brazil

Lula’s victory matters well beyond Brazil’s borders, also in three ways.

Globally, Brazil remains a bulwark against the rise of the far right. In recent elections across Latin America and Europe, far-right parties and leaders have advanced almost everywhere.

Brazil, the world’s fourth-largest democracy, has now bucked the trend, and is a symbol that democrats elsewhere will not ignore.

Regionally, Lula has defied the so-called “incumbent curse”. Over the past decade in Latin America, governing parties have lost election after election, punished by voters for inflation, insecurity and economic stagnation.

Brazil’s economy was in reasonable shape, but its gains were modest and unevenly felt. Everything pointed to a defeat, and Lula beat the odds anyway.

His win is also a check on what critics have called the “Donroe Doctrine”, referring to the Trump administration’s push to bring the Western Hemisphere more firmly into the US sphere of influence through tariffs, threats and political patronage.

Bolsonaro had campaigned as Washington’s preferred partner in South America. Brazil’s voters turned that offer down.

Domestically, the result also shows the power of popular mobilisation on the left. After Lula’s poor first-round showing, Lula’s campaign re-energised demoralised supporters and built a broad coalition of voters, some of whom were voting less for Lula than against what Bolsonaro represents. It also mobilised people who had stayed home in the first round to get out to vote.



Image Brazil's presidential candidate Flavio Bolsonaro of the Liberal Party (PL) reacts after the country's electoral authority said he will face President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva in the runoff of a presidential election, in Brasilia, Brazil, Oct 4, 2026. Source: REUTERS

The battle is not over

Lula should not mistake survival for vindication. Yes, he corrected course. In three weeks, he acknowledged the mistakes he made over four years in office, especially during a lacklustre first-round campaign. He sharpened his message, widened his alliances and spoke directly to the voters he had lost. That is no small achievement for a politician, however experienced he may be.

But he now has to govern a country more polarised than ever. Political violence on the streets has increased, and hate speech circulates freely online.

Prominent figures on the far right, including Nikolas Ferreira and Lucas Pavanato, have already said they will not accept this election result. Bolsonaro said late Sunday he will not concede, and will seek an annulment of the vote.



And then there is Washington. Given the White House’s close ties to the Bolsonaro family, there is a real risk the Trump administration will question, or even refuse to recognise, the outcome of the election. That would be extraordinary, and a few years ago, it would have been unthinkable.

Things are further complicated by a legal battle on election day itself. After allegations of voter suppression of Lula’s supporters in several cities, the justices of Brazil’s Supreme Court and Supreme Electoral Court clashed over whether to extend voting hours. Whatever the legal merits, the dispute gives the losing side a ready-made narrative of “voting irregularities”. This could be a matter of serious concern, and it may last for weeks.



Image Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, the Workers' Party (PT) candidate for presidential re-election, is embraced by Andre Janones, a member of the Chamber of Deputies of Brazil, as he speaks after winning the presidential runoff election, in Sao Paulo, Brazil, Oct 25, 2026. Sources: REUTERS

Three questions for Lula’s next term

When Lula is inaugurated on January 5, three questions will define his fourth term.

The first is how Lula will govern a deeply divided country with a conservative majority in Congress and over a dozen right-wing state governors.

The legislature that held him hostage over the past four years has grown more hostile, not less. Every budget, every reform and every appointment will be a tough negotiation, with the possibility of an impeachment hanging over Lula’s head.



The second is repair. How will he deal with problems that go well beyond partisan disputes?

These include fiscal pressures from rising government spending, a steady loss of trust in democratic institutions, and an institutional system that no longer works as designed.

The Supreme Court, once the guarantor of the democratic order, has seen its legitimacy eroded by a major financial scandal surrounding Banco Master. Although the president cannot “repair” a court, he can refuse to treat the crisis as someone else’s problem.

The third question is the most important. Will Lula, his Workers’ Party (PT) and Brazil’s broader democratic forces use this reprieve to renew Brazilian politics? That would mean:

new political leadership alternatives beyond the ageing leaders who have dominated the left for 40 years

new forms of popular political participation that do not depend on a single charismatic figure

a new narrative that speaks to the precarious workers, religious families and angry voters who have drifted toward the far right.

This is the only real antidote to polarisation, and it will not come from a single election or a single leader.

Lula’s comeback has bought Brazil time. Whether it buys anything more depends on what he and his allies do over the next four years, one step at a time.

Lula has worked another miracle. His last task is to make sure Brazil does not need another one.

This article was first published under the title “Lula wins a ‘miracle’ election in Brazil. Now comes the hard part: putting the country back on the right track" in The Conversation, The Daily Star, on October 26, 2026.

Guilherme Casarões is an associate Professor of Brazilian Studies, Florida International University.

title: Bangladesh-Germany relations in a changing world order
text:
Dr Rüdiger Lotz, German Ambassador to Bangladesh, speaks to The Daily Star about Bangladesh’s growing significance in Germany’s Indo-Pacific outlook, opportunities to deepen bilateral trade and investment, democratic transition and institutional reform, cooperation in renewable energy and skilled migration, the Rohingya crisis, and lessons from German reunification.

The Daily Star (TDS): As the global order becomes increasingly multipolar and Asia gains greater economic and geopolitical significance, how does Germany view Bangladesh’s role in its broader Indo-Pacific strategy?

Rüdiger Lotz (RL): We have seen a significant shift in world politics. When I grew up in the 1980s, we lived in a world dominated by two major power blocs, the East and the West, with non-aligned countries in between. Today, we have a truly polycentric world order with multiple centres of influence, and Asia is becoming vastly more important.

Asia is crucial not only because of its population, with South Asia alone accounting for about a quarter of the world's population, but also because it is the primary growth region of the 21st century. While Europe maintains a high level of economic development, sustaining it requires investment in dynamic new growth markets.

On the political front, Berlin prioritises its bilateral relationship with Bangladesh, viewing it on its own merits rather than through the lens of its relations with other countries. We seek to work closely with partners who share our core values: the rule of law, democracy and a rules-based international order. Bangladesh has impressively demonstrated these shared values through its transition to a democratic government and democratic elections.

Image Dr Rüdiger Lotz, German Ambassador to Bangladesh. Photo: Star

TDS: Bangladesh and Germany have built a longstanding economic partnership, particularly in the ready-made garment sector. Which sectors offer the greatest potential for diversifying bilateral trade and investment, and how can the two countries strengthen cooperation in technology transfer?

RL: It is remarkable that Bangladesh has built an internationally competitive ready-made garment (RMG) sector. Even as we talk about diversification, Bangladesh should maintain this sector. About 20 per cent of all textiles sold in German shops are produced in Bangladesh, so the RMG sector is definitely here to stay.

However, economic diversification is essential. The lowest-hanging fruit for expansion is likely the leather sector, which holds excellent potential. Additionally, I see strong opportunities in agro-industry, light manufacturing and pharmaceutical products. Expanding into these sectors will also facilitate important forms of technology transfer between our nations.

TDS: As Bangladesh approaches graduation from least-developed-country status, how can Germany support its transition in terms of EU market access and trade preferences? What reforms would help Bangladesh attract greater German investment?

RL: When I was growing up, Bangladesh was synonymous with a poor country facing severe living conditions; today, it is, in macroeconomic terms, a middle-income country that has achieved impressive development.

To ensure a smooth economic transition regarding EU market access, negotiations on a free trade agreement (FTA) are set to begin very soon. Currently, Bangladesh benefits from tariff-free access under the EU's "Everything But Arms" (EBA) initiative. Because large-scale RMG production operates on thin margins, where even minor cost increases affect competitiveness, securing an FTA is key to retaining trade preferences and mitigating risks when LDC preferences expire.

To attract further German investment, the overall business climate must be addressed. Over the past few decades, Bangladesh has maintained an impressive rate of annual economic growth. If this trend continues over the next 20 to 40 years, the country could rank among the world’s 20 largest economies, supported by a middle class of more than 40 million people. To realise this potential, foreign investors need good governance, clear regulations, legal certainty and a reliable rule of law, under which legal disputes are resolved fairly and predictably in court. Furthermore, greater investment in infrastructure and education is required to develop the skilled workforce needed for more sophisticated manufacturing.

TDS: Bangladesh is undergoing a significant political transition following the February elections. How does Germany view these developments, and what opportunities exist for strengthening democratic institutions, governance and engagement between the two countries?

RL: A major Asian country returning from autocracy to democracy is a significant and uncommon event in today's global landscape, and one that has a positive regional impact. Working together with partners who share fundamental democratic values is naturally easier and more effective.

Sustainable development requires political stability. Since the new government took office following the February elections, Bangladesh has experienced a period of considerable stability compared with previous periods in its history, which is commendable and crucial for building long-term, sustainable bilateral relations.

Regarding institutional strengthening, Germany supports Bangladesh through development projects focused on areas such as access to justice and institutional independence. Beyond traditional government-to-government diplomacy, the key opportunity lies in fostering ongoing dialogue across different sectors of society, enabling experts and civil society members from both nations to engage directly with one another.

To attract further German investment, the overall business climate must be addressed. Over the past few decades, Bangladesh has maintained an impressive rate of annual economic growth. If this trend continues over the next 20 to 40 years, the country could rank among the world’s 20 largest economies, supported by a middle class of more than 40 million people. To realise this potential, foreign investors need good governance, clear regulations, legal certainty and a reliable rule of law

TDS: Renewable energy and energy efficiency have long been important areas of Bangladesh-Germany cooperation. How can the two countries expand this partnership to help Bangladesh meet its growing energy demand while advancing its climate and sustainability goals?

RL: Recent global events have highlighted the risks of relying heavily on fossil fuels and concentrating energy supplies in regions vulnerable to crises. Renewable energy and energy efficiency have long been core components of our bilateral cooperation portfolio, and they will remain central to our joint efforts to combat climate change.

Although per capita energy consumption in Bangladesh is currently relatively low by international standards, it could double or triple over the next 20 years as the economy grows. Meeting this growing demand sustainably requires greater reliance on clean energy sources. Our cooperation focuses particularly on initiatives such as rooftop solar installations, which offer considerable potential.

TDS: As European consumers and businesses place increasing emphasis on environmental, social and labour standards, how can Bangladesh strengthen its position as a sustainable manufacturing hub and maintain its competitiveness in the European market?

RL: European consumers are increasingly conscious of social, environmental and labour standards in producing countries. For European companies, sourcing from facilities associated with poor working conditions presents serious reputational and economic risks.

This shift offers Bangladesh a major competitive opportunity to position itself as a sustainable manufacturing hub. By ensuring that "Made in Bangladesh" signifies clean, environmentally friendly and socially responsible production, the country can strengthen its international reputation. While Bangladesh is still making progress towards meeting these standards fully, moving in this direction is vital for maintaining long-term market access.

Image Members of the German-South Asian Parliamentary Group meet Jatiya Sangsad Speaker Hafiz Uddin Ahmad Bir Bikram on 17 September 2026 to discuss trade, energy cooperation, the Rohingya crisis and a potential EU–Bangladesh free trade agreement (FTA). Photo: Jatiya Sangsad.

TDS: Germany faces growing demand for skilled workers, while Bangladesh has a large and increasingly skilled workforce. How can the two countries build mutually beneficial pathways for skilled migration, professional training and the recognition of qualifications?

RL: Demographics present a natural opportunity: Germany’s median age is 46, whereas Bangladesh’s median age is 26. Germany requires young workers, and Bangladesh has a vibrant youth population. Already, around 7,000 Bangladeshi students are studying in Germany, a number that continues to grow.

However, key challenges must be navigated to build effective pathways, starting with the German language, which requires dedicated effort but is well within reach for bright young individuals.

A more significant hurdle is aligning skill levels with German labour market expectations because of Germany's highly structured dual vocational training system, under which people entering trades such as electrical work or plumbing undergo three years of combined classroom instruction and practical training. To bridge this gap, Bangladesh needs a comprehensive, holistic national approach to vocational training. Rather than copying the longstanding German model directly, Bangladesh should develop a system tailored to its own economic needs. Germany supports these efforts through development projects focused on vocational skills development.

TDS: Beyond humanitarian assistance, what diplomatic initiatives could Germany and the EU pursue, together with Bangladesh and regional partners, to help create conditions for the safe, voluntary, dignified and sustainable repatriation of Rohingya refugees to Myanmar?

RL: Bangladesh has performed a tremendous humanitarian service by accommodating 1.3 million displaced Rohingya refugees. The international donor community must continue supporting these efforts and keep the issue prominent on the global agenda, a task aided by Bangladesh’s Foreign Minister serving as President of the UN General Assembly. Non-traditional donors should also be encouraged to contribute alongside Western nations.

At present, safe, voluntary repatriation remains unfeasible due to prevailing conditions inside Myanmar. However, keeping more than a million displaced people in cramped conditions for nearly a decade carries serious long-term risks of radicalisation and security challenges.

While full long-term integration is a politically sensitive topic, my advice would be to explore pragmatic measures that grant displaced individuals basic work permits and broader educational or livelihood opportunities, giving them a sense of direction and hope while they remain in Bangladesh.

Several lessons from Germany’s experience may resonate with Bangladesh’s transformation. Unifying societies with different historical experiences and perspectives is a gradual process that requires patience and reconciliation. Societal attitudes cannot be changed overnight, and lasting progress depends on bringing all citizens along rather than declaring one side superior to the other. Equally important is the establishment of strong, independent public institutions that can ensure long-term stability.

TDS: Germany’s reunification offers important lessons in democratic transformation, reconciliation and institution-building. Drawing on that experience, what lessons might be relevant to Bangladesh as it navigates its own political and institutional transition?

RL: German reunification in 1989 and 1990 was an immense historical blessing. Today, it has resulted in a stable democracy with strong institutions established across the entire country. For the younger generation, including my children, the division between East and West is no longer a defining mental barrier.

Several lessons from Germany’s experience may resonate with Bangladesh’s transformation. Unifying societies with different historical experiences and perspectives is a gradual process that requires patience and reconciliation. Societal attitudes cannot be changed overnight, and lasting progress depends on bringing all citizens along rather than declaring one side superior to the other.

Equally important is the establishment of strong, independent public institutions that can ensure long-term stability.

Major societal transformations also require practical, incremental progress. As the saying goes, even a journey of a thousand miles begins with a single step. Above all, sustainable change depends on continuous, open dialogue across all levels of society, allowing people with different experiences and perspectives to contribute to shaping a shared future.

The interview was taken by Ystiaque Ahmed and Khairul Hassan Jahin.

title: Rabindranath, Sher-e-Bangla and the mystery of a historic photograph
text:
Two luminous stars sit side by side: Rabindranath Tagore, the world-renowned poet, and Sher-e-Bangla A K Fazlul Huq, the first Prime Minister of undivided Bengal. Even after so many years, their historic encounter remains alive within the frame of a photograph. The poet, his face framed by a flowing white beard, holds a white teacup and saucer in his left hand. His gaze is fixed on Sher-e-Bangla, as though he is expressing some profound thought. Dressed in light-coloured clothes, Sher-e-Bangla leans slightly forward, his hands resting on his lap, listening intently to the poet's words.

This meeting of politics and literature, thought and action, the pen and administration, represents a unique, rare and enduring moment in Bengali culture and history. One had awakened the human spirit, while the other had devoted his life to fighting for the rights of those awakened people. When culture and politics come together in this way at the altar of humanity, the darkness enveloping society is bound to recede.

I remember reading somewhere a remark about this historic moment by Justice Abu Sayeed Chowdhury, the second President of Bangladesh, which continues to resonate with me. He wrote: "The day Rabindranath met A K Fazlul Huq, the Chief Minister of undivided Bengal, marked the beginning of the Bengali Muslim renaissance."



Image Sher-e-Bangla A K Fazlul Huq (26 October 1871–27 April 1962). Courtesy: Zaidis Photographers.

My first encounter with this historic photograph was in the pages of The Pakistan Observer. On 27 April 1963, in a special issue marking the first death anniversary of Sher-e-Bangla, the photograph appeared without a caption above an article titled "The Historic Lahore Resolution".

Many years later, I came across the photograph again in Swadhinatar Sangram O Sheikh Mujib (The Struggle for Independence and Sheikh Mujib), a book by the distinguished photojournalist Khandaker Kamrul Huda. Published in March 1995, the book reproduced the photograph on page 21, identifying it as "collected". The caption read: "1937: Rabindranath Tagore, the world-renowned poet, and Fazlul Huq, the Prime Minister of Bengal. Two great figures who are the pride of the Bengali nation. Sher-e-Bangla meets the poet at the Tagore family residence in Jorasanko, Calcutta."

Later, I saw a large framed print of the same photograph hanging on the wall of the home of pioneering photographer Sayeeda Khanam.

I became increasingly eager to discover the circumstances behind this extraordinary meeting between two remarkable personalities who had emerged from different currents of history. Seeking a detailed account of that day in 1937, and hoping to establish who had captured this compelling moment on camera, where and how, I turned to the authoritative four-volume Rabijibani, written by Prabhat Kumar Mukhopadhyay.

Mukhopadhyay meticulously documented the visits of distinguished personalities from home and abroad who came to meet the poet. Yet, to my astonishment, I found no mention of this momentous meeting with Bengal's Prime Minister in his monumental, almost epic, biography. Even after approaching contemporary Rabindranath scholars, I could find no definitive explanation of the mystery surrounding the photograph.



Determined to uncover the truth, on 8 May this year I posted a question on Facebook: "Does anyone know who took this historic photograph of Rabindranath and Sher-e-Bangla?"

In the comments section, theatre director Alok Basu opened a new window onto history:

"In 1937, Sher-e-Bangla became the Prime Minister of undivided Bengal. Although his Krishak Praja Party had not secured an absolute majority of seats, he was able to form a government. The opposing positions of the Congress and the Muslim League helped him come to power.

"The Krishak Praja Party's electoral success that year was largely attributable to the support of ordinary peasants and the backing Fazlul Huq received from both Hindus and Muslims. Fazlul Huq had announced his intention to abolish the zamindari system.



Image Sher-e-Bangla A K Fazlul Huq’s historic residence in Dhaka, photographed in 1954. The building has since been demolished. Photo: James Burke/LIFE Magazine.

"Meanwhile, the condition of Bengal's jute cultivators had deteriorated considerably since the First World War. British jute mill owners had introduced certain regulations that caused immense hardship to local jute growers and mill workers. At that time, around 100,000 jute mill workers became unemployed. They joined a strike.

"Rabindranath expressed solidarity with the jute mill workers' movement. He met Prime Minister Fazlul Huq and appealed to him to take measures to alleviate the suffering of the workers. This is the photograph of that meeting."

To support his explanation, Alok Basu referred to Rabindranath: Koyekti Rajnaitik Prasanga (Rabindranath: Some Political Issues), written by Nepal Majumdar and published by Dey's Publishing, Calcutta, in January 1999. He sent me photographs of the pages from the chapter titled "Rabindranath in Support of Jute Cultivators and Jute Mill Workers".

Although Nepal Majumdar's book does not directly describe a meeting between Rabindranath and Sher-e-Bangla, his account offers some insight into the historical circumstances surrounding the photograph.

At the heart of Rabindranath's vision of his homeland stood the people. Throughout his life, he spoke out against the suffering, exploitation and oppression of ordinary people, particularly impoverished peasants and working-class communities.



In early February 1937, jute mill workers in Calcutta, Howrah and Bhagirathi began a prolonged strike. Nearly 175,000 workers joined the movement. The strike had begun even before Fazlul Huq formed his ministry. The new government adopted repressive measures in an attempt to break it.

At the time, Rabindranath was spending his summer holiday in Almora, a hill town in what is now the Indian state of Uttarakhand. Reports of the workers' strike gradually reached him through newspapers, causing him considerable distress.

Upon returning to Calcutta, he heard the full account from the labour leaders. On 29 April, through United Press, he issued a press statement making an impassioned appeal to the government to accept the workers' legitimate demands.

Just ten days after the poet's humanitarian appeal, on 10 May, the workers called off their strike and returned to work, placing their trust in certain encouraging assurances given by Prime Minister Fazlul Huq.

This historic photograph is, in essence, a silent witness to that movement.

One morning, in search of the photographer behind the image, I made my way to Bangla Academy. There, I discovered a rare photographic album of Rabindranath titled Tumi Ki Keboli Chhobi (Are You Merely a Picture?), published in June 2012.

The 230-page album was also published by Bangla Academy. The photograph appeared on page 121, in a section titled "Distinguished Personalities and Rabindranath". Yet its caption stated only: "With A K Fazlul Huq."



Image The historic meeting between Rabindranath Tagore and Sher-e-Bangla A K Fazlul Huq in Calcutta, 1937.

A deeply disappointing fact emerged. Although the substantial collection contained 184 invaluable photographs, not a single photographer was identified or credited. By contrast, the artworks reproduced in the volume had been properly attributed to their creators.

Professor Anisuzzaman, then President of Bangla Academy, acknowledged this omission with evident regret in his foreword:

"These photographs have been collected from various sources. Owing to their sheer number, it was not possible to acknowledge the photographers. In some cases, we were unable even to obtain their names. The source publications have been acknowledged with gratitude, but the photographers have remained unnamed. Nevertheless, this does not mean that we are unwilling to acknowledge our debt to those who took the photographs. It is because of them that such a collection could be assembled."

My investigation continued as I turned to the pages of Sher-e-Bangla, a biography by B D Habibullah, published by East Bengal Publishers in Dhaka in June 1962. The book had been written during Sher-e-Bangla's lifetime but was published two months after his death. Its author had been a lifelong, devoted political associate of Sher-e-Bangla. Following page 77 of the book, the familiar photograph of Rabindranath and Sher-e-Bangla was reproduced on a separate sheet of art paper. The caption read: "Fazlul Huq, Prime Minister of Bengal, and Rabindranath Tagore." Yet nowhere in the book's 188 pages was there any further reference to their historic meeting.

Nor could I find any information about the photograph in Sher-e-Bangla A K Fazlul Huq by Sirajuddin Ahmed, Ek Shatabdi (A Century) by Khondkar Abdul Khalek, or Pakistan Prastab O Fazlul Huq (The Pakistan Resolution and Fazlul Huq) by Amalendu De. However, the photograph appeared prominently at the beginning of Rabindranath O Musalman Samaj (Rabindranath and Muslim Society), written by Bhuiyan Iqbal and published by Prothoma in 2010. Although the caption read "A K Fazlul Huq with Rabindranath", there was no mention of the photographer's name or the precise year in which the photograph was taken. Nor did the extensive chronology titled "A Record of the Poet's Interactions with Muslims", included towards the end of the book, offer any account of the circumstances surrounding the photograph. Nevertheless, the book provides a clear account of how Rabindranath's non-sectarian outlook and Sher-e-Bangla's progressive politics together profoundly influenced Bengali society.



I then turned the pages of history once again, this time examining the special issue of Kolkata Purashree, the Bengali-language publication of the Kolkata Municipal Corporation, published on 27 January 1999 to commemorate the 125th birth anniversary of A K Fazlul Huq. The photograph appeared in an article titled "Sher-e-Bangala" by Hirendranath Mukhopadhyay, but once again the photographer remained unidentified. The caption simply stated: "Fazlul Huq with Rabindranath Tagore in 1937." No further information was provided.

However, an article by Ganesh Mukhopadhyay titled "Shilpa-Sanskriti Daradi Fazlul Huq" (Fazlul Huq, a Patron of Art and Culture) revealed the deep emotional bond between these two great personalities. He wrote: "Huq Saheb was extremely dear to Rabindranath. During the poet's final days, he suspended all his administrative duties for more than a week and remained at the Jorasanko residence. According to eyewitness accounts, when the poet breathed his last, one of his hands was clasped between Huq Saheb's two hands."

Shambhu Saha was Rabindranath's personal photographer. Between 1935 and 1941, he photographed the poet extensively at Santiniketan, earning international recognition for his work. With renewed hope and a sense of anticipation, I began examining two photographic albums published from Santiniketan featuring his photographs: Faces and Places of Visva-Bharati and Rabindranath Tagore. Although the albums contained photographs of Rabindranath with many prominent personalities, including Mahatma Gandhi and Jawaharlal Nehru, the photograph with Sher-e-Bangla was nowhere to be found.



Image Caption Sher-e-Bangla A. K. Fazlul Huq with his cabinet after becoming the first Premier of Bengal under provincial autonomy in 1937.



As a final attempt, on 4 August, I sent the photograph via WhatsApp to Nilanjan Bandyopadhyay, an official at Rabindra Bhavana, Visva-Bharati, asking whether the Santiniketan archives held any information about it. After making enquiries with the photography department, he informed me that they had no knowledge of the person behind the camera. Indeed, there was no trace of the photograph even in the Santiniketan archives.

Yet hope is not easily extinguished. Something within me urged me to continue the search. On 9 September, as I turned the pages of dusty documents at the Bangladesh National Archives, a faint hope still lingered in my mind. But once again, the elusive photograph remained beyond my reach.

I reassured myself that other sources must exist. What if I visited Sher-e-Bangla's old residence? Perhaps his descendants held some clue to the photograph's origins.

The following afternoon, I made my way to Tikatuli. Since Partition, the house at 27 K M Das Lane had been graced by Sher-e-Bangla's presence. But today, that history has vanished. The once-familiar courtyard has disappeared beneath a nine-storey concrete structure built by a property developer.



Din Islam, the security guard at the modern apartment building named "Sher", told me: "No one from Sher-e-Bangla's family lives here. They sold the property many years ago and moved to Gulshan. Nobody here has any contact with them."

My heart sank. It was difficult to accept such an erasure of memory.

As I made my way back through the unfamiliar crowds of Tikatuli, a name suddenly came to mind: Tasnim Karim Baby, Sher-e-Bangla's great-granddaughter and the daughter of his eldest granddaughter, Razia Banu.

When I contacted her by mobile phone, she offered me a glimmer of hope, providing the telephone number and Facebook profile of Sher-e-Bangla's grandson, A K Faiyazul Huq Raju, son of former minister A K Faizul Huq.

But that promising connection soon reached an impasse. His phone was switched off. Left with no alternative, I sent him an earnest message through Facebook Messenger. No reply came.

After waiting 13 days, I approached Tasnim Karim Baby again on 22 September. She immediately contacted Faiyazul Huq Raju's wife, Salma Faiyaz, and gave me the address of their residence in Gulshan.

The following afternoon, I arrived at their home. In the drawing room of their luxurious apartment overlooking Gulshan Lake hung a large framed print of the very photograph I had been searching for.

Over lunch, in an atmosphere of genuine warmth and hospitality, I discussed the historic photograph with the couple.

Faiyazul Huq explained that, following Sher-e-Bangla's death, his father had obtained a copy of the photograph from Syed Azizul Huq, popularly known as Nanna Mia. Azizul Huq was Sher-e-Bangla's nephew and a former minister.

Salma Faiyaz told me that they had presented large framed prints of the photograph to the directors-general of Bangla Academy, Shilpakala Academy and the National Museum for preservation. However, neither of them could provide any definite information about when, where or by whom the photograph had been taken.



This long journey in search of the history and photographer behind a single image confronts us with a deeply painful reality. There is a profound lack of research in Bangladesh on the great pioneers of photography and their timeless creations. It is precisely because of this neglect that the people behind the camera, who captured countless invaluable images that have left an indelible mark on history, remain forever shrouded in obscurity. Their stories fade into oblivion.

To do justice to our glorious past and keep these silent yet powerful historical documents alive, there is now an urgent need for thoughtful, aesthetically informed research into Bangladesh's iconic photographs and the photographers who created them.

Yet a close reading of the photograph's own visual language opens another remarkable window onto history.

Rabindranath is dressed in the Tagore family's signature flowing robe, wearing his familiar tall black cap and heavy-framed spectacles. His appearance is elegant and distinguished. Beside him sits Sher-e-Bangla, the Tiger of Bengal, leaning slightly forward, his lowered gaze reflecting profound respect and extraordinary attentiveness.

Behind Rabindranath, a sofa adorned with flowers lends a touch of aesthetic grandeur to the otherwise solemn atmosphere. The setting appears considerably more formal than the domestic or familial surroundings of the Tagore residence at Jorasanko. This strongly suggests that the meeting may have taken place in the office of Fazlul Huq, the first Prime Minister of undivided Bengal.

If this historic encounter did indeed take place in the Prime Minister's office, then the credit for capturing this epic moment for posterity may belong to none other than W A Khan, the dedicated official photographer attached to the Prime Minister's office at the time.

Amid the uncertainties that continue to surround the photograph's history, this carefully considered inference may be the closest we have yet come to an answer.

Shahadat Parvez is a photographer and researcher.

title: The limits of Bangladesh’s low-wage growth
text:
Bangladesh's factories have created millions of jobs. Employment in industry rose from 9.5 million in 2010 to nearly 12 million in 2022. Two types of industry drove this growth. The first is the ready-made garment (RMG) industry. Firms in rich countries move simple, labour-intensive work to poorer countries, and Bangladesh, with its abundant workforce, seized the opportunity. Garments became the country's main source of foreign earnings and provided millions of poor women with paid work. The second is a newer group of industries, such as food processing, plastics, electronics and light engineering, which have grown by selling to the domestic market.

We usually assume that a factory job is a ladder out of poverty. A person leaves the village, gets a regular wage, and the family's life slowly improves. But a factory job is not always a way out of poverty. In early 2024, we surveyed 3,005 factory workers in Dhaka, Gazipur and Narayanganj. We did not survey the entire manufacturing workforce: owners, managers, engineers, supervisors and office staff were not included in our sample. The survey covered workers engaged in production on the factory floor: machine operators, assemblers, craft and trade workers, technicians and helpers. Workers like these make up about 85 per cent of all manufacturing jobs, and they are among the lowest-paid workers in manufacturing. We found that about 28 out of every 100 of these workers live in households below the upper poverty line, compared with about 19 out of every 100 people in the country as a whole. Eight out of every 100 fall below the lower, or extreme, poverty line.

Image Women work at sewing machines in a garment factory. Bangladesh’s manufacturing sector has created millions of jobs, but factory employment does not always lift workers and their families out of poverty. Photo: Mehedi Hasan

In other words, a person can work in a factory all year and still be poor. This essay asks three questions. Why does factory work not always lift workers and their families out of poverty? If it does not, why do people still leave agriculture for factory work? And what should wage policy do about it?

The first reason is simple: wages remain close to the minimum wage, and the minimum wage is too low. On average, a worker in our survey earns a basic wage of about Tk 12,500 per month, which is almost exactly the minimum wage in the garment industry. Overtime and bonuses add only about Tk 2,000, bringing the total to about Tk 14,500. When we asked workers what monthly salary they expected, the average answer was about Tk 23,000, far above what they actually earn. Even with the earnings of a spouse or other family members added, the average household earns about Tk 23,900 a month. A household of four needs roughly Tk 19,800 a month just to stay above the upper poverty line in the city. So household income sits only just above the poverty line, and any illness or loss of income can push a household below it.

The second reason is the cost of city life. A factory worker earns more in cash than a rural non-farm day labourer, about Tk 14,500 per month compared with Tk 10,000. Yet the two groups have similar poverty rates. Rent, food and transport in the city eat up the gain. People migrate for better pay and a better life, but because the city costs so much, they end up living little better than they did in the village. A larger family makes this worse, since each additional member adds to the cost of city life.

A household of four needs roughly Tk 19,800 a month just to stay above the upper poverty line in the city. So household income sits only just above the poverty line, and any illness or loss of income can push a household below it.

The third reason is that extra work does not pay much. Workers in our survey put in an average of 12 or more extra hours a week, at the cost of rest and family time. Yet overtime and bonuses together add only about Tk 2,000 a month. In many non-RMG and domestic factories, less overtime is available, and it is also underpaid.

The fourth reason is the number of earners in a household. Most workers depend solely on their wages, which are very close to the minimum. On one income, it is hard to meet the cost of city life. When both husband and wife can work, the family has a real chance of escaping poverty. In our survey, workers whose households had another earner were less likely to be poor. The garment industry offers this opportunity because about half of its workers are women, compared with a quarter in other industries.

The last reason is low levels of education and a lack of voice at work. Most factory workers have studied only up to primary or secondary level, and those with little education are paid less. Workers who studied beyond secondary school were less likely to be poor.

Workers also have little power to bargain for better pay. Where a factory has a trade union, workers earn more and are less likely to be poor.

Given the high cost of city life, crowded housing and the slim chance of escaping poverty, it may seem surprising that so many people still move from villages to cities. The economists John Harris and Michael Todaro offered a simple explanation: people move when the wages they expect to earn in the city exceed what they earn at home. In the city, a factory offers full-time work year-round at a higher wage. In the village, farm work is seasonal. There is plenty of work at harvest time, but little in between, and in the lean months, many families have no income at all. Rural non-farm work, such as driving, working as a bus helper or running a tea stall, pays more than farm work. But it is informal, pays less than a factory job and offers less security. So people migrate for the certainty of work. A monthly wage, however small, is something a family can plan around.

Image A child looks out of a window in a corrugated-tin dwelling in a Lalbag slum. For low-paid factory workers, the high cost of housing, food and transport in cities often erodes the financial benefits of regular employment. Photo: Anisur Rahman

But this migration places a new burden on cities. The number of unskilled workers arriving has grown much faster than the number of jobs available to them, which keeps wages down. Many who come looking for factory work end up in casual jobs instead. They are better off than they were in the village, but often not by enough to escape poverty in the city.

Urban poverty is falling much more slowly than rural poverty, so it needs to become a policy priority. Between 2010 and 2022, the upper poverty rate fell by about 15 percentage points in rural areas but by less than 7 percentage points in urban areas. Unless poverty among factory workers comes down, urban poverty as a whole will be difficult to reduce.

The place to start is the minimum wage. Bangladesh does not have one minimum wage; it has many. The Minimum Wage Board has so far set minimum wages for 47 sectors, and the RMG minimum wage is higher than those in other sectors. The minimum wage for leather workers is Tk 7,100, set in 2020. For jute workers, it is Tk 8,000, set in 2014. For pharmaceutical workers, it is Tk 8,050, set in 2017. In several industries, such as light engineering, electrical appliances, iron and steel, furniture and ceramics, no minimum wage has been set.

Minimum wage across industries

Industry Minimum wage (Tk) Year declared RMG export Woven garments (trousers, shirts, sweaters and others) 12,500 2023 Garments (hosiery) 12,000 2023 Non-RMG export Leather and leather goods, export-oriented (shoes, bags and other articles) 7,100 2020 Jute and jute products 8,000 2014 Agro-food processing (cold storage) 6,050 2022 Agro-food processing (tea packing) 7,080 2017 Pharmaceuticals and medical equipment 8,050 2017 Domestic industries Plastics 8,000 2020 Textiles and spinning 1,0001 2024 Light engineering Not fixed Electrical appliances Not fixed Paper and printing 8,150 2022 Metal (iron and steel) Not fixed Furniture Not fixed Ceramics Not fixed

Source: Minimum Wage Board

Note: The table shows a selection of industries. It illustrates that many industries still have no minimum wage and that existing minimum wages are rarely revised.

This creates three problems. Where an industry has no minimum wage, its workers can easily be underpaid. Where a minimum wage exists but is rarely revised, inflation gradually erodes its value. And large differences in minimum wages between industries mean that workers doing similar work are paid very differently. To address this, Bangladesh needs a uniform minimum-wage system across all industries. The idea is not new. In 2001, the government moved to introduce a universal minimum wage, but the plan did not go ahead because industry owners opposed it.

Image Pedestrians cross a busy road amid heavy traffic. Although factory workers generally earn more than rural day labourers, higher living costs in cities often leave them little better off than their rural counterparts. Photo: Rashed Sumon

Instead, the Minimum Wage Board was formed in 2004 to set wages sector by sector. Workers and trade unions now demand a uniform minimum wage or a single national wage structure, as in Vietnam or Cambodia. Industry owners usually oppose such a system, arguing that they would lose access to cheap labour and their competitive advantage. Yet empirical evidence does not conclusively show that minimum wages necessarily reduce employment. In practice, minimum wages are often set or revised only in response to strikes, pressure from trade unions and demands from international buyers.

Three things need to change. First, there should be a minimum wage for all manufacturing industries, a floor below which no factory worker should be paid. Second, the minimum wage should be revised regularly, in line with the cost of living in cities, rather than only after strikes. Third, overtime and attendance bonuses need to be paid properly, so that extra hours actually add to a family's income.

But a minimum wage alone will not end poverty on the factory floor. Our findings point to four other conditions that help working households escape poverty. The first is employment opportunities for women. Households with two earners do much better than households with one. Every industry, not just the garment industry, needs to provide women with workplaces that offer safe transport, childcare and fair treatment.

Image Garment workers protest outside the Bangladesh Secretariat on 25 March 2025, demanding unpaid wages and Eid bonuses. Photo: Amran Hossain

The second is education and skills. The third is factory size. Unlike the garment industry, which was "born to export", many domestic industries grew step by step, from retailer to importer to assembler to manufacturer. Most remain small and cannot pay the wages that large firms can. Promising domestic industries need support, including tariff protection where justified, so they can grow, meet domestic demand and eventually become large enterprises. The fourth is having a voice at work. A factory-level trade union allows workers to bargain collectively. The rules governing the formation of trade unions should be eased.

Bangladesh's manufacturing story began with low-cost labour. That was enough to get the factories running and to bring millions of people out of the fields. But a model built only on cheap labour cannot also end poverty for the people who do the work. If Bangladesh wants factory jobs to be a way out of poverty, and not just a way out of the village, the next stage of its growth must share more of its gains with the workers who made it possible.

Md Nadim Uddin is a Research Fellow at the Bangladesh Institute of Development Studies (BIDS).

title: Where Chamunda still dances: The living heritage of Naogaon
text:
A child wears a wooden face larger than his own. Its bulging eyes, exposed teeth and long crimson tongue transform his appearance. Nearby, older performers move to the rhythms of the dhak, accompanied by ringing metal percussion and the penetrating voice of the sanai. Women watch closely, encourage their children and offer small sums of money as expressions of reverence. Around the dancers, the village gathers.

When I witnessed the Chamunda mukha dance in Bhandarpur, in Naogaon’s Badalgachhi upazila, what struck me most was the community’s spontaneous involvement. Children, adolescents, young men and elderly performers were all part of the same ritual occasion.Their neighbours and relatives surrounded them, participating through attention, encouragement and devotion. Here, heritage takes place among people who recognise it as part of their lives.

According to local legend, this dance tradition has continued in Bhandarpur for more than four hundred years. Although this claim has yet to be verified through documentary research, it reflects the community’s understanding of a tradition passed down through generations. Its continuation depends on people who return to the observance, prepare children to join it and sustain the music and worship that give it meaning.

Image Masked dancers perform the traditional Chamunda mukha dance as villagers gather to witness the ritual in Bhandarpur, Naogaon. Photo: Courtesy of the author

A wooden face, a moving presence

The wooden mukha is the most immediately arresting feature of the dance. The photographs I took show vividly painted faces with prominent eyes, conspicuous teeth, projecting red tongues and elaborate crowns. Their exaggerated features make the goddess recognisable even within a dense gathering.

The mask acquires its expressive force through the performer’s body. Dancers bend their knees, lower themselves towards the earth, extend their arms and incline their masked heads. Some dance close to the ground; others adopt wider, more expansive positions. Their gathered garments spread around their legs, giving their movements a distinctive silhouette.

The costumes vary. Bright skirts, patterned cloth, necklaces and waist bindings appear alongside ordinary shirts and T-shirts. This combination reveals how inherited ceremonial forms remain embedded in contemporary village life. Each performer brings a living body and present-day circumstances to an established devotional practice.

Among the practitioners recorded in my documentation are Nikhil Chandra Mali, Nirmal Mali, Nirab Mali, Shanta Mali, Pranta Mali, Sagar Mondal, Arun Chandra Mali, Subrata Mali and Tapas Mali. Children associated with the observance include Lakshmi Rani, Rupa Rani, Sonali Rani, Jitu Malakar, Pramit Mali, Mohan Mali and Amrita Mali.

Recording their names matters. Too often, photographs of traditional performances circulate while the people who sustain them remain unidentified. Bhandarpur’s inheritance belongs to particular practitioners and families whose knowledge deserves recognition.

Image A woman pays homage to a masked Chamunda performer during a traditional religious observance in Bhandarpur. Photo: Courtesy of the author

Mothers, children and the work of transmission

Women did not perform the Chamunda mask dance during the observance I documented. Their contribution, however, was integral to its social and devotional life.

Mothers helped dress their children and encouraged them to participate. Through this preparation, they supported the children’s entry into a practice that requires confidence, familiarity and the approval of those closest to them.

During the dance, women also approached the performers with reverence and offered small amounts of money as devotional gifts. These gestures situated the masked dancer within a relationship of worship. The offerings acknowledged the sacred significance of the enactment.

This distinction helps us understand participation more fully. Dancing is one responsibility within the observance; preparing children, encouraging them and expressing devotion are others. Women’s contribution to transmission deserves attention in its own right.

The photographs capture a close relationship between performers and those around them. Women stand or sit within immediate reach of the masked figures. Children watch from among the adults. The dance unfolds within a gathering whose members continually respond to it.

Image A Chamunda mukha performer dances to the rhythms of traditional percussion instruments during a religious observance in Bhandarpur, Naogaon. Photo: Courtesy of the author

Learning the rhythm

The musicians provide another compelling picture of continuity across generations.

The rhythms of the dhak, the metallic sounds of kansa percussion and the melodies of the sanai accompany the dance. Older musicians bring experience to the ensemble, while children and younger participants contribute to the instrumental performance. The photographs show young percussion players sharing the occasion with adult drummers and an older wind-instrument player.

This is a setting in which musical knowledge can pass through participation. Young people encounter the rhythm in relation to dancing bodies, ritual actions and the responses of the gathering. They learn when to enter, how to listen and how their contribution fits into the larger event.

Image Women and children gather around a Chamunda performer, highlighting the community’s role in preserving and passing down this living cultural tradition. Photo: Courtesy of the author

The presence of children is especially significant because it makes transmission visible in the present. Their participation already forms part of the observance, even as their skills continue to develop.

Wood, clay, metal, cloth and breath come together in this performance. Its continuation therefore involves several kinds of knowledge: caring for masks, preparing costumes, playing instruments, moving in rhythm and understanding the religious occasion.

Kali beyond the mask

The ritual world of Bhandarpur also includes an enactment of Kali in which the performer’s own face and body become the principal expressive surfaces.

Akhil Mali is identified in my field documentation as a practitioner of this role. With his face and body blackened, a crimson tongue extended and a da, a sharp cutting blade, in hand, he dances to the dhak.

This enactment differs materially from wearing a wooden mukha. Paint, facial expression, bodily gesture and the weapon establish the divine appearance. Together with the masked dance, it reveals the range of expressive means through which fierce goddess forms enter the ceremonial space.

Image A performer wears an elaborate wooden Chamunda mask, featuring prominent eyes, exposed teeth and a projecting red tongue that evoke the goddess’s fierce appearance. Photo: Courtesy of the author

These images require interpretation within their devotional setting. The blade, tongue and fearsome face can dominate an outsider’s attention, while villagers approach the occasion through reverence and attachment. Ferocity and maternal protection can occupy the same religious imagination.

The relationship between Chamunda, Kali and Burakali within this local practice deserves careful study. Their presence within a shared observance should prompt attention to the community’s own explanations of their identities and relationships.

From Paharpur’s terracotta to Bhandarpur’s dancers

The comparison with Paharpur gives the Bhandarpur dance a particularly thought-provoking historical setting.

In the photographs of terracotta plaques accompanying my documentation, a dancing figure wears a waist-bound lower garment whose folds extend outwards around the thighs. The knees are bent, the legs held apart and the arms arranged in an expressive posture. The flaring lower garments and bent-knee positions of several Bhandarpur performers invite comparison.

The resemblance is strongest in the positioning of the dancing body: the emphasis on the waist, the outward spread of cloth and the articulation of the limbs. These features provide a meaningful starting point for investigating the region’s performance history.

Image A terracotta plaque from Paharpur depicts a dancing figure whose posture and costume invite comparison with contemporary ritual performances in Bhandarpur. (Left)

A dancer demonstrates the distinctive movements and flaring costume associated with Bhandarpur’s traditional Chamunda mukha dance. (Right)

Photo: Courtesy of the author



They cannot, on their own, establish that the terracotta figure depicts the Chamunda mukha dance. Its face is damaged, and the photograph does not allow for a confident identification of a mask. Nor can a visual resemblance bridge every intervening century.

Nevertheless, the comparison deserves sustained attention. An ancient representation of dance and a contemporary ritual practice exist within the same broader cultural landscape. Exploring their possible relationship requires bringing archaeological evidence into conversation with costume history, local memory and living performance.

At Paharpur, movement survives in a sculpted image. In Bhandarpur, movement continues through bodies taught and encouraged by other bodies. Studying them together could deepen our understanding of how regional forms are inherited, adapted and renewed.

An ancient landscape with living practices

Northern Bengal has a rich and well-documented history. Mahasthangarh, identified with ancient Pundranagara, preserves evidence of early urban life. Somapura Mahavihara at Paharpur became a major Buddhist intellectual centre under Pala patronage, while Jagaddala and Halud Vihara further enrich the region’s archaeological landscape.

The Charyapada offers a related perspective on the religious importance of performance. Its Buddhist esoteric songs convey spiritual meanings through figurative language grounded in bodies, occupations and everyday experience. Their musical character reminds us that knowledge circulated through singing and embodied practice as well as through manuscripts. The Charyapada belongs to a wider eastern Indian cultural context; attributing the entire corpus to Somapura would go beyond the available evidence.

Chamunda’s presence in Bengal also has a historical basis in religious art. Medieval images and iconographic scholarship situate her within the region’s goddess traditions and Tantric milieu. They provide a context for studying contemporary worship, although the history connecting particular ancient images to present-day village practices remains to be reconstructed.

What is remarkable is that the landscape surrounding Paharpur continues to support vigorous ritual performance. Archaeological remains and living devotional practices occupy the same region, inviting us to consider its history through both material objects and community knowledge.

A goddess’s claim on water and land

The story of Bhandarpur’s origins connects its temple, settlement and founding family through an encounter with the goddess. According to local tradition, Ramlochan Chandra Chowdhury stopped in the area while travelling to Nawab Alivardi Khan’s court during the 1740s. His attendants brought water from a pond beside a religious establishment. That night, a fierce goddess appeared in his dream and demanded repayment for drinking water that belonged to her.

Her demand was for service from Ramlochan and his descendants. The narrative continues that he subsequently obtained four mouzas and established a settlement and a place of worship around the shrine.

The story gives a sacred explanation for the relationship between landholding and religious responsibility. Possession of land carries an obligation to maintain worship; the use of water creates a debt extending across generations.

Image Women gather near old brick structures in Bhandarpur, where community participation plays an important role in sustaining traditional religious observances. Photo: Courtesy of the author

This eighteenth-century account should be distinguished from the community’s broader claim that the dance has continued for more than four hundred years. The chronology of the patron family, the history of the shrine and the beginnings of the dance may represent different layers of local memory.

The account of ascetics living in the area before Ramlochan’s arrival is particularly significant. According to local tradition, they were concerned about who would care for the deity after their departure. The question of who would carry on the tradition, which remains central to preserving living heritage today, was therefore already an important part of the village’s understanding of its past.

Beyond a single village

Bhandarpur is one important location within a wider field of practice. Local accounts identify Chamunda worship and dance in Mahadebpur, Naogaon Sadar and other upazilas of Naogaon. These observances remain animated by people’s devotion and affection. A fuller understanding will require documentation across villages, allowing practitioners to explain local variations in masks, music, ritual calendars and ceremonial responsibilities.

The association with esoteric Tantric worship helps explain why these practices have attracted relatively limited publicity. Some knowledge may circulate within particular families or ritual communities. The absence of extensive public discussion should encourage patient research conducted through relationships of trust.

Such work must respect practitioners’ decisions about what can be recorded and shared. Public visibility is only one possible outcome of documentation. Returning photographs, recordings and written accounts to the people who contributed them is equally valuable.

Image A dancer wearing a wooden Chamunda mask and a red costume performs during a traditional ritual in Bhandarpur, Naogaon. Photo: Courtesy of the author

The people who keep the dance alive

The strongest impression Bhandarpur left on me was of a community making participation possible. A mother prepared her child. An older musician played while younger participants joined the rhythm. A woman offered money with reverence. A dancer lowered a crowned wooden face towards the people gathered around him.

These actions sustain a cultural inheritance through relationships between generations. They also give substance to the idea of a living historical landscape.

Around ancient Somapura, the past remains open to investigation in earth, brick and terracotta. In the villages of Naogaon, inherited ritual knowledge continues through worship, music and movement. Bhandarpur’s Chamunda mukha dance brings that knowledge into the present through the care and commitment of its people.

Saymon Zakaria is a researcher, playwright and poet. He serves as Deputy Director at Bangla Academy and Chairman of the Vabnagar Foundation.

title: Tarique Rahman's Japan visit: The next frontier of Bangladesh-Japan relations
text:
Prime Minister Tarique Rahman’s scheduled visit to Japan on 26 October 2026 comes at a significant moment in Bangladesh-Japan relations, as Dhaka seeks to deepen economic and strategic engagement with Tokyo. During the visit, Bangladesh is set to propose a US$14 billion investment and cooperation package spanning 12 priority sectors, including transport, technology and energy. The visit provides an opportunity to assess the evolving bilateral partnership and identify avenues for expanding cooperation in an increasingly complex regional geopolitical environment.

Bangladesh’s strategic location at the crossroads of South and Southeast Asia holds considerable significance for regional and global powers, including Japan. This importance has long been recognised in Japan’s official foreign policy assessments. The 2021 Diplomatic Bluebook describes Bangladesh as “geopolitically very important as an intersection between India and ASEAN” (MOFA, Japan, 2021, p. 79). Bangladesh’s geographical position, together with its growing geostrategic relevance amid evolving regional dynamics, has also been a key consideration underpinning Japan’s Bay of Bengal Industrial Growth Belt (BIG-B) Initiative, which places Bangladesh at the centre of its regional connectivity and economic development strategy.

Deepening Bangladesh-Japan investment ties

According to a survey conducted by the Japan External Trade Organization (JETRO), 73.2 per cent of the 57 companies interviewed said Bangladesh was their top priority for business expansion; 61 per cent said the country had high growth potential. The survey covered Japanese firms across 20 countries in Asia and Oceania. Among these 20 countries, Bangladesh ranked second in terms of profitability for Japanese companies, owing to low wages and production costs. Bangladesh has also taken steps to create a more favourable investment environment. One notable example is the Bangladesh Special Economic Zone (BSEZ) in Araihazar, Narayanganj, developed in partnership with Japan to attract Japanese and other foreign investors.

Image Foreign Secretary Asad Alam Siam and Japan's Senior Deputy Foreign Minister Namazu Hiroyuki lead their respective delegations at the seventh Bangladesh-Japan Foreign Office Consultations in Dhaka on 12 August 2026. The consultations formed part of ongoing diplomatic engagement to strengthen bilateral relations. Photo: MOFA, Bangladesh.

In recent years, several leading Japanese companies have expressed interest in investing in Bangladesh or expanding their existing operations in the country. Japanese businesses are also exploring opportunities in Bangladesh and neighbouring markets as part of their “China Plus One” strategy, which seeks to diversify production and investment beyond China and reduce dependence on a single market. Bangladesh and Japan signed an Economic Partnership Agreement (EPA) in February 2026, marking an important step towards deepening bilateral economic cooperation. Its effective implementation could further strengthen trade and investment ties and generate mutual economic benefits.

Promoting trade relations

Trade between Bangladesh and Japan has expanded steadily over the past decade, driven largely by growing demand for competitively priced Bangladeshi garments. Bangladesh’s exports to Japan have increased significantly since 2011, when Japan relaxed its rules of origin for knitwear imports from least-developed countries (LDCs), enabling Bangladeshi products to benefit from duty-free market access. According to data from the Export Promotion Bureau (EPB) and Bangladesh Bank (BB), Bangladesh’s annual exports to Japan first exceeded US$1 billion in FY2015–16, rising sharply to US$2.8 billion in FY2021–22. Japan is now Bangladesh’s ninth-largest export destination globally and second-largest in Asia.

Nevertheless, there is ample scope to expand Bangladesh-Japan bilateral trade. For instance, Bangladesh has considerable potential to increase its exports of ready-made garments and pharmaceuticals to the Japanese market. Japan’s Finance Ministry data show that the country imported US$24.72 billion worth of apparel, with the bulk (US$22.96 billion) coming from Asia, including US$13.57 billion from China alone. China's share of Japan's textile product imports fell below 50 per cent in 2025, reaching a 31-year low. The resulting gap is increasingly being filled by Southeast and South Asian countries. Vietnam's share rose by 7.7 percentage points over the past decade to 17.4 per cent, while Bangladesh gained two percentage points to reach only 4.3 per cent. It is also encouraging that Bangladesh has already begun exporting ICT products to Japan, which could become another promising area of bilateral trade.

Expanding Bangladesh-Japan labour cooperation

From Bangladesh’s perspective, labour migration and diaspora connections are critical to its relations with Japan. According to BMET, between 1976 and 2020, of the 1.3 crore Bangladeshi migrant workers who went abroad for employment, only 0.02 per cent went to Japan. Several factors make Bangladesh a promising source of skilled workers to meet Japan’s growing labour demand.

Bangladesh and Japan should move beyond immediate economic gains to deepen cooperation in maritime security, technology transfer and sustainable development. Japan has much to offer in terms of technology, expertise and institutional experience, while Bangladesh brings a young workforce, a growing market and a strategically important position in the Bay of Bengal. The challenge lies in translating these complementary strengths into a lasting partnership grounded in mutual respect and shared prosperity.

First, Bangladesh offers a large pool of semi-skilled and skilled workers, while Japan faces a severe shortage of people of working age. According to a joint survey by Persol Research and Consulting and Chuo University, Japan will face a shortage of approximately 6.44 million workers by 2030. The proportion of people aged over 65 had already reached 28 per cent, one of the highest in the world, as reported by The Washington Post. Although there is considerable discussion about the Fourth Industrial Revolution, in which machines may replace human workers, human resources remain essential. The demand for human labour is unlikely to disappear anytime soon. Therefore, to address its labour shortages, Japan has increasingly opened its doors to foreign workers. In this context, Japan introduced legal amendments in 2018 to grant visas to more foreign workers and address its tightening labour market.

Against this backdrop, labour migration presents a promising avenue for cooperation between Bangladesh and Japan. Encouragingly, in August 2019, Bangladesh and Japan signed a Memorandum of Cooperation (MoC) to facilitate the recruitment of Bangladeshi workers under Japan’s Specified Skilled Worker (SSW) programme across 14 sectors. Bangladesh was the ninth country to sign such an MoC with Japan as a sending country for specified skilled workers. In addition, in May 2025, Bangladesh and Japan reached an agreement to recruit at least 100,000 Bangladeshi workers over the following five years to help address Japan’s severe labour shortage.

Building on these bilateral arrangements for labour cooperation, Bangladesh and Japan signed a five-year Memorandum of Cooperation on Employment Skills Development (ESDP-MoC) on 17 October 2026. The agreement, which will be automatically renewable for another five years, aims to facilitate the recruitment of Bangladeshi workers in Japan from 1 April 2027. The agreement marks a significant step towards expanding employment opportunities for Bangladeshi workers in Japan. With a formal framework for labour cooperation now in place, Bangladesh needs to focus on its effective implementation to maximise the opportunities it offers.

Image Prime Minister Tarique Rahman meets a Japanese delegation led by Parliamentary Vice-Minister for Foreign Affairs Shimada Tomaki at the Prime Minister's Office in Dhaka on 1 July 2026. Discussions covered bilateral cooperation in energy, airport infrastructure development and Rohingya repatriation. Photo: PMO

Strengthening Bangladesh-Japan maritime security and blue economy cooperation

The Bay of Bengal and the wider Indian Ocean region have become increasingly important arenas of strategic competition among regional and extra-regional powers. Against this backdrop, closer cooperation between Bangladesh and Japan is essential to address growing non-traditional security challenges, including climate change, piracy and illegal, unreported and unregulated (IUU) fishing.

During Japanese Prime Minister Shinzo Abe’s visit to Bangladesh in September 2014, the two countries agreed to strengthen cooperation in the blue economy. However, progress in this area has remained limited despite its growing strategic and economic significance. Bangladesh continues to face constraints in investment, technology and skilled human resources, limiting its ability to harness marine resources sustainably. As a major maritime nation with advanced technological capabilities and expertise, Japan is well positioned to support Bangladesh in developing its blue economy while strengthening maritime cooperation.

Looking ahead, Bangladesh and Japan should move beyond immediate economic gains to deepen cooperation in maritime security, technology transfer and sustainable development. Japan has much to offer in terms of technology, expertise and institutional experience, while Bangladesh brings a young workforce, a growing market and a strategically important position in the Bay of Bengal. The challenge lies in translating these complementary strengths into a lasting partnership grounded in mutual respect and shared prosperity.

Dr Md Shariful Islam is Associate Professor and Chairman of the Department of International Relations at the University of Rajshahi. He can be contacted at [email protected].
