title: Why Bangladesh needs a new growth model
text:
For four decades, garment exports have driven Bangladesh's development. The garment industry has created jobs, earned foreign exchange and helped transform a country once dismissed as an economic basket case into one of the world's leading apparel exporters. That achievement is worth preserving. But the model that delivered yesterday's success cannot, on its own, secure tomorrow's prosperity.

Bangladesh now confronts an increasingly inhospitable global economy. Its own weaknesses make matters worse: a narrow export base, pervasive low-productivity employment, an education system poorly aligned with economic needs and institutions undermined by corruption. These problems reinforce one another. Faster growth alone will not suffice; Bangladesh also needs new sources of productivity, better jobs and more widely shared prosperity.

Image A combine harvester cuts paddy in a field. Raising agricultural productivity will require greater mechanisation, modern technology, improved storage facilities and stronger linkages between farmers and markets. Photo: Sheikh Nasir

A recent essay by Gordon Hanson, Dani Rodrik and Rohan Sandhu in the IMF's Finance & Development offers a useful starting point. They argue that export-led industrialisation has become a less dependable engine of mass employment and that development strategies must focus more on raising productivity in domestic services, where most workers earn their living. The argument applies to Bangladesh, but it needs a broader framework: exports still earn the foreign exchange needed to pay for imports, expose firms to the discipline of world markets and drive technological upgrading.

Bangladesh needs a new growth model built on four mutually reinforcing pillars: first, a more productive domestic economy; second, education that builds real capabilities; third, effective governance and corruption control; and finally, smart industrial policy across both domestic and export sectors.

A less forgiving global economy

Bangladesh's export success emerged during the heyday of globalisation, when expanding markets, predictable trade rules and strong demand for labour-intensive goods opened doors for developing countries.

That world has changed. The pandemic exposed the fragility of supply chains; resurgent protectionism, especially under President Donald Trump, has made markets less predictable; and geopolitical conflicts have disrupted energy, shipping and food markets. According to the WTO, merchandise trade volume will grow in 2026, but most of that growth will come from AI-related goods, such as semiconductors and servers, rather than labour-intensive products such as garments. Geoeconomic fragmentation is also narrowing the scope for export growth in low- and middle-income countries. For Bangladesh, these shocks threaten its exports, access to essential imports, migrant employment opportunities and remittance inflows. Meanwhile, automation is reducing manufacturing's capacity to absorb labour, making it harder for Bangladesh to follow the development path of earlier Asian success stories.

Bangladesh also faces a vulnerability of its own making. Garments became a remarkable success, but the country failed to develop a comparably competitive range of other export industries. This narrow base exposes the economy to external shocks and is also a sign of an unfinished structural transformation. Bangladesh should not retreat from exports. Instead, it should diversify its sources of growth by continuing to upgrade export industries while raising productivity across the domestic economy.

First pillar: Make the domestic economy an engine of growth

In Bangladesh, as across much of the developing world, development policy has focused disproportionately on modern export industries. Garments dominate exports, but most workers earn their living in agriculture, construction, transport, retail, repair services, restaurants and countless small, informal enterprises. About 84 per cent of employed workers are in informal employment, often without formal contracts or social protection.

These activities are often treated as part of a residual economy, a waiting room until factory jobs become available. But for the vast majority of Bangladeshis, they are the economy, and their productivity will largely determine future living standards. A development strategy centred solely on export manufacturing leaves most of the workforce behind.

Transforming this economy requires more than microcredit or exhortations to pursue entrepreneurship. Small businesses need reliable electricity, efficient transport, access to finance, better management, modern technology and access to larger markets. Agriculture needs better storage facilities, cold chains, mechanisation and processing capabilities.

Transforming this economy requires more than microcredit or exhortations to pursue entrepreneurship. Small businesses need reliable electricity, efficient transport, access to finance, better management, modern technology and access to larger markets. Agriculture needs better storage facilities, cold chains, mechanisation and processing capabilities. Construction, transport and repair services need improved skills, equipment and professional standards. Digital platforms and mobile financial services can help, but their contribution should be judged by improvements in productivity and net earnings, rather than simply by user numbers. Policy should also strengthen linkages between large firms and small suppliers, as such connections can facilitate the spread of technology, management expertise and quality standards.

A domestic focus has its limits. A more productive shop improves livelihoods but earns no foreign exchange to pay for machinery, fuel, fertiliser and technology. Domestic services, too, cannot grow without rising purchasing power. The domestic and external sectors are complementary engines of growth, not substitutes for one another.

Second pillar: Turn education into productive capabilities

Bangladesh has expanded access to schooling remarkably, but schooling alone does not guarantee education. Too many students leave the education system without adequate literacy, numeracy, analytical abilities or practical skills. The result, as the World Bank suggests, is graduate unemployment alongside shortages of competent workers.

The problem goes beyond funding. Exam- and credential-driven learning, rote memorisation, poor teaching standards, politicisation and malpractice have eroded educational quality. The focus must shift from enrolment and certificates to learning and employability. The system needs stronger foundational education; credible technical and vocational training built around apprenticeships and internships; closer ties with employers; and universities that reward merit, effective teaching and serious research. Yet funding matters too: public spending on education has remained below 2 per cent of GDP for two decades, far short of the 4–6 per cent of GDP recommended by UNESCO. Greater investment is essential, but without accountability, it may simply produce more expensive failures.

Education policy is also industrial policy. Raising productivity on farms and in workshops and diversifying into new industries will require workers, engineers, technicians, and managers equipped with increasingly sophisticated skills. No tax break or tariff can compensate for a workforce that lacks these capabilities.

Bangladesh risks growing old before it grows skilled. Its next economic transformation will depend less on how cheaply its people work than on how productively they contribute.

Automation, AI and a narrowing demographic window add further urgency. Bangladesh risks growing old before it grows skilled. Its next economic transformation will depend less on how cheaply its people work than on how productively they contribute.

Third pillar: Put governance and corruption control at the centre

In Bangladesh, corruption has become a structural barrier to economic transformation. Access to credit, contracts, land, licences and regulatory favours too often depends on political connections rather than merit. Many entrepreneurs therefore invest in cultivating influence instead of improving technology and productivity, while resources flow to the politically connected rather than the capable.

The damage extends beyond slower economic growth. Corruption diverts money from education, health and infrastructure. It also hollows out the tax base: Bangladesh collects less than 7 per cent of GDP in taxes, one of the lowest tax-to-GDP ratios in the world. Tax exemptions and selective enforcement shift the fiscal burden onto ordinary citizens. The result is a system in which privilege, rather than merit or productivity, determines prosperity.

Transparent procurement, financial-sector discipline, predictable regulation, independent oversight and credible law enforcement must replace discretion and patronage. Singapore demonstrates how institutions that make corruption difficult and unrewarding can underpin economic transformation. Bangladesh need not replicate its political system to learn that lesson.

Image Bottles move along a pharmaceutical production line. Pharmaceuticals are among the industries with the potential to diversify Bangladesh's exports, reduce dependence on garments and create new sources of economic growth. Photo: Collected

Bangladesh does not lack anti-corruption machinery. What it lacks is machinery that points in every direction. Anti-corruption bodies have too often been perceived as instruments of those in power, pursuing the leaders and officials of previous regimes while the wrongdoing of the incumbent authorities goes unexamined. Justice that looks only backwards is not justice; it is score-settling in legal dress. Corruption carries no party card. A credible anti-corruption system must pursue the corrupt wherever they sit: in government or opposition, at the highest levels or the lowest. An anti-corruption institution earns its credibility only when it subjects today's powerful to the same scrutiny as yesterday's fallen.

Good governance is especially critical for industrial policy. A developmental state must support promising firms and withdraw that support when they underperform. Without such discipline, industrial policy rewards connections rather than competence; finance serves the politically favoured; and regulation becomes a tool for private enrichment. A state that cannot discipline itself will fail to discipline the firms it supports.

Fourth pillar: Pursue smart industrial policy across the economy

Bangladesh's history shows that industrialisation rests on deliberate learning and supportive public policies, as well as market forces. In 1979, 130 workers from Desh Garments travelled to Busan, South Korea, to receive training at Daewoo, its international partner. They returned with knowledge of production management, procurement, quality control and factory organisation, and subsequently spread those capabilities across the industry. Public policy mattered too: bonded warehouse facilities and back-to-back letters of credit enabled exporters to import inputs and finance production against foreign orders.

But the garment industry's success story also exposes a significant gap. Bangladesh nurtured one globally competitive industry without developing an effective mechanism to build others. Successive policies proclaimed export diversification, yet garments continue to dominate the country's exports. The problem has been less a shortage of policy declarations than weak implementation, poor coordination and inadequate performance discipline. In South Korea, the government used export performance to assess whether firms receiving public support were actually learning and becoming more competitive. Bangladesh absorbed the lesson that public support can nurture industries but largely ignored the equally important principle that such support must be conditional on measurable results.

Image Students receive hands-on training in operating machinery. Bangladesh's next economic transformation will depend less on cheap labour and more on developing a skilled workforce capable of driving productivity, technological upgrading and industrial diversification. Photo: UCEP

The answer lies between indiscriminate intervention and passive reliance on markets: smart industrial policy. In practice, this means:

Diagnose constraints before selecting industries. Identify and address specific obstacles, such as unreliable power supplies, skills shortages, poor logistics, costly finance, inadequate testing facilities or cumbersome regulations, rather than distributing subsidies indiscriminately. Extend industrial policy to the domestic economy. Agricultural extension services, cold chains, supplier development, management training and technological support can benefit far more workers than policies confined to export-oriented industrial enclaves. Make export diversification operational. Continue upgrading the garment industry towards higher-value products and man-made fibres, while assessing sectors such as light engineering, pharmaceuticals, footwear, agro-processing, IT and business services for their market potential, competitiveness and capability gaps. Make support conditional and time-bound. Subsidised finance, tax incentives and temporary protection should be tied to measurable benchmarks for productivity, technological upgrading, exports or employment generation, with support withdrawn when firms fail to deliver the expected results. Establish clear accountability. Each intervention needs a designated lead agency, adequate funding, publicly disclosed targets and independent evaluation. Business input should inform policymaking without allowing private interests to capture the process. Reduce anti-export bias. High tariffs that guarantee comfortable profits in the domestic market weaken incentives for firms to compete internationally. Protection without performance requirements merely sustains inefficiency and discourages innovation and productivity improvements.

None of this requires the government to predict which industries will succeed. Rather, it requires the institutional capacity to identify obstacles, encourage experimentation, coordinate investments and discontinue interventions that fail to deliver results. Nor can Bangladesh simply replicate South Korea's historical policy instruments; international trade rules, technology and the global economic environment have all changed. The underlying principle, however, remains relevant: public support should help firms develop productive capabilities, while competition and accountability ensure that such support delivers results. The task is to build a state that works with markets without allowing industrial policy to become another instrument of patronage.

Four pillars, but one strategy

The four pillars reinforce one another. Greater domestic productivity raises incomes and creates employment; education supplies the skills needed for economic upgrading; industrial policy helps firms overcome structural barriers; and good governance ensures that public resources reward productive effort rather than political connections.

These complementarities, however, are not automatic. Skills achieve little without productive employment opportunities, while incentives fail without effective accountability. The central challenge lies in coordination and implementation: identifying binding constraints, concentrating resources where returns can be demonstrated, and holding public agencies and beneficiaries accountable for results. Policies should ultimately be judged by whether they deliver higher productivity, better jobs and more widely shared prosperity.

The cost of business as usual

Bangladesh's greatest danger is not that its garment industry will collapse. Rather, it is that the wider economy will fail to generate the productivity, employment opportunities and capabilities needed to sustain another generation of development.

Image Workers operate machinery at a jute mill. Bangladesh's dependence on a narrow export base underscores its unfinished structural transformation and the need to develop competitive industries beyond ready-made garments. Photo: Rashed Sumon

Under a business-as-usual scenario, the country would remain dependent on a narrow export base, while much of its workforce would continue to be trapped in low-productivity employment. More graduates would enter the labour market without the skills employers need, and public resources would continue flowing to the politically connected rather than the most productive. The result would be an economy increasingly unable to meet the aspirations of its young people, characterised by a shortage of quality jobs, declining opportunities for upward mobility and widening inequality. When education fails to translate into opportunity and economic success depends more on connections than competence, public frustration and distrust inevitably deepen.

Bangladesh must keep its sewing machines running. But it must also raise productivity on farms and in workshops, rural shops, transport and service industries; transform education from a conveyor belt of credentials into a source of genuine capabilities; and replace patronage with transparent, accountable and effective institutions.

The workers who travelled to Busan in 1979 demonstrated what focused learning, entrepreneurial initiative and supportive public policy can achieve. Today's challenge is considerably larger: to spread that dynamism throughout the economy and bring meaningful economic opportunities within reach of the many, rather than the privileged few. Bangladesh's next economic miracle, if there is one, will emerge as much from its farms, workshops and classrooms as from its factories.

Dr M.G. Quibria is an economist and public policy commentator whose work explores trade, development, governance and democratic change in Bangladesh and beyond. He can be reached at [email protected].

title: Without reform, Bangladesh cannot escape the low growth trap
text:
The latest growth forecasts from international organisations are troubling: Bangladesh may not just grow more slowly this year, but its economy could remain weak for years—unless its underlying problems are addressed. In its October 2026 report, the International Monetary Fund (IMF) projected the growth to be 3.2 percent in FY2026-27, down from 4.3 percent in April. It expects growth to fall to 2.2 percent in FY2027-28, then recover gradually to around 3 percent by FY2030-31. The World Bank forecasts 3.4 percent growth and the Asian Development Bank (ADB) 4 percent, compared with the government’s projection of 6.5 percent growth in FY2026-27. The IMF also projects an average inflation of 10.9 percent, whereas the government has projected inflation to be 7.5 percent in FY2026-27.

These forecasts are not certainties, nor do they make the government’s target impossible. But they show how far the economy’s current course is from the recovery the country needs. While the IMF, World Bank and ADB all differ in their estimates, they all point to weak growth and persistent inflation. This convergence should prompt an honest assessment of what is holding the economy back. After eight months in power, the government should treat the current economic context as a serious crisis, one that requires coordinated action and deep structural reforms.

Both international and domestic factors contribute to the country’s weaker outlook. Immediate pressures include conflicts in the Middle East, rising energy costs, and disruptions in major trade routes. These factors raise import, transport and production costs. Bangladesh is particularly exposed because it depends heavily on imported energy. Weaker demand in export markets and uncertainty in global trade can further constrain manufacturers. The IMF also identifies conflict, trade tensions, and fiscal vulnerabilities as risks to the global outlook, projecting a 3.1 percent growth.

Domestic obstacles are more persistent. Investment has weakened, businesses face high borrowing and operating costs, and policy uncertainty has undermined confidence. The World Bank reports that private investment contracted for the second consecutive year due to energy shortages, banking sector weaknesses, low revenue collection, and limited public investment capacity. Even when a business sees an opportunity, it may hesitate to invest if it cannot count on a reliable energy supply, access affordable credit, or predict the rules it will face.

Banking problems are central to this impasse. Non-performing loans (NPLs) constituted 32.78 percent of total outstanding loans as of June 2026. A banking system weighed down by bad loans and weak governance cannot reliably channel savings to productive firms. At the same time, businesses with heavy debt or falling revenues may be unable to borrow to invest. Their balance sheet problems reinforce the banks’ vulnerabilities, and vice versa. New credit alone will not solve the problem while losses remain unrecognised, and viable businesses cannot be distinguished from borrowers unable to repay.

The cost of weak growth is already being borne by households. According to World Bank estimates, around 21 lakh more people fell into poverty in FY2025-26 than in the previous fiscal year. High inflation has reduced the real value of wages, while weak labour demand has shrunk income opportunities. Meanwhile, job creation stalled and women lost jobs; female labour force participation fell from 42.8 percent in 2022 to 38.4 percent in 2024, according to the World Bank’s Bangladesh Development Update in October 2026. Remittances have helped families and supported foreign exchange inflows. But they cannot substitute for employment generated by investment and productive businesses.

The ongoing fiscal pressures also make reform increasingly urgent. Revenue collection stood at around 8 percent of GDP in FY2025-26. This constrains the resources available to finance services, infrastructure, and household support. Interest payments also absorb funds that could otherwise be directed to development priorities. Public debt continues to rise, while a wider current account deficit and higher energy import costs could put further pressure on the taka. Depreciation is a risk, not a certainty, but prolonged financial sector problems and weak external inflows could make stability harder to maintain.

The next phase should be built around a few measurable commitments. First, ensuring discipline in the banking sector is crucial because banks must safeguard depositors’ money and channel credit to productive businesses. The Bangladesh Bank should publish the findings of its asset quality reviews and require weak banks to submit time-bound plans to recognise losses, recover loans, and meet capital requirements. Taxpayers’ money should not be used to bail out banks or companies without strict conditions and a credible recovery plan. Any public support for banks must be tied to stronger governance, accountability and measurable progress in recovering bad loans. Indebted companies that remain viable should be offered a transparent, time-bound path to restore their finances.

Second, fiscal and monetary policies should promote stability while safeguarding productive activity. The government should curb low priority spending and avoid excessive domestic borrowing as the monetary policy focuses on containing persistent inflation. It should broaden the tax base, review exemptions, and strengthen compliance through digital records and risk-based audits. The National Board of Revenue should publish its transition plan and timetable. If agreed, a future IMF programme, which the government is currently negotiating, should support a Bangladesh-led reform agenda the country can implement. Measures should be sequenced according to domestic conditions, with realistic milestones and safeguards for vulnerable groups.

Third, the government must ensure that public spending delivers lasting results. Infrastructure projects should undergo rigorous appraisal and begin only once land, designs, financing, and procurement arrangements are in place. Project costs, progress and expected outcomes, and fund maintenance alongside construction should be made public. Ministries should regularly report what public money has delivered. Increased spending alone will not sustain growth if projects are delayed, poorly selected, or fail to improve transport, energy, logistics, or access to services.

Finally, restoring confidence requires dependable energy and predictable investment rules. The government should publish the status, costs and completion dates of the solar tenders, disclose power purchase agreements, and review capacity payments. It should strengthen efforts to expand domestic gas exploration, upgrade the grid, and expand renewable energy connections. It should also speed up business approvals and customs procedures, make them more predictable, and link skills programmes to employers’ needs. Supporting the RMG industry while enabling new export sectors would reduce concentration and create more opportunities for job growth.

Bangladesh does not need a one-size-fits-all policy package; it needs politically owned reforms that address the interplay among banks, indebted businesses, energy costs, weak revenue collection, and poor investment. The government should be transparent to the public about the scale of the challenges, report progress, and explain the costs of delay.

Building towards a trillion-dollar economy depends on sustained growth in productivity, investment, exports, and employment. Bangladesh cannot overcome low growth, high inflation and weak job creation unless it tackles the long-recognised obstacles that it has only partially addressed. The government must now translate laws, commissions and policy announcements into measurable results. Doing so will require difficult decisions and resistance to vested interests. But without these reforms, the country may face prolonged stagflation.

Dr Fahmida Khatun is an economist and distinguished fellow at the Centre for Policy Dialogue (CPD). Views expressed in this article are the author’s own.

title: Our dengue response needs a fundamental overhaul
text:
As of October 25, dengue claimed 384 lives in Bangladesh this year. Just how grim the situation has become is clear from the 123,948 patients admitted to hospitals so far. Year after year, vast sums of money are spent on mosquito control, accompanied by cosmetic, often high-profile drives launched with great fanfare. Yet the same disaster keeps returning. There is no room left to shift the blame for this persistent failure. Structural weaknesses in our prevention system have proven as dangerous as the mosquito. At its core, a lack of sound planning, execution, and coordination needed for such a multidimensional public health threat is what makes its recurrence predictable every year.

Figures from recent years illustrate the chronic nature of this crisis. In 2023, the country recorded 1,705 dengue deaths and more than 321,000 hospitalisations. Deaths declined to 575 in 2024 and 413 in 2025, but both years still saw more than 100,000 hospitalisations. In October 2026, hospitals continued to admit thousands of dengue patients. These figures raise serious questions about how effectively lessons from previous outbreaks have been translated into sustained mosquito-control efforts.

The biggest flaw in our dengue response is that it is still largely reactive rather than preventive. Authorities launch drives after hospital admissions surge. Finding high-risk zones before the monsoon is patchy at best. Dhaka South’s May survey found Aedes density above the threshold in 63 of its 75 wards. Dhaka North, which gets far more of the mosquito-control budget, had run no formal survey as of June.

The methods being used are also not sufficiently scientific. There is an overreliance on fogging, whereas mechanisms for larval control, eliminating breeding grounds, and testing the efficacy of insecticides remain weak. There are no clear benchmarks to measure what these drives actually achieve. On top of that, gaps in surveillance and data use are glaring. Above all, although responsibilities are divided among the health department, city corporations, and local government bodies, their coordination is weak. Without an overhaul of these operations, there is no way out of this crisis.

Moreover, unplanned urbanisation and poor civic management cannot escape blame. Stagnant water at construction sites, poor drainage systems, discarded containers, and uncollected solid waste serve as prime breeding grounds for Aedes mosquitoes. While unusual shifts in temperature, rainfall, and humidity driven by climate change are indeed creating favourable conditions for mosquitoes to thrive, climate change alone cannot be an excuse. It is the mismanagement of urban infrastructure and institutional failure to respond and maintain year-round mosquito control that help the crisis persist.

In June, the health minister announced that private hospitals would reserve 10 percent of their beds for free dengue treatment, waive consultation fees for patients receiving treatment in those beds, and offer discounts of up to 80 percent on diagnostic tests. In July, the government also made dengue NS1 tests free at public hospitals until December 31. The health minister subsequently told parliament that private hospital owners had agreed to comply with the directives. However, as of October, there is still no publicly available comprehensive assessment showing how many private hospitals have implemented these measures.

City corporations, the Directorate General of Health Services, and local government institutions each have distinct responsibilities. Huge budgets are allocated, but the public does not know what each agency did, or how success was measured.

Breaking out of this cycle requires adopting effective solutions. Prevention must be built as a year-round effort. High-risk areas need to be mapped before the monsoon, and breeding grounds must be cleared regularly. Greater emphasis must be placed on science-based mosquito control. Monitoring mosquito density, destroying larvae through appropriate methods, and routinely testing whether insecticides actually work are essential. Integrated urban management also needs to be ensured through regular waste removal and strict inspections of construction sites. At the same time, setting specific targets, publishing regular progress reports, and expanding treatment capacity are necessary to improve the response. Effective dengue prevention demands sustained planning, coordination, and accountability at all levels.

title: We must make formalisation easier than staying in the cash economy
text:
In early September, in an article published by this newspaper, I highlighted how the country’s underground economy was not only depriving the government of much-needed revenue but also sustaining inequality, rewarding tax evasion, distorting competition, and weakening the government’s capacity to deliver public services. Bangladesh has two economies: one regulated and taxed, the other generating income, employing people, transferring money, and building wealth largely out of sight. Bangladesh Bank has now put a price on the gap between them.

In a policy paper titled “The Cost of Cash Study in Bangladesh: A Comparative Analysis of Cash and Digital Payment”—published in May 2026 but brought to public attention through media coverage only last week—the central bank estimates that the economic cost of using cash in 2023 was about Tk 1.70 trillion, or 3.24 percent of GDP, while that of the entire digital payments ecosystem was about Tk 59.64 billion, or 0.11 percent of GDP. On that headline comparison, cash was roughly 28 times more costly than digital payments.

The number deserves attention, but the more important finding sits inside it. More than half the total, about Tk 933 billion, is not the cost of printing, moving or guarding notes. It is estimated government revenue forgone in a shadow economy that the study puts at 27.2 percent of GDP. In other words, the cost attributed to cash largely reflects what remains hidden from the tax system.

The study’s accounting deserves further scrutiny. Forgone tax is an estimate of what a more capable revenue system might collect, not money that digital payments will automatically recover. Strip it out and cash still costs about Tk 770 billion a year, or 1.47 percent of GDP—roughly 12 times what the digital payments system costs, and broadly in line with estimates for India and South Africa. That narrower bill falls largely on banks, households, small firms, and microfinance institutions. Bangladesh Bank’s own costs of handling cash are about Tk 4 billion; commercial banks bear Tk 368 billion, consumers Tk 280 billion, micro-merchants Tk 62 billion, and microfinance institutions Tk 56 billion. Cash may look free at the counter, but it is clearly not.

The larger bill—the forgone revenue—is the one my earlier article addressed. In 1997, using a monetary approach, I estimated that underground activities comprised about 23.5 percent of the formal economy on average during 1972-1995. Bangladesh Bank’s estimate of 27.2 percent of GDP rests on a different method, period, and denominator, so the two cannot be compared directly. What they share is the message that a large part of the economic life has stayed outside the tax net for half a century, while tax revenue reached only 6.9 percent of GDP in FY2025, according to the IMF.

The central bank deserves credit for building a remedy alongside the diagnosis. Since July 1, Bangla QR has been mandatory for merchants, replacing a clutter of proprietary codes with one interoperable payment standard. Reportedly, the average daily transaction value rose from about Tk 28 crore in June to Tk 143.54 crore in September, in a more than five-fold increase, reflecting the rapid growth of Bangla QR payments. The central bank set the interchange fee for such transactions to zero from October 1, mandated instant settlement for merchants, created a Tk 100 crore incentive fund, and is due to introduce person-to-person QR transfers on November 1.

Digital trails can make formalisation cheaper and enforcement smarter. That said, the distinction I drew in September matters even more now. A street vendor who has never registered a business is not the same as a firm under-reporting sales or an importer misinvoicing to move money abroad. If digital payments are used to treat the vendor like an evader, the people they should help may avoid using them.

Three obstacles stand out. First, merchants may still face fees for QR payments, which can matter on thin margins when cash appears free. Second, the study estimates that about 75 percent of retail transactions take place in cash, partly because wholesalers and suppliers continue to demand it; a code at the till changes little if the distributor still wants notes. Third, only 28 percent of adults are financially literate, and nearly half of mobile-money users cannot use their accounts without assistance, according to data cited in the study.

Behind all three sits a fourth obstacle: fear. If a small trader believes a digital receipt means a tax notice down the line, they may stick to cash. The final report of the Economic Census 2024 found that only 3.3 million of Bangladesh’s 11.7 million economic units were registered, while 7.6 million, or 65 percent, operated without registration. Much of this informality reflects the realities of small-scale and subsistence activity, not deliberate tax evasion. Policy must recognise that distinction clearly.

So, what should we do going forward? Getting back to my starting point, the goal remains simple: make formalisation of informal businesses easier, make tax evasion harder, and make enforcement credible. Applied to digital payments, that means six steps.

First, make small-ticket QR payments free for micro-merchants below a specified turnover threshold, with the policy reviewed after two years. Second, have the National Board of Revenue (NBR) and Bangladesh Bank jointly announce that small merchants’ digital receipts will not trigger retroactive tax assessments, alongside a simple presumptive tax regime for those who register. Third, digitise upstream, bringing distributors, wholesale markets, government fees, utility bills, and social transfers onto Bangla QR.

Fourth, enforce instant settlement and automatic reversals of failed payments, and publish provider-level compliance data. Fifth, adopt enforceable data-protection rules before payment data reach scale. Sixth, direct the revenue gains towards tackling serious evasion by linking NBR, customs, land, company and financial records for large taxpayers, and repeat the cost-of-cash study every three years to measure progress.

Without such steps, Bangla QR payments may grow without building sufficient trust in the formalisation process. Leaving a large share of the economic life outside oversight is no longer a technical problem but rather a governance decision. Bangladesh Bank’s recent study only served to sharpen this point. The rails now exist, and the cost of not using them well has a number attached.

Cash, however, will not disappear because a code is printed on a counter, nor should the state try to force it out of the lives of those who depend on it. The hidden economy will shrink when paying digitally is cheaper than paying in cash, registering is easier than staying invisible, and the revenue system is seen to pursue the powerful evader before the pavement vendor. This is a test for the revenue board and the finance ministry as much as for the central bank.

Dr M Kabir Hassan is professor of finance and Moffett Chair at the University of New Orleans in the US, recipient of the 2016 IsDB Prize in Islamic banking and finance, and member of the AAOIFI Ethics and Governance Board.

title: Bangladesh needs a strategy to wean itself off imported gas
text:
Energy has rarely been treated as anything more than a question of tariffs and subsidies in the concurrent policy discourse of Bangladesh. However, the war that began with the US-Israeli strikes on Iran on February 28 and the resulting disruption of shipping through the Strait of Hormuz have changed the scenario. By April, Qatar invoked force majeure on its LNG contracts, diesel stocks fell below 10 days of cover, and Bangladesh had to ration fuel sales. Nearly eight months on, the emergency has settled into a chronic condition. We still rely on imported fuel to keep our power plants, factories and farms running, leaving us exposed to shocks beyond our control. It is now clear that energy is a matter of national security.

The price of this exposure is visible across the economy. By mid-September, Bangladesh was paying nearly $30 per million British thermal units (MMBtu) for spot LNG, almost three times the pre-war rate. Zero Carbon Analytics, an international research group, projected that the country’s annual energy import bill of roughly $12 billion could rise by $4.8 billion, or 40 percent, if the elevated prices persist. The energy ministry projects this year’s LNG subsidy bill at Tk 40,000 crore, nearly triple last year’s payout, while electricity subsidies could reach Tk 50,000 crore. Consumers have not been spared either, as retail electricity prices were raised by 16.68 percent in June. More recently, the World Bank’s forecast cut Bangladesh’s growth to 3.4 percent in FY2026-27, citing a more protracted drag from energy shortages.

The roots of the problem go back almost a decade. In 2018, Bangladesh began importing LNG as a stopgap to address declining domestic gas output, which has since fallen by about 30 percent over six fiscal years. That stopgap has now become a crutch, and an expensive one, with Petrobangla’s LNG import bill rising from Tk 16,505 crore in FY2020-21 to around Tk 59,000 crore in FY2025-26. Domestic fields currently produce around 1,620 million cubic feet per day (mmcfd) of gas against an estimated demand of 3,860 mmcfd. Even with imported LNG, this leaves a shortfall of roughly 32 percent. Domestic production is itself concentrated, with a single field in Habiganj supplying about half of it. Meanwhile, imported fossil fuel now accounts for about 59 percent of our trade deficit.

What makes this dependence dangerous is the level of concentration. Between January 2025 and March 2026, the Middle East supplied 64 percent of our LNG, 69 percent of our LPG, and about 63 percent of our crude oil, as well as accounting for nearly half of over $30 billion in remittances received in FY2025-26. A single shock therefore inflates the import bill while threatening the inflows that pay for it.

Fuel rationing during the Boro season also endangers irrigation and food security. The concentration is physical as well as geographical. All imported LNG enters through just two floating terminals in Moheshkhali, which have been disrupted at least three times in as many years: Cyclone Mocha forced both terminals offline in May 2023; Cyclone Remal reduced capacity for nearly four months in 2024; and a terminal experienced a temporary, partial outage again in July 2026. Each time, the shortfall’s impact spread quickly and was felt across the country.

Japan, which imports almost all of its oil, was able to release supply worth 45 days of consumption from state and private reserves in March. This was possible because stockholding is a legal obligation in the country, rather than an administrative aspiration. By contrast, India’s strategic petroleum reserve, despite having a capacity of 5.33 million tonnes, can meet only about 9.5 days of crude requirement. Bangladesh is in an even weaker position, with no formal strategic fuel reserve at all. A legal obligation on the Bangladesh Petroleum Corporation (BPC) to hold 90 days of stock, phased in as storage expands and with stock levels published every month, should therefore be our first priority.

Bhutan offers a different lesson. Hydropower sold to India is its primary export and a major source of revenue. Bangladesh, by comparison, imports only 40 MW from Nepal and only during June-November, while India has withheld approval for an additional 20 MW, citing transmission constraints. In this regard, Dhaka should actively press New Delhi for a dedicated Bangladesh-Nepal transmission corridor. A four-country power trading agreement among Bangladesh, Bhutan, India and Nepal would also give the government’s Saarc ambitions their first concrete deliverable. At the same time, power imports must also be diversified so that cross-border trade does not simply replace one single-supplier dependence with another.

Meanwhile, more than a decade after settling our maritime boundaries, we have yet to make a major offshore gas discovery, even as India, Myanmar and Pakistan have expanded deepwater exploration. The Offshore Bidding Round 2026, with bids for 26 blocks due by November 30, must not see a repetition of the bidless 2024 round. Petrobangla should release seismic data free to pre-qualified bidders, clear approvals within 90 days through a single window, and reserve a carried stake for Bapex in each contract to keep offshore expertise at home.

Supply contracts need similar reform. Qatar has extended its supply disruption notices to Bangladesh while, in August, 22 cargoes were approved without tender. The recent deal for 117 US LNG cargoes up to 2038 is a start, but diversification must become the rule. Still, diversified contracts will mean little without the capacity to receive them, which is why the government’s decision to fast-track a third floating terminal at Kutubjom must translate into delivery.

Future long-term agreements should cap Gulf-sourced volumes at no more than half of all annual LNG imports, with the balance contracted from the US, Australia or Malaysia, and include supplier substitution clauses. Spot purchases should be made only from a panel of suppliers pre-qualified through an open tender each quarter, with the price and supplier of every emergency cargo disclosed within 30 days.

Finally, none of this will hold without an institutional home. An energy security council under the Prime Minister’s Office, bringing together the energy, finance, foreign and expatriates’ welfare ministries, should run quarterly stress tests against 30-, 90-, and 180-day closures of Hormuz and publish the results.

In 2022, the Russia-Ukraine war triggered fuel price hikes and nationwide load-shedding, a warning we largely failed to heed. Recent weeks offer a further lesson. Only a month after signing a sweeping sanctions law against Russia, the US president announced a deal to import Russian diesel, reversing a policy that was in place since 2022.

Large economies can afford such abrupt turns. Bangladesh cannot. Our contracts and terminals lock in choices for decades, so every decision in this crisis must be weighed carefully.

title: Motherhood must not end sporting careers
text:
In Bangladesh women’s cricket, motherhood can mean losing both an income and the chance to continue a career due to the lack of a formal maternity policy as well as adequate institutional support. The experience of former pacer Suraiya Azmin, as reported by this daily, highlights this issue. When she emailed the Bangladesh Cricket Board (BCB) on May 9 to request paid maternity leave, she received no response. After giving birth in August, she found herself dropped from the national contract list, while her leave request and unpaid salary remained unresolved. The question is: should motherhood be a penalty for women cricketers who have dedicated their lives to represent our country?

Suraiya is not the only one to face this reality. Former national team batter Sanjida Islam Moyna, who played 16 ODIs and 54 T20Is between 2012 and 2020, went through a similar situation. While she continued playing domestic cricket after her marriage in 2020, she had to eventually step away after giving birth in 2025 to raise her child. Former cricketer and international umpire Sathira Jakir Jessy also struggled to balance motherhood and cricket. According to Sanjida, officials and selectors often assume that married players or those who have children will not continue playing for long, so they do not want to invest further in them. Such attitudes undermine women’s careers and risk wasting the talent and experience the country has already invested in developing.

While our women players are expected to choose between family life and professional ambitions, the situation in many other countries is different. Australia and New Zealand provide paid maternity leave to contracted players, while Pakistan introduced a parental support policy in 2021. These measures demonstrate that supporting players through pregnancy and childbirth is compatible with sustaining their careers. The International Cricket Council (ICC) has recently introduced return-to-play guidelines for female cricketers after pregnancy, covering medical assessments, recovery, gradual training, and monitoring. The guidelines provide a framework for member boards but do not guarantee paid leave, making a clear national policy all the more necessary.

We welcome BCB’s assurance that it will follow the ICC guidelines. But promises to address these matters on a case-by-case basis are not enough. BCB should urgently introduce a comprehensive maternity policy, establishing the right to paid maternity leave clearly, protecting contracts and salaries during pregnancy and recovery, and providing appropriate medical care and fitness assessments to support their return to competition. It should also set out transparent procedures for contract renewal and selection so that marriage or motherhood does not become an unofficial ground for excluding players. These protections should also extend to other cricketing individuals, including coaches and match officials, so that their careers are not similarly disrupted by inadequate maternity support. In Suraiya’s case, the board must settle her outstanding dues promptly and clarify her contractual position.

title: Amite hits third double ton as Dhaka bag first win
text:
Amite Hasan struck his third double century in first-class cricket against Khulna in Cox’s Bazar, while Dhaka Division registered their first victory of the season with an innings-and-103-run win over Rajshahi in the fourth round of the National Cricket League (NCL) on Tuesday.

Despite three of the four matches ending in draws, the round produced several notable individual performances, with Chattogram’s Shah Paran scoring his maiden first-class century and Rangpur’s Mim Mosaddeq and Nabin Islam also reaching three figures.

Amite resumed the final day unbeaten on 171 in Cox’s Bazar and went on to score 201 not out, becoming the seventh Bangladeshi batter to register three double centuries in first-class cricket. His 335-ball innings featured 16 fours and two sixes.

The landmark marked Amite’s third consecutive season with a double century. Sylhet declared at 632 after he reached the milestone, putting Khulna under pressure. However, Khulna finished their first innings at 199 for seven before the teams settled for a draw. The opening day had been washed out by rain.

Ashraful Hasan, who had scored a century on the previous day, was dismissed for 114.

Dhaka, meanwhile, secured a comprehensive victory over Rajshahi to open their account for the season. Resuming the final day at 215 for five in their second innings, Rajshahi were bowled out for 256 in just 11.3 overs on Tuesday, handing Dhaka an innings-and-103-run victory.

Sabbir Rahman, who had been unbeaten on 64 overnight, fell in the second over without adding to his score. Rajshahi lost their last four wickets for just 16 runs.

The victory earned Dhaka eight points, along with a bonus point for an innings win. Their nine-point haul took them to 15 points and second place in the standings. Khulna remained top with 21 points, while Rajshahi suffered their first defeat of the campaign.

In Bogura, Shah Paran struck a blistering unbeaten 163 to put Chattogram in control against Mymensingh, although the match eventually ended in a draw.

Paran, who was dismissed for 91 on his first-class debut last season, registered his maiden century in the format in just his third match. Batting at No 7, he struck 11 fours and 12 sixes in a 166-ball innings.

He also shared a valuable 79-run partnership for the 10th wicket with Ifran Hossain, who contributed just five runs. Chattogram, who resumed the day at 424 for six, went on to declare at 599, securing a 133-run first-innings lead.

Mymensingh were reduced to 28 for four in their second innings, raising the prospect of a defeat. Poor light, however, denied Chattogram the chance to force a result. Play was called off at 4:35pm, with Mymensingh struggling at 61 for five.

The Barishal-Rangpur encounter in Sylhet also ended in a draw, with Rangpur reaching 288 for five in their second innings.

Resuming at five without loss, Rangpur built their innings around opener Mim Mosaddeq, who scored 121, and Nabin Islam, who made 104 at No 5. Both batters registered their second first-class centuries as the teams settled for a draw.

title: 'Cinema is a massive undertaking. For now, I am focusing on television'
text:
Television actor Naznin Niha has carved out a steady following in the country's small-screen circuit, earning the trust of directors and viewers alike.

Yet, despite recurring offers to transition to film, the actor said she wants to remain deliberate about keeping her focus on television for now, citing the need for further artistic preparation.



Image

"I am not prepared to work in what is typically understood as commercial cinema," Niha said. "I will act in films eventually, but not right now. I feel there is still a lot of preparation left. When the time is right, I will step into the cinema."

"To be honest, I still feel comfortable acting in television dramas," she explained. "Cinema is a massive undertaking. I want to step into it only when I am completely prepared. That is why I am taking my time."

Image

Niha's small-screen output continues to draw significant viewership. She recently starred alongside Ziaul Faruq Apurba in Jakaria Showkhin's drama “Bhalo Acho To?”, which crossed one million views on CMV's YouTube channel within two days of its release—marking a notable milestone for a Bangladeshi single-episode drama.

In addition to her television work, she is slated to appear in Mohammad Mostafa Kamal Raz's YouTube film “Instagram”, co-starring Khairul Basar.

title: Five familiar titles that have reappeared in Bangladeshi cinema
text:
Bangladeshi cinema has often revisited familiar film titles, with some later productions remaking earlier films while others use the same name to tell entirely different stories. From “Sujon Sokhi” to “Nayok”, several titles have appeared on the big screen across different generations of actors and filmmakers.

Here are five notable examples.

1. “Sujon Sokhi”

Khan Ataur Rahman’s “Sujon Sokhi”, starring Farooque and Kabori, was released in 1975. Nearly two decades later, director Shah Alam Kiron made another film under the same title, featuring Salman Shah and Shabnoor. The two productions brought the familiar name to audiences of different generations.

2. “Priyotoma”

Ashok Ghosh’s “Priyotoma”, starring Nayak Raj Razzak and Babita, was released in 1973. Fifty years later, the title returned to cinemas with Himel Ashraf’s 2023 romantic drama, featuring Shakib Khan and Idhika Paul.

Although the films share a name, they belong to different eras of Bangladeshi cinema, with separate casts and creative teams.

3. “Toofan”

Ashok Ghosh’s “Toofan”, released in 1978, featured Shabana, Wasim, Suchorita and Mahmud Koli.

The title resurfaced in 2024 with Raihan Rafi’s film starring Shakib Khan, Mimi Chakraborty, Nabila and Chanchal Chowdhury. The two films have different stories and filmmaking approaches, despite sharing the same name.

4. “Rangbaaz”

Directed by Zahirul Haque, the 1973 film “Rangbaaz” starred Razzak and Kabori and attracted considerable attention at the time.

In 2017, another film bearing the same title was released, featuring Shakib Khan and Shobnom Bubly. The later production brought the name back to the screen with a new cast and creative direction.

5. “Nayok”

The 2002 film “Nayok”, directed by Ispahani Arif Jahan, starred Manna and Purnima. The director returned to the same title in 2018 with a separate film featuring Bappy Chowdhury and Adhora Khan.

The two productions illustrate how a familiar title can be used for different films, even under the direction of the same filmmaker.

The reuse of film titles reflects a recurring feature of Bangladeshi cinema, where productions from different periods have shared names while introducing new casts, stories and creative approaches. In some cases, the films are remakes; in others, the connection ends with the title itself.

title: Manipuri Rasleela veteran Krishnakumari Sinha passes away at 82
text:
Krishnakumari Sinha, a veteran exponent and revered guru of Manipuri Rasleela, passed away at her residence in Jhapergaon village on Tuesday morning due to age-related complications. She was 82.

A central figure in preserving traditional Manipuri performing arts, Sinha devoted over six decades to the sacred tradition of Rasleela, which combines classical dance, music, and narrative theatre.



Image



She began her career as a sutradhari, leading all-night devotional performances as a narrator and singer in over 300 productions, while also appearing as a principal dancer in more than 100 enactments.

After training under Guru Aja Chandramohan Sinha, she transitioned into the role of rasdhari, directing nearly 30 full-scale productions, including “Maha Rasleela”, “Rakhal Ras”, “Noukabilash”, and “Mathur Pala”.



Image



Beyond her directorship, Sinha was instrumental in sustaining the art form through teaching, mentoring generations of artists across Bangladesh and India, and guiding Manipuri Theatre from its inception as a director and adviser.

In recognition of her lifelong contributions to indigenous culture, she received numerous honors, including accolades from the Bangladesh Shilpakala Academy.



Cultural institutions across the region have expressed deep grief over the loss of a foundational guardian of Manipuri heritage. Her last rites will be performed at the Manipuri community’s cremation ground in Madhabpur.

title: ‘Timeless Testament’: Exhibition revisits Abdur Razzaque’s artistic legacy
text:
A face emerges from a few decisive strokes of charcoal. In another frame, a young boy’s features take shape through restless lines and overlapping marks. Nearby, a seated figure is rendered in loose washes of colour, while a more abstract composition breaks into a dense arrangement of shapes, textures and contrasting hues. Together, the works on display at Desh Art Gallery offer a glimpse into the range of Professor Abdur Razzaque’s artistic practice.

Image



The exhibition, “Timeless Testament | Professor Abdur Razzaque (1932–2005)”, opened on October 2 and ran until October 12. It revisits the work of an artist whose influence extended across painting, sculpture, printmaking and art education, at a time when modern art in Bangladesh was developing its own visual language.

Image



Born in Shariatpur in 1932, Razzaque graduated from the Government Institute of Arts in Dhaka in 1954. A Fulbright scholarship later took him to the State University of Iowa in the United States for higher studies. On returning home, he joined the institution that had trained him, contributing to its academic development and helping establish its Sculpture Department in 1963. His career would span several artistic disciplines, earning him recognition as one of the important figures in Bangladesh’s modern art movement.

Image



Several works in the exhibition demonstrate his interest in the expressive possibilities of line. “Self Portrait” (1957), an engraving, uses spare marks to establish his own 22-year-old facial structure and expression. In “Head of a Boy” (1956), a drypoint print, layered strokes and areas of darkness give the portrait a rough, immediate quality.

The paintings introduce another dimension to the collection. A seated figure, depicted through broad brushstrokes and muted earth tones, is defined as much by the movement of the paint as by the outline of the body. Elsewhere, an abstract composition layers fragmented shapes, bold colours and varied textures across the surface. The contrast between these works and the closely observed portraits reveals an artist adapting his methods to the demands of each subject.

Image



Razzaque’s legacy also extends beyond the gallery wall. His sculpture “Jagrata Chourangi”, associated with the memory of the Liberation War, occupies an important place in Bangladesh’s public sculpture tradition. His contributions to art education helped shape generations of artists, while his receipt of the Ekushey Padak recognised his wider contribution to the country’s cultural life.



Image



At Desh Art Gallery, “Timeless Testament” brings together works from different periods and across multiple mediums, offering a glimpse into the breadth of Razzaque’s artistic practice and enduring legacy.

title: Colombian rapper Chelo Hop steps on Israeli flag, chants ‘Free Palestine’
text:
Colombian rapper Chelo Hop made a political statement in support of Palestine during her performance at the 2026 edition of Hip Hop al Parque, a major free hip-hop festival held in Bogotá, Colombia. Instead of waving an Israeli flag presented to her on stage, the rapper placed it on the ground and stepped on it.

The 28th edition of Hip Hop al Parque took place on October 24 and 25 at Simón Bolívar Metropolitan Park.

Image

During the festival, Chelo Hop performed her latest track, “Anatomía”, produced by Astrallbass. According to a post shared by El Enemigo Co and the rapper, the song calls on popular movements to remain patient and persistent in their resistance, while looking towards 2030 as the starting point for a new world.

Image

Videos circulating on social media show a man holding an Israeli flag on stage before it is placed on the ground. Chelo Hop then steps on the flag while continuing her performance, chanting “Palestina Libre” (“Free Palestine”) and “Afuera lo que no pertenece” (“Out with what does not belong”).

The gesture drew attention to the Palestinian cause, with the rapper using her festival appearance to express solidarity with the Palestinian people's struggle for freedom and liberation.

title: Misir Ali: The man who solved mysteries but remained one
text:
When we think of fictional detectives, characters such as Sherlock Holmes and Hercule Poirot usually come to mind. Their sharp intelligence, remarkable observational skills, and ability to solve seemingly impossible mysteries have shaped how we imagine a detective novel. But, Humayun Ahmed's Misir Ali breaks away from this familiar image. He is neither physically impressive nor particularly charismatic. Instead, we meet a thin, sickly, somewhat absent-minded psychology teacher who appears to be an ordinary man. His intelligence is extraordinary, but his everyday life is filled with rather ordinary difficulties. For someone who spends much of his life trying to understand the human mind, Misir Ali himself remains a difficult person to understand.

Introduced in Debi (1985), Misir Ali is physically frail, with a thin face, sharp eyes, and unusually long fingers. In Brihonnola, Humayun Ahmed describes him as exceptionally thin and tall, with thick glasses, an untidy beard, and dishevelled clothes. His appearance changes slightly across the novels, but the impression remains much the same: an unremarkable man who hardly resembles a conventional detective. His health is equally troublesome.

Yet his fascination with understanding people reveals only one side of his personality. His childhood, relationships, fears, and emotional responses offer a more complicated picture.

Image Illustration: Maisha Syeda

In Sinduk, we encounter important details about Misir Ali's early life. His mother died when he was two, leaving him to grow up under the care of his deeply religious father. One of his childhood memories involves a mysterious chest belonging to his father, from which he believed a woman's voice could be heard. When the chest was eventually opened following his father's death, nothing was found inside.

The incident is significant because it introduces uncertainty into his life long before he becomes an investigator. One might wonder whether his later fascination with unexplained events has something to do with this early experience. The unanswered mystery becomes part of his personal history, suggesting that his intellectual curiosity may be connected to experiences he could never fully understand.

His relationship with Durga, the wife of a mathematics teacher who sheltered him after his father's death, reveals another important dimension. Although she initially treats him with prejudice because of his Muslim identity, Misir Ali gradually becomes attached to her and begins regarding her as a mother. He later honours her final wishes by participating in her funeral rites.

This relationship complicates the image of Misir Ali as an emotionally detached intellectual. Having lost his biological mother so early, he develops a meaningful attachment to someone who initially offers him little affection. From the perspective of attachment psychology, his relationship with Durga may suggest a desire for maternal security and belonging. However, his actions also demonstrate something simpler: he is capable of recognising affection beyond the social and religious divisions surrounding him.

His relationship with solitude is similarly complicated. In Nishad, Misir Ali acknowledges the conflicting desires within himself, particularly his wish for companionship and his preference for being alone. This distinction matters because solitude and loneliness are not necessarily the same. While solitude can be comforting, loneliness emerges when the desire for meaningful connection remains unfulfilled.

Misir Ali seems to occupy a space between these conditions. He values his independence but is not entirely free from the need for affection. His solitary lifestyle therefore appears less like an absence of emotion than an ongoing negotiation between personal freedom and emotional attachment.

His compassion becomes particularly evident in Misir Ali! Apni Kothay?. During a classroom exercise, he asks students questions about their economic circumstances and everyday habits, apparently to investigate the relationship between financial conditions and patterns of thinking. The exercise, however, has another purpose. He uses it to identify three financially disadvantaged students whose educational expenses he intends to support.

The incident reveals how Misir Ali often expresses care indirectly. Instead of openly displaying sympathy, he approaches the problem through observation and analysis. His intelligence becomes a means of helping others. It also suggests that his emotional restraint should not be confused with indifference.

A similar sense of responsibility appears in Nishithini. While working with Firoz, a young man experiencing severe psychological disturbances, Misir Ali receives an invitation to attend an international psychology conference in Sweden. He refuses because he does not want to abandon Firoz's case.

For someone whose life revolves around intellectual pursuits, declining such an opportunity is revealing. His commitment to another person's well-being outweighs professional recognition. Although curiosity initially draws him towards unusual cases, his involvement often develops into a personal responsibility that he takes seriously.

Image Illustration: Maisha Syeda

Nevertheless, this commitment has its limitations. Misir Ali is neither infallible nor immune to fear. In Nishithini, Firoz eventually attacks him with an iron rod, leaving him seriously injured. During his suffering, Misir Ali experiences the appearance of a mysterious goddess and asks her to relieve his pain.

The encounter exposes an important contradiction in his personality. Throughout his investigations, Misir Ali relies on rational explanations, but when faced with unbearable physical suffering, he appeals to a presence whose existence he continues to question. This need not indicate the collapse of his rationalism. Rather, it demonstrates how intellectual convictions and immediate emotional needs can coexist, even when they appear contradictory.

The relationship between reason and uncertainty remains central to Misir Ali's character. In Debi, he carefully investigates Ranu's unusual experiences, searching her childhood for possible psychological explanations. He examines her memories, questions witnesses, and attempts to understand the relationship between trauma and perception. Yet the novel does not allow every mystery to be comfortably resolved.

His investigations in Misir Ali! Apni Kothay? similarly demonstrate his willingness to consider competing explanations. Faced with the strange experiences surrounding Ayna and her husband Faruk, he develops several hypotheses rather than immediately accepting a single interpretation.

These examples suggest that his rationality is better understood as a method of inquiry than an absolute certainty about the world.

There is, however, a contradiction between Misir Ali's capacity to understand others and his limited ability to resolve the uncertainties of his own life. He can recognise psychological patterns in strangers, yet his own emotional needs remain comparatively unexplored. His intellectual pursuits provide purpose, but they cannot entirely replace companionship or protect him from suffering.

Humayun Ahmed thus constructs a character whose humanity lies in his imperfections. Misir Ali can be stubborn, curious to the point of recklessness, emotionally reserved, and unexpectedly affectionate. He is capable of extraordinary patience but not extraordinary control over his circumstances.

Perhaps this explains why Misir Ali remains compelling beyond the mysteries surrounding him. His intelligence does not eliminate his vulnerability, and his commitment to reason does not free him from the contradictions of ordinary human experience. He spends his life searching for explanations, while his own thoughts, feelings, and desires resist any single interpretation.

The psychologist who understands so much about others remains, in the end, as complicated as the people he investigates.

The writer is a sub-editor at Star Books and Literature.
