title: Why imaginary friends are important for healthy child brain development
text:
Picture a three-year-old pulling out a chair at the dining table. Nobody is sitting there, yet she insists you leave it alone. “That’s Tutul’s seat,” she says, and hands him an empty spoon.

For many parents, this is where the worrying begins. Is this normal? Should we play along? Is something wrong? According to Dr Helal Uddin Ahmed, Professor of Child, Adolescent and Family Psychiatry at Faridpur Medical College, the answer is usually reassuring.

A sign of a growing mind

“Having imaginary friends is an important part of a child’s development, and we should see it positively,” says Dr Ahmed.

Imagining means holding in your mind something that is not in front of you. He explains that this process is a core part of cognitive development, the way a child’s thinking and understanding grow. It usually starts around the age of three and is most common between three and seven.

Image Photo: Collected / luthfi alfarizi / Unsplash

Swiss psychologist Jean Piaget, whose work on child development remains a staple in education, provided an excellent description of this stage. In simple terms, young children learn about the world by pretending. A cushion becomes a boat, a spoon becomes a microphone, and a friend nobody else can see becomes someone to talk to.

The benefits go beyond fun. Imaginary play builds communication skills, Dr Ahmed confirms, and helps children learn to read other people’s feelings. When doctors assess a child for developmental concerns, they ask parents whether the child plays imaginary games. “If they can, we consider it normal,” Dr Ahmed says, expressing relief. “If they cannot, it may point to a neurodevelopmental disorder.”

As for screens, he says no direct link has been found. Too much screen time can make a child withdraw and weaken social skills, while a child busy talking and playing with an imaginary companion may actually spend less time on a device.

How parents can respond

Many working parents drop their child at school and come home in the evening eager to hear about the day. Instead of answers, they get, "My friend knows everything.”

Dr Ahmed emphasises that this situation is not a big problem. “Parents must not forbid it. They have to listen to the child, with full attention. If the child says the friend was talking to them today, ask what the friend said, what game they played, where the friend is now, and whether the friend has rested or slept.”

There are things to avoid, too. Do not insist the friend is real, and do not make fun of the child either. “Don’t say, ‘Stop this nonsense,’ or ‘You have no friend; there is nobody in this room,’” he warns. Parents should also resist adding new characters, inventing scary events or cross-examining the child. And if the child has cousins or classmates to play with, real relationships should not be pushed aside for the imaginary one.

Laughing about the friend in front of relatives is another mistake. Dr Ahmed points out that it can embarrass the child, which can be a very bad experience for them.

Ghosts at the window

Many of us grew up hearing, “Go to sleep, or a ghost will come through the window.” Dr Ahmed has no objection to imaginary characters, but not when they are used as a threat.

“Say something positive instead,” he suggests.

Childhood lessons stick, he asserts. Telling a child that the doctor will give an injection if they refuse medicine can plant a lasting fear of doctors. Warning that a cat will bite can grow into fear of animals, and he alerts us by mentioning that some adults who hurt animals are carrying a bad early lesson, as they were taught negative things in their childhood.

When to seek help

Only in a small number of cases does imaginary play become a real problem. Dr Ahmed indicates a few clear signs.

One is fear so strong that daily life suffers. The child stops sleeping, refuses to eat, avoids the washroom or trembles with fright. Another is a friend who gives harmful instructions. “I hit him because my friend told me to" or “I threw the phone out of the window because my friend said so” are the kinds of statements that should get a parent’s attention. A sudden, major change in behaviour, with the child seeming overwhelmed or obsessed, is a third warning.

In such cases, the cause may be obsessive-compulsive disorder or panic attacks, and sometimes an intellectual disability, he says.

For most children, an imaginary friend is a healthy imagination at play. Listen with patience, and seek professional help only if daily life suffers.

title: High risk, no return: Is capital moving in the right direction in Bangladesh's startup ecosystem?
text:
Bangladesh has never lacked entrepreneurs. What it has lacked is patient capital. For more than a decade, policymakers, investors, and ecosystem builders have celebrated the country's 'startup era'. Pitch competitions multiplied, venture capital entered the national vocabulary, and unicorns became an aspiration.

Yet beneath the optimism lies a paradox. Bangladesh has produced thousands of founders, promising technology companies, and millions of digitally connected consumers. But institutional venture capital remains limited, angel investing fragmented, and bank lending tied to collateral. Much domestic capital still flows into real estate, textiles, trading, and fixed-income assets.

The result is an ecosystem with companies capable of becoming regional champions, but too little capital to help them get there. The question is no longer simply how Bangladesh produces its next unicorn. It is whether the country is starving dozens of Royal Bengal tigers while searching for one mythical unicorn.

A decade of momentum

Over the past 15 years, Bangladesh has laid much of the groundwork for a technology economy. Internet access expanded, mobile financial services entered everyday life, digital commerce grew, and government programmes accelerated the adoption of digital services. International investors backed companies including Pathao, ShopUp, Chaldal, Truck Lagbe, Maya, and Sheba.xyz. The government entered venture investing through Startup Bangladesh Limited. Funding strengthened between 2018 and 2022 before rising interest rates and tighter global liquidity made foreign investors more selective. The correction exposed a weakness that had been there all along: Bangladesh had not developed enough domestic risk capital.

Mature startup ecosystems have a financing ladder, from family backing and angel investment to seed funds, venture capital, growth equity, debt, and public markets. Bangladesh's ladder is missing several rungs. Founders navigate grants, accelerators, and scattered angel networks before reaching institutional investors. Companies with growing revenue also struggle to finance expansion. They fall between traditional small-business lending and the rapid growth sought by venture funds.

The banker's dilemma

Commercial banks are not irrational. Their business is to protect capital, while startups are built around uncertainty. A lender asks about collateral, current cash flow, and recoverable assets. A venture investor asks whether a company can capture a market, scale efficiently, and execute its strategy. These are fundamentally different ways of assessing risk. Expecting banks to behave like venture capitalists misunderstands banking itself.

Bangladesh Bank established a BDT 500 crore startup refinancing fund in 2021. Revised rules in 2025 expanded financing limits, retained concessional lending, and opened routes for equity investment. These changes matter, but implementation will determine whether founders can actually access the money. Startup Bangladesh Limited, central bank financing, ICT innovation programmes, and SME support have given startups greater policy recognition. These are meaningful steps, but public money cannot build a venture ecosystem on its own.

Successful ecosystems combine government support with private capital, including corporate investors, family offices, and institutions. Bangladesh still leans heavily on public intervention when international investors pull back. That dependence is neither sustainable nor desirable.

Where are the institutional investors?

Bangladesh has pension funds, insurers, banks, non-bank financial institutions, and large corporate balance sheets. Yet allocations to venture capital and other alternative investments remain limited. Elsewhere, institutions and family offices help fund innovation over long horizons. In Bangladesh, founders remain heavily dependent on overseas investors. When global venture markets slow, domestic startups can suddenly find themselves without oxygen.

The greatest blind spot may be neither seed-stage startups nor billion-dollar companies, but businesses between the two. Many generate revenue, employ substantial teams, and have demonstrated customer demand. With patient expansion capital, some could become regional leaders. Instead, they are too risky for conventional lenders, too small for growth equity, too mature for grants, and too large for angels.

This 'missing middle' may hold one of Bangladesh's greatest unrealised opportunities. LightCastle's investment data suggest startups have raised roughly $1 billion through more than 450 deals between 2010 and 2025, yet access to capital remains uneven.

SMEs versus startups: a false choice

The debate over whether to prioritise SMEs or startups presents a false choice. SMEs sustain employment and local economies; technology startups can also improve productivity and transform industries. Both matter, but they do not always need the same financing.

A manufacturer should not be financed on the same terms as an early-stage software company. Nor should a software business be judged solely by collateral standards designed for factories.

The broader investment picture also reveals how concentrated funding remains. LightCastle recorded $124 million across just 12 startup deals in 2025. The $110 million ShopUp–Sary transaction, which formed SILQ Group, accounted for about 89% of the total. A strong headline figure concealed much thinner investment activity elsewhere. Billion-dollar valuations make headlines, and governments often embrace them as benchmarks. But unicorns are outliers, not an economic strategy.

An ecosystem producing hundreds of sustainable, profitable technology businesses may generate more employment, exports, and tax revenue than one focused on a handful of valuations. Bangladesh should pursue resilience before rarity. Royal Bengal tigers are real. Unicorns mostly live in PowerPoint presentations.

Capital should follow capability

Bangladeshi founders have demonstrated their ability to build businesses in logistics, fintech, commerce, healthcare, education, and enterprise software. The question is how to finance their next stage. Well-directed investment in innovation can support higher-value jobs, export diversification, technology transfer, productivity, digital infrastructure, and future tax revenue. Innovation is not merely an ICT issue. It is also an industrial, employment, and economic policy. The next chapter requires each part of the financial system to reconsider its role.

Policymakers must improve regulatory certainty, tax treatment, cross-border investment rules, and governance. Bangladesh Bank must turn financing reforms into consistent implementation. Commercial banks need specialist lending expertise rather than applying conventional SME tests to every startup. Non-bank financial institutions could explore venture debt and revenue-based financing, while institutional investors could consider measured allocations to innovation funds, subject to their mandates and risk limits. Corporations can become customers, investors, and acquisition partners. Founders, meanwhile, must remember that raising capital is not proof of success. Sustainable businesses ultimately matter more than inflated valuations.

Bangladesh has spent years asking where its next unicorn will come from. Perhaps the better question is whether its financial system can recognise extraordinary businesses before they become obvious. Royal Bengal tigers already roam this ecosystem: resilient, adaptable, and accustomed to difficult terrain. If capital keeps chasing mythical unicorns instead of backing capable founders, Bangladesh may discover too late that its greatest competitive advantage was never missing: it was simply overlooked.

Nomrota Sarker is a consumer brand founder and operator based in Bangladesh. Her work focuses on unit economics, cross-border scalability, and culture-led brand building across South Asia.

title: The Bengali ghosts we see in ourselves
text:
In Bengali ghost stories, even the dead have preferences. The Mechho Bhoot wants a share of your fish. The Shakchunni cannot quite give up her attachment to domestic life. The Gechho Bhoot has settled into a tree, and so, everyone else has to take the longer route home.

Their habits are part of what makes them memorable. Look past the frightening appearances, and you might recognise the relative who plans every visit around lunch, the friend who struggles to let go of the past, or yourself refusing to leave your favourite corner of the house.

With a little imagination, these familiar spirits make an entertaining guide to our own personalities. So, which Bengali ghost sounds most like you?

Image Representational image — AI generated

Mechho Bhoot knows what is for lunch

The Mechho Bhoot pesters fishermen and people carrying fish until they surrender a share. Here is a creature that has crossed into the afterlife without losing interest in dinner.

You might recognise yourself if a family lunch becomes more exciting at the mention of ilish. You have a preferred piece, notice when fish has been overcooked and find “all fish tastes the same” personally upsetting.

Food keeps you connected to people and places. Just remember that someone beside you may also have an emotional attachment to the largest piece.

Image Photo: Silvia Mahjabin

Shakchunni is the assertive voice

Recognised by the shankha bangles or traditional jewellery associated with married South Asian women, the Shakchunni remains attached to domestic life. In some stories, she takes another woman’s place in a household. Often described as a woman who died unmarried or with unfulfilled wishes, the Shakchunni may have loose hair, a dark green skin tone, luring features and backwards-facing feet. Her story varies, but she rarely seems interested in pleasing anyone.

Perhaps you understand the feeling. A relative asks when you will marry, then explains why your answer is wrong. Someone comments on your weight before saying hello. Once, you smiled. Now, you have a follow-up question.

Your Shakchunni tendencies emerge when you stop submitting every decision for family approval. Some call it attitude. You call it having answered this already. The challenge is deciding which arguments deserve your afternoon.

Image Representational image — AI generated

Brahmadaitya would like to add some context

Commonly portrayed as a Brahmin spirit wearing a dhoti and sacred thread, the Brahmadaitya is often learned, helpful or protective. You suspect he would contribute enthusiastically to an adda.

You may recognise yourself if friends come to you for explanations and book recommendations. You enjoy being useful, although a passing remark sometimes activates everything you know. Someone mentions a film and receives its production history. Lunch takes a detour through agricultural policy. Meanwhile, somebody has quietly gone to make tea. Your curiosity is a strength. Knowing when everyone has enough information would make you even better company.

Image Representational image — AI generated

Gechho Bhoot has found a comfortable spot

The tree-dwelling Gechho Bhoot has chosen its address and settled in. You understand this if you have a particular chair that other people are technically allowed to use.

You enjoy company, preferably on your balcony, where everything is already comfortable. Friends say you are difficult to bring out. You wonder why they cannot come over. Your ideal village holiday involves sitting under a tree while relatives ask what you plan to do all day. You have already begun doing it.

There is much to admire in being content where you are. Still, after declining six invitations, it may be time to leave your branch.

However, you may discover that your inner ghost changes with the occasion. The Mechho Bhoot appears when someone reaches for the last piece of ilish, or the Petni takes over when a relative asks about marriage for the third time. Perhaps that is why these ghosts may feel so familiar. Their habits are ours, exaggerated just enough to make a good story.

Nevertheless, keep that in mind the next time you call someone a Petni, they might have a convincing case for what you are.

title: Do young people still feel connected to traditional jewellery?
text:
Traditional jewellery is more than an accessory; its designs reflect craftsmanship, aesthetics, and cultural identity. However, maintaining a connection with Bengali traditions does not necessarily require wearing heavy gold ornaments. It may also mean appreciating distinctive designs and adapting them to contemporary tastes.

Shulogna Barua, 26, expressed her love for deshi ornaments. “I love traditional jewellery because I feel Bangladeshi traditional pieces are unique. It stands apart even from that of other South Asian countries. But I would not wear heavy ornaments. I absolutely love the minimal versions, the smaller pieces with intricate detailing.”

Image Photo: Silvia Mahjabin





Barua added, “Take the mukut, for example. It used to be very popular, but hardly anyone wears it now. People no longer want to wear ornaments to make them the centre of attention.”

Image Photo: Silvia Mahjabin

For Raka Islam, 28, tradition has taken a different meaning. She loves gold ornaments but more as a financial asset than a piece of fashion accessory.

“I really like designs in muted, matte finishes rather than that bright, shiny gold colour. I want to have gold in my collection, but when it comes to wearing jewellery, I prefer something that can be matched with different outfits.”

Many from this generation can relate to her preference immensely. The distinction between ownership and appreciation is worth exploring. Gold can be both an ornament and a financial asset, but the jewellery someone wants to own may differ from what they prefer to wear daily. With the metal becoming increasingly expensive, silver, copper-toned metals, and imitation jewellery offer accessible ways to enjoy traditional designs.

Image Photo: Silvia Mahjabin

Sharmin Akhter, 24, shared a different perspective. Although she prefers simple jewellery for everyday wear, she believes elaborate ornaments have their place at weddings.

“I feel heavy jewellery looks best at weddings. For everyday wear, I prefer something simple. But I have no problem wearing heavy traditional jewellery at my wedding. Mantasha, haattana, haatpasha, kanpasha, kantana, and a large nose ring can all enhance the beauty of a bridal look.”

Image Photo: Silvia Mahjabin

The experiences of a few young people cannot represent an entire generation, but they raise an important question: Does cultural connection depend on how much traditional jewellery young people own, or can it also be expressed through the designs they appreciate and choose to wear?

Perhaps traditional jewellery is not losing its place among young people so much as finding new ways to remain relevant. For a tradition to survive, it does not always have to remain unchanged. Sometimes, it evolves with the people who carry it forward.

title: Essential skincare steps most people skip after turning 40
text:
If your mirror shows growing dryness and sagging despite trying every moisturiser, you might be missing the true culprit. Rebuilding your skin’s natural barrier — not buying ten different serums — is the missing key to youthful radiance.

What changes after 40

Your skin often becomes drier, thinner, and more sensitive as you age. This change occurs because your skin retains less moisture. A decrease in collagen production makes fine lines, sagging, and wrinkles more noticeable. Additionally, years of exposure to ultraviolet (UV) rays can lead to uneven pigmentation, a rough texture, and an increased risk of skin cancer.

These changes are a normal part of ageing and do not warrant a harsh routine. In fact, mature skin typically benefits from less irritation and more consistency in care.

Image Photo: Collected / xandro Vandewalle / Unsplash

Sunscreen, EVERY DAY

This has turned into a cliché. Yet, people forget it every time they step out in the sun, or casually skip it because winter is coming. But to slow the ageing process and reduce the appearance of dark patches, it is essential to use a broad-spectrum, water-resistant sunscreen with an SPF of 30 or higher on all exposed areas.

Apply sunscreen before going outside and reapply about every two hours while outdoors, or after heavy sweating. Additionally, seeking shade, sunglasses, and protective clothing can provide extra protection.

Image Photo: Collected / kimia kazemi / Unsplash

A gentle cleanser

To cleanse your face, use lukewarm water and a mild, fragrance-free cleanser. It is important to wash your face at night to remove sunscreen, makeup, sweat, and pollution. In the morning, a simple water rinse or a gentle cleanser is usually sufficient, especially for those with dry or sensitive skin.

Avoid harsh soaps and deodorant bars, as they can dry out your face.

A barrier-supporting moisturiser

If you are the one who picks up any cream from the supershop or sneaks moisturiser from your spouse’s vanity, “barrier-supporting moisturiser” might seem like a Hebrew word to you. It is more like a moisturiser that not only hydrates your outer layer, but also protects and rebuilds it — something essential after 40.

Apply it soon after washing, while skin is still slightly damp. Look for fragrance-free formulas with glycerine, hyaluronic acid, ceramides, or peptides.

Retinoids and retinol

Over-the-counter retinol is a milder option that can help improve uneven tone, texture, pigmentation, and fine lines. Start at night with the lowest-strength product available. Apply a pea-sized amount to completely dry skin two nights a week for several weeks.

Avoid the eyelids and the corners of the nose and mouth. It is also crucial to wear sunscreen every morning. Retinoids can increase sun sensitivity, and irritation may worsen discolouration.

title: UK pledges $800 million to defend against AI threats
text:
Britain has set out around £600 million ($800 million) in funding largely aimed at defending against health and security threats posed by artificial intelligence, with the largest share going to a new biosecurity initiative.

According to a recent report by Reuters on the matter, this funding includes £100 million for a laboratory using AI to detect biological threats and £65 million to develop countermeasures against pathogens. UK's AI minister, Kanishka Narayan, said the aim was for the AI Biosecurity Lab to become a major global institution, "bringing together world-leading scientific expertise to protect people from emerging biological threats."

OpenAI and Anthropic will contribute up to £200 million in model credits to the initiative, while Google DeepMind and London-based life sciences startup Basecamp Research will offer other support, adds the report.

The package spreads across several areas. The existing AI Security Institute receives an extra £120 million, and £130 million goes to new projects improving cyber defences for critical infrastructure and the wider economy, known as the National Cyber Shield and the National Exposure and Real-Time Vulnerability Centre.

A further £60 million will fund a vehicle investing in British companies using AI for robotics, autonomous systems, and manufacturing, with another £60 million for AI research and procurement contracts. Research on AI's economic impact gets £23 million, a new chip design academy £18 million, and a prize for AI solutions to public policy problems, initially healthcare, £15 million. Regional mayors will receive £30 million to support local AI work, Reuters adds.

The National Cyber Security Centre will also get an unspecified sum to expand in Manchester, the Reuters report further states.

title: Reddit's r/opensource bans AI projects
text:
The r/opensource community on Reddit has banned any project that uses AI, is made by AI, or is aimed at AI. The announcement on the subreddit says AI in its current form does not fit with the open source community.

The new rules also set a high bar for everything else. Projects must be at least a year old, actively maintained, and have an existing community. They also need multiple contributors, which the post says means roughly three or more, and an OSI-approved licence. Common student capstone projects, such as note-taking apps, PDF viewers, and command-line music players, are not allowed.

Posters need a Reddit account that is at least a year old and has significant activity. Temporary bans are kept for members who briefly lose their cool, while those who post AI output will never be welcome back, the moderators say. Non-English speakers are also told to look elsewhere, because the moderators cannot tell AI-written text from AI-translated text.

The Verge reports that the rules sparked a backlash and led to a rival forum, r/trueopensource. Critics call them too broad or vague, and many point out that the Linux kernel now contains some AI-generated code, so projects using it could be caught out. Moderator Wolvereness said in the comments that there is room for selective enforcement, such as for software with AI-powered accessibility features like automatic captioning.

title: The fascinating science behind why we love horror stories
text:
Perhaps the elementary drive that makes the paranormal so popular amongst the masses is the fear factor itself. While ghost stories instil that feeling in people, it also comes with a fun factor, and this combination is what makes them so popular. Research even suggests that frightening experiences might help us prepare for how to deal with scary situations and unpleasant emotions while being in a safe environment.

Think about the ghost stories and horror movie experiences from your own life. You were at your home; you were safe. Your brain knew it was safe; at the same time, you were experiencing the terror. This safety of the environment is what makes it appealing to your brain.

It’s in our nature

There have been many studies regarding fear, both from neurological and sociological perspectives. One study found that the central amygdala of the brain harbours neurons that fuel pleasure-inducing behaviour. The central amygdala is also linked to fear. Which means getting scared and feeling good about it might be just biology: we are supposed to like the supernatural!

Good horror stories successfully trigger our fight-or-flight response, followed by a flood of adrenaline, endorphins, and dopamine. Think of your most intense or scary memories. Remember how the hairs stood on end all over your body? Or that unique feeling of a chill running down your spine. While those are not ideally the best experiences, they can be quite enjoyable when you feel them for just a few seconds.

The brain can process your surroundings and conclude that the experience is not a genuine threat. Naturally, the accelerated heart rate, heavy breathing, and other physical reactions wear off very soon, and we enjoy a sense of intense relief.

In short, horror gives us a concoction of “feel-good chemicals”.

There are a lot of people who enjoy gothic literature but hate scary movies as they rely heavily on gore, jump-scares and disturbing images. The use of imagination from literature itself is a great and enjoyable experience.

Besides, many people enjoy the feeling of accomplishment that comes from experiencing and overcoming that frightened feeling, not the fear itself. It’s essentially the same emotion that drives people to climb mountains or take on risky adventures. Sure, the task itself is terrifying, but the feeling of accomplishment that comes afterwards makes it worth it.

The culture of ghost stories

It’s not just the brain chemicals that drive our love for fear. Our nostalgia and culture also play a part. Think of your earliest memory surrounding the supernatural. What were you doing? You were probably in your childhood home, surrounded by siblings and cousins, and your parents or grandparents were narrating a story.

That’s a precious childhood memory. When we think of ghost stories, these nostalgic memories make them more appealing.

Besides, many ghost stories had some sort of moral lesson to them, and the stories have been passed down from generation to generation. They are so embedded in our culture that we might as well call them traditions.

To make things more interesting, the curiosity of human beings in general also plays a great part in it. In some people, that curiosity is so strong that they will go to extreme lengths. Many people actually go to so-called “haunted houses” out of sheer curiosity. Ghost stories might just be a warm-up to them!

Of course, not everyone likes to be scared. Some people enjoy the cosy feeling of being wrapped in a blanket with a warm cup of coffee without any shred of the paranormal. But most people enjoy the thrill of ghost stories, even unwittingly.

So, which one are you?

title: Millennials and the most sought-after Mexican restaurant in Dhaka
text:
For those of us who grew up in Dhaka in the 1990s, it is more than just a Mexican restaurant. It is a window to somewhere else — a world that exists somewhere between the movies we watch, the places we imagine visiting, and the lives we think we will eventually lead.

This is Dhaka before the internet takes over our lives. Before Instagram tells us where to eat, before Google Maps makes finding a restaurant a matter of seconds, and before every meal needs to be photographed, reviewed and shared.

Going out to eat is an event. Finding a restaurant is an adventure. And sometimes, the restaurant itself becomes part of our personal history. Tucked away in Gulshan 1, El Toro is one such place.

Image Photo: Collected / Coffeefy Workafe / Unsplash

University life is a curious mix of ambition, youthful rebellion, and the discovery of things we have never experienced before. Food is a big part of that discovery. Mexican food feels exotic. Tacos and nachos aren't things we grow up eating at home. They belong to another world; one we are only beginning to understand.

And then there is the piña colada.

There is something wonderfully grown-up about ordering a drink whose name sounds as though it belongs on a beach somewhere far away. Even if we aren't quite sure what the world outside Dhaka looks like, we can, for a little while, imagine ourselves somewhere else.

El Toro becomes the setting for university dates, conversations that seem capable of going on forever, and evenings that feel significant simply because we are young enough to believe everything is significant.

Image Photo: Collected / Kike Salazar N / Unsplash

It is also a time when eating out means discovering more than just new dishes. It is about testing boundaries, trying things our parents might not have ordered, and finding little pockets of the world within a city that is still figuring out what it wants to become.

That is what El Toro represents for me.

It isn't simply about the food, or whether the tacos meet today's standards of authenticity. It isn't about comparing the restaurant with places we visit now, armed with years of travel, better information and more sophisticated palates.

It is about what the place means at the time.

Image Photo: Collected / Deborah Rainford / Unsplash

It is about being young in a city that is changing, discovering new tastes, falling in and out of love, and believing the world is waiting for us to figure it out.

Perhaps nostalgia is a generous editor. It softens the edges, makes the ordinary extraordinary, and allows us to remember not just what happens but how it feels to be there.

But perhaps that is precisely the point.

Image Photo: Collected / Hybrid Storytellers / Unsplash

The places we remember most fondly aren't always the ones that serve the best food. Sometimes they are the ones that happen to be there when we are becoming who we are.

A restaurant can be a time capsule. Its tables, its menu and even the familiar journey to get there can bring back a version of ourselves we haven't thought about in years. We may return with different tastes, different expectations and a few more miles behind us, but a part of us remains exactly where it was.

El Toro is one of those places.

And somewhere between the tacos, the nachos, the piña coladas and those university dates, a little bit of our story is written.

For many of us, that is where the miles begin.

title: Grok's AI-made 'Odyssey' arrives, and it is hard to watch
text:
On July, Elon Musk said that Grok Imagine, the AI image and video generator from his company SpaceXSI, would deliver a full-length, “historically accurate” version of Homer’s The Odyssey before the year was out. Three months later, the first result has landed: a seven-minute video that Grok calls Episode 1 of an 'Odyssey series'.

It was made in collaboration with AI film studio Wonder Studios, with AI content creator Dev Walker as director. However, it arrives in the shadow of a very different adaptation. Christopher Nolan’s film opened in July and has been more than a hit. It took over $1.1 billion worldwide in under a month, the highest total of his career, and earned his best-ever critics’ score on Rotten Tomatoes. Many classicists have embraced it as a spectacle, including the IMAX visual design, though some criticised how it handles Homer’s complex themes.

So, how does Grok's version compare? Not well, as you would expect.

If you do not already know the story, you will end the seven minutes knowing even less than when you started. The video jumps from clip to clip with no clear direction, and nothing tells you who anyone is. The sudden time skips make the whole thing feel like a poorly made trailer, not an episode of what would be called a movie or a series.

The dialogue is corny and random, and it explains nothing about what is happening on screen. An ominous voiceover runs throughout, yet it adds no context either. In fairness, a few shots look lifelike, and anyone who did not know this was AI-generated might be fooled for the first few seconds. But the bad lighting and the stiff way the characters move will soon give it away. Some of the action and scenery also felt too similar to scenes from Game of Thrones, which made me wonder if Musk fed the show to this model.

Historical accuracy - the thing Musk was striving for - is hard to judge in this video, as there is little on screen to test it against. The characters speak English with a slightly British accent, and the island looked to me more like Scotland than Greece. Neither is a good sign for a project that promised to stay true to Homer.

What remains is a run of clips of men shouting at each other, with no context and no backstory. Even as a trailer, I doubt it would stir any emotion in a human audience, and I do not think many people would want to watch beyond these seven minutes. I barely managed to.

If you want to marvel at a bad AI-generated film, you can watch it here. If not, you will thank yourself for skipping it, like all the other AI slop that pops up on your X (formerly Twitter) feed these days.

title: Sher-e-Bangla A. K. Fazlul Huq: His Life and LegacySher-e-Bangla A K Fazlul Huq: Revisiting a complex legacy
text: One of the most influential political figures in the history of Bengal, Sher-e-Bangla A K Fazlul Huq left an enduring legacy through his advocacy for peasant rights, his challenge to entrenched political and economic power, and his role in shaping the politics of colonial and postcolonial Bengal. Yet his political thought, achievements and contradictions deserve renewed attention beyond familiar historical narratives. Through a collection of essays and historical analyses, The Daily Star's Slow Reads revisits his life, political struggles, ideas and legacy, exploring how his vision and actions shaped Bengal's past and continue to resonate in Bangladesh today.

title: Beyond the remittance economy: How Gulf migration reshaped power, religion and gender in Bangladesh
text:
Bangladesh knows how much money its migrant workers send home. It knows far less about how those earnings have reorganised power in the communities those workers leave behind. We can count the houses built with Saudi wages, the tuition fees paid from Riyadh, and the foreign exchange entering the banking system. Yet we have no comparable national accounting for the authority acquired by a local patron, the autonomy exercised by a migrant’s wife, or the cultural practices that become vulnerable when a new definition of religious respectability acquires financial backing. These are not sentimental additions to the economic story. They are integral to the story itself.

The question is not whether migration has benefited Bangladesh. Millions of families have depended on it, and the benefits have been substantial. The question is why an economic arrangement that transforms social relations continues to be judged principally by its monetary returns. What happens when an economy becomes better at exporting labour than at protecting the lives, relationships and freedoms associated with that labour?

Image In 2025, more than 750,000 Bangladeshi workers reportedly travelled to Saudi Arabia, accounting for roughly two-thirds of overseas employment departures. This dependence extends beyond remittances, shaping the economic security and social lives of Bangladeshi households. Photo: Star



The bargain forged in the 1970s

The relationship emerged from two very different national circumstances. Bangladesh became independent in 1971 with damaged infrastructure, a narrow industrial base and a formidable employment challenge. Across the Arabian Peninsula, the oil-price shock of 1973 accelerated construction, infrastructure investment and demand for imported labour. Saudi Arabia and its neighbours could recruit foreign workers on a scale that Bangladesh could not employ at home. The connection was primarily economic before it became a familiar feature of family life, religious discourse and village status.

Official overseas employment records begin in 1976, when 6,087 Bangladeshis departed for work abroad. By the 1980s, temporary contracts in Gulf states had become a major route for men seeking incomes unavailable in their own communities. Recruiters, brokers, travel arrangements, household borrowing and informal networks developed around that route. The state gained foreign exchange without first having to create an equivalent number of domestic jobs. Families assumed the risks associated with departure, debt and separation, while employers and destination governments retained considerable control over wages, residence and working conditions.

During the 1990s, the geography of migration broadened, with Malaysia and other destinations becoming increasingly important. Yet the Gulf remained central. Migration was no longer an exceptional journey undertaken by a few pioneers; it had become a recurring household strategy. A brother followed another brother, a neighbour financed another neighbour’s recruitment, and families began planning marriages, house construction and schooling around expected overseas income. The migrant became both an absent family member and a powerful presence in the family budget.

The 2000s brought a more visible remittance economy, reflected in concrete houses, consumer goods, land purchases, private education and small enterprises. Money could loosen older hierarchies, allowing families without inherited property to acquire assets and social standing. However, new money entered institutions that already distributed power unequally. It could help a daughter attend university or strengthen the authority of the person deciding whether she should attend. The same transfer that expanded a household’s opportunities could leave its internal hierarchy largely intact.

In the 2010s, mobile phones and digital communication transformed the experience of separation. Families could communicate across borders every day. Money moved faster, but so did instructions, disputes and expectations. A husband who was physically absent could remain closely involved in decisions concerning spending, movement and social relationships. Equally, a wife who managed remittances might use that responsibility to develop greater confidence and bargaining power. Technology did not determine either outcome. Existing relationships of trust, education, property ownership and gender shaped what constant connectivity meant for individual households.

This dependence has not disappeared. In 2025, more than 750,000 Bangladeshi workers reportedly travelled to Saudi Arabia, accounting for roughly two-thirds of overseas employment departures. Such concentration matters beyond economics. When a single destination absorbs such a substantial share of migrant labour, its employment regulations, judicial institutions and diplomatic relationship with Dhaka become central to the security of Bangladeshi households. The issue is not simply the amount of money arriving. It is also the bargaining position from which that money is earned.

Image Women migrant workers, particularly those employed as domestic workers in private households, face distinct vulnerabilities, including limited bargaining power and difficulties in seeking protection against exploitation and abuse. Photo: Star



How wages become authority

Economic change does not stop at the family doorstep. Pierre Bourdieu’s distinction between economic, social and symbolic capital helps explain why. Savings can be used to purchase land, finance a business, support a mosque or school, and establish an individual as a local patron. Patronage can generate networks and public recognition, while that recognition can translate into influence over communal decisions. None of this is peculiar to migrants or to religion. Wealth has long been converted into authority through charitable giving, political involvement and local institutions. Gulf earnings introduced an important new source of wealth into that process.

A donation to a religious institution may be generous, socially valuable and sincerely motivated. Yet religious institutions are also spaces where prestige and influence are cultivated. Who chooses the preacher, funds the programme, defines respectable conduct, or claims to speak on behalf of the neighbourhood? These are questions of power as much as belief. The central analytical issue is the conversion of financial contributions into moral authority, particularly when that authority is used to regulate the lives of people who have not consented to it. A benefactor may fund a building, but that donation does not confer ownership over everyone else’s conscience.

Class further complicates this picture. Many Gulf workers left Bangladesh with limited formal education because opportunities at home were unequally distributed. Their labour, experiences and accumulated knowledge deserve recognition rather than contempt. The danger is not that a worker with limited schooling earns money or acquires social status. Rather, it is that any society may mistake wealth for intellectual authority and social influence for the right to command others. University degrees do not necessarily protect the affluent from authoritarian tendencies either. The question is how institutions can prevent money, whether inherited or newly acquired, from overriding the principles of equal citizenship.

Ideas travel with money

Sociologist Peggy Levitt’s concept of ‘social remittances’ draws attention to what travels alongside earnings: habits, ideas, identities and expectations about how a community should live. Such transfers are neither automatic nor unidirectional. Migrants interpret what they encounter, select what they adopt and renegotiate those ideas when they return home. The communities to which they return are not passive recipients. Relatives, clerics, political organisers, schools and the media can welcome, resist or reinterpret particular ideas according to their own circumstances and interests.

The Bangladesh–Saudi Arabia relationship offers an especially revealing case. In a 2022 study, Nazli Kibria and Sultan Mohammed Zakaria examined Saudi labour migration and the transmission of Wahhabi religious influence. Their qualitative findings describe migration as an important but contested channel of religious and social change, with differing effects depending on gender, employment histories and migrants’ individual experiences. That complexity is essential to understanding the relationship. The existence of religious influence does not mean that every returnee shares the same outlook or that an entire village changes simply because one of its residents worked in Jeddah.

Bangladesh’s Islamic traditions have long interacted with the Bengali language, Sufi practices, religious scholarship, popular music and regional customs. Those traditions were never entirely free from hierarchy or conflict. Nor did disagreements over music, women’s conduct or religious purity begin with Gulf migration. The question is how particular religious interpretations acquired new channels of circulation and new sources of patronage. Overseas employment connected Bangladeshi households to Saudi religious environments, while domestic political actors and institutions determined how those connections were translated into local claims of religious and social legitimacy.

This distinction is historically important. Changes in state religious policy, the growth of Islamic organisations, international funding, print and broadcast preaching, and, later, online platforms all influenced the religious public sphere. Labour migration interacted with these developments rather than replacing them. A convincing historical account cannot attribute every cultural restriction to Saudi influence, but neither can it assume that half a century of intensive interaction between two societies involved only the movement of wages and consumer goods.

The result can be a struggle over who possesses the authority to define legitimate cultural practices. A song, festival, a woman’s choice of clothing, or a mixed-gender gathering may become the subject of public disputes over religious authenticity. Such disagreements are not simply about whether individuals are becoming more devout. They concern whether one interpretation of religious devotion can establish enforceable boundaries for others. The important question is not how religious a society appears, but how much freedom remains for those who practise their faith differently, hold different beliefs, or do not believe at all.

The Saudi paradox

Saudi Arabia itself illustrates why religious authority and social change should never be treated as fixed or timeless. The kingdom has reopened cinemas, promoted concerts and entertainment, allowed women to drive, and sought to increase female participation in the workforce. These reforms are linked to a broader economic transformation programme aimed at diversifying the economy beyond oil. A state once associated with restrictive public regulations now actively promotes itself through tourism, entertainment, cultural events and investment. Meanwhile, older Saudi-derived interpretations of religious propriety can continue to circulate in Bangladeshi debates as though they represent fixed and unchanging social commandments.

The paradox should not be mistaken for a celebration of Saudi liberalism. Social liberalisation is not equivalent to political freedom. Human Rights Watch recorded at least 356 executions in Saudi Arabia in 2025, a new annual record, and has documented serious concerns about the treatment of migrant workers and restrictions on dissent. A government can promote concerts while retaining formidable coercive powers. The distinction between cultural consumption and legally enforceable rights is fundamental to any assessment of the kingdom’s reforms.

Image Migrant workers wait at an airport. While overseas employment offers opportunities for better incomes, families often bear the risks of departure, recruitment debt and prolonged separation, with limited control over working conditions abroad. Photo: Rashed Sumon



Nor is ‘Saudi culture’ a single, homogeneous entity. Saudi citizens, including women, artists and human rights advocates, hold diverse perspectives, and state policies do not fully represent their experiences. For Bangladesh, the more useful question is which elements of Saudi religious authority have been selectively adopted and amplified by local institutions, and why. The answer lies in the interaction between money, social status, politics and pre-existing forms of patriarchy, rather than in a simplistic portrayal of either society.

The household as a political institution

Consider the different women connected to a single migrant household. A wife may manage remittances, negotiate with builders, supervise her children’s education and care for elderly relatives. A daughter may attend a private college because of her father’s earnings. A sister may use the family’s newly acquired resources to enter paid employment. These represent genuine expansions of opportunity, and any argument that ignores them risks mistaking its own thesis for evidence. Migration has enabled forms of social and economic mobility that would otherwise have been considerably more difficult to achieve.

Yet responsibility is not the same as authority. A wife who manages every practical household task may still require permission for major expenditure, travel or employment. A daughter whose tuition fees are covered may find her choices of academic subjects, clothing, friends or marriage subject to strict supervision. The contradiction is not that remittances necessarily diminish women’s freedom. Rather, it is that increased household resources do not automatically redistribute decision-making power. Who owns the assets? Who controls the bank account? Who can refuse a demand without facing punishment? These questions reveal far more about the distribution of power than household income alone.

Distance further intensifies this ambiguity. Prolonged separation may produce loneliness, emotional strain and suspicion. Digital communication can sustain affection and facilitate shared decision-making, but it can also enable surveillance from abroad. Relatives who remain at home may serve as caregivers or informal enforcers of a husband’s preferences. Whether the outcome is greater autonomy or increased constraint depends on family relationships and social institutions, rather than the mere fact of migration. The prevailing moral double standard remains revealing: a man’s absence may be publicly honoured as a sacrifice, while a woman’s independent social presence becomes a subject of scrutiny.

Women who migrate face a different set of risks. Female domestic workers may earn money and support dependants while working inside private households where they have limited practical opportunities to challenge their employers. Allegations of unpaid wages, confinement and abuse demand serious investigation and accessible legal remedies. Their experiences should not be conflated with those of wives who remain in Bangladesh. One group negotiates power within transnational families, while the other may also confront coercive structures within the destination country’s labour market.

This is why a gender analysis of migration must move beyond simply asking whether women are better or worse off. It must examine which women, with what levels of education, assets, legal status and family arrangements, acquire particular forms of freedom and autonomy. The same migration economy can finance a young woman’s education, increase her mother’s unpaid care responsibilities and expose another woman to exploitative employment conditions abroad. A national remittance total cannot capture these differences.

Image The parents of Sweety Akhtar, who was executed alongside another Bangladeshi national in Saudi Arabia in October 2026. The case has raised urgent questions about consular notification, due process and communication with the families of detained migrant workers. Photo: Star



The unequal bargain exposed

In October 2026, the execution of two Bangladeshi nationals in Saudi Arabia brought the vulnerability of foreign workers into sharp focus as an urgent diplomatic concern. According to reporting based on a confidential memorandum from the Bangladesh consulate in Jeddah, Nazrul Islam Abdul Basir and Sweety Akhtar had been detained since August 2023. A prisoner list recorded a cybercrime allegation against him and an adultery allegation against her. Saudi authorities subsequently announced their executions for what they described as an immoral act in a mosque in Makkah. The available memorandum did not explain the relationship between these differing descriptions of the alleged offences.

The prisoner list provided to the consulate reportedly did not indicate that either individual had received a death sentence. The consulate stated that it had not been informed of the sentences or executions and had sought copies of the judgments and details of the judicial proceedings. The same memorandum referred to 306 Bangladeshis imprisoned in Saudi Arabia’s western region. These facts do not establish every detail of what occurred during the court proceedings, nor do they demonstrate that consular officials were never able to communicate with the detainees. However, they establish a compelling need for the relevant authorities to provide a documented chronology of the detentions, notification procedures, access to legal counsel, interpretation services, appeals and communication with the detainees’ families.

Article 36 of the Vienna Convention on Consular Relations protects a detained foreign national’s right to communicate with consular officials and requires the authorities to inform the detainee without delay of their right to have the consulate notified. If the detainee so requests, the authorities must inform the relevant consular post without delay. Whether those obligations were fulfilled in these cases requires evidence. Separate questions concern the fairness and proportionality of the proceedings and the information provided to the families. Bangladesh should not allow religious disapproval of an alleged offence to substitute for scrutiny of the legal process. A state’s obligation to protect the rights and interests of its citizens does not expire when their alleged conduct is unpopular.

The executions also expose a structural tension. Bangladesh needs Saudi employment opportunities, and Saudi employers need foreign labour, but the relationship operates within a system in which workers often have limited bargaining power. Diplomatic friendship can obscure this imbalance when the relationship is measured primarily by labour quotas, remittance flows and official visits. A more meaningful test is whether a Bangladeshi worker facing imprisonment can obtain timely information, competent legal representation and the support of a government willing to press for answers before it is too late.

A different measure of development

Amartya Sen’s account of development as an expansion of substantive freedoms offers a more demanding standard than the volume of money transferred. Income matters because it can widen people’s choices. Yet the ability to choose also depends on education, health, bodily security, political voice and social relations. A household may become wealthier while a daughter’s mobility remains restricted. A village may acquire new buildings while dissenting cultural practices lose space. A government may celebrate remittances while migrants remain vulnerable to recruitment debt and inadequate legal support.

Image Nazrul Islam Abdul Basir, one of two Bangladeshi nationals executed in Saudi Arabia in October 2026. Their executions raised serious questions about consular protection, access to legal representation and transparency in judicial proceedings. Photo: Courtesy



A better policy framework would therefore measure more than overseas departures and remittance receipts. It would track recruitment costs relative to earnings, unpaid wages, access to legal representation, deaths and injuries, and the practical effectiveness of consular interventions. At home, research should examine who controls remittance-financed property, how care responsibilities are distributed, and whether women’s education and decision-making power change over time. Local studies should investigate how religious philanthropy and political patronage influence cultural participation without presuming that every donor or returnee exercises coercive authority.

There is an economic dimension to reform as well. Lower recruitment costs, higher skill levels, enforceable contracts, diversified destinations and productive investment at home would reduce families’ dependence on repeated cycles of migration. Stronger public services could make remittances a source of greater choice rather than a substitute for inadequate employment opportunities and welfare institutions. The point is not to end migration. It is to prevent the necessity of migration from becoming the organising principle of national development.

The historical contribution of Bangladeshi migrants is undeniable. Their earnings have transformed the material circumstances of millions of people, sometimes weakening the grip of inherited class privilege and expanding women’s opportunities. The same history has also created new arenas in which wealth can be converted into authority, religious interpretations can acquire institutional power, and workers’ rights can be subordinated to the maintenance of a vital foreign labour market. These outcomes have been shaped by political decisions and social institutions; they were not the inevitable price of receiving money from abroad.

Image For millions of Bangladeshis, overseas employment has opened pathways to higher incomes, better education and improved living standards. Yet recruitment costs, debt and prolonged family separation remain significant burdens of the migration economy. Photo: Star



For fifty years, Bangladesh has built increasingly sophisticated systems for counting the dollars arriving from its citizens’ labour. It has not developed an equally serious public account of who gains power from those dollars, who bears the costs of separation and care, and how securely the workers themselves are protected. That is the unfinished history of the remittance economy. The question for the next fifty years is whether Bangladesh will continue to measure the success of migration mainly by what it extracts from workers, or whether it will also measure that success by the freedoms and protections it makes possible for them and for the people they leave behind.

Dr Lubna Ferdowsi is a researcher and educator whose work engages with society, culture, identity, public policy and questions of citizenship.

title: Rethinking development beyond Western prescriptions
text:
Development is conventionally understood as a long-term process of structural transformation and societal progress, with economic growth traditionally regarded as its defining characteristic. For decades, gross domestic product (GDP) served as the principal measure of a society’s development. However, this growth-centred approach increasingly came under criticism, prompting scholars to recognise the importance of assessing human and social well-being through measures such as the Human Development Index (HDI), rather than relying solely on GDP. Over time, the understanding of development has broadened considerably, incorporating indicators ranging from inequality and carbon emissions to freedom of choice, alongside comprehensive frameworks such as the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). This proliferation of indicators and frameworks has made development an increasingly complex concept, raising a fundamental question: when we speak of development, which measures or criteria should we use to define and assess it?

Image An uncovered manhole on a busy road. Akbar Ali Khan's "open manhole" metaphor exposes the pitfalls of development approaches that overlook local contexts and people's everyday realities. Photo: Star

To avoid this confusion, I find Akbar Ali Khan’s “open manhole” metaphor a simple yet powerful conceptualisation of development. With a sense of humour, Khan remarked that if you find a place where the cover of a manhole has disappeared (perhaps because it has been stolen), it is not a developed country. This metaphor exposes the limitations of conventional approaches to national economic development, particularly their superficial, top-down promises that often fail to account for local contexts and the lived realities of ordinary people. Such a contextualised understanding of development highlights the importance of Southern approaches alongside dominant Western models.

Background to the Southern perspective on development

If the ultimate goal of development is human well-being, what is wrong with adopting Western models when they prove effective? Bangladesh's garment industry offers an example. By following the neoliberal economic model associated with the Global North, the industry has become the backbone of Bangladesh's economic growth. It has also expanded women's economic participation and mobility, creating new opportunities for employment and financial independence.

If development approaches originating in the Global North have produced tangible benefits, why should we question them? The answer lies in the politics of development. In his influential book Orientalism, Edward Said argues that the Third World has been managed politically, sociologically, militarily, ideologically, scientifically and imaginatively through Western perspectives. A declaration made by US President Harry Truman in 1949 illustrates this approach: “We must embark on a bold new programme for making the benefits of our scientific advances and industrial progress available for the improvement and growth of underdeveloped areas.” Led largely by the United States, Western countries initiated an ambitious development project aimed at transforming so-called Third World countries through Western scientific knowledge, industrial practices and economic models.

Image Adamjee Jute Mill, once the world's largest jute mill, was shut down in 2002 amid economic restructuring. Yet Bangladesh now promotes jute as an environmentally sustainable alternative to plastic, raising questions about the development priorities behind the mill's closure. Photo: James Burke/The LIFE Picture.

This process can also be understood as a project of domination through development. Its historical roots lie in colonialism, which enabled Western powers to control, exploit and plunder resources across Africa, Asia and Latin America. Political independence did not necessarily bring an end to these unequal relationships. In the postcolonial period, Western powers continued to exercise influence and advance their economic and political interests through new forms of imperialism and neocolonialism.

Joseph Stiglitz has highlighted how the conditionalities imposed by the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and the World Bank have undermined the sovereignty of states in the Global South. Bangladesh's experience illustrates these contradictions. Adamjee Jute Mill, once the world's largest jute mill, was shut down in 2002 amid economic restructuring. Yet today, Bangladesh is promoting jute bags as an environmentally sustainable alternative to plastic. Environmental sustainability was not a priority for global financial institutions when they prescribed the closure of Adamjee Jute Mill. This contradiction illustrates the problems associated with viewing development predominantly through a Western lens.

Image Bangladesh's ready-made garment (RMG) industry demonstrates how Western neoliberal economic models can drive economic growth and expand women's participation in the workforce, even as their broader implications for development remain contested. Photo: Star

The application of Western development policies often produces contradictory outcomes, particularly in the context of Bangladesh. On the one hand, the closure of potentially viable local jute-based industries under development policies associated with the Global North effectively undermined opportunities for locally contextualised and environmentally sustainable development. On the other hand, the subsequent expansion of the garment industry demonstrates how Western development models can also create pathways to economic advancement, particularly through export-oriented production and profit generation. These contrasting experiences highlight the complexity of development and the importance of evaluating policies in relation to local circumstances rather than assuming that a single model will produce equally beneficial outcomes everywhere.

The Global South has not merely been a passive recipient of Western development models. Countries and communities across the Global South possess their own indigenous knowledge, practices and approaches to development.

Indigenous knowledge and development innovations from the Global South

To counter the adverse effects of imperialism, we must strengthen our capacity for self-sufficiency. However, the Global South has not merely been a passive recipient of Western development models. Countries and communities across the Global South possess their own indigenous knowledge, practices and approaches to development. Indeed, many development practices that are widely recognised today originated from successful initiatives and practitioners in this part of the world.

For example, BRAC pioneered the ‘Ultra-Poor Graduation Model’ to support people living in extreme poverty who could not benefit from conventional microfinance programmes. Operating across four interconnected areas- livelihood promotion, financial inclusion, social mobilisation and social protection- the graduation approach seeks to unlock people's potential through holistic, time-bound and context-specific interventions lasting between 12 and 36 months. These interventions strengthen individual agency, restore dignity and place people on a pathway towards greater self-reliance and improved well-being.

Abhijit Banerjee and Esther Duflo presented an example from Mumbai that illustrates the remarkable capacity for innovation and entrepreneurship often demonstrated by people living in poverty. The Nobel Prize-winning economists described how, every morning before dawn, a group of women would visit the beach to collect wet sand from the sea. They would then spread it evenly across the street before traffic began to move. As cars started passing over the sand, the heat generated by their wheels helped dry it. The women would subsequently collect the dried sand, return to their settlement, package it into small packets and sell it to local women, who used it to scrub dishes.

Southern approaches to development can be found not only in the work of Bangladeshi NGOs and the resourcefulness of communities living in Indian slums but also in innovative approaches to urban governance in Bogotá, Colombia.

In 1995, Antanas Mockus was elected mayor of Bogotá. Among his popular initiatives was the recruitment of 420 mimes to mock traffic violators, reflecting his belief that Colombians were more afraid of public ridicule than financial penalties. He also introduced a “Night without Men”, during which men across the city were encouraged to stay at home for an evening and take care of their households and children, while women were encouraged to venture outside and enjoy public spaces.

Image The cover of Edward Said's Orientalism. Said examined how Western perspectives have shaped political, intellectual and cultural understandings of the East, often portraying Eastern societies as inferior.

Numerous examples from around the world, therefore, illustrate what can be understood as Southern approaches to addressing development challenges. These initiatives demonstrate how locally grounded knowledge, community participation and innovative solutions can provide alternative ways of understanding and pursuing development, rather than depending exclusively on models developed in the Global North.

Universalising Western ideas of development

The examples discussed above demonstrate that we possess considerable potential for innovation and development. However, a fundamental problem is that we often undermine our own progress by perceiving ourselves negatively, as inferior, backward and incapable of producing valuable knowledge. This tendency can be understood through Edward Said's concept of Orientalism, which explains how the Western world historically constructed representations of the East as inferior. The irony is that we frequently accept and internalise these ethnocentric representations produced by the West, allowing them to shape how we perceive ourselves and our capabilities.

Similarly, Frantz Fanon explains how colonialism creates an internalised sense of inferiority, leading colonised people to regard whiteness and Western culture as inherently superior. Deep down, we aspire to become like them and seek to emulate the West. Consequently, we develop negative perceptions of ourselves, and one particularly revealing example is our attitude towards language. I remember encountering a German speaker at a conference in Bangladesh who questioned why we were speaking English when there was only one international speaker present.

I had a similar experience during an interview with a Japanese documentary film producer. While I was speaking English, he interrupted me and asked, “Why are you speaking English? Why not Bangla?” I felt ashamed. The encounter made me realise how, in our attempts to be accommodating, we sometimes inadvertently undermine and disrespect our mother tongue. This sense of linguistic inferiority has profound implications not only for how we perceive and conduct ourselves as individuals but also for how we conceptualise and pursue development.

The first question we must ask ourselves is whether we genuinely aspire to develop a Southern approach to development. If we are sincere about this aspiration, the most important task is to look within ourselves and critically examine our own perceptions, values, intellectual traditions and ways of understanding the world.

Structural inequalities in knowledge production

In my view, one of the major shortcomings is the limited theoretical and scholarly contribution of the Global South to academic knowledge production through research publications. Patterns of academic publishing reveal substantial disparities between the Global South and the Global North in terms of research output, visibility, funding, authorship and citation impact. The Global North generally produces a greater number of internationally indexed publications and enjoys stronger representation in prestigious academic journals, benefiting from greater access to research funding, infrastructure, academic databases, international networks and institutional resources.

Researchers in the Global South, despite their growing contributions to academic research, continue to encounter significant barriers, including inadequate funding, limited research infrastructure, high publication fees, language barriers and restricted access to high-impact journals. These disparities reflect broader structural inequalities embedded within the global research and academic publishing system.

Bangladesh offers a clear illustration of this disparity. According to Scientific Bangladesh, the country's Scopus-indexed publications increased from 15,413 in 2024 to 18,613 in 2025. Over the same period, India's publications rose from 334,617 to 364,782, while Pakistan's increased from 42,353 to 45,260. This gap is associated with limited research facilities and funding, restricted access to academic journals, insufficient time devoted to research and publication practices driven primarily by academic promotion requirements. Moreover, research priorities are often influenced by external donors: nine of the top 15 research funding agencies in 2025 were foreign organisations.

The central concern, therefore, is not necessarily how much research the Global South produces, but rather who determines what should be studied, whose interests such research serves and how it contributes to our own development priorities.

The central concern, therefore, is not necessarily how much research the Global South produces, but rather who determines what should be studied, whose interests such research serves and how it contributes to our own development priorities. How can we expect meaningful Southern perspectives on development to emerge when we lack sufficient control over the systems through which academic knowledge is produced and disseminated?

Image A woman works with traditional textiles. Southern approaches to development recognise the value of indigenous knowledge, local practices and community-led initiatives rather than relying exclusively on development models originating in the Global North. Photo: Star

Southern approaches to development cannot be fully realised without greater academic autonomy and more equitable participation by researchers and institutions from both the Global South and the Global North. Addressing these structural imbalances is essential if Southern perspectives are to contribute meaningfully to the global production of knowledge and the broader development discourse.

Conclusion

In conclusion, there is nothing inherently wrong with adopting Western development models, provided they contribute to the well-being of people in the Global South without generating adverse consequences. However, development should not be understood or measured exclusively through Western-prescribed indicators. Instead, it should incorporate multiple principles, perspectives and forms of knowledge, including those originating in the Global South. Striking a balance between these approaches is essential for achieving more equitable and sustainable development outcomes. Global development models must be adapted to local contexts rather than applied uniformly without sufficient consideration of the distinct needs, experiences, priorities and circumstances of different societies.

The Global South should not remain merely a recipient of knowledge produced elsewhere. It must also become an active producer of knowledge and contribute to shaping the global discourse on development. Greater investment in research, more equitable international collaboration, stronger leadership by local researchers and institutions, and improved access to international research platforms are necessary to address existing disparities and establish a more inclusive and equitable system of knowledge production.
