title: Is lead exposure making South Asia more violent?
text:
Lead is an oddly discreet villain.

It does not announce itself with smoke. It has no sinister smell. You cannot look at a plate of rice, a child’s toy or a shiny aluminium cooking pot and say, “Ah yes, neurotoxin.” It can sit quietly in soil, dust, paint, spices, cookware and cosmetics. It can travel home from a battery recycling workshop on somebody’s clothes. And once it gets into a child’s body, it can interfere with the one organ we spend decades trying to develop and approximately five minutes destroying on social media: the brain.

For Bangladesh, this is not some abstract environmental health concern discussed in conference rooms and policy papers. The latest nationally representative data are fairly terrifying.

The Bangladesh Multiple Indicator Cluster Survey 2025, conducted by the Bangladesh Bureau of Statistics with UNICEF, tested around 11,000 children aged 12–59 months. It found that 38.4 per cent had blood lead levels of at least 5 micrograms per decilitre (µg/dL). The mean was 5.21 µg/dL. Among pregnant women, 7.5 per cent crossed that same benchmark.

A necessary clarification here: 5 µg/dL is not a magical line below which everything is fine. The World Health Organization says there is no known safe level of lead exposure, and adverse effects in children have been observed at blood concentrations as low as 3.5 µg/dL. WHO estimates that lead exposure contributed to more than 3.5 million deaths worldwide in 2023, overwhelmingly through cardiovascular effects.

So yes, Bangladesh has a lead problem.

Back in 2020, UNICEF and Pure Earth estimated that around 800 million children worldwide had blood lead levels above 5 µg/dL. Nearly half lived in South Asia. India alone accounted for an estimated 275.6 million children; Pakistan for 41.1 million; and Bangladesh for 35.5 million. At the time, Bangladesh ranked fourth in the world by the number of affected children.



Image Unsafe recycling of used lead-acid batteries releases toxic lead into the surrounding environment, contaminating soil, dust and air and exposing workers and nearby communities to serious health risks. File photo: Rajib Raihan

Those figures were modelled estimates and are now several years old, so they should be read with appropriate caution.

A comprehensive review published in August this year, covering Bangladesh, Nepal, Sri Lanka, India and Pakistan, reached a similarly grim conclusion: blood lead concentrations across South Asia frequently exceeded the US CDC reference value of 3.5 µg/dL. Importantly, the researchers found that since leaded petrol disappeared, the villains have diversified. Food, spices, vegetables, rice, contaminated air and consumer products now form a messy web of exposure.

India remains staggering simply because of its scale. A 2025 systematic review of 51 studies estimated a pooled mean blood lead level of 10.4 µg/dL among Indian children. Even children without a known high-risk exposure averaged 8.71 µg/dL. The authors were careful to note considerable heterogeneity and generally weak underlying evidence, but there is no plausible reading of those numbers in which everything is hunky-dory.

Pakistan is still assembling its national picture. In May 2026, a government-UNICEF study of more than 2,100 toddlers living in high-risk areas of seven cities found elevated lead exposure in roughly four out of ten children; in Hattar, Haripur, the figure reached 88 per cent. UNICEF says modelling suggests that as many as eight in ten Pakistani children could be affected, among the highest proportions globally, but a nationally representative survey is still needed.

If there was ever a case for South Asian regional cooperation that did not involve border disputes or arguments over water-sharing, this may be it.



How did lead get everywhere?

For decades, the obvious source was petrol. South Asian countries eventually removed lead from fuel, producing enormous public health gains. Unfortunately, lead did not receive the memo that its services were no longer required.

Bangladesh is believed to have had more than 1,100 informal or illegal used lead-acid battery recycling operations, according to a UNEP assessment. Backyard smelting and crude recycling can contaminate surrounding soil, dust and air, while workers can carry lead home to their families.

Researchers also discovered that some Bangladeshi turmeric processors were adding lead chromate, an industrial yellow pigment, to make inferior turmeric look brighter. A 2019 investigation found evidence of the practice in seven of nine major turmeric-producing districts, with some turmeric exceeding the national lead limit by up to 500 times. Isotope analysis linked the adulterated spice to lead in pregnant women’s blood.



Image Some turmeric processors in Bangladesh have used lead chromate, a toxic industrial yellow pigment, to make low-quality turmeric appear brighter and more appealing, creating a dangerous source of lead exposure. Photo: Star

Lead has also turned up in paints, ceramics, toys, cosmetics and recycled-metal cookware. A Pure Earth market survey in Bangladesh detected it across nine categories of consumer products. South Asian surma and kajal have produced spectacularly high readings in some international investigations, while recent research has shown that lead can leach from recycled aluminium and brass cookware made in the region.

Lead damages the developing brain. That much is not controversial.

Childhood exposure has been associated with lower intelligence, poorer attention, weaker working memory and executive function, behavioural difficulties and impaired educational performance. MRI research following children into adulthood has found that higher childhood lead levels are associated with reduced grey matter volume in parts of the prefrontal cortex and anterior cingulate cortex, areas involved in decision-making, mood regulation and executive control.

So, what happens when millions of children grow up with a neurotoxin capable of affecting impulse control and behaviour circulating in their bodies?

This is where the conversation gets fascinating. It is also where we need to put down the sensational headline and behave like adults.



Higher childhood lead exposure was associated with higher arrest rates, including arrests for violent crimes in some analyses. Another strand of research noted that violent crime in several wealthy countries fell roughly a generation after leaded petrol was phased out.

For decades, researchers have investigated what is sometimes called the “lead-crime hypothesis”. One famous US study tracked children whose blood lead levels had been repeatedly measured and later examined their arrest records. Higher childhood lead exposure was associated with higher arrest rates, including arrests for violent crimes in some analyses. Another strand of research noted that violent crime in several wealthy countries fell roughly a generation after leaded petrol was phased out.

Compelling? Absolutely. Case closed? Absolutely not.

A 2023 systematic review of individual-level research found considerable inconsistency across studies, exposure windows and outcomes.

Then came an important update in 2025. Researchers reviewed 43 human epidemiological studies and 37 animal studies on lead exposure and antisocial behaviour. Their conclusion was striking: taken together, the evidence indicated a “likely causal association” between lead exposure and antisocial behaviour.

The evidence specifically concerning aggression was rated only “slight”. Evidence for antisocial disorders and violations of social norms was stronger, rated as “moderate”, but “lead makes people violent” is not an accurate summary of the science.



Image Lead exposure during childhood can cause lasting damage to the developing brain, affecting cognitive abilities, behavioural development and learning, with consequences that may extend well into adulthood.

An Indian study offers a useful South Asian glimpse. Researchers examining 756 young children in Chennai found that higher blood lead levels were associated with poorer executive function, anxiety, social problems and ADHD-related behaviour. That is important evidence of neurobehavioural effects. It is not evidence that those children would grow up to become violent criminals.

Bangladesh has certainly experienced disturbing forms of violence. Ain o Salish Kendra recorded 197 deaths from mob violence in 2025, up from 128 the year before, alongside extensive political clashes. Any Bangladeshi who has watched footage of someone being beaten by a mob because a rumour travelled faster than the police will reasonably ask what produces that kind of collective loss of restraint.

But this article is emphatically not arguing that lead exposure caused those killings or violent crimes in Bangladesh, India or Pakistan.

There is no credible evidence allowing us to draw that line.

Human violence does not come with one convenient laboratory label. Poverty, inequality, childhood trauma, gender norms, political conflict, drugs and alcohol, firearms, policing, institutional trust, impunity, education and socialisation all matter. Trying to explain a society’s violence through blood chemistry alone would not merely be bad science; it would also be an excellent way of absolving governments, institutions and offenders of responsibility.

Lead should be understood as a possible risk factor, not a puppet master.

That may sound less sexy than “Pollution is making us violent”, but reality has an annoying habit of refusing to fit inside headlines.

There is another reason to take the lead question seriously without exaggerating it: removing exposure works.

After researchers, regulators and media campaigns tackled the problem, the proportion of contaminated turmeric samples fell from 47 per cent in September 2019 to 5 per cent in early 2020 and then to no detectable adulteration in 2021. Blood lead levels among sampled participants subsequently fell by a median of 30 per cent.



Image Informal recycling of lead-acid batteries, including those used in electric three-wheelers, is a major source of lead contamination in Bangladesh, putting workers and surrounding communities at risk. Photo: Rashed Shumon

At Kathgora, north of Dhaka, where informal battery recyclers had left heavily contaminated land behind, a clean-up led to an average 42 per cent reduction in children’s blood lead levels after about 18 months.



These are not tiny victories. They tell us something unfashionable: regulation works, enforcement works, and cleaning contaminated land works. Making producers stop putting poison into food works.

Bangladesh has finally moved towards a national response. In August 2026, the Cabinet approved the draft National Strategy and Multi-Year Action Plan for a Lead-Free Bangladesh 2026–2035, setting targets to reduce the prevalence of elevated blood lead levels in children by 50 per cent from the MICS baseline by 2030 and by 95 per cent by 2035.

The urgency is difficult to overstate. A World Bank-linked modelling study estimated that South Asian children under five lost some 230 million IQ points from lead exposure in 2019, with lost future income equivalent to about 3.5 per cent of regional GDP. The study’s broader estimate put the total health and economic cost of lead exposure in South Asia at roughly 9 per cent of GDP, although such modelling carries substantial uncertainty.

If a toxin can quietly diminish children’s cognitive potential, affect their behaviour, damage their hearts and kidneys, and shave away possibilities from millions of lives, and if much of that exposure is preventable, how much more evidence do we need before treating it as the public health emergency it already is?

Whatever questions remain about lead and violence, there is no ambiguity about this: children should not have to grow up carrying poison in their blood.

title: Tarique Rahman’s Japan visit: Turning trust into tangible gains
text:
Prime Minister Tarique Rahman should arrive in Tokyo with a clear message: Bangladesh is ready to become a dependable economic and strategic partner for Japan. But goodwill alone will not be enough. He must show what Bangladesh can offer, how it intends to protect investment and why Japan should place greater confidence in its future.

The reported four-day visit, beginning on October 26, is expected to focus on economic cooperation, investment and a possible arrangement for Bangladeshi workers. These are promising areas, but negotiations are not achievements. The visit should produce practical commitments that both countries can follow through on.

Japan has been one of Bangladesh’s most trusted development partners. Its contributions to infrastructure development have been substantial. The challenge now is to build on that relationship through stronger trade, industrial investment, skilled employment and maritime cooperation.

The partnership has a long history. Japan recognised Bangladesh in February 1972, and Sheikh Mujibur Rahman visited Tokyo the following year. President Ziaur Rahman visited in 1978 and 1980. An air services agreement and the first bilateral meeting on commerce and economic cooperation in 1980 showed that relations were moving beyond diplomatic goodwill.

Begum Khaleda Zia’s visits in 1994 and 2005 carried this engagement forward. The 2002 technical cooperation agreement provided an institutional framework, while her July 2005 talks with Prime Minister Junichiro Koizumi gave the relationship a wider economic and strategic direction. Their joint statement recognised Bangladesh as a bridge between South and East Asia and placed Japan within Dhaka’s “Look East” diplomacy. Investment, technology, training and good governance were already priorities. Two decades later, the question is how much Bangladesh has delivered on them.

The 2014 comprehensive partnership and the 2023 strategic partnership deepened cooperation in infrastructure, connectivity and economic security. Tarique Rahman inherits these commitments, along with the responsibility to make them work. Relations with Japan must remain a national priority, not a political possession that changes hands with each government.

Bangladesh offers more than a need for development assistance. It has a sizeable domestic market, a growing industrial base and a strategic position on the Bay of Bengal. Japan wants reliable supply chains, commercial opportunities and secure maritime routes. Dhaka should understand these interests and negotiate from a position of confidence.

Image The seventh Bangladesh–Japan Foreign Office Consultations (FOC) were held in Dhaka on August 12, 2026. Foreign Secretary Asad Alam Siam and Japanese Senior Deputy Foreign Minister Namazu Hiroyuki led their respective delegations. Photo: MOFA, Bangladesh

Matarbari’s deep-sea port and the Bay of Bengal Industrial Growth Belt, or BIG-B, illustrate the possibilities. Together, they could strengthen logistics, energy and industrial connectivity, including links with India's northeast.

Yet geography does not guarantee success. A modern port is of limited value without efficient customs, dependable transport, competitive charges and industries that generate cargo. Bangladesh has spent too many years celebrating ambitious projects before asking whether they will deliver. Matarbari must not become another example. The government should be clear about the costs, deadlines and benefits, particularly when regional connectivity is involved.

The immediate trade priority is the Economic Partnership Agreement signed on February 6, 2026, Bangladesh’s first. Covering far more than tariffs, it includes customs, services, investment, electronic commerce, procurement, labour and environmental provisions. The Tokyo visit should help turn this agreement into something businesses can use. That will require administrative preparation, clear rules and support for exporters.

With Bangladesh scheduled to graduate from least developed country status on November 24, 2026, although it has requested an extension, preparation is urgent. Whatever happens to the timetable, the country cannot depend indefinitely on preferential market access.

Japanese assistance with product testing, certification and supplier development could help Bangladeshi firms meet demanding international standards. Footwear, processed foods, light engineering and technology services deserve attention alongside garments.

Investment is another area where opportunity and frustration coexist. Japan’s foreign ministry recorded 338 Japanese companies operating in Bangladesh as of October 2025. A JETRO survey presented in March 2026 found that 56.9 per cent of surveyed firms planned to expand within one or two years.

That interest is encouraging, but investors will judge Bangladesh by their everyday experience. Delayed approvals, inconsistent tax decisions, unreliable utilities and difficulties in resolving disputes can undermine even attractive investment prospects.

A successful visit should leave behind more than a joint declaration. Bangladesh needs a clear plan to implement the Economic Partnership Agreement, firm infrastructure deadlines, specific reforms to improve the investment climate, a credible worker recruitment system and concrete commitments on maritime and humanitarian cooperation.

The Japanese-backed economic zone at Araihazar should become a working example of how Bangladesh can do better. Businesses need predictable services, published deadlines and effective grievance mechanisms. Routine problems should not require intervention from the highest levels of government.

Financial discipline matters equally. JICA’s June 2026 emergency support agreement offers up to ¥50 billion for economic resilience and a stable energy supply, with a published annual interest rate of 3.05 per cent. Such financing can help, but every commitment must be assessed against its economic benefits, repayment obligations and currency risks.

Bangladesh cannot afford projects that look impressive at inauguration but become costly burdens afterwards. Transparent procurement, timely completion and sound financial management are essential. Energy cooperation should also place greater weight on efficiency, grid reliability and renewables rather than creating further dependence on imported fuels.

Employment cooperation could produce some of the visit’s most direct benefits. Japan needs skilled workers, and Bangladesh has young people seeking opportunities. But sending workers abroad is not simply a matter of signing an agreement.

Language proficiency, technical training and recognised qualifications must match employers’ needs. Recruitment costs should be reasonable, contracts should be understandable and workers should be protected against exploitation. Success should be measured by actual placements, wages and working conditions, not ambitious recruitment announcements.

Security cooperation is also growing. The defence equipment and technology transfer agreement signed on February 3, 2026, established a framework for future transfers. Japan’s handover of five patrol boats in July under its Official Security Assistance programme added a practical maritime dimension.

Bangladesh should focus on surveillance, search and rescue, disaster response, training and maintenance. It must also preserve strategic flexibility. Japan is a US ally, while Bangladesh has important relationships with India, China and others. Cooperation with one partner need not come at the expense of another. Sovereignty, international law and independent decision-making should remain the guiding principles.

Image Prime Minister Tarique Rahman meets a Japanese delegation led by Parliamentary Vice-Minister for Foreign Affairs Shimada Tomaki at the Prime Minister’s Office on July 1, 2026. Discussions covered key issues, including the energy crisis, airport terminal development and Rohingya repatriation. Photo: PMO

The Rohingya crisis also deserves attention. In March 2026, Japan announced ¥2.57 billion in additional assistance for refugees and host communities. Bangladesh should seek continued humanitarian support and stronger diplomatic engagement towards safe, voluntary and dignified repatriation. Instability across the border threatens the very regional connectivity both countries hope to develop.

Nor should Bangladesh forget the seven Japanese citizens killed in the July 2016 terrorist attack while working on preparations for Dhaka’s mass transit development. Japan continued supporting Bangladesh afterwards. Protecting foreign professionals and everyone working for the country’s development is an obligation that goes beyond diplomacy.

A successful visit should leave behind more than a joint declaration. Bangladesh needs a clear plan to implement the Economic Partnership Agreement, firm infrastructure deadlines, specific reforms to improve the investment climate, a credible worker recruitment system and concrete commitments on maritime and humanitarian cooperation.

Ultimately, the harder test lies at home. The 2005 joint statement recognised the importance of governance to investment. That lesson remains unfinished. Predictable rules, credible courts, accountable institutions and respect for contracts will attract lasting Japanese investment more than repeated assurances in Tokyo.

Tarique Rahman has an opportunity to build on a relationship nurtured by successive generations of leaders. Japan’s trust is a national asset. The visit should honour that history, but its success will be judged by something more immediate: better jobs, stronger businesses and lasting opportunities for Bangladeshis.

Zillur Rahman is a political analyst and President of the Centre for Governance Studies (CGS). He hosts Tritiyo Matra on Channel i and writes on geopolitics, strategic affairs and governance. Follow him on X: @zillur.

title: What does Napoleon have to do with Gen Z's gym obsession?
text:
More than one quarter of young adults in Britain now say their gym memberships matter more to them than holidays or eating out.

Sport England data shows that Gen Z has begun to turn away from running, swimming and fitness classes towards gym and strength training. For them, weight training is seen as the best form of exercise because it can help build strength, improve appearance and boost overall health.

People have argued about the best forms of exercise for over two centuries. While today’s fitness trends tend to be more about improving the body and overall fitness, health has rarely been the sole reason why certain exercise trends gained popularity through the eras.

Image Napoleon Bonaparte’s invasion of Prussia in 1806 helped inspire Friedrich Ludwig Jahn to establish an open-air gymnasium in 1811, laying the groundwork for modern fitness culture. Photo: Collected

Napoleon and gymnastics

In 1806, Napoleon Bonaparte invaded Prussia and, inadvertently, created the modern fitness industry.

As Napoleon’s troops stormed their way eastward, one Prussian man, Friedrich Ludwig Jahn, began to seethe with anger. For Jahn, Prussian men had lost because they were physically weaker than the French.

Image The belief that strong nations needed physically strong people helped popularise gymnastics and calisthenics for men and women throughout the 19th century. Photo: Johnston, Frances Benjamin, 1864-1952, photographer, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons



The nation’s solution, according to Jahn, lay not in muskets – but muscles. So in 1811 Jahn opened a Turnplatz – an open-air gymnasium. Young men ran, jumped, climbed ropes, wrestled and vaulted. They also swung on two pieces of equipment that Jahn is believed to have invented: the parallel bars and the horizontal bar. Soon the trend spread to other nations, with England’s first outdoor gymnastics school opening in 1825.

The underlying logic behind Jahn’s Turnplatz system – that strong nations demanded physically strong troops – became a rallying cry for a wave of gymnastic and calisthenic systems for men and women across the century.

The birth of bodybuilding

A popular form of entertainment in the Victorian era were strongmen shows, where muscular men would perform theatrical acts of strength. One of the most popular performers of the time was Charles “Samson” Sampson, whose act involved snapping chains with his chest.

But in 1889, a new kind of strongman arrived on the scene. During one of Sampson’s performances, a moustachioed strongman named Eugen Sandow stripped down to his pants in a London theatre, responding to a challenge from Sampson. But what made Sandow different from Sampson and other strongmen of the era was his physique. He was lean and sculpted.

From 1889 until his death in 1925, Sandow became synonymous with the ideal body. He was deemed the “best specimen of manhood” by Harvard University physical educationalist Dudley Sargent. Sandow hosted the first major bodybuilding contest in London in 1901 and ran a health enterprise which spread across the British Empire, the Americas and Australasia. Thousands followed his mail-order courses, read his magazine and drank his cocoa.

Those lifting dumbbells and barbells to build their bodies like Sandow classed themselves as “physical culturists” in the same way that modern trainees may define themselves by Pilates, Hyrox or weight training.

Following Sandow and others, people trained for health but they also trained to become better workers, better spouses, to be more attractive or dynamic.

Although the state still mattered – Sandow even trained British troops for the second South African war – the emphasis slowly shifted to building the body for its own sake.

The post-war aerobics boom

The approach to exercise in the post-war era shifted due to an emerging new health concern: people were sitting down too much. This fear was fuelled by a 1953 work published by epidemiologist Jerry Morris which found that London bus drivers experienced higher instances of heart disease than conductors, who spent their day climbing stairs. The cause? Inactivity.

Image Eugen Sandow became synonymous with the ideal male physique, popularising bodybuilding through performances, publications and a fitness enterprise that spread across continents. Photo: The Strobridge Lith. Co., Cin'ti & New York., Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons



In the US, physicians began rallying against rising heart disease. Their radical solution was to advise people to run slowly for set periods of time – an activity we today call jogging. Pioneered in New Zealand and brought to the US in the 1960s, jogging soon kickstarted an “aerobics” boom.

New gym chains filled up with previously untrained enthusiasts running and doing aerobics classes. Aerobics classes were particularly popular with women. And in 1969, fitness instructor Jacki Sorenson originated the aerobics dance movement after she began setting routines to pop music, stitching together steps from jazz, folk, cha-cha and square dancing.

The popularity of aerobics only continued to grow throughout the 80s, thanks to actor Jane Fonda’s best-selling 1982 workout video which brought aerobics into the living room.

Image Fitness instructor Jacki Sorensen pioneered aerobic dancing in 1969, combining dance routines with pop music and helping popularise a new form of exercise. Photo: Employee of Aerobic Dancing, Inc., Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

The muscle builders

In 1977 the world was introduced to Austrian bodybuilder Arnold Schwarzenegger in the hit documentary Pumping Iron. Brash but charming, muscular but beautiful, Schwarzenegger and the entrepreneur pushing him, Joe Weider, popularised bodybuilding as we now understand it.

Pumping Iron hit cinemas at a time when aerobics had driven more people into gyms and new gym equipment made lifting weights far more accessible.

Schwarzenegger’s physique soon became a template for heroic figures in pop culture. Action stars, children’s toys and athletes all succumbed to the bodybuilding effect. Leading 80s megastar Sylvester Stallone even transformed his body with Schwarzenegger’s training partner Franco Columbu in preparation for Rambo and the Rocky movies.

Image From Napoleon’s invasion of Prussia to today’s social media-driven fitness trends, exercise has been shaped by political, cultural and social influences. Visual: Adrin Sarwar

Women were lifting, too. Lisa Lyon won the first women’s world bodybuilding championship in 1979. Two decades later women’s weightlifting reached the Olympics.

By the 2000s, lifting weights was no longer a fringe activity. Budget and 24-hour gyms were commonplace while sports such as CrossFit and powerlifting swelled with men and women. In recent years the hashtag #strongnotskinny has spread across Instagram and TikTok.

Exercise scientist Andrew Scott says that influencers have been a big part of this shift. None of this is new. Sandow sold his body on postcards and cocoa tins, Fonda sold hers on VHS and Schwarzenegger sold his at the cinema.

Once again, the world around us is changing how people move their bodies. Two hundred years ago, fitness served the country. Now it serves the algorithm.

This article was first published under the title “Napoleon can be partly blamed for Gen Z’s weightlifting obsession – here’s why” The Conversation, an ANN partner of The Daily Star, on October 22, 2026.

Claire Warden is a professor of Performance and Physical Culture, Loughborough University.

Conor Heffernan is a lecturer in the Sociology of Sport, Ulster University.

title: What is Pakistan really seeking from its new defence alliances?
text:
SINCE September 2025, Pakistan has signed multilayered and multi-domain defence agreem­e­nts with several Arab and Muslim states. It has sig­­ned a Strategic Mutual Defence Agreement (SMDA) with Saudi Arabia, the Makkah Joint Def­­ence Agreement (MJDA) with Turkiye and Saudi Arabia, and a defence pact with Kuwait. Pak­istan has recently signed another defence agree­ment — the Badr agreement. Pakistan, Turkiye, Qatar, and Indonesia are signatories to this pact.

These defence deals have, in the past year, increased Pakistan’s strategic relevance in the Middle East. Interestingly, each accord carries the explicit provision for joint defence production and investment in the defence industry. This clause in every defence pact reveals Islamabad’s long-term strategic objective of moving from a buyer-seller relationship to a co-production partnership with reliable partners in the region.

Image Turkish President Tayyip Erdogan, Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman and Pakistan's Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif sign a joint defence agreement in Makkah, Saudi Arabia, on August 7, 2026. Photo: Reuters

There are four primary strategic factors that have driven Islamabad’s emphasis on the joint defence production clause in each defence pact.

The India factor remains the primary driver. New Delhi’s defence budget now exceeds $80 billion, and its rapid induction of advanced platforms has widened the qualitative gap. Joint production arrangements with middle powers are likely to allow Pakistan to accelerate defence modernisation without bearing the full research and development cost. By manufacturing components and subsystems domestically, Pakistan can sustain a higher operational tempo and maintain credible conventional deterrence.

Islamabad believes that strategic parity in South Asia does not require numerical equivalence. It primarily requires the ability to absorb, adapt, and indigenise technology at a pace that may prevent New Delhi from achieving decisive superiority over Islamabad

Islamabad believes that strategic parity in South Asia does not require numerical equivalence. It primarily requires the ability to absorb, adapt, and indigenise technology at a pace that may prevent New Delhi from achieving decisive superiority over Islamabad. These defence deals, therefore, function as a force-multiplier for Pakis­tan’s conventional and strategic capabilities.

Islamabad’s second strategic objective is the diversification of defence suppliers and reduced reliance of its defence supply chain on Western weapons.

Historically, Islamabad has relied on Chinese weapons, but the extent of dependency has increased significantly in the last two decades. The Stockholm International Peace Research Institute has noted that this dependency is nearly 80 per cent. Although Pakistan and China enjoy unprecedented trust and depth in their all-weather strategic relationship, in theoretical terms, heavy reliance on any single external source worries Islamabad.

Similarly, Islamabad is increasingly seeking to decouple its military procurement from Western-reliant supply chains. This approach is rooted in Pakistan’s historically bitter experiences with sudden embargoes and sanctions, alongside Islamabad’s broader resistance to the West’s tendency to use defence exports as political leverage over the Global South during geopolitical crises.

Primarily, Islamabad is eager to cultivate robu­­st, non-Western defence partnerships to secure reliable and uninterrupted arms supplies free from the influence of foreign powers. By integrating affluent Saudi and Qatari capital with the technologically advanced Turkish weapons industry, Pakistan is building an insulated, collaborative defence network with the middle powers to achieve this strategic objective. Islamabad belie­ves that these defence deals, alongside its strategic alliance with China, may allow Islamabad to minimise its conventional vulnerabilities, help mod­­ernise its armed forces, and ultimately achieve a much higher degree of long-term strategic autonomy.

Image Turkish Chief of General Staff General Selçuk Bayraktaroğlu meets Saudi Arabia's Chief of General Staff General Fayyadh bin Hamed Al-Ruwaili and Pakistan's Chief of Defence Forces and Chief of Army Staff Field Marshal Asim Munir in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, on 25 September 2026. Growing defence cooperation among the three countries reflects efforts to develop regional security arrangements amid uncertainty over traditional American security guarantees. Photo: Reuters

Moreover, Islamabad is acutely aware that the intensifying US-China strategic competition will make it increasingly difficult to maintain a purely China-centric defence supply chain in the long run. Therefore, by building parallel defence production partnerships with Saudi Arabia, Qatar, Turkiye, and Indonesia, Pakistan is creating a middle-power buffer to avoid unwanted political pressure from the US. Interestingly, these countries are not fully aligned with either Washington or Beijing, and provide Islamabad greater room for manoeuvre.

Third, the economic factor equally occupies the strategic motivations of Islamabad. Pakistan wants to enhance its ability to modernise the defence production industry and increase defence exports. Pakistan’s official defence exports stood at approximately $280m in 2024. The recently concluded deals can significantly enhance defence exports to $650-700m by 2027, crossing the $1bn mark by 2030.

The Gulf states, seeking to reduce their own dependence on Western suppliers, constitute the most immediate and lucrative market for Pakistani defence exports. Joint ventures under the Badr agreement, MJDA and SMDA, are designed to produce systems that meet the Gulf’s operational requirements, while carrying Pakistani certification and, crucially, a lower price tag. Successful penetration of these markets would generate much-needed foreign exchange for Pakistan, create skilled employment, and justify further capital investment in the domestic defence industry.

Beyond the Gulf, there is also potential for niche exports to African and Central Asian countries that face similar budgetary constraints and seek cost-effective, reliable platforms.

The fourth objective linked to the third is to attract foreign direct investment to Pakistan’s defence sector. The joint production clauses are structured to encourage equity participation rather than simple technology licensing. Early commitments already indicate potential inflows of $1.2-1.5bn over the next five years in manufacturing facilities, testing ranges, and human capital development. These investments will upgrade the physical infrastructure of Pakistan’s public-sector defence industry. These inflows can stimulate related industries, including electronics, metallurgy, and software, while creating thousands of high-skill jobs for individuals who would otherwise migrate overseas.

Image Ministers of Turkiye, Qatar, Pakistan and Indonesia sign a military cooperation pact in Qatar on October 21, 2026. Photo: Turkish Defence Ministry

Time will tell whether these defence deals can deliver a meaningful technology transfer. The most important question is whether such a multipronged approach can genuinely enhance Pakis­tan’s long-term strategic autonomy or will merely redistribute its dependencies. It is also unclear to what extent these defence deals can genuinely reduce Pakistan’s strategic vulnerabilities.

However, despite these uncertainties, these defence deals will bring critical capital and technical know-how, while reducing vulnerability to external supply shocks. Yet Islamabad must calibrate its exposure with precision. Over-commitment in the complex security theatres of the Middle East can risk entangling Pakistan in conflicts whose political and military logic lies beyond Islamabad’s core interests. Therefore, Pakistan must pursue these opportunities with strategic clarity and within well-defined red lines.

title: The real test of Bangladesh's 25 crore tree pledge
text:
The gap between planting a seedling and keeping it alive is the real test of the pledge to plant 25 crore (250 million) trees in five years. The Prime Minister formally launched the programme on 13 June at the Malumghat reserved forest in Cox's Bazar. According to the progress report prepared for the implementation cell's fifth meeting on 7 October, the programme planted about 3.57 crore seedlings between 17 February and 15 September: 69 per cent of this year's target of 5.15 crore.

Guidance to keep those seedlings alive already exists. In June 2025, the Forest Department updated its 161-page Nursery and Plantation Manual. It explains which tree suits which soil, how big a pit should be, how much fertiliser to use and when to weed. But the department wrote it for its field staff, and people planting seedlings in courtyards or school fields have rarely seen it.

Yet much of the programme is in ordinary hands. Under the "One Tree One Child" initiative alone, the education divisions' five-year targets total 13.34 crore seedlings, more than half the national goal. Children will plant them; parents and teachers will decide whether they survive.

Image Prime Minister Tarique Rahman launches the five-year programme to plant 25 crore trees at the Malumghat reserved forest in Cox’s Bazar on 13 June 2026. The programme’s success will depend not only on the number of seedlings planted but also on their long-term survival. Photo: PMO

As a member of the advisory pool supporting the programme, I have read the manual cover to cover. This essay draws on it and on experience abroad to set out what citizens should know, how to verify the figures, where the manual needs updating and what could strengthen the programme.

How will we know how many trees survive?

At present, the figures come from agency reports. Of the 3.57 crore, about 3.04 crore came from 11 government offices reporting in a prescribed format every 15 days, and about 53 lakh from other agencies. The cell is planning a tree-monitoring app, a central database and a dashboard; in October, a sub-committee recommended a common data format and a feasibility and cost study. The cell has also asked every ministry to record where it plants, and its chair has said it will not tolerate irregularities. As the system takes shape, six questions will help make the numbers credible:

What counts as "planted"? A seedling handed over by a nursery, or one in the ground? The Air Force plans to drop seed balls from helicopters over coastal and hill areas; should seed balls be counted separately? How is double counting avoided? Forest Department nurseries supply schools, local bodies and other agencies. If supplier and planter both report, one seedling may appear twice. What is additional? Counting began on 17 February, before the June launch, and agencies plant every year through social forestry and roadside programmes. Separating routine planting from new effort would strengthen the record. Can each site be found again? A GPS or location record lets anyone return in two years to see what survived. Who checks a sample? Universities or the Bangladesh Forest Research Institute could verify a random sample of sites each year. When will survival be reported? The planting figure is updated fortnightly; a date for the first survival figure would complete the picture.

None of this casts doubt on the effort behind the numbers. Verification turns a reported figure into a result the public can trust.

What other countries have learned

Survival, not planting, is the measure that counts. A 2022 study in Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society B, covering 176 restoration sites across tropical and subtropical Asia, found that on average 18 per cent of planted saplings died in the first year and 44 per cent within five. Results ranged widely: some sites kept over 80 per cent alive. Saplings planted near mature trees had roughly 20 per cent better odds of survival. Only 28 per cent of sites were monitored for five years or more. If this year's 5.15 crore seedlings followed the Asian average, about 93 lakh would die in the first year and some 2.3 crore within five.

Numbers planted can also mislead. In India's Himachal Pradesh, a 2021 Nature Sustainability study used satellite imagery of 430 plantations and found that, on average, decades of planting had not increased forest canopy cover and had shifted forests away from broadleaf species local people valued.

Verification can be built in from the start. Pakistan asked a consortium led by IUCN, with FAO and WWF-Pakistan, to provide independent third-party monitoring of its Ten Billion Tree Tsunami programme.

Ownership may count for most. After Nepal handed forests to community groups in 1993, forest cover rose from 26 per cent in 1992 to 45 per cent in 2016; over 22,000 groups now manage about a third of the country's forests. Bangladesh's social forestry, which shares timber income with participants, is a homegrown model worth extending to schools and homesteads.

Right tree, right place

Before planting, decide why. Greening and forestry are different. On a city street, a tree's job is shade and cooling; in a homestead, fruit, timber, fuel and income; on the coast, a shield against storms and surges; in forest restoration, a mix of native species for biodiversity. Whatever the purpose, a surviving tree stores carbon, holds soil and water, and shelters birds. A dead seedling does none of these.

The manual's central lesson fits in one line: a seedling in the wrong place will not survive, however well it is cared for. Jackfruit must never go where water stands in the monsoon. A tall tree under a power line will be cut down within years. Wherever possible, choose native species suited to the area.

Image Eucalyptus trees line a road in the Khalilganj area of Kurigram. In May 2025, Bangladesh banned the raising, planting and sale of eucalyptus seedlings over environmental concerns. Photo: Abdul Wahed

One rule is missing from the manual: on 15 May 2025, the environment ministry banned raising, planting and selling eucalyptus and acacia (akashmoni) seedlings. If a market stall or nursery offers them, do not buy.

From the manual's own lists:

Where Suitable trees Watch out South side of a house Lemon, guava, amloki, sajna, pomegranate, kul Small trees, so light reaches the house North and northwest of a house Bamboo, jam, gamar, koroi Large trees belong here High ground that never floods Jackfruit, lychee, bel, jambura These die in standing water Low or waterlogged land Kadam, hijal, mandar, pitali, babla Never jackfruit Pond banks Coconut, betel nut, palmyra, date palm, arjun, hijal Avoid trees whose falling leaves foul the water Edges of crop fields Date palm, betel nut, babla, bokain Avoid heavy shade Village roads Neem, jarul, arjun, amloki, palmyra, date palm No tall trees under power lines Flood embankments Lower slope: shil koroi, shimul, kadam, neem; upper slope: grass, dhaincha, arhar No trees on the crest; unpicked fruit draws rats that damage embankments City footpaths Sonalu, mini jarul, kanchan, tagar, shefali Under wires, nothing taller than 10 to 15 feet Road dividers Sonalu, mini jarul, kamini, kanchan, tagar Nothing taller than 8 to 10 feet Rooftops Dwarf mango, guava, lemon, pomegranate, tulsi Avoid deep-rooted trees Haors and wetlands Hijal, koroch, tamal, barun Water-tolerant trees only New coastal chars Keora, baen, golpata On sandy soil, jhau and babla

Six rules for planting

Timing: The monsoon, from mid-June to mid-October, is best. Plant at other times only if you can water regularly. Mangroves go in from August to September, or December to January; this winter, the programme plans to plant 2 crore mangrove seedlings. Seedling: Choose a healthy, sturdy one; bigger seedlings survive better. For homesteads, the manual recommends seedlings at least two metres tall, beyond the reach of goats and cattle. Pit: Generally 30 centimetres (one foot) wide and deep; 45 centimetres for homesteads. Dig it two to three weeks ahead and keep topsoil and subsoil apart. Where water collects, plant on a 20 to 30 centimetre mound. Fertiliser: At least 15 days before planting, mix one kilogram of well-rotted cow dung, 25 grams of TSP and 25 grams of MoP into each pit. Never use fresh dung. Three weeks after planting, apply 25 grams of urea in a ring 20 centimetres from the stem. Planting: Remove and dispose of the polythene bag; it pollutes. Jute bags can stay. Set the seedling at the depth it grew in the nursery, refill with topsoil first and press firmly. Stake and water: Tie the seedling to a stake with jute twine, and water if it does not rain.

Keep two metres between timber trees and more for fruit trees. These are general rules that vary by species, soil and site. For pests or disease, consult an agriculture or forest officer before spraying anything.

Planting takes a day; survival takes three years

The manual expects up to 20 per cent of seedlings in a forest plantation to die in the first year. It says dead seedlings must be replaced in July to August and October to November of that year, and by May to June of the next. For this monsoon's plantings, that means now. With the dry season starting, now is also the time to mulch.

Fence: a bamboo cage about 1.5 metres high; in cities, a reusable iron guard.

Where the manual needs updating

As the manual reaches schools and households, its advice becomes public guidance, so a few sections deserve prompt revision.

Pesticide guidance has fallen behind the law. Page 85 rightly lists dieldrin, aldrin, heptachlor, chlordane, lindane and DDT as never to be used in nurseries; Bangladesh has banned the first four as "dirty dozen" pollutants. Yet earlier text still recommends them on pages 37, 87, 88, 103, 105 and 149. Furadan (carbofuran) appears on pages 90, 99 and 149, although Bangladesh banned it in January 2023. Dursban (chlorpyrifos) is listed as approved, even though Stockholm Convention parties agreed in May 2025 to list it for global elimination. Bangladesh's own experience shows the value of acting: a 2018 study in the International Journal of Epidemiology linked the 2000 ban on the most toxic pesticides to large falls in poisoning deaths, with no apparent loss of farm output.

Species lists predate the ban and include invasive trees. The manual does not yet mention the eucalyptus and acacia ban, and page 89 still covers eucalyptus nursery pests. It recommends ipil-ipil, a widely invasive tree, for roadsides. Its "stand improvement" model, meant to replace invasive species with native ones, lists exotic mahogany. And sissoo, which page 126 advises avoiding because of dieback, still appears in the models on pages 128 to 141.

Nursery planning needs a bigger buffer. The planning formula on page 54 allows 10 per cent for replacing dead seedlings, while page 147 expects up to 20 per cent first-year mortality. At roughly 5 crore seedlings a year, nurseries could fall short by up to 50 lakh replacement seedlings.

A careful edit would also fix smaller slips: 98 plus 341 nurseries totalled as "413"; two site-quality classes both labelled "good"; cortisol described as a plant hormone; a fertiliser ratio printed as 2:141; differing thinning schedules; and unsourced Miyawaki carbon claims.

What could strengthen the programme?

Before the next monsoon:

A one-page errata with every copy, withdrawing banned pesticide recommendations and stating the eucalyptus and acacia ban.

A nursery replacement allowance of at least 20 per cent.

A survival protocol: a location record for every planting, survival counts at one, two and three years, independent sample checks, a survival target, and planting and survival reported separately by district, upazila and institution.

A clear definition of "planted", separating programme plantings from routine ones.

In the full revision:

A pest chapter built with the Department of Agricultural Extension around integrated pest management, with soil and species chapters checked by the Soil Resource Development Institute and the Bangladesh Forest Research Institute.

A species appendix: banned and invasive trees, native priorities by agro-ecological zone, drought-, salt- and flood-tolerant options, and a cap on any single species per block.

Chapters for schools and for agencies such as LGED, Roads and Highways, and the Water Development Board.

Measurable seedling standards, registration of private nurseries and a shift from polythene bags to jute or coir pots and root trainers.

Dry-season watering guidance.

A named caretaker and a three-year maintenance budget for every planting.

Urban standards, including heat-reducing species, and protection for existing trees during construction; felling one mature tree for two saplings does not balance the books.

A simple carbon accounting method linking surviving trees to national climate commitments and climate finance.

Free online publication, a four-page Bangla citizens' guide, upazila species posters at nurseries and a channel for reporting irregularities.

Image An acacia monoculture plantation in Sherpur illustrates the limitations of relying on a single tree species for forest restoration, particularly in landslide-prone areas. Selecting suitable native species is essential for sustainable forest restoration. Photo: Dr Reza Khan

What the rest of us can do

Buy seedlings from the Forest Department or other reliable nurseries, and refuse eucalyptus and acacia. Take responsibility for one tree for three years: fence it, weed it, water it, replace it if it dies and photograph it each year. Schools, mosques, temples and offices can plant spare land, with a committee in charge. Where space is scarce, the Miyawaki method packs three to four native seedlings into each square metre, though it requires digging and enriching the soil a metre deep. Give seedlings as gifts. Companies can adopt nearby roads and budget for care, not just saplings. Do not nail signboards to trees or let goats loose near seedlings, and report fake plantings to the forest office or upazila administration.

Divide 25 crore trees among more than 20 crore people, and it comes to less than one and a half trees each. The question is whether, in 2031, we will be able to walk past most of them. A manual in a cupboard saves no seedlings; an updated one in every school, mosque and union parishad, plus a counting system people trust, could turn the programme into a social movement and save crores of trees.

Subail Bin Alam is an engineer-economist. He is Chief Operating Officer of Rancon Infrastructures and Engineering Limited, a Director of the Bangladesh Sustainable and Renewable Energy Association, a guest faculty of ULAB, a Trustee of the Panam Institute and a founding member of the Centre for Science, Technology and Policy Diplomacy. title: Police and media have no right to shame detainees
text:
A police outpost stood barely 30 yards from a house in Purbachal where “drug parties” had apparently been held for nearly a year. The house belonged to a senior police officer. When detectives finally raided it early Tuesday, October 20, 85 people—26 women and 59 men—were detained and sentenced to varying terms of imprisonment.

Thanks to the broadcast of the raid and the disclosure of the backgrounds of these otherwise affluent detainees by a section of the media, the episode has since generated considerable curiosity on social media. Ideally, the questions following such a raid should have concerned the police and the alleged offences: what the police knew, why the gatherings and DJ parties went unchecked for so long if they were being held illegally, and what evidence justified the sentences imposed. Some of the media coverage, however, turned elsewhere: Who were their fathers? Where did they study, work, or live? These personal details along with the footage, supplied by the officers themselves, established nothing about the alleged offences. Yet, such public exposure and shaming of people caught in police operations have become routine, both among law enforcers and in sections of the media, despite repeated High Court directives against parading detainees before cameras.

The Daily Star found that residents often saw cars outside the Purbachal property and heard loud music late at night. Local police acknowledged knowing about the gatherings but denied prior knowledge of drug-related activities. Officers of the Detective Branch (DB), however, alleged that 20 to 22 parties were held monthly, accusing the property’s owner, Additional DIG Abdullah Al Jahir, of obtaining profits from them. Jahir, however, disputed the allegations, saying he had rented out the premises for private functions and prohibited drugs.

DB’s limited seizure list, however, raised questions about the police accounts of widespread drug consumption, especially given that the nearly three-hour raid led to the detention of 85 people. Among the items recovered were one yaba tablet, some bottles of liquor, and a small quantity of a substance described as “kush”. When asked, investigators claimed the participants had already consumed drugs before the arrival of officers. That explanation warrants scrutiny alongside the evidence and procedures underpinning the summary proceedings. Limited physical recovery alone does not establish that the sentences were unjustified, but how each sentence was reached, why “unlawful” gatherings went unchecked for so long, or whether the police followed due process during the raid are matters of public interest.

The test for the media, meanwhile, is straightforward. Did the coverage establish what evidence supported the sentences, how the premises were supervised, and whether anyone received preferential treatment? These questions need documents and verification, not pictures or videos sensationalising the raid. Yes, naming someone convicted of an offence can serve the public interest. A person’s identity, family connections, or place of employment may help verify information or uncover a wider network of wrongdoing. But these details do not deserve publication merely because they are readily available. If a relative of the detainees participated in wrongdoing or an employer helped conceal it, that is a story worth investigating. Without such evidence, why should their identities enter a crime report?

For police, their responsibility begins before anything reaches a newsroom. Officers control a scene, determine who can enter, and have custody of those detained. This puts them in a position of power, making it particularly important that they ensure the dignity and privacy of detainees. Journalists can observe police operations, but no one should be compelled to uncover their face for a camera. Unfortunately, this distinction was also disregarded during an August raid at a residential hotel in Abdullahpur, where video footage showed female officers trying to uncover detained women’s faces. One woman was crying, and an officer was seen threatening violence if the women kept their faces covered.

The practice extends beyond cameras brought by journalists, however. A September investigation by Prothom Alo identified 107 Facebook accounts run by police officers. Videos posted there, showing encounters with members of the public, attracted large audiences. But under Article 10.12 of the Bangladesh Police Social Media Use Guidelines 2025, officers cannot post photographs or videos of their operations without prior approval. Police Headquarters, in the same report, acknowledged violations and said action had been taken against some officers. It remains unclear how consistently such violations are detected and addressed, particularly when they attract little public attention.

In 2012, the High Court directed law enforcers not to expose arrested or detained people before the media, describing such conduct as illegal and unconstitutional. In 2015, it asked the police chief to stop presenting accused persons before cameras prior to their court appearances. A 2019 ruling called for regulations governing the presentation of detainees and the disclosure of information while investigations are under way. The constitution also points in the same direction: Article 31 protects people against actions detrimental to their reputation except in accordance with law, while Article 39 guarantees freedom of the press, subject to restrictions provided by law. Importantly, these interventions concern the treatment and exposure of detainees by law enforcers; they do not amount to a ban on reporting arrests, investigations, etc.

In fact, filming police operations can sometimes be essential. Video evidence can expose an unlawful search, an assault, or a misleading official account. Where influence has been used to obstruct justice, identifying those responsible can be essential to accountability. The question here is not whether cameras should be present at a crime scene, but what they record, who controls access to the footage, and what editors choose to publish. The Society of Professional Journalists’ code makes it clear that journalists’ ethical responsibilities go beyond what they can legally obtain and broadcast. Producers choose the footage, digital editors select the clips and thumbnails, and news editors decide whether to name relatives or employers. Each has a responsibility to ask whether a certain detail advances the public’s understanding or merely satisfies curiosity.

That said, failings along that line must not become a pretext for giving the state new powers over journalism. Such powers could just as easily be used to suppress footage exposing official abuse. The answer lies instead in enforcing professional standards within news platforms, explaining difficult editorial decisions, and correcting errors across videos and social media posts, not just in written articles. Police Headquarters should also publish clear procedures governing camera access during raids but, at the same time, take responsibility for how they investigate and discipline officers who violate existing instructions.

The questions raised by the Purbachal raid remain, and the police must answer them. As for journalists, they must think what purpose their disclosure of detainees’ faces and personal details—especially those of women—served. Did these help uncover wrongdoing, or did they simply turn people in police custody into objects of public humiliation? If they added nothing to the public’s understanding of the alleged offences, why were they necessary? We cannot demand accountability from the police while refusing to account for our own editorial decisions.

Arafat Rahaman is a journalist at The Daily Star. He covers education and writes on governance, rights, and public accountability. He can be reached at [email protected].

title: Remittance and fuel: Bangladesh's double exposure to the Gulf crisis
text:
While the direct impact of the Houthi missile strike in Riyadh is being clearly felt in Dhaka with the suspended flights and long queues at the airport, the longer term repercussions are likely to be more debilitating for the economy.

Saudi Arabia, home to around 3.5 million Bangladeshi expatriates, is Bangladesh’s largest single source of remittances, accounting for about a fifth of inflows during July-September. If a stronger Houthi presence translates into control over the crucial Bab el-Mandeb Strait, a key Red Sea chokepoint, it could have serious implications for global oil markets.

This would effectively mean that Iran exercises control over two straits (Hormuz and Bab el-Mandeb) that are crucial not just for Saudi oil but also for all kinds of fuel from the Persian Gulf. The ongoing war in the Persian Gulf has also affected Bangladesh's exports, directly by way of shutting down export destinations in the region, and indirectly by way of more expensive energy prices.

The missile strike, which killed two Bangladeshis and critically injured several others, also underscored the extent of Bangladesh’s integration with both the global economy and the international energy order. Ironically, Riyadh was hosting the World Energy Congress at the time, with several ministers attending virtually and the chief executives of ExxonMobil, TotalEnergies, BP and Shell cancelling their trips.

The energy minister, Abdulaziz bin Salman, an elder step-brother of the all powerful Saudi crown prince, did not mention the strikes as he addressed the gathering but expressed his dismay that some of the invitees could not join because of certain safety concerns.

Mohammad bin Salman, the crown prince, had waded into this conflict in Yemen soon after his father had ascended to the throne and appointed him defence minister in January 2015. More than a decade later, it is evident that try as they might, the Saudis are not going to be able to root out the Houthis short of putting ground troops in Yemen with military muscle on their own. If anything, the Houthis have only become battle-hardened and perhaps more resolute in the meantime.

But this is not just a rebel group trying to run over the Saudi-backed government. There are other factors as well. The Houthis are backed by Iran and, by extension, Russia and China. The one in government, supported by Saudi, is also supported by the US. Then there are the recent parties of the Makkah agreement, Pakistan and Turkey to consider. Notably, Turkey has clarified that it will not deploy troops for an offensive into Yemen but will actively defend the oil-rich kingdom. To a large extent, this tangled web of interests and allegiances within and among these countries could be resolved if the US and Israel cease their attacks on Iran.

Now that the Houthis have brought the war right inside his home, the crown prince will discover that it is no longer possible to extricate Saudi Arabia, without resolving what US and Israel had started. He is most likely going to become another one in a long line of people impressing upon the Trump administration that the impasse needs to be resolved.

And given the repercussions Bangladesh is feeling already, that resolution will be in Saudi interest as much as it will be in ours.

title: Why does Tagore still trouble Bangladesh’s idea of ‘us’?
text:
There is a particular kind of argument about Rabindranath Tagore that is difficult to treat as literary criticism because very little literature is involved. One version says, with the confidence of a joke that has somehow become an argument, that everything Tagore wrote was really for his sister-in-law, Kadambari Devi. Another asks what this ‘Indian Hindu poet’ ever wrote for ‘us’.

If the ‘sister-in-law’ line were merely a bad joke, it would not deserve much attention. But repeated alongside the insistence that Tagore was Hindu, Indian and therefore culturally external to Bengali Muslims, it begins to do something more interesting politically. The word I find most revealing in the argument is not ‘Hindu’, ‘Indian’ or even ‘boudi’. It is ‘us’. Who is being included in that pronoun, and who has the authority to decide what belongs inside it?

The literary reduction is almost comic in its ambition. Tagore wrote poetry, songs, novels, short stories, plays, essays and letters, as well as works on education, society, religion, nature, colonialism and nationalism. Yet apparently the interpretive key to all of this is ‘boudi’. If reading literature were really that economical, Gitanjali, Gora, Ghare Baire, Chandalika and Streer Patra could be placed on one side of the desk and a single word on the other. A new discipline could be founded: boudi tattva.

Whatever the precise character of Tagore’s relationship with Kadambari Devi, it is a legitimate subject of biography and historical inquiry. It cannot plausibly serve as an explanatory key to his entire intellectual production. There is also something revealing about reducing Kadambari herself to ‘the sister-in-law’ who supposedly explains a male writer’s work. She disappears as a historical person and becomes a sexual and romantic punchline. The joke that claims to expose Tagore ends up flattening a woman as well.

The more consequential reduction is the attempt to settle Tagore’s cultural citizenship through the words ‘Hindu’ and ‘Indian’. Both descriptions can contain historical information, but neither can carry all the political meaning now placed upon them.



Image A torn image of Rabindranath Tagore at Chhayanaut following the mob attack on the cultural institution on December 19, 2025.

Tagore was born into the Brahmo tradition, and Upanishadic thought shaped his intellectual world. He was also a poet, novelist, short-story writer, dramatist, composer, painter, educational thinker, social critic and institution-builder. He won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1913. His politics cannot be fitted comfortably into a nationalist box either. He participated in the Swadeshi movement against the partition of Bengal but became a powerful critic of aggressive nationalism. After the Jallianwala Bagh massacre, he renounced the knighthood he had received from the British Crown.

None of this requires turning him into a saint. Tagore was also a zamindar, and his class position, contradictions and limitations deserve scrutiny. Intellectual history is not improved by replacing criticism with reverence. Recognising Tagore as part of Bangladesh’s cultural inheritance does not require treating his particular Bengali world as the whole of Bengal, still less as the only legitimate version of Bengali culture.

The problem with describing him as a foreign cultural presence in Bangladesh becomes clearer when we look at geography. Tagore died in 1941. India and Pakistan were created six years later; Bangladesh appeared three decades after his death. To decide his cultural nationality retrospectively through today’s passport borders is therefore historically awkward. More importantly, a substantial part of his life and literary imagination was formed in places that are now in Bangladesh.



Image Protesters hold a banner at Dhaka University following the disappearance of a statue of Rabindranath Tagore, amid debate over the poet’s cultural legacy.

He first came to Shilaidaha in 1889 and spent long periods there between 1891 and 1901 while managing the family estates. He travelled through Shilaidaha, Shahzadpur, Patisar, Kaligram and other parts of East Bengal. The Padma, river life, rural poverty, ordinary people and the landscape entered his letters, stories and poetry. Many of the stories later collected in Galpaguchchha, as well as the world depicted in Chhinnapatra, emerged from these encounters. At Shilaidaha, he wrote or developed major works including Sonar Tari, Chitra and Chaitali; in 1912, he began translating Gitanjali into English there.

The soil of present-day Bangladesh is therefore not an incidental footnote to Tagore’s literary life. If we want to deport him culturally from Bangladesh, we would first have to deport the Padma from his imagination.



The same experience of East Bengal complicates another familiar question: what did he do for ordinary people? At Patisar, in present-day Naogaon, Tagore established schools, a charitable dispensary and an agricultural bank, and supported cooperative initiatives connected with agriculture and rural industry. Accounts of his estate work also record experiments involving education, health, water supply, roads and attempts to reduce peasants’ dependence on exploitative credit. None of this erases the unequal structure of zamindari. It does make the claim that he had no engagement with the lives of the people around him difficult to sustain.

What makes this argument especially difficult to dismiss as a passing social media quarrel is that Bangladesh has encountered versions of it before.

During the Pakistan period, Bengali culture became one of the arenas in which competing ideas of nationhood were fought over. In 1961, resistance to official hostility surrounding Tagore’s birth centenary drew together intellectuals and cultural activists in East Pakistan and formed part of the context in which Chhayanaut emerged. In 1967, Pakistan’s information and broadcasting minister, Khwaja Shahabuddin, announced restrictions on broadcasting Tagore songs regarded as inconsistent with Pakistan’s cultural ideology. Writers, artists and intellectuals protested.



Image Chhayanaut’s celebration of the Bengali New Year at Ramna Batamul. Photo: Anisur Rahman

The logic was recognisable: Tagore could be represented as Hindu, Indian and therefore culturally suspect within a Pakistan officially imagined through a Muslim national identity. Yet attempts to push him out of East Bengal helped give Rabindra Sangeet a different political life. It became entangled with resistance to the state’s attempt to define Bengali Muslim culture from above.

Amar Sonar Bangla makes that history particularly difficult to ignore. The song had emerged from the movement against the 1905 partition of Bengal, but its political life did not end there. Banglapedia records its performance at the Paltan Maidan meeting on 3 March 1971, before Sheikh Mujibur Rahman’s 7 March speech, and again during the 23 March programme of the Swadhin Bangla Kendriya Chhatra Sangram Parishad. Before Bangladesh formally existed as a sovereign state, the song had already entered the political imagination of independence.

Cultural texts do not remain permanently owned by the author’s religious identity or by the political geography into which the author is later placed. Communities receive them, argue with them, reinterpret them and sometimes make them part of a new political language. Tagore came from a Brahmo background in colonial Bengal. In 1971, Amar Sonar Bangla was being sung by people in East Bengal imagining a sovereign Bangladesh.



Bangladeshis did not import Tagore from India after independence. His place in the country’s cultural history had already been fought over under Pakistan. In that struggle, Tagore often came to signify something larger than the writer himself: the right of Bengali language and culture to possess a history that could not be reduced to the religious ideology of the Pakistani state.

That dispute did not disappear with Pakistan. After the political upheaval of August 2024, a public demand to change Bangladesh’s national anthem revived arguments over Amar Sonar Bangla and, inevitably, over Tagore’s place in the national imagination. The interim government said it had no plan to change the anthem, while 48 prominent citizens publicly condemned the demand. Jamaat-e-Islami also said that the remarks made by former brigadier general Abdullahil Amaan Azmi were his personal views and not the party’s position. The episode matters here not because every proposal to change a national symbol has the same motive, but because objections to the anthem repeatedly return to questions about Tagore’s religion, nationality and cultural belonging.

So when I hear the apparently simple question, ‘What did Tagore write for us?’, I find myself wondering what kind of relationship between literature and belonging the question assumes. Literature is not a parliamentary development allocation. A writer does not become part of a culture because he set aside a certain number of poems for a future constituency. Shakespeare did not write his plays for every person who would later call themselves English. Rumi did not compose poetry with the passport politics of modern Iran, Turkey or Afghanistan in mind. Cultural inheritance is created through language, circulation, memory, reinterpretation and historical experience, often long after an author has died.



Image Sanjida Khatun and others at Ramna Batamul during a Pahela Baishakh celebration in the late 1960s or early 1970s. Photo courtesy: Late Asir Uddin Ahmed (Editor, Jhinuk Magazine) / Dhaka – 400 Years of History in Photographs

This is why I keep coming back to the word ‘us’. It carries much more of the argument than it first appears to. If Bangladesh’s cultural inheritance is defined retrospectively by the present majority religion, the consequences do not stop with Tagore. What do we do with Michael Madhusudan Dutt’s Christianity? Where do we place Lalon’s resistance to fixed religious identity? If Kazi Nazrul Islam is reduced to a ‘Muslim poet’, what happens to his Shyama Sangeet, his extensive use of Hindu mythology, his attacks on religious orthodoxy and his language of human equality?

Bengali culture itself makes the search for purity difficult. Its language and cultural forms developed through centuries of exchange among Sanskritic, Persian, Arabic, Vaishnava, Sufi, Baul, folk, colonial and modern traditions. The existence of those entanglements does not mean that Bengal’s history was harmonious or that all communities experienced it in the same way.

The movement against the 1905 partition of Bengal is an important reminder. It should not be romanticised as an uncomplicated expression of Bengali unity. Hindu bhadralok dominance and the use of Hindu religious symbolism were real, as were the economic and political concerns of many Muslims in eastern Bengal. Tagore himself later criticised the temptation to explain Hindu and Muslim estrangement entirely through British manipulation while ignoring inequalities within Bengali society. Cultural inheritance can belong to us without its history having to be innocent.

Bangladesh became a sovereign state in 1971, but the cultural histories from which Bangladeshis inherited their language, literature, music and political vocabulary obviously did not begin that year. Reading the pre-1947 history of Bengal only through today’s India-Bangladesh border, or testing pre-1971 culture against contemporary religious nationalism, produces a past arranged according to categories that did not exist in the same form when much of that past was made.



This is why saying ‘Tagore is not ours’ interests me more than the familiar argument over whether Tagore is overrated. On the surface, the statement classifies the poet. What interests me more is what happens to the meaning of ‘ours’ when we say it. Does the word refer to the complicated historical inheritance of people who have lived in this region, or only to cultural forms that can be made compatible with a particular religious and national identity in the present?

This is why saying ‘Tagore is not ours’ interests me more than the familiar argument over whether Tagore is overrated. On the surface, the statement classifies the poet. What interests me more is what happens to the meaning of ‘ours’ when we say it. Does the word refer to the complicated historical inheritance of people who have lived in this region, or only to cultural forms that can be made compatible with a particular religious and national identity in the present?

Once the second test becomes normal, the argument cannot remain confined to one poet. A writer can become too Indian; a song can become too Hindu; a festival can be asked to prove its religious pedigree. Music, sculpture, theatre, clothing and public ritual can all be subjected to the same question of cultural legitimacy. The issue then is no longer whether something forms part of the history of this society, but whether it fits comfortably enough within the identity of the majority.

There is no obligation to like all of Tagore’s writing, to treat him as beyond criticism, or to ignore the privileges of the world from which he came. His politics, personal life, class position and literary reputation should remain open to arguments grounded in evidence. But there is a difference between criticism and reducing a historical figure until only the identity category useful to a present argument is left.



Image Tagore’s Kuthibari in Shilaidaha, Kushtia, where he spent long periods and wrote several major works. Photo: Mahmuda Tuli

Tagore can be placed outside Bangladesh easily enough in contemporary political rhetoric. The historical record is less accommodating. Shilaidaha remains in Kushtia. Patisar remains in Naogaon. The Padma remains inside his writing. Amar Sonar Bangla remains Bangladesh’s national anthem, carrying with it a political history that includes March 1971.

For me, the question at the end of all this is not whether Bangladesh must admire Tagore. It is whether a plural society can recognise a cultural inheritance that was made by people with different religions, class positions, political commitments and historical contradictions. A country does not have to make its past pure in order to claim it. But if the present becomes too narrow to accommodate that past, eventually history itself has to be rewritten to fit it.

Dr Lubna Ferdowsi is a researcher and educator whose work engages with society, culture, identity, public policy and questions of citizenship.
