title: Mustafizur seeks BCB clearance for BBL debut
text:
Bangladesh pacer Mustafizur Rahman has applied for a No Objection Certificate (NOC) from the Bangladesh Cricket Board (BCB) to play in the Big Bash League (BBL) for the first time.

If all goes according to plan, he will represent the Melbourne Renegades.

The development was confirmed on Monday during the auction for the domestic tournament 'D3'.

BCB president Tamim Iqbal told reporters that Mustafizur, alongside Rishad Hossain, had sought an NOC from the board.

The pacer did not spark an intense bidding war at the auction, as he is set to miss part of the D3 tournament due to his BBL commitments. Mustafizur will only feature in the ODI format, with Seven Rings Cement securing his services for 70 lakh virtual points.

Shakib Al Hasan was the first Bangladeshi cricketer to feature in the BBL, where he also represented the Melbourne Renegades. Meanwhile, Bangladesh leg-spinner Rishad Hossain, who impressed with the Hobart Hurricanes last season, will return to the same franchise for the upcoming edition.

The next edition of the BBL is scheduled to take place in December-January, coinciding with the T20 format of the D3 tournament. Having stepped away from red-ball cricket, Mustafizur is not part of domestic first-class competitions.

title: Mbappe hits 100 for Real, but Clasico victory means more
text:
Kylian Mbappe said reaching a milestone 100 goals for Real Madrid during the 2-1 Clasico win over Barcelona in La Liga on Monday was "just a detail" compared to the team's victory.

The French forward hit a brace to bring up his century for Los Blancos across all competitions since joining in 2024.

Mbappe's double, either side of a Raphinha strike for the hosts at Camp Nou, brought third-place Real Madrid within three points of the La Liga leaders and reigning Spanish champions.

"I'm very happy, I think everyone knows I like to score goals, I like to help the team with that, but I think today it's just a detail, because... the most important thing is the team's win," Mbappe told Real Madrid TV.

"Honestly, the real star of the game today is the team, the group, because we knew we had to play a big game, a team game...

"We know that in the end it was a great game, but it still only counts as three points, and we need to pick up a lot of points to win La Liga."

Jose Mourinho's Madrid have now won five matches in a row and seem to be coming into strong form.

"It doesn't mean anything, we have to continue, because five games for us is nothing, we want to win every game," added Mbappe, 27.

"(Winning) is a good message today, but we can't think the season is done -- next week (at Racing) Santander we have to put in the same intensity."

title: Carrick’s tears, United’s turmoil, and a future on the line
text:
Michael Carrick insisted it was not a farewell, but the emotion on his face after Manchester United’s 3-0 home defeat to Bournemouth told its own story.

As United supporters sang his name at full-time on Sunday, the 45-year-old made a lap of the pitch to applaud them, visibly moved by their backing. Yet, with results continuing to deteriorate, his future as manager is hanging in the balance.

The defeat left United 16th in the Premier League, 14 points off the top, having won just one of their opening eight matches. Senior figures at Old Trafford are understood to be discussing Carrick’s position after a dismal start to the campaign.

“See what happens,” Carrick told BBC Sport when asked whether he expected discussions about his future.

“I’m not expecting anything. It’s just digesting today. We knew it was an important day to try and get us moving forward, and we haven’t done that.

“For me, it’s just digesting that, and the emotions at the end of the game is something I’ve not really had before.”

Speaking to Sky Sports, Carrick was equally keen to dismiss the suggestion that his lap of appreciation had been a goodbye.

“It wasn’t a farewell from me,” he said.

“I’ve mixed emotions. I’m feeling it for my players. They’re going through a tough spell. Some of it we can help, some of it the situation unravels, and the boys are feeling it at the moment.

Emotional exit by Michael Carrick as fans sing his name. A farewell? Supporters turn on players once Carrick down tunnel. #MUFC https://t.co/WLYqqHg6vF — Laurie Whitwell (@lauriewhitwell) October 25, 2026

“Mixed emotions for the supporters to respond in that way. To have that connection with the supporters, it’s mixed emotions. It’ll take a bit of time to digest, but I certainly appreciate their support.

“The situation is where we are, and we haven’t had results or performances that have been good enough.”

That connection with the supporters remains one of Carrick’s strongest assets. A former United midfielder who made 464 appearances for the club over 12 years, he remains a popular figure among the Old Trafford faithful. But the warmth of that relationship may not be enough to protect him from the consequences of United’s results.

The contrast was striking at full-time. While Carrick received a chorus of support, the chants turned to boos after he had left the pitch, with the players and the club’s hierarchy bearing the brunt of the supporters’ frustration.

Former United defender Gary Neville believes the fans’ reaction could reflect their fear that a popular figure is about to pay the price for problems that run deeper than the manager.

The Old Trafford faithful showed their true colours today. 👏🔴 Despite watching their team get humiliated on the pitch, they stood firmly behind Michael Carrick, singing his name throughout the game and making it clear where their loyalty lies. Then, as the players made their way down the tunnel, the boos rang out. The fans are absolutely disgusted with what they've witnessed since the start of the season, and they know the problems at Manchester United go far beyond the manager. Carrick has done more for that football club than most of those players ever will, yet he could be sacked tonight because, once again, a group of players appear to have downed tools when things got tough. Another manager potentially sacrificed while the same problems remain. It's a disgrace. — Football Tweet ⚽ (@Footballtweet) October 25, 2026

“The Manchester United fans are singing the Michael Carrick song because I think they know what’s going to happen here. They’ve seen this before. He’s one of their own and he’s popular,” Neville said on Sky Sports.

“But the owners, the sporting department and the players are not popular, and they’ve badly let this football club down.

“Those two [Omar Berrada and Jason Wilcox] tomorrow are probably going to make a decision that will disgust Manchester United fans, but it’s probably necessary.

“It’s just an absolute mess.”

Former Premier League striker Clinton Morrison also noted the difference between the reception for Carrick and that for his players.

“They’re with Carrick, the fans, but they’re not with the players. Wow, that was alarming,” Morrison said.

“Carrick got a big cheer, but as soon as it was just the players, they got booed. But they’ve not been good enough, and they deserve to get booed. There’s only so much a manager can do.”

Former United full-back Ashley Young was similarly critical of the players’ performance, saying they had shown little fight or unity against Bournemouth.

“The fans are behind him and backing him, and of course they are, because he’s a legend of the football club. But the players on the pitch showed nothing. They didn’t run, they didn’t look like a team together,” Young said.

Carrick, however, has received public support from within the dressing room. Harry Maguire, who wore the captain’s armband against Bournemouth with Bruno Fernandes left on the bench, insisted that the players remained behind their manager.

“We’re fully behind Michael [Carrick],” Maguire told BBC Sport.

“Coming into the team last season, he turned things around and got Champions League football this season. As individuals, we’re not playing well enough.”

Yet the decision to leave Fernandes out added another layer of intrigue to an already fraught situation. The Portugal international had questioned Carrick’s tactics following Wednesday’s 4-1 Champions League defeat to Como, making his omission from the starting line-up a significant talking point.

The episode came amid wider unrest at the club, with defender Lisandro Martinez having apologised after making controversial remarks about United’s hierarchy. Martinez had said he expected greater investment in the squad and “more from our technical director [Jason Wilcox]”.

Carrick took interim charge in January following Ruben Amorim’s departure and was handed the permanent job in May after an impressive run that secured Champions League qualification and a third-place finish. That progress now feels distant, with United struggling to find consistency and the pressure mounting after another damaging defeat.

For Carrick, Sunday was a night of conflicting emotions: the affection of supporters who still see him as one of their own, the public backing of his players and the uncomfortable reality that performances have fallen well short of expectations.

title: Ashraful’s abrupt removal leaves more questions than answers
text:
Mohammad Ashraful oversaw Bangladesh’s training on Saturday ahead of their crucial two-Test series against West Indies. By night, he had been removed as national batting coach without prior notice or any reason publicly stated by the Bangladesh Cricket Board (BCB), raising fresh questions over its handling of a role marked by frequent changes.

His appointment in November last year had drawn criticism, with many questioning whether the former national captain had sufficient coaching experience for such a key position.

Yet, his tenure brought notable results in Test cricket. Bangladesh won five of eight Tests under him and drew one, including a historic victory over Australia in Darwin. They also secured three consecutive ODI series wins at home. However, their struggles away from home, particularly during the recent UAE ODI tri-series, appear to have proved decisive.

Ashraful, speaking after his removal on Saturday, defended his record in the longer format, arguing that Bangladesh’s Test side remained settled and that the batters had performed consistently under his watch.

“Since I joined, we have won five of eight Tests and drawn one. Our batters have scored nine centuries and 22 or 23 half-centuries, with a century partnership in almost every Test,” he told reporters yeterday.

“The cricket board can best explain why I am no longer there.”

The numbers offer a more nuanced picture of his tenure. Bangladesh averaged 202.8 runs per innings across 14 matches under Ashraful, with no totals exceeding 300. In the preceding 14 matches under Mohammad Salahuddin, the average was 217.6. Salahuddin, who previously oversaw batting as senior assistant coach, has now been appointed interim batting coach for the West Indies series.

The change adds to a history of uncertainty surrounding the role. Following Neil McKenzie’s resignation for family reasons, the BCB appointed Ashwell Prince, who sources suggest helped several batters. However, Prince resigned in 2022 after the board had already brought in Jamie Siddons as batting consultant a month earlier.

Siddons was expected to address Bangladesh’s longstanding batting problems, given his previous stint with the team, but some considered his methods outdated. David Hemp followed, yet concerns persisted within the BCB that his work remained focused on basics without delivering the desired improvements.

Ashraful is the latest to make way. While some believe he has strong mentoring qualities, there are suggestions that players were less receptive to working with him on individual technical issues, having established relationships with domestic coaches before his appointment.

There is also a question of consistency in the board’s judgement. Salahuddin was in charge during the recent Asian Games, where Bangladesh’s batting failures were also apparent. As the BCB keeps searching for a high-profile batting coach, Ashraful’s departure leaves a familiar question unanswered: can frequent changes deliver the stability the team’s batting needs?

title: Kane primed to pip Yamal, Mbappe to Ballon d'Or glory
text:
England captain Harry Kane is the favourite to win a wide open race to be crowned Ballon d'Or winner at a glitzy London ceremony on Monday, with Lamine Yamal and Kylian Mbappe also in the running to be named the world's best footballer.

The 70th edition of the award, established by the magazine France Football, will be hosted in England for the first time in recognition of the first winner Stanley Matthews and fittingly could have a first English winner for 25 years.

Bayern Munich striker Kane struck a remarkable 73 goals in 65 games for club and country last season, leading the German giants to a league and cup double and England to the semi-finals of the World Cup.

"I'd love to be able to achieve something like that. I would be a massive milestone in my career," said the 33-year-old.

But semi-final exits in both the Champions League and World Cup for Kane means the outcome is far from certain.

"I think my wife would prefer to know and my family … it’s very stressful for everyone," he added.

"I can see why they don't tell people. They want everyone to go, all the big names, and there will be more people watching it if they don't know."

Yamal finished second to Paris Saint-Germain's Ousmane Dembele last year and the 19-year-old Barcelona superstar seems destined to be a Ballon d'Or winner one day.

However, after a hamstring injury ended his club season early, he was far from the shining light of Spain's World Cup triumph that was built on being the best collective unit.

Yamal was pipped to both the player and young player of the tournament by his Barcelona team-mates Rodri and Pau Cubarsi.

That has not diminished his bullish confidence ahead of the ceremony.

"For me, Mbappe and me, we're the two best players in the world," Yamal said last month.

"I honestly think that, as the best in the world, maybe there are two of us, and this year I would deserve it because of what I've won."

Mbappe, by contrast, boasts plenty of personal milestones without medals for either Real Madrid or France.

The 27-year-old was top goalscorer in La Liga, the Champions League and the World Cup without winning any of those trophies.

His 10 World Cup goals made him the top goalscorer in the competition's history on 22.

"Being the all-time top scorer in World Cup history, overtaking all the great legends in the history of the sport in the most important tournament there is, is something that really stands out," said Mbappe.

"Who am I voting for? Myself."

One football journalist from each of the 100 top nations in FIFA's rankings is invited to cast votes for their top 10 players from a 30-man shortlist, allocating a maximum of 15 points down to one based on their ranking.

The Ballon d'Or goes to the player who accrued the most points.

Although the award carries no cash prize, it can generate huge bonuses from clubs and commercial partners as well as increasing a player's overall marketing value.

Alexia Putellas is the frontrunner to win the women's award for the third time with Aitana Bonmati's three-year reign to come to an end after an injury-hit year.

Putellas, winner in 2021 and 2022, was part of the Barcelona side that regained the Champions League last season before moving to London City Lionesses.

Her former club team-mate, Poland's Ewa Pajor is the main challenger to Putellas after she netted 11 Champions League goals in Barca's latest triumph.

title: Ronan, Mahe tasked with filling No 9 void
text:
Bangladesh coach Thomas Dooley has turned to overseas-based forwards Ronan Sullivan and Mohammed Mahe Khan in a bid to solve the national team’s long-standing No 9 problem ahead of the SAFF Championship, which begins in Dhaka on November 5.

The German-American coach has overlooked local forwards such as Sourav Dewan and Shahriar Emon, while promising Raphael Tudu has also missed out, instead banking on the US-based Sullivan and English ninth-tier forward Mahe to provide the goals Bangladesh have been lacking.

Since taking charge in June, Dooley has seen Bangladesh score just four goals in as many international matches. Defender Topu Barman scored twice, while Farhaan Ali Wahid and Shuki Itofusa netted once each.

“Everybody knows that we're looking for a number 9 because we don't have a number 9,” Dooley told reporters at a hotel on Sunday, after 21 players from the 28-member preliminary squad reported for the residential camp.

The coach explained that a traditional centre-forward needed the physical presence, courage and positional awareness to compete with defenders and get to the ball first inside the penalty area.

“You have to have as a centre-forward a specific player who needs to go in front of the goalkeeper, in front of the defender, to be the first one to get that ball,” he said.

“If you are not afraid to go in there where it hurts, then you are a number 9, then you are a centre-forward, but we don't have that.”

Dooley identified Sullivan and Mahe as the two candidates he hopes can fill the role.

“Ronan is one of them and Mahe Khan is also one of them. So those are obviously with us to fulfil that number 9 position that we so desperately need,” he said.

Mahe, who recently represented Bangladesh at the AFC U-20 Asian Cup qualifiers, had initially faced uncertainty over his inclusion. Dooley said he wanted the forward to join the camp for assessment but was informed two days later that the final 28-man squad had to be announced, leaving him no time to evaluate the player.

Despite playing in England's ninth tier, Mahe has impressed the coach with his profile as a traditional striker.

“Maybe he doesn't play at the highest level, but he is a typical number 9. He scores goals,” Dooley said, adding that he had encouraged the forward to seize the opportunity to establish himself.

Sullivan, who has also represented Bangladesh at the youth level, became an option after the coach received confirmation that his college would release him to join the national team.

“He played for the U-20, scored. He is a typical number 9, fantastic,” Dooley said.

The coach believes finding a reliable centre-forward is essential to Bangladesh's hopes of winning the regional title.

“If we go to the SAFF tournament and we don't have a number 9, it will also be very difficult to be successful,” he said.

title: Mourinho offers Real a blueprint to beat Barca
text:
Real Madrid recorded just a second victory in eight games against Barcelona on Sunday night, with the return of Jose Mourinho to the fixture haunting the reigning champions.

In the first Clasico of Mourinho's first spell at Real Madrid, Barcelona ripped his side to shreds in a 5-0 win at Camp Nou. A 2-1 win in the first Clasico of his second spell suggests Mourinho's Real Madrid can challenge Barcelona's recent LaLiga dominance in his first season back in Spain.

Although the chances were shared out evenly, with Barcelona racking up more shots on goal, more possession and more passes throughout the match, those statistics were not an honest reflection of the game. Real Madrid played as if they had the answers to the test Barcelona posed.

"The lads played an extraordinary match," said Mourinho in his press conference afterwards.

"Very organised, focused, and showing the courage to play the ball out from the back against an opponent that applied a lot of pressure."

Time and again, Mourinho's side moved the ball with urgency and precision in their own half to escape Barcelona's pressing.

Fede Valverde was praised for playing through injury by Mourinho, but above all he embodied the presence of mind to identify where the space was whenever the ball was turned over.

The Uruguayan did so from the right-back position, despite stating in September 2025 that he was "not born to play as a full-back."

Valverde later denied he had expressed any unwillingness to play in defence, but a number of Spanish outlets took this as a suggestion he was not pleased about doing so, and perhaps he was not on board with then-manager Xabi Alonso's style of management.

For a third game in a row, the Real Madrid captain started at right-back and delivered a captain's performance. Valverde's impressive showing in his unfavoured position demonstrated Mourinho not only is finding tactical solutions to get the best out of his players, but is winning over the Real Madrid dressing room.

Mourinho remarked that leaving Camp Nou just three points behind Barcelona "gives us peace of mind, and it's well deserved."

The victory over Barcelona should help to boost morale and build unity within the Real Madrid squad. More importantly, Mourinho now has evidence his methods can help return Real Madrid to the summit of Spanish football.

"If we win today but lose at El Sardinero, it counts for nothing, because Madrid isn't playing to win at the Camp Nou," Mourinho said.

"They’re playing to win the championship" — a statement that now looks closer to reality after two defeats in September had sown early doubts about Mourinho's plans.

title: Inter snatch Serie A summit, depleted Bayern return to the top, Rennes soar in Ligue 1
text:
It was a weekend of dramatic shifts, emotional triumphs, and late chaos across Europe's top leagues as the race for domestic supremacy intensified. In Italy, Inter Milan pulled off a spectacular stoppage-time heist to reclaim the Serie A summit, matching the resilience of a depleted Bayern Munich side that returned to the top of the Bundesliga despite the hospitalisation of head coach Vincent Kompany. Meanwhile, in France, Rennes capitalised on a tense, red-card marred draw between Monaco and Lille to vault to the top of Ligue 1, capping off a breathless round of football.

Serie A: Stoppage-time madness sends Inter top as Juve stop the rot



Inter Milan staged a breathtaking late comeback at San Siro, striking twice in stoppage time to overturn a deficit and beat struggling Fiorentina 2-1 on Sunday.

Alex Jimenez's audacious long-range strike against the run of play in the 65th minute looked set to hand the visitors a shock victory after Inter failed to beat an inspired David de Gea. However, Marcus Thuram leveled the scores in the 91st minute and then won a 98th-minute penalty, which Piotr Zielinski calmly converted to send the Nerazzurri back to first place alongside Lazio on 22 points.

Inter head coach Cristian Chivu praised his team's unwavering mentality. "The important thing is not to let your heads drop," Chivu said. "I don't want to see people feel sorry for themselves. I want to see players respond to setbacks."

Elsewhere in Italy, Juventus eased the mounting pressure on head coach Luciano Spalletti by securing a much-needed 2-0 win away at Lecce. Following a dismal run of one win in five league games, Weston McKennie and Douglas Luiz found the net in the first half to lift Juve to seventh. Lecce’s frustrating evening ended with a late red card for Kialonda Gasper.

In other action, Atalanta and Frosinone played out a frantic 4-4 draw where both sides came from behind twice, extending Atalanta's winless run to three games. Genoa climbed to 16th by edging out bottom club Venezia 1-0 through a Mikael Ellertsson goal, while AC Milan were scheduled to face Udinese in the late fixture.

Bundesliga: Depleted Bayern win for hospitalised Kompany as Hoffenheim make history

Over in Germany, Bayern Munich navigated a tumultuous week to reclaim the Bundesliga summit with a 3-1 victory at Freiburg.

Operating under assistant coach Aaron Danks while head coach Vincent Kompany recovers in the hospital from a mystery virus, a depleted Bayern squad -- missing several key figures including Manuel Neuer and Joshua Kimmich -- cruised to a two-goal halftime lead. Dayot Upamecano finished off a brilliant length-of-the-field counterattack, and Serge Gnabry doubled the advantage just before the break.

Freiburg found late hope via a Tom Bischof own goal, forcing Bayern keeper Jonas Urbig into crucial saves. But with Freiburg pushing high in stoppage time, Michael Olise capitalised on goalkeeper Mio Backhaus being caught up the pitch to slide the ball into an empty net. The victory allowed Bayern to leapfrog Borussia Dortmund ahead of their highly anticipated clash next week.

"I just opened my phone to a message from Vince saying 'well done' and he was happy," Danks shared after the match, noting that Kompany is stable and resting.

Meanwhile, Hoffenheim made history with a late flurry to snap Bayer Leverkusen's six-game winning streak in a 3-0 victory. Andrej Kramaric's 79th-minute penalty broke the deadlock and marked the 1,000th league goal in Hoffenheim's history. Alexander Prass added a second on the counter -- bizarrely earning a red card for taking his shirt off in celebration -- before Max Moerstedt capped off the win deep into stoppage time despite the one-man disadvantage.

Ligue 1: Rennes capitalise to seize top spot as red card drama derails Lille



In France, Rennes took full advantage of dropped points by their rivals to climb to the top of Ligue 1 with a commanding 3-0 win over 16th-placed Strasbourg. First-half goals from Boulaye Dia and Sebastian Szymanski, who later netted again to secure a brace, wrapped up the points for Franck Haise's men, putting them on 16 points.

The door had been left open after Monaco fought back to hold Lille to a 1-1 draw at the Stade Louis II. Ethan Mbappe gave Lille the lead in the 24th minute with a crisp left-footed strike, but the momentum shifted when Lille defender Tanguy Nianzou was shown a straight red for a reckless challenge in the 65th minute. Monaco leveled nine minutes later when Edan Diop's cross evaded everyone and nestled into the far corner, leaving both sides tied on 15 points.

In the day's most chaotic fixture, eighth-placed Marseille held on to beat bottom-side Le Havre 4-3 at the Stade Velodrome. Cruising at 4-0 up with just 15 minutes remaining, Marseille nearly collapsed entirely as a Josh Maja brace and a Lamine Ndiaye strike set up a nerve-wracking finale.

Elsewhere, Toulouse and Troyes, as well as Angers and Lorient, played out goalless stalemates, while Auxerre and Le Mans finished 1-1. The Ligue 1 picture could shift once more on Monday when PSG -- missing Ballon d'Or winner Ousmane Dembele, Marquinhos, and the recently injured Khvicha Kvaratskhelia -- face Lyon in a match delayed by nationwide protests.

title: Mbappe reigns supreme at Camp Nou as Real clinch Clasico win
text:
Kylian Mbappe struck twice to earn Jose Mourinho's Real Madrid a 2-1 Clasico victory over La Liga leaders Barcelona on Sunday at Camp Nou, cutting the gap to three points.

French superstar Mbappe opened the scoring before the interval and then slotted home late on to inflict Barca's first domestic defeat of the campaign after Raphinha had equalised for the champions.

Real Madrid remain third, behind Atletico Madrid and Hansi Flick's Barca, who had won their first nine games before a chastening week.

The Catalans suffered a second straight defeat after losing on Tuesday against Paris Saint-Germain in the Champions League.

Barca had won six of the seven previous Clasicos since the German arrived but were surprisingly subdued against Mourinho's side.

Los Blancos, without suspended winger Vinicius Junior, won their fifth straight game across all competitions and are finding their footing under veteran Portuguese coach Mourinho.

The opening period of the game was cagey, with few opportunities.

Barca defender Pau Cubarsi twice reacted well to shut down Mbappe, while Real Madrid's Marc Cucurella took a rapid liking for Lamine Yamal's shirt, constantly grabbing at the 19-year-old winger.

Anthony Gordon, playing in his first Clasico since joining Barcelona from Newcastle, backheeled the ball to Raphinha, who fired narrowly wide as Barca threatened.

The hosts were dealt a setback when young defender Xavi Espart pulled up hurt and needed to be replaced by Alejandro Balde before the half-hour mark.

Andriy Lunin, playing in goal for Madrid after Thibaut Courtois pulled out of the squad with flu, saved at his near post from Gordon before the visitors took the lead.

Mbappe scored his 10th league goal of the season and also his easiest, with Barca's Gerard Martin clearing a cross straight at the Frenchman, who deflected it into the net.

Barca responded by carving out a glorious chance for an equaliser but teenage sensation Yamal for once miscued in front of goal, firing wide when poised to level.

The game opened up and Yan Diomande came close to doubling Madrid's lead before half-time, drilling into the side-netting.

Sting in the tail



Martin redeemed himself early in the second half as he held off Jude Bellingham, who could neither beat the defender nor find a free Mbappe.

Raphinha, who had a quiet first half, pulled Barcelona level just after the hour mark.

Pedri fed the Brazilian, La Liga's top goalscorer with 13, who fired through Bellingham's legs and Lunin could not keep the shot out.

The Ukrainian goalkeeper did make a superb save to deny Martin at a corner, as Barcelona flowed forward with the wind finally in their sails.

Yamal bent an effort wide with Lunin at full stretch and Barca substitute Frenkie de Jong had a shot desperately blocked by Dean Huijsen.

There was a sting in the tail for the Catalans though as substitute Gabriel Jesus lost possession and Madrid raced through on goal.

Eduardo Camavinga beat Cubarsi and unselfishly cut the ball back for Mbappe to tuck home his second of the night into an empty net with Joan Garcia drawn out of position.

title: Maternity blind spot in Bangladesh cricket
text:
When former Bangladesh pacer Suraiya Azmin emailed Bangladesh Cricket Board (BCB) on May 9 to request paid maternity leave, she received no response.

After giving birth in August, she found herself dropped from the national contract list, while her leave request and unpaid salary remained unresolved.

Suraiya’s experience is not an isolated case.

Her experience exposes a wider gap in Bangladesh women’s cricket: the lack of a formal maternity policy to protect players’ income, contracts and prospects of returning to the game.

Former Bangladesh batter Sanjida Islam Moyna, who played 16 Women’s ODIs and 54 T20Is between 2012 and 2020, married first-class cricketer Mim Mosaddek in 2020, continued playing domestically until 2024 and gave birth in 2025. She has since stepped away from the game to raise her child.

Image Sanjida Islam had dreams of a successful cricketing career when she got married. Photo: Facebook

Sanjida believes assumptions about marriage and motherhood shape how officials and selectors view women players. Some cricketers delay marriage to prolong their careers, while others conceal their marital status.

“In the BCB's system, there is a stigma against married players. Officials and selectors assume that once a female player marries or has a child, she won't play long, viewing further investment in her as a waste of time,” Sanjida said.

She believes proper maternity support would allow women to continue playing much longer after marriage and childbirth. Sanjida recently interviewed for a women’s divisional coaching position but was not selected, for reasons that remain unclear.

In the BCB's system, there is a stigma against married players. Officials and selectors assume that once a female player marries or has a child, she won't play long, viewing further investment in her as a waste of time. Sanjida Islam Moyna

Suraiya’s experience reflects the same assumptions about marriage and motherhood. “Once a player gets married or reaches a certain age, people assume she won't play anymore. And if she has a baby, then playing again is completely out of the question.”

The board’s silence also affected her willingness to continue. “If I saw they had responded positively, if my willingness for return was 60 percent it would have increased to 100 percent,” she said. Although encouraged by her husband to seek leave, she felt the board had failed to value her. She last played for Gulshan Youth Club in the 2025 Dhaka Premier Division Women’s Cricket League.

Former national cricketer and international umpire Sathira Jakir Jessy also struggled to balance motherhood and cricket. “Even when I got married, I was the vice-captain of the national team, and I had a feeling that I might not be able to continue for long. I continued playing after becoming a mother, but it wasn’t easy at all.

Image Sathira Jakir Jessy has carved out an inspiring career for herself. Photo: Facebook

“Many are still afraid of having a baby because they feel it could bring their careers to an end."

She added, “Even at the stage I am at now, I think twice about having another baby because I wonder whether BCB would support me during that time, allowing me to return to the level of umpiring I have reached."

Many are still afraid of having a baby because they feel it could bring their careers to an end. Sathira Jakir Jessy

LESSONS FROM ABROAD

On June 22, International Cricket Council (ICC) introduced Return to Play Post-Pregnancy Guidelines for female cricketers. Its six stages -- Ready, Review, Restore, Recondition, Return and Refine -- cover recovery, medical assessments, gradual training and monitoring. The guidelines help member boards develop policies but do not guarantee paid leave.

Cricket Australia and New Zealand Cricket provide paid maternity leave to contracted players, while Pakistan introduced a Parental Support Policy in 2021. A year later, Bismah Maroof captained Pakistan at the World Cup, six months after giving birth, with her child and a support person.

Former Bangladesh player and current Qatar women’s team head coach Fatema Tuz Jahara, who has worked in Australia and China, said the contrast was stark. In Australia, she said, maternity leave is fully paid, with board-supervised medical care and health and fitness assessments before a player returns.

“In our country, when they get contracted as national players, [they] rely on that salary to support not just themselves but their entire family. So when pregnancy comes up, she has to think ten times.” she said.

“That's why our female players get married very late… [and] cannot think long-term about family life or pregnancy during their active playing careers, because there is no security provided in our country. When it comes to protecting women, economically or socially, we are far behind compared to other countries."

WHAT BCB SAYS

BCB Women’s Wing chairman Rafiqul Islam Babu said the board would follow ICC guidelines. “In the future, anyone who becomes pregnant or takes maternity leave will certainly be granted leave, and we will follow ICC’s policy in this regard,” he said, adding that he did not know why a guideline had not been introduced by this time.

Asked about Suraiya’s unpaid salary, leave and contract, Babu said her dues would be paid soon. “Everything is under process."

BCB CEO Nizamuddin Chowdhury acknowledged the absence of a formal maternity policy. “These matters are being addressed on a case-by-case basis.

“The POSH [Prevention of Sexual Harassment] Policy and the Safeguarding Policy have already been introduced,” he added. “As for the other issues, we will implement the other policies as soon as possible.”

As it stands, BCB has no maternity policy in place, despite pledging to follow ICC guidelines and address outstanding payments. A policy must clarify whether leave is paid, how contracts are protected and what support players receive when returning to competition.

The POSH [Prevention of Sexual Harassment] Policy and the Safeguarding Policy have already been introduced,” he added. “As for the other issues, we will implement the other policies as soon as possible. BCB CEO Nizamuddin Chowdhury

Until such a policy is introduced, women cricketers will continue to face uncertainty over whether motherhood and a sustained career can coexist.

title: When marriage becomes a financial trap
text:
I had a friend at school whose mother used to steal money from her husband’s wallet on a regular basis. When my mother shared this gossip with us, I remember being a bit put off by my auntie’s apparent lack of virtue. My younger self had been taught that stealing was a sinful act, and thus, I could not understand what reason there could be for an adult woman to engage in such an act. The 12-year-old version of me could barely realise back then that many unfortunate women like my friend’s mother resort to petty theft because they have been financially abused throughout their lives.

There are millions of women all over the world who have absolutely no access to money. Not a single paisa to their name. Many of them even live in houses with granite countertops and a Toyota RAV4 or Land Cruiser in the garage, yet every time they need to purchase even the most basic necessities, such as groceries, they have to ask their husbands for permission and show them receipts afterwards. These might seem like extreme cases to some, but in a world that has long been dominated by patriarchy, these are the real stories of real women who have experienced financial abuse in more ways than one. They are your mothers, your sisters, your friends, your neighbours and maybe even you. And they live like hostages behind the grey concrete walls of high-rise towers or amid the dust and squalor of the city’s underbelly.

Contrary to popular opinion, financial abuse does not always look like financial struggle. While it can look like a middle-class mother scavenging for stray coins in her purse to afford new school supplies for her daughter, it can also look like a woman travelling in her family’s new Mercedes to Espresso Lounge and spending more than 5,000 taka in one sitting. What makes their stories similar is that both women have to remember to ask their husbands for permission before making any financial decision, whether it involves buying school supplies for their children from a local shop or buying brunch for themselves at a posh restaurant.

Every single day, these women require “approval” to spend money on everything, even common household items such as kitchen utensils or personal necessities such as menstrual hygiene products. Like my friend’s mother, some of them, finding no other alternative, resort to stealing cash from their partners and hiding it in their jewellery boxes.

The most intriguing thing about financial abuse is that it is not always obvious. It does not always occur openly, so for a woman, beyond empty bank accounts, it can mean having no monthly allowance, little to no share of her partner’s monthly income, no access to joint funds, no debit or credit cards in her name, no income of her own, no bank account and, consequently, no safety net at all. It can also mean a husband who questions, “What do you even need money for when I am paying for everything?” Or a husband who quite lovingly says to her, “Don’t worry about money. I’ll handle it.” And then, years later, when her marriage turns upside down, she is afraid to leave because she does not have any money in her account. Why? Because she never had to worry about money or bank accounts in the first place.

And that is how financial abuse works: slowly, silently and, most of the time, strategically. By the time these women finally realise that they have been subjected to financial abuse by their partners in one way or another, they wish somebody had told them sooner: you need your own money.

Image Having personal savings and access to money provides women with financial protection against life's uncertainties. Photo: Collected

According to data sourced from the World Bank Group’s Gender Data Portal, women comprised only 38.6 per cent of the labour force in Bangladesh in 2025; in other words, around 61.4 per cent of Bangladeshi women of working age do not participate in the formal labour market and thus have no personal income from formal employment. Additionally, according to data from the same portal, in 2024, only 33.3 per cent of Bangladesh’s female population reportedly had an account, either individually or jointly with someone else, at a bank or another type of financial institution, or had used a mobile money service in the previous 12 months. This indicates that about 66.7 per cent of Bangladeshi women neither have a bank account nor use mobile financial services. Data from ActionAid Bangladesh reveals that Bangladeshi women perform 85 per cent of all household chores as unpaid labour, spending an average of nearly 6.8 hours on such work every day.

Every single one of these women needs her own money. Not because they plan to leave their husbands or families without any valid reason. Not because they cannot or do not trust their partners. Not because they want to live their lives wilfully or recklessly, without a care in the world. But because life happens in the most unpredictable ways. People lose jobs at the most crucial moments of their lives. Businesses fail, and bank accounts get frozen. Accidents and disasters happen, resulting in the loss of lives, property and stability. Love goes awry. People change because their minds change. The world can shift overnight. And when any of these misfortunes befall a family, having an additional source of income, a second bank account and/or a certain amount of savings provides financial protection, allowing women to protect themselves, their children and the rest of their families against such hardships.

One of the most enduring mechanisms through which patriarchy has maintained its hold over women has been to keep them financially dependent; not just broke in the moment, but systemically, structurally and generationally broke. Forcing women out of the workforce is one of the most insidious forms of social control exercised by patriarchal societies. These societies, in many devious ways, try to make it an unavoidable “choice” for women to prioritise their homes over their careers. “You are allowed to continue working as long as meals have been prepared for everyone, your children’s homework has been completed, routine household chores have been done, and all other needs of your family members have been sufficiently met,” the husband and in-laws declare. With little to no support from their immediate families, the burden of these double shifts often becomes unbearable for working women. Next, we see their families vehemently encouraging, and even forcing, them to leave their jobs on the grounds that their husbands are already earning enough to support the family.

Stripped of her earnings, a woman loses not just her confidence and identity but also her financial cushion. This, in turn, ensures that every taka in the household passes through someone else’s hands, usually her husband’s. If any untoward event affects her marital relationship, she may find herself powerless to leave simply because she cannot afford to. We call a woman’s decision to quit her job and focus on household responsibilities her “choice”, but without any personal income, her choices eventually narrow down to one: stay.

In Bangladesh, the percentage of ever-married women aged between 15 and 49 who have experienced physical or sexual violence by their husband or partner, widely known as intimate partner violence, is 48.9 per cent, which is 27 percentage points higher than the world average. For many of these women with no income of their own, the only choice is to stay. Stay in the marriage, no matter how abusive it is. Stay in the house, no matter how toxic its environment is. Stay in the role, no matter how suffocating it feels. This is neither a coincidence nor bad luck. This is an entire system working exactly as it was designed.

Money is freedom, yet too many women are still being taught that dependence is just another name for devotion and that unquestioning silence is a badge of honour. This has to change. Families must fully understand the importance of education and financial independence for their daughters. Before deciding to marry them off hastily at a young age, parents must ensure that their daughters have their own sources of income. Also, instead of spending millions on their weddings, parents need to invest that money in their daughters’ education and save a substantial amount of it in a bank account as a safeguard. Most importantly, parents must respect their daughters’ property rights under the country's existing legal framework. Government intervention, when these rights are violated, must be strengthened and strictly enforced. Educational institutions need to make classes on personal finance mandatory so that female students can formally learn how to make important financial decisions. Both public and private organisations need to make necessary adjustments to their workplaces for female employees, particularly working mothers, by offering flexible working arrangements, paid maternity leave, in-house childcare facilities and opportunities for remote work.

Image Financial abuse can leave women without control over their own money, trapping them in dependence and making it difficult to leave an unhappy or abusive marriage. Visual: Adrin Sarwar

Easier said than done, of course. Expecting an entire social system that has endured for generations to change its mindsets, norms and practices overnight is simply unrealistic. But combined, dedicated efforts on all fronts can certainly have transformative effects on numerous women’s lives. If the measures outlined above are properly implemented, perhaps these women will no longer have to choose between their careers and their homes. Perhaps they will no longer have to ask anyone for permission to spend money. And perhaps they will no longer feel compelled to stay if they experience financial abuse at any point in their lives.

Nadia Afroze Disha is a lecturer at BRAC Business School, BRAC University.

title: AI boom is making computers way more expensive
text:
Arifuzzaman Biplob has spent the past two decades selling computers across a range of price points to businesses, individuals and students.

His company, Ryans Computers Limited, builds desktop computers and sells laptops from global brands such as HP, Dell, Acer and Asus. Building desktops requires solid-state drives (SSDs), which store data, and random-access memory (RAM), which temporarily holds data while other chips crunch numbers and display graphics.

Over the past year, Ryans Computers, one of the largest computer retail chains in Bangladesh, has faced a massive rise in RAM and SSD prices. Laptop import costs have also climbed, pushing the price of an entry-level model to Tk 65,000-Tk 70,000 from Tk 48,000 a year ago.

“Standard laptop prices have increased by 35 to 49 percent,” said Arifuzzaman.

A mid-range laptop that previously cost Tk 65,000-Tk 70,000 now sells for around Tk 80,000-Tk 85,000. Higher-end models that once cost Tk 80,000-Tk 90,000 can now fetch Tk 110,000-Tk 125,000 or more, depending on their specifications, he said.

The surge is being driven by the global race to develop artificial intelligence (AI). OpenAI, Meta, Google and other technology giants are ordering increasing quantities of memory chips for their data centres, tightening supplies for personal computers and pushing up prices.

“The situation is worse than during the Covid-19 pandemic, when manufacturing units were largely shut,” said Arifuzzaman. “There is no possibility that computer prices would cool off anytime soon in Bangladesh as prices are ticking up across the globe.”

He said memory chips, SSDs and processors are among the main components driving up computer prices. Graphics cards have also become more expensive.

Image

As AI companies place large orders for high-performance memory and other chips to build their computing infrastructure, manufacturers are giving priority to these more lucrative products, according to Mohammad Zahirul Islam, president of Bangladesh Computer Samity (BCS), the country’s leading ICT trade and business organisation.

Zahirul said a small number of major semiconductor manufacturers supply much of the global market, while large technology companies are securing components for their AI infrastructure.

He said as manufacturers redirect production towards these customers, supplies for consumer devices are tightening, raising procurement costs for computer makers and retailers.

Global market intelligence and consulting firm TrendForce forecast in a September report that contract prices for conventional dynamic random-access memory (DRAM) would rise by 10-15 percent in the October-December quarter of 2026 compared with July-September.

The price of NAND flash, the technology used in SSDs, was forecast to increase by 15-20 percent over the same period.

The rising costs are already affecting computer sales in Bangladesh.

BCS President Zahirul said laptop and desktop sales volumes have fallen by around 20-25 percent over the past year, although the total value of sales has increased.

During the Covid-19 pandemic, movement restrictions, working from home and online classes triggered a sudden surge in demand for computers. The subsequent wave of pent-up purchases added to price pressures. The depreciation of the taka then dealt another blow to the IT business, followed by the latest disruption from the AI boom.

Industry insiders estimate that monthly laptop and desktop sales now stand at around just 20,000 units.

Global forecasts point to similar pressures. International Data Corporation (IDC), a technology research firm, forecast in June that worldwide PC shipments would fall by 11.3 percent in 2026, while average selling prices would rise by 18.3 percent.

IDC said the memory shortage is likely to persist until the end of 2027, with no meaningful relief expected before then.

HIGHER PRICES PUT COMPUTERS OUT OF REACH

Al Amin Mollah, a student at Independent University, Bangladesh, bought his laptop for Tk 60,000 three years ago. He now works part-time at an office in Uttara and recently decided to buy another laptop for his job, with his employer covering the cost.

A week ago, he visited Multiplan Centre, a computer market in Dhaka, to look for a laptop. But he was shocked by the prices. Retailers quoted Tk 90,000 for the same model he had bought three years earlier.

“It has become too expensive for me and exceeded the budget my office had. I returned home without buying it,” said Al Amin.

For businesses, rising computer prices mean higher cost for setting up offices, expanding operations and replacing ageing equipment.

Steel manufacturer Rahim Group, for example, had planned to buy a large quantity of computers and other IT equipment for a new office. But the conglomerate put the plan on hold after finding that IT costs had risen alongside borrowing costs.

“Due to the higher prices, we had to put our expansion plans on hold for now,” said Asaduzzaman Shawon, head of IT at the group.

Students are also feeling the impact, particularly those who need computers for university assignments, online learning, programming, research and professional training.

At BCS Computer City in IDB Bhaban, one of Bangladesh’s largest computer retail hubs, The Daily Star spoke to two customers on Tuesday. Both said laptop prices have become prohibitively high, making it difficult to find devices with the specifications they need within their budgets.

“It is very difficult to find a laptop with the configuration I need within my budget,” said Rayhan Ahmed, a Dhaka resident.

Bangladesh Computer Samity said import duties of 15-20 percent had previously applied to computer and laptop components. The government withdrew those duties entirely in the national budget for fiscal year 2026-27.

Without the tax cuts, prices would have been even higher.

Computer Samity President Zahirul said the government has done its part by cutting duties, but global supply constraints are likely to keep computer prices high at least until 2027.

title: History of Bangladesh’s coffee industry
text:
From coffee shrubs in the Chattogram Hill Tracts to espresso machines in Dhaka, two very different landscapes frame the same story. A nation historically defined by tea leaves is now, quietly and unevenly, building a coffee identity of its own. That story reaches back well beyond the cafés that have made coffee a familiar part of urban life.

Colonial roots and early beginnings

Coffee’s presence in this land is older than most of us assume. Chattogram had coffee gardens in the nineteenth century. In an archival account published in The Business Standard, researcher Haroon Rashid traced references to coffee plants as far back as 1786, although their origins remained uncertain. An old map places one coffee garden near the present-day Chittagong Medical College and War Cemetery, a reminder of how thoroughly that earlier landscape has changed.

In 1843, a proposal for the Chittagong Joint Stock Coffee Company reached colonial authorities before a proposal for tea plantations that year. Local merchant Sheikh Obaidullah was also cultivating coffee, sending samples to Calcutta for assessment.

Coffee’s prospects eventually faded amid competing interest in tea, staffing shortages and disputes over land. Its later cultivation in the hills belongs to a separate chapter: farmers brought seeds and saplings from Mizoram, with coffee reportedly being grown in Lama, Bandarban, from the 1950s.

The experimentation

Decades later, the state’s interest grew. Government attention increased during the 1990s, followed by organised cultivation at the Khagrachhari Agricultural Research Station in 2001. Arabica and Robusta found a foothold in the hills, with Bandarban, Khagrachhari and Rangamati becoming the main producing districts. Some growers now plant coffee beneath mango trees, adding a crop within an existing orchard.

Since then, cultivation has expanded beyond the hills. In 2021, the government launched a Tk 211 crore research, development and extension project covering both cashew nuts and coffee. Sapling distribution and training helped growers move from scattered experiments towards more organised cultivation.

Coffee enters Bangladesh society

While farmers were experimenting with cultivation, many consumers found coffee through another door: the tin and the packet.

Imported instant coffee offered a convenient introduction. Prothom Alo’s account of the market dates Nestlé’s formal coffee marketing in Bangladesh to 1998, distinct from the company’s wider commercial operations beginning in 1994.

Nescafé became a familiar name, while subsequent entrants widened the choice. PRAN-RFL entered the coffee business in 2013, and Abul Khair Group’s AMA Coffee later joined the instant segment. Small sachets offered an alternative to buying a jar, while premixes simplified preparation.

Vending machines and kiosks provided another route into daily routines. Nestlé’s offerings cover offices and food outlets, with kiosks aimed at universities, hospitals and transport hubs. Coffee could fit into a working day or a journey, as well as an evening out.

The café years

Coffee was also becoming a destination, something people went out for. Café Mango opened in Dhanmondi in November 2000, offering a place to linger over a drink and conversation. Coffee World followed with a Banani outlet in 2005, bringing an international chain into the developing market. The appeal extended beyond the beverage. In The Daily Star’s 2004 account of Café Mango, its founder described a space for reading, meeting people and spending time together. The social life around a cup was already taking shape.

Rick and Chris Hubbard visited Bangladesh in 2001 and opened North End Coffee Roasters in Shahjadpur in 2011. What started with small batches of freshly roasted coffee attracted expatriates and, increasingly, local customers.

The café was only part of the business. Roasting and supplying beans to other establishments helped North End’s influence travel beyond its own tables. Its sourcing of hill-grown coffee also linked the urban market with local producers.

Industry boom

The following years brought a wider market. Gloria Jean’s arrived in 2012, while Crimson Cup coffee reached Dhaka through Columbus Coffee Shop in 2015. Independent cafés and local roasters added their own approaches. East Bengal Coffee Roasters, for example, has introduced a Bandarban Blend.

Urbanisation, changing tastes, social media and the appeal of cafés as informal workplaces helped sustain demand. Students and young professionals brought coursework, meetings and laptops to café tables, making the surroundings part of what customers were paying for. Yet the opportunities came with expensive premises, imported inputs and a need for trained baristas.

The growth was visible in trade figures. Import data reported by Prothom Alo showed volumes rising from 264 tonnes in 2012 to 1,745 tonnes in 2022. That increase helps explain the interest from businesses, although imports alone cannot measure the value of café sales or the size of the speciality market.

Coffee’s history in Bangladesh reaches back well before the café boom, with references to plants in eighteenth-century Chattogram



Café Mango opened in 2000 and Coffee World in 2005, preceding North End’s arrival in 2011



Local growers need processing skills and reliable buyers to turn coffee cultivation into a dependable source of income

The business opportunity

The real opportunity is in the space between supply and appetite. For local growers, reaching that market involves more than planting coffee shrubs. Beans need careful handling, consistent processing and buyers willing to return for the next harvest.

Women producers offer one example of how those connections can work. In a 2021 account, Helen Keller Intl described the experience of Zing Pian Bawm of Bandarban’s Happy Hill Para. After training supported by Helen Keller and USAID, she developed her coffee-growing skills and went on to train dozens of neighbouring producers.

By 2020, she had nearly tripled her earlier annual income, with coffee becoming an additional source of earnings. The programme also introduced processing equipment and partnered with North End to connect growers with a market for their beans.

That relationship matters because farmers face a wait of several years before their first harvest, alongside gaps in processing facilities and access to buyers. The Daily Star’s recent reporting also identified changing weather and uneven quality as continuing challenges.

Looking ahead

Bangladesh’s coffee future will depend on how these different parts grow together. Local cultivation offers farmers another source of income, while roasting, distribution and hospitality can create value around both local and imported beans. Equipment suppliers and the people who install, maintain and repair coffee machines also belong to this expanding business, alongside cafés and roasters.

For the grower in the hills and the barista in Dhaka, the connection is becoming more tangible. A nation raised on tea is now finding room for a second cup.

title: El Nino rewrites the menu in the world's top restaurants
text:
A record-breaking El Nino will likely force the world's top chefs to rethink their menus ahead of droughts, floods and heatwaves upending global food systems.

Ants are disappearing from the table in Brazil, one Danish chef is opting for cocoa-free chocolate and Japan is serving up warm-water fish, culinary stars disclosed at the Apapaxoa gastronomic festival on Mexico's Caribbean coast.

United Nations experts have predicted an exceptionally strong cycle of the El Nino climate phenomenon, which causes global changes in winds and rainfall as well as erratic weather conditions.

The cream of the culinary crop, looking ahead to unpredictable ingredient availability, quality and prices, are rearranging their shelves accordingly.

But for these acclaimed chefs, extreme weather events and their habit of turning the kitchen upside down are nothing new.

"In the last three years, I've been creating an annual menu that I end up adjusting many times, almost weekly, because certain products aren't available," Brazilian chef Alex Atala told AFP.

"Ants, for example, this year are only available for customers who specifically ask to try them," said Atala, whose Sao Paulo restaurant D.O.M. plucks ingredients from the Amazonian wilderness to reinterpret Indigenous traditions.

El Nino can also massively disrupt transportation, said Atala.

Flooded roads or wildfires "delay a product that should be fresh, and by the time it arrives, it's no longer in good condition," he said.

'People just don't come anymore'

The renowned Brazilian chef also emphasized the "cultural loss" provoked by El Nino, referring to the disappearance of tradition along with the unavailable ingredient.

The climate crisis has wreaked havoc on the Mediterranean, says Spain's Quique Dacosta, whose restaurant in the port city of Denia sits near Valencia, which was pummelled by torrential rain in 2024.

Almost 250 people died, while vineyards, orange groves and plots used to grow Albufera rice, an essential paella ingredient, were decimated.

An event of such intensity "directly attacks the raw materials that are the natural foundation on which we build our cuisine," Dacosta told AFP.

Footfall also takes a hit, he said, noting that a stormy season has once again descended and fearful customers are canceling their reservations.

"It's going to rain a lot and people just don't come anymore -- imagine how vulnerable our businesses are," he said.

'First year without hurricanes'

While El Nino ramps up weather conditions in some parts, it produces a vacuum in others.

"This is the first year without hurricanes" in the Mexican Caribbean, said chef Roberto Solis.

While Hurricane Polo hurtles around the Pacific, there isn't a trace of the usual cyclones off Mexico's opposite coast, near Solis's native Yucatan.

"Hurricanes carry moisture and move ocean currents and plankton," he said, noting the consequences for seafood dishes at his restaurant Huniik, where he reimagines Mayan specialties.

Danish chef Rasmus Munk has a reputation for inventiveness and is calling on his peers to think about future food resilience.

His Copenhagen restaurant Alchemist is experimenting with chocolate alternatives because "the chocolate market is also under pressure," he said.

"The non-chocolate we're making now, we make it from BSG, which is the brewer's spent grains," he added.

The fibrous leftover from beer production also serves as a "local alternative," Munk said.

Rationing water

Japanese cooks are working with a brand-new selection of seafood, since El Nino has altered ocean migratory routes.

"In Japan it's not a problem, there's always product available," said Yusuke Takada, who combines Japanese ingredients with French cooking techniques in La Cime, Osaka.

But concern is the prevailing mood among the culinary greats gathered in Mexico.

El Nino "is changing everything," warned Dominique Crenn, a French-born chef in San Francisco, where Atelier Crenn uses its menu to stress the gravity of the situation to customers.

The weather pattern "hits Colombia very hard," echoed Alvaro Clavijo.

At Clavijo's Bogota-based El Chato, ingredients like cacao pulp and Andean tubers are already running low.

But the chef is most worried about water shortages, recalling a severe drought in 2024.

"Two years ago rationing already started to be felt, and that in a restaurant is super complicated," he said.

title: Retailers lose up to 30% of sales after early closures
text:
Closing shopping malls earlier to save electricity amid an energy shortage has wiped out up to 30 percent of retail sales, according to traders, who say customers are particularly used to buying footwear and fashion items after finishing work in the afternoon.

In August, the authorities instructed shops, markets and shopping malls across the country to close by 8 pm, bringing the deadline forward from 10 pm.

The shorter shopping hours came at a time when retailers were already dealing with prolonged inflationary pressure, which had weakened people’s purchasing power and hit sales.

Yet businesses still have to pay the same, if not more, for shop rents, staff salaries and other operating costs, putting further pressure on already shrinking profit margins.

“Sales have fallen over the past month, putting significant pressure on cash flows,” said Khalid Mahmood Khan, co-founder and managing director of Kay Kraft, a popular fashion retailer.

Khalid said people in Bangladesh generally feel more comfortable shopping after sunset, especially during hot weather. Reducing shopping hours is disrupting a long-established lifestyle pattern.

He estimated that sales in the fashion and lifestyle sector have fallen by around 25 percent to 30 percent over the past month because of the combined impact of inflation and reduced shopping hours.

“Costs have increased, but revenue has declined. Salaries and shop rents, however, have not come down,” he said.

In April, the government initially ordered shops, markets and shopping malls to close by 6 pm as part of energy-saving measures. The deadline was later relaxed to 7 pm following pressure from business groups and temporarily extended to 10 pm during Eid-ul-Azha.

It was then restored to 7 pm before being extended to 9 pm from June 11. The latest order cut the closing time to 8 pm.

According to businesses, the repeated changes to operating hours have made it harder for retailers to plan sales and staffing.

EVENING SALES TAKE A HIT

The impact has been particularly pronounced for retailers whose sales peak in the evening.

Apex Footwear, one of the country’s major footwear brands, says about 60 percent of its domestic sales normally take place after 8 pm.

Firoze Mohammad, chief executive officer of the company, said domestic business had fallen by 20 percent to 30 percent following the latest restriction on operating hours.

“Closing shops at 8 pm is having a very significant impact on our business,” he said.

Kazi Jamil Islam, managing director of Lotto Bangladesh, which operates 240 outlets, said the company’s sales fell by around 20 percent within a month of the latest restriction.

“Our major sales take place between 7 pm and 9 pm,” he said, adding that rents and other operating costs had remained unchanged despite the decline in sales.

International retail chain Mustafa Mart has also seen a sharp decline in business since the latest restriction.

BM Saleh Musa, manager (accounts and finance) at Mustafa Mart Pvt Ltd, said customers generally feel more comfortable shopping between 6 pm and 10 pm.

“Our revenue has declined by around 30 percent over the past month compared with the regular sales level of the previous month,” he said, adding that at one outlet, daily revenue fell from around Tk 3 lakh to Tk 70,000.

“Even after 8 pm, salesmen are compelled to turn away customers who want to make purchases,” Saleh said.

Local retail chain Daily Shopping, a concern of PRAN-RFL Group, also said it had seen an immediate impact from the restrictions.

“Customers are yet to get accustomed to completing their necessary shopping by 8 pm. As a result, we have seen an immediate impact on sales and revenue earning,” said Heron Mahmud, manager of an outlet of the retail chain in Uttara.

At Transcom Electronics Ltd, sales at its Gausul Azam Avenue outlet in Uttara have fallen by around 10 percent since the closing time was reduced, said Md Shorif Sarker, branch operation head.

“If our average daily sales were Tk 4 lakh, a 10 percent decline means Tk 40,000 less in sales. We are now doing around Tk 3 lakh to Tk 3.5 lakh a day,” Shorif said.

The outlet previously remained open until after 10 pm.

COSTS KEEP RISING

The shorter selling window comes as retailers are already dealing with weaker purchasing power and higher operating costs.

Footwear retailers are also facing higher prices for petrochemical-based inputs, which have reduced margins.

“Our business is a mix of exports and the local market. The export business generates only a small manufacturing margin,” said Apex’s Firoze.

Apex has absorbed much of the increase in input costs rather than passing the full increase on to customers, he said.

For smaller retailers, the combination of lower sales and unchanged fixed costs has become increasingly difficult to sustain.

Md Nasir Khan, vice-president of the Footwear and Leather Industries Association of Bangladesh and managing director of Five-R Footwear, said the company had permanently closed around 70 outlets amid weak demand, rising costs and the broader energy crisis.

“Running a business in the domestic market has become extremely difficult in Bangladesh,” he said.

NO EARLY RELIEF IN SIGHT

The government, however, says the 8 pm closing requirement is unlikely to be relaxed while the power supply remains inadequate.

“Currently, we still have loadshedding and the supply is not enough. Unless the situation improves, we cannot consider that,” said Muhammad Arif Sadeq, public relations officer of the Ministry of Power, Energy and Mineral Resources.

Power Grid Bangladesh PLC data show that the power shortage remains significant during the evening. At 9 pm on September 14, during the evening peak, power demand stood at 17,348MW while supply stood at 15,435MW, leaving a deficit of 1,913MW.

When asked if there was a possibility of the restrictions being lifted during winter, when energy consumption typically falls, he said it would have to be seen.

“We will reconsider if the situation improves,” he reiterated.

title: World's water cycle becoming more unpredictable, UN warns
text:
The planet's water cycle is becoming increasingly erratic, swinging between too little and too much, the United Nations warned Thursday, with an unprecedented El Nino expected to exacerbate the long-term trend.

Last year was among the driest for the world's rivers in over three decades, the UN's World Meteorological Organization said in a report.

In 2025 -- one of the warmest years on record -- glaciers also shrank across all regions, even as groundwater levels in many parts of the world are in multi-year decline, it found.

Overall, the WMO's annual State of Global Water Resources report showed that the Earth's freshwater storage -- the total amount of water stored in groundwater, lakes and rivers, soil moisture, vegetation and ice and snow -- continued a decade-long decline.

Some elements of the water cycle change rapidly -- like precipitation, river flow and soil moisture, responding to weather within days or weeks.

WMO Secretary-General Celeste Saulo voiced particular concern about the decline in "slow reserves", like groundwater and glaciers, which she said had traditionally served as the planet's "savings account".

They have served as "a buffer that absorbs bad years so that a single drought or a single dry season does not translate directly into a water crisis", she told reporters.

'Spending our reserves'

Now, "we are depleting that savings account", she warned. "We are spending our reserves."

Glaciers have also been shrinking at a precipitous rate, with 2025 marking the fourth consecutive year where they shed significant ice mass across all regions.

Between 2023 and 2025, the report estimated that glaciers lost a cumulative global glacier mass of 1,400 gigatonnes of water -- roughly equal to the water required to fill 560 million Olympic-sized swimming pools, or about a third of the world's annual freshwater withdrawals.

"Groundwater tells a similar story: nearly two-thirds of monitored wells worldwide showed conditions outside the historical norm in 2025," Saulo said.

She highlighted that this was happening in parallel with "more water-related disasters".

In particular, she pointed to the current El Nino pattern, which is expected to be the strongest since comparable records began four decades ago.

El Nino is the warm phase of a natural climate cycle that occurs every two to seven years and is characterised by above average ocean temperatures across the Pacific, and brings worldwide changes in winds and rainfall patterns and erratic weather.

"The strengthening El Nino will increase the risk of drought in some areas, and flooding in others," Saulo cautioned.

'Abnormal'

Already before El Nino hit, rivers worldwide were showing "abnormal" flows, WMO said, with 2025 among the three driest years for rivers in 35 years.

For a seventh year in a row, the number of river basins globally experiencing "normal" conditions were in a clear minority in 2025.

Only around 36 percent saw normal flows, while an equal percentage saw below-normal discharge conditions and 21 percent were above normal, the report found.

The WMO stressed the importance of good data to map the developments in the water cycle, warning that significants gaps remained in hard-hit areas.

"Weather respects no borders, and this is especially true for water," Saulo said, arguing for the importance of "shared data, shared standards and shared early warnings".

"A river basin is fed by water upstream, often in another country," she pointed out.

And "a glacier disaster in one country can lead to devastation in another as we saw with the recent tragedy of China and Nepal".

title: CAAB issues Air Navigation Order ahead of int’l audit
text:
Bangladesh has issued its first dedicated Air Navigation Order (ANO) on aviation security as the country moves to strengthen its civil aviation rules ahead of an International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO) audit next month.

The audit is scheduled to begin on October 26, and the dedicated aviation security ANO is one of the major issues auditors will examine, said Air Commodore Md Asif Iqbal, member (security) of the Civil Aviation Authority of Bangladesh (CAAB).

“If I cannot answer that question, I lose marks, and that affects the overall grading,” he told The Daily Star.

The ANO is a legal instrument issued by CAAB under the Civil Aviation Act, 2017, that sets out binding rules and procedures for a specific area of aviation operations. Violations of the order will be treated as offences punishable under the Act.

The security-specific ANO was gazetted on September 3 and came into force the same day. It sets out security responsibilities for airports, aircraft operators, passengers and other stakeholders and gives effect to standards and recommended practices.

The order does not, however, bring major changes to security measures already being followed.

Asif said the National Civil Aviation Security Programme (NCASP) contains detailed security requirements but cannot be made public because it includes sensitive information.

The ANO, he said, is essentially a generalised, publicly available version of the NCASP with classified information removed. “It’s not new.”

Group Captain SM Ragib Samad, executive director of Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport, also said no new passenger screening measures had been introduced following the issuance of the order.

“We are following the existing protocols,” he said.

Screening before entry into airside or security-restricted areas, for instance, was already in practice, he said, but had previously existed through other instructions rather than in the form of a navigation order. “This has basically given it a legal basis through the ANO.”

The order brings together a wide range of requirements concerning passengers, airport staff, baggage, aircraft and cargo.

It classifies disruptive passenger behaviour into four levels, ranging from suspicious or verbally threatening behaviour to an attempted or actual breach of the flight crew compartment.

Under the order, airlines may halt check-in or deny boarding over a passenger’s condition or behaviour. If boarding is denied at the gate, hold baggage should be offloaded, the passenger escorted to the landside area, and their name removed from the flight manifest.

Serious cases may be referred to law enforcement.

The ANO also says liquids, aerosols and gels must be carried in containers not exceeding 100ml each and placed in a transparent, resealable plastic bag with a maximum capacity of 1 litre. Containers larger than 100ml will not be accepted even if only partly filled.

Passengers who refuse security searches or do not allow their cabin and hold baggage to be screened or searched will not be allowed to board.

The order also requires background checks for people implementing security controls, those with unescorted access to security-restricted areas and those with access to sensitive aviation security information. The Special Branch of Bangladesh Police is responsible for conducting the checks.

Asif acknowledged that CAAB still faces shortages of manpower and some security equipment.

“We have some human-resource shortages. Our recruitment process is ongoing,” he said.

He said the Armed Police Battalion had been given responsibility for landside security while recruitment continued. Once CAAB reaches its full staffing strength, it plans to take over those responsibilities itself.

There are also equipment shortages, although procurement is under way, he said.

CAAB recently received 25 explosive trace detectors from China, while dual-view baggage screening machines have also been procured. The authority has recently added four body scanners, Asif said.

He described improvements in manpower, equipment, infrastructure and facilities as a continuous process.

“Even if you reach 100 percent today, tomorrow you may see a new requirement,” he said.

More sophisticated and modern equipment will be available once the third terminal becomes operational, he added.

The publication of the ANO comes as the government moves to replace the Civil Aviation Rules, 1984, which have remained in force for more than four decades.

The new rules are intended to bring the country’s civil aviation regulatory framework in line with international standards and address shortcomings identified in previous assessments.

The upcoming ICAO audit will assess Bangladesh’s compliance with international standards and recommended practices, with the findings affecting the country’s overall audit grading.

title: Karnaphuli EPZ: From a defunct steel mill to an export hub
text:
Safety shoes made by Bangladeshi workers in Chattogram are being used by workers in the oil and gas extraction and pipeline industries in the United States, miners in China and mountaineers in Europe.

The shoes are produced by Xin Chang Shoes (BD) Limited, a Taiwanese company that has been operating in the Karnaphuli Export Processing Zone (EPZ) since 2010.

Xin Chang runs two units in the EPZ, employing around 6,000 workers and staff and producing 4.2 million pairs of safety shoes a year.

“Last fiscal year, our export volume stood at over $100 million,” the company’s operations manager Tony Hsieh said yesterday.

According to him, 60 percent of the company’s products go to the US market, 30 percent to the EU and 10 percent to Asian markets.

The plant has nine production lines and plans to add four more over the next three years, he added.

The zone was inaugurated on September 12, 2006, and is operated by the Bangladesh Export Processing Zones Authority (BEPZA).
