title: Dhaka built flyovers and a metro, but forgot the bus
text:
More than a decade ago, four of us at Bangladesh University of Engineering and Technology (Buet) wrote a paper titled “Bus Rapid Transit (BRT): What is it and Why Do We Need it for Dhaka.” The argument was not complicated. Dhaka had over 1.5 crore people making about 2.1 crore trips a day. Buses were only 9.7 percent of the vehicles on the road but carried 77 percent of public transport users. More than 5,500 buses and minibuses were run by a crowd of small companies with no schedule at all. The low-income group, 48 percent of the population, made 73 percent of walking trips and 41 percent of transit trips. Fix the bus, we said, and you fix the city for the people who need it most.

Look at where we are now. We could not even restructure bus operations. We could not make the government see what the industry should look like, or accept that it needs public money to get there. We built flyovers, an expressway, and a metro, while ordinary people, the urban poor, above all, are still stuck in traffic.

Where the money went

MRT Line-6 cost Tk 33,472 crore. On September 16, Ecnec approved three more metro lines with a combined cost of nearly Tk 2.5 lakh crore. Construction cost of the Dhaka Elevated Expressway alone was estimated at Tk 8,940 crore. The bus, meanwhile, has received pilot projects and press conferences, and the contrast is not presented here as an argument against the metro. In fact, Line-6 carried a record 499,756 passengers on September 10, 2026, and it is a good service. But it is one corridor, and its fare of Tk 5 per km is about double the bus rate. Prothom Alo reported last month that an end-to-end metro trip costs Tk 90, against a government bus fare of about Tk 50 for the same distance, and that poor people are rarely seen on the trains.

The report also stated that ticket revenue was around Tk 400 crore last fiscal year, against loan instalments of between Tk 465 crore and Tk 740 crore a year from 2025 to 2031. If the state is willing to carry that gap for a line used mostly by the middle and upper-middle class, it cannot claim that supporting buses is unaffordable. Congestion is the bill we already pay. Buet’s Accident Research Institute (ARI) put the annual loss at Tk 37,000 crore in 2018 and about Tk 56,000 crore in 2020. The World Bank found average speeds had fallen from 21 km/h to under 7 km/h in a decade. In 2018, the institute’s then director, Prof Dr Moazzem Hossain, argued that a Tk 1,000 crore subsidy in the transport sector could return Tk 5,000 crore. Nobody took up the offer.

The BRT that never was

Critics would say, pointing to the Gazipur–Airport BRT, that attempts have been made to improve bus transit, but failed. ECNEC approved the project in December 2012 at Tk 2,040 crore. Revisions pushed the cost to Tk 4,268 crore, and The Daily Star reports that around Tk 2,800 crore of that has already been spent. Ecnec sent back a fourth revision of Tk 6,598 crore. A Buet review this year (2026) recommended dropping BRT operations altogether and turning the lanes into a tolled road. Not one dedicated bus was bought. Before even operating for a single day, the project was scrapped.

That is a failure of planning and execution, not of buses. A 20 km stub that ends at the airport, never connected to the city and never given an operator, was never going to work. In 2006, when Bogotá launched its BRT system TransMilenio, the number of buses on its busiest link was reduced from 650 to about 270 an hour and yet speed increased from 18 to 26 km/h, because the system ran as a network with one operating logic. Guangzhou’s BRT raised bus speeds by 29 percent. Converting our corridor into a toll road for cars would turn a bad project into a permanent loss for bus users, or rather for all public transport users.

An industry built to race

Only 98 of Dhaka’s 418 approved bus routes are operational, served by more than 7,000 buses. Most crews work on daily deposit, the “chukti” or “zoma” system. The owner is paid a fixed sum each day, and the crew keeps only what is left after fuel and roadside payments. So, they race, block the road, and stop wherever a passenger waves. The owners’ association promised in 2019 to end daily contracts. It did not. Transparency International Bangladesh (TIB) estimated in March 2024 that Tk 1,059.37 crore is extorted from private buses each year, a figure TIB itself called “very conservative”, and found politicians involved in managing about 92 percent of the largest bus companies. After August 2024, the faces at the top of the owners’ association changed. The system did not.

This is why Dhaka Nagar Paribahan stalled. It started on December 26, 2021, with 50 buses on the Ghatarchar–Kanchpur route, but private operators did not join, and in February 2025 it was relaunched on a single route because owners resisted. We asked owners to give up daily cash for a franchise with no guaranteed income. No sensible operator accepts that deal.

What must happen now

The prime minister ordered one designated company per route: franchises for 32 routes finalised within two months, and the full system running within six months. We welcome it. Here is how we can make this attempt different.

First, use gross-cost contracts. Pay operators a fixed rate per km for running scheduled services to a set standard, and send fare revenue to a public account. When income stops depending on how many passengers a driver grabs, the race ends. Second, make salaried crews a condition of every franchise. Third, fund the gap. Since the publication of our paper, the city fare has followed diesel from Tk 2.45 per km down to Tk 2.42, then up to Tk 2.53 and now Tk 2.70. Every rise hammers the poorest riders. The World Bank’s $290 million Clean Air Project already plans 400 electric buses under gross-cost contracts, but unfortunately the procurement has slipped. This needs to be approved, because it will change the shape of the bus sector and the look of the buses in Dhaka.

Other countries treat bus subsidy as normal. Jakarta has kept the Transjakarta fare at 3,500 Indonesian rupiah since 2005, and the city pays about 9,700 Indonesian rupiah per passenger on top. India’s PM e-Bus Sewa scheme puts 10,000 electric buses on gross-cost contracts, backed by a 3,435 crore Indian rupees fund that guarantees operators are paid even if a city defaults. In addition to similar subsidy models, the draft Route Franchise Act should be finalised and approved, buses should get priority lanes, and the routes should be enforced.

A city of over two crore people, a great many of whom are urban poor, cannot move on metros and flyovers alone. It moves on buses, and it needs them badly. The people standing at Mohakhali in the rain do not write columns or sit on committees, and the bus is the only service the state offers them. Somebody has to make the case for it. A chance like this does not come around twice, and if we let this one go, we will be writing the same article in 2040.

Dhrubo Alam is deputy transport planner at Dhaka Transport Coordination Authority.

title: Crossfire must never return
text:
The police chief’s recent remark about using “crossfire” “if (the) government allows it” is not only alarming but also raises the question of whether any real change has taken place within our disciplined forces since the July uprising. One of the core issues that drove the uprising was extrajudicial killings, which had almost become a norm during the Awami League regime. We spent months forming commissions and drawing up reform proposals so that all the human rights violations that the country saw during the 15-plus years of Sheikh Hasina’s tyrannical rule would never occur again. And yet, a little over two years on, the person who heads the force primarily responsible for citizens’ protection is using the term “crossfire” most irresponsibly and unconstitutionally. Shouldn’t this make us concerned that police are still playing by the old partisan book, whereby they stand ready to carry out any unlawful and unconstitutional act that the party in power may demand?

Since 2004, when the Rapid Action Battalion was created, the term “crossfire” has been used in Bangladesh to mean alleged extrajudicial killing. An analysis published by The Business Standard, based on data compiled by Ain O Salish Kendra (ASK), shows that 2,957 people were killed in crossfires involving law enforcement agencies between 2004 and September 2026, of which police were involved in 1,371 cases. How, then, could the IGP not know about the gravity of the term? And as a law enforcer, he surely has read our constitution, Articles 31 and 32 of which clearly states a person’s right to life and protection under the law. Not even the country’s government has the right to take away a person’s life without proper judicial process—a point clarified by the Prime Minister’s Adviser on Information and Cultural Affairs Zahed Ur Rahman.

What makes the remark more troubling is that the police don’t have a fully clean book even under the current administration. Per ASK data, 10 custodial deaths occurred in the country between March and September 2026. While not all custodial deaths occur from torture, and data on human rights violations vary across organisations because of differences in their methodologies, unlawful excesses by police or their inaction favouring ruling party activities have made the headlines several times. Moreover, the police chief’s comment appears more concerning when it is read in the context of the questionable amendments made to the National Human Rights Commission (NHRC) Act, 2026 and the Enforced Disappearance Prevention and Redress Act, 2026, which stripped the NHRC of its power to probe human rights abuse by members of law enforcement agencies.

We second the opposition’s and rights bodies’ call for accountability and withdrawal of the remark. The colonial and partisan mindset of our police and other security forces must change. To achieve this, comprehensive reforms, an independent commission, and a modern, updated law governing the ethics and conduct of law enforcement personnel are essential.

title: Profits must not trump conservation
text:
The government’s decision to ease tourism restrictions at St Martin’s Island, rolling back some of the stricter measures introduced earlier, raises questions about its commitment to environmental protection. From November 1, the island will be open to tourists until March 15, with the daily visitor limit increased from 2,000 to 3,500. Previously, the tourism season on the island ran from November 1 till January 31. While the decision has understandably been welcomed by tourism businesses and residents, we must ask: what evidence of ecological recovery justifies increasing the daily visitor limit by 75 percent and extending the tourism season? Has any credible assessment established that this ecologically critical area can withstand the additional pressure?

These questions are especially relevant given reports of continued resort construction and environmental degradation on the island. Although the authorities have retained restrictions on overnight stays, noise, beach lighting, and activities harmful to biodiversity, their possibility of enforcement remains a concern. The introduction of a Tk 100 environmental conservation fee is a good move, but how will the money be spent, and who will ensure compliance with the restrictions?

St Martin’s predicament reflects a much wider and persistent pattern in which commercial interests repeatedly trump environmental considerations. In Bandarban, resorts operating under the banner of ecotourism have reportedly cleared forests, cut hills, and obstructed natural streams. Similar developments are unfolding around the Sundarbans, where reports indicate that 21 resorts and cottages have emerged in its ecologically critical surroundings, many without environmental clearance or registration. Another 10 are reportedly in the pipeline.

The threats extend well beyond tourism. The government is reportedly considering locations near or within the Sundarbans, including Akram Point, for LNG terminals despite serious concerns raised by forest officials about potential damage to mangroves, dolphins and other wildlife. In Gazipur, the city corporation reportedly proceeded with constructing a waste transfer station inside Bhawal National Park despite objections from the Department of Forest and without environmental clearance. In Patuakhali’s Rangabali, hundreds of trees have been felled in a reserved forest following a land lease granted by the district administration.

Together, these developments indicate a troubling disregard for environmental safeguards, sometimes by the authorities themselves. It is particularly disappointing that the current government, from which a stronger environmental stewardship was expected, appears to be falling short. Development that destroys forests, biodiversity and fragile ecosystems is ultimately self-defeating. The government must explain the scientific basis for relaxing tourism restrictions at St Martin’s Island as well as why it is allowing the other developments. It must ensure strict enforcement of conservation laws and reconsider projects that threaten protected areas.

title: Why risk relaxing environmental safeguards in shipbreaking?
text:
The government’s recent decision to downgrade shipbreaking yards from “red” to “orange” category, potentially easing the environmental assessment requirements, is a dangerous move that may backfire. In fact, we fail to see how this move could be justified when recent incidents raised the need for stricter safeguards. In an industry widely known for being occupationally and environmentally hazardous, risking workers’ safety and known environmental damage is indeed baffling.

The stakes are quite clear. Even with the existing safeguards, at least 150 workers have been killed and 264 injured in shipbreaking accidents in Chattogram’s Sitakunda—where most of the country’s shipbreaking yards are located—between 2015 and 2026 (till October), according to records maintained by the Bangladesh Institute of Labour Studies (BILS). In August this year, 10 workers died from toxic gas exposure while dismantling a scrapped ship at Ferdous Steel Ship Recycling Yard. Ferdous Steel was one of the 23 “green” yards, which means it had checked all the safety boxes on paper. However, safety deficiencies were identified during an inspection six months before the accident. Ferdous Steel was also flagged by the authorities for repeatedly flouting labour law. If even certification cannot guarantee basic safety, the government should be strengthening monitoring rather than relaxing scrutiny.

Under the Environment Conservation Rules 2023, shipbreaking activities and yards fall under the red category because of their potential impacts on the environment and human health. The existing approval process includes an environmental impact assessment (EIA), public consultation, and scrutiny by the Department of Environment. Reclassifying the industry may make the EIA discretionary rather than obligatory, depriving regulators and the affected communities of a crucial means of assessing risks. Industry representatives argue that environmental clearance takes around 90 days and imposes financial costs. These concerns certainly deserve attention, but the solution is making approvals faster and more transparent, not lowering safety standards. Moreover, a decision affecting coastal ecosystems, public health and workers’ safety should not have been made without consulting the relevant experts.

Lowering safeguards to boost industrial growth and attract investment can never be a solution. Strict enforcement of the existing measures is essential, including regular independent inspections, adequate protective equipment, effective emergency response and meaningful penalties for violations. A competitive shipbreaking industry should be measured by its ability to protect the workers and the environment, not by the speed and volume of business it brings in.

title: Ramp up health worker recruitment
text:
Our healthcare system cannot provide quality services with inadequate healthcare workers to meet patients’ needs. Despite an increase in the number of doctors, nurses and midwives in recent years, the country remains far below the World Health Organisation’s recommended threshold. According to the latest health ministry data, the country had only 15.16 doctors, nurses and midwives per 10,000 people in 2025, against the WHO benchmark of 44.5. At the current pace of training and recruitment, this density is projected to reach 31.77 by 2030, leaving a substantial gap. To match the country’s growing healthcare needs, the government therefore needs a comprehensive workforce plan.

While the recommended ratio is one doctor to three nurses and midwives and five allied health professionals, including laboratory and imaging technologists, our hospitals have fewer than one nurse or midwife for every doctor and fewer than two allied health workers. Successive governments have often emphasised recruiting doctors without giving equal attention to nurses and other essential professionals. In our public hospitals, wards designed for around 24 patients sometimes accommodate 48 or more, while doctors at upazila health complexes may have to see 100-150 outpatients a day, leaving them barely a few minutes for each consultation. Specialist services are similarly overstretched, with patients waiting months for appointments and some specialists attending to hundreds of patients a day. Such conditions are hardly conducive to proper diagnosis, treatment and follow-up care. They also place an unreasonable burden on existing health workers.

The growing disease burden makes these gaps even more concerning. Non-communicable diseases require regular monitoring and long-term treatment, while maternal and child healthcare needs remain high. The country must also address communicable diseases such as measles and tuberculosis, as well as recurring dengue outbreaks that put additional pressure on hospitals. Without sufficient health workers, these multiple healthcare needs will continue to overwhelm facilities and limit access to timely treatment, particularly for people in rural areas who have fewer alternatives to public healthcare.

However, the government’s acknowledgement of the shortage and announcement of plans to create around one lakh additional posts for health workers is positive. It has decided to recruit 5,000 doctors, while proposals to create 15,000 nursing posts and recruit around 25,000 midwives over the coming years are under consideration or in progress. These initiatives must translate into actual appointments within clear timelines. The authorities must also expand training capacity, improve working conditions and ensure health workers are supported well enough to remain in public service.

Workforce planning must also guide the government’s recent decisions on hospital expansion. The government’s plan to expand upazila health complexes to 151 beds each cannot succeed without adequate doctors, nurses, medical technologists, equipment, space and operating budgets. In primary healthcare, properly staffed facilities can provide preventive care and early treatment, reducing the need for hospital admission. In other words, we need a balanced, adequately staffed workforce capable of meeting patients’ needs at every level of care.

title: Ensure transparency in BR online ticketing
text:
The allegations against Shohoz-Synesis-Vincen JV—the online ticketing contractor for Bangladesh Railway (BR) since 2022—of using bots to “secure” train tickets as soon as online sales opened and reselling them at higher prices are deeply disconcerting. Reportedly, the state rail authority sought an explanation from the company regarding these allegations, which Shohoz has already submitted and is currently being examined, alongside the possibility of Shohoz’s involvement in ticket black marketing. As the company’s five-year contract with BR is nearing its end in January 2027, the railway is taking over administrative controls at some stations and preparing to invite tenders for a new ticketing agency.

It has been alleged that bots operating through an unauthorised website are holding large numbers of tickets for resale at inflated prices, putting into question Shohoz’s fulfilment of its contractual security obligations. BR’s own audit has flagged security weaknesses, identified around 169 suspicious administrator accounts, and found that the administrator dashboard allowed tickets to be held several days before sales opened. The audit suspects black marketing of train tickets via collusion between Shohoz representatives and railway booking assistants using administrator accounts operated by the contracted company’s employees. According to our report, an audit covering fiscal years 2021-2026 alleged a shortfall in deposits to the government treasury against revenue from online ticket sales, citing a staggering Tk 1.4 crore in fines that had not been recovered from Shohoz. Besides these major issues, the contractor had previously been warned and fined several times over slow servers, outages, and other system flaws. These fines were recovered from payments BR owed to Shohoz.

It should be noted that Shohoz’s role as a contractor for the national railway has seen controversies in the past as well. In its first year after being appointed, Shohoz was fined at least twice, for Tk 4.15 lakh in total, by the Directorate of National Consumer Rights Protection (DNCRP) over allegations of mismanagement in selling tickets. Both times, Shohoz’s writ petitions to the High Court succeeded in having the fines suspended. We hope the recent audit will finally lead to accountability.

The allegations discovered from the railway authority’s audits must be investigated thoroughly. Both Shohoz as well as any colluders within BR must be held to account for obstructing the right of citizens to proper train ticketing services. Any security issues within the online system itself must be resolved. Sending out a tender for a new contractor come 2027 must not translate to any offenders being allowed to slip through without accountability.

title: Crop insurance needs a clear plan before it can take off
text:
On March 18, Agriculture Minister Amin Ur Rashid said at a rice distribution event in Cumilla that farmers whose crops are lost to floods or other disasters will be compensated through insurance. On May 8, State Minister for Power, Energy and Mineral Resources Aninda Islam Amit reiterated the pledge while inaugurating the government’s Boro paddy procurement drive for the current season. The Farmers Card, which lists agricultural insurance among its 10 promised benefits, is supposed to carry this insurance.

There is no information yet on who will pay the premium, what will trigger a payout, who will sell the policy, or who will regulate it. That the second announcement came from a power minister at a paddy procurement event suggests that no ministry has claimed the design. But these decisions will determine whether the scheme survives or not, and Bangladesh already has a case showing how it could go wrong.

The state-owned Sadharan Bima Corporation (SBC) ran a crop insurance scheme from 1977 to 1995. It insured 18,782 farmers in all and claims averaged 508 percent of premiums a year. Premium rates were capped at 3 to 5 percent, below what the risk required, and the scheme had no government subsidy and no reinsurance. SBC carried the losses itself and suspended the scheme in 1995. Weak demand played a part, but design may be the bigger cause since a product priced below cost would have struggled even with willing buyers.

The pilots since then show that delivery is possible. In 2014, SBC and the Asian Development Bank enrolled at least 9,641 policyholders in Rajshahi, Sirajganj, and Noakhali, backed by 20 weather stations and a 50-percent premium subsidy. Green Delta Insurance has gone further, as its weather-index programmes grew from 215 farmers in 2015 to 15.3 lakh in 35 districts by 2025, with about Tk 18.8 crore paid to 3,36,000 claimants.

If those numbers hold, delivery would no longer be a weak point. What is still missing is public backing, that is, a legal basis for index cover and premium support for farmers who cannot pay. Trust is a second gap, because a farmer who loses a crop while the index pays nothing is unlikely to renew.

The first question is about who pays. According to the Finance Division, revenue collection by the National Board of Revenue (NBR) was only 6.78 percent of GDP, while expenditure stood at 11.33 percent at the end of last year. India has shown how the bill grows, since its crop insurance scheme cost the government roughly 25,000 to 30,000 crore Indian rupees a year in 2022-24, or about $2.6 billion to $3.1 billion as per the current rate, and several states, including Bihar, Jharkhand, and West Bengal, have opted out of the scheme.

My view is that premium support should go to the poorest farmers only, with an end date and with the budget naming where the money comes from. The trigger decides whether farmers believe in the product or not. An index pays on rainfall or river levels, and what it records can differ from what happened in a farmer’s field.

The 2014 pilot relied on 20 weather stations across three districts. In a choice experiment on one coastal island, most farmers were averse to insurance, and those who did choose cover preferred physical verification of losses to an index. The study dates from 2017 and covers one island, so it is a warning, not a verdict. Farmers who distrust the trigger may not renew.

The study of the aforementioned ADB pilot found a higher uptake of crop insurance schemes by farmers where NGOs and microfinance institutions acted as intermediaries. At a roundtable held last year, SBC’s general manager said that regulators must clarify how microfinance institutions can legally distribute cover and be paid for it. The then chairman of the Insurance Development and Regulatory Authority (IDRA) offered one answer: a corporate agent model in which microfinance institutions and banks sell policies for a commission of up to 15 percent. Indeed, a generous commission would push premiums up and cancel part of any subsidy.

Of course, the law is yet to catch up. The same IDRA chairman said parametric cover falls outside the current indemnity-based insurance law and that the Insurance Act is being amended. Microfinance institutions answer to a different regulator, the Microcredit Regulatory Authority, so cover sold through them can fall between two rulebooks. The World Bank said in 2018 that the legal, regulatory and supervisory environment would need strengthening before any scheme. The government has not said whether its cover will be parametric. If it is, the amendment is what I would watch, because until it passes the scheme has no clear legal footing.

The obvious objection is cost. Reportedly, the agriculture ministry has shown reluctance regarding index cover, citing undue claims and existing subsidies. Waiving VAT on premiums has been proposed since 2022. Green Delta says dropping the 15 percent tax could widen cover, and a UNDP official said at the abovementioned roundtable it would cost revenue. These are fair points, and they are reasons to name a payer. Donors cannot be the plan, since the then IDRA chairman advised after COP30 last year that Bangladesh should expect to rely on its own resources. The recent pledge suggests the ministry’s view has shifted, and it should say so.

The Ministry of Agriculture should publish a design note that answers the four questions by December 15, before Boro planting gathers pace. The Finance Division should show a premium-support line, with an end date, in the budget due in June 2027. Lastly, the IDRA should publish a timetable for the Insurance Act amendment by November 30. Without those answers, the pledge may only be a repetition of the 1977 venture, with better technology and the same arithmetic.

Swarupam Barua is an economics research professional working on climate finance, monitoring, evaluation and learning (MEL), and socioeconomic data analysis in Bangladesh.

title: Why Bangladesh needs legal literacy in its schools
text:
Imagine a college student whose phone has just been snatched. He asks a friend: “Does it cost money to file a GD at the police station?” He is enrolled in a bachelor’s programme and speaks good English, but he may not know that lodging a general diary (GD) is his right, not a favour. And the burden of his ignorance does not solely lie with him, but with an education system that has not covered the subject.

Every law student learns that ignorance of law is generally no excuse: ignorantia juris non excusat. The law applies to everyone, whether or not they have read it. This principle works best when citizens also have a reasonable opportunity to learn the law.

In Bangladesh, such knowledge is presumed but rarely taught. How many people can say which parts of the Constitution are the “Fundamental Principles of State Policy” and which are “Fundamental Rights”? The difference is important, as while the principles are not judicially enforceable, the rights can be enforced, including through the High Court Division’s writ jurisdiction under Article 102. Citizens who confuse the two may wait for a court to enforce what the Constitution does not make enforceable, or may not realise that they hold a right they could claim today.

Law students here typically begin with a foundational course on the legal system. They learn how courts are organised, where laws come from, and how a case begins. Most other students receive no comparable introduction, which is unfortunate because law is present in rented homes, employment contracts, land deeds, public services, and online conduct.

Scholars increasingly treat the ability to recognise and act on a legal problem as a component of justice itself. Research on legal aid in Bangladesh points to procedural hurdles and funding constraints. One consequence may be described as legal dependency: reliance on intermediaries even for basic questions, because the basics were never explained. This can expose people to unreliable advice and encourage informal remedies.

The aim here is not to train junior lawyers or to memorise sections of the Penal Code. I propose a school-level version of the law student’s foundation, introduced in stages across all streams and types of school. Primary pupils would learn fairness, responsibility, and trusted institutions through stories and classroom rules. Lower secondary students would study rights, duties, and lawful ways of settling disputes. In secondary and higher secondary, students would learn the Constitution’s structure, including the distinction between principles and rights; how to lodge a GD and how it differs from a First Information Report (FIR); how legal aid works; how to use the Right to Information Act 2009; when to call 999; and how a legal proceeding begins. Methods should be interactive: simulations, debates, and mock complaints, with ideas revisited at greater depth.

A study of 842 elementary schoolchildren found that a structured child-rights programme improved recognition of major rights. A recent field experiment found that young people who were informed of their entitlements to public services, and supported in claiming them, gained more self-efficacy and political knowledge than those who were only informed. Practice appears to strengthen learning.

Some caution is needed. A review of US civic education research found limited evidence of direct effects on voting, so how a subject is taught matters as much as whether it is taught. Experience with Street Law in Bangladesh and South Africa shows both promise and the need for institutional continuity.

The government has announced a new curriculum from 2028 for both primary and secondary levels, with learning outcomes for every grade and an exit profile at the end of Class Five. The proposed framework names civic education as a component, and in early October the education minister said more books could be added if needed.

Room in the framework is not yet a commitment. The language so far refers to civic responsibility and social awareness, and does not mention rights, the Constitution, or how to seek a remedy. Civic education that addresses only duties toward the state would be incomplete. Legal literacy need not mean heavy textbooks or more examinations, and its content can be factual and non-partisan.

A constitution defines the relationship between citizen and state. Article 21 makes it a citizen’s duty to observe the Constitution and the laws, while Articles 27 and 31 provide for equality before the law and its protection. Where citizens are expected to observe the law, it is reasonable that they also be informed of these protections. Four steps could be crucial to do so.

For example, legal literacy should be treated as an educational goal for everyone, not only for those in law schools. Age-specific learning outcomes should be added to the 2028 curriculum for every stream. Teachers must be trained and given shared lesson plans and case studies. The new curriculum needs to be piloted in a few districts first before national rollout, measuring whether students can identify a legal problem and find the right institution, not only recall facts. None of this replaces lawyers, courts, or legal aid. It helps citizens arrive at those institutions knowing what to ask.

Courts deliver justice, but understanding of it can begin earlier. A student may complete 12 years of schooling in Bangladesh without learning what the Constitution provides. If citizens are expected to claim their rights, they first need to know that those rights exist.

Thohedul Alam Nowel is a legal researcher at the Department of Law, Port City International University, Chattogram.

title: Patients' need, not political clout, should guide hospital expansion
text:
When patients are forced to lie on hospital floors for lack of beds, allocating public funds to hospitals should be guided by one principle: patients’ medical need, not political influence. Recent data on health facilities expansion shows that hospitals located in places linked to ministers and state ministers have received an overwhelming share of additional beds while other overcrowded hospitals remain neglected. Public healthcare is a national responsibility, not a political reward. No constituency should receive preferential treatment simply because its representative holds power.

According to a recent report in The Daily Star, between February 17 and September 22, 2026, the government added 2,879 beds in 19 public hospitals, including several medical college hospitals and two specialised hospitals. Of these, 2,688 beds, or approximately 93 percent, were allocated to hospitals in districts or constituencies associated with ministers and state ministers. Only 191 beds were approved for five hospitals outside these areas. Meanwhile, several hospitals experiencing severe pressure on their existing capacity received no comparable expansion.

These figures do not necessarily prove that political considerations determined every decision. Hospitals in politically influential constituencies also have genuine needs. However, such a concentration of investment demands a clear explanation, particularly when hospitals elsewhere face more severe overcrowding. The fundamental question is simple: are we expanding hospitals to serve patients, or allocating healthcare infrastructure according to political influence?

Our public hospitals are under enormous pressure. A shortage of hospital beds is a chronic problem. Healthcare professionals struggle with excessive workloads, while diagnostic facilities, essential medicines and functioning equipment remain inadequate in many facilities. Expanding hospital capacity is undoubtedly necessary, but where and how that capacity is expanded matter as much as the decision itself.

The concentration of hospital expansion in politically influential areas raises a more fundamental question about the roles and responsibilities of elected representatives. A Member of Parliament (MP) represents a particular constituency and is expected to raise its concerns and advocate for its development. A minister, however, holds a position in the national government and has responsibilities that extend beyond the constituency from which they were elected. So ministers are duty-bound to consider the needs of the entire country and ensure that public resources are allocated according to national priorities.

When ministers appear to prioritise hospitals in their own constituencies over facilities elsewhere with equally urgent or greater needs, it raises concerns about whether they are fulfilling their national responsibilities or continuing to act primarily as constituency representatives.

A minister must think and act as a minister, not merely as an MP. Public leadership requires looking beyond local interests and making decisions in the interests of the entire population. A minister’s responsibility is not to secure the largest possible share of public investment for their own constituency, but to ensure that resources reach the people and places where they can generate the greatest public benefit.

This distinction is particularly important in healthcare, where inequitable investment can have direct consequences for people’s lives. Citizens should not have to depend on the political influence of their representatives to access essential healthcare services.

In this connection, another fundamental misconception is that increasing the number of sanctioned beds automatically improves healthcare. A bed becomes useful only when supported by adequate doctors, nurses, medical technologists, support staff, medicines, diagnostic services, and functioning equipment. Constructing additional wards without these complementary resources may increase nominal capacity without improving actual service delivery.

Hospital expansion must, therefore, be based on a comprehensive assessment of existing capacity and future demand. Bangladesh urgently needs a transparent, evidence-based mechanism for prioritising healthcare investment.

First, the government should establish standard criteria for assessing hospital expansion proposals. These should include bed occupancy rates, inpatient, and outpatient volumes, population projections, disease burden, travel time to appropriate facilities, referral patterns, and workforce availability.

Second, every major proposal should undergo an assessment of both capital and recurrent costs. The government must consider not only construction expenditure but also the long-term costs of staffing, medicines procurement, equipment, utilities, and maintenance.

Third, the rationale for approving major projects should be publicly disclosed. Citizens should understand why one hospital receives priority over another and what evidence supports the decision. Where a less overcrowded hospital is prioritised over a more congested facility, the government should explain the reasons.

Fourth, an independent technical body should review major expansion proposals before approval. Periodic evaluations should establish whether investments have reduced overcrowding, improved service availability, and generated better health outcomes.

Finally, equity must be an explicit consideration. Remote, disadvantaged, and historically underserved communities may require additional investment even when their hospitals report lower occupancy rates, because geographical barriers and limited access can suppress demand. Investment decisions must balance efficiency with fairness.

These measures would not prevent ministers and MPs from identifying and advocating for local healthcare needs. Rather, they would ensure that every proposal is assessed against the same transparent criteria, regardless of the political importance of the constituency concerned.

The challenge facing Bangladesh is not simply a shortage of hospital beds. It is also the need to allocate scarce public resources efficiently, fairly and transparently. When investment decisions appear to favour locations connected to influential politicians from the ruling party, public confidence suffers, while underserved communities continue to face overcrowding, delayed treatment and unnecessary travel.

Ultimately, the success of health policy should not be measured by the number of beds approved or hospital buildings constructed. It should be measured by whether people receive timely, affordable and quality healthcare, regardless of where they live or whom they elect. In a fair health system, the urgency of patients’ needs, not political power, must determine the priority for public investment.

Dr Syed Abdul Hamid is professor at the Institute of Health Economics of the University of Dhaka, and convener of Alliance for Health Reforms Bangladesh.

title: The 'time tax' we have to pay every day
text:
When a citizen visits a government office to obtain a simple service, the direct fee may be small, but the person may lose half a day in the process. The opportunity cost of time is not readily discernible. But the time lost still has an economic value. This is what may be described as the time tax—the hidden cost of the time and mental energy people spend filling out paperwork, waiting in queues, and navigating complex bureaucracy simply to access basic services, receive government benefits, or exercise their rights.

People stand in long queues and spend substantial amounts of time obtaining services from government offices. Some of the most time-consuming services are associated with obtaining passports, permits/licences for businesses or vehicles, land documents, resolving tax issues, accessing low-cost healthcare, to name just a few.

Moreover, a wealthy person can reduce the opportunity cost of time by hiring an agent or intermediary, while some people may resort to informal payments to speed up a service. A poor person, however, usually has fewer options. The relative loss of time can therefore be much greater for poorer citizens. For a low-income household, the forgone wages of days spent in queues are far more consequential than it would be for a richer household.

Bangladesh has, to some extent, recognised the importance of reducing this burden. The country’s digital reforms have used Time, Cost and Visit (TCV) as measures of improvement in public service delivery. A World Bank document reports that Bangladesh’s service delivery initiatives have measured reductions in the time, cost and number of visits required to obtain services, with substantial aggregate reductions attributed to digitisation.

But despite digitisation and innovation in public-service delivery, some sectors remain mired in delays and administrative hassles. According to the World Bank’s Bangladesh Development Update published in April this year, senior managers in Bangladesh spend an average of 13 percent of their time dealing with government regulations, higher than in any comparable country in the region. This national average, however, masks substantially heavier burdens in some parts of the country. In Chattogram, managers spend about 40 percent of their time dealing with regulatory compliance, while in Barishal, the figure rises to 60 percent, leaving little room for productive management and strategic decision-making.

The burden is also unevenly distributed across firms. As per the report, frontier firms—defined in the report as the most productive companies in the formal sector—”spend around five percentage points less time dealing with regulators and face fewer tax inspections than non-frontier firms.” Regulatory delays further compound these challenges. Obtaining an operating licence takes an average of 28 days, while construction permits and import licences each take about 49 days—nearly twice as long as in China or India, per the report. These regulatory burdens have tangible economic consequences: firms facing heavier regulatory demands are 19 percent less likely to invest.

The concept of time tax can be extended beyond government offices to another major source of lost time: traffic congestion. For millions of Bangladeshis, commuting has become an everyday tax on their time. A 2018 study estimated that around five million work hours are lost annually in Dhaka because of persistent traffic congestion, with an associated economic loss of an average of Tk 37,000 crore. Direct and indirect losses can be 6-10 percent of national GDP.

Time tax also has an important relationship with bribery. When bureaucratic procedures impose substantial costs in time, an unofficial payment may become, from the individual’s perspective, a way of escaping queues, delays and uncertainty. This creates a troubling incentive structure. If a person believes that paying a bribe can expedite a task that takes several weeks, the time tax itself can create a demand for speed money.

Besides, when entrepreneurs and firms spend substantial time obtaining licences, complying with regulations, or dealing with government agencies, that time becomes part of the cost of production. Firms may respond by reducing investment, delaying expansion or passing some of the additional costs on to consumers through higher prices. Ultimately, consumers may bear part of the burden through reduced purchasing power and lower welfare.

What, then, can be done? First, every major public service should publish a small set of measurable indicators: average processing time, average citizen waiting time, number of visits required, number of documents required, and number of physical interactions. This would make the time tax visible and allow citizens and policymakers to compare services and institutions.

Second, digitalisation should not simply transfer an inefficient paper-based procedure to an online platform. The underlying process itself should also be simplified. If a citizen has to upload the same information repeatedly, visit an office for physical verification, and then wait for several approvals, an online interface alone cannot eliminate the time tax.

Third, traffic congestion needs to be treated as a time-tax problem as well as a transport problem. Several measures have already been taken to ease congestion in Dhaka and Chattogram, but rapid urbanisation means that other divisional and major cities are increasingly facing similar problems. These cities also deserve greater policy attention. Finally, existing roads must be effectively used, as poor planning, roadside markets, illegal parking, and weak enforcement limit expanded highway capacity.

Time is one of the few economic resources that cannot be produced, imported or recovered once it is lost. Bangladesh has traditionally measured the cost of government services in terms of money. It is time that we also measure them in terms of hours lost. A tax collected in money appears in the government’s accounts. A tax collected in time does not. But it is no less real for citizens, businesses and the economy.

Professor Dr Md Bakhtiar Uddin is head of the Department of Economics at Jatiya Kabi Kazi Nazrul Islam University in Trishal, Mymensingh. He can be reached at [email protected].

title: A trillion-dollar economy sounds good, but it must benefit the people
text:
A few months ago, Prime Minister Tarique Rahman said that the BNP-led government is working to transform Bangladesh into a trillion-dollar economy by 2034. Bangladeshis have heard ambitious promises before. During the Awami League government’s tenure, Sheikh Hasina also spoke of making Bangladesh a trillion-dollar economy and a fully developed Smart Bangladesh by 2041. As a matter of fact, Bangladesh became a lower-middle-income country in 2015. The question, therefore, is not simply how large Bangladesh’s economy becomes, but how much that growth improves the lives of ordinary people.

During the Awami League period, Bangladesh recorded impressive GDP growth. But this did not create enough decent jobs for a young and growing population. Between 2013 and 2017, GDP grew by an average of 6.6 percent a year, while employment grew by only about 0.9 percent a year. Economists described this as “jobless growth”. Employment elasticity also declined from 0.54 during 1995-2000 to 0.25 during 2010-2018, showing how slowly job creation responded to economic growth.

The benefits of growth were also unevenly shared. According to the Bangladesh Bureau of Statistics’ Household Income and Expenditure Survey 2016, the income share of the richest 5 percent rose from 24.61 percent in 2010 to 27.89 percent in 2016. During the same period, the share of the poorest 5 percent fell sharply from 0.78 percent to just 0.23 percent. This is why many ordinary people feel disconnected from politicians’ celebration of GDP growth or rising per capita income. For an ordinary citizen struggling to pay rent, buy food, send their children to school, or deal with expensive medical costs, a higher GDP figure means little unless it visibly improves their quality of life.

A 2025 survey by the Power and Participation Research Centre estimated that 27.93 percent of the population was living below the upper poverty line, while 9.35 percent was living in extreme poverty. The situation is also being made worse by high living costs and pressure on household incomes.

Food security remains another serious concern. The 2026 Global Hunger Index found that 8.2 percent of Bangladesh’s population was undernourished, while 24 percent of children under five were stunted. Unicef has also reported that two in every three children under five in Bangladesh face child food poverty. More recently, the Food and Agriculture Organization reported that about 1.81 crore people are projected to face high levels of acute food insecurity between September and December 2026.

Housing, water, and sanitation remain major challenges. According to various reports from 2019, more than 50 lakh people in Bangladesh have no homes to live in. According to the Household Income and Expenditure Survey (HIES) 2019, 74.87 percent of families live in permanent mud houses, while only 4.95 percent of households have pucca buildings. Another 2.13 percent of people reside in slums and makeshift mud houses. The World Bank says 6.83 crore people lack safely managed drinking water, while 10.3 crore people lack safely managed sanitation facilities.

Meanwhile, more than seven crore people are employed in Bangladesh, but around 85 percent of them are engaged in the informal sector, where wages are low, jobs are insecure, and there is no social protection. The number of unemployed people in the country stands at around 27.3 lakh as per the Bangladesh Bureau of Statistics (BBS) data for 2025. An International Monetary Fund report published in 2026 noted that unemployment among highly educated young people in Bangladesh is around 36 percent.

It is unfortunate that, since independence, governments have come and gone, but ordinary citizens continue to struggle with the same basic problems.

BNP won the February 2026 election and Tarique Rahman became prime minister with a clear opportunity to present a different model of governance. Having spent many years in the United Kingdom, he has had the opportunity to observe how a developed country manages public services, healthcare, education, housing, transport, social protection, and institutions. It is therefore understandable that people expect his experience abroad to be reflected in his approach to state-building at home. Of course, no one expects Bangladesh to become a developed country overnight, as building effective institutions and public services takes time. But people do expect to see evidence that the government is moving in the right direction.

This is where the government could have made a visible difference through a few practical pilot projects. For example, our public hospitals are in dire straits, so why not transform at least one into a genuine model hospital, with modern equipment, clean facilities, proper nursing standards and reliable services? Similarly, why not develop affordable flats of 300 to 500 square feet for low-income families in selected areas? Why not turn one public school, college, or university into a model institution with modern classrooms, libraries, laboratories, playgrounds, and research facilities? Of course, such projects would not solve the country’s problems overnight. But they would show people that change is possible and that the government is serious about delivering it.

People do not oppose ambitious economic goals, but they want to see the benefits of growth reflected in their own lives as well. That is why the government’s performance cannot be judged by economic targets alone. Law and order are equally important. In the first eight months of 2026, police recorded 14,602 incidents of violence against women and children, while Ain o Salish Kendra reported that 254 children died in various forms of violence during the same period. Such figures are a reminder that economic progress has little meaning if people do not feel safe. The attack, looting, and demolition of the Radda MCH-FP Centre in Mirpur and a studio at ECB Chattar attacked and ransacked are troubling examples. For ordinary citizens, this is not an abstract issue of governance, but about whether the state can protect a public-serving institution and enforce the law.

Therefore, the lesson for the government is simple. Bangladesh does not need another development slogan. It needs visible results that ordinary people can see and feel in their daily lives. A trillion-dollar economy should not be measured only by the size of GDP, but by the quality of life it creates.

title: Our jute industry needs more than tariff relief
text:
India has revised its anti-dumping duties on Bangladeshi jute again. Some jute mills in the country now face no anti-dumping duty on specified products, while yarn from producers outside India’s list of 36 named firms attracts a duty of $445 per tonne. Days later, India’s trade remedies authority recommended countervailing duties of up to $140 a tonne, with some components payable on top of existing anti-dumping duties. India first put duties on our jute in 2017, and the routine since then has been familiar: exporters protest, associations appeal, and everyone hopes the next review goes easier.

India’s trade remedies authority found that dumping still hurts Indian mills. It sampled 10 Bangladeshi producers and found three selling below their home market prices. Reported margins ranged from 5 to 55 percent. According to the chairman of Bangladesh Jute Spinners Association (BJSA’s), production costs here are higher than India’s and that the earlier duties already cut our exports. Delhi reads the data differently: Indian demand fell 20 percent, imports from Bangladesh and Nepal fell by only 13 percent, and so foreign suppliers gained share.

Bangladesh should keep contesting all of it through every legal and diplomatic channel. Spinners argue that General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade (GATT) rules bar countervailing duties on goods already under anti-dumping duties. India says its design avoids counting any subsidy twice. But even a win would only reset the clock. The more important number is one that nobody in this dispute contests. Bangladesh’s jute goods exports to India fell 18 percent in FY2024-25, from 1.43 lakh tonnes to 1.17 lakh tonnes. That April-to-March decline came before this revision took effect. Last year, India also restricted a range of Bangladeshi jute products to one entry point: the Nhava Sheva port in Mumbai. A market we have long treated as a default destination is already contracting. Building a strategy around recovering it is building on sand.

India was never our only customer, though. According to the textiles and jute minister, Bangladesh exported jute goods to 138 countries in FY2024-25. The larger problem is that the whole sector has been shrinking. Export earnings fell from $1.16 billion in FY2020-21 to about $820 million in FY2024-25. They recovered to $883.7 million last fiscal year, but mostly on higher prices, not higher volumes.

Jute yarn earned $545.8 million in FY2025-26, about 62 percent of the total, on 2 percent less volume than the year before. Diversified jute products, the category beyond raw jute, yarn and sacks, earned $74.4 million, about 8 percent, and that figure fell 11 percent. India holds that Bangladeshi and Indian jute goods are interchangeable, so the contest is on price. Its countervailing case expressly excludes floor coverings, shopping bags and geotextiles: the products we should be selling.

Product comes first. The government wants jute export earnings to reach $2 billion within five years. More yarn will not get us there. Straits Research projects the global jute market to grow about 6 percent a year through 2034. To claim a share of that, mills need design, testing and certification capacity, and support that does not hinge on exports. India’s countervailing case targets cash grants tied to shipments, and Bangladesh’s WTO room for them narrows sharply with upcoming LDC graduation.

The next priority is market expansion. Bangladesh already exports jute goods to 138 countries, but it needs to strengthen its presence in these markets. This requires a well-defined export strategy that identifies priority markets across different regions, builds lasting relationships with buyers, and ensures compliance with international quality standards. The millers’ association reports growth in some new markets. Even the European Union, a major buyer of diversified products, is no safe harbour. Entrepreneurs say orders have fallen by 20 to 25 percent as higher energy costs hit sales of non-essential goods.

Then there are cost records. India asked 54 Bangladeshi mills for information, and 38 answered. Named firms got individual rates starting at $59 a tonne, some at zero, while yarn from anyone outside the list pays $445. The notification also requires exporters seeking producer-specific rates to document who made the goods. Mills need auditable cost and pricing records before the next review, and trade bodies should help the smaller ones get there.

Nepal was targeted in the same review, with estimated margins of 20 to 30 percent, and the two countries have shared these duties for years. Dhaka and Kathmandu have reasons to press Delhi together on how trade remedies are applied.

For years, our jute policy has followed the calendar of someone else’s investigations. The above-mentioned revision is one more setback and also a fair warning. The market we keep defending is shrinking. Jute still has buyers. We just need to sell them something better than yarn.

title: Of public spectacles and hidden crime masters
text:
Two visible actions related to illegal drug trade made headlines in the country last weekend. On October 15, gunmen shot dead Lutfozzaman Fakir Alif, an investigative journalist based in Netrokona. Less than a year ago, he had expressed fear of being killed in the hands of the local crime organisations during a meeting with the district police chief. His fear was grounded in the knife attack he had survived just a few weeks earlier. The Netrokona SP instructed his colleagues to provide protection to Lutfozzaman. Now his death and the consequent arrests of two suspects have probably proven his fear right. The other incident, just two days later, involves a sitting cabinet member whose derring-do involved raiding an alleged drug joint while openly carrying a pistol. Party high-ups deemed his movie-like stunt—notwithstanding his noble intention of dismantling drug rings—irresponsible and demanded his resignation as a state minister.

One died and the other lost his job in two visible cases to remind us of the invisible drug menace plaguing society. Alif’s visibility was evident on his Facebook page titled “Detective Article”, where he tried to expose the people and interests behind the crimes in Netrokona. Alif built a rapport with the local police and used to share information about criminals with them. He was reportedly a former army member who entered journalism after retirement. Alongside working as the Netrokona correspondent of private IPTV channel Ruposhi Bangla, he used his own social media platform to detail criminal activities. In the video footage of the meeting with police officials, Alif was seen saying he feared for the safety of his family and relatives.

We can posthumously credit Alif’s courage and even apply the attractive word “maverick” to describe him. He took initiatives to shed light on the dark side of life. He was courting danger, hoping those of whom he was helping would protect him. His death, instead of being brave, can now be considered foolish.

Drug trade has the negative reputation of making a fool of anyone and everyone who has tried to resist it. The network in which drug peddling happens involves financiers, suppliers, transporters, sellers and intermediaries. A reporter without any organisational support is unlikely to deal with the structure behind it. Alif was like David, but his slingshot missed its target, Goliath.

In contrast, when Ishraque Hossain, the Dhaka-6 MP and the then state minister for Liberation War affairs, unleashed a raid on an alleged drug joint in Gandaria with his men and weapons, he appeared to be a Goliath chasing tiny Davids. Video footage shows how Ishraque and some of his men alighted from a vehicle and went after alleged peddlers and users in a city slum, pointing his pistol at the people who were running away. When his actions drew controversies, he defended his conduct by citing security concerns and police shortcomings. Police disagreed, citing a joint operation in which they collaborated with the local lawmaker. His reckless behaviour made the prime minister ask for his resignation, which was formally accepted on October 20.

The two episodes are unlikely to have any operational connection. A journalist’s investigation and an elected official’s armed intervention can never be the same. Yet, their juxtaposition reveals how easily public attention settles on an individual confrontation. The pistol, the information collection, the dramatic declaration, and the personal risk become the content in this image-driven era. But while we remain glued to the wagging tail, the lizards who run the drug trade remain evasive as ever.

Law enforcement agencies should not simply focus on nabbing suspected perpetrators. They should instead focus on the system that necessitated or caused a murder or the removal of the enthusiastic individual who singlehandedly wanted to arm a wretch against an organised crime. Has the master of the ring changed their colour after the change in political echelon? Would it be possible to follow the money trail? Who finances a consignment? How are payments collected and transferred? Who absorbs the loss when drugs are seized? Does an operation disrupt supply or move a selling point elsewhere? Where allegations of protection arise, what evidence is collected and what happens to it?

A reporter in disguise or a lawmaker experiencing an adrenaline rush may only scratch the surface of the problem without fully understanding its extent. Alif’s relationship with law enforcement adds another layer. The Daily Star reported that he had supplied information about criminals to the authorities. That does not establish that he held a formal role as an informant. But it does raise questions about the boundaries local reporters must negotiate when they investigate dangerous subjects.

Did Alif become overconfident that his contact with senior police officers would offer him protection? Surely, the SP instructed his colleagues to do so. What safeguards supported his independence and his sources? The available reporting on detained murderers does not settle these questions.

But the greater danger that Alif faced involves the pitfalls of digital publishing. Unlike crime reporters working for established channels or news outlets, Alif’s Facebook page allows reporting to circulate without waiting for space in a newspaper or a television bulletin. It also concentrates recognition around its operator. The person gathering evidence becomes the publisher, the presenter, and the most identifiable point of contact. Such a journalist can obtain quick public recognition without any practical protection.

Meanwhile, Alif’s family faces consequences that will outlast public attention. His widow and children must live with the loss and the uncertainty surrounding their future.

This is where celebrating courage becomes inadequate. News organisations and professional bodies need arrangements for legal assistance, emergency relocation, insurance and sustained family support. A correspondent’s ingenuity should not conceal the resources required to investigate safely.

We should therefore be a bit cautious in celebrating the courage that takes an extraordinary path. Alif’s face is now familiar to people who never encountered his work while he was alive. The task is to ensure that the inquiry does not end with that recognition. His family needs support; his murder requires justice. The questions that both Alif and Ishraque brought into public view deserve scrutiny so that the structures that brought them down get exposed.

Dr Shamsad Mortuza is vice-chancellor at the University of Liberal Arts Bangladesh (ULAB).

title: ‘Some form of change will have to happen following India protests’
text:
Jahnavi Sen, managing editor of The Wire, speaks to Md. Shariful Hoque of The Daily Star about the ongoing protests in India demanding the resignation of its chief election commissioner and raising concerns over voter deletions and potential disenfranchisement linked to the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls.

The Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) movement began as a meme and social campaign, but gradually became a major force in Indian political discourse. Do you think it has become more of a political movement now amid the ongoing protests?

CJP started as an online movement, but during June and July, it turned into a street protest. It was barely a few weeks old then. We saw how, in Delhi, it grew into a large sit-in protest, with protesters attempting to march to parliament before being stopped by the police. Quite soon, it became clear that the movement had captured people’s imagination and was not going to remain confined to the internet and social media.

The current movement is a little different. CJP is one player in it, and its leaders have come out to say that the right to vote is essential and that they want to put all their strength behind the cause. But different groups also seem to have been involved from the start, organising different kinds of protests and applying different forms of pressure.

For CJP, it still remains a youth pressure group. It still does a lot of online campaigning while holding physical protests. But I don’t think the protest this time is as centred around them.

The protests have escalated, especially since October 10, with demands for the chief election commissioner’s resignation. Given that BJP has been in power for more than 12 years, how significant a political challenge does this movement pose to the government?

It has turned into an extremely significant challenge. The protests actually started a little earlier, around October 2, when civil society activists tried to gather in Delhi. The police immediately adopted a playbook of preventing any gatherings with detentions and roadblocks. Metro stations were closed down and a lot of traffic was diverted.

BJP leaders have been saying that the protests are an attempt to cause anarchy. They have tried to blame it on the leader of the opposition and the main opposition parties. But I don’t think anyone watching the footage of protests can say that this is an opposition-driven political agenda, because people from different walks of life have come together at these demonstrations.

They have all been affected by the issue at hand, which is the way the Election Commission has been functioning over the last few years. This has become particularly stark since last year, with the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of voter rolls and the inordinate pressure placed on citizens to prove their identities. I don’t think the government will be able to ignore the fact that such a basic right of every citizen is, in some way, being seen as under attack.

Congress leaders Rahul Gandhi and Priyanka Gandhi, along with internet personalities and celebrities, have joined the movement. Is the opposition amplifying a genuine movement or attempting to turn public anger into a broader political campaign of its own?

For this particular movement, it has been easy for Rahul Gandhi to come out and own it, because the voter-roll issue is something that he has been raising for much longer than the past few weeks. He has been holding press conferences and questioning the way voters are being added to and deleted from electoral rolls in different states just before elections. But while opposition parties are playing a big role, many of the street protests are being led by youth groups.

Does India’s response to the protests suggest that the government is becoming increasingly intolerant of dissent?

We have been witnessing intolerance towards dissent for several years now. We have seen cases brought against rights activists and people who have participated in protests. We also saw the big farmers’ movement in 2021 and the way the roads to Delhi were blocked.

One of the first glimpses into how far protesters managed to bring this into the heart of the national capital came in July, when pellet guns were fired at student protesters on July 20 as they were trying to march to parliament. Something like that had never happened there before. There was a lot of outrage, and we still have not received a clear answer as to why such force was considered necessary against a peaceful protest.

The Union government has been trying very hard to prevent a similar situation this time, using the Delhi Police and paramilitary forces. However, the police are detaining even small groups of people. They may be allowed to protest for 15 or 20 minutes, raise some slogans and gather, and then they are put on police buses, driven to the outskirts of the city, and let off. There have also been reports of phones being taken and attempts to delete footage. Many journalists and lawyers have been detained.

What has led to the erosion of trust in the EC? What evidence supports allegations that CEC Gyanesh Kumar has favoured BJP, and how should we distinguish legitimate concerns about institutional neutrality from allegations that have yet to be established?

The issues with the Election Commission predate Gyanesh Kumar’s appointment. During the 2019 general elections, one of the three election commissioners, Ashok Lavasa, suddenly resigned. It was later revealed that he had wanted notices to be issued to Prime Minister Narendra Modi and other top BJP leaders over speeches violating the model code of conduct. Likewise, we have seen different ways in which the commission has been used to favour BJP.

Creating a voter roll from scratch is an extremely complicated exercise. Anyone willing to do it seriously would give it adequate time and care. An interesting finding emerged from transparency activist Anjali Bhardwaj, who asked the Election Commission for the documents or notes on which the decision to conduct the SIR was based. The response was that the commission had no record of such a decision being taken. The question, then, is who decided that this exercise should take place in certain states where elections were approaching and that it should be conducted in such a rushed manner. West Bengal is one of the states where the extent to which this was used to keep people off the voter list was particularly stark. We saw how Muslim-majority areas experienced much larger numbers of deletions.

BJP has portrayed CJP and the youth-led protests as part of an anti-Modi agenda, while some have questioned whether the movement is influenced by foreign interests. How effective has this attempt to delegitimise the movement been?

BJP keeps insisting that the Election Commission of India is an autonomous and independent body. But all the defence of what has happened at the Election Commission has come from BJP leaders. None of the election commissioners has held a press conference. There has been just one press note, which did not really refute any of the allegations.

There was a report that two of the three election commissioners—not Gyanesh Kumar, but the other two—had dissented against EC decisions at least 14 times in 10 months. That is an extremely serious matter, something that the EC must answer for. There has certainly been an attempt to change the narrative, but it does not appear to be sticking.

South Asia has witnessed repeated confrontations between citizens and political establishments, from Sri Lanka and Bangladesh to Nepal and now India. What needs to happen for public anger to translate into lasting democratic reform?

South Asia has a very large youth population. There are many reasons why these street protests have captured people’s imagination, whether they concern education, public exams or recruitment systems. Quality employment, in particular, has become a major issue. The dream that big investments would mean better jobs and better lives for everyone is slowly being shattered.

As for what it takes for democratic dissent to succeed, a few months ago, the Union education minister had to resign following large-scale protests led by CJP. That was the first resignation of a minister in the Modi years resulting from public protest. The scale of the current protests means that some form of change will have to take place for people to feel that there has been a response. For that to become a lasting change, there needs to be greater investment in education, infrastructure, and healthcare, along with a concerted effort to create the futures people want.

This is an abridged version of an interview conducted by The Daily Star on October 13, 2026. To watch the full interview, visit @TheDailyStarNews.
