title: ‘ACC must be freed from political and bureaucratic influence’
text:
Dr Iftekharuzzaman, executive director of Transparency International Bangladesh (TIB) and former head of the Anti-Corruption Commission (ACC) Reform Commission, speaks to Tasneem Tayeb of The Daily Star about the state of corruption in Bangladesh, the fate of reform efforts, and the changes needed to hold those in power accountable.

ACC was established in 2004 as an independent institution to combat corruption. More than two decades later, corruption remains deeply embedded in the public sector. What was the original thinking behind the commission, and where did it fail in practice?

The former Bureau of Anti-Corruption, which ACC replaced, was part of the government and directly under its control. Since government departments and those in power were themselves often accused of corruption, the bureau could not function effectively. It rather became an instrument for harassing political opponents. We wanted a specialised, independent institution free from government influence.

Fighting corruption, however, needs more than one institution. Parliament, the judiciary, law enforcement agencies, and the bureaucracy must also fulfil their responsibilities. Parliamentary committees, for example, are supposed to hold the government accountable, but whether they function properly remains a major question.

Moreover, since its beginning, appointments to the commission reflected partisan political choices. Its leadership favoured the ruling authorities while targeting political opponents, allowing the bureau’s culture to continue under a new identity. Bureaucratic influence compounded the problem as senior positions below the commissioners came to be dominated by deputed officials whose allegiance remained with the bureaucracy. This damaged ACC’s capacity and credibility. People saw minor offenders pursued while powerful figures escaped accountability.

We recommended limiting the number of deputed bureaucrats and addressing corruption within ACC itself. Officials implicated in corruption should be removed and handed over to the relevant law enforcement agencies.

Does this chequered history suggest that policymakers failed to understand how corruption operates in Bangladesh, or that their knowledge has not translated into action?

I would not say policymakers do not understand corruption. Having engaged with those in power over the years, I know there is a clear understanding of what corruption is, how it can be combated, and what their responsibilities are. These are documented in laws, policies, codes of conduct, and reform recommendations. What’s missing is execution, as those who are supposed to apply this knowledge are often beneficiaries of corruption themselves. They protect the system and thus enable further corruption.

Ironically, fighting corruption has become central to political rhetoric. Election manifestos or government statements are full of commitments. The current ruling party’s 31-point agenda, election manifesto, and the July Charter, which its leaders have pledged to implement word for word, also contain specific commitments against corruption. So political will exists on paper, but it is not reflected in practice.

TIB’s household surveys have found that 85 percent of respondents who paid bribes said they would not have received their service otherwise. This shows how deeply systemic corruption is. Catching individual offenders cannot solve the problem while the wider system remains unchanged. Expectations naturally focus on ACC as the institution specifically mandated to fight corruption, but other institutions responsible for strengthening the state’s capacity to control corruption have also failed to fulfil their roles.

To be clear, corruption does not mean just bribery. It involves the abuse of power for private gain often through collusion among political actors, public officials, and business interests. So to tackle it, we must dismantle the wider ecosystem that allows such practices to persist.

The government has recently decided to set up separate anti-corruption committees in every ministry. What gaps could these committees fill when the existing mechanisms have failed to ensure accountability?

I think this may turn out to be another example of rhetoric as the government is not approaching the problem strategically. In Bangladesh, committees are often formed to deflect attention from key issues, while their reports remain unpublished and their effectiveness is rarely evident. Their work is also likely to be hampered by conflicts of interest. As things stand, the most senior officials in each ministry already have responsibilities for ensuring accountability, integrity, and corruption-free administration. There is, moreover, no clear indication of what these new committees will actually do.

Speaking of strategic interventions, we recommended a national anti-corruption strategy assigning specific responsibilities to the institutions concerned. The government has yet to act on this proposal, even though the ruling party, like other political parties, fully endorsed it. The idea is to transform the existing National Integrity Strategy into a national anti-corruption strategy. But these committees, representing an ad hoc approach, may, at best, recommend transferring a corrupt official from one ministry or department to another. Such departmental action has already proved ineffective and could become another way of protecting corrupt officials by simply shifting them around.

Higher salaries are often presented as a way to curb corruption in the public sector. How can the new pay scale help achieve this when previous increases have failed to do so?

Public officials are a fixed-income group, so we cannot expect them to perform to the best of their ability and with integrity unless their salaries and benefits are commensurate with the cost of living. Reviewing salaries periodically is also a standard practice. That said, better pay must be linked to accountability. We recommended making annual public disclosure of assets and income a condition for receiving the revised pay scale. Officials agreeing to disclose their assets and update their statements annually would receive the increase, while those unwilling to do so would not. The purpose was to make the salary revision an effective tool for controlling corruption.

But the proposal was not accepted because of resistance from bureaucrats. Without accountability, I fear that higher salaries could simply lead to demands for higher bribes rather than help curb corruption.

The interim government established reform commissions but left many of their recommendations unimplemented. Where did it fall short, particularly in relation to the ACC reforms you proposed?

Forming the commissions was a positive step, but the interim government lacked a clear vision for what to do with their reports. It committed to implementing the recommendations that could be acted upon immediately through executive authority or by the relevant institutions, without needing to wait for a new government or constitutional changes. But most recommendations were left aside, apart from a few selected on an ad hoc basis as a token gesture. Where legal changes were made, they often reflected the government’s own ideas rather than the commissions’ recommendations. The ACC ordinance left out critical recommendations of the ACC Reform Commission.

We wanted ACC to have full independence alongside accountability. Independence cannot mean the absence of accountability. ACC must answer for protecting those in power or harassing political opponents. Our proposed reforms sought to address both political influence and bureaucratic control, but those critical changes remain unimplemented. The promise that cabinet members and public officials would disclose their wealth statements was also delayed until shortly before the interim government stepped down. What was eventually disclosed was controversial, to say the least. These examples raise questions about the seriousness of the interim government’s commitment to transparency and the foundation it left for reform.

What should the current government prioritise to give substance to its commitments against corruption?

It must abandon the mindset that “it is now our turn” and the winner-takes-all politics: the idea that we have been deprived of opportunities for so long, so winning the election entitles us to capture everything. Political positions, elected or unelected, within parties or the government, are unfortunately being treated as a licence for profiteering and personal gain. After the former regime fell on August 5, 2024, the space it had occupied through extortion and corruption was taken over by those who emerged as victors. This continued under the interim government and persists today.

This political culture, in which the abuse of power simply changes hands, must end. Political commitment must be demonstrated by enabling institutions to hold those in power to account. People must also be able to reject and report corruption without facing retaliation. Harassing those who expose corruption while protecting the corrupt only allows it to flourish.

Four elements must work in concert—political commitment, the capacity to hold offenders accountable, independent and effective institutions, and people’s ability to stand against corruption. If any of these is missing, the system cannot deliver what is promised.

If you could begin making changes now, what would be your first priority, and what results would convince people that accountability is finally possible?

There is no single magic bullet for fighting corruption. My first priority nevertheless would be to create the conditions for the governing authorities to address the two major drivers of unabated corruption: cleansing the ruling party of corruption at all levels and overhauling a bureaucracy that has become deeply entrenched in preserving systemic corruption. The first step to that end would be to require public officials to disclose their annually updated assets for public scrutiny. Equally important is a truly independent, corruption-free, efficient, and accountable ACC. The recommendations are already there on how to make it effective. Its ability to function properly depends on the government allowing it to exercise its mandate without partisan influence or bureaucratic control.

We need to see corruption, especially at higher levels, punished. The commission has hundreds of cases; it cannot, nor does it need to, handle all of them at once. Prioritising high-profile cases and securing exemplary punishments in, say, even 10 cases a year could send a powerful signal to society.

ACC cannot deliver this alone. It needs, among other things, a truly independent judicial system that upholds the highest standards of integrity. Fighting corruption needs a comprehensive strategy combining both prevention and control and involving the whole of the state and society.

title: ‘New mothers must be supported to recover in every way, not just physically’
text:
In Bangladesh, it is still uncommon for new mothers to receive help to deal with postpartum mental health shifts. On the occasion of World Mental Health Day, Dr Sahar Raza, a public health researcher and mental health expert, speaks to Afia Jahin of The Daily Star detailing the life-altering changes new mothers go through and discussing how communities and the healthcare sector can help narrow the existing gaps in care.

How do postpartum mental health issues manifest in new mothers, and how long can they last?

There is a normal level of emotional adjustment for all new mothers. Once you have a baby, it can be overwhelming as the postpartum period involves a major physical, psychological and even a social transition. That adjustment period may last up to two weeks or even longer. But then there is a mental health condition where symptoms are more persistent, severe, and which interfere more with the mother’s everyday life. For example, a new mother may feel persistently sad and empty, worry excessively, and lose interest in the activities she usually enjoys. In many cases, she may even struggle to connect with her baby emotionally. This is when an assessment may be required.

Postpartum mental health issues can include anxiety and depression, but there can also be severe issues such as hallucinations, delusions, confusion, suicidal thoughts, or even thoughts of harming the baby which can signal postpartum psychosis. These severe issues are medical emergencies and need prompt attention. There cannot be a wait-and-watch approach.

In terms of how long postpartum mental health changes can last, the World Health Organization (WHO) conventionally defines the postpartum period as the first six weeks after giving birth. But there is no biological switch that turns off on Day 40 or 42. As much as we try to quantify the postpartum period, we need to make sure the mother is getting better beyond this point, too. Women still need support as their existing mental health issues may become more severe or they may develop new conditions after the six-week mark. One Lancet series titled “Maternal health in the perinatal period and beyond” states that there should be consideration about extending the postpartum period and that women should be coming in contact with health systems in order to be kept in check regarding their mental, physical and emotional health.

How common is it for new mothers in Bangladesh to seek professional help in dealing with postpartum mental health issues?

We found in one study that about 22 percent of reproductive-age women with anxiety or depression sought care from a healthcare provider, and only 8 percent used prescribed medication. During the postpartum period, the focus is more on the new baby than on the mother. Even during this time, when people visit to see the baby, the mother has to make sure that she is presentable. She will often be criticised or blamed for any issues with the baby, to the point of having her basic maternal instincts being questioned. This disallows her the space needed to navigate the first few weeks with her baby, which is an adjustment period for both of them.

Also, in order to seek help, a new mother has to first realise that she is suffering. Many a time, new mothers’ concerns are dismissed, with elders minimising the gravity of childbirth. At other times, the family may assume it is a period of adjustment that will eventually pass. Even for those who may recognise the problem, the stigma around mental health issues often becomes a barrier to seeking help.

There can also be uncertainty about where mental health services can be availed. And in our context, the decision-making is usually not with the mother as she may be dependent on a family member for money and mobility.

It should also be noted that the onus of seeking help should not be imposed on the mother. A woman may recognise her mental health condition, but she may not know what to do about it. The people around her need to create an enabling, non-judgemental environment where she can have time, privacy, and the reassurance that her concerns are being taken seriously. This also means training healthcare providers to handle such cases. It has to be a holistic approach wherein everybody plays a role.

In the rural areas, where lack of adequate services often deprives mothers of proper physical treatment during and after pregnancy, what is the level of awareness about postpartum mental health?

I would avoid saying that there is no awareness at all. Because of the level of connectivity we have now, even in rural areas, women do recognise when they are struggling. But a postpartum mother may not know that her symptoms could be part of a treatable mental health condition.

One local study evidenced this, finding that rural women often do not know which providers or facilities offer maternal mental healthcare. A new mother might also not realise that whatever she is going through is something other women feel too. That form of an enabling environment, which makes it easier for mothers to speak up, is lacking.

How can families and communities help new mothers cope better mentally during the postpartum period?

Families should offer practical support and active listening. This means helping the new mother with the baby, any older children, and with other responsibilities. Rather than making it all about the baby, relatives can ask after the mother as well. Families should foster a positive environment and avoid any unnecessary conflicts. A study done in Chandpur’s Matlab area, for instance, highlighted how strained relationships with the mother-in-law and marital conflicts were associated with postnatal depression.

A new mother may seem functional, but could be struggling internally. Regardless of how many generations we have been giving birth for, childbirth will always be a massive physical, mental and psychological change. New mothers must be supported to recover in every way, not just physically. Also, different women may have different timelines for recovery, so it is important to eliminate any pressure for a new mother to bounce back quickly.

What should be done at the government level to raise awareness about postpartum mental health?

Mental healthcare should be an ordinary, expected and integrated element of maternal care that continues into postnatal care, rather than being a separate service that women are burdened to discover if they feel something is wrong. Starting from the antenatal period, mental health check-ups should be part of routine screenings.

This won’t require the government to come up with a whole new screening system. For example, when a mother takes her baby to be vaccinated, that opportunity can be used to do a quick questionnaire-based screening to check on her mental state. The contact mothers are already making with the health system should be utilised as such.

Accessing mental healthcare providers can be challenging, so having these services within a regular health facility, where women can walk in, discuss whatever is on their mind, and get a primary screening done can be a good model. It is all about ensuring that a mother can say it openly when she is struggling mentally, that she is taken seriously, and that she receives care even after the first 40 days have passed.

Afia Jahin is a member of the editorial team at The Daily Star.

title: ‘Every child has the right to be taught by a properly trained teacher’
text:
Samir Ranjan Nath, programme head at the BRAC Institute of Educational Development, BRAC University, talks with Naznin Tithi of The Daily Star about the persistent learning gaps in primary education, the need for properly trained teachers, teacher redistribution, and other issues.

Recently, an inspection by the Compulsory Primary Education Implementation and Monitoring Unit (CPEIMU) found significant learning deficits among students in nearly 2,100 government primary schools across four areas, including the Dhaka Metropolitan Area. How would you evaluate its findings?

To be frank, the CPEIMU report does not reveal anything entirely new. The findings are largely consistent with the results of various studies and assessments conducted over the past few years. For example, BBS and Unicef’s National Survey on Children’s Education in Bangladesh 2021, the Directorate of Primary Education’s National Student Assessment (NSA) 2022, and earlier studies have all revealed a similar picture. These studies found substantial deficiencies in students’ foundational literacy and numeracy skills.

In the BBS-Unicef survey, students were asked to read and comprehend a short paragraph consisting of just 72 Bangla words. The result showed that many students were unable to understand even this simple passage. Likewise, their basic mathematical skills were found to be weak. The Directorate of Primary Education’s assessments have also shown that many Class 3 students fail to achieve the competencies expected for their grade. Those who fall behind at an early stage tend to fall even further behind by the time they reach Class 5. In other words, instead of narrowing over time, the learning gap continues to widen.

Research conducted by the BRAC Institute of Educational Development during the Covid pandemic also identified significant learning losses. This latest assessment is particularly alarming because it shows that many students cannot even pronounce the Bangla alphabet or read common words correctly. Earlier studies generally reported that students struggled with reading comprehension or solving mathematical problems; the latest assessment highlights an even more fundamental problem.

What reforms are needed in primary education to address these deficits? How should struggling students be identified and supported?

I don’t think any major policy reforms are necessary. What is needed is for everyone involved in primary education to carry out their responsibilities properly. Teachers’ primary responsibility is to teach effectively in the classroom and ensure that students are learning. Unfortunately, this is where our greatest weakness lies. Headteachers provide leadership at the school level, and the quality of that leadership is extremely important. Above them are upazila and district education officials, whose responsibilities include regularly visiting schools, supporting teachers, and monitoring the quality of education. If classroom teaching is given the highest priority, with proper support and oversight from those in leadership roles, much of this problem can be addressed.

Another important issue is strengthening the connection between schools and students’ families. Maintaining regular communication with parents is very important. Government schools used to hold regular parent-teacher meetings, but this practice has largely disappeared over time. Overall, weaknesses in classroom teaching, school leadership, regular supervision, teacher support, and parental engagement all reflect a persistent lack of accountability and commitment. In my view, the learning deficit is fundamentally a reflection of weak accountability across the system.

Teacher shortages and the lack of qualified teachers have long been major concerns in primary schools. How can these shortages be addressed?

Teacher shortages certainly exist, but the issue is not just about the number of teachers; it is also about how they are allocated among the schools. There are now 65,567 government primary schools across the country. Of these, 133 schools have only one teacher, while 633 schools have only two. At a minimum, a school needs five teachers to teach the five grades, along with one headteacher. If a school has a pre-primary class, another teacher is required. Based on my calculations, nearly one-fifth of government primary schools have fewer than five teachers. This shows that the crisis is real.

At the same time, it is important to recognise that a large number of teachers have been recruited over the past two decades. In 2001, there were, on average, 67 students for every teacher. By 2024, that ratio fell to around 29 students per teacher. However, this improvement has not translated into better learning outcomes. One reason may be the unequal distribution of teachers. Some schools may still have 50 students per teacher, while others may have only 20.

Therefore, the government’s first priority should be to redistribute teachers more evenly across schools. Additional recruitment should then be carried out where necessary.

How important is teacher training to improve their skills?

The number of teachers and their competence must be considered together. Unfortunately, while there have been numerous studies on students’ learning outcomes, there has been very little research on teachers’ competencies. I think CPEIMU could assess teachers’ competencies just as it assesses students’. It is important to know how many teachers can effectively teach Bangla, mathematics, and other subjects. Teachers found to have skill gaps should receive needs-based professional training. If, even after receiving training, a teacher is found unable to teach effectively, difficult decisions may have to be made regarding the continuation of their service.

Unfortunately, nearly one-quarter of primary school teachers have still not received the necessary professional training. This is unacceptable. Every child has a fundamental right to be taught by a properly trained teacher.

What special measures can schools and the government take to help students who fall behind because of social, family, or economic disadvantages?

Every school should have a clear understanding of the socioeconomic backgrounds of its students. Schools should maintain a database of this information. Regardless of family background, every child deserves equal attention in the classroom. However, we know that children from disadvantaged families often do not receive adequate academic support at home. They, therefore, require additional assistance. A school’s responsibility does not end with delivering regular lessons; it must also ensure that students who are falling behind receive the support they need to catch up.

Teachers can identify struggling students through continuous classroom assessment. Based on that information, schools should organise appropriate remedial programmes. Schools can arrange remedial classes after school or during holidays. Schools with sufficient teachers can begin these interventions immediately. But those facing teacher shortages should first address the problem through teacher redistribution and then gradually recruit additional teachers where needed.

Do you find government supervision of schools to be adequate?

Most of the supervision that currently takes place focuses on infrastructure, while academic supervision and evaluation of classroom teaching are almost absent. Education officials at the upazila level should visit schools regularly to identify academic problems, provide guidance, and follow up to see whether their recommendations have been implemented. In other words, they need to work with schools continuously rather than conducting one-off inspections. Some NGOs have extensive experience working closely with families and teachers to promote quality education. So, a collaborative effort can be considered, as was done during the Education for All (EFA) movement.

Following a recent policy shift, children seeking admission to Class 1 will now be required to sit for entrance exams, raising concerns among parents about the likely effects on children. What changes do you think are needed in the admission policy and school system to ensure equal opportunities for all children?

I think the lottery-based admission system was better than admission through competitive examinations. The current policy may force many to resort to coaching centres or private tutoring even before entering school. Financially well-off families will be able to afford that, while others will not. As a result, inequality will increase. If a child becomes familiar with coaching before becoming familiar with school, it is a serious injustice. It encourages a coaching-dependent culture from the very beginning of a child’s education journey. Therefore, I believe the lottery-based admission system should be reinstated for the time being.

In the medium term, however, the best solution would be to introduce a catchment area-based admission system. Each school should have a clearly defined catchment area, and all children living within that area should attend that school. Such a system can be introduced immediately where possible. At the same time, the government must ensure that every school has adequate infrastructure, properly trained teachers, and the resources needed to provide quality education.

title: ‘Textbooks should not undermine girls' confidence or reinforce the beauty myth’
text:
Dr Samina Luthfa, professor in the Department of Sociology at Dhaka University, speaks with Monorom Polok of The Daily Star about the contents of national curriculum textbooks, their revisions, and possible impact on students.

The Class-7 Home Economics textbook has recently drawn criticism for the way it presented girls’ appearance and gender roles. What concerns you most about this content?

My first concern is that Home Economics itself has traditionally been treated as a highly gendered subject. It is almost always taught to girls, while boys are excluded, even though household management is a life skill that everyone should learn. If the subject is to remain in the curriculum, it should be compulsory for both boys and girls. Learning how to manage a household or do basic stitching is not something to be ashamed of. The fact that boys are generally not taught these only reinforces unequal gender roles in society.

I am also deeply concerned by the textbook’s advice telling girls what to wear based on their body shape or skin complexion. Such prescriptions amount to body shaming. They suggest that certain skin tones or body types are more attractive than others, which can seriously undermine young girls’ confidence and reinforce what we call the “beauty myth”. This kind of content should be removed entirely. And, textbook writers should involve experts from the social sciences and gender studies so that these kinds of insensitive messages are identified before publication.

How does teaching these ideas at a young age reinforce the culture of body shaming in society?

When children are taught that only certain complexions or body types are beautiful, they begin comparing themselves against those standards from an early age. That comparison can have a profoundly negative impact on their confidence and identity formation later on. Given how widespread body shaming already is, particularly on digital platforms, educational materials should promote inclusivity rather than reinforce harmful stereotypes.

You were directly involved with the 2024 textbook revision process. Were you aware of this change? What were the biggest challenges you encountered?

It is important to note that my role did not involve the Home Economics textbook review; instead, I led the social sciences group. Our committee was a diverse collective, featuring sociologists, anthropologists, and specialists in gender, media, archaeology, and Islamic history. Together, we meticulously examined every social science text from Classes 2 through 12, engaging in rigorous debate to determine which sections should be retained, excised, or fundamentally revised. These expert committees functioned primarily to evaluate current material rather than authoring new works. After reaching a consensus on necessary changes, we produced revised drafts that reflected the collective approval of all committee members.

One challenge involved terminology relating to indigenous communities. The expert committee wanted to replace the phrase “small ethnic groups” with “Indigenous”, but government officials objected because the constitutional wording was different. Eventually, we agreed to use the term “different ethnic groups” instead, ensuring that the word “small” was removed altogether.

I was also part of the overall coordination committee that brought together around 57 experts alongside NCTB officials. Unfortunately, after considerable controversy and online pressure, the Ministry of Education dissolved the committee. That, in my view, was a major setback. I think one of the interim government’s earliest failures was repeatedly retreating in the face of pressure. That established a pattern of compromising decisions instead of standing by expert recommendations.

We also argued strongly that education researchers should be included at every stage of textbook development. Subject specialists can judge factual accuracy, but education researchers understand whether content is developmentally appropriate for children of different ages. Another issue we repeatedly raised concerned the poor quality of textbook printing. Contracts may specify higher-quality paper, but in practice the required standards are often ignored. We believed corruption surrounding textbook printing and procurement was a serious problem.

What changes did the expert committee actually recommend, and what do you see as the biggest challenge facing NCTB today?

We made several content revisions. For example, we ensured that works by recognised researchers on the Language Movement were included where appropriate. We added material on Nawab Faizunnesa, included references to Maulana Abdul Hamid Khan Bhashani, and made other modest corrections to improve representation and historical balance. These were not sweeping ideological changes but measured revisions based on evidence.

We also felt that including the July uprising in textbooks for very young children may not be appropriate because it is a recent and highly violent event. We believed students should study it later, perhaps in Classes 8 or 9, when they are better able to understand it in context.

In my view, the biggest challenge facing NCTB is not the experts. It is the bureaucracy within the institution and the nexus between sections of that bureaucracy and business syndicates. That remains the most serious structural problem.

Textbooks in Bangladesh are often revised whenever governments change. What impact does this have on education, and how should the revision process be handled?

I believe this is a very harmful practice, particularly for children. Imagine a student learning one version of history in primary school and then encountering an entirely different version a few years later because the government has changed. That creates confusion and undermines a child’s understanding of the country’s past. If we could simply acknowledge historical contributions regardless of political affiliation, many of these unnecessary revisions could be avoided.

Besides, textbook development should be carried out through expert committees. History books require historians, and even within history there are specialists for different periods. Similarly, every subject should be reviewed by experts in that field. However, the responsibility for implementing their recommendations lies with the bureaucracy. As I said before, when we revised textbooks in 2024, NCTB formed expert committees comprising university teachers and specialists. However, I do not know what happened after our work was completed.

title: ‘Waterlogging is now more a problem of governance than of rainfall’
text:
Dr Efadul Huq, assistant professor of environmental science and policy at Smith College in the US, speaks with Marzana Tasnim of The Daily Star about the governance failures behind persistent urban waterlogging, climate resilience, and the future of cities in Bangladesh.

Bangladesh’s weather forecasting capacity has improved considerably over the years. Yet, heavy rain predictions often fail to translate into timely anticipatory action on the ground. Why does this gap persist?

The main problem is that the responsible authorities, such as the city corporations, don’t make the connection between the forecast and the required action. Unless officials are held accountable for the response, or lack thereof, better forecasting will not lead to better preparedness.

How much of the recent severe waterlogging can be attributed to heavy rainfall, and how much to poor urban planning, inadequate drainage capacity, canal encroachment, or weak enforcement?

For chronic waterlogging, I would say this is primarily a governance problem. In a genuinely extreme event, some flooding may be unavoidable. But repeated and prolonged waterlogging at the same known hotspots points to failures of maintenance and response. Dhaka received 196 mm of rain in one day in May 2025 and 97 mm on July 12, 2026, yet the smaller rainfall event caused much greater disruption. If inadequate drainage infrastructure were a decisive factor, how did the water drain last year?

I want to push back strongly against the claim that Dhaka waterlogs simply because its wetlands were filled. Wetland loss has reduced the city’s capacity to hold water, but it does not make chronic waterlogging inevitable. The city did not suddenly lose a major share of its wetlands between May 2025 and July 2026. It had essentially the same wetland deficit in both years. What changed was governance, or the lack of it. The broader claim that a city built on wetlands or beside rivers is destined to remain waterlogged is also simply untrue.

Take a look at the Netherlands. It is a low-lying delta where substantial areas were reclaimed from water, and millions of people live below sea level. It manages that vulnerability through clearly assigned responsibilities, continuous maintenance, flood protection, and coordination among public authorities. Wetland loss is a serious structural problem for Bangladesh, but it has become a politically convenient explanation by turning a preventable failure into geographical destiny. Wetland loss does not leave pumps unrepaired, canal mouths blocked, or agencies unprepared despite an advance forecast.

Some canals in Dhaka still connect directly to the surrounding rivers, alongside a wider interconnected network that can still carry water. Those connections must be restored and kept open. Some targeted infrastructure investment will be necessary, but anyone explaining the current crisis mainly through rainfall, wetland loss, or drainage capacity is downplaying the governance failure within the city corporations in the capital.

One recurring criticism during monsoons is that responsibility for preventing waterlogging is divided among multiple agencies, with no single institution accountable for coordinating the overall response. What do you have to say about this fragmentation of governance?

Sure, many agencies are involved, but fragmentation should not become an excuse for inaction. Historically and practically, the city corporation has to take responsibility for the overall coordination. The city mayor’s ministerial status gives the office the political standing to convene the relevant agencies, press them to act, and follow up across institutional boundaries.

Ideally, the entire drainage system would be placed under one unified metropolitan authority. But we don’t need to wait for that restructuring before acting. Under the current arrangement, the city corporation is still best positioned to lead. What is needed is the competence and will to coordinate, rather than allowing each agency to hide behind the question of who owns which drain or canal.

In a genuinely extreme event, some flooding may be unavoidable. But repeated and prolonged waterlogging at the same known hotspots points to failures of maintenance and response. Dhaka received 196 mm of rain in one day in May 2025 and 97 mm on July 12, 2026, yet the smaller rainfall event caused much greater disruption. If inadequate drainage infrastructure were a decisive factor, how did the water drain last year?

Media reports have been highlighting that, despite large investments made in improving the drainage infrastructure, major cities like Dhaka, Chattogram and Khulna experience waterlogging even after a moderate rainfall. Why are these costly projects falling short?

Focusing on infrastructure alone would be misleading. The more immediate problem is the lack of proper operation and maintenance of the existing infrastructure. Canal mouths and outfalls are not regularly cleared. Pumps and sluice gates are not kept functional. The list goes on. That said, Dhaka, Khulna or Chattogram should not be treated as if they face the same problem.

In Khulna, the low-lying geography and still-incomplete drainage investments mean that major infrastructure gaps remain. In Chattogram, rivalry among agencies has produced competing plans and different drainage designs, so institutional conflict is part of the problem. Dhaka is different. Its stormwater and sewerage networks are incomplete, but the city still has considerable capacity to drain water through its existing canals, outfalls, and interconnected channels. Restoration is still possible. The city authorities need to take the upper hand in coordinating the agencies, maintaining these connections, and deciding where targeted infrastructure is actually needed.

So, the lesson here is not that investment produces no result. It is that investment fails when it is not scientific, people-oriented, coordinated, or followed by proper operation and maintenance. We should assess these projects by how quickly water recedes and whose neighbourhoods remain flooded.

Not to downplay the severity of the extreme rainfall events being caused by climate change, but at this stage, is climate change becoming an excuse for our governance failures?

Yes. Climate change should not be used to lower the standard of accountability. But in practice, climate change has become an instrument for avoiding responsibility. Dhaka has always experienced intense monsoon rainfall, and the historical rainfall pattern has not changed so abruptly that it can explain why the same drainage system performed relatively well in 2025 and failed under less rain in 2026. Climate change does not absolve public authorities of maintaining and operating the system they already have.

Should Bangladesh adopt formal trigger mechanisms whereby forecasts above certain thresholds automatically prompt reviews of decisions such as school closures, public transport arrangements, etc?

Sure, formal trigger mechanisms can be introduced. But we should not mistake that for governance. We could, for example, build a waterlogging app tomorrow, but the app alone will not help. Such tools are useful only when public offices are accountable, staffed by competent people, and motivated to act on the information they receive.

Urban waterlogging affects not only people but also street animals or urban wildlife. These impacts rarely feature in urban planning or disaster preparedness. How should cities incorporate the protection of vulnerable human and non-human populations into resilience planning?

At present, there is no meaningful urban safety net for poor people. Informal settlements—the so-called slums—are among the most exposed to various environmental risks, yet they are often left out of infrastructure planning. They need drainage, safe shelters, drinking water, sanitation, transport support, and emergency assistance. You are also right about animals. Flood preparedness has to include urban wildlife, rather than treating animals and other living systems as separate from the city.

For street animals and urban wildlife, community involvement is essential because residents and grassroots groups usually know where animals gather and can respond quickly. City corporations should fund and empower these groups to organise rescue, temporary shelter, feeding, and veterinary support. Citizen-led action can fill some immediate gaps when the government response is weak, as we saw in 2025, but it should complement public responsibility rather than replace it.

If you had the authority to implement just three reforms before the next monsoon season, what would they be?

First, I would return to the 2025 DNCC playbook. The then DNCC administration showed that it could audit known hotspots before the monsoon, clear canal mouths and outfalls, repair pumps and sluice gates, and prepare for forecast rainfall. The condition of these sites and the work completed should be digitally monitored and made public.

Second, I would establish response teams ahead of time that can be deployed before and during heavy rain, rather than assembling an ad hoc response after streets are already flooded. These teams should work under the city corporations and have the authority to act across agency and jurisdictional boundaries.

Third, for the longer term, I would require the agencies to follow a coordinated drainage master plan. That means restoring and connecting canals, drains, outfalls and rivers, and making targeted infrastructure investments where they are actually needed.

title: 'Don't wait until El Niño risks become a real crisis'
text:
Dr Rashed Chowdhury, a climatologist and adjunct faculty member at Arizona State University in the US, speaks with Pinaki Roy of The Daily Star about the possible impacts of El Niño on Bangladesh, why its different variants matter, and how the country should prepare for the risks ahead.

Last month, the UN weather agency warned of the likelihood of El Niño intensifying later this year. What are the most likely impacts of El Niño on Bangladesh?

We have seen extensive media coverage of El Niño, including from the UN, but much less attention has been paid to its different variants. This distinction is particularly important for Bangladesh because the two main types—Eastern Pacific El Niño (EPE) and Central Pacific El Niño (CPE), also known as El Niño Modoki—can have different impacts.

For example, EPE events during 1982-83, 1991-92, and 1997-98 brought dry conditions and drought to Bangladesh, whereas CPE events during 1987, 2015-16, and 2023-24 were associated with wetter conditions and flooding. The EPE is characterised by the strongest sea surface temperature (SST) warming in the Eastern Pacific Ocean, while the CPE exhibits maximum SST warming farther west in the Central Pacific. Therefore, before linking El Niño to seasonal climate variability in Bangladesh, we must first understand which variant is developing.

Normally, if El Niño develops before or around the onset of monsoon in South Asia, it can have a significant influence on rainfall across the region, including Bangladesh. This year, however, El Niño is expected to develop relatively late, towards late summer or even winter. Because of this timing, Bangladesh may not experience the more typical impacts associated with a strong EPE event, such as the major monsoon failures of 1982-83 or 1997-98.

It is also worth noting that, although the SST pattern associated with the developing 2026 El Niño currently resembles an Eastern Pacific event, the atmospheric response is more characteristic of a Central Pacific El Niño. This is one reason why Bangladesh has so far experienced wetter-than-normal conditions.

People often confuse El Niño with climate change. How are they different?

Yes, El Niño and climate change are not the same thing. El Niño is a naturally occurring climate phenomenon that develops periodically, whereas climate change is a long-term shift in the Earth’s climate driven primarily by human activities. Global warming does not cause El Niño. That said, it can amplify its impacts. In Bangladesh, this can mean more intense heat, greater water stress, increased flood risks, and more severe impacts on agriculture and livelihoods.

A simple way to think about it is: climate change is like raising the baseline temperature, while El Niño is a temporary push on top of that. Climate change gradually increases temperatures and climate risks over decades, while El Niño alters temperature and rainfall patterns over several months.

What risks does El Niño pose to Bangladesh’s rice production and overall food security?

El Niño can reduce rice production by bringing higher temperatures, delayed or weaker monsoon rainfall, and drought conditions, all of which can lower crop yields. Lower rice production can lead to food shortages, higher prices, and increased food insecurity, particularly among low-income households. Overall, El Niño threatens Bangladesh’s food security by affecting agricultural livelihoods, reducing food availability, and increasing the cost of staple foods.

What steps should the government take for farmers if El Niño conditions persist?

If El Niño conditions persist, the government should strengthen early warning systems, promote drought-tolerant crop varieties, improve irrigation facilities, provide financial and technical support to farmers, expand crop insurance, and maintain adequate food reserves to safeguard food security.

In the longer term, Bangladesh could consider developing a comprehensive weather-based insurance programme similar to the Total Weather Insurance (TWI) schemes used in several countries. TWI provides season-long protection against weather-related risks that reduce crop yields and farmers’ incomes. Such programmes use detailed information on weather patterns, climate trends, soil conditions, crop types, field locations, and other factors to design more accurate, farm-specific insurance coverage. This approach could help reduce farmers’ financial losses during climate extremes associated with El Niño, La Niña, and other weather-related events.

Could El Niño worsen water shortages or reduce river flows, especially during the dry season?

Yes. El Niño can have a major impact on Bangladesh’s water resources. It can reduce rainfall and weaken the monsoon, leading to lower river flows and water shortages, especially during the dry season. This can affect irrigation, drinking water supplies, fisheries, and agriculture, increasing the risk of drought in vulnerable regions. Reduced water availability can also put additional pressure on water needed for farming, industry, and households.

If the 2026 El Niño strengthens as projected by some climate-monitoring agencies, Bangladesh may face increased risks of water stress and energy shortages in late 2026 and early 2027. Prolonged dry conditions could reduce water levels in rivers, reservoirs, and other sources, affecting hydropower generation and increasing pressure on electricity supplies. Experience from other countries shows that severe droughts can force the authorities to introduce water conservation measures and manage electricity demand when water shortages disrupt power production.

What effects might it have on groundwater, drinking water availability, and irrigation?

Because El Niño can reduce rainfall and river flows, it can mean less water being available to recharge groundwater. As a result, groundwater levels may decline, especially in drought-prone areas such as northwestern Bangladesh. This can make it more difficult for people to access safe drinking water, worsen salinity intrusion in coastal areas, and create irrigation challenges for crops like Boro rice. For farmers, water shortages can increase production costs and lower crop yields.

How well prepared is Bangladesh to cope with an El Niño year? What should the government prioritise?

Bangladesh has some capacity to cope with El Niño through weather forecasting, irrigation infrastructure, and agricultural support programmes. However, the country still has limited capacity to independently forecast El Niño and prepare for its longer-term impacts, particularly in drought-prone regions. So, as I have indicated earlier, to better manage El Niño risks, the government should prioritise improving early warning systems, promoting drought-tolerant crop varieties, strengthening water management, supporting farmers, protecting groundwater resources, and maintaining adequate food reserves.

An important step forward would be to strengthen the capacity for monitoring and forecasting the El Niño-Southern Oscillation (ENSO). This can be achieved through closer collaboration between Bangladesh’s weather and climate institutions and leading international ENSO research centres. Such partnerships would improve access to climate information and support the development of more localised seasonal forecasts for farmers, policymakers, and disaster managers.

If you could give one message to policymakers and one to ordinary citizens about preparing for El Niño, what would that be?

Although there is still some uncertainty, current indications suggest that we may be heading towards a strong Eastern Pacific El Niño. If this develops as expected, Bangladesh could experience significantly drier-than-normal conditions during the latter part of 2026 and early 2027.

It is also important to remember that El Niño is only one component of a much larger climate system. Bangladesh’s rainfall patterns are influenced by several interacting climate drivers, including the Indian Ocean Dipole (IOD), the Madden-Julian Oscillation (MJO), and other large-scale oceanic and atmospheric processes. A reliable assessment, therefore, would require continuous monitoring of not only El Niño but also these other factors in the coming months.

My message to policymakers, therefore, would be: Do not wait until a crisis develops. Invest in early warning systems, strengthen water management, support farmers, and improve preparedness so that communities across the country are better equipped to cope with heat, drought, and possible water shortages.

My message to citizens: Stay informed through regular weather updates, use water wisely, and follow official guidance. Small actions by individuals and communities can collectively make a meaningful difference in reducing the impacts of El Niño.

title: ‘Unequal rural load-shedding is a symptom of a deeper structural crisis’
text:
Prof Dr M. Shamsul Alam, dean at the faculty of engineering at Daffodil International University and energy adviser at Consumers Association of Bangladesh (CAB), speaks with Monorom Polok of The Daily Star about the ongoing power crisis, persistent rural-urban disparities in electricity distribution, financial challenges facing the power sector, and the reforms needed to ensure a more reliable and equitable energy system in the country.

As always, rural areas have been facing far more power cuts than the cities this summer. Why has the gap become so severe? Is this a technical problem or a policy failure?

This is neither simply a technical problem nor merely a policy failure. It reflects a lacking in our collective understanding of equality.

Load-shedding is one of the clearest examples of discrimination. Rural areas experience far more outages than cities even though their electricity demand is lower and often concentrated during the evening. If rural consumers are subjected to load-shedding while urban consumers continue receiving electricity, then public services are being distributed unequally.

There is also a policy dimension. Consumers connected above the 33kV level are generally exempt from load-shedding. Most large commercial, industrial and institutional consumers in urban areas receive electricity through 132kV or 230kV networks. As a result, policy itself shields them from outages.

Our constitution says citizens should not face discrimination in receiving state services. If load-shedding becomes unavoidable because the state cannot meet demand, then that burden should be shared equally.

The impact of this burden goes far beyond households, of course. Rural economy also suffers heavily. Without electricity, irrigation is disrupted, fish die in the ponds during the dry season, poultry production declines, and small industries cannot operate as expected. When these and other rural sectors lose electricity, production falls, incomes decline, and government tax revenues also suffer.

Many experts say Bangladesh generates electricity based on fuel availability rather than actual demand. What does that mean, and how has it contributed to the current crisis?

The real issue is not whether electricity is generated according to fuel availability or demand. The real issue is how Bangladesh designed its generation capacity and fuel mix. Power systems should operate according to the principle of least-cost dispatch. The cheapest available fuel should always be used first. If sufficient domestic gas were available, gas-fired plants could operate first because they generate electricity at the cheapest cost. But domestic gas production has declined while imported LNG is expensive. As a result, only a fraction of existing gas-based capacity is being utilised.

Coal-fired electricity is also cheaper than oil-fired generation. Bangladesh has substantial coal-fired capacity, but it is not fully utilised apparently because importing coal also requires foreign currency that the government struggles to afford. Despite that, expensive oil-fired plants continue operating even though electricity from them can cost Tk 25 to Tk 26 per unit. Meanwhile, the cheaper coal-based capacity remains underutilised.

Bangladesh’s fuel mix also reflects policy choices made over many years. The country significantly expanded oil-based electricity generation capacity even though oil is among the most expensive fuels. At one stage, around a quarter of the country’s electricity came from oil-fired plants, and even today oil still accounts for more than one-fifth of generation. Maintaining this system places a huge financial burden on the government because imported fuel must be purchased with scarce foreign currency.

This creates the impression that electricity generation depends on fuel availability. In reality, generation is constrained by the government’s financial capacity. The government purchases only as much fuel as it can afford, and electricity production is limited accordingly.

As generation costs have risen, the government has struggled to pay fuel suppliers, repay infrastructure loans, and meet other financial obligations. The result is that electricity generation is increasingly determined not by consumer demand or installed capacity, but by how much fuel the government can actually afford to buy. That constraint has become one of the main drivers of recurring load-shedding.

Hence, the current crisis is less about technical shortages than about financial constraints. Bangladesh’s dependency on imported fuels has made electricity generation increasingly expensive. As fuel imports are rationed because of dollar shortages, electricity production is falling below demand, making load-shedding unavoidable.

How much of the power crisis is linked to the country’s dependency on expensive private power plants and the financial problems in the power sector?

The crisis has several dimensions. First, as I said before, heavy dependency on imported fuels has sharply increased generation costs. Had there been a least-cost fuel strategy, electricity could have been produced much more cheaply. Second, the issue is not simply that the private sector has been encouraged; private investment can work if it is properly regulated. The real problem is that regulation has failed.

The Bangladesh Energy Regulatory Commission (BERC) was created to regulate the sector, but a regulatory culture has never developed properly. Independent power producers, merchant plants, and other private generation models were introduced, but effective oversight remained weak. The state weakened many of the safeguards. Competitive procurement was relaxed under emergency legislation, reducing transparency and accountability. Once competition disappears, it becomes much easier for excessive costs and inflated profits to become embedded in the system. When private investment expands without strong regulation, the sector becomes vulnerable to exploitation. In Bangladesh, private investors have gained enormous influence over state decision-making, creating what I would describe as an oligarchic structure.

It should also be remembered that private generation has not necessarily been cheaper. Government data shows that in 2022, electricity generated with gas cost around Tk 5 per unit in the private sector but only around Tk 3 in the public sector. Hence, the current crisis is not simply about expensive private power plants; it is about the state’s declining ability to regulate the sector effectively. When regulatory institutions become weak while private interests become stronger, the balance shifts away from public interest.

Today’s crisis should not simply be described as an electricity shortage. The deeper problem is that the power sector itself has become financially distressed. Its liabilities exceed its financial capacity, it cannot repay its debts, and it faces an acute liquidity crisis. This crisis ultimately affects electricity generation itself and spreads into the wider economy. As electricity shortages reduce industrial production, government revenues decline. The state then borrows more, crowds out private investment, and eventually faces even greater fiscal pressure.

What are the most important reforms that Bangladesh should make to reduce recurring summer power cuts and ensure a more reliable electricity supply?

First, the government must recognise that this is not primarily a technical problem but a structural governance issue. Simply building more infrastructure without changing the institutions that manage the sector will only create further opportunities for waste and corruption. The existing administrative structure has lost public confidence and is not capable of delivering meaningful reform in its current form.

Second, Bangladesh should rapidly expand distributed renewable energy. Renewable electricity currently contributes only a small share of the national grid despite much larger potential. Instead of relying solely on centralised generation, the country should encourage thousands of small entrepreneurs to develop decentralised solar and other renewable projects. This would expand generation capacity while creating employment and gradually reducing dependency on imported fuels.

The original “electricity for all” policy has lost public credibility because many people believe inflated demand projections were used to justify unnecessary infrastructure projects that created opportunities for rent-seeking. The government must acknowledge that loss of confidence if it wants to rebuild trust.

Moreover, government-owned energy companies should operate on a cost-recovery basis rather than seeking profits. Their purpose should be to provide public services, not to maximise commercial returns. Electricity tariffs should reflect only the actual cost of providing the service. At the same time, the government must rebuild confidence in regulatory institutions. Public trust has declined because many people no longer believe regulators are acting independently or effectively. Regulation should protect consumers, not merely approve tariff increases or accommodate commercial interests.

Finally, energy should be established as a legal right. Citizens should have the right to receive electricity at a fair price, in the correct quantity and quality. Consumers should be able to challenge utility companies in court when they are harmed and should also have the legal right to propose tariff reductions before BERC. Without stronger public accountability, reforms in infrastructure or generation alone will not solve the underlying problems. Genuine energy justice requires enforceable rights, transparent regulation, and accountability throughout the sector.

title: ‘We need action-oriented research that explores solutions to drug addiction aligned with local contexts’
text:
Dr Md Tawohidul Haque, criminologist and associate professor at the Institute of Social Welfare and Research in Dhaka University, speaks with Marzana Tasnim of The Daily Star about the shifting drug scenario in Bangladesh, the failure of ‘zero tolerance’ policy, border smuggling, and the urgent need for structured rehabilitation.

A recent survey by Bangladesh Medical University found that around 82 lakh people use illicit drugs in the country, and nearly 90 percent of respondents said drugs are very easy to access. What do these findings reveal about the situation?

The statistics are frightening. They show that a large segment of our population is addicted, and the ease of access, both online and offline, is deeply concerning. When the availability of drugs increases in a society, the number of drug addicts naturally rises. While the study estimates around 82 lakh users, private information and our own assumptions suggest the actual number exceeds 1.5 crore. No matter how much the authorities talk about “zero tolerance” or how many measures the law enforcement agencies employ, they will bring no results at the end of the day if we cannot control the production of illicit drugs and their entry into the country. Easy availability completely defeats any recovery or enforcement efforts.

Respondents identified unemployment, peer pressure, and accessibility as the three main reasons for drug addiction. Are these factors sufficiently addressed in policy discussions?

They are major factors, but they are not unique to Bangladesh. There is no logical explanation for the idea that taking drugs will solve an unemployment situation. However, when an individual is unemployed for a long time, they become frustrated, lonely, and isolated. Under family and social pressure, they seek psychological relief and turn to drugs because they are readily available. Peer pressure is also universal, especially among school and college students. Personal observations show that most users in our country develop drug addiction during college, often beginning with smoking. When drugs are easily accessible, these triggers—frustration, unemployment, and peer pressure—become highly active, but without easy availability, people would seek healthier, alternative ways to cope.

The state currently lacks a proper system to address these root causes. We need our families, educational institutions, and religious and cultural bodies to actively build awareness and promote responsible behaviour. When these social institutions fail to engage, the tendency among young people to turn to drugs increases significantly. There is also a visible deficit in social movements to prevent this. Previously, social leaders were vocal against drugs. Now, those involved in the drug trade, their godfathers, and field-level dealers are so violent and dangerous that they attack anyone who protests.

Is there a realistic global model that Bangladesh can follow to control this problem?

Every country must design a model based on its own reality. A preventive model works best for us because most drugs available here are not locally produced; they come from outside. To be drug-free, the state must do two things: ensure zero drug production inside the country, and completely seal the borders, international couriers, and airports against drug entry.

In Bangladesh, the meaning of “zero tolerance” has become compromised. Some argue that we should control supply by controlling demand. It means that if people stop using drugs, dealers will stop importing. This demand-side model will not work here because supply comes first, and drugs are made available before people even become addicted. So, we must use a preventive model that completely cuts off the supply. Bangladesh is no longer in the initial stages of a drug problem; a large population has reached the final stages of addiction. Applying initial-stage solutions now will yield no results.

How do our neighbouring countries factor into this supply chain?

Reports and media sources indicate that there are numerous yaba factories along the borders of India and Myanmar. Unofficial information suggests that the majority of the yaba pills produced in these border factories are sold in Bangladesh. For producers, drugs are simply a profitable product, and Bangladesh is a lucrative market.

While we share a historical relationship with India, citizens expect two things: no border killings and no drug smuggling. Unfortunately, we have failed to keep our borders crime-free because of the immense financial transactions involved. If those tasked with border control and law enforcement fail to prevent these criminals, any internal discussion, research, or rehabilitation effort becomes futile.

Why is it so difficult for governments to get to the root of the drug trade?

Governments often prioritise popular rhetoric over strict implementation. While the number of arrests, cases, and drug seizures is high, the trade continues due to procedural loopholes. Cases are often drafted in a way that makes bail easily obtainable, allowing dealers to return to the trade immediately.

Although agencies like the Department of Narcotics Control and police have compiled extensive lists of drug dealers, the godfathers and main beneficiaries remain untouched. Their names are never revealed, which mostly happens due to political sheltering. Those providing shelter receive massive financial benefits without any investment. For them, the drug crisis is highly profitable, so they have no interest in stopping it.

We are seeing seizures of amphetamine-type stimulants (ATS). Is there a shift towards more dangerous substances, and is this linked to the rising violence in society?

There is a direct link between chronic drug addiction and crime, including sexual assault, rape, domestic violence, and theft. But I don’t think classifying drugs into “hard” and “soft” categories will benefit the country. Look at e-cigarettes or shisha lounges: even when regulations exist, enforcement is weak, and the fines are too minor to deter business owners. Furthermore, deceptive campaigns, like those claiming that yaba pills make people look beautiful, which circulated widely in the past, target and attract young people. The long-term impact of addiction is devastating, leading to job losses, financial ruin, and family breakdown.

We also hear reports of counterfeit drugs being manufactured locally. What is the situation regarding fake yaba?

There are numerous factories inside Bangladesh manufacturing fake yaba pills. This cannot be unknown to the state or law enforcement. The physiological damage caused by these counterfeit, chemical-laden drugs is even more terrifying than that of the original substances.

What would be an ideal rehabilitation environment for someone struggling with drugs, and what is your message to someone struggling with drug addiction?

We want those who have already become addicted to be rehabilitated and bring them back into society as healthy, functional human beings and citizens. For those who are chronically addicted, we certainly need rehabilitation services. We view these services in two ways: institutional support and community-based actions.

Institutional support involves keeping individuals in rehabilitation centres for a specific period, applying existing treatment methods, and taking initiatives to make them drug-free. Community-based actions are needed when someone returns from rehabilitation or is in the initial stage of drug consumption. Often, the drug-addicted person or their family is socially stigmatised. This acts as an obstacle to maintaining social relations or building new relationships. If society does not come forward to help these individuals get better, recovery cannot be achieved through institutional support alone.

However, we don’t have the slightest trust in the way rehabilitation centres have been established in Bangladesh. Most of these centres face allegations of torture, keeping patients asleep for long periods by administering sleeping pills, and taking large sums of money without providing proper rehabilitation. The alternative could be establishing government-run rehabilitation centres, managed according to modern, evidence-based models.

Do we have enough academic research to guide our drug policies?

Most current research is highly quantitative and focused on statistics. We need action-oriented research that explores solutions aligned with our unique socio-cultural, religious, and institutional contexts. While academics want to conduct large-scale studies, we are limited by funding, which restricts our respondent pool and makes broad generalisations difficult. If the government, the Department of Narcotics Control, or law enforcement agencies allocate research funds to academic institutions, we can conduct area-specific studies to map addiction patterns and design effective preventive frameworks. At the Institute of Social Welfare and Research, we continue our academic efforts to train students in drug prevention, but a comprehensive solution requires strong political will and state cooperation. We want to use our academic lenses and methodological processes to help transform society and rehabilitate drug users, but this requires the genuine cooperation and will of the government.
