title: Return of bangles as an everyday modern wardrobe staple
text:
Without warning, classic wristwear has slipped out of storage boxes and straight into daily rotation. This subtle styling shift proves that timeless pieces never truly disappear; they just wait for a new generation to wear them.

Be it traditional, western, or a mix of both, from festive wear to casuals, the new generation is embracing bangles as nearly an outfit staple. This versatile piece of jewellery comes in a wide range of colours, sizes and designs, with small local vendors and online businesses utilising the hype in full swing.

While contemporary designs like the “Turkish enamel” bangles or the translucent, multicolour and embellished with stones “Kashmiri” sets have been an online sensation, classics made of traditional glass never went out of style either.

Image Photo: Adnan Rahman

“Chunky” and thicker ones are also very widely adorned by women, especially recently. Previously they were limited to only being traditional “balas”, often painted with intricate details and sometimes, golden borders, but now they are even seen in plain silver or rose gold, with a metallic finish on the top-coat.

The latter is styled very commonly nowadays, with western outfits like midi gowns or short-sleeved frocks and tops.

Among those who have openly welcomed this new style, a vast majority are people who prefer maximalist fashion over simple ones.

Being tasked with the ever so difficult choice of selecting which bangle will make it outside the jewellery box to complete today’s look and listening to the “clattering” chime of bangles as they walk through the busy aisles of Dhaka, are only few of the many reasons that turn such a jewellery into more than just an ornament for women.

Image Photo: Adnan Rahman

Aside from the trendy and rapidly evolving designs, bold and statement pieces like those in oxidised sets and intricate, thinner bracelets, are also flourishing in the market. In other words, whatever the stylistic preferences may be, when it comes to bangles, there is usually something for everyone.

With the merging of traditional clothing with western elements becoming increasingly popular, incorporating bangles with all outfits has become a major contributor to this sort of fusion fashion. While a traditional kurta with jeans is quite common, a shirt and jeans paired with large bangles often proves to be an equally fitting look for that kind of wardrobe.

Image Photo: Adnan Rahman

Although recent trends have made it seem like the fascination for bangles among young girls is back and it is here to stay, looking back at the older generations' jewellery collections may make us wonder; Did this ornament truly ever leave the conversation? Or did the internet simply rediscover a timeless piece that has been loved by Bengali women for generations.

title: How to style a classic red saree for any modern occasion
text:
Mastering the art of wearing a red saree goes beyond the traditional drape. Discover smart blouse pairings, modern accessories, and unique draping tricks to make your favourite red piece pop.

Maybe it is the depth of Venetian red or maybe the sharp pop of crimson that just grabs attention. Put any of these reds on a saree and the same thing happens: she brightens from the inside and lights up a room. Maybe that is why it feels natural to us. We see it early, even before we understand style. It is in wedding photos, festivals, family albums, and old movies. In so many of these red sarees, colour, memories, and rituals seem to be tied together.

Image Photo: Salek Bin Taher

Of bridal and beyond

For Bangladeshi brides, red has been around for a long time. A classic Benarasi saree can make her look like a living painting. Adorned with gold ornaments or held together with zari design, it brings out a newlywed bride’s blush and beauty. Oftentimes, with the classic bridal ghumta, the saree becomes warm and soft.

A red Dhakaiya Jamdani gives a whole different vibe, which looks calm and graceful. With its woven scenes, it makes the whole saree seem like a tale. That seems quite similar to the red tant that often feels light and close, with small motifs and an easy way of falling.

Image Photo: Salek Bin Taher

Of draping and blouse

Then comes the part most people forget: draping matters. The athpourey style has its own look throughout the years. The anchal is set in a clear way, and the shape feels roomy.

The Nivi drape, which is the most popular and classic way to wear a saree, creates a different outline. If the anchal is open, or if there is a belt, it changes the mood of the saree to something modern.

A red drape can also look fabulous with several style combinations. Think of a vermilion saree with a dark green blouse. That combo can feel like the Bangladeshi landscape. If you want a sharper finish, try an ivory, black, or antique gold blouse with the red. For a gentler mood, choose a dusty rose or blush blouse. These shades calm the look but keep the same warmth.

Moreover, a red saree can look totally different with a high-neck blouse. You can also go for sleeves that stand out, or a more modern intricate back detail. But if your saree already has a lot going on, a plain blouse helps the most.

Image Photo: Salek Bin Taher

Of accessories and aesthetics

Adding accessories could also elevate a saree significantly — a few glass bangles for a classic touch, a watch with a vintage feel, or bold sunglasses when you want a more current vibe. Styling is not a strict rule. It is more about how you make that red saree match your own style.

Red sarees also look wonderful in photos. Red grabs the light and keeps focus, as you get a sweep of colour along the floor, pleats shifting when you move, and an Anchal sliding over one shoulder. The small changes add up, so the picture feels like a lovely moment.

Jewellery makes this moment even stronger. Gold beside red brings out warmth in both. It can be a bridal necklace, a traditional choker, or jhumkas that catch the eye. On the other hand, pearls and diamonds make red feel softer, and silver makes it cooler. Some days, though, the classic red saree only needs a tip, kohl-lined eyes, and a flower pinned into a bun.

Image Photo: Salek Bin Taher

Of an evergreen culture

A Bangladeshi woman can wear red in her own way. She might choose scarlet red with a plain, well-cut blouse. Or she may pick a red border that is deep and looks different from what others expect. She can also blend old family jewellery with newer items.

Yet, why does a red saree on a woman look so unmatched? Maybe there is not one clear reason. The colour matters, yes. But so does the beauty of carrying that shade through ages, cultures, customs, and styles. The zari can catch the light in little flashes while the border can be familiar. The flowers in hair can add softness while the anchal moves gracefully. Ultimately, a red saree is not just an outfit on women; it lingers like a tune and weaves through hearts like an age-old tale.

title: Effortlessly style every skirt cut for any occasion
text:
Transforming a garment from formal office wear to a relaxed weekend look is simpler than you think. By pairing structured pencil skirts with tucked tops or matching asymmetric hemlines with minimalist bases, you can elevate any outfit instantly.

Rumoured to have been around since prehistoric times, there are very few garments quite as versatile as skirts. Their evolution should be proof enough of their diversity in fashion.

Despite their potential for enhancing almost every outfit, they often remain neglected, a big reason for which is not knowing what kind of skirt is the right pick and the outfits each type of skirt flourishes in.

Starting off with the basics, the classic A-line is quite literally shaped as the letter “A”. It is fitted at the waist and grows outwards, usually staying above the ankles or even shorter, though longer maxi versions are seen too.

Image Photo: Sazzad Ibne Sayed

Often closer in looks to the A-line, the bell and godet offer similar features but are distinctive at the same time. The bell skirt is also fitted at the waist, but it “puffs” out and flares into outward pleats, mimicking a bell shape, while the godet skirt remains fitted till the hip-line and then grows outwards, usually with pleats. Both are more flowy than the A-line and offer dramatic movement below the waist.

All three of these skirts are usually relatively short in length, often seen in popular Hollywood depictions of girls’ school uniforms. They pair well with short tops, sweaters, or tucked-in shirts.

A fan favourite and very popular in the fashion world, you can never really go wrong with a sleek pencil skirt. It is associated with being very narrow and straight-cut, outlining and hugging the body from the waist to below the knees, though shorter versions also exist.

From formal office-wear to party outfits, pencil skirts can be styled with nearly any top, as long as it is short or tucked in, allowing the waistline and hourglass silhouette to steal the show. It is not flowy, and designers often recommend this type for curvy figures.

Another widely known and loved skirt variant, miniskirts have always remained in fashion and can be a classy addition to any outfit. Staying above the knee length, they may easily be one of the most versatile skirts, pairing well with both fitted and relaxed tops, tucked in or short in length. Jackets or blazers can also be styled with them, sometimes coming in matching sets too. Similar to the pencil skirt, miniskirts can also effortlessly handle both formal and festive looks.

Known for their length and comfort, midi skirts are considered a wardrobe staple, especially for people who style skirts in everyday outfits. They are usually below the knee, reaching only as far as the calf, and offer incredible flow and movement. They can be straight from the waist down or grow a little outward, often coming with relaxed pleats.

Unlike most other skirts, they pair well with longer and baggy tops such as those below the waistline and can be styled with cardigans and sweaters too.

Image Photo: Sazzad Ibne Sayed

Widely seen during summer at music festivals and carnivals, asymmetric skirts are a bold choice among the younger generation. Unlike other skirts with their rigid designs and fabrics, asymmetric skirts come in hemlines of unequal length and offer a diverse range of fabrics, colours, patterns and designs, with more room for styling. They usually speak for the entire outfit and can be paired with minimal base-colour tops or short blouses.

Aside from cuts, the fabric and design also classify skirts into different types. They can be lace-trimmed and made of silk or satin for an elegant look, while leather pencil skirts or denim miniskirts can easily add a bold touch to an outfit. Heavy georgette can be ideal for formal straight skirts, while lighter georgette in bright colours makes vibrant long pleated skirts.

To the average individual, most skirts may look the same. While the differences in each type of skirt can be harder to spot at first glance, a big reason why they are always so restrictively categorised is due to the differences in methods of stitching.

Both pleated skirts and bell or godet skirts have frequent, vertical pleats, but pleated skirts are stitched by repeated folding of fabric, while the others are made using flared fabric cut-outs and triangular inserts. A generalisation would therefore be a great dishonour to the craftsmanship of fashion designers and garment workers.

title: Why lightweight printed sarees are the ultimate everyday wear
text:
For generations of Bangladeshi women, watching a mother meticulously pin and tuck her saree was the ultimate lesson in personal style. Today, that legacy is getting a fresh, versatile update. Blending nostalgic elegance with lightweight modern fabrics, printed sarees are proving to be the most adaptable piece in a woman's wardrobe — effortlessly transitioning from corporate offices to weekend trips and celebrations.

Indeed, that little girl is still inside all of us. She may be a grown woman with children of her own, and yet she fondly remembers watching her mother putting on her saree, adjusting the anchal ever so delightfully on the shoulders. And then as soon as she unfurls the anchal over her arms, in a heartbeat she is transformed into an epitome of chic and poetic beauty.

Image Photo: Adnan Rahman

Always gracious and beautiful in her printed sarees, she is a vision of our mothers that will stay with us till we are grey and ancient.

Speaking of printed sarees, they are in a league of their own when it comes to the sheer variety. Soft, light and always a delight to wear and carry, printed sarees in georgette, chiffon, crepe, silk and other such flowy fabrics are perfect for a hot and humid climate like ours. What’s more, they are extremely flattering and have an instant slimming effect on all body types.

Versatility is another factor. Printed sarees are great for office wear, leisurely lunches with girlfriends, and everyday wear.

Imagine a busy day in your life: dropping children off at school and heading to your office where back-to-back meetings await you. Foreigner clients are due for an all-important meeting that you are heading to, and your attire of choice is a breezy, beautiful mint and peach georgette saree. Some pearls on your ears and neck bring elegance to your look, and your clients are impressed with your style and substance. That a woman draped in the most traditional of attires is a brilliant corporate leader is incredible- how!

Image Photo: Adnan Rahman

A saree can be so many different things, just like the woman in you. For a fun day out with your friends in the country, choose a funky striped georgette number to match with your friends’ crazy fun personalities. Amidst the lush green fields and clear blue skies, your vibrant saree will make you look ever so lovely and happy.

And then it’s that time of the year when your best friend is turning a year older and is throwing a fantastic party. You must put your best fashionable feet forward, and a fantastic cocktail piece is the only attire for it! Sleek and seductive, a golden cocktail saree with sparkling sequins will make you look like a belle of your friend’s birthday bash.

Floral chiffons are elegant and timeless. They flatter every woman. When in doubt, it is that one attire that will make every lady feel confident and beautiful. For your next ladies’ lunch, parent-teacher meeting, book club get-together, or dinner with your parents, a floral-printed saree is the best answer for all your sartorial questions.

title: Tangail taant: A classic saree for every weekday
text:
On a weekday morning, Tasfia Mumtarin is not thinking about making a fashion statement. She is thinking about Dhaka traffic. The dancer and sales executive at an automobile company has meetings ahead, several hours at her desk, perhaps a client visit, and dance practice later in the evening. Her question is simple: could a saree realistically survive all of that?

“I would wear sarees more often if I stopped thinking that wearing one meant I had to dress up,” explains Mumtarin. “If I can wear a cotton saree with a comfortable blouse, flats, a big work bag and almost no jewellery, then it becomes clothing rather than an occasion.”

That distinction may be precisely what the Tangail saree needs.

For a textile so deeply connected to Bengal’s clothing history, the Tangail saree increasingly finds itself in a curious position. We bring it out for Pahela Baishakh, Puja, weddings, office celebrations, and cultural programmes. Yet, the saree that could be one of the most practical pieces in a Bangladeshi wardrobe often waits patiently for an “occasion.”

Perhaps, the more interesting question is not how to preserve the Tangail saree, but how to wear it again.

A saree made for real life

There is little about traditional Tangail that inherently demands ceremony.

Tangail sarees are known for their fine texture, local motifs and detailed weaving, and can be made using cotton, silk or jute.

In 2025, UNESCO inscribed the traditional saree weaving art of Tangail on the Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity, recognising a weaving tradition sustained across generations of Basak and Jhola communities.

However, cultural importance does not mean a garment needs to become precious to the point of impracticality.

In fact, some of the qualities associated with taant make it especially appropriate for Bangladesh. Lightweight cotton, breathability and relatively uncomplicated care have long made handloom sarees suitable for humid weather and regular use

Fashion director and stylist Sonia Yeasmin Isha points first to accessibility.

“First of all, Tangail sarees are reasonably priced. They are affordable for almost everyone,” she remarks. There is, of course, enormous variation within the category. Everyday cotton Tangails coexist with elaborate, highly valuable pieces. A weaver from Tangail Saree Kutir Ltd. explains that Tangail should not be automatically equated with inexpensive casual wear.

“There are many expensive Tangail sarees. Some cost more than Tk 1,00,000,” he says. “These sarees can easily be worn at weddings or any kind of party.”

That range may actually be one of Tangail’s greatest strengths. It does not have to choose between the everyday and the extraordinary. The same weaving tradition can occupy both spaces.

Image Photo: Adnan Rahman

The problem may not be the saree

Ask many young women why they do not wear sarees regularly and the answers are predictable: too difficult to drape, too formal, too much fabric, difficult for commuting, uncomfortable for a full working day.

Some of these concerns are genuine. Others have as much to do with how we have learned to style a saree as with the garment itself.

We often construct a complete ritual around it. A matching blouse must be made. Jewellery needs to be chosen. The anchal needs to behave. The pleats must be exact. Hair and makeup suddenly require attention.

By the time the look is complete, what began as six yards of cotton has turned into an event.

Isha proposes treating Tangail much more freely. “It can be paired with almost anything and styled in many different ways,” she says.

For office wear, she suggests a blazer over the saree. A shirt can be knotted and worn as a blouse. In winter, a high-neck or black turtleneck can replace the conventional blouse, with a belt or jacket added if desired.

Even a familiar Tangail can therefore behave differently depending on what surrounds it. That may be particularly relevant for younger wearers who do not necessarily want to look “traditional” simply because they are wearing a traditional textile.

Stop saving your good sarees

There is another habit worth questioning: the Bangladeshi tendency to save clothes.

The beautiful saree remains folded because it is “too good” for work. Another is reserved for an invitation that never quite matches it. Years later, a wardrobe can contain perfectly wearable handloom sarees that have appeared in public only twice.

For Nafisa Raidah, a communications professional, repeat wear would make sarees much more appealing.

“If I buy a Tangail saree, I want to know I can wear it to work on Monday, to lunch with friends a month later, and then to a family dinner with different accessories,” she shares. “I don't want every saree to have one fixed identity.”

It is a useful way of thinking about sustainability too. Sustainable fashion is not only about what something is made from. It is also about whether we actually wear what we own.

An everyday Tangail does not require five separate sarees for five looks. One muted saree might be paired with a white shirt for work, a sleeveless blouse and silver jewellery for dinner, a contrasting cotton blouse for daytime, and a jacket during winter.

The repeat is not a styling failure. The repeat is the point.

Image Photo: Adnan Rahman

What about the stiffness?

One practical complaint about new cotton Tangail sarees is that they can initially feel crisp or slightly voluminous.

Isha acknowledges this. “Many people avoid Tangail sarees because the fabric can feel slightly stiff or puffy,” she clarifies. “However, after a few washes, it usually becomes much softer.”

That is an important everyday detail because we often judge handloom clothing straight from the shop rather than considering how natural fabrics change with use.

A saree that softens over time develops familiarity. It becomes easier to pleat, easier to move in and less intimidating. In that sense, an often-worn Tangail may actually become more useful than one permanently preserved in pristine condition.

For a workday, practical choices matter too: secure the pleats with pins, keep the pallu manageable, choose shoes that allow walking, avoid unnecessarily heavy jewellery and select a blouse that lets the arms move freely.

A saree does not have to be worn as though one is perpetually arriving at a reception.

Let the border do the talking

Tangail also lends itself naturally to restrained dressing.

Isha notes the variety within its visual language. Some sarees have broad, striking borders; others have narrow ones, while some place greater emphasis on motifs across the body. “In most Tangail sarees, however, the border is one of the main attractions,” she elaborates.

For someone beginning an everyday saree wardrobe, that means the textile can supply its own decoration.

A strong border hardly needs a statement necklace. A saree with small motifs can work with a plain blouse. Black, white, beige, indigo and other versatile blouse colours can remove the pressure to tailor something new for every saree.

The goal is not to make Tangail resemble Western clothing to call it contemporary. It is to remove unnecessary rules around how it must be worn.

The saree does not need rescuing. It needs wearing

The Tangail saree has already demonstrated an extraordinary ability to adapt. Weavers have long responded to changing tastes through new colours, designs and motifs. Historical reporting from Tangail likewise shows artisans producing both casual handloom sarees and more expensive versions while adapting designs to contemporary demand.

Its relevance therefore does not have to depend on nostalgia. Nor does honouring craftsmanship require keeping it behind glass.

UNESCO recognition understandably places renewed attention on Tangail’s weaving knowledge, communities and cultural importance. Bangladesh also lists Tangail saree as a registered geographical indication product. Perhaps, one of the most meaningful forms of this appreciation happens far away from exhibitions and ceremonies. It is when someone reaches into the wardrobe before work and chooses a Tangail.

Isha believes younger wearers are already drawn towards cotton and softer, more comfortable fabrics. What remains is to show them the possibilities. “We now need to introduce Tangail sarees to a wider audience,” she says. “People should be shown that these sarees can be worn in many different ways and styled in a variety of contemporary looks.”

For generations, Tangail's looms have produced extraordinary clothing. Perhaps the next chapter is wonderfully ordinary.

title: What inspires Gen Z’s funky hair colours?
text:
Want a trick to spot Gen Z in a crowd? Just take a look around. If your eyes catch flashes of lavender or burgundy, cherry red, electric blue, or any other funky hue splashed across someone’s hair, you’ve got it.

A flash of lavender at a coffee shop, ombre green and black curls on a university campus, or perhaps cherry red bangs peeking out from under a bandana! Colourful hair has become one of Gen Z’s favourite ways to express themselves, and they are nailing it effortlessly. In a world where trends come and go overnight, vibrant hair remains one of the generation’s boldest forms of self-expression.

“I usually colour my hair when I feel sad or down,” said Nabila Tabassum, a university student. “I always go for electric blue because somehow I feel that blue represents my personality and aesthetics.”

Image Photo: Collected / "Jessie Dee" Dabrowski www.jessiedee.net / Unsplash

For this generation, hair colour means more than what it looks like. They paint their hair not just to look cool but to let you know their personality.

Some dye it impulsively; some do it after a breakup. Others simply wake up one morning and decide black or brown isn’t cutting it anymore. Whatever the reason, one thing is clear: this generation is not afraid to wear its personality, quite literally on its head.

Muntaha Rahi, an artist, still remembers the first time she dyed her hair red. “I felt powerful, to be honest.” She added, “It gave me an incredible sense of confidence.”

For Rahi, experimenting with hair colour is not just about changing her appearance; it’s about how it makes her feel. “Once you discover the power of hair colour, you might keep changing the shades, but you will probably never want to go back to plain black,” she expressed with a laugh.

It’s hard to scroll through social media without watching a dramatic hair transformation video. One minute, someone’s showing off their natural brunette locks; the next, they are rocking icy silver or bubble-gum pink. Before you know it, you are wondering if maybe burgundy highlights would not be such a bad idea after all.

“I’ve definitely been influenced," stated Sabit Ahmed, a 26-year-old university student. “It was very impulsive. I was watching hair transformation videos, and then I felt like I had to paint my hair blue.”

Social media may spark the idea, but K-pop often seals the deal. With every comeback, idols seem to debut a new hair colour: platinum blond one month, mint green the next, followed by cherry red or ash grey.

Fans do not really copy the exact look, but they do borrow the confidence to experiment.

Image Photo: Collected / Maks Styazhkin / Unsplash

Western musicians and influencers have embraced the same playful approach, treating hair colour like an accessory that changes with the mood, the season or even the playlist.

Yet for many young people, colouring their hair goes beyond keeping up with trends. Sometimes, it’s less about the colour itself and more about how it makes them feel.

In Bangladesh, this hair colour revolution is quietly gaining momentum too. From university campuses to trendy cafes, these places are becoming showcases for ash grey, wine red, deep violet, copper orange and peekaboo highlights.

And of course, colourful hair comes with its own set of responsibilities. Sulphate-free shampoos become your bestie, maintaining a hair care routine becomes a regular thing, and you will probably learn more about hair masks than you ever expected. However, ask anyone rocking cobalt blue curls, and they will probably tell you it is worth every faded towel and every extra minute in the shower.

Because at the end of the day, funky hair is not just about following the trend. It’s a feeling that stays with you.

title: How to style corsets with sarees for every occasion
text:
Corsets were invented in the early sixteenth century to attain an hourglass shape by cinching the waist into submission! The earliest corsets were made by inserting wooden panels and whalebone into silk or layered linen bodices, and were worn by aristocratic men and women to attain better posture and structure. From being a marker of status to attaining a desired body silhouette, corsets have transformed from being an undergarment to being an essential element of an upper-class Victorian woman’s wardrobe, then eventually being discarded for their rigidity and impracticality.

Image Photo: Adnan Rahman

Corsets of yore were demonised by women forced to wear and endure them; their accounts have been immortalised in literature and various accounts of that time as being extremely restrictive. Fainting was a regular occurrence as blood circulation was severely limited, and bruises and wounds were commonplace from ‘tightlacing’ the corsets, well, too tightly!

Modern corsets are anything but; appealing, stylish and elegant, they look and feel fabulous and fierce!

Image Photo: Adnan Rahman

A saree, traditional as it is, when worn with a corset is a match made in sartorial heaven! A refreshingly modern way to pair two ancient pieces together to fantastic effect. In the Western world, corsets have always been a great reference point for legendary designers such as Jean Paul Gaultier, whose entire repertoire is based on it. Worn with pants, skirts, on top of shirts and even dresses, corsets are highly versatile. However, wearing corsets with sarees and lehenga is remarkably stylish and unique too. Not for the faint of heart, sarees worn with corsets make a fantastic statement and are a mark of a true-blue fashionista.

Image Photo: Adnan Rahman

When planning to wear a corset with a saree, keep the occasion in mind. A slinky sheer georgette number with a black lace corset will look fabulous for your next cocktail night.

Pick a lovely floral one for the next ladies’ lunch; contrasting colours also look lovely. For a chic dinner at your friend’s new penthouse apartment, pick an elegant corset with pearls and pull up your hair in a sleek bun. And that’s not all. Traditional sarees look drop-dead gorgeous when worn with a corset too!

Image Photo: Adnan Rahman

Pair your Kanjeevaram with a sheer, detailed corset and kundan jewellery and wow everyone at your cousin’s wedding!

title: Summer makeup tips for a long-lasting look
text:
Every year as summer returns, so does the challenge of doing long-lasting makeup. Along with the high temperatures and humidity, the search for the right products and techniques to have a durable makeup look becomes a part of our everyday struggles.

To make that search a little easier, we have curated a short guide containing some simple ways to ensure your makeup stays on longer during the heat.

Almost all long-lasting makeup guides begin by stating the importance of skin prep before doing makeup, and rightfully so.

As we all know, the biggest hurdle in having makeup last longer during hot days is sweat. The skin’s pre-condition before any makeup products are applied is a major contributing factor to sweating. Rubbing ice cubes or spraying some cold water on the face and letting it dry out is a great way to soothe the skin before the main show begins.

According to experts, for a long-lasting makeup look during summer, primers are non-negotiable.

They are always applied before foundation or any other product and are formulated to fill the pores of the skin and help control oil. Regardless of the skin type, primers are highly recommended as they help the other makeup products “grip” onto the skin. For dry skin, liquid-based primers containing hyaluronic acid can be a good choice.

While “glowy” makeup looks and creamy formulas have become more popular recently, in summer they can be the biggest enemy of makeup.

Swapping cream-based foundations and blush for powdered products and a matte makeup look is the ideal solution for humid weather. The powder also helps limit sweating by absorbing moisture.

Image Photo: Shahrear Kabir Heemel

Though the heat and humidity force many people to opt for more minimalist makeup looks, makeup artists often encourage using this opportunity to maximise on eye makeup instead.

Even if areas of the face such as the T-zone are at risk of excess sweat and oil, the eyelids and their nearby regions are at less of a disadvantage. Matte eyeshadow and waterproof eye-makeup products are the way to go during such weather.

Products and formulas aside, the techniques of applying and blending the makeup are also crucial in ensuring it stays on longer.

Instead of smearing or strongly blending the products against the skin, tapping it gently using brushes or a makeup sponge is highly advised. It is widely believed that relaxed skin is less likely to sweat profusely during and immediately after applying the makeup.

Another non-negotiable product for makeup during summer is setting spray or setting powder. They are a must to ensure all the products are locked in and remain intact for as long as possible. This is usually the final step in the makeup routine, and the product must be applied generously for it to work.

Most of these products are widely available and offer a great variety of brands to choose from. Some small changes to the regular makeup routine, replacement of certain products and adjusting to some new techniques can make a big difference in ensuring your makeup stays put longer during this heat.

title: Rising from the ashes: Ahmed Tuhin Reza and Tanzila Elma return with renewed purpose
text:
A fashion house’s return can mean more than reopening its doors. For House of Ahmed, it became an opportunity to rebuild with a clearer sense of identity and to make a stronger case for what contemporary luxury from Bangladesh can look like.

On 21 August, House of Ahmed marked the beginning of its Chapter 2 with the grand launch of its new space on the entire Level 6 of Ventura Mall in Gulshan. The evening brought together members of the fashion industry, media, clients and supporters, while the space itself offered a visual introduction to the brand’s renewed direction.

The launch followed a major setback caused by a fire that disrupted the brand’s operations. For Reza, however, the return was not about recreating what existed before. According to Tanzila Elma, Co-Founder, House of Ahmed, around 24,000 fresh red roses were used across the event space, from the backdrop to the welcoming area.

Inside the store, House of Ahmed’s signature zardozi craftsmanship appeared in installations inspired by Bangladesh. Ahsan Manzil, Lalbagh Fort, a handmade map of Bangladesh, a Dhaka rickshaw and a sewing machine were recreated through intricate zardozi work.

Another display celebrated Nakshi Kantha, Benarosi, Muslin and Jamdani, centred around the shapla motif. References to the Sundarbans, a Cox’s Bazar sampan, Jessore’s date palm and Barishal’s palki further connected the interiors to different parts of the country.

The overall concept and ideation for the space came from Ahmed Tuhin Reza and Tanzila Elma, while Saimul Karim of Eskay Décor was responsible for translating that vision into the final interior design with meticulous attention to detail.

With Chapter 2, House of Ahmed’s return was therefore not simply a reopening, but a renewed statement of ambition, craftsmanship and confidence in Made in Bangladesh luxury.

Who Wore What

title: Giving children a voice through fashion
text:
Bangladesh Street Kids Aid uses skateboarding to connect with street-involved and underprivileged children. It also links them to education, medical and hygiene support. The children of BSKA have found confidence, discipline and a powerful form of self-expression through skateboarding. For a special Star Lifestyle project, that spirit became the starting point of a collaboration with three creative professionals who approached the children not simply as subjects of a photoshoot, but as individuals with their own stories and identities.

Image Photo: Shadab Shahrokh Hai

“When they are in motion, they look like a flock of butterflies”

For Sara Hossain, Director of Craftsman Footwear & Accessories Ltd, designing shoes for the children began with an image that stayed with her. She had seen photographs of girls skateboarding in sarees during Pahela Baishakh, moving with a confidence that challenged familiar ideas about how girls should dress or occupy public space.

“To me, it felt like a rainbow in a cloudy sky,” Hossain recalls. “When they are in motion, they look like a flock of butterflies.”

That sense of movement, colour and freedom shaped the footwear she created for the Star Lifestyle photoshoot. Bright mustard, green, magenta and contrasting combinations were chosen with the children’s ages and energy in mind.

“Being a girl in Bangladesh is difficult,” she says. “Doing something out of the norm is even harder.”

For the BSKA children, that philosophy resulted in shoes designed not to tone down their energy, but to keep up with it.

Image Photo: Shadab Shahrokh Hai

“They should hold their heads high when they are wearing something they created themselves”

I saw a couple of videos of the children on social media and fell in love with the statement of freedom and self-expression they demonstrated,” recalls Sharmin Rahman, creative director and designer.

For the photoshoot, Rahman decided the clothes should begin with the children themselves. She wrote to them and asked them to draw whatever they liked. Those drawings became the visual language of the 11 outfits.

Rather than refining the drawings into conventional motifs, Rahman preserved their uneven lines, spontaneous colours and individual character.

“I thought these children are extraordinary and they should be presented as who they are and in their true spirit,” she explains. “They should hold their heads high when they are wearing something they created themselves.”

The project reflects Rahman’s broader design philosophy. Before thinking about silhouette or decoration, she considers who a garment is made for, its purpose and the story it should portray. For her, responsible fashion extends beyond sustainable fabric to the use of local materials, techniques, artisans and community capabilities.

Image Photo: Shadab Shahrokh Hai

“We wanted to be a part of their happiness”

Khalid Mahmood Khan and the Kay Kraft team helped turn the creative language of the outfits into wearable garments.

“We felt connected to the concept when Sharmin Rahman shared the idea in her very own way,” says Khan, Entrepreneur, Kay Kraft.

Each outfit was designed around an individual child’s artwork, making the project closer to made-to-order work.

“Usually, Kay Kraft does ready-to-wear products. This collection was like individual samples for the children, with their own drawings incorporated in individual pieces,” Khan explains.

Preserving the individuality of those drawings required extra attention.

“From a production point of view, it needs a bit more effort and care to keep individuality and uniqueness,” he says.

The team approached the work enthusiastically, knowing the children would eventually see their own drawings transformed into garments. Khan credits Rahman for developing the concept and guiding its execution, while noting that the project also aligned naturally with Kay Kraft’s broader mindset.

For him, however, the most rewarding part was emotional rather than technical.

“We know that the children will be happy and more spirited, inspired wearing this,” Khan says. “We wanted to be a part of their happiness.”

title: The hidden language we speak through jewellery
text:
Long before jewellery became a fashion statement, it was a way of saying something without uttering a word. Across cultures and centuries, people have worn different kinds of jewellery made from gold, silver, iron, or beads to communicate who they are, where they belong, and what they value.

If we think about that for a moment, some of the oldest known jewellery, tiny shell beads discovered in Morocco, dates back more than 140,000 years. That indicates humans were making and wearing ornaments long before agriculture, cities, or even writing!

From an anthropological perspective, this tells us that jewellery was never simply about looking beautiful; it was an early form of symbolic communication.

Image Photo: Sazzad Ibne Sayed

What makes this even more fascinating is that jewellery was completely unnecessary for survival if we think logically. Someone had to find a shell, make a hole in it and carefully turn it into something wearable. And why make that effort? Simply because humans have always attached meaning to objects, using material things to express identity and enhance social connections.

Across many African societies, jewellery has functioned as a visible social language. Take beadwork, for example, which can communicate age, marital status, social position and ethnic identity.

Among the Maasai of Kenya and Tanzania, the colours or stones indicate wealth or ethnic identity, while certain materials, motifs and arrangements of beads carry special meanings; in parts of West Africa, gold jewellery has historically been associated with status, authority, and wealth.

Image Photo: Sazzad Ibne Sayed

These things may look decorative to outsiders but can work almost like a social code within the community.

We can find a similar idea among the indigenous communities of Bangladesh, although each group has its own traditions. This includes communities such as the Chakma, Marma, Garo, and Santal. Ornaments made from beads, silver, coins and locally available materials have been part of cultural identity forever.

In Mongolia, traditional jewellery has also conveyed information about the wearer’s identity and social status. Silver ornaments and pieces of coral, turquoise and other stones have been incorporated into elaborate headdresses, earrings, necklaces and clothing decorations, with styles diverse among different Mongolian groups.

Different types of colour or stones indicate wealth or ethnic identity, while certain materials and motifs were also associated with protection and spiritual beliefs.

Image Photo: Sazzad Ibne Sayed

East Asia offers another fascinating example. Traditional Chinese jade has historically been connected with virtues, protection and social status, while Korean norigae ornaments conveyed symbolic and aesthetic meanings.

In Japan, kanzashi hair ornaments could indicate the wearer’s age, social setting and occasion. The object itself signified meaning, but cultural knowledge is also important to understand.

Across Bangladesh, we see this communication take another shape in everyday life. We often see gold ornaments, bangles and especially nose rings have long been associated with marriage. The meaning depends not only on how they look but also on who wears them and what occasion they are worn for.

Image Photo: Sazzad Ibne Sayed

And lastly, there is the jewellery we choose simply because it feels like us. We might wear silver. It suits our attire, colourful beads because they reflect our personality, or a handmade statement. After all, we want something unique.

Even without knowing the cultural history behind it, our ornament choice tells people something about how we see ourselves. That is why naming jewellery merely an accessory feels incomplete.

The materials of the jewellery have changed, from shell and bones to gold and silver, gemstones and beads, but the tendency remains remarkably familiar: we decorate ourselves to communicate about ourselves.

title: 7 historic Bangladesh temples to visit this Durga Puja season
text:
Looking to experience authentic autumn festivities beyond urban crowds this Durga Puja? From the intricate terracotta walls of Dinajpur to Sitakunda’s misty hilltop shrines, Bangladesh offers remarkable heritage trails. Here is your curated guide to seven ancient temples offering unforgettable history, culture, and architecture.

As Durga Puja approaches this autumn, temples across Bangladesh prepare to come alive with worship, colour, music and gatherings of devotees. But beyond the festive atmosphere, many of these temples carry stories that stretch back centuries, preserved through distinctive architecture, enduring traditions and generations of worshippers.

From elaborate terracotta walls to hilltop shrines and temples that have survived war and upheaval, each offers a different glimpse into the country’s religious and cultural heritage. This Puja season, here are seven temples worth visiting for the stories they hold as much as the sights they offer.

Image Photo taken from Facebook

Kantajew Temple, Dinajpur

Including Kantajew Temple in a list of Bangladesh's must-visit temples almost feels inevitable. Built in the 18th century under the patronage of Maharaja Prannath, the temple is best known for its extraordinary terracotta work, with its walls carrying scenes from the Ramayana, Mahabharata and Krishna's life, alongside glimpses of life in Bengal.

Originally built in the Navaratna style, its nine spires were destroyed by the 1897 earthquake, but the elaborate terracotta panels survived. The temple also comes alive during the annual Rash Mela around Rash Purnima, when the month-long fair draws devotees and visitors to the area. Even without the festivities, however, Kantajew is the kind of place where simply walking around the walls can keep you looking for another detail.

Image Photo: Sazzad Ibne Sayed

Dhakeshwari National Temple, Dhaka

Dhakeshwari National Temple has a long history, with its name, meaning “Goddess of Dhaka”, closely tied to the city's identity. The temple is traditionally associated with King Ballal Sen of the Sena dynasty and is believed to date back to the 12th century, although its present structure has changed considerably through repeated renovations. The complex includes four small Shiva temples beside its historic pond.

This temple hosts the city’s largest Sharadiya celebrations, with Mahalaya marked by Chandipath recitations and the Chokkhu Daan ritual that “opens” the goddess’s eyes. On Dashami morning, the iconic procession winds from the temple to Wiseghat for immersion, while devotees fill the grounds.

Puthia Temple Complex, Rajshahi

Puthia feels more like an entire temple landscape than a single architectural masterpiece. The historic complex in Rajshahi is home to a remarkable collection of temples, ponds, and remainders of the Puthia Raj family’s estate. The complex includes the Govinda Temple, the lakeside Bhubaneshwar Shiva Temple and curved Dolmancha used for Rath Jatra.

Built mainly between the 18th and 19th centuries, the temples showcase different forms of Bengal’s religious architecture, with terracotta and traditional silhouettes appearing across several structures. The large Shiv Sagar pond adds another layer to the setting. Rather than rushing from one shrine to another, Puthia is best experienced as a place to wander, look around, and take in how closely its temples and old landscape fit together.

Chandranath Temple, Sitakunda

Reaching Chandranath Temple is part of the experience. Perched on 350‑metre Chandranath Hill in Sitakunda, the temple is one of Bangladesh's best-known pilgrimage sites, and is regarded as one of the 51 Shakti Peethas where part of Goddess Sati's body fell.

Thousands of devotees make the climb each year during the Shiva Chaturdashi festival, turning the usually quiet hill into a lively pilgrimage route. While Mahashivratri brings the largest crowds, Sharadiya Puja also draws devotees who combine Navaratri worship with the hill’s panoramic views. For visitors who enjoy places where the journey is almost as memorable as the destination, Chandranath is difficult to overlook.

Bhabanipur Shaktipeeth, Bogura

Set beside the Karatoya River in rural Bogura, Bhabanipur temple complex is regarded as one of the Shakti Peethas, where devotees worship Goddess Bhavani, also known as Aparna. Bhabanipur has grown into a larger sacred complex with several shrines, Shiva temples and a pond known as Shankha Pukur.

Daily Devi puja, recitations of the Devi Mahatmyam and seasonal festivals keep the complex alive. During Sharadiya Puja, pilgrims from across Bangladesh and neighbouring India gather for special rituals. Its quieter setting makes Bhabanipur particularly interesting for anyone curious about Bangladesh’s older traditions of goddess worship and living pilgrimage culture.

Ramna Kali Temple, Dhaka

Ramna Kali Temple carries a history that goes far beyond its role as a place of worship. Located beside Suhrawardy Udyan, the temple is believed to have originated as an ashram several centuries ago before the main temple was built and expanded under Rani Bilashmoni Devi. Its most devastating chapter came in 1971, when the temple and the adjoining Ma Anandamoyee Ashram were destroyed during the Liberation War.

The site was later rebuilt, with the reconstructed temple inaugurated in 2021. Today, the temple hosts major Kali Puja and Sharadiya Durga Puja celebrations, with pushpanjali, arati and Sindur Khela drawing thousands on Dashami. Today, Ramna Kali stands as more than an old temple in the heart of Dhaka, bringing together religious heritage and national history.

Jeshoreshwari Kali Temple, Satkhira

In the village of Ishwaripur in Satkhira, Jeshoreshwari Kali Temple is one of Bangladesh's most significant pilgrimage sites. The temple is believed to have been established centuries ago and has undergone several changes over time. Its surviving Natmandir, with its rows of pillars, is one of the most recognisable parts of the site.

While Kali Puja is the main annual draw, Sharadiya Navaratri and Durga Puja are also observed with village‑wide festivities. For visitors willing to travel beyond the usual tourist circuit, Jeshoreshwari offers a quieter encounter with one of Bengal's oldest traditions of Goddess worship.

title: Marriage should not be a ban on travelling with friends
text:
There is a strange transformation that supposedly takes place after marriage. You get a spouse, perhaps a new home, a few additional responsibilities, and, according to some people, an automatic cancellation of your friends-only travel plans.

Before marriage, a weekend in Sylhet with university friends requires little more than a group chat, a bus ticket and someone trustworthy enough to book the hotel. After marriage, the same trip can suddenly become a family discussion.

Who is going? Where are you staying? Why are you going without your wife? Why is your husband going without you?

Somewhere along the way, travelling with friends after marriage started looking less like a holiday and more like a suspicious activity.

But perhaps marriage does not have to mean that every trip must now be a joint venture.

For many couples, travelling separately is simply another part of maintaining an individual life within a shared one.

“Getting married did not suddenly make my friends disappear,” says Farhan Rahman, a software engineer. “I still enjoy travelling with them. My wife knows my friends, knows where we are going and knows when I am coming back. That is enough. Going on a trip without her does not mean I am trying to escape my marriage,” he laughs.

A common myth is that couples who truly love spending time together should naturally want to do everything together. But marriage does not erase personal preferences. One partner may dream of a quiet beach holiday, while the other considers waking up at five in the morning to hike a mountain peak.

There is also something healthy about maintaining friendships outside the marriage. Friends knew you before you became somebody’s husband or wife. They have witnessed your terrible haircut, your university disasters and possibly the phase when you thought you would become a professional photographer after buying a camera phone.

Why should marriage require abandoning that history?

"There is a huge myth that if you love your husband, you should want to do everything together," exclaims Nishat Tasnim, a school teacher who recently returned from a trip to India with her girlfriends.

"My husband stayed back managing our cat and office work, while I ate street food in Kolkata until midnight. When I came back, we actually had things to talk about besides grocery bills and laundry. My advice is to stop falling for the trap that independence equals a lack of commitment. Absence makes the heart fonder, not distant."

Of course, freedom does not mean disappearing without explanation. Separate travel works best when it comes with communication. Discussing the dates, budget, accommodation and responsibilities at home is not asking for permission. That is a kind of consideration that both partners should have for one another.

“If one person is always travelling while the other is handling everything at home, resentment will obviously build,” explains Adnan Karim, a business analyst. “The point is not that you should do whatever you want. It means that both people should have the same space to enjoy their friendships. Fairness matters more than keeping score.”

For couples with children or other family responsibilities, planning may require even more effort. Someone may need to manage school runs, elderly parents or household work while the other is away. This simply means that the freedom to travel comes with responsibility.

Moreover, travelling separately does not automatically mean that a couple is emotionally distant.

Sometimes a few days apart can be a reminder that two people entered a marriage as individuals before becoming partners.

“People sometimes think if your partner wants to travel with her friends, you should feel threatened,” says Rafia Chowdhury, a biotechnology professor. “I do not see it that way. Trust is not built by keeping someone beside you all the time. If anything, knowing that we can have our own experiences makes our relationship feel more secure.”

A married person going on a trip with friends should not immediately trigger a neighbourhood investigation. Nor should a wife booking a girls’ trip require a courtroom defence.

You can miss your spouse while sitting beside your oldest friends on a bus. You can spend three days eating questionable food with your college group and still come home excited to show your partner the photographs. You can have a life together without having to share every single moment of it.

After all, getting married should give you someone to come home to. Travelling after marriage does not have to give you a reason to stop going anywhere.

title: A visitor’s guide to exploring Old Dhaka’s Armenian heritage
text:
Discovering one of Old Dhaka’s best-kept secrets require knowing exactly where to look behind the bustling market stalls of Armanitola. Use this guide to experience the striking architecture, sacred courtyards, and centuries-old stories of the Armenian Church.

Old Dhaka rarely offers a moment of silence. Its narrow streets are almost permanently in motion, but step inside the Armenian Church compound in Armanitola and the city suddenly feels different. The noise recedes as birds replace horns. White walls edged in gold rise above a quiet courtyard of trees, flowers, and gravestones. At the centre stands the Armenian Apostolic Church of the Holy Resurrection, its dome and cross visible against the Dhaka sky.

Image The white-and-gold Armenian Apostolic Church of the Holy Resurrection rises above Armanitola in Old Dhaka. Photo: Imama Karim

The calm is striking. However, the most interesting thing about this place is not its tranquillity or even its architecture. It is what the church reveals about Dhaka itself!

Long before Armanitola became simply another familiar name on the city's map, an Armenian community lived, traded, worshipped and buried its dead here. Most of that community is gone. Remarkably, much of its physical story is not.

Armenians of Dhaka

Armenian merchants had established themselves in Bengal by the 1600s and became particularly influential in Dhaka's commercial life during the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries. Their trading networks connected Bengal's goods, particularly textiles, with markets beyond the subcontinent.

Their community was never particularly large, but its presence mattered. They became involved in trade, property and civic life. Nicholas Pogose, one of nineteenth-century Dhaka's prominent Armenian figures, founded Pogose School in 1848. The name Armanitola itself carries that history.

Image The cemetery surrounding the Armenian Church holds the graves of generations of Dhaka's Armenian community. Photo: Imama Karim

The Church of the Holy Resurrection was built in 1781 on land associated with an Armenian burial ground. More than 350 burials have historically been linked to the site. And today, those graves are impossible to ignore.

They sit across the churchyard and beneath its covered corridors. Some gravestones are incorporated into the ground itself, so visitors quite literally move through the names and inscriptions of people who lived here generations ago. It makes the compound feel less like a conventional historical attraction and more like a surviving piece of the community itself.

Image The cemetery surrounding the Armenian Church holds the graves of generations of Dhaka's Armenian community. Photo: Imama Karim

A church that does not overwhelm

Historic churches are often associated with scale and elaborate decoration. This one is different. It is compact, bright and unusually intimate.

White dominates the building, with gold used around arches, columns and architectural details. The decoration is noticeable without becoming overwhelming. Sunlight against the white surfaces makes the interior feel almost luminous.

Then there are the smaller details.

Image White surfaces, gold accents and restrained ornamentation shape the church's distinctive architectural character. Photo: Imama Karim

Old wooden furniture sits inside the church. Gold floral patterns run along parts of the interior. Religious paintings and objects occupy the altar. A carved eagle forms part of the Gospel stand, traditionally associated with St John the Evangelist.

Individually, these might seem like minor details. Together, they make the church feel lived-in rather than monumental. There is also something interesting about seeing this architecture in Dhaka. The church belongs unmistakably to an Armenian Christian tradition, but it has existed in Bengal for more than two centuries. Its surroundings, climate and long relationship with the city make it difficult to think of it simply as a foreign object transplanted onto Bangladeshi soil. It has become part of Old Dhaka's landscape.

A piece of Armenia

That connection becomes particularly visible outside the church.

Among the greenery stands a khachkar, or Armenian cross-stone. They are part of a centuries-old Armenian tradition, typically featuring a carved cross surrounded by intricate geometric and botanical patterns. The craftsmanship and symbolism associated with them are recognised by UNESCO as Armenian intangible cultural heritage.

Image A khachkar, or Armenian cross-stone, stands amid the greenery of the church compound in Armanitola. Photo: Imama Karim

Seeing one surrounded by tropical plants in the middle of Old Dhaka is an unusual sight. But perhaps it shouldn't feel strange.

Cities have always been shaped by people who moved into them. Communities brought languages, religions, food, businesses, craftsmanship and architecture with them. Over time, those influences became part of the cities themselves.

Dhaka is no exception.

The Armenian Church therefore raises an interesting question: when does the heritage of one community become the heritage of an entire city? In this case, the answer seems fairly clear. The church may be Armenian in origin, but its history is also Dhaka's history.

Image Armenian inscriptions and intricate carvings survive on gravestones across the church compound, leaving a tangible record of the community that once called Dhaka home. Photo: Imama Karim

More than preserving an old building

Dhaka changes quickly. Old buildings disappear, neighbourhoods transform and traces of earlier versions of the city become harder to find. Against that reality, the condition of the Armenian Church is remarkable. The compound is clean, maintained and clearly cared for.

But preserving a heritage site involves more than protecting its walls. If people stop knowing why the church exists, who built it or why the surrounding neighbourhood is called Armanitola, something important is still lost.

The building survives, but its meaning begins to disappear. That is why places like the Armenian Church matter. Not because every old building must be romanticised, and not simply because the church is beautiful; it matters because it complicates the story we tell about Dhaka.

The city's history was never created by a single community. Armenians were one of many groups whose lives became intertwined with it, and Armanitola is one of the places where that layered history remains visible.

Outside the compound, Old Dhaka continues at full volume. Inside, the white-and-gold church, gravestones and Armenian cross-stone quietly tell another version of the city. You only have to know what you are looking at.

title: Solo travel can teach you more than any group trip ever
text:
The cultural expectation to travel in packs is quietly fading away. More explorers are trading crowded itineraries for quiet streets, discovering that travelling alone unlocks a deeper sense of confidence and inner resilience.

In an era of group chats, constant connectivity, and the deep-rooted cultural expectation to travel in packs, booking a ticket for one can feel like a radical act. Whether it is a weekend getaway or a backpacking trip, travelling alone is often met with unsolicited warnings about safety, boredom, or isolation. However, embarking on that journey is one of the most transformative experiences a person can have, irrespective of gender.

Psychological research backs this up. Studies published in the International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health note that solo travel forces individuals out of their social comfort zones, accelerating personal growth, cognitive flexibility, and self-reliance in ways group travel rarely allows.

When you are entirely responsible for navigating foreign streets, making split-second decisions, and solving your own problems, a quiet resilience begins to build from within.

When you travel with others, vacations are often built on compromise. You adjust your sleep schedule, debate over restaurants, and visit attractions to please the crowd. Solo travel strips away all of that noise, leaving an itinerary that belongs completely to you.

For first-timers, the thought of dining alone in a restaurant can be overwhelming, but overcoming this challenge is worthwhile.

"I spent three days in Oslo without speaking a single word to anyone outside of hotel staff, and it was the most liberating experience of my life," shares Lamia Ahmed, a 28-year-old engineer. "There was no pressure to rush through museums or match someone else's energy. I could sit in a park and watch the clouds over the Oslo Fjord for four hours, and that stillness taught me how to enjoy my own company.

Image Photo: Collected / Redd Francisco / Unsplash

“My biggest advice to anyone trying solo travel for the first time is to drop the rigid itinerary. Do not map out every single minute of your day. Allow yourself the discomfort of getting lost, because that is usually where you find the best hidden cafes and unexpected moments of peace," Lamia announced excitedly.

This sentiment captures the essence of “solomaxxing”, the modern lifestyle movement that reframes being only by yourself not as a sign of isolation, but as a deliberate choice for self-discovery and mental clarity.

For many, particularly women, the hesitation to travel solo is deeply tied to safety concerns. While caution is always necessary, letting fear dictate your horizons keeps you confined. Cities like Oslo or Tokyo, frequently ranked among the safest and most pedestrian-friendly capitals in the world, offer an ideal testing ground for first-time solo explorers looking to build confidence.

"As a man, society tells you that you should always be the protector and provider, but solo travelling taught me how to be comfortably vulnerable," notes Zahin Rahman, a 34-year-old corporate strategist who recently spent a week wandering through Japan's capital.

"When you are in a city where nobody knows your name, you drop all your social masks. You realise that you are entirely capable of taking care of yourself in a completely unfamiliar environment. My advice for men considering a solo trip is to leave the ego at home. Avoid approaching the city as a tourist who is merely ticking off items on a checklist. Let the city happen to you,” Rahman added.

A common misconception about solo travel is that it is a lonely endeavour. In reality, travelling this way often makes you more approachable. Without the barrier of a companion or a group, you are far more likely to strike up conversations with locals, sit at communal coffee tables, and notice the microscopic details of a city that crowds usually blur out.

"When you are not in a group, the world feels louder, sharper, and somehow more intimate. If you are planning a solo trip, try to spend at least one afternoon walking without headphones or maps. Just listen to the city breathe. It changes your entire perspective on how small you are, and yet, how much of the world is open to you,” fathomed Sumaiya Raka, a freelance journalist and a frequent solo traveller.

Ultimately, a solo trip is an exercise in profound trust. It teaches you that you are good company. In a world that constantly demands our attention, time, and energy for others, a solo journey gives those resources back to you. You return home not just with photographs of new landscapes, but with a renewed sense of confidence. You learn that you can get lost, figure it out, and still find your way. And that is a lesson worth travelling for.

title: ‘Congratulations to Boeing and Biman’: US ambassador on 11-aircraft deal
text:
Biman Bangladesh Airlines, the country’s national flag carrier, is set to sign an agreement with US aircraft manufacturer Boeing to acquire 11 additional aircraft during Prime Minister Tarique Rahman’s visit to New York for the 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly.

The agreement is scheduled to be signed at 4:15pm (local time) on Wednesday at the prime minister’s place of residence, in the presence of senior Bangladeshi and US officials.

"Congratulations to Boeing and Biman on the agreement to purchase 11 more of the world’s best commercial planes. Another win-win for the US-Bangladesh relationship! Will be tuning in to the signing ceremony in New York later today," US Ambassador to Bangladesh Brent T Christensen said on Wednesday.

The ambassador said this in a post from his verified X handle.

In April, Bangladesh signed a $3.7 billion deal with US aircraft manufacturer Boeing to buy 14 planes for national carrier Biman Bangladesh Airlines, marking the airline’s biggest-ever aircraft order.

title: How actress Sonia Hossain redefined pregnancy and motherhood at 40
text:
She feels that her decision to become a mother and her experience of pregnancy were not defined by her age. She had food aversions in her first trimester, including a strong aversion to meat. “But those are your body’s natural reactions to hormonal changes, and not connected to the mother’s age at all!” she said.

Other than these, Hossain remembers no complications. Her energy levels improved in the second trimester, and she continued to dance and swim until the very end.

“I have always been an energetic person, and I wanted to be honest to my daughter as well,” she said.

Image

Hossain thought of the baby as an extension of herself, as the ultrasounds began to suspiciously look like her baby was trying to emulate yoga asanas!

“It’s also got a lot to do with the people around you,” notes the actress. “Everyone was trying to keep me happy. My husband was being a rock for me to lean on, ensuring that I am the happiest home for my Imaan. There seemed to be no reason to stress about anything.”

Hossain mentioned that ever since she was in her 20s, she had lived by a mindset that allowed her to receive, rather than to chase. “I didn’t want to have a child in Bangladesh, and I shared as much with Hansa Yogendra, founder of the Yoga Institute, during a podcast.”

Image

She also shared that she was close to her 40s and apprehensive about her ageing body.

Hansa Ma encouraged her to think beyond age alone, saying that a healthy 40-year-old can have a good pregnancy just as an unhealthy 25-year-old can have a difficult one. Sonia remembers having been told that she would be entrusted with this blessing when the Almighty thought she was ready for it.

“And that is exactly what happened. Even after moving to the States, I was not ready to have a baby. But it happened naturally, and I accepted it,” she said.

Sonia Hossain never went for IVF treatments or for egg freezing as she believed in the divine plan and had long tried to approach life with trust rather than fixation. “I felt that it would happen if it was meant to happen, and if not, I would accept that as part of the bigger plan.”

Image

During the pregnancy, Hossain not only drew inspiration from regular recitations of the Holy book, but her spiritual and mental preparation also included Garbh Sanskar classes. The classes helped her think of the child as a person in their own right, with Sonia Hossain serving as a beloved vessel, caretaker and mentor.

“This sort of a mindset allowed me to shake off undue pressure about the birth or my role as a mother, and view pregnancy as a rite of passage for my daughter’s arrival,” Hossain said.

When asked whether choosing to breastfeed her child had made her a healthier eater, Sonia Hossain said she had not consciously changed her habits after the baby.

Image

“It was my child who was changing me for her own needs,” she mused. She remembered a teaching from class: the baby had “built her home” before coming into her.

She remembers that while not specifically for pregnancy, she had made a lot of steady, positive changes to her lifestyle over the last three years. “I dropped unhealthy habits, got into dance, fitness, yoga, good food, deep sleep, and mindful thoughts. I did it for myself, and for my health, and I believe that these changes helped me a lot to get pregnant at 40 as I was already on track.”

Sonia Hossain’s story is personal, not a prescription. Pregnancy after 35 can involve additional considerations, and people’s health and circumstances do differ. This article in no way tries to invalidate the struggles of those who are facing trouble in their personal journeys of family life, pregnancy and childbirth. However, Sonia Hossain’s message is really for those who are scared to try, who are worried before there is a reason to be. It is an effort to demystify pregnancies above 35 and usher in positivity in place of anxiety.

“Prepare yourself, prepare your future baby’s home with good food, sleep, happy thoughts and good people. And above all, trust the divine. The beauty of surrendering to the will of the Almighty is that there is no scope to be worried,” Sonia Hossain concluded.

Photo: Sanjaya Das Joy
