title: How cancer counselling helps you navigate treatment and rebuild confidence
text:
Facing a life-changing diagnosis involves far more than medical appointments and prescriptions. From handling treatment burnout to easing difficult family conversations, working with a therapist provides essential tools to navigate the emotional side of recovery.

Most of us picture counselling sessions as a chair, a box of tissues and an hour of talking about chronic depression. And for someone fighting cancer, that picture can be the very first thing that keeps them from walking through the door.

The reality, however, is broader. A psychologist or counsellor is not there only to hear about your feelings of distress, but also to help you manage the many challenges that come with a diagnosis, including fear, treatment-related stress, changes in your body, difficult conversations at home, questions about work, and a future that suddenly feels uncertain.

The first thing many patients meet, though, is not sadness but disbelief.

Abdul Hamid, who is a prominent psychotherapist at the Monobikash Foundation, says, "The most common reactions after a diagnosis are non-acceptance and denial. 'This can't be happening to me' is a way of protecting oneself from something too large to take in at once."

That is why a psychologist primarily assists cancer patients in coming to terms with their diagnosis and gradually accepting the changes it brings to their lives. Hamid clarifies that encouraging patients to "stay positive all the time" is not how counselling sessions work. It is more about creating a safe space for them to express their fears, frustrations, and uncertainties without judgment.

Through emotional support, realistic reassurance, and positive encouragement, they assist patients in recognising their strengths, acknowledging their efforts, and rebuilding their confidence in their ability to navigate the journey ahead.

Even small affirmations such as acknowledging their courage in attending treatment or their determination to keep going despite challenging days can strengthen their sense of self-worth and agency.

The goal is not to deny the reality of the illness but to empower patients to confront it with greater emotional resilience, hope, and confidence. In Hamid’s experience, individuals who are psychologically and mentally strong tend to respond better to medication.

In practice, most psychologists begin by simply listening. They want to know what has happened, what worries you most, and what support you currently have in place. You do not have to share your entire story all at once, nor do you need to have the "right" words to express yourself. And over the course of several sessions, the conversation typically shifts to specific issues and how to address them.

Along the way, many patients arrive carrying fears and uncertainties: fear of pain, treatment, and the unknown. Hamid says a counsellor helps identify these fears so they no longer operate in the dark. Treatment itself can often be a source of stress. Side effects, waiting for scan results, making difficult decisions, and the exhaustion that comes with hospital routines can wear a person down, even when the treatment is progressing well.

The body’s changes bring their own struggles. "The physical changes may lead individuals to feel self-conscious, prompting them to avoid social interactions," Hamid mentions. "In such cases, counselling can be beneficial in helping to rebuild confidence and comfort in being seen by others."

Hamid mentions how relationships change too, as partners take on caregiving roles, intimacy shifts, and some friendships fade. Returning to work after treatment raises further questions about energy, disclosure, and how colleagues will react. These changes are worth discussing rather than keeping silent.

Throughout, counselling is not only about talking. Practical tools, such as ways to manage anxious thoughts, coping with negative rumination, and ways to pace daily life, are part of the work.

Ultimately, a psychologist cannot change a diagnosis. However, they can provide a supportive, non-judgmental environment and assistance in initiating difficult conversations. While medicine addresses the illness, counselling supports the individual experiencing it.

title: 6 everyday habits for stronger bones beyond calcium supplements
text:
Building resilient bones requires far more than taking daily calcium pills. From pairing local small fish with leafy greens to incorporating simple weight-bearing exercises, here is how to craft an actionable, everyday lifestyle plan for lifelong strength.

When we hear the words “strong bones”, most of us immediately think of calcium. There is a problem with this line of thinking. Bone health is much more than calcium. It is a living tissue. Throughout our lives, old bone is continuously broken down, and new tissue is formed. This complex process depends not only on calcium, but also on vitamin D, protein, other micronutrients, physical activity, hormones, body weight and overall nutritional status.

Bangladesh receives abundant sunlight throughout much of the year. Yet, vitamin D deficiency and insufficiency remain surprisingly common. A recent laboratory-based study of adults in Bangladesh found that only 12.2 per cent of participants had sufficient vitamin D; 49.3 per cent were deficient, and another 38.5 per cent were insufficient. Women had a higher prevalence of deficiency than men.

Image Photo: Collected / rohit choudhari / Unsplash

Calcium remains a fundamental nutrient for bone health. However, the question should not simply be, “How much calcium am I taking?” The better question is, “Am I getting enough calcium from an overall balanced diet?”

Milk and yoghurt are familiar calcium sources. But Bangladesh has many other possibilities, such as small fish eaten with their edible bones, appropriate leafy vegetables, and calcium-fortified foods where available, and calcium-containing soy products.

The problem is that dietary calcium intake can be inadequate in some Bangladeshi populations. Research among premenopausal Bangladeshi women has demonstrated low calcium intake and suggested that inadequate intake may compromise bone accretion and increase future osteoporosis risk. This is why calcium supplements should not become a substitute for a nutritious diet.

Image Photo: Collected / Mathew Schwartz / Unsplash

Bone contains an organic matrix in which collagen and other proteins provide an important structural framework. Adequate protein is particularly important during childhood and adolescence, when peak bone mass is being developed, and later in life when muscle and bone loss become increasingly important.

Along with a nutritious diet. bones need mechanical stimulation. Weight-bearing and resistance exercises stimulate bone and muscle. Regular physical activity also improves strength and balance, which can help reduce the risk of falls.

For a healthy adult, brisk walking, stair climbing, resistance exercises, and appropriate sports can all contribute to a bone-friendly lifestyle.

For older adults, balance and strength exercises become particularly important. However, exercise should be individualised. Someone with osteoporosis, a previous fracture or significant musculoskeletal disease may need professional guidance before starting high-impact activity.

Image Photo: Collected / Ekaterina Kuznetsova / Unsplash

Osteoporosis is often regarded as an “old person's disease.” This is misleading. Bone health is built across the life course. Childhood and adolescence are crucial periods for accumulating bone mass. Research among Bangladeshi women has shown that bone mineral density begins declining relatively early in adulthood and declines more rapidly with advancing age. This means that waiting until the age of 50 or 60 to think about bone health is too late. Healthy eating, adequate protein and calcium, appropriate vitamin D status, physical activity and maintaining a healthy body weight should begin much earlier. This is particularly important for girls and young women because inadequate nutrition during the years when peak bone mass is being established can have consequences decades later.

Women experience accelerated bone loss around menopause because the protective effect of estrogen decreases. Bangladesh-specific research highlights the concern. Women with low body weight, poor nutritional intake, limited physical activity, vitamin D deficiency, early menopause or other clinical risk factors may require additional assessment. And osteoporosis is not exclusively a women's disease. Men can also develop osteoporosis, particularly with ageing, chronic illness, nutritional deficiencies and certain medications.

So, what does a bone-friendly Bangladeshi diet look like? It does not have to be complicated or expensive.

Include a calcium source regularly: Milk, yoghurt, small fish with edible bones, suitable leafy vegetables and fortified foods can contribute calcium.

Eat adequate protein every day: Include fish, eggs, dairy, poultry, lean meat, dal, beans, soy, nuts and seeds according to individual needs.

Pay attention to vitamin D: Safe, appropriate sunlight exposure and vitamin-D-containing foods can contribute to maintaining vitamin D status. Individuals with deficiency may require supplementation under medical supervision.

Eat plenty of vegetables and fruits: A varied diet supplies magnesium, vitamin K, potassium and other micronutrients and bioactive compounds involved in overall musculoskeletal health.

Stay physically active: Combine weight-bearing activity with muscle-strengthening and balance exercises where appropriate.

Maintain a healthy body weight: Being underweight is associated with poorer bone health, while obesity can also create musculoskeletal and mobility problems.

​The author is the Chief Clinical Dietitian and Head of the Department, Dietetics and Nutrition Department, Continental Hospital PLC

title: How private fitting room questions inspired the Breast Health Hub
text:
Understanding your body doesn't require complex medical jargon—just three simple steps practiced once a month. Discover how the simple routine on the Breast Health Hub empowers you to recognize subtle changes early and navigate local care with total confidence.

For many women, questions about their breasts begin early. What does a lump mean? If breast cancer runs in the family, should one be worried? And if someone has never had a breast check-up, where should she even begin? These are some of the questions Monoshita Ayruani, founder of a lingerie brand, says her team has repeatedly heard from women during private bra fittings. Now, those conversations have led to the launch of the SHAPE Breast Health Hub, a free online resource designed to help women understand what is normal for their own bodies and recognise changes that may need medical attention.

Launched on October 7, during Breast Cancer Awareness Month, the Hub is available in both Bangla and English.

Image

“Bangladesh makes bras for the whole world, and none of them were cut for our women. So, I began measuring women, one at a time,” Ayruani said. Seven years later, they design seamless, wire-free bras for Bangladeshi women using their own sizing system based on measurements of local women.

A fitting session at SHAPE is twenty private minutes with a fit advisor, and in those minutes women ask questions that have nothing to do with bras. For years, Monoshita Ayruani says, the team could only advise women to see a doctor. “But the questions kept coming, in the fitting room and in our women’s community late at night. They came from women who had nowhere else to ask.”

That gap in accessible information became one of the reasons behind the Breast Health Hub.

A simple habit: Look, Feel, Notice

At the centre of the Hub is a three-word monthly awareness habit: Look, Feel, Notice. The idea is to help women become familiar with how their breasts normally look and feel, so they can recognise when something changes. The Hub explains changes that should be discussed with a healthcare professional and provides information on where women can begin seeking care in Bangladesh, including public hospitals and private clinics.

Users can also set a monthly reminder for themselves, either through their calendar or by writing a reminder to themselves or someone they trust on WhatsApp. The Hub is deliberately positioned as an awareness resource, rather than a medical tool.

Image

“It is not a diagnosis. It is not screening, and it says so clearly: knowing your normal does not replace the screening a doctor recommends for your age and history,” Ayruani explains.

It is also not a shopping page. No products are displayed while users are reading the health information, and Ayruani says information entered or ticked on the page is not saved or sent to the store.

Awareness, not diagnosis

The Hub contains a Signs section covering eight changes, including a new lump, changes in breast size or shape, skin dimpling, new nipple inversion or discharge, redness or warmth, and pain that remains in one place. For each, the Hub explains in plain language what the change can mean and advises users that a new or persistent change should be assessed by a healthcare professional.

The Hub does not provide users with a numerical risk score or categorise them as low or high risk.

“The boundary is this: the Hub will never give a woman a score, a tier or a ‘low risk’ label,” Ayruani says. “A short quiz cannot know anyone’s risk, and a reassuring label from a bra company could delay real care.”

The distinction is central to how they describe the platform: awareness, yes; assessment, no.

Building the information responsibly

The page lists sources for its figures and clinical information. It draws on public education materials from relevant organisations. The Hub also distinguishes US-based figures and explains that such figures do not automatically apply to Bangladesh.

Before its launch, the complete text was reviewed by two practising doctors. Their feedback resulted in changes to the description of the awareness habit, the removal of symptom time-frames, the wording around survival statistics, care navigation and privacy.

Taking the message beyond the website

The Breast Health Hub launched on October 7 and will remain available throughout the year.

Over the next two weeks, they plan to promote it through posters in hospitals and clinics across Bangladesh with partner Green Delta Life Insurance, cards at reception desks around Dhaka, and the brand’s own digital channels.

For Ayruani, the desired impact is both simple and ambitious. “I want ‘know your normal’ to become an ordinary phrase among Bangladeshi women, as ordinary as asking your bra size,” she says. She hopes women who notice a change will know that seeking medical advice is the appropriate next step, without panic or shame.

For details on the breast health hub, visit: https://shapelingerie.com/pages/breast-health-hub

title: Is depression contagious? What psychotherapists want you to know
text:
Moods and stress can quickly spread between close partners, but feeling low after supporting a friend isn't always clinical depression. Experts break down the fine line between temporary emotional contagion and a serious mental health condition.

We often think of depression as a deeply personal struggle, something that exists within the mind of the person experiencing it. But what happens when someone close to us is depressed? Can their sadness, hopelessness, and emotional exhaustion begin affecting us too? While depression itself is not an infectious disease, the emotions surrounding it can influence people who share a close relationship with someone experiencing depression.

In a recent interview with psychotherapist Abdul Hamid of the Monobikash Foundation, he explained that depression can be emotionally contagious. “When someone very close to us is depressed, we may end up carrying their emotions,” he explains. In some situations, this emotional impact can extend beyond one person and affect an entire group.

However, feeling low after witnessing someone else’s suffering does not automatically mean that a person has depression. Hamid explains that if someone experiences deep sadness, emptiness, or loss of interest for 14 days or more, and these feelings significantly interfere with everyday activities, relationships, and lifestyle, it may indicate depression. The distinction between temporary emotional distress and clinical depression therefore remains important.

The emotional weight of close relationships

The impact can become particularly significant when the relationship is emotionally close. A partner, family member, close friend or caregiver may spend considerable time listening to the depressed person’s struggles and witnessing their difficulties. Over time, this constant exposure can create emotional exhaustion. The caregiver may begin feeling helpless, hopeless or overwhelmed, especially when they feel responsible for helping the other person recover.

This does not mean that we should become emotionally detached from someone who is suffering. In fact, empathy remains essential. “We cannot become robots,” Hamid says. We need to understand another person’s pain and respond with compassion, but there is a difference between feeling someone’s emotion and making that emotion our own. The goal is to remain empathetic without taking ownership of another person’s suffering.

Image Photo: Collected / Stormseeker / Unsplash

That is where healthy emotional boundaries become important. If someone else’s depression is beginning to affect our own emotional wellbeing, we need to recognise the change and establish boundaries. Hamid suggests that we can listen and remain supportive without allowing the other person’s emotional state to completely take over our own. If necessary, maintaining some distance while continuing to show empathy can also be healthy.

For caregivers, this distinction becomes even more important. Hamid compares emotional wellbeing with physical health: just as we do not physically take another person’s illness into our own body, we should not carry their emotional problems as our own. Caregivers need to remain conscious of their own emotional state and watch for signs that they are mirroring the depressed person’s feelings.

When professional help is needed

So, what should someone do when a close person’s depression begins affecting them? Hamid suggests first paying attention to whether the person’s suffering appears to have reached a clinical level. Sometimes, an accident, traumatic event or difficult experience can deeply affect someone and create significant emotional distress. Instead of trying to personally solve the person’s depression, suggesting professional help may be a more appropriate response.

Trying to become someone’s personal therapist can also create another problem: judgement. When we desperately want to help someone, we may start giving unsolicited advice, comparing their experience with ours or telling them what they should do. Even when our intentions are good, such responses can make a depressed person feel misunderstood. Professional support can provide a safer and more appropriate space for addressing serious psychological difficulties.

At the same time, caregivers should not silently absorb their own discomfort. If someone feels that another person’s depression is affecting them, sharing that discomfort with a trusted person can be helpful. However, confidentiality must also be respected, particularly when the person is acting as a caregiver. Supporting someone does not give us permission to disclose their private struggles without considering their dignity and privacy.

Recognising the warning signs

The warning signs can sometimes become surprisingly similar. According to Hamid, when emotional distress becomes strongly mirrored between a depressed person and their caregiver, the caregiver may begin experiencing symptoms such as losing interest in activities they previously enjoyed, changes in sleeping patterns, significant changes in appetite, social withdrawal and persistent negative thoughts about themselves.

These changes should not simply be dismissed as the price of caring for someone. If a caregiver feels that another person’s depression is gradually consuming their own emotional wellbeing, early intervention is important. Seeking professional guidance at the primary level can help the caregiver understand what they are experiencing and develop healthier ways of supporting the other person without sacrificing their own psychological wellbeing.

The digital spread of emotional distress

Technology has added another dimension to this emotional influence. We are increasingly individualised while remaining deeply connected through technology, particularly social media. Emotional states can now travel far beyond close personal relationships. A person’s posts, videos or public expressions of distress can reach thousands or even millions of people, potentially influencing the emotions of audiences who have never met them.

Consider a social media influencer openly expressing their experience with depression. If that content reaches hundreds of thousands of followers, a portion of that audience may emotionally identify with the person’s experience. For some viewers, particularly those already struggling emotionally, such content may become triggering. What begins as one person’s personal experience can therefore have a much wider emotional impact in the digital environment.

This does not mean people experiencing depression should hide their stories or remain silent. Sharing personal experiences can reduce stigma and encourage people to seek help. The concern is about how audiences consume and respond to emotionally intense content. Social media users should recognise that repeatedly consuming another person’s distress can affect their own emotional state, particularly when they already feel vulnerable.

Empathy without absorbing the pain

Supporting someone with depression requires more than empathy. It requires boundaries, awareness and, when necessary, professional help. We can listen without absorbing, care without carrying, and support without trying to become the person responsible for another’s recovery. As Hamid explains, we need to acknowledge another person’s feelings without taking ownership of their suffering. Sometimes, protecting our own emotional wellbeing is also part of being able to care for someone else.

title: How to get enough Vitamin D without ruining your skin
text:
Soaking up natural sunlight doesn't mean risking skin damage or spending hours outdoors. Exposing just 20 per cent of your skin between 10 AM and 3 PM for 15 to 30 minutes gives your body the exact boost it needs to absorb calcium and protect your bones.

Bangladesh is blessed with abundant sunshine. Yet vitamin D deficiency is an important nutritional concern. Vitamin D is essential for calcium absorption, bone mineralisation, muscle function and skeletal health. Severe deficiency can cause rickets in children and osteomalacia in adults.

A review of studies conducted in Bangladesh between 2002 and 2022 found a substantial burden of vitamin D deficiency, particularly among women, pregnant women and older adults.

Why deficiency in a country full of sunshine?

The answer lies in the difference between sunlight availability and meaningful sunlight exposure. Urbanisation and modern lifestyles have reduced outdoor activity. Many people spend most of their day indoors. Women who spend limited time outdoors may be particularly vulnerable.

Sociocultural clothing styles that cover most of the skin reduce the area available for vitamin D production. Sunscreen, cosmetics and skin pigmentation also play a role. People with darker skin generally require greater ultraviolet-B exposure to produce the same amount of vitamin D as people with lighter skin. Older adults have a reduced capacity to synthesise vitamin D through the skin, while obesity and limited physical activity may also contribute.

What does vitamin D deficiency do?

The strongest evidence relates to bone and muscle health. In children, severe deficiency can impair bone mineralisation and cause nutritional rickets. In adults, prolonged severe deficiency can result in osteomalacia, bone pain and muscle weakness. Adequate vitamin D should therefore be viewed as one component of broader bone health, alongside calcium, protein and physical activity.

Low vitamin D levels have also been associated with obesity, diabetes, cardiovascular disease, autoimmune disorders and infections. However, an association does not necessarily mean supplementation prevents or treats these diseases. Vitamin D is an essential nutrient, not a universal cure.

Who needs particular attention?

Some people deserve closer nutritional and clinical attention, including:

• Pregnant and breastfeeding women

• Infants, children and adolescents with limited outdoor exposure or inadequate dietary intake

• Older adults

• People who spend very little time outdoors

• Individuals with obesity

• People with disorders or medications affecting vitamin D metabolism

Assessment should be based on individual risk rather than indiscriminate testing.

Food first—but food alone may not always be enough

Naturally occurring dietary sources of vitamin D are relatively limited. Fatty sea fish such as hilsa and rupchanda are good sources. Egg yolk, liver and meat provide smaller amounts, while fortified foods can contribute where available. Improving access to appropriately fortified foods could be an important public-health strategy.

Sensible sunlight has a role

Regular outdoor activity can contribute to vitamin D production and offers additional health benefits. However, there is no universal amount of sun exposure that guarantees adequate vitamin D. Production depends on skin pigmentation, age, season, time of day, clothing, exposed skin area and air pollution.

There is a thumb rule that the best time to get natural vitamin D from sunlight in Bangladesh is between 10am and 3pm, when UVB rays are strongest. Exposing at least 20 per cent of the body for 15 to 30 minutes is generally enough, although needs vary by skin tone.

Therefore, “more sun” is not necessarily the answer. Sensible exposure should be balanced with protection from excessive ultraviolet radiation and skin damage.

Should everyone take vitamin D supplements?

Not necessarily. Supplementation can be useful when deficiency is diagnosed or an individual has a recognised indication. Taking large doses without medical or nutritional guidance is not harmless.

Vitamin D is fat-soluble, and excessive intake can lead to toxicity and hypercalcaemia, with potentially serious complications.

The 2024 Endocrine Society clinical practice guideline does not recommend routine vitamin D testing or supplementation above the recommended dietary intake for generally healthy adults under 75 without specific indications. Certain groups may benefit from supplementation according to age and clinical circumstances.

What Bangladesh needs

Vitamin D deficiency is not simply a problem to be solved by prescribing tablets. A sustainable solution requires sunlight, a healthy diet, physical activity, appropriate fortification, targeted supplementation and evidence-based clinical care.

The bottom line

Bangladesh may have abundant sunshine, but sunshine alone does not guarantee adequate vitamin D. The better approach is to spend sensible time outdoors, eat a balanced diet, remain physically active, identify those at risk and use supplements when clinically appropriate.

The author is Chief Clinical Dietitian and HOD, Dietetics and Nutrition Department, Continental Hospital PLC

title: The ultimate guide to daily caffeine limits and timing
text:
Juggling coffee, tea, and soda throughout the day makes tracking milligrams nearly impossible. Knowing your exact limits and setting a firm afternoon cutoff can completely transform your daily energy levels.

For many of us, the day starts with a cup of coffee and runs on a few more. A cup of tea at 11 AM, a cola with lunch, and an espresso before the evening meeting. The milligrams add up faster than we realise.

Chowdhury Tasneem Hasin, Chief Clinical Dietitian and Head of the Dietetics and Nutrition Department at Continental Hospital PLC, explains where the limits lie and why they matter.

Know your numbers

Healthy adults can take 350 to 400mg of caffeine a day, according to Hasin. "That comes to around four small cups," she says. During pregnancy and breastfeeding, the limit drops by half.

Children need stricter rules. "Children under two should not have caffeine at all," she says. For children aged 8 to 12, she caps intake at 100 mg a day.

Your drink of choice changes the count.

Tasneem puts a cup of black tea at 47 to 50 mg and a can of caffeinated drink at around 40 mg. A regular cup of coffee carries about 100 mg, instant coffee holds less at 50 to 60 mg, and a single shot of espresso delivers roughly 70 mg.

Image Photo: Collected / Jocelyn Morales / Unsplash

In cups, she keeps it simple. "Three to four cups is the maximum. If you drink it black, without milk or sugar, keep it to two or three. During pregnancy and lactation, one to two cups."

Caffeine has real medical uses. Hasin notes that doctors give caffeine to semi-sedated patients to raise alertness, and certain pain relievers contain it as well.

It lifts your mood too. "Caffeine triggers dopamine and norepinephrine, and that improves how you feel," she explains. Coffee also contains polyphenols, and she adds that caffeine may reduce the effects of Parkinson's and Alzheimer's disease.

Coffee will not do all the work for you

Plenty of people drink coffee to lose weight. Chowdhury Tasneem Hasin confirms that caffeine speeds up metabolism, so your internal organs use more calories. She warns against relying on it.

"Weight loss does not come from coffee alone. You need a calorie deficit," she says. "And adding sugar defeats the purpose."

Sugar complicates the picture further. According to her, coffee makes you alert while the sugar gives you a quick hit, and the two work together to make the habit harder to break.

A higher dose does not mean faster results. "Too much caffeine causes jitters and raises your heart rate," she says. Sleep plays a part here. Your body burns calories while you sleep, so a late cup that costs you rest also costs you progress.

When it goes too far

“Excess caffeine brings stomach upset, headaches, and anxiety,” Hasin says. Caffeine also acts as a diuretic, pulling water out of your body. "Too much caffeine causes dehydration, and that is dangerous," she warns.

Dependence worries her most. "The brain can easily become dependent on caffeine. It is much more difficult to control than people think," she says. She describes caffeine as a major addictive substance, one people underestimate because it sits in drinks they have every day.

Timing your cup

Tasneem draws a firm line in the afternoon. "No coffee after sunset. Have your last cup by 4 or 5 PM so you get proper sleep and your brain gets rest," she advises. Drinking coffee close to bedtime, she adds, can even cause nightmares.

Mealtimes matter as well. The tannins in coffee reduce how much iron your body absorbs from food, so she recommends waiting 40 to 60 minutes after a main meal before you reach for a cup.

None of this means giving up your morning coffee or evening tea. Hasin's advice comes down to counting your cups, cutting out sugar, and finishing your last one before the sun goes down.

title: Truth about menopause and your suddenly rising heart risk
text:
Many women assume heart disease is an inevitable consequence of ageing after midlife. Cardiological insights prove that proactive habits and timely screenings can keep your heart strong.

When people think of heart disease, they often picture an older man clutching his chest, rather than a middle-aged woman. However, heart disease has long been one of the leading causes of death in women, and the risk does not increase gradually over a lifetime; it rises sharply after menopause. Fortunately, it is largely preventable when the groundwork for prevention begins from adolescence.

Why menopause changes a woman's heart risk

Dr Ashraful-Ur-Rahman, who is a Medicine Specialist and a Cardiologist at the National Institute of Cardiovascular Diseases (NICVD), explains that before menopause, estrogen hormone levels provide real protection for heart health. “Before menopause, men are roughly twice as likely to have a heart attack or develop heart disease compared to women of the same age. But later the risk is almost the same.”

What can women do during and after menopause?

Dr Rahman emphasises the importance of annual screenings to detect potential health risks.

It is recommended that individuals undergo an EKG (electrocardiogram) and check their lipid profile and blood sugar levels every year starting at around the age of 45. Additionally, women with a family history of cardiac diseases should be particularly alert about their health.

Sleep and stress levels require attention as well.

Hot flashes and night sweats are not only uncomfortable but are also increasingly associated with cardiovascular risk, especially in women under 60. Smoking and vaping should be completely avoided starting from the teenage years. Not to mention, it is important to maintain a healthy body weight according to the Body Mass Index (BMI).

Avoiding self-diagnosis

Dr Rahman points out that heart disease can be particularly dangerous for women because it does not always present in the typical way. The classic heart attack symptom, often described as an "elephant on the chest," differs from what many women experience. Instead, they may show subtler signs such as unusual fatigue, nausea, shortness of breath, or pain in the jaw, neck, or back, which are often dismissed as stress, indigestion, or simply a sign of ageing.

Dr Ashraful-Ur-Rahman also cautions against self-managing hormonal therapies, which are used to manage menopausal symptoms and protect bone density. They can raise the risk of stroke and blood clots when done without expert supervision.

In the end, ensuring a healthy heart starts long before menopause, with a teenage girl who stays active and intakes nutritious food.

The evidence is clear: most of the risks associated with heart health are modifiable. Warning signs can be identified, and the sooner these signals are addressed through proper diet, regular physical activity, routine screenings, and informed discussions with a doctor, the better the long-term outcomes will be.

title: Dhaka’s office lunch: What are we actually eating?
text:
Healthy office eating does not mean giving up traditional Bangladeshi food. It means building a more balanced plate and a better routine around it.

A typical Bangladeshi office lunch may feature a generous portion of white rice with fish, chicken or meat, perhaps some daal and vegetables, and sometimes a soft drink or a dessert.

It is important to remember that rice itself is not the problem. It is a traditional staple and can absolutely be part of a healthy diet. The bigger question is: What is on the rest of the plate? If rice occupies most of the meal while vegetables, daal and other forms of protein are limited, the lunch may be filling without being nutritionally balanced. Similarly, generous amounts of oil, fried foods, rich gravies, and sugary beverages can add considerable calories without improving nutritional quality.

Image Photo: Collected / Bayu Syaits / Unsplash

A healthier office lunch should provide a sensible balance of whole or minimally processed carbohydrates, protein, vegetables, fibres, and healthy fats.

In a city where healthy food choices around the workplace may not always be readily available, bringing lunch from home can provide greater control over ingredients, portion sizes, cooking oil, salt and overall balance.

A simple home-packed lunch does not have to be elaborate. Rice or rooti, fish or chicken, daal, two types of vegetables and some salad and a fruit or handful of mixed nuts for mid-morning or afternoon can make a nutritious and culturally appropriate meal. Even a sandwich with a combination of brown bread, egg or meat, salad and yoghurt as a dry lunch could also be a good choice. The goal is not to make office lunch complicated. The target is to make it complete.

However, it’s time to look at the whole day and simply not be obsessed with one office meal. When we talk about “office lunch”, we often focus only on what is inside the lunchbox. But nutrition does not work meal by meal in isolation. The real picture is the entire day's eating pattern.

Image Photo: Collected / Haricharan Boganatham / Unsplash

A person who skips breakfast, eats an unbalanced brunch outside, has a rice-heavy lunch and then consumes a very large dinner late at night may technically be eating three times, but the pattern is still far from ideal.

The answer is not crash dieting, eliminating rice or following complicated food rules. It is regularity, balance, variety and moderation.

Office-day routine

Don't skip breakfast. Even a simple, balanced meal is preferable to beginning the day on an empty stomach.

During the workday, choose outside food carefully. Look for options containing protein, vegetables and less fried food. Carry lunch from home whenever possible; it makes portion and ingredient control easier.

Build a balanced plate consisting of moderate rice or rooti, adequate proteins, plenty of vegetables, daal/salad, fruits, and nuts.

Limit soft drinks and other sugar-sweetened beverages and measure your drinks.

Don't allow yourself to become excessively hungry before going home. A sensible snack, when needed, can help prevent overeating at dinner.

At dinner, avoid turning it into the day's largest meal. Keep portions sensible and include vegetables and protein. Eat mindfully rather than rushing through the meal.

The bottom line: Dhaka's office workers do not necessarily need to abandon traditional Bangladeshi food to eat better; they need to rethink the pattern. A healthier office lifestyle begins with a simple shift: do not wait until you are extremely hungry to think about food.

Plan the day before hunger makes the decisions for you, because the real question is not simply, “What are we eating for lunch?” It is: “What does our entire working day look like on the plate?”

The writer is the Chief Clinical Dietician & HOD, Continental Hospital PLC

title: Why a simple bowl of daal is a total nutritional masterclass
text:
Long before modern wellness trends introduced protein pairing, generations of home cooks already had it figured out. Combining lentils with pantry staples creates a complete protein profile that is both incredibly nourishing and remarkably light on your wallet.

Nobody has ever queued up for lentils. Nobody takes a photo of the steel bowl sitting at the corner of the table. And yet, take it away and see how lunch goes. The rice looks lost, and the bhorta feels lonely. And someone always asks, "daal nei?"

You can tell daal is coming before you see it. Around one in the afternoon, there is a hiss from the kitchen, garlic and dried chillies hitting hot oil, and the whole flat knows lunch is minutes away. That sound is the chonk. It lasts ten seconds, and no one has ever been annoyed by it.

A plain plate of daal-bhaat is a small miracle. Rice by itself is just rice. Pour a little over it, and it becomes a meal you want to keep eating. Add alu bhorta with a lot of mustard oil, a begun bhaja, and maybe a fried egg with lacy edges, and you have the kind of lunch nobody describes as special, but everybody remembers.

A cooked cup of lentils has about 18 grams of protein, plus fibre, iron and folate. Eaten with rice, the two cover each other's gaps in amino acids, so the plate ends up healthier than it looks. Our grandmothers figured this out long before anyone printed it on a packet.

It is also affordable and very forgiving. Too thin, let it simmer. Too thick, add water. Forgot the salt; add it at the table. Daal never complains!

Ask people about daal, and they rarely talk about protein. They tell you about one particular bowl. A grandmother's, a hostel mess's, the one that appeared during exams and fevers and the weeks when nothing was going right. Most of us didn't have a favourite dish on those days. We just wanted the thing that was already in the kitchen.

Then there is the eating itself. Mashing rice and daal together with your fingers, warm enough to loosen the grains, is something no spoon has ever managed. The smell of turmeric, garlic and toasted spice hanging around the kitchen afterwards is the closest thing we have to a family perfume.

We talk a lot about the dishes that show off, the biryani, the kachchi, the naans and kebabs that need a nap afterwards. Daal does not need any of that. It sits on the table, gets scraped clean, and somebody always asks for a second helping!

Image Photo: Sazzad Ibne Sayed

DAAL-BHORA POTOL (LENTIL STUFFED POINTED GOURD)

Ingredients

For the stuffed pointed gourd —

10–12 medium-sized potol (pointed gourds); ½ cup chana daal (Bengal gram), soaked for 1 hour; 1 tsp ginger paste; ½ tsp cumin powder; ½ tsp coriander powder; ½ tsp turmeric powder; 1 green chilli, finely chopped; salt to taste; 3–4 tbsp mustard oil

For the gravy —

1 medium tomato, finely chopped; 1 tsp ginger paste; ½ tsp cumin seeds; 1 bay leaf; ½ tsp cumin powder; ½ tsp coriander powder; ½ tsp red chilli powder; ½ tsp garam masala powder; 1 tsp sugar (optional); salt to taste; 1½ cups warm water

Method

Peel the pointed gourds lightly, leaving a little green skin for texture, and trim both ends.

Carefully make a lengthwise slit in each pointed gourd and remove the seeds to create a hollow centre. Boil the soaked chana daal until tender but not mushy, then drain thoroughly and coarsely mash it. Heat a little mustard oil in a pan and add ginger paste, chopped green chilli, cumin powder, coriander powder, turmeric and salt. Add the mashed daal and cook for 4–5 minutes until the mixture becomes fairly dry and aromatic.

Allow the filling to cool slightly, then stuff each pointed gourd with the prepared daal mixture. Heat the remaining mustard oil in a pan and lightly fry the stuffed pointed gourds until golden on all sides. Remove and set aside.

In the same pan, add the bay leaf and cumin seeds. Once fragrant, add ginger paste and chopped tomato, followed by cumin powder, coriander powder, turmeric, red chilli powder, salt and sugar. Cook until the tomatoes soften and the masala releases oil. Add warm water and bring the gravy to a gentle boil. Carefully arrange the fried stuffed pointed gourd in the gravy, cover and simmer for 10–15 minutes until tender and well coated with the spices. Finish with garam masala and a drizzle of mustard oil. Serve hot with steamed rice, pulao or luchi.

BEGUN WITH MOONG DAAL CRUST

Ingredients

2 large eggplants (begun), cut into thick round slices; ¾ cup yellow moong daal; 2 tbsp rice flour; ½ tsp turmeric powder; ½ tsp red chilli powder; ½ tsp cumin powder; ½ tsp ginger paste; salt to taste; 1 tsp poppy seeds (optional); mustard oil, for shallow-frying

Image Photo: Sazzad Ibne Sayed

Method

Wash the moong daal thoroughly and soak it in water for 2–3 hours. Drain and grind the daal into a thick, coarse paste, adding very little water. Transfer the paste to a bowl and mix in the rice flour, turmeric powder, red chilli powder, cumin powder, ginger paste, salt and poppy seeds. Add a little water if necessary to make a thick coating batter. Wash the eggplant slices, pat them dry and sprinkle lightly with salt and turmeric.

Heat mustard oil in a frying pan over medium heat. Dip each eggplant slice into the moong daal batter, ensuring it is evenly coated on both sides. Carefully place the coated slices in the hot oil and shallow-fry over medium-low heat until the lentil crust becomes golden and crisp and the eggplant is tender inside. Turn gently and cook the other side. Remove and drain on kitchen paper. Serve hot as a delicious Bengali-style starter or side dish with steamed rice and daal.

DAAL WITH TARO STEMS (KOCHUR DATA DIYE DAAL)

Ingredients

1 cup masoor daal (red lentils); 2 cups tender taro stems (kochu data), peeled and cut into 2-inch pieces; 1 medium tomato, chopped; 1 tsp ginger paste; 2 green chillies; ½ tsp turmeric powder; ½ tsp cumin seeds; 1 dried red chilli; 2 tbsp mustard oil; salt to taste; 4 cups water; ½ tsp cumin powder (optional)

Method

Wash the daal thoroughly and soak for 20 minutes. Wash the taro stems, remove their tough outer fibres, and cut them into pieces. Boil the stems separately until completely tender, then drain.

Cook the daal with turmeric and water until soft. Heat mustard oil in a pan and add cumin seeds and dried red chilli. Add the ginger paste and chopped tomato, and sauté until the tomato softens. Stir in the boiled taro stems, cumin powder and salt, and cook for a few minutes to allow the flavours to develop.

Add the cooked daal and green chillies, mix well, and simmer for 10–15 minutes until the daal reaches the desired consistency. Adjust the seasoning and add hot water if needed. Serve warm with steamed rice.

Important tip: Taro stems must be cooked thoroughly, as insufficiently cooked taro can cause itching or irritation in the mouth and throat. Choose tender stems and cook them until completely soft.

Recipes by Salina Parvin

title: How to host a perfect Durga Puja feast with easy recipes
text:
Durga Puja is as much a celebration of rich, unforgettable flavours as it is of tradition and togetherness. Whether you are hosting a festive gathering for friends or preparing a cosy meal for your family, serving the right balance of classic Bengali comfort foods and festive centrepieces makes all the difference. From crispy Luchi with sweet Suji to flavourful Bhuna Khichuri, tender Mutton Curry, and delicate Patishapta, these 15 authentic, easy-to-follow recipes bring the magic and warmth of traditional festive dining straight to your home kitchen.

Image Photo: Sazzad Ibne Sayed

VEGETABLE BATTER FRY

Ingredients

2/3 cup maida (refined flour)

1/3 cup corn flour, 1 tsp rice flour

½ tsp turmeric powder

1/3 tsp cooking soda

Salt and sugar, to taste, 1 cup oil

Sliced potato, brinjal and pumpkin or any other combination of vegetables

Method

Wash the sliced vegetables and add salt and sugar to them and keep aside. In a bowl, add maida, corn flour, rice flour, turmeric powder, cooking soda and salt and mix well. Add water to make a batter thick enough to coat the vegetables and set aside. Heat oil in a wok. Drain the vegetables of the salt and sugar water. Dip in batter and deep fry.

LABRA (MIXED VEGETABLES)

Ingredients

½ tsp turmeric powder

1/3 tsp chili powder

½ tsp cumin powder (jeera)

1/3 tsp coriander powder

¼ tsp asafoetida (Hing), optional

¾ tsp panch phoron

4 green chilies, split

½ tsp wheat flour(atta)

1 tsp ghee, 2 tbsp oil

6 daaler bori (optional)

Vegetables such as potato, pumpkin, brinjal, radish, cauliflower, cabbage, bean and whatever else you have available in the refrigerator

Method

Heat oil in wok. If you add daaler bori, fry first and keep aside. Temper oil with two slit green chilies and paanch phoron. Add the cut vegetables and the turmeric, chilli, cumin, asafoetida and coriander powder and salt and sugar. Fry till the raw flavour is gone and a fried smell prevails. Then add water and cook till it is completely absorbed and the vegetables are cooked. When done, add the bori, remaining green chillies, ghee and wheat flour and mix. Cover to allow standing time and serve.

CREAM PANEER (COTTAGE CHEESE)

Ingredients

250g paneer, cut into small cubes

1 cup fresh milk or powder milk

3-4 tsp fresh cream or coffee mate (you can also use milk powder)

1 black cardamom, 4 green cardamom

3 cloves, 1 bay leaf

1 medium sized potato, boiled and cubed

1 green capsicum, cubed

1 tbsp ghee

2 tbsp oil

½ tsp ginger paste

4 green chilies, slightly slit

Salt to taste

Method

Heat oil in wok. Fry the paneer and keep aside. Fry capsicum and keep aside. Add ghee to the oil and temper with the whole spices. Add the ginger paste. Then put the boiled potato cubes and fry them. Add milk, coffee mate and then cover it and let it cook. Add the paneer cubes and green chilies and cook on low flame so that the flavour of milk infuses into the paneer. Add the capsicum, and then allow a 1-minute standing time and remove from flame.

CHOLAR DAAL (BENGAL GRAM)

Ingredients

1 cup Bengal gram

½ tsp turmeric powder

½ tsp cumin powder

1/3 tsp chili powder

Salt and sugar to taste

For temper

1 tbsp oil

1tbsp ghee

½ tsp cumin seeds

2 dried red chillies

1 bay leaf

1½ tsp coconut, freshly grated

Method

Boil daal in sufficient water. Remove all the dirt that floats up. Add powdered turmeric, cumin and chilli and salt and then cook till the daal can be mashed by the finger. Then add sugar and keep aside.

Heat oil in a separate pan. Add ghee, chillies and fry. Temper with red chillies, cumin seeds, bay leaf and the grated coconut and fry till the coconut turns golden brown. Add the tempered oil to daal and heat with split green chilies and serve.

Image Photo: Sazzad Ibne Sayed

CAULIFLOWER AND POTATO CURRY

Ingredients

1 small cauliflower, cut into small flowerets

2 medium potatoes, cut into wedges

1 green capsicum, cut into half-inch squares (optional)

1½ tsp turmeric powder

¾ tsp chilli powder

1 tsp cumin powder

1 bay leaf

3 tbsp oil

1 tsp ghee

½ tsp garam masala powder

1 tsp wheat flour(atta)

2 green chillies, split

Method

Heat oil in a pan. If you use capsicum, fry it in some oil until it softens and keep aside. Add the cauliflower to the oil. Add salt and sugar as per taste and fry until all the water is absorbed and the raw smell is gone. Add ½ tsp of turmeric powder and fry till a nice aroma pervades, then remove from oil.

In the same oil, add 1 bay leaf and the potatoes and fry. Make sure to season it with some salt. Add the remaining turmeric powder, chilli powder and cumin powder with 2 tbsp of water and cook until all the water evaporates and the oil starts to float on top. Then add ½ cup of water and cover to allow the potatoes to boil. When the potatoes become soft, add the cauliflower, but do not cover the lid, or else the trapped vapour will make the cauliflowers soggy. The curry needs to have a thick consistency so don't be afraid to add more water and wheat flour if needed at this stage.

Finally, add the capsicum, ghee, garam masala powder, green chillies and salt and sugar as per taste before serving.

VEGETARIAN EGG

Ingredients

For the egg

500ml full cream milk made into paneer

Saffron, for food colouring

4 medium potatoes, boiled and mashed

1 tsp ginger paste

Salt, to taste

3 tbsp cornflour, mixed with ½ cup of water

4 tbsp of oil

For gravy —

½ tsp turmeric powder

½ tsp chilli powder

½ tsp cumin powder

½ tsp ginger paste

1 medium tomato, chopped

1tsp white Vinegar

Salt, to taste

½ tsp garam masala

1tsp ghee

1 bay leaf

Method

Mash the paneer and add a pinch of salt and the saffron colour. If needed, add a little bit more of the saffron colour to resemble the colour of an egg yolk and mould into balls.

Add the ginger paste and salt to mashed potatoes and make oval shaped balls surrounding the paneer balls. Dip into the cornflour batter and then deep fry them.

For gravy —

Add 1 bay leaf to the leftover oil from frying the vegetarian eggs. Then one by one, add powdered chilli, cumin, ginger paste, chopped tomatoes and salt. Pour ½ cup of water and fry till it evaporates.

Add the vinegar and 1 cup of water to make the curry. Then place the vegetarian eggs into the curry, garam masala powder, ghee and serve.

DHOKAR DALNA

Ingredients

For dhoka

1 cup gram lentil, washed and immersed in water

1-inch ginger

½ tsp turmeric powder

3 green chillies (or as per taste)

Salt and sugar, for taste

1 tbsp of oil

For the curry —

1 tsp turmeric powder

½ tsp chilli powder

½ tsp jeera powder

½ tsp ginger paste

1 tbsp tomato puree

1 bay leaf

2 cinnamon sticks

3 green cardamoms

2 cloves

¼ tsp of asafoetida powder

1 tsp vinegar

1 cup oil

1 tsp ghee

green chillies, as per taste

Method

To make dhoka —

Blend the gram lentil with ginger and green chillies and a little bit of water to make a paste. Add the turmeric powder, salt, and sugar to the paste to make a thick batter. In a pan, heat oil, add the batter and keep stirring till the water is absorbed. Spread on a greased plate and allow to cool. Cut into rectangular pieces.

To make the curry —

Heat oil in a pan and fry the dhokas and then keep aside. In the remaining pan, add the whole spices. Add the powdered turmeric, cumin, asafoetida and chilli and ginger paste, tomato puree, vinegar, salt, and sugar (as per taste) and some warm water. Cook until there is a layer of oil floating on the top and the raw smell of the spices are gone. Then incorporate the fried dhokas into the sauce and add sufficient water (for the dhokas to boil) as they tend to absorb a lot of the water in general. Add ghee, garam masala and split green chillies and mix well. Remove from flame and serve.

Image Photo: Sazzad Ibne Sayed

FRIED HILSA (ILISH BHAJA)

Ingredients

6 pieces Hilsa fish

1 tsp onion paste

½ tsp garlic paste

½ tsp turmeric powder

1 tsp vinegar, Cornflour

Salt, to taste

Method

Marinate the fish with all the ingredients. In a separate bowl, combine water and cornflour to make a thin batter. Heat oil in a pan, there should be enough oil to shallow fry the Hilsa. Dip the pieces of fish in the batter and then the oil and fry till golden brown.

Image Photo: Sazzad Ibne Sayed

TOMATO CHUTNEY

Ingredients

8 tomatoes, cut into thick slices

4 tbsp sugar

½ tsp salt

2 seeds of tamarind or 6 dried plums (shuknaboroi)

Water, to soften

1 tbsp oil

1 tsp of mustard seeds

1 dried red chilli

1 tbsp oil

3 mango bars (store bought), cut into squared, or raisins (optional)

Method

For the syrup —

In a pan, boil the tomatoes with salt and add 1/3 cup of water till the tomatoes soften. Add the tamarind or dried plums and sugar. You may also add the mango bar pieces and raisins. Remove from flame and set aside.

In a separate pan, heat oil for tempering. Add the red chillies and fry. Add the mustard seeds and after they start cracking, pour only the oil directly into the syrup. Without adding any extra oil, heat the temper until the oil is absorbed and mix into the syrup. Serve in desired bowl.

Image Photo: Sazzad Ibne Sayed

MUTTON CURRY

Ingredients

500g mutton, washed and drained

2 tbsp yoghurt

3 desi onions, finely sliced for 'beresta'

1/3 tsp nutmeg powder

1 tsp ginger paste

½ tsp garlic paste

1 tsp onion paste

1 tsp chilli powder

1 tsp coriander powder

2 tsp almond and raisin paste

2 potatoes, peeled and cut into halves and washed (optional)

1 bay leaf

2-inch pieces of cinnamon stick

1 black cardamom

4 cloves

4 tbsp butter oil

3 green chillies

Salt, to taste

Method

Marinate mutton with yoghurt, salt and nutmeg for about 30 minutes. Heat the butter oil and fry the onion slices with a little bit of salt till the onions become golden brown, and place in a bowl draining the oil as much as you can from it. In the same pan, without adding any extra oil, fry the potatoes with a pinch of salt and keep aside as well.

In a separate pan, temper oil with the whole spices and add the ginger, garlic, and onion paste.

Add powdered chilli and coriander, salt and ¾ cups of water and cook until the water completely evaporates and the raw smell of masalas disappear. Add the marinated mutton and half of the fried onions and cover. Cook on medium flame. The mutton will cook in its own juices.

Add the fried potatoes, green chillies and ½ cup of water and cover for 5-10 minutes to allow the mutton and potatoes to absorb the flavours in the curry. Add the remaining fried onions as garnishing and serve.

BHUNA KHICHURI

Ingredients

1 cup pulao rice

1 cup dry roasted mung daal

1½ tsp freshly grated coconut

1 bay leaf

1 black cardamom

4 green cardamoms

2 cinnamon sticks, roughly 1½ inches thick

6 peppercorns

1 tbsp ginger paste

1 tsp turmeric powder

½ tsp chilli powder

½ tsp coriander powder

½ tsp cumin powder

4 tbsp ghee

6 green chillies

½ tsp garam masala powder

Hot water

Method

Wash and soak the pulao and mung daal before starting. Drain water from rice and daal. Heat ghee in a pot and temper with the whole spices. Add the coconut and fry until golden brown. Add the rice, 2-3 split green chillies and ginger paste, salt and fry till a rich aroma pervades. Add sugar and stir well so that it coats the rice.

Add the daal and further fry so that the daal absorbs the ghee and spices. Add all the other dry masalas (except for the garam masala powder) and fry well till the raw smell of the masalas is gone. Add 5 cups of water, and cover and cook on high flame.

When almost done, add the garam masala powder, the remaining green chillies and ghee (optional)

Over a low flame, let the khichuri cook for 5 more minutes before serving.

Image Photo: Sazzad Ibne Sayed

LUCHI

Ingredients

1½ cup maida flour

1/3 tsp salt

1 tbsp ghee or oil

3 cups oil, for deep frying

Method

Add the salt and ghee to the flour and mix it in well. Then start mixing in the water, little at a time to make a stiff dough. The end result should be a dough with a rubber like texture. Cover and allow to rest for 15 to 30 minutes.

Then make small round balls from the dough. For this amount of flour, you should get 10-12 balls. Heat oil in a pan. Roll out the balls into flat disc-like shapes with a diameter of 4-4" and deep fry the oil.

PLAIN ALU BHAJA

Ingredients

4 medium potatoes, peeled and cut into small squares

2 tbsp ghee

½ tsp panch phoron

4 green chillies

Salt, to taste

Method

Heat ghee in a pan. Temper with 2 green chillies and panch phoron. Add the potatoes, salt and lightly fry. Add warm water (sufficient to allow potatoes to boil) and cover. Allow the potatoes to cook and the water to be completely absorbed. Add the remaining green chillies and cover for one minute. Mash a few of the cooked potatoes for desired texture and then serve.

SUJI (WITH LUCHI)

Ingredients

1 cup semolina (suji)

1 cup sugar

3 tbsp ghee

1 tbsp raisins

6 green cardamoms, crushed

Warm water

Method

Heat ghee in a pan and temper it with the crushed cardamoms. Add the semolina and lightly fry it till it turns golden brown and then mix in the sugar, raisins, and enough water to cook the semolina. When the water is absorbed and semolina is cooked, remove from the flame and serve.

Note: This semolina is fried lightly and more ghee and sugar are added to get a runny texture so that it complements the luchi. When adding the sugar, you can start of by adding ¾ of a cup of sugar and check before adding more to adjust how sweet you want it to.

PATISHAPTA

Ingredients

For the filling —

½ coconut, grated

1/3 piece of jaggery (khejur gur)

For the batter —

2/3 cup of flour (maida)

1 tsp semolina (suji)

Method

To make the filling —

In a pan, heat coconut and ghee and cook over low flame until it turns into a sticky consistency and then remove aside.

For the batter —

Mix the flour with ½ cup of water. The consistency of the batter should be runny, so if needed, add a little bit more of water. Lightly grease a non-stick pan with oil. Pour a large spoon of the batter and allow it to spread out, covering the pan. Take a dollop of the filling and place it at the centre and spread it out a little. Start folding the batter in the same way you would while making an omelette. Slightly tap the two ends with a spoon so that the filling stays in place and then place in plate. Repeat this process for the remaining batter and filling.

title: Can Dhaka’s rare pet cafés survive beyond the social media trend?
text:
Walk into a café in Dhaka today and you might not just be handed a menu — you might also get a rule board telling you how to greet a cat. That is the reality of the city’s newest experiment: the pet café.

There are only two keeping the concept alive in Dhaka — A T M Ragib Raihan, owner of Furrycafe in Tejgaon, and Zeeshan Sadeque, owner of Robbie Bobbie Café, along with his co-owner Mayisha Alamgir in Bashundhara R/A.

The pet café concept remains small, but it raises a bigger question: can Dhaka’s pet café industry survive in a market where several ventures have already closed down?

For animal lovers, the idea sounds appealing. Instead of scrolling through our phones over a favourite drink, there is a cat at our table.

But behind that adorable experience lies a complicated and costly industry.

According to Raihan and Alamgir, their motivations came from their love for cats and their desire to support animal welfare and foster homes.

Image

A pet café here is not just a café with cats added to the decor. Alamgir mentioned that the café itself helps create a support system for stray and rescued cats. The business and welfare initiative therefore become intertwined.

Dhaka’s pet culture has changed noticeably over the years. More people are keeping pets, rescuing animals from the streets, and speaking up about animal rights, with rescue stories and adoption opportunities frequently appearing on social media. Perhaps it was only a matter of time before that affection moved beyond people’s homes and into cafés.

The customers are not limited to pet owners. Animal lovers who cannot keep pets at home can still experience that connection, while families can introduce their children to animals in a controlled environment.

Image

Raihan mentioned that children who are initially afraid of animals can gradually overcome that fear after spending time with the cats.

A pet café can also become someone’s first comfortable interaction with an animal. A child who gets anxious around cats might leave having learned that an animal does not need to be chased, picked up, or touched to be loved.

Running a pet café comes with a responsibility that a regular café does not have: the animals cannot be treated like furniture.

Both Raihan and Alamgir emphasised the importance of keeping food and cats separate. The cafés use partitioned areas so that cats do not come into direct contact with food preparation and serving spaces.

Image

At Furrycafe, Raihan said, "There is a rule board in front of the cat area door for the visitors, and the area is monitored." The message is simple: do not force an interaction because you paid to enter.

If a cat wants to sleep under a chair, it should be allowed to do so. A cat that approaches you may be welcomed, while one that retreats should be left undisturbed.

But the biggest challenge is not regulation; it is sustainability.

A lot of pet cafés have come and gone in Dhaka before. According to Raihan and Alamgir, several cafés eventually shut down, making survival one of the biggest challenges for those still operating.

Image

Unlike conventional cafés, the expenses do not stop at rent, ingredients, and staff salaries. There are additional costs such as vaccinations, healthcare, specialised food, regular deep cleaning, and constant monitoring.

This makes us question whether there is enough demand in Dhaka to sustain more pet cafés, or whether the concept will remain a niche experience.

The answer depends on whether we stop seeing these spaces simply as a trend. Bangladesh’s growing pet culture indicates there is an audience, and with continued support, the cafés can sustain themselves and help more cats.

The city is already learning to make space for animals in people’s homes, online communities, and everyday conversations. The next step is making space for them in our cafés too — patiently, responsibly, and with more support.
