title: How ancient spices built empires and defined human history
text:
Modern pantries treat spices as ordinary, but history tells a far wilder story. Centuries ago, rare aromatics were so valuable that kingdoms waged wars and guarded trade routes with fierce secrecy.

“No man should die if he can afford cinnamon,” remarked a writer in the 14th century, capturing a truth that once governed global commerce, politics and power. Long before oil and gold became the currencies of empires, spices transformed economies, drew ships across unknown oceans and inspired voyages that altered the course of history.

In medieval Europe, dockworkers in London were sometimes paid in cloves, while Roman soldiers received allowances in salt, giving rise to the expression “a man worth his salt.” Such was the value of spices that kingdoms guarded the origins of these precious commodities with extraordinary secrecy. The quest for pepper, cinnamon, cloves, and nutmeg helped create vast trading networks, fuelled maritime exploration and ultimately contributed to the European search for new sea routes — a journey that led to the discovery of the Americas.

Today, a pinch of spice is an everyday pleasure, but there was a time when wars were fought, fortunes made and empires built in pursuit of these fragrant treasures.

The story of spices on the Indian subcontinent stretches back thousands of years. An ordinary meal in the cities of the Indus Valley Civilization may have included salt, asafoetida (hing), pepper or chillies, accompanied by vegetables and staple grains. By the time of the Mauryan Empire, culinary choices had become even more diverse. Kautilya, the renowned strategist and author of the Arthashastra, wrote about the cultivation and trade of several varieties of salt, including sea salt, black salt, rock salt and mineral salts, underlining the importance of flavouring agents in both diet and statecraft.

Image Photo: Collected / marion botella / Unsplash

Buddhist traditions, however, favoured simplicity. Salt, mustard seeds, pepper, and amloki formed part of a restrained cuisine, while foods such as garlic and onion were often avoided. Even humble ingredients carried profound meaning. One of Buddhism’s best-known stories recounts how the Buddha asked a grieving mother to bring him mustard seeds from a household untouched by death. When she found no such home, she realised that suffering was universal and that she was not alone in her loss.

Among all spices, few have commanded as much fascination as black pepper. Known as “Black Gold”, pepper travelled from the Malabar Coast of Kerala to distant markets in Greece as early as the fourth century BCE. Its immense value attracted merchants, adventurers, and empires, from the Romans to the Portuguese. When Vasco da Gama arrived in India at the end of the 15th century in search of spices, he discovered that he was far from the first claimant to this lucrative trade.

Legend has it that when the Portuguese attempted to carry pepper plants back to Europe, their hosts in Kerala offered a gentle reminder: “You may grow the plant in your country, but how will you give it our rain?” The rich pre- and post-monsoon climate of Kerala — often called “God’s Own Country” — gives its pepper a distinctive intensity that proved difficult to replicate elsewhere.

Competition for spices reshaped the world map. The Portuguese were followed by the Dutch, who found more efficient sea routes around the Cape of Good Hope, and eventually by the British, whose arrival in South Asia was deeply tied to the spice trade. Ironically, British cuisine was once far more heavily seasoned than it is today. As spices became cheaper and more widely available, sections of the aristocracy adopted simpler, blander food as a way of distinguishing themselves from the broader population.

The Mughals brought yet another layer to the subcontinent’s culinary heritage. Arriving from Central Asia, Emperor Babur reportedly found Indian food lacking in fragrance. By the reign of Akbar, Mughal kitchens had introduced new aromas and refinements, including the use of rose water to perfume dishes. The Mughals also popularised elaborate desserts and the custom of ending meals with paan, shaping dining traditions that continue across South Asia today.

From the healing qualities associated with turmeric to the astonishing prices once commanded by nutmeg, spices have long been far more than mere ingredients. They are stories of trade, migration, conquest, faith and culture — tiny seeds and powders that connected distant worlds and continue, even now, to awaken our senses.

title: Why your constant scrolling is quietly destroying your closest personal relationships
text:
A 2025 meta-analysis published in Frontiers in Psychology, which examined 52 studies covering nearly 19,700 participants, found that "partner phubbing", the act of ignoring your partner by using your phone in their presence, significantly reduces relationship satisfaction, marital satisfaction, intimacy, and responsiveness towards each other. It also increases conflict and jealousy.

The picture is painfully familiar closer to home.

Nasima Begum, 52, says, "At the end of the day, the people I wait to talk to sit down at the dinner table with a mobile in hand."

"I stay home alone all day," she adds. "Once the housework is done, I wait for my child and my husband to return so I can talk to them. But even after coming home, everyone seems to enter a separate world of their own. Someone plays games on the phone, someone watches reels. Even my husband now spends most of his time talking while staring at his screen."

There was a time when leisure meant quality time with the family, when everyone spoke and listened to the day's stories with enthusiasm, because no one on the other side was holding a phone. That familial bond is fading.

Mental health advocate Tawhida Shiropa mentions that the phone should not come to the dining table at all. For those fifteen minutes, it can easily stay aside. Eating without mindfulness, she points out, harms not just relationships but one's own digestive system. And for those who do not use phones, a grandmother or a mother, their very presence is made to feel unimportant.

A little connectivity, checking in on people, sharing photos, is fine, she says. But with this level of social media and phone addiction, real conversation no longer happens.

People now become so engaged in the virtual world that its emotions begin to feel real. Long hours on the phone become a form of escape, Shiropa adds; thoughts turn inward, and people gradually become self-centric and isolated.

Image Photo: Collected / Adrian Swancar / Unsplash

Not every household has surrendered, though. Isabella, a graphic designer, says that the mobile is undoubtedly valuable. It keeps you updated, connects you fast, and teaches you a great deal. But this blessing, she feels, is sometimes overused and misused. Excess of anything is never good; used with control, it is genuinely helpful. She usually chats with her mother about friends and colleagues. In those moments, it feels like beautiful time can be spent without a mobile. And it truly can.

Yet, Moner Bondhu, a mental health care centre, observes that while good hours without the phone are possible, in reality, after long stretches on the screen, the very habit of talking wears away.

Texting starts to feel like the easier option. The confrontation and genuine emotion of a real conversation are something many no longer want to face. Our capacity to listen is shrinking so fast that we want to rush to the end of every story, which is why this generation shows such reluctance to spend time with family.

Nayeem, a young jobholder, speaks with a touch of sadness. "I honestly cannot remember the last time a full hour passed without checking my phone. Even when I am with my parents or friends, I scroll reels or reply to messages. It has become second nature now; it has become a habit."

At any friend’s meetup, he adds, everyone seems only half-present. They sit in front of you, apparently listening, but with a phone in hand, scrolling Facebook. You can never be sure whether your story matters to them. To many, maintaining relationships now feels like a hassle, so the phone becomes the friend, and being alone becomes the comfortable choice.

Sinking into an unreal world at every free moment carries a mental cost, one that can leave a life devoid of relationships and terribly lonely.

Tawhida Shiropa echoes this. After hours spent online, people feel lonelier, she says. If sending a meme or a reel to a WhatsApp group is mistaken for connectivity, the habit of real conversation itself is lost. This is how emptiness and loneliness are born.

Shiropa notes that researchers have long warned that excessive dependence on the mobile can reach the level of behavioural addiction.

A generation is growing up whose entertainment, social life, and even sense of identity flow largely through a screen. Many can no longer recognise their own loneliness, because the phone keeps the silence filled. It offers instant gratification: novelty, distraction, and a feeling of connection without the risk of real presence. But the ability to sustain attention declines, and being with people face-to-face starts to feel uncomfortable. That is what destroys relationships.

These days, we keep piling on the work, forgetting what leisure means. We wake up reaching for the phone and fall asleep holding it. But habits can be changed. When the mobile stays untouched during time spent together, conversation among family members becomes easier and more meaningful.

In relationships, real conversation is what works best: giving time, being there, staying beside someone. Family bonds and friendships need care. And that care can be as simple as setting the device aside and valuing the time we get with each other.

title: Why modern women are choosing life and peace over broken marriages
text:
When a marriage unravels despite years of devotion, holding on can cause more damage than letting go. For modern women, walking away isn't an admission of defeat, but a brave leap toward rebuilding dignity and quiet emotional healing.

As undesirable as it may be, sometimes divorce becomes an inevitability of life. In the pursuit of making marriages work, couples often suffer immensely. And when every effort falls short, love and respect are replaced with anger and resentment; the best course of action is to separate amiably.

Women in 2026 are more well-informed, financially responsible, and capable of taking care of themselves in ways their previous generations were not. Hence, more and more women are choosing mental peace over conflict.

Amelia shares her experience beautifully.

Hers was a happy marriage by most standards. As professionals, she and her husband built a life together for nearly two decades. She made their house a home by pouring her heart, soul, and finances. And when it fell apart because of infidelity, the consequences were too severe to bear.

“When you've lived with someone for thirteen years, you don't just develop a relationship with that person; you develop habits, routines and an entire ecosystem around the marriage,” she shares. “And then when that ceases to exist, the void and the chasm initially seem impossible to grasp and fill,” she said.

Amelia, while nursing a broken heart that sent her to hospital twice in the course of her divorce proceedings, picked herself up with boundless courage and determination.

“I threw myself into work and focused on my children because I did not want to wallow in my misery. After all, I had a thriving career, and I am financially stable enough to have my own home and provide for my children. So, I didn’t have a lot to complain about, unlike a lot of other women in my position,’ she remarks assertively.

It was not easy at first. With her husband no longer in the picture, she realised people around her changed a lot. Renting a house and employing new staff brought a lot of judgment, as our society is still largely patriarchal. Both her parents and good friends stood by her side. The idea of raising her children alone was daunting, but they were supportive of Amelia’s decision to break free and helped her every step of the way in that journey.

“Emotionally, they (the children) were devastated as the life they knew no longer existed. Slowly they understood happy, separated couples are better than miserable parents who stay together,” she states affirmatively.

Now, co-parenting with her former husband, she and her children are thriving.

In the truest sense of the word, partnership needs two people to function as a unit. Sometimes one person falls short, and that’s perfectly normal; the other person fills the void. But if this pattern continues, then resentment surfaces, which eventually leads to bitterness.

To that end, Manzima shares her experience.

She shares with a sense of ease, “I came out of a difficult marriage, so even though this new life comes with its own struggles, it also comes with peace. I now have to manage everything on my own, from the children and finances to making every important decision. It can feel overwhelming, but I no longer live with the same emotional stress and uncertainty. Life is harder in many ways, but it is also calmer, safer and more honest.”

Manzima decided not to co-parent with her husband due to conflicting values, and that plays a big role.

“The greatest challenge is knowing that everything rests on me. I have to be emotionally available for my children, take care of their education and everyday needs, manage the household, and think of our financial security,” she says with a sense of relief.

And that’s the greatest takeaway. Divorce is not an easy decision for anyone to make, especially when children are involved. Navigating through many different stages of personal grief and a profound sense of loss while being the primary caregiver is no mean feat.

Being a parent is like being a doctor in the ER; there are no days off. But in the hardest days, mothers rise to the occasion with grit, determination and fierce love. They are capable of taking on many roles and fulfilling them with aplomb.

Divorce is not desirable to anyone, but sometimes that’s the only way, but it’s definitely not the end. Women are stronger than they realise, and are capable of taking on the world. The road may be treacherous, the journey may be difficult, but in pursuit of peace, dignity, and happiness, women have always come out as winners and how!

Names have been changed upon request.

title: It’s time we stopped treating marriage as a community project
text:
Long after public rituals of the past faded away, the instinct to scrutinize a couple's private life remains stubbornly alive. For many couples today, the biggest challenge isn't finding love—it's keeping the rest of the world out of it.

The morning after a wedding, a blood-stained bedsheet is carried out from a balcony like a flag, held aloft for an audience waiting below. Heads turn upwards. Eyes remain fixed on the balcony. And when the white sheet, marked by a generous stain of blood, is finally put on display, the crowd erupts in cheers. The marriage has been consummated; its most private moment has become a public spectacle.

The night before, when the husband asks his wife what she actually hopes to gain from the marriage, her answer is telling: she is looking forward to showing the world that she is no longer a virgin bride.

The sequence appears in the Netflix series Monster: The Lizzie Borden Story, a dramatised retelling of the 19th-century Lizzie Borden case. Watching it today, the ritual feels almost impossible to imagine. Few people, after all, would think of carrying a bloodied bedsheet out into the neighbourhood and putting it on display.

But perhaps the more uncomfortable question is not how much we have changed, but how much we have not. The ritual may have disappeared, yet the larger idea behind it that a marriage is not quite the private business of two people remains familiar.

Historically, marriage determined inheritance, property, social alliances, family status and the continuation of a lineage. Modern marriage, however, is increasingly associated with companionship, emotional compatibility, personal choice and intimacy.

Image Photo: Sazzad Ibne Sayed

Yet older social expectations have not disappeared. The result is a curious hybrid: we expect people to choose their partners for themselves, but we still reserve the right to comment on the choice.

Marriage may be entered into by two people, but in most (almost all) Bangladeshi families, it is rarely allowed to remain private. Before the wedding, everyone has an opinion on who you should marry, what he should earn, and what family she should come from. Is he too old? Is she too career-focused? Is the family respectable enough? What religion, profession, education and social background do they have?

Then comes the wedding, and the questions do not stop: When are you having children? Why are you living separately? Why does your wife work so late? Why does your husband not visit his in-laws enough? Why don't you buy a flat?

Some questions are asked out of affection while some are asked out of curiosity. Some are expressions of genuine concern, but somewhere along the way, concern can become entitlement.

The moment a person reaches a certain age, marriage can become a community project. Parents ask. Aunts investigate. Family friends recommend candidates. Colleagues make introductions. Matchmaking happens through Facebook groups, dating apps, and social media. These days some matchmakers are even turning to AI-powered tools to suggest potential matches.

There is nothing inherently wrong with seeking advice or involving trusted people in an important life decision. The question is: when does advice become interference?

Anthropologist Fatama Sultana Suvra says, “In the new capitalist society, everything is sellable. We once had the narrative that it takes an entire village to raise a child, but now even marriage has become something that can be sold and marketed. We are neither fully individualistic nor fully community oriented.

“Marriage is also sold as a symbol of status and dignity. Through social media, however, it has increasingly become light, almost trivialised. People sometimes seem less interested in the reality of marriage than in consuming the idea of marriage,” says Suvra, associate professor, Jagannath University.

“We look at marriage like a picture we want to paint in a particular way, rather than asking what the reality of that marriage looks like. It is still not fully individualistic. Just as we see with many of our other social systems, we have not quite figured out how to move from the old structure to the new one.”

A disagreement between two people can quickly become an argument involving parents. A quarrel can become a conversation between siblings. A private complaint can travel through family WhatsApp groups. A separation can produce competing versions of events, with relatives taking sides.

Image Photo: Sazzad Ibne Sayed

There are, of course, situations in which family intervention is necessary. Abuse, violence, coercion, serious financial exploitation or other forms of harm should not be romanticised as matters that couples must simply resolve behind closed doors.

However, there is a difference between supporting someone in a difficult marriage and taking ownership of the marriage's decisions.

Mehadi Mobarak Aman, senior psychosocial counsellor at Moner Bondhu, says, “Whether outside interference is helpful or harmful depends on the situation. In an arranged marriage, involving the families can sometimes be positive, but in a love marriage, it may not have the same impact.

“It is best to try to resolve conflicts between the couple first. If they need outside support, they can turn to someone reliable in the family. If there is no such person, they should seek help from a professional counsellor,” he adds.

For some couples, the problem is not that their families care too much. It is that the couple has never been given enough space to become a separate unit.

Sreshtha Habib (pseudonym), a woman in her early 40s going through a bit of a rough patch in her marriage, says, “Professional mediators can certainly help, but I think friends and the wider community can sometimes be better than families because families are generally biased.

“A husband will naturally want his family to take his side, just as a wife will want hers to do the same. Friends, on the other hand, can offer more objective perspectives and advice. Ultimately, though, it depends on the couple and whether they genuinely want to find a solution,” she says.

Marriage is no longer simply discussed within the neighbourhood. It can be displayed online.

Engagement photographs, wedding albums, anniversary posts, pregnancy announcements and family celebrations can turn private milestones into public content. And the public interest does not always end with the happy photographs. People notice when couples stop posting together. They notice when one person disappears from another's photographs. They ask mutual friends what happened. They speculate.

“Today, we have a very specific picture of what a marriage is supposed to look like — the dancing, the groom lifting the bride into his arms, the elaborate celebrations. Social media then becomes a form of surveillance, constantly showing how other people's marriages look and, in turn, shaping what we think ours should look like,” says Fatama Sultana Suvra.

Perhaps the most persistent form of interference is also the most casually delivered. “Adjust” — the word is often presented as wisdom.

Every long-term relationship requires compromise. Two people cannot live together without accommodating each other's habits, expectations and imperfections. But adjustment can mean very different things depending on who is being asked to do it.

For generations, women in particular have been told to adjust to their husband's family, household expectations, financial limitations, unequal domestic responsibilities or even mistreatment. At other times, men may be pressured to remain in marriages because leaving would embarrass the family or damage social standing.

“With our clients, we do not approach marriage as a matter of making or breaking it, or of rescuing the relationship. Generally, however, friends and family will tell couples to adjust, especially women. Rarely will anyone suggest divorce; that is the usual practice,” says Mehadi Mobarak Aman.

The problem is when society decides, from the outside, what a person should tolerate inside their marriage.

We have moved far from a world in which a bride's virginity could be publicly established through a bedsheet displayed before her community. We have changed our laws, our ideas of consent and our understanding of individual rights. For many people, marriage is now fundamentally about companionship and personal choice.

But the social instinct to treat marriage as a collective affair has proved much harder to leave behind. Perhaps the real measure of how modern our understanding of marriage is does not lie in how elaborate our weddings have become, or how freely couples choose their partners.

Marriage may involve two families, communities and, often, a much wider social circle. But the life being lived inside it belongs to the two people who chose to enter it.

Sometimes, care means offering a hand when someone asks for it. Sometimes, it means speaking up when there is harm. And sometimes, it means resisting the urge to turn someone else's marriage into a matter for public discussion. The blood-stained bedsheet may have disappeared. Perhaps it is time the audience did too.

title: Embracing a smaller social circle without feeling guilty
text:
Living abroad taught me that shallow conversations drain more energy than solitude ever could. Trimming my social circle in my 40s was not about being unsocial—it was about protecting my peace and cherishing the few who truly know my heart.

One can call me unsocial, although I will disagree with them. I think I am just socially selective, because in my mid-40s, I love depth over noise.

Yes, my friend circle has shrunk over the years. However, the people I call friends today have stood the test of time, which means that together, these people make my support system.

Just like people change over time, friendships change, too. At some point in life, you may begin to seek genuine friendships rather than surround yourself with people merely because you need someone to talk to. As for me, I would rather spend my time alone than socialise with people with whom I have little in common.

At this point in life, I simply cannot make small talk; it drains me. I have been an expat for more than 18 years now, and in all this time, I have managed to make only two genuine friendships. With the others I knew, our conversations always revolved around food, clothes, jewellery, and other people.

At one point, I realised that I had limited interest in these subjects and that discussing them with people, with whom I began to socialise simply because I thought life abroad could be lonely, was actually a source of stress. Having said that, I do enjoy discussions around food and clothes, when and if the focus is on healthy eating and sustainable fashion. But more than these, I enjoy conversations on current affairs.

Slowly, we drifted apart. Do I miss them and their friendship? No, I really do not.

I would choose solitude and long-distance conversations with people I really connect with over relationships that carry little value for me.

My annual trip to Dhaka is a breather. These trips mean so much to me because I get to meet old friends, people who have known me since I was a child or an adolescent. When I converse with them, I do not have to think and re-think before saying anything; I can simply pour my heart out.

At this stage of life, I am only comfortable around people who allow me to be myself.

Image Photo: Collected / Robin Canfield / Unsplash

I am sure you have one or more people in your life with whom you once had so much in common but are no longer in contact. Work, family commitments, and other responsibilities do not give us the same amount of free time that we had as children and young adults, which means that we gradually become more selective about the kinds of friends we want to keep in our lives.

As a result, as we grow older, our friend circles tend to get smaller. And when we reach the life-altering years of middle age, our circles often shrink even more. In our middle age, it not only becomes more difficult to make new friends, but at this stage of life, we only seek friends with whom we can connect on a deeper level. Small talk with acquaintances is no longer entertaining.

No two stages of life are the same. Our priorities change with age and time.

In our teenage, having a big circle of friends often signifies popularity; the more popular a young person is, the more friends they tend to have. However, this perception often changes as we get older and gain more life experience. At some point in life, you no longer seek the same kind of popularity (after all, popularity also comes with its own baggage), you seek peace. And the source of that peace is often friends; not just any friends, but genuine friends in whom you can safely confide.

Throughout my 30s, my circle had gotten smaller; it was then when I learned to prioritise quality over quantity. By removing noise, I had learnt to identify true friends and cherish them for their unconditional love and support.

Let me wrap this up by sharing an anecdote. I was talking to one of my best friends over the phone, and all of a sudden, I said, “Please don’t die before I do.” She replied, with confidence, “Don’t worry, I won’t!” A genuine friend is like that, she always gives you hope, even when she does not know what the future holds. I cannot imagine how difficult it is going be to live this life without the handful of friends I have.

title: Six modern safety habits every parent needs today
text:
When 13-year-old Ishiat Shahriar Opratim walked out the door with his mother's iPhone last Friday, his family expected photo-snapping with friends — not a tragedy. Another child who did not come home leaves parents asking agonizing questions. Yet, child-protection bodies like UNICEF point to subtle daily safety routines that offer a line of defence.

Know the where, the who, and the when

Professionals advise parents to set boundaries about where children go. Build it into the household routine, the way you build in washing hands before dinner. “Where are you going?” “Who is with you?” “When will you be back?”

Ask every time, and it stops feeling like an interrogation. What matters is the gap between the plan and what the child does, so make one rule the house lives by: plans change only after a phone call, never on the spot.

Beyond stranger danger

Organisations working with child safety warn that the person who harms a child is often someone the child already knows.

Tell your child that an adult who wants them to come somewhere quiet is a warning sign, however warm he seems. The tells are ordinary: gifts and a grown-up who asks the child to keep a secret from you.

Schools and coaching centres can carry their share by refusing one-on-one sessions behind a closed door, and parents should ask if that rule exists before enrolling anyone.

Give them permission to refuse

Many of us grew up believing we could never refuse anyone older. Saying it once is not enough, so rehearse it: give them a sentence to reach for without thinking, like "No, I have to ask my mother first," and practise it until it is automatic.

And stop rewarding the opposite. The child who obeys any adult without question is praised as well-mannered, and that is the exact instinct that puts them at risk.

Talk often and keep your voice level

The hard part is teaching caution without planting fear. Short conversations in the car or over dinner work better than one frightening lecture, so keep the channel open before you need it.

Ask about their day, who they sat with, and what was funny, so talking to you is ordinary, not the alarm.

Organisations advise watching for a child who turns secretive or low. It looks like a boy who suddenly will not hand over his phone or goes quiet when one name comes up. Ask gently: a child who expects to be shouted at will stop telling you things.

Get to know their online life

UNICEF USA advises that children ask a parent before meeting anyone they know only from the internet and that parents hold their sign-in details and check their social media and gaming profiles.

Do it in the open, as something the family agreed, so it reads as protection, not surveillance.

For younger children, keep the phone in a shared room, not the bedroom. One line is worth more than any filter: nobody you met online becomes someone you meet in person without a parent there.

Be ready for the hour you hope never comes

Child welfare workers note that police work faster when parents can hand over height, weight, and a recent photograph without hunting for them.

Keep a current photo on your phone and notice what your child is wearing each morning, because "what did he have on" is the first question anyone asks.

Teach even young children their full name, a parent's number, and how to make a call, including the emergency number, 999. Settle the school-pickup rule in advance: if anyone else is collecting your child, the school knows, and your child knows, every time!

None of this sits with parents alone. Safer streets, working police, and schools that notice an absent student matter as much as anything said over dinner. Still, a child who knows they can refuse and knows they can come home and tell you anything walks out of the door with something.

title: Adult phone addiction: A problem we often overlook
text:
Most research over the years has concentrated on excessive screen time for children and everything it takes away from them. However, in a surprising turn of events, children between the ages of 8 and 16 are now flipping the tables on their parents, saying that phone addiction in adults causes them to overlook important family moments. Suddenly, it seems as if the older generation must do some soul-searching of its own.

Fairly concerning results came to light in a study conducted in the UK. Through responses from 16,000 people and a separate poll of 1,000 children, the research that spanned 18 months made it evident that intentional or unintentional scrolling by the parents of children under 18 chips away at precious family time.

The research shows that parents spend, on average, 88 hours (almost 4 days) on unconscious phone activity. Over this time, they miss moments that matter to their children, such as talking or playing together, family days out, and so on. In fact, 63 per cent of the children who were part of the survey believed that their parents had no idea how much time they were actually spending online.

Image Photo: Collected / camilo jimenez / Unsplash

The results of the study indicate something even more puzzling: parents of minors spend more than two hours a day on their smartphones unintentionally, 40 minutes more than an average adult who is not a parent.

This means that parents check their phones more than non-parents and often, without a concrete reason.

“Scrolling is a break from reality,” shares Shoily, mother to a 6-year-old. “It’s mindless, and that’s precisely why I indulge in it.”

Many parents like Shoily say they often pick up their phones without thinking after a long day at work, and do not realise that they may be overdoing it or overlooking their children while doing so. Often, this is not the same for people without children.

“I make it a point to consciously use my phone as little as possible once I’m off work,” says Alvi Mannan, a 36-year-old graphic designer. “My wife and I both feel like our work is heavily screen-dominated, and we opt to read books, go walking or explore cafes instead.”

Of course, there is a very evident reason for all this. Non-parents have time after work to spend as they wish.

Taking care of a young child is not a burden they have to carry, and therefore, they can see scrolling for the mindless, soul-sucking activity that it is, rather than an escape. For parents, the scenario is vastly different. Their timetables revolve around their children and, for lack of a break, they turn towards the screen. The consequences that follow such an activity are, however, more far-reaching than parents realise.

According to psychologist Inara Salim, when parents are physically present but mentally on their phones, children learn they are less important than a screen.

Image Photo: Collected / Warren / Unsplash

“Every child who has to repeat themselves because a parent was on their phone, or has to turn back from a parent without having shown them or told them what they wanted to, feels unseen, and teaches them that love is something that must be earned.”

According to the psychologist, this dent in confidence can show up as doubt in class, anxiety in friendships, and a belief that they must compete to be chosen.

“The repair is simple: children don’t need perfect parents; they need present ones. Even 10 minutes a day of phone-down attention tells a child: ‘You matter.'”

Perhaps then, the real question simmers down to what message adults are willing to impart to children. It is no more about how much time the children are spending on their phones. Rather, it is what they learn from the behaviours modelled by the adults around them. Each time a parent chooses a device over a conversation, even unintentionally, that choice becomes part of a child’s understanding of attention, love, and importance.

This in no way means that parents can never disconnect from their role or catch a break. It simply means that if adults want children to develop a healthy relationship with technology, they must be willing to be honest about their own habits first.

Sometimes, putting the phone down is more than a break from scrolling; it is a way of saying, without words, that the children will always come first.

title: Why doing nothing on the weekend has become ultimate luxury
text:
After five grueling days of commuting and city chaos, the most appealing weekend plan is no plan at all. Staying home has transformed from a sign of having nowhere to go into the ultimate form of self-care.

“What are you doing this weekend?” used to mean plans involving friends, food, or a new place. Increasingly, however, the most appealing answer is simply nothing!

After five days of university, work, commuting and constant social interaction, many people no longer want their weekends to feel like another task. By the time the week ends, the city has extracted every drop of energy they had to offer. But for a generation whose weekdays are increasingly packed, a weekend with no plans has become a luxury in itself. Staying home is no longer necessarily a sign that someone has nowhere to go. Sometimes, it means they have finally found somewhere they actually want to be.

Going out, of course, can still be fun. But in a city like Dhaka, even a simple plan can require more effort than it seems. Getting ready, deciding where to go, arranging transport, sitting through traffic and eventually getting back home can turn a few hours of leisure into a tiring affair.

Cost alone often settles the question. In many urban neighbourhoods, leisure options are largely limited to restaurants, cafés, and shopping malls. A casual outing can mean an expensive meal, transport fares and other small expenses that quickly add up. Add weekend traffic to the equation, and a plan meant to be relaxing can become exhausting before it even begins.

The alternatives are not always ideal either. Parks and walking spaces may not offer the quiet, comfortable environment most people want, while rooftops and other casual spaces are increasingly harder to find than before. For students and young workers trying to stick to a budget, even a seemingly simple plan can become an expense hard to justify every weekend.

Staying home, therefore, offers something increasingly valuable: the freedom to do very little. It can feel restful and boring at the same time, but after an exhausting week, even boredom can be welcome.

But there is another side to spending more time at home. It does not necessarily mean being together. If weekdays leave little room for family time, weekends should offer a chance to make up for it. Yet even then, everyone's routines can remain surprisingly separate. Home has quietly become a place where everyone is mostly there to eat, recharge, and sleep.

Everyone's schedule now seems to run on a different clock. There are early birds and night owls. Meal times no longer necessarily bring everyone together. Dinner happens at different times, and some may prefer eating late at night in their rooms while watching something on their screens. Everyone is absorbed in their own corner of the digital world. The family shares an address but barely shares the day.

And even on the weekends, someone may use the day to catch up on assignments or work. The smallest moments are often lost amidst these. Sitting around the dining table for a meal, having tea and snacks in the living room, watching a film together or simply talking about something that happened during the day rarely requires planning, but these are the moments through which families stay connected.

There is nothing wrong with spending the weekend at home. After a demanding week, rest is not something we need to justify, and every day off does not need an exciting plan. We embrace the stay-at-home weekend as a victory over the exhausting city. And it gives us a chance to remember what home is supposed to offer beyond comfort. But the urban fatigue that drove us indoors didn't bring us closer to the people under our roof.

title: How solomaxxing is changing the way we look at being alone
text:
There was a time when going alone to a restaurant made us wonder what people were going to think. Watching a movie alone felt slightly sad, travelling alone sounded like a vivid dream, and being single for too long came with inevitable questions.

However, people seem to have silently decided that none of these things are taboo anymore. Welcome to the era of solomaxxing — the art of doing everything by yourself, intentionally choosing your own company and enjoying it. The term has recently started appearing across social media all over the world, describing young people who are choosing to invest their time, money and energy in themselves rather than constantly pursuing a company.

And we can see the shift in the everyday choices. Solo dinners, cinema trips, solo travels, and attending concerts alone are no longer viewed as a sign of being "alone" or as a sign that someone has “no one”. They are increasingly becoming experiences people actively choose.

And honestly, there is something strangely beautiful about that.

Image Photo: Collected / vladimir fedotov / Unsplash

Think about the last time you wanted to try a new cuisine but nobody else was interested, or there was a movie you desperately wanted to watch but your friends wanted to watch it with their partners. Or you badly needed a break from the busy life and planned a trip, but everyone’s schedules refused to match.

For years, we have been taught to cancel or postpone these little joys until someone can join us.

What if we simply went to that restaurant? Watched that movie? Or planned that trip?

Sarwat Sameen, a Bangladeshi restaurant owner, talks about solo travels and puts it beautifully, “If you want to discover yourself, understand yourself and learn to love yourself and life, then travel alone; it will teach you a lot.”

And for women especially, choosing to travel alone can carry a whole different weight. There is something so rebellious yet beautiful in that sentence. For years women were taught that travelling alone invites judgement or considered incapable of handling situations alone.

But women choosing their peace over society's permission feel less like another trend and more like a quiet act of reclaiming her own life. Sometimes solomaxxing does not always have to mean booking a flight or planning a big adventure.

Nusrat Kamal, 23, says, “I used to feel weird sitting alone at a coffee shop, but now I actually enjoy having that little time to myself. I rearrange my thoughts while having my cappuccino and observe surroundings.”

It is such a simple but relatable example of how our relationship with being alone is changing. We often assume that sitting alone means that the person must have been stood up, when in reality, they might simply be enjoying their coffee without having to make conversation.

Solomaxxing is not necessarily about avoiding people entirely. It is about learning that independence and companionship can exist together. You can cherish your family, adore your friends, aspire to have a relationship someday and still enjoy spending an entire afternoon alone.

Image Photo: Collected / ismail hamzah / Unsplash

Being alone can sometimes make us notice small things we usually miss. It can be as simple as enjoying the taste of the food silence, reading a new book while sipping coffee in a cosy café or wandering down a street without worrying about being somewhere else.

Labib Rahman, a 28-year-old graphic designer, shared, “I started going to cinema, art exhibitions, and even attending concerts alone because I realised I was missing so many experiences because I was simply waiting for a plus-one."

And honestly, I agree; we started to miss a lot of things the moment we made our plans according to someone else’s availability. That is where solomaxxing starts making sense. Why should you put something you are excited about on hold just because nobody else is available?

We are so used to a plus-one for everything that initially it feels unusual, but once we stop seeing it as sad or embarrassing, we start enjoying life on our own terms.

Being alone does not mean being sad and lonely. Being single does not mean being sad and incomplete. And being unmarried definitely does not mean sitting in some imaginary waiting room. It is simply refusing to put life on pause while waiting for someone.

If company arrives, wonderful. If it does not arrive tomorrow, that is fine too. Life goes on.

So, the next time you see someone eating alone at a restaurant with their headphones on while enjoying the food, resist the urge to feel sorry for them. Chances are, they picked the specific table on purpose and had a better evening than us.

title: 10 realities of moving abroad nobody warns you about
text:
Nobody talks about what happens after you move abroad. They talk about courage. They talk about opportunities. They talk about new beginnings and fresh starts.

Nobody talks about the random Tuesday when homesickness hits you out of nowhere, and suddenly you are crying because a stranger’s cooking smells like something your mother used to make. Nobody talks about how lonely it can feel to build a life from scratch. How exhausting it is to always be adapting. How sometimes you can be surrounded by people and still feel completely alone.

Maybe that’s the thing about moving abroad.

You do not just leave a country. You leave a version of yourself behind. The version that knew where they belonged. The version that never had to explain their accent. The version that could call someone and have them at their door in ten minutes. And then one day you wake up in a different country and realise there is no guidebook for this part.

Just survival. Just trial and error. Just learning as you go.

Over the years, I have learned a few things that helped me cope when everything felt too heavy. Not because they fixed the loneliness. But because they made it easier to carry.

So, here are 10 things I wish someone had told me when I moved abroad:

Image Photo: Collected / mana5280 / Unsplash

Stop trying to be strong all the time. Missing home does not make you weak. It means you came from somewhere that mattered.

Call your people regularly. Not just when you are struggling. Relationships need maintenance when they are separated by oceans and time zones.

Create routines. A morning coffee, a Sunday grocery run, an evening walk. Small routines create stability when everything else feels uncertain.

Find one place that feels like yours. A café, a library, a park bench, a bookstore. Somewhere you can go when life feels overwhelming.

Cook food at home. It will not taste the same, but sometimes comfort matters more than perfection.

Build a support system before you think you need one. Loneliness is much easier to manage when you already have people around you.

Stop comparing your journey to others. Some people seem to have everything figured out. Most of them are improvising too.

Get out of the house. Fresh air won’t solve your problems, but neither will lying in bed creating twenty-seven imaginary worst-case scenarios.

Laugh at the absurd moments. One day, you will be explaining your culture. Next, you will be explaining why you cried over a particular brand of biscuits. Both are valid experiences.

Allow yourself to grow. You are not supposed to be the same person you were before you left.

That’s the whole point.

The funny thing about living abroad is that nobody warns you about the identity crisis. You miss home when you are overseas. Then you visit home and realise you have changed. You belong there. But you also belong somewhere else now. You find yourself living between two worlds, carrying pieces of both.

And sometimes that’s beautiful. Sometimes it’s heartbreaking. Most of the time, it’s both. But here’s what I’ve learned.

The goal was never to stop missing home. The goal was never to become fearless. The goal was simply to keep building a life anyway. To keep showing up. To keep making connections. To keep finding joy in small things. To keep choosing hope on the days when everything feels uncertain, because eventually the city that felt foreign becomes familiar. The streets become part of your story. The people become part of your life.

And one day, without even noticing, you realise that while you were busy trying to survive abroad, you were quietly creating a home. Not the one you left behind. A new one. One built from resilience, memories, friendships, heartbreak, growth, and all the little moments that nobody posts about on social media.

And maybe that’s what moving abroad really teaches you. That home isn’t always where you came from. Sometimes it’s who you become when you have no choice but to start over.

title: New cigarette prices could be your best reason to quit
text:
The new fiscal year budget has been announced and as always, people are paying close attention to which expenses are set to rise and which might offer a little relief. While most of these changes affect our wallets, some also have the potential to affect our habits.

Cigarettes are among the items that have seen an increase in price, adding to the cost of a habit that was never cheap to begin with.

For those who have spent months or even years, telling themselves that they would quit "one day", this price hike could offer a reason to finally start. Quitting smoking is rarely easy, but if the latest price increase feels like the final push you needed, here are a few practical ways to make that decision stick.

Do the math

Smokers are aware that cigarettes cost money, but they do not calculate how much they actually spend over time. Imagine someone spending Tk 200 a day on cigarettes. That amounts to Tk 1,400 a week, roughly Tk 6,000 a month and more than Tk 70,000 a year!

The figure will vary from person to person, but the principle remains the same. Small daily purchases add up to a significant amount over time and looking at that may prompt different thoughts. This money could contribute to a holiday, a new gadget, or even a small investment. Seeing the annual cost rather than daily terms can be a source of motivation for those considering quitting.

Let technology help

Breaking a long-standing habit can feel overwhelming, which is why many people find it helpful to focus on small milestones rather than the end goal. Several smoking cessation apps are designed around this idea. They track smoke-free days, celebrate progress through badges, estimate money saved and provide regular reminders of how far a user has come.

What makes these tools effective is that they turn quitting into a series of manageable challenges. Users are encouraged to focus on reaching the next milestone, whether that is a day, a week or a month without a cigarette. For people who enjoy tracking progress or staying motivated through goals, these apps can help to accomplish.

Know your triggers

Quitting smoking is not only about willpower, but also about understanding the situations that quietly keep the habit alive. Most smokers do not light up randomly. There are usually patterns behind it. It could be a cigarette with morning tea, one after meals or during work breaks.

Identifying these triggers is an important step. Some people find it useful to observe their smoking patterns for a few days and note when cravings appear most strongly. Once these moments are recognised, they become easier to anticipate and gradually avoid or replace with other actions.

Replace the habit

Quitting something often works better when something else replaces the habit. Smoking is not just nicotine for many people, it is a ritual for them.

Simple substitutes like chewing gum, mints or even a bottle of water can keep the mouth engaged during cravings. Some people also find it helpful to distract themselves with small activities, whether it is scrolling through something, listening to music or playing games.

The goal is not to find a perfect replacement, but to interrupt the loop that leads from craving to cigarette. Over time, the urge weakens when it is no longer paired with the familiar action that follows it.

Change your environment

Willpower alone often struggles when the environment keeps reinforcing the habit. That is why small changes in surroundings can make difference. Spending more time in smoke-free places such as cafés, libraries or study spaces can reduce exposure to situations where smoking feels automatic.

It also helps to avoid carrying extra cigarette or keeping them within easy reach. Minor frictions, like making cigarettes less accessible, can interrupt impulsive decisions. Over time, these small barriers add up and make smoking less convenient, which is often enough to reduce frequency without relying purely on self-control.

Quitting smoking is rarely a straight or simple journey. The intention may be strong, but setbacks are part of the process. A price increase alone may not force anyone to quit, but it can serve as a reminder of what the habit is costing in the long run. Sometimes, even a small shift in perspective is enough to take the first step in a different direction.

title: Simple habits that can ease financial stress
text:
If you ever felt the correct way to get rid of financial anxiety is to get rich, you are absolutely wrong. Of course, theoretically, it should work, but practically, maybe not much. So, here we present the simplest guide to shoo away the overwhelming thoughts of economic insecurity.

Name your fear

Financial anxiety is never solely about money. Underneath might hide a specific fear, the apprehension of being judged, not being able to retire at the desired age, or maybe not being able to fulfil one's expectations. Before you can address the problem, you need to declutter your mind and pinpoint what exactly scares you.

Save an emergency fund

It is one of the quietest, yet most powerful things you can do for fixing your relationship with money. Most importantly, it does not have to be large; the equivalent of two or three weeks of essential expenses sitting untouched in a separate account changes everything. At the end of the day, the size of the fund matters far less than the fact that it exists.

Know your digits

Avoiding checking the accounts might make you feel safer for the time being, but avoidance triggers anxiety in the long run. Sitting down once a month and simply looking at your savings and bills gives you a clear idea of whether you are overspending intentionally or it is slipping without notice. When you know your monthly expense limits, spending stops feeling like a gamble, and it alone takes a huge burden off your chest.

Change in mindset

Financial anxiety thrives on extremes, either “I have nothing” or “I must have everything figured out right now.” A steadier mindset sits in the middle.

Thinking about small wins is the baby step you can take, tracking one week of expenses, saving a tiny amount, and saying no to one unnecessary purchase, is undoubtedly boring, but effective.

In the end, a constant worry about finances is more about the fear of not being enough in a world that keeps raising the price of “enough”, and there is always someone ahead of you. Counting your expenses, worrying sometimes is perfectly fine, but that should not own you. And that quiet shift, where fear begins to fade just enough for you to move forward, is where real stability begins.

title: Clayface pushes the DCU into disturbing body horror territory
text:
*This review contains spoilers.

Clayface is the third feature film in James Gunn and Peter Safran’s DC Universe (DCU), following Superman (2025) and Supergirl (2026), based on the Batman villain of the same name. The movie provides a unique take on the genre, focusing on body horror and portraying a complex take on a person’s loss of identity and the desperation that ensues ‌after.

The film is a horror-revenge thriller centred on Matt Hagen, a successful actor who is horribly disfigured by a Gotham City crime boss and receives experimental treatment to repair the damage, resulting in unexpected changes to his body. The root of the story is based on Matt’s loss of self and desire for revenge.

Clayface is ‌more of an experimental mixed-genre film than a straightforward horror or superhero film, blending elements of a crime-thriller, revenge quest and body horror. There are very few jump scares in the movie, with the horror stemming purely from the gore and disturbing scenes of Matt Hagen’s body transformation. The superhero (or, in this case, supervillain) aspects of the movie come from Matt’s revenge quest. While this side of the plot is satisfying, it does slightly undercut the scares and existential dread built through the gruesome body horror side of the story.

Image

Matt Hagen’s descent into madness is done with masterful complexity, as from the beginning of the film his true personality is left ambiguous. Matt is neither completely heroic nor villainous; his profession as an actor and “becoming other people” is hinted at as being his coping mechanism for having an abusive childhood. His gradual transformation and ability to not just portray but physically become other people are both tragic and poetic to his character. He is a character with no sense of self, and he values himself by how others perceive him and the validation he receives as an actor. Subsequently, he values others based on that same philosophy, as demonstrated by his relationship with Dr Caitlyn Corr.

Caitlyn is the only character who helps Matt, and thus he begins to develop an idealised version of her and fails to perceive her as anything more than that. While his pursuit of revenge may seem somewhat “heroic”, his relationship with Caitlyn devolves into a one-sided obsession, and when she ultimately rejects him, it drives him toward his inevitable villainous turn. After finally entering his comic-accurate monstrous form at the end of the film, he holds on to that idealised version of Caitlyn. This aspect of the story can be interpreted as a subtle commentary on consent and unhealthy relationships based on idealisation and desire, and not taking into account the other person’s individuality.

Image

A minor aspect that may disappoint certain fans is the absence of any reference to Batman, even though Clayface is primarily a Batman villain and the movie is set in Gotham City. On its own, the plot does work well as solely a Clayface origin story; however, the lack of Batman connections is a bit of a missed opportunity. Furthermore, the film’s approach to blending genres does make it more of a “jack of all trades”, as the elements of horror and revenge thriller make it so that the movie doesn’t excel at either but still manages to be sufficiently well enough to be enjoyable.

Clayface is yet another unconventional addition to the DCU, delivering a brilliant mix of body horror and revenge thriller within the superhero genre. It does not vastly expand the lore of the cinematic universe; however, it does give a solid, standalone character study on identity and self. Clayface is an easy recommendation not just for fans of DC Comics, but also for horror enthusiasts and people looking to see a satisfying revenge story.

title: Durga Puja for Bangladeshi students abroad
text:
Image Illustration: Arindom Kundu

As the riverbanks around the country are increasingly adorned with the blinding white hue of the kash-phool, the Hindu community prepares for the annual Durga Puja – the largest celebration of ethnically Bangalee Hindus on both sides of the border. It is a time which for many symbolises the community aspect of the social group — from families coming together to listen to the recital of Chandipath on the auspicious morning of the Mahalaya to shopping for one’s friends and family. However, for students who have moved away from Bangladesh, it can be a difficult time as they not only struggle to adjust to their new lifestyles but also navigate feelings of homesickness while missing out on the celebrations back home.

Durga Puja, for them, does not feel the same without the shared anticipation with their loved ones. “The Bangladeshi Hindu community has a separate spark in the days leading up to the festivities,” said Atoshi Golder, a second-year undergraduate student at Rhodes College. Recalling experiences from her childhood, she said that the entire calendar in a Bangladeshi Hindu household is orientated around Durga Puja – an aspect of celebration she misses being in the air every October. Despite her homesickness during the period, Atoshi feels lucky to be able to go to a Durga Puja hosted by the Bangladeshi Hindu community nearby. However, many do not share a fate similar to hers.

Nabonita Paul, a third-year undergraduate student at The University of Sheffield, shared how Durga Puja is not something that is often at the back of her mind these days. “Sometimes I will just forget that it is Durga Puja, and I will only realise it when I talk to my parents back home,” she shared. The lack of a Bangalee Hindu temple in Sheffield means that she misses out on any and all festivities surrounding Durga Puja.

Image Photo: Hrishik Roy

“While there is a lot that happens on campus during Diwali, I cannot really say the same thing about Durga Puja.” When asked if she thinks that Diwali might be able to make up for some of the missed aspects of Durga Puja, she said, “Nothing really replaces Durga Puja for me because I miss dressing up for it, the food that my mother would make, and just being able to invite my friends to our house.” For her, celebrating Durga Puja now boils down to just going out and getting a meal with her friends, and that too, if she actually remembers that it is the day of the puja.

Even for those who have a Durga Puja celebration near them, the idea of going to a puja pandal can be daunting because of their unfamiliarity with the community. Aritra Saha, an undergraduate student at the University of British Columbia, shared that he was hesitant to go out for the festivities last year because he didn’t know anyone involved with the Bangalee community in Vancouver. “I am researching my options this year,” he said. Speaking about his experience last year, he said that he attended his school’s Diwali festivities to compensate for the fact that he was unable to celebrate Durga Puja.

Unlike Nabonita, however, Aritra feels that it is plausible that Diwali can make up for some of the missed festivities during Durga Puja. Shedding light on his brother’s experience – who lives in a part of Canada where there aren’t many Bangalee Hindus – Aritra said that his brother celebrates Diwali and Navratri with his friends. The former is a festival that is also dedicated to the Goddess Durga, which coincides with the festivities of Durga Puja.

"My brother now engages in Gujarati festivities such as going to a ‘Garba Night’ with his friends during Navratri because all his friends are from that part of South Asia,” he shared.

Reflecting on this, he stated that people seek out that festive essence from other celebrations such as Diwali or Navratri when their own festivities are not available. On the other hand, Shawhardo Shopan Singha, a first-year student at the University of New South Wales, is attempting to convince the Hindu student groups on campus to celebrate Durga Puja in a more active fashion. “I believe that if many people can show up for Garba – a predominantly Gujarati tradition, as a part of Navratri celebrations – there has to be interest in celebrating Durga Puja amongst non-Bangalee Hindus too,” he commented.

Image Durga Puja mandap in East London in 2025. Photo: Dipita Saha Shweta

While some do have a community of people to celebrate Durga Puja with while abroad, several core aspects of the celebration might feel imperfect to them. According to Shawhardo, the pujas which happen in Sydney often happen over a span of two days or a weekend. “It just feels wrong to be celebrating Durga Puja on the wrong day, especially when it is constrained within two days,” he shared. He further added that this is the only feasible option for many members of the community given that Durga Puja is not a public holiday in Australia. Similarly, students studying abroad often do not take holidays for religious observation, even if they are allowed to take a break.

The difficulty of having to catch up with academics and other extracurricular commitments means that religious or cultural commitments often have to take a backseat. “My engineering degree is extremely intensive, and I am often attending lectures for very long periods of time, so taking a day off means that I have to miss out on material which is difficult for me to later catch up on,” said Nabonita. “I literally had a midterm exam during the puja last year, so taking a day off was not an option for me at all,” noted Aritra.

The students pursuing their education and other career opportunities abroad often have to give up on important aspects of their culture as a trade-off. As such, the feeling of alienation can feel more pronounced when you are so removed from the festivities.

Sharing her melancholy surrounding the issue, Atoshi remarked, “I honestly do not have a strong desire for any holidays during any other time of the year, but I really wish that I could get time off during that period and visit Bangladesh.” She further shared how she sometimes thinks about the implications of permanently settling in a country that is not her own and how she pensively wonders if she’ll ever even be able to go back to celebrate it in a proper manner.

It is rather ironic that, while Durga Puja is celebrated as homecoming for the Mother Goddess as she returns from her husband’s abode to unite with her family, it is that one time of the year that Bangladeshi students cannot afford to return home, given that it often overlaps with the midterm examination season of the academic term. As one learns to adapt to these social changes around them when studying abroad, there is still a part of them that clings to aspects of their culture and traditions. While one might tweak or shed some aspects of the culture, they still try to retain the core essence, whether through participation in Diwali festivities for a sense of belonging or just celebrating through a meal with their friends.

title: Why everyone should try chess at least once
text:
Everything we consume now is built for speed. Videos are 15 seconds long, articles are skimmed, and we have all been quietly trained to value the output and skip the process.

Chess is the exact opposite of that. You cannot rush it, you cannot skim it, and there is no version of it where you get good in a fortnight. You sit with one problem, concentrate for longer than feels comfortable, and slowly get better.

Chess is also simple to learn and impossible to master. The rules take an afternoon, and after that, you have a game with more possible sequences than there are atoms in the observable universe, which means no two games you play will ever be quite the same. A game from the sixth century still manages to feel new every single time someone plays it, which is quite fascinating.

The best part about chess is definitely the grind. You will get stuck, and you will sit at the same rating for weeks, lose six in a row, and want to throw away your phone. What chess teaches you in this scenario is pretty introspective: step away, come back later, and look again at how you are actually playing rather than blaming your luck. And when you finally break through, when you cross that golden 1000 rating, the feeling is euphoric in a way that very few things are.

Now, the myth. Most people picture chess as two silent old men staring at a board for six hours. That format exists, but it is not where the game lives now. Blitz and rapid are what everyone actually plays, and over the board, they are chaotic in the best way. There is banter. There is trash talk. When both clocks fall under 30 seconds, people start slapping pieces down and knocking half the board over.

Chess is also free. Chess.com and Lichess have millions of players between them, so you can find a game at two in the morning at whatever level you are. Every opening, tactic, and endgame has been explained on YouTube by someone better than you. The barrier to entry is essentially zero.

I should be honest about one thing, because it gets overstated. The research on whether chess makes you academically sharper is mixed. One large meta-analysis found a moderate benefit for maths and general cognitive skills, but other controlled studies found no meaningful transfer at all. I would not sell it as a brain upgrade but as a way to build discipline.

What I did not expect was how social the game actually is. Chess clubs exist at most universities and many schools as well, but they are tiny compared to the sports clubs, which feels like a missed opportunity. A chessboard is one of the easiest excuses to talk to a stranger that I have ever come across. It got me talking to people at university I would never have met otherwise, and at work, it put me in conversation with an entire department I had no professional reason to know.

Nobody intends to network over a chessboard. They just play, and the networking happens anyway. Hence, I think campuses should take it more seriously. You need a board, a clock and a room, or nothing at all if you play online.

Add proper tournaments with real prizes and actual stakes, and it becomes a spectacle rather than a hobby. If that sounds far-fetched, consider that chess is now a certified esport.

So, try it once. If it clicks, you are in for a treat. If it does not, you at least know the rules and can accept a game whenever one is offered. My only advice is to take it slowly and stop being afraid of losing, because the learning curve is steep and you will lose more than you win at first. You cannot become Magnus Carlsen in a month. Trust me, I have tried.

1. Esports World Cup (2026). Chess at the Esports World Cup 2026.

2. Educational Research Review (2016). Do the benefits of chess instruction transfer to academic and cognitive skills? A meta-analysis.

3. Learning & Behavior (2017). Does chess instruction improve mathematical problem-solving ability? Two experimental studies with an active control group.

title: Blue Valentine still stings in your 20s
text:
*This review contains spoilers for the movie

I keep coming back to one thing about Blue Valentine, which is how it shows you the right person at the right time, then shows you those same two people turn into the wrong ones. It never lets you decipher where the switch happened.

The film cuts between the two timelines on purpose. One minute, Dean and Cindy are walking the streets at night, half-strangers convinced they have found the one. The next, they have been married for six years and cannot stand to share a room. Putting the falling-in-love next to the falling-apart is why the film hurts the way it does.

The romance is real. The nighttime wandering, Dean playing ukulele on the pavement while Cindy taps her feet in a shop doorway: none of it is ironic. You believe them – which is the trap – because underneath all that tenderness, the film is showing you two people in their 20s rushing into a marriage without ever asking the boring questions. What do you actually want? Where do you see yourself in 10 years? Cindy is pregnant, scared, and on her own. Dean shows up and chooses her completely. He marries her, raises the baby as his own, and asks for nothing back. It is the most generous thing in the film. It is also the decision that quietly dooms them.

Being chosen at your lowest is not the same as being right for each other once you have climbed back up. Cindy was training to be a doctor. Dean is content painting houses and indulging in his vices. He says, more or less, that being a husband and a father is dream enough for him. Maybe he means it. But Cindy ends up married to a man whose ambitions she never actually knew, because when they met, all she could see was someone who wanted her and the baby. She did not fall for his future, as there was not one to fall for.

There's a Jeff Buckley song, “Lover, You Should've Come Over”, that names her exact bind: the feeling of being too young to stay put and far too old to break free and start again. That is Cindy by the end. She is suffocating, but there is a child now, and she grew up watching her own parents stay locked in a cold, loveless marriage. She knows what that does to the kid caught in the middle. So, she takes the harder stance and lets go, not out of cruelty, but because she refuses to hand her daughter the same childhood.

Here is what I really cannot resolve: who is the bad guy? Cindy, for leaving a man who was good to her when she had nobody? Or Dean, who refuses to grow past his resentment, takes offence at every word, and treats her ambition like an attack until she cannot breathe? I have gone back and forth, and I do not think the film wants me to land anywhere. There is no villain, but rather, there are two people who made an enormous decision on the back of one tender, desperate night and woke up years later as strangers.

That is why it still feels honest at 20-something. We are sold the idea that loving someone hard enough is supposed to be enough. Blue Valentine says outgrowing someone is real, even someone kind, even someone you once meant it with. The decent thing to do in that situation is to say so out loud, to talk about who you are becoming, instead of clinging to who you used to be for each other.

It is complicated, the way real relationships are complicated. No bad guy. Just bad timing, a few bad decisions, and the plain fact that people grow in different directions. The film does not try to comfort you about that; it refuses to pretend otherwise. At this age, that honesty is worth more than reassurance.
