title: DU student Amio Paul on carrying forward a 150-year-old legacy of idol-making
text:
On the occasion of Durga Puja, we must acknowledge the artisans behind the idols we see in mandaps. Campus spoke with Amio Paul, a student of the 33rd batch of the Department of Oriental Art at the Faculty of Fine Art, Dhaka University (DU), who, along with his family, has been involved in this craft for approximately 150 years. Generation after generation, his family has continued to make idols with pride.

Image

Campus (C): You grew up in a family that has made idols for generations. What is your earliest memory of watching your father or grandfather make an idol, and when did you first feel you wanted to learn this craft too?

Amio Paul (A): There is always some work going on at my home or workshop, so the whole working period becomes a collection of small memories. We do the work with great joy.

As a child, I especially enjoyed the time of painting Durga idols with my father, Achinto Paul. I have felt a special fondness for art since childhood, and because work is always going on at home, I have been watching and learning since I was little.

C: What have you learnt from your father and grandfather about making idols that cannot be learnt from books or at art school?

A: The biggest lesson I received from my father is that making an idol is not just art; it is work that involves feeling, faith, and patience. I learnt how to understand clay, how to work by judging its quality and moisture, and how to bring life to an idol’s facial expression.

Above all, I learnt from my father how to work in the traditional method. At art school or the Faculty of Fine Arts, the entire process of making a sculpture follows academic rules, and every measurement is taken precisely. The traditional method, however, I learnt from my father.

C: How has formal art education as a student of Oriental Art at DU influenced your idol-making? And how has your experience as an idol-maker helped you see what you learn in the classroom?

A: Formal art education has made my idol-making far more conscious and refined. The ideas I gained there about drawing, form, proportion, colour, composition, aesthetics, and art history are useful when I make idols.

Earlier, I perhaps relied more on experience and family teaching, but formal education has given me a new way of analysing my own work.

Image

At the same time, my long practical experience as an idol-maker has helped me understand classroom lessons differently. The theories of proportion, form, and balance taught in books and classes, I see applied in practice right before my eyes as I make idols.

So, theoretical knowledge and practical experience have complemented each other. For me, the union of formal art education and the idol-making education I received from my family has enriched my art practice the most.

C: What does making an idol mean to you: simply creating a work of art, or something more?

A: For me, making an idol is not just creating a work of art. It carries a deep connection with tradition, emotion, and people. When I make an idol, I do not merely shape a form out of clay. I try to express the form of a goddess and people’s feelings of faith and devotion.

This work has been done in our family for generations, so for me, idol-making is at once an art, a family heritage, and a responsibility. When an idol is installed in a puja pandal, and people pray before it with devotion and reverence, my work as an artist takes on a different meaning. Being part of that faith and joy is the greatest reward for me.

So, I believe idol-making is not just creating a beautiful form from clay, straw, colour, and ornaments; it holds a culture, a tradition, and people’s feelings.

C: You are part of a young generation joining a craft that has been passed down through families for generations. What changes have you seen in idol-making compared to your father’s and grandfather’s time?

A: Quite a few changes have come to idol-making compared with my father’s and grandfather’s time. Earlier, the work depended largely on conventional methods and family experience. From collecting materials like clay, straw, and bamboo to the idol’s structure, ornaments, and colours, everything was done mostly by hand, drawing on long experience.

Image

Today, new kinds of designs, colours, and decoration are being used more. The demands of buyers and puja organisers have changed too, so alongside traditional styles, modern design and creativity are gaining importance. Because of social media and technology, it is easy to learn about idol work from different parts of the country, which has created opportunities to work with new ideas and designs.

Even amid so much change, we try to hold on to our core tradition and our family’s technical knowledge. What matters most to me is that, while keeping pace with modernity, this traditional art form should not be lost. Rather, I hope it becomes richer through the new generation and moves forward.

C: Do you feel interest in learning traditional crafts like idol-making is declining among young people today? If so, what do you think could be lost if this knowledge and skill are not passed on to the next generation?

A: I feel that interest in learning this traditional art is declining somewhat among young people. If this chain breaks, it is not only the techniques of idol-making that could be lost, but also our family heritage, technical knowledge, and generational experience. That is why it is important to get the new generation involved in this art.

C: Do you want to continue idol-making professionally in the future and carry your family’s heritage forward? What do you want to preserve in your work, what do you want to change, and what do you want to add anew?

A: Yes, I want to continue idol-making professionally in the future and pass our family’s heritage on to the next generation. I want to preserve the traditional methods of construction and the technical skills we have received from our forebears. At the same time, I want to bring some changes in design, materials, and technology to keep pace with the times. By adding modern artistic thinking and creativity, I will try to make idols more aesthetic and diverse.

I dream that one day our art will spread beyond the country. I dream of exhibiting my work internationally.

Azra Humayra is a sub-editor at Campus, Rising Stars, and Star Youth.

title: Inside the eating habits of corporate professionals
text:
Across Dhaka’s corporate hubs, 7 AM is considered an exceptionally early start to the day. After all, most offices do not start their operations for another two hours. Yet, these areas have their own unique rhythm of busyness in these early hours. Shopkeepers chitchat with one another as they prepare breakfast items that will soon fill the offices around them. The most common breakfast served in these eateries is shingara and a cup of tea – a combination considered a snack at best across the country.

Most employees rely on these makeshift eateries to start their day. Md Mahidul Islam, an assistant manager at a leading conglomerate, shared that he has observed a tendency among people around him to skip breakfast in order to reach the office on time. He says, “Most people do not live close to the corporate hubs, especially those situated in Gulshan and Banani. These areas currently do not fall within the metro-rail network, which leaves many employees with the public bus as the other affordable transportation option.”

“Unfortunately, public buses not only have a negative reputation for their unpredictable schedules but also often take the longest to reach the destination compared to other available transportation alternatives. Thus, corporate employees like me usually leave home by 7 in the morning to reach the office by 9 in order to cross a distance of maybe just 10 kilometres,” he adds.

But long commutes are not the only reason employees may sacrifice breakfast. For some, the morning begins after a night of caregiving and interrupted sleep.

“Being the mother of a one-and-a-half-year-old, I rarely get the privilege of eight hours of uninterrupted sleep,” says Maisha Tabassum, a graphic designer by profession. “I have to wake up several times every night to feed my baby and soothe her. This is why I subconsciously trade having a balanced, nutritious breakfast for 30 minutes of extra sleep before my office commute.”

Maisha's experience points to another pressure on working professionals: the struggle to fit personal needs around work and caregiving responsibilities. For postpartum mothers, this can be particularly challenging, as childcare responsibilities often disproportionately fall on mothers. In such circumstances, breakfast can become one of the first things to be sacrificed, potentially compromising nutrition during a period when adequate nourishment is important for recovery and long-term health.

Image Photo: Orchid Chakma

Yet, skipping breakfast or relying on unhealthy alternatives does not come without consequences, particularly for professionals whose work demands sustained concentration and decision-making.

“I have noticed a significant difference in my energy levels on the days I have skipped breakfast,” says Kowshik Acharjee, an accounts payable lead at a multinational corporation (MNC).

“My work entails leading my team, dealing with different stakeholders, and communicating my perspective – tasks that require considerable mental effort. Thus, I usually avoid running on low fuel, as I find it difficult to focus on an empty stomach,” Kowshik elaborates.

From 10:30 AM to 11:00 AM is the unofficial snack break in the corporate world. Colleagues put a short pause on their hustle for a quick cup of tea, usually from the stalls nearby. Tea, with milk and sugar, is the common beverage of choice here.

Kowshik says, “Since I work at an international organisation, I have had the opportunity to work closely with colleagues from India and China, two major tea-producing countries. It surprised me that they are usually more conscious about their caffeine intake compared to us, limiting themselves to just two cups of tea per day, and that too without any milk or sugar.”

A cup of milk tea can contain roughly 35–60 calories, depending on how much milk and sugar is added. “For someone like me, who drinks around three cups a day, that could amount to roughly 105–180 calories, before considering the biscuits or snacks commonly eaten alongside tea. I have seen my colleagues consume even five to six cups of tea per day,” he sighed.

This is an alarming statistic because the survival of South Asian populations during famines has led to a genetic adaptation that results in increased fat storage, leading to a greater risk of metabolic diseases such as type-2 diabetes and cardiovascular diseases.

An eight-hour workday, five to six days a week, leaves little room for recreation for corporate professionals. In this environment, food has become a significant part of socialising. Nusrat Sultana, a communication professional, says colleagues often meet over lunch as a common team-bonding activity.

“Training sessions, birthday parties, and farewells are all very common corporate events which are incomplete without a feast. As someone transitioning from university to the workplace, I struggled to maintain my existing healthy eating habits while trying to navigate through this transition. The excess calorie intake, accompanied by a sedentary lifestyle, caused a 10-kilogram weight gain within my first year of joining the workforce.”

Beyond being an integral part of workplace socialising, food has also become a coping mechanism for workplace loneliness.

Gallup’s 2024 global report found that one in five employees feel lonely at work. Despite spending hours communicating with colleagues, some employees still miss having a “real” connection – moments of shared laughter, heartfelt conversations, and emotional support from their peers.

Nusrat mentioned that as careers progress, work responsibilities tend to increase significantly by the late 20s. As a result, it can become increasingly difficult to find a common time when all her friends are available.

She says, “I have noticed that cafes have come as a rescue to these individuals. Having a quiet cup of coffee there allows them a break from the monotony of life, without the subconscious need to justify their solitude to anyone.”

Image Photo: Mehedi Hasan

In addition to workplace loneliness, a toxic work environment can also influence employees’ eating habits. In the APA’s 2024 Work in America survey, 15 percent of respondents described their workplace as somewhat or very toxic. The situation may be no different in Bangladesh, where workplace stress can take a toll on both employee well-being and productivity.

For some, food becomes an easy way to seek temporary relief from a stressful work environment. Kowshik recalls, “At one point in my life, I used to go out for lunch every other day. My office at that time was surrounded by restaurants offering a wide array of cuisines. Trying a new restaurant every other day not only gave me breathing space from my workspace but also acted as a quick dopamine hit. This is not a sustainable way of living, as I gained a substantial amount of weight within a short span of time – not only because of the higher calorie intake, but also, I believe, because of the higher cortisol levels.”

On days when employees choose not to eat out, they often have access to subsidised meals at their workplace. These usually consist of rice, a source of protein such as fish or poultry, lentils, vegetable curry, and, sometimes, a fruit. The subsidy not only allows employees to have a relatively healthy and hygienic meal within their budget but also saves them the time and hassle of preparing and bringing lunch to work.

However, with food prices continuing to rise, Mahidul fears that corporations may eventually pass these additional costs on to employees. He adds, “Businesses usually have a greater ability to absorb these expenses than we do as individuals. Thus, they should consider not putting tangible cost benefits over employee welfare, which I see as the key to an organisation’s success in the long run.”

For many office goers, subsidised workplace lunches aren't always a viable option, either because their employer doesn't offer the perk or because the food lacks appeal. On the other hand, bringing a homemade lunch presents its own challenge, which is a lack of preparation time.

Faced with these constraints, professionals like Didar Hossain, an HR manager at a garments company, frequently turn to local Bangla hotels near their offices.

“I prefer home-cooked food because the subsidised meals at work don't always taste good, even if they are affordably priced,” Didar explains. “However, bringing lunch from home is only feasible occasionally. We rarely have time to cook in the morning or pack leftovers from the night before.”

He adds, "Dining at nice restaurants or ordering food delivery every day gets too expensive, so roadside Bangla hotels become our fallback. My main worry is hygiene. Every so often, government inspectors raid these places and uncover unsanitary kitchens or harmful ingredients. I don't fully trust the food, but when options are limited, I have no choice."

Water consumption is another often-overlooked aspect of their workday habits.

Nusrat said, “It is often difficult to keep track of how much water one consumes during a busy workday. I experience this even more so on days I must go for field visits. Although this may go unnoticed for a big chunk of the workday, I experience severe headaches caused by dehydration.”

These pressures can make it difficult for corporate professionals to maintain healthy eating habits. Chowdhury Tasneem Hasin, Chief Clinical Dietician & HOD, Dietetics & Nutrition Department, at Continental Hospital PLC, says that, given these circumstances, corporate professionals can adopt a few personal initiatives to better navigate the structural limitations they face.

“Many corporate professionals say that they tend to miss breakfast because they are juggling responsibilities such as getting their children ready and dropping them off at school. As a result, they may subconsciously put their own needs at the end of the priority list. Many may notice the impact soon enough, such as poor focus and irritability throughout the day. For some, it may also contribute to weight gain in the long run if it leads to overeating during the next eating window,” says Hasin.

“Where possible, making small adjustments to the routine may help. For instance, going to bed earlier could allow those who cite lack of sleep as a reason for skipping breakfast to make more time for it,” she adds.

On the topic of caffeine consumption, Hasin advises against villainising tea and coffee, while also encouraging people to be mindful of their consumption. She says, “Tea and coffee are popular pick-me-up beverages that may stimulate one and invigorate them for the next work session. However, it is advised to limit ourselves to two-three cups of tea or coffee and make it a priority to drink two-three litres of water a day at the same time. Many aren’t aware, but excessive caffeine intake can cause dehydration in some individuals. In a busy working environment, particularly in an air-conditioned room, it can be easy to lose track of how much water we are consuming, as one may not face the physical symptoms of dehydration as much.”

Additionally, Hasin acknowledges that communal meals and corporate events are an integral part of workplace culture. However, she believes that maintaining a balance is key to a healthy lifestyle. Thus, she suggests that organising committees of these events can place healthier and nutrient-rich options alongside the usual fare.

“These changes do not necessarily require drastic adjustments. Rather, small, sustainable changes to daily routines can help professionals make healthier choices while managing the demands of their workday,” she says.

The corporate diet, thus, is shaped by more than appetite. It is a product of the commute, the clock, the office culture, and the demands that fill the working day. For many professionals, eating better may therefore require not just better choices but also a workplace in which those choices are easier to make.

title: Unpacking the abuse inflicted by teachers
text:
Image Illustration: Mong Shonie

Trigger Warning: Mentions of verbal, physical, and sexual abuse

I can still feel the humidity of my sixth-grade classroom. As a natural reaction to the heat, some of us had opened one or two shirt buttons. Suddenly, the teacher, who had been conducting the lesson, called out one of our classmates. She pointed at the girl and started disparaging her because she had opened a few too many buttons for the teacher's liking. This went on for several minutes – one word after the other being thrown at her, insinuating that she did it to grab the attention of the boys in the classroom.

My classmate had started crying by the end of that interaction. The rest of us quietly began closing the buttons we had opened for momentary relief. Sadly, this wasn't that rare a situation for us. This particular teacher's "strict guidance" was known to almost every student in my school. We were simply expected to deal with it, and to pray that we didn't face the brunt of her wrath on any given day.

Schools are often the place where we spend most of our adolescence besides our home. It is the main focal point of a lot of students' socialising as well. Therefore, the fact that the authority figures in such an important environment can be bullies themselves is an extremely uncomfortable truth. A lot of people think that teachers are far more lenient towards us these days. Some are under the impression that children are becoming too sensitive and soft, simply because corporal punishment has been prohibited — that too in 2011.

Image

A report titled "The prevalence of teachers who bully students in schools with differing levels of behavioral problems" defines a bullying teacher as a teacher “who uses his or her power to punish, manipulate, or disparage a student beyond what would be a reasonable disciplinary procedure."

Bullying comes in many forms. Sometimes it happens at such a young age that the victim can't even identify it for what it is; they end up blaming themselves for being berated. Such is what happened to Pia*. She says, "Back when I was in class one, I had just been admitted to a new school and was told to draw an octopus. As I was only six years old, I couldn't draw very well, and my science teacher took my drawing in front of the class and humiliated me. As a timid child, this really affected me. She carried on berating me for every little thing. Once she started on her tirade, it took a long time for her to calm down. I became even quieter after facing such treatment from her."

Asked to shed some light on this, Laila Akter, a psychological counsellor, says that neurodivergent students tend to be more vulnerable to teachers’ rebukes. Not all neurodivergent students are bullied, of course. It depends on their communication style and sensory issues, with their behaviour often being misinterpreted by teachers.

Back when Nusrat Shabnam was in the fifth grade, her ADHD was still undiagnosed. Even though she used to complete her homework, she would sometimes forget to bring the note copy to class. This would enrage her maths teacher to the point that he would punish her on other days for no reason. It became particularly bad one day in class when, as the teacher's phone was ringing, she simply pointed it out.

She alleges that he began marching towards her and hitting her on the face with a rolled-up notebook so hard that her glasses fell off. Her friend tried to pull her away from the attack, but he didn't stop. He carried on tormenting her for the rest of the school year.

Bullying isn't limited to insults or physical retaliation. Sometimes it takes the form of active sabotage. Such is what happened in the case of Farhan*, who did not want to enrol in his class teacher's private coaching centre. Following this, the award for ranking first in his batch eluded him.

The procedure required that the class teacher submit his name to the school authorities for the prize to be authorised, which Farhan recalls the teacher forgot to do. Yet, another student, who did attend the teacher’s coaching centre, received it instead.

Image Illustration: Abir Hossain

Students may think that at least in university they won't have to put up with any sort of abuse or humiliation anymore. However, the start of their academic journey may be tainted by some faculty members’ awful behaviour.

Rafi* explains a distressing encounter that he faced. On one particular day, during class, everyone had been talking amongst themselves while the attendance sheet was being passed around. Rafi merely asked a classmate whether they had signed their name, following which the professor came rushing towards him. Rafi alleges that he almost hit him as he charged to the end of the bench and also screamed at him.

He then forced Rafi to call his father and berated him, asking why he had sent his son to that particular university. He proceeded to call Rafi’s mother as well. The student says that the most traumatic part was the fact that the professor decided to humiliate his parents in front of his whole class. Rafi says that he was the subject of horrible nicknames and gossip following the incident.

Through all of this, students are more often than not told to just accept it. They are also scared off from reporting a teacher's behaviour to the school authorities on the basis of a single question: who would they believe – a young student or a grown adult with a long history at the institution?

Mustering up the courage to report incidents is not easy either, as victims are often hounded simply for speaking up. Sadly, there are also extreme cases where students have lost their lives for speaking out against an authority figure, such as in the infamous case of Nusrat Jahan Rafi, a young girl who was set on fire for speaking up against her school’s headmaster, who had sexually assaulted her.

It's quite daunting to be treated so harshly by the person who is supposed to be your guide, at the place that is supposed to shape you.

Asked about the effects this type of bullying has on people, Laila opines, "When exposed to prolonged bullying like this, strong psychological effects can be seen in students. They get depressed, they're anxious, and they have self-esteem issues, which can devolve into not performing well academically and developing an aversion towards going to the institution. The worst part is that they sometimes blame themselves for these situations and try to make themselves smaller in social settings."

Image

She also offers insight into why teachers act this way: "A lot of our teachers, sadly, aren't trained properly to handle neurodivergent students. They may also not have a proper work-life balance and use the classroom as a way to let out their frustration. They're often so burnt out that their personal authoritarian teaching style overrides the training they do receive on how to handle students."

Laila believes that educational institutions shouldn't simply try to hide these cases. Rather, they should stand beside their students through difficult periods. Beyond support from the institutions themselves, some also struggle with opening up to their parents, as they may minimise the severity of the teacher's actions. As such, while institutional support remains imperative, it is just as vital that the prevailing mentality of people also change.

The inner lives of students are left in turmoil through no fault of their own. As we strive towards a better future, it is imperative that we recognise that teachers’ unwanted, aggressive behaviour is not only called out but deemed unacceptable.

*Names have been changed upon request.

title: "If the art is yours, it is enough"
text:
Image

Dhaka-based musician Swar, the artist behind Porcelain Kiss, creates dreamy yet unsettling electronic music that explores isolation, derealisation, and the strange distance of living in a hyper-connected world. Starting with little more than a smartphone and headphones, she turned her bedroom setup into an intimate sound that exists outside Bangladesh’s mainstream indie landscape.

For Swar, the DIY approach is part of the project’s identity. Rather than chasing numbers or algorithmic reach, she remains committed to making music that feels honest to her. Through Porcelain Kiss, she gives shape to the quiet disconnection of a generation that is constantly online yet often feels alone.

Campus sat down with Swar to discuss building Porcelain Kiss from her bedroom, finding an audience across borders, and turning feelings of detachment and grief into sound.

Campus (C): For someone discovering your music today, who is Porcelain Kiss? Where does the name come from, and how would you describe your sound in three words?

Swar (S): Porcelain Kiss is basically the part of me that I can’t really explain normally, so I put it into music. I am an independent artist from Bangladesh, making dark, emotional, and electronic music with dreamy or ethereal, and sometimes unsettling textures.

The name “Porcelain Kiss” came from the contrast I liked between something fragile and something intimate. It felt soft but a little strange, which is kind of what I wanted the project to feel like. If I had to describe the sound in three words, it would be ethereal, dark, and emotional.

C: You started making music on your phone instead of waiting to access a studio. What first inspired you to create your own music, and how has that DIY approach shaped the sound of Porcelain Kiss?

S: I started on my phone because I didn’t really have access to a studio or expensive equipment, and I knew it wasn’t coming to me any sooner. Honestly, I didn’t want that to be the reason I never started. I had a phone, headphones, and a lot of ideas. So, I just started experimenting.

Making everything myself definitely shaped Porcelain Kiss. I learned by doing things badly at first and slowly figuring out what sounded right. It also made the music very personal because I resonated with the imperfect audio of older acts like Crim3s and Crystal Castles. To me, the imperfections themselves carried that emotion, so I was trying to translate what I feel directly into sound.

C: What has it been like making dark electronic and dreamscape music in Bangladesh's indie scene, where acoustic, rock, and pop tend to dominate?

S: It can feel as though I am being outcast sometimes because the scene here naturally leans more toward acoustic, rock, pop, metal, and other mainstream sounds. There aren't always many people around you making the same kind of music. But I actually like that part of it too. I never really wanted Porcelain Kiss to sound like everything else around me. There are young people discovering music from all over the world now, so I think the audience is changing too. I am happy to pursue international listeners.

C: On your platform, you stand by the rule: "If the art is yours, it is enough". In an algorithm-driven era where young independent artists constantly chase external validation, how do you maintain that creative boundary?

S: I think the internet makes you feel like everything needs to be measured. Views, followers, streams, comments, whether people think you're good enough. It’s very easy to start making things for an algorithm instead of making things because you actually have something to say.

That rule reminds me that the reason I started was never to impress everyone. If I make something and it genuinely feels like me, then it already has a reason to exist. Of course, I still want people to listen to it, but I don't want numbers to decide whether something I created has value. I hope I keep this mindset till the end.

C: "Under The Moon" turns private grief into a quiet memorial, while "Fog" captures the jarring derealisation of waking up in a haze. When a song begins with a feeling like grief or detachment rather than a melody, what does the creative process look like from there?

S: With something like “Under the Moon”, the emotion came first. I wasn't trying to make a sad song. I was trying to capture a very specific feeling of missing something or someone, and not really knowing what to do with that feeling.

“Fog” came from a completely different kind of emotion. It was my second ever self-produced song, and the feeling of being awake but not completely present, like everything around you is real but somehow distant.

Once I have that feeling, I try to build a world around it with sound. Sometimes the production becomes more important than the lyrics because I want the listener to actually feel the emotion instead of just being told what it is.

C: Across songs like "out of frame" and "Blur", your work explores the isolation of feeling like an outsider watching life from behind glass. Why do you think this sense of digital disconnect and social displacement resonates so deeply with young listeners today, and how has creating music helped you process those feelings?

S: I think a lot of young people are constantly connected now, but somehow still feel incredibly alone. You can talk to hundreds of people online and still feel like nobody actually knows you. You see people going places, having relationships and friends, becoming successful, and you start comparing your real life to tiny edited pieces of someone else's. I think that's where the feeling behind songs like “Out of Frame” and “Blur” comes from. Creating music gives me some place to put those feelings instead of keeping them in my head. Sometimes I don't even fully understand what I am feeling until I have turned it into a song.

C: What would you say to a teenager in Bangladesh sitting alone in their bedroom, feeling like they don't fit in but dreaming of making music with nothing more than a phone and a pair of headphones?

S: Don't wait until you have everything. I started with basically nothing except a phone and a pair of headphones. You don't need the perfect microphone, the perfect computer, the perfect room, or someone's permission to call yourself an artist.

Start with whatever you have and learn as you go. And don't be embarrassed if your first songs aren't amazing. Mine weren't either. You're allowed to be bad at something while you're learning. And don't let people convince you that your music isn't real because you made it differently from them. Start there. The rest can come later.

title: In conversation with three O and A level top performers
text:
For most students, the significance of their grades – particularly of their board examinations – is not lost on them. In fact, they’re reminded, time and again, about its gravity, sometimes with a frequency that can border on annoyingly obsessive. Though a lot may be said about our collective fixation on the need to excel academically, there is little doubt that there is something awe-inspiring about a student who doesn’t just adhere to that aspiration but embodies it. Their achievement serves as a reminder of what dedication, diligence, and sincerity can get you. Then, there are some who go the extra mile and set a benchmark.

​Samara Sharleez Emdad, Md Faiyaz Siddiquee, and Sazin Mustafa Muntakim fall squarely within that category. All three of them are students of Glenrich International School. Faiyaz and Sazin are both students of the twelfth grade and have attained the “World Top Scorer” title, with each having scored a perfect grade in AS Mathematics. They have also received A grades across all their AS subjects.

​Similarly, Samara achieved a perfect score in IGCSE Mathematics along with A* grades in all the other subjects she sat for.

​When asked what was going through their heads when they received their results, Samara could barely believe it. “It felt as though things had finally settled into place and that all the effort I put in over the last two years paid off,” she explains.

​Faiyaz recalls feeling a profound sense of gratitude. “What makes moments like this special is not only the results on paper but also the people around me – the teachers who encouraged my questions, my family who supported my interest, and friends who shared my mutual enthusiasm for problem solving,” he says. “It felt more like a milestone in a journey that is still unfolding.”

​Sazin, on the other hand, was quite nervous. “The AS level examination is known for heartbreaks, so I was quite afraid of how my results would turn out. However, when I first saw my results, the nervousness morphed into happiness as I performed better than I thought I would,” he recalls.

​Though the students were initially gripped by a great deal of anxiety, it ultimately faded away, giving way to jubilation and gratitude. For Sazin, the results are a reflection of his hard work. And the reward, he says, is making the people around him proud.

​Likewise, Samara feels more determined than ever. The results instilled in her the belief to approach challenges with greater self-assurance, as she regards it as a great milestone. She also expresses gratitude to her family, friends, and teachers for providing support to her.

​Faiyaz views his results as a by-product of the intellectual autonomy that he was granted. Having relied on explorative learning rather than traditional study methods, he seeks to understand the underlying mechanisms of the laws of our universe. Such a sentiment inspired him, along with Samara and Sazin, to pursue their own individual interests and extracurricular activities.

​The distinction between academic and extracurricular activities is blurry for Faiyaz. Ranging from research and mentoring to composing original music pieces and participating in olympiads, he believes that his many endeavours have shaped how he thinks. “Something that has helped me in my academic journey is authoring a book; it's called A Quest for Clarity. It taught me that explaining genuinely difficult ideas can also help me understand concepts on my own,” he says.

​Sazin is of the belief that extracurricular pursuits are an important way for him to avoid academic burnout, as they provide an outlet to unwind and ease his mind. He partakes in playing football, video games, and cooking, as it provides a renewed sense of focus and motivation. Having also participated in olympiads and research, he echoes Faiyaz’s sentiments, stating that it proved to be effective in helping him academically.

​As for Samara, she says that karate is the most important asset to her. “It's what helps me keep a clear mind and prepare for the future,” she explains. Much like her seniors, she also attributed participating in olympiads as well as group competitions to helping her practice curiosity.

​Exploring one’s curiosity allows students to develop a better sense of what works for them. This rings true for all three students who undertook study methods tailored to their needs.

​Samara says, “My main study method was to bookmark tough or uncommon past paper questions instead of doing complete past papers. I accepted and learned from the mistakes I made in tests. The most important thing was that I discussed difficult problems, especially in physics and mathematics, with my friends, which I believed helped me a lot.”

​To deal with tumultuous periods, she made an imaginary list of people she felt grateful for and why she wanted to work hard for them.

​Faiyaz states, “My core approach has always been reasoning with the principles first; really understanding the rigorous why behind the theorems and formulas rather than settling for the procedural ‘hows’.”

​When studying A level Further Mathematics, he came across an exponential formula for hyperbolic trigonometric functions. Unsatisfied with just the formula, Faiyaz then attempted to derive the formula himself.

​On the other hand, Sazin tried to maintain a balanced and organised study routine. “I can't study well if I put excessive pressure on myself. So, I try my best not to do so.” His daily routine involved solving mock exams, identifying weaknesses, reviewing mistakes, revising topics, and then preparing himself for the next day. All of this wasn’t done in one continuous stretch but rather in focused increments throughout the day.

​As recipients of the top world scores in their mathematics exams, they were asked about the fear commonly associated with the subject. All three of them assert that maths, even when it's complex, can become enjoyable if students are allowed to understand it more intuitively.

​“Once students believe that the same logic they use in video games, cooking, or even in formulating a social media post can be applied to a math problem, it can prove to be an important skill,” asserts Samara.

​Sazin stresses, “Students should mainly focus, especially at AS level, on building a strong conceptual foundation. When they experience the satisfaction of solving difficult problems, they’re more likely to appreciate the subject.”

“If you let students see the connections between pure mathematics and its application in physics and computation, rather than presenting it as a set of procedures, that really helps. In the mathematics and physics club that I founded, I tried to build a culture of open discussion where ‘whys’ were welcomed,” explains Faiyaz.

​Having done exceptionally well in their academics, the results are sure to spur them on to pursue their goals with a great degree of fervour. After all, the results don’t just signify excellence; they are also representative of their abilities.

​Faiyaz says, “I want to study mathematics and physics deeply, and explore the connections between them. My long-term interest can maybe extend into astrophysics and scientific computing.” He also wants to continue writing, researching, and expanding his organisation.

​“These results have opened up a wider range of opportunities for my future. They have made it possible for me to apply to strong universities and consider a variety of academic pathways,” asserts Sazin. He also states that it has carved out a pathway for him at City University of Hong Kong and also imparted more confidence in him to aim higher.

​Samara emphasises that the results have taught her greater discipline as well as reminded her that it is okay to fail sometimes. “My results fueled my ambition to make a positive impact in the world. And since I've just finished my O levels, a lot of people – including myself – have had some trouble with consolidating their A level subject choices, but now I believe that my subject choices of math, chemistry, physics, and further mathematics are pulling me towards the right direction in the future.”

​Their wisdom, of course, isn’t just limited to their own individual feats. Each one of them extended advice to their younger counterparts as well.

​Samara advises her juniors not to compare themselves to others. Instead, she tells them to compare their present progress with the past.

​Faiyaz underpins the importance of enjoying life. He also urges them to view maths not merely as a subject but rather as a universe to explore.

​Lastly, Sazin says that while exams may appear overwhelming, they can be managed with consistent effort and the right approach. He reminds them to remain positive and that their results are a reflection of their preparation, not their potential.

title: Bangladesh's young mathematicians shine at WMI 2026
text:
Image Team Bangladesh at WMI 2026. Photos: Courtesy

Bangladesh returned from the World Mathematics Invitational (WMI) 2026, held in Chiba, Japan, with an achievement matched by few nations at the competition: every single member of its 27-member national team won an award. Competing against roughly 2,300 students from more than 30 countries, the Bangladeshi contingent secured two diamond awards, two gold medals, six silver medals, 14 bronze medals, and three merit Awards, achieved under the management, training and international coordination of Banglar Math.

Among the many young mathematicians who represented the country four names stand out: Ahbab Zulkifal Zahin of Rajshahi Collegiate School, who won a diamond award; Jeet Bala of Swarnakali High School in Gopalganj, also a diamond medallist and the country's top-3 second-place finisher; Sajidul Haq of St Joseph International School, a sixth grade student who won gold and was named “Star of the World” for posting the highest score among all Bangladeshi participants; and Rahid Azad Ahan, a ninth grader from Khulna Public College, gold medallist. Their accounts, gathered after the competition, trace a common thread of confidence, discipline, mentorship, and tenacity that carried Bangladesh's flag to Chiba and back.

A shared pull toward numbers

For many of the medallists, the pull toward mathematics began long before the WMI ever entered the picture, and the invitation to compete in Japan simply became the natural next step in a much longer relationship with the subject.

“Ever since my childhood, I have been deeply attracted to numerical problems and mathematics, and due to my parents' support, it has only been enhanced further. Bangladesh Math Olympiad (BdMO), Banglar Math Excellency Championship (BMEC), and Banglar Math appeared to me as an opportunity to showcase my love and interest through the various problems that were introduced in this olympiad, so I was highly motivated to take part,” says Zahin, who recently passed his SSC examination.

Jeet Bala, competing among the strongest performers in the entire contingent, described a similarly deep-rooted attachment to the subject, sharpened further by the chance to test himself against peers from around the world. He says, “My deep-seated passion for mathematical problem-solving, abstract thinking, and exploring core disciplines, like number theory, Euclidean geometry, combinatorics, and inequalities, pushed me to enter the olympiad scene. I have always derived immense joy from testing my analytical limits against complex, non-routine problems that stretch far beyond the standard school curricula.”

For Bala, beyond the personal intellectual thrill, the drive to represent Bangladesh on an international platform and benchmark his skills against the brightest young mathematical minds around the world was a massive motivation.

Months of methodical preparation

Behind the medals lay months, and in some cases years, of structured preparation. Zahin drew on lessons from his earlier appearance at WMI Thailand 2025, building a study routine around his own strengths and weaknesses, and credited the organisation's trainers with helping the wider Bangladeshi contingent cut a figure on the international stage. Bala's route was more formal and academic. He immersed himself in advanced problem-solving techniques, functional equations, and rigorous proof-writing, trained alongside other hopefuls at national BdMO camps and selection tests, and supplemented that structured work with independent study of classical contest literature.

Image From the left: Jeet Bala, Sajidul Haq, Rahid Azad Ahan, and Ahbab Zulkifal Zahin.

For Ahan, the step up from national to international competition initially felt disorienting. His BdMO preparation had already given him a strong foundation, which meant BMEC felt like a natural progression, but WMI level left him unsure whether his existing methods would be enough. Banglar Math's problem-solving classes, he said, became a reliable space to verify his reasoning and catch the subtle errors that slip past a solitary solver. He also worked through the organisation's practice book and built in time to reflect on a problem's shape before diving into calculations.

Haq's route to the podium began earlier still, through the BMEC advertised at his school, which led to his selection for the WMI 2026 team trial. His preparation included independent practice on previous years' papers – a formula that, by his own account, was less about elaborate strategy than sustained effort.

Carrying the flag under pressure

Representing a country at an international competition carries a weight that differs from student to student, and the two youngest medallists among the group described handling it in markedly different registers.

For Haq, the youngest of the four grade six Bangladeshi participants, earlier experience on the international stage had already taken the edge off any nerves.

“I already participated in several competitions, including international competitions, and received awards there, so there was not much pressure for me, as I was confident enough to get an award from here. I was also confident to keep my country's honour in front of the whole world,” he says.

Ahan answered the same question framing years of relentless preparation as having already settled the outcome long before he sat down to compete in Chiba. He expands, “I knew I would win. Pressure is for people who are unsure. I wasn't. I had already seen every problem the country could design. WMI was already finished while BdMO was still just my warm-up. The international arena wasn't a mystery. It was just a bigger board with the same rules.”

Building an ecosystem, not just a medal count

Ahmed Shahriar, coach of the Bangladesh Mathematics Team at WMI and co-founder of Banglar Math, views the results as validation of a broader project rather than the product of individual brilliance alone. Looking beyond the next olympiad cycle, he outlined a calendar built around two flagship national competitions: the Banglar Math Team Championship (BMTC), held between August and September, and the Bangladeshi Math Excellence Championship (BMEC), held between March and April, both open to students from grades 3-12.

“Through these competitions, we aim not only to identify talented students but also to nurture their problem-solving abilities, teamwork, confidence, and competitive mindset,” he states, noting that Bangladeshi students have now collected more than 150 international medals and recognitions across competitions including the World Mathematics Team Championship, the International Mathematics Competition, WMI, and the American Regions Mathematics League.

Asked what they would tell the next generation of hopeful Olympiad participants, each of the four medallists offered a version of the same underlying message, even as their tone ranged from gentle encouragement to something closer to a full-throated rallying call.

“If you have a good understanding of the topic of the olympiad or any competition and try hard enough, Inshallah you can easily get an award,” says Haq.

“Cultivate a genuine curiosity for understanding mathematical concepts from first principles rather than relying on rote memorisation or shortcuts. Never be intimidated by difficult problems or initial failures. Resilience in mathematics is forged precisely by wrestling with complex proofs, making mistakes, and rigorously analysing where you went wrong. Stay consistent with your daily practice, embrace the intrinsic elegance of problem-solving,” added Bala.

“Can't solve math in 10 minutes? Try an hour. Still, no? Try two. Still, no? Try three,” says Ahan, before tempering the intensity of his own advice. “And before you grind, take a moment to reflect. Reflection isn't hesitation. It's reconnaissance. Look at the battlefield before you charge.”

“Participating in the olympiad would help them to work with their fear of mathematics and develop their problem-solving skills to a very high level. We should remember that at the end it is not over when they lose; it is only over when they give up,” says Zahin.

For Shahriar, that spirit of persistence is precisely the point: “We want to build a nation of problem solvers. We dream that one day, the students who are solving mathematical problems today will grow up to solve the big problems for Bangladesh”

title: Tufan Chakma on his Erasmus Mundus Joint Master’s in Animation journey
text:
Tufan Chakma, an Indigenous visual artist from the Chittagong Hill Tracts (CHT), Bangladesh, recently completed the fully funded Erasmus Mundus Joint Master’s Degree (EMJMD) in Animation, Re:Anima. A Bachelor of Fine Arts (BFA) graduate from Jahangirnagar University (JU) and founder of the widely followed Facebook page “Tufan’s Artbin”, Tufan works with painting, illustration, and animation, using visual storytelling to highlight the identity, history, culture, and social realities of indigenous communities in the CHT.

Campus sat down with Tufan to get a closer look at his journey.

Campus (C): How did you discover Re:Anima and determine that it was the right programme for you?

Tufan Chakma (T): After completing my BFA from JU in 2023, which took seven years instead of four, I was hesitant to spend another three to four years on a master’s degree there, but I also didn’t want to quit studying. Ultimately, I decided to enrol at JU, so I wouldn’t lose a year while looking for an alternative—which had to be a fully funded scholarship, since neither my family nor I could afford the expenses of studying abroad or at a private university.

The first thing that came to my mind was the Erasmus Mundus scholarship, which I’d first learnt about in the fourth year of my bachelor’s. I had very little knowledge of its requirements, so I started by watching YouTube videos and reviewing the official catalogue. I was very sad to find no painting-related programme, as I wanted to continue my master’s in painting.

One day, I found the programme called Re:Anima. But I wasn’t taught animation academically or professionally. However, as a visual artist, I had been practising animation irregularly since 2019 to tell my stories and reach a wider audience. My only experience with animation was watching Studio Ghibli movies and making some animated videos following YouTube tutorials.

Nevertheless, the course was the only programme that interested me. When I realised animation could bring to life the stories in my head and portray the unseen and unheard history, trauma, loss, and existential crisis of indigenous peoples, I was convinced to apply.

I dug deeper into the requirements, without worrying whether the scholarship committee would select me or not due to my limited animation knowledge. I just felt a connection with animation and started preparing, including the IELTS exam and writing my statement of purpose (SOP).

C: Re:Anima looks for applicants with advanced animation skills, but you had only some self-taught experience in animation. How did you address that in your application?

T: My self-taught animations were created to represent the CHT and address its under-representation and misrepresentation in mainstream media, not for academic purposes. However, Re:Anima required the submission of a four-minute animation showreel to prove sufficient general knowledge. Since I didn’t have one, I decided to use my illustrations and paintings, combined with a few animation clips – as illustration connects to animation through storytelling, character design, and concept art. I hesitated over whether it would be accepted but kept shaping it regardless.

Around then, I learnt from seniors at JU about Mreethmandir Gunjan Kumar Roy, who was studying Re:Anima in the 2023–2025 session. Once I connected with him on social media, his feedback helped improve the showreel and gave me confidence to apply with what I had.

What I realised is that they don’t just look for advanced animation skills—they look for people with passion for animation, experience in a related field, and the ability to bring change, diversity, and new ideas.

Image

C: For your portfolio, how did you decide what to include?

T: I included work that showed what I actually do, why I do it, and what I wanted to do in the future if selected, which, I now realise, mattered most, even though it was unconscious at the time.

I was clear about what I wanted to achieve through this programme. As someone from an indigenous community in the CHT, all my work is based on the rights, struggles, and existential crises we face as under-represented peoples in Bangladesh. Even before knowing about Re:Anima, I had been telling stories from the CHT through my art and wanted to carry those stories into a bigger canvas like an animation film, since the CHT has no notable animation filmmakers to represent stories kept in the dark for so long. So, I chose the pieces that best represented those stories, along with my achievements as an artist.

Image

C: Limited to just 1,000 characters for the motivation letter, how did you present yourself to the selection committee?

T: For Re:Anima, we had to submit a letter of motivation, expectations concerning knowledge to acquire, and a project proposal, each limited to 1000 characters.

I tried to represent the true me—how I started my artistic journey, what motivated me to create art and animation, what I wanted to learn through the programme and why, and the project proposal for my final short film. I believe this is what led the committee to see me as a passionate storyteller—pursuing the degree to represent the CHT creatively.

Firstly, I wrote everything I wanted to include, then shortened it as much as I could. Then, I asked my senior from JU, Dinalo Chakma, to review my writing and give feedback, which helped me shape my words. This is something every candidate should do: never hesitate to reach out to someone experienced who can provide proper guidelines.

C: What project idea did you propose, and how much did it change during the master’s programme?

T: It was tough to decide what to include in this section without proper knowledge of animation filmmaking at the time, but I was motivated to make something no one had made yet—something sustainable about the indigenous peoples of CHT that could be used as a visual example in the future.

There are many untold stories of the CHT that need to be heard and seen. The Kaptai Dam tragedy is one of them, especially in terms of visual documentation; we have no archive with enough visual data on this historical tragedy.

But once the programme started, the story of my final project kept transforming, which is common in filmmaking. So, the film I eventually made is not just about the Kaptai Dam tragedy, but more than that—to discover the full film, audiences will have to wait at least a year. I’m excited to show it to the world and feel very fortunate for this opportunity.

C: How did you decide whom to approach for recommendation letters?

T: Before applying, I had very little knowledge about this and was confused about who and how to ask. My requirement was two or three letters, so I collected three. I wanted people who knew me well, either through teaching or working with me. Since it was an academic application, at least one recommender had to be from JU. I asked two respected teachers from the Fine Art Department, who were supportive and wrote the best letters—which is one of the key documents for any fully funded scholarship. I got another from an organisation I had worked with, which I believe also played a great role.

I spoke to each of them personally, shared my desire to pursue the scholarship, and once they agreed, shared the programme website so they could connect it to my personality, education, and experience.

C: What advice would you give to students with unconventional dreams who are unsure about their career path?

T: Firstly, don’t doubt yourself. Don’t question whether you’re capable of applying for a scholarship. If you want an unforgettable journey full of learning, sharing, and growing, believe in yourself and start working on it. Don’t wait to feel ready; start your journey today.

Secondly, try to be honest, true, and the most authentic version of yourself—someone interested in learning, sharing ideas, bringing diversity, and being creatively different from others. The more genuine you are, the stronger a candidate you become.

Thirdly, the Erasmus Mundus scholarship journey is a chance to transform yourself academically, personally, and professionally and a lifetime opportunity to study at top universities across Europe, explore multicultural societies, and build international connections.

Finally, reserve at least two to three months before applying to prepare for the IELTS exam, research the programme thoroughly, and get to know the universities it’s affiliated with. Your SOP and recommendation letters should reflect that you know the programme, the connection between your previous studies and this one, how your work experience ties in, and how you intend to contribute—not just study it. The committee needs to see that you’re not simply someone who wants a scholarship but someone worth investing in.

Although there’s no universal scoring method across Erasmus Mundus Master’s programmes, remember—it’s not all about your CV, CGPA, motivation letter, or IELTS score—it’s about presenting who you are; what you do and why; the reason why you’re applying for that particular programme; what you’ve already accomplished; and what you intend to do afterwards. Try to submit the best and most unique version of yourself in every way possible.

title: A Bangladeshi photojournalist's Chevening journey
text:
For years, I wanted to become part of the Chevening community. I knew about Chevening and admired its reputation for developing leaders, but there was always one question in my mind: would a photojournalist fit into a journalism fellowship that seemed to attract mostly reporters, editors, and broadcasters?

That question stayed with me for a long time.

My career has been built around documentary photography and photojournalism. For more than a decade, I have documented some of Bangladesh's defining moments, from political unrest and humanitarian crises to climate change, migration, and the Rohingya refugee emergency. Through my work with the Associated Press, Al Jazeera, and other international publications, I learnt that photographs can often communicate what thousands of words often cannot.

Yet, I also understood that journalism is constantly evolving. To remain relevant, journalists must continue learning.

That realisation led me to apply for the Chevening South Asia Journalism Fellowship (SAJP) at the University of Westminster.

A last-minute decision that changed everything

Ironically, I almost missed the opportunity.

In September 2025, while planning my upcoming political assignments and thinking about Bangladesh's rapidly changing political landscape, I came across the SAJP on LinkedIn. I was busy preparing for what I believed would be one of the most important periods of my career as a photojournalist. My focus was entirely on the next assignment, the next story, and the next photograph.

The application form itself surprised me.

Instead of feeling like an ordinary online form, it felt like a professional assessment of my entire journalism career. Every question encouraged me to reflect on my experiences, leadership, achievements, and the impact of my work. Since the fellowship requires several years of professional journalism experience, I realised that every assignment I had covered over the years mattered.

I submitted my application on the final day. One of the most valuable lessons I learnt during the application process is that you should never underestimate your own experience. Sometimes the work you consider routine becomes the strongest evidence of your professional growth.

The email I will never forget

On December 29, 2025, I received an email informing me that I had been shortlisted for the interview.

I still remember exactly where I was.

At that moment, I was covering the funeral of former Prime Minister Begum Khaleda Zia while simultaneously working on political assignments for the Associated Press. Like many photojournalists, I was balancing multiple deadlines with very little time to celebrate.

But reading that email gave me a new sense of confidence. It reminded me that years of consistent work do not go unnoticed.

Preparing for the interview was different from preparing for any job interview I had experienced before. It wasn't about giving perfect answers; it was about honestly explaining my professional journey, why journalism matters to me, and how I wanted to contribute to the future of the profession.

When the award letter arrived

Receiving the final Chevening award letter was one of the most emotional moments of my career. I was genuinely stunned. Although I had worked hard on my application, I never allowed myself to assume I would be selected.

Looking back, another international opportunity had already transformed my perspective. In 2024, I studied documentary practice and visual journalism at the International Center of Photography (ICP) in New York. That experience introduced me to photographers and journalists from around the world and showed me the importance of global collaboration, cultural exchange, and lifelong learning.

Chevening became the next chapter of that journey.

Learning beyond the classroom

Arriving in London and beginning classes at the University of Westminster was inspiring from the very first day. Our fellowship brought together journalists from Bangladesh, India, Pakistan, and Sri Lanka. Although we came from different countries, our professional challenges were remarkably similar.

We debated media ethics, press freedom, conflict reporting, misinformation, digital journalism, and the future of news in an era increasingly shaped by artificial intelligence.

The fellowship itself extended far beyond lectures. We visited some of Britain's most respected media and cultural institutions, including the BBC, The Guardian, the British Library, and several museums that preserve centuries of history and knowledge. These visits allowed us to observe how globally respected news organisations operate and how journalism continues to evolve while maintaining public trust.

One moment remains especially personal. As someone who has spent years documenting humanity through a camera lens, seeing the works of Renaissance master Raphael (Raffaello Sanzio da Urbino) in London for the first time was unforgettable. Standing before paintings I had previously known only from books reminded me that visual storytelling has always shaped the way societies understand the world. Whether through Renaissance art or modern photojournalism, powerful images continue to influence history.

Learning from extraordinary mentors

One of the greatest privileges of the fellowship was learning from distinguished scholars and journalists. Prof. Jean Seaton, an internationally respected media historian and the Official Historian of the BBC, challenged us to think beyond daily headlines and understand journalism within its broader historical, political, and democratic context. Her discussions reminded us that journalism is not only about reporting events; it is about protecting public memory and accountability.

Prof. David Loyn, an acclaimed foreign correspondent with decades of international reporting experience, shared invaluable lessons from covering conflicts, diplomacy, and global affairs. His practical insights into international reporting, editorial judgement, and ethical decision-making demonstrated that great journalism depends not only on courage, but also on accuracy, context, and empathy.

Learning from professionals of their calibre was both humbling and inspiring.

Every experience counts

People often ask me what made my application successful. There is no single answer. I believe it was the accumulation of experiences over many years: covering humanitarian disasters, photographing elections, documenting the lives of refugees, reporting on climate change, working with international news organisations, and receiving opportunities such as the US Department of State's International Visitor Leadership Program (IVLP) in 2021–2022, which introduced me to American institutions and strengthened my understanding of international journalism and leadership.

None of these experiences existed in isolation. Together, they told a story about who I am as a journalist.

My advice to future applicants

If you are considering applying for the Chevening South Asia Journalism Fellowship, my advice is simple: don't wait until you think your career is perfect. Apply when your work genuinely reflects your passion, leadership, and commitment to journalism.

Write honestly and reflect deeply. Don't try to become the person you think the selection committee wants to meet. Instead, help them understand the journalist you have already become.

Most importantly, remember that every assignment, every challenge, and every lesson you have experienced may become part of your story.

Why this fellowship matters

The world is becoming increasingly connected, yet journalism faces unprecedented challenges.

Artificial intelligence is reshaping newsrooms. Disinformation spreads faster than facts. Public trust in the media continues to be tested.

This is precisely why international fellowships like Chevening matter.

They allow journalists to step outside their daily routines, exchange ideas across borders, learn from global experts, and return home with new perspectives that strengthen their reporting and leadership.

For me, Chevening was less about studying in London and more about joining a global community of journalists committed to improving our profession. Because journalism doesn't stop at national borders. Neither should learning.

title: Dr Arifin Sandhi on building Bangladesh's environmental future
text:
Dr Arifin Sandhi, a scientist in the domain of environmental biosciences in Sweden, has spent over a decade studying toxic metal contamination in ecological systems. This remains a crisis with direct stakes for Bangladesh, where groundwater arsenic is a perpetual concern for the rural masses with tubewells. He earned his PhD in Land and Water Resources Engineering at KTH Royal Institute of Technology, Sweden, and has since built a body of work in nature-based solutions. The weight of his work holds great implications for the revival of municipal rivers where open industrial dumping is practised, costing our government and citizens alike. Campus sat down with Dr Sandhi to get a closer look at his thoughts for the future.

Campus (C): What drew you to natural sciences?

Arifin Sandhi (A): Choosing environmental science was quite easy; it was my natural inclination towards the magic of ecosystems. Having attended Dhanmondi Government Boys School, Dhaka College, and Sher-e-Bangla Agricultural University in Bangladesh, I became closely acquainted with the realities of the urban sprawl. The metalloid-laden effluents that bring about a slow death to all rivers that were once the heart of the city tightened the grip. As such, it would be a lie if I went on to say the pastures and ruralities inspired me to pursue this particular modus operandi in academia. Since my master’s study at Stockholm University, I have focused on bioenergy plants and how to clean up the toxic metal mess. And for my PhD, I leaned towards arsenic remediation in mining waters and food crops. Sweden’s culture, entrenched in its policy, is one of stewardship. They are stringent on keeping industrial pollution in check. Industries pay fat margins in order to fulfil their binding obligations, quite a different scene when compared to what we’re used to in the rest of the world. I found this to align with my views. I then became a researcher at Linnaeus University, Sweden, and have been involved in several projects as a principal investigator. I am about to join the Department of Landscape Architecture, Planning and Management at the Swedish University of Agricultural Sciences as an assistant professor.

C: Bangladesh is home to one of the largest arsenic contamination crises in the world, affecting millions through groundwater and agricultural irrigation. From your vantage point, how would you describe the current state of the problem?

A: As far as I’m aware, the arsenic crisis in Bangladesh is still not fully resolved. In our review article published in Environmental Science and Pollution Research in 2023, we highlighted that although the Bangladeshi government has implemented vital awareness campaigns and alternative water sourcing initiatives since 1997, critical gaps remain in implementation. District-level data is scarce, and over five crore people are still at heightened risk. What we need now is a comprehensive nationwide survey and the development of an efficient, data-driven water monitoring system to effectively identify and mitigate arsenic exposure on a mass scale. International cooperation may abate this.

C: What kind of frontier research, particularly in bioremediation, do you think Bangladesh could benefit from in pursuing?

A: Generally, the application of phytoremediation is recommended, using local, endemic plant species, since it reduces the threat to biodiversity and genetically modified ones don’t adapt quickly to the monsoon climate. Moreover, this is an economically sound option. If research institutions come forward, then a number of potential bioremediation options could be developed in Bangladesh. Other than this, biofortification (breeding plant strains and introducing needed elements to increase their nutritional value) and hyperaccumulator species (plants capable of absorbing and storing exceptionally high concentrations of toxic metals) should be explored.

C: In 2018, you and your team identified a first arsenic hyperfilter aquatic moss species — a discovery that generated international attention, including a feature in The Independent. What does "hyperfilter" actually mean in practical terms?

A: It started with the investigation of arsenic content in iron mining sites in northern Sweden. We found that these aquatic mosses grow naturally in arsenic-rich aquatic environments, and we became interested in investigating them. Fortunately, we received funding from the Swedish Engineers Association. We ran experiments in the lab to discover that this moss has a very high, very rapid arsenic uptake capacity from arsenic-contaminated waters. In waters containing 74 micrograms per litre of arsenic, the level of arsenic in water could reduce 82 percent within an hour by using this arsenic hyperfilter species (Warnstorfia fluitans). The World Health Organization (WHO) safety standard is 10 micrograms per litre, and the Bangladesh national standard arsenic limit for drinking water is 50 micrograms per litre.

C: Could a version of this technology be deployed in Bangladesh's river systems and industrial zones?

A: In one of our recently completed research projects, we tested constructed floating wetland systems in old industrial (glassworks) sites in Sweden. We obtained satisfactory results and are waiting to publish. So, from that point of view, the development of constructed wetlands near lead battery factories could also reduce the loading of toxic heavy metals from effluents. Sites like Kamrangirchar and Tongi, tannery sites in Hazaribagh, and the Buriganga River could benefit from an updated regulatory framework. Of course, before planning such a wetland system, both economic variables and viability simulations need to be assessed, and bureaucratic hurdles overcome. If corporate social responsibility (CSR) policy and government subsidies are implemented, these areas could finally be appraised.

C: For a student reader unfamiliar with biosensors, can you explain what these devices are and why they might be game-changing for environmental monitoring in a low-resource context like Bangladesh?

A: To clarify, the “biosensor” we developed is not an electronic gadget; rather, it is a biological unit utilising actomyosin, a protein that is also found in your muscles. This was an exciting collaboration between the Chemistry and Biomedicine and Environment Science departments at Linnaeus University. Our goal was to create a rapid, low-cost primary screening tool for developing countries where expensive high-tech instrumentation, such as ICP mass spectrometry or AAS, is unavailable. By placing these muscle proteins in water samples, we observe how toxic metals affect the mortality of the proteins. We then can flag high concentrations of toxicity in water samples in the field – useful for developing countries.

C: Bangladesh produces talented science graduates every year, yet much of the frontier environmental research on Bangladesh is being conducted from laboratories abroad. What, in your view, are the structural barriers in funding and institutional culture that prevent this research from happening at home, and what might it take to change that?

A: Research Funding plays a significant role in research, regardless of the country. To change this situation, universities should also approach different industrial partners, the private sector, and philanthropic networks. Frontier research should be advanced through collaboration between academia and industry. Universities could play a big role in promoting their research by organising more roadshows, conferences and grant-raising networking events.

C: If you were designing a curriculum for Bangladeshi university students to get an idea of the current market trends for environmental sciences, what would be the three topics you would introduce?

A: I could say the framework needs to be developed in such a way that it maps pollution sources and sinks, management philosophies, and modernised research methodologies. First, students need a comprehensive understanding of contaminant cycles, specifically tracking how agricultural and industrial pollutants migrate and accumulate within a country's ecosystem – the hard science. Second, this must be paired with practical and management strategies that focus on systems thinking and nature-based solutions to actively mitigate soil, water, and air contamination. Particular emphasis should be given to cultural change by comparative analysis of techniques used by developed nations and their practical adoption. Finally, to future-proof this knowledge in the era of artificial intelligence, the curriculum must urgently upgrade its research methodologies by equipping students with advanced skills in applied statistics, modern data management, ethics and stewardship, and most critically, the practise of AI applications.

C: For a Bangladeshi student reading this today, what is the most honest and useful advice you can give them?

A: First and foremost, protect your academic grading. Good grades are an essential gatekeeper for entering top-tier global institutions in the next level of academia and for securing funding. The transcript is a screening process, the first judgement – explain if you have low grades, show your ECAs, and explain properly any shortcomings and gaps you may have. Keep in mind that good grades don't require many explanations. Honesty goes further than you think. Being talented across multiple domains also helps. Second, a technical toolkit should be mastered. Think of data science, coding, and advanced modelling software, and place particular attention on the communication of your research to laymen. Modern research is entirely data-driven, and having strong dry-lab skills will instantly set you apart from your peers. Read up on contemporary developments in your domain in open-access journals. Finally, expand your horizons. Attend international seminars to understand how science is conducted globally and get involved in university clubs, academic societies, non-profits and think tanks to pad your CV.

title: IDP's Razib Mahbubul on making smarter study-abroad decisions
text:
As more students explore opportunities to pursue higher education overseas, choosing the right destination and navigating the application process can feel both exciting and overwhelming. In this interview, Campus speaks with Razib Mahbubul, Country Director of IDP Education Bangladesh, about the evolving study abroad landscape, the support IDP provides to aspiring international students, and practical advice for those preparing to take the next step in their academic journey.

Campus (C): What are some of the key factors students should look into when choosing a study abroad destination?

Razib Mahbubul (R): One of the most common questions we face whenever a student comes to our office or sits down for a one-to-one discussion is, "Which country should I choose?"

My advice is this: don't start with the country. Our major focus should be on the student because every student is different. Their academic and financial backgrounds, career ambitions, and personalities are completely different. The focus should be on the student's long-term plan.

For example, if a student is interested in technology or business, they should focus on which university is strong in that area and what post-study opportunities, global exposure, or internships are available.

Secondly, affordability and cultural adaptability come into the picture as well.

From the IDP side, there are five key points that should be considered carefully: the quality of the course, the reputation and support system of the universities, the total cost of study and living, visa and post-study opportunities, safety, and lifestyle.
