Fundraising applications to the World Bank, Asian Development Bank (ADB), and Bangladesh Bank may tie it altogether, as joint-funding applications by universities show promise to grant avenues.

“If a logical view of evolution is observed, collaboration has always benefitted the insects on the forest floor more than competition has benefited the birds that prey upon them,” said Dr Akhter Hossain Khan, the Vice-Chancellor of State University of Bangladesh. “The birds are the ones to pass in fighting over the not-so-scarce resources. Find common ground in sharing resources; don’t promote infighting. I say that having taught at the ‘coaching centre’.”

"The only thing more thoroughly researched at DU than the question of why DU does no research is the question of whose turn it is to say 'Bangladesh means Dhaka University',” said Nusrat Jahan, a fourth-year statistics student at DU.

Jahan added that she had applied for an undergraduate research assistantship the previous semester and been told, in writing, that her department's research budget for the year would be spent on a single international journal subscription.

A counterpart at NSU’s Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering, Sayad Zaman Ador, was less amused by his own institution's victory lap. “We are much better at flash mobs than any other institution, but DU takes the cake for a more ‘informal gathering’ when criticism strikes. Though it goes without saying, most of NSU's high-impact output comes from maybe forty faculty members, and we strive for joint research with no avenues yet to be seen.”

Tahmid Karim, a sophomore at the Department of Chemical Engineering at BUET, said, "We have spent a week arguing whether or not DU is a coaching centre. Nobody has asked whether the system, as a whole, is a dispensary that happens to issue degrees, with no real prestige outside of the borders of the nation."

The mission itself has been drifting away from both types of institutions – public and private – while they fought. And every ranking system tells the same underlying story of a country home to 178 million people that has not produced a single institution inside the global top 500.

A*STAR was not built in a decade by Singaporean pride. Fraunhofer was not designed for Bavarian nostalgia. Bangladesh, if it is to mean anything in the next century – a knowledge economy, a prospective industrial super-hub, and a country that manufactures its own answers instead of importing them – will mean public and private universities working on the same problems, in the same rooms, and with the same resources.

The country's leading public and private universities may frequently argue about which is the legitimate heir to the national academic mission. The question is what both might build together, lest we be ruled by division.

Reference:

The Daily Star (July 1, 2026). DU gets no UGC research fund for first time.

Shoumik Zubyer is a researcher of the soils of Mars at the Atomic Energy Commission and SERC, and a peripatetic. Find him at [email protected].

title: The prospects of pursuing a degree in theatre studies
text:
The re-evolution of theatre in Bangladesh took place through social commentary, political engagement, and community dialogue. This intricate form of artistic expression has its roots in Sanskrit and indigenous traditions, where its prominent role as a space for entertainment, reflection, and cultural expression laid the foundation for the theatre we practise today across South Asia.

The emergence of theatre as a field for formal education in our country surfaced in the late 1980s, transitioning stage drama from a non-formal genre to a recognised academic discipline. Currently, several public universities, including Dhaka University (DU), Jahangirnagar University (JU), Chittagong University (CU), and Rajshahi University (RU), have active departments of theatre studies within the Faculty of Arts.

I spoke to Dr AKM Yusuf Hassan, a professor in the Department of Drama and Dramatics at JU, regarding the relevance of theatre in today’s landscape. According to him, “Theatre is an art form that has remained relevant time and time again because of its fundamental ability to connect people. The impact of this live art is far more potent than any audio-visual medium, as it thrives on the vibrant, immediate human interaction shared between the stage and the audience. This is precisely why theatre has endured for millennia, despite the rise of technology-driven mediums like film and radio.”

To master and rehearse the art of stage drama, numerous independent institutions also offer training programmes to enthusiastic learners. Why, then, is there a need to pursue a formal degree in theatrical studies?

In response to such a question, he says, “Pursuing higher education in the said discipline encompasses both the rigorous practice and the profound philosophy required to understand the human condition. Training is only a part of that education for enhancing skills. So, I may opine that actors may not necessarily require a formal education degree. However, a university curriculum in theatre, dramatics, or performance studies provides a comprehensive intellectual foundation. It cultivates an in-depth understanding of life, society, and art, equipping students with a critical lens that independent workshops cannot replicate.”

In the undergraduate curriculum, other than acting, courses on prop making, stage lighting design, set design, costume design, makeup, direction, dance choreography, and fieldwork are also included. This multi-disciplinary approach ensures that students understand the collaborative ecosystem required to bring a script to life.

Arpita Zohra, a third-year student in the Theatre and Performance Studies Department at DU, says, “When an artist performs in theatre, even if they are a solo performer, they require the support of a few other people. Suppose you are an actor; you are supposed to deliver a dialogue upon reaching the downstage. You arrive at the spot, but the light doesn't turn on. You will remain in the dark, and no one will be able to see your performance. In such circumstances, we absolutely need the assistance of a lighting designer who knows exactly when, where, and how much light to cast. Some people might think about working with AI or robots, but theatre is a live medium — where the audience and the actor coexist in the same space and time.”

Photo: Orchid Chakma

Alongside practical arts, students are acquainted with numerous theory-driven aspects, such as the history of global art and the socio-economic and political history of Bangladesh.

Erfanul Islam Iftu, an ongoing master’s student in the Department of Drama and Dramatics at the JU, mentions, “The core element of theatre is 'acting'. A student must understand the technical and theoretical concepts that shape an actor. Beyond that, a key arena for a student’s intellectual development is ‘writing’— the space for expressing creative thought.”

He elaborates, “At the bachelor’s level, we are taught the rules of dictionary usage, linguistic purity, syntax, and the use of rhythm and rhetoric as part of our coursework. Gradually, alongside writing analytically and editing any given subject, students can master the art of playwriting across various media. We also undergo rigorous training in elocution, phonetics, and vocal projection that helps us develop high proficiency in the vocal and verbal arts.”

Theatre majors are not confined solely to stage acting; another crucial lesson in art is cinema. Some universities also require students to take up certain courses related to media production, where they receive hands-on, foundational training on filmmaking. Hence, the academic and professional landscape for a graduate can be extensive.

With an undergraduate degree in this discipline, one can transition into a diverse range of career prospects. In the creative and entertainment industries, graduates can build careers as directors, scriptwriters, and actors across stage, television, and film or step into critical technical design roles such as scenographers, costume stylists, makeup artists, and light and sound designers. The training in broadcast media and cinematography also opens pathways into digital content creation, independent filmmaking, and technical positions within media houses and OTT platforms.

One of the students I spoke to talked about the success of her juniors with pride to exemplify how theatre can open doors to exceptional possibilities. The students of the 2022-23 academic session at her university, during their first year, made a documentary Pronayopakhyaner Satkahon based on the behind-the-scenes story of the play Pronayopakhyan as part of their final examination. That documentary was selected for the 24th Dhaka International Film Festival in 2026. This proves how diverse routes of new creation can emerge from theatre.

But there are more options if students want to pursue other avenues. In education, they can become teachers or researchers. Many students are also working with strong reputations in non-governmental organisations (NGOs), banking, and the corporate sector, while others are securing opportunities in government civil services.

When it comes to higher education, theatre studies offer excellent global pathways. For advanced studies in fields like applied theatre and dramaturgy, there are wonderful opportunities such as the Erasmus Mundus scholarship and the ICCR scholarship in India. Additionally, theatre students are eligible to apply for various programmes under prestigious fellowships like the Chevening and Commonwealth scholarships.

However, choosing to pursue dramatics, much like any other discipline, does come with its own set of challenges. One might dream of becoming a professional theatre artist after completing their studies, but for Bangladeshi students, that ambition faces a tough reality.

Igimi Chakma, currently completing her master's degree in the specialised discipline of Art of Performance at JU, shares, “As a theatre artist, choosing stage drama as a sole profession after graduation is extremely difficult. This is because most people who perform theatre in our country are involved in other professions alongside it. They continue to practise theatre and keep this art form alive primarily out of love, passion, and personal urge.”

“Another major challenge is commuting and financial pressure. When I first started practising theatre in my first year, I regularly had to travel from JU to Dhaka for rehearsals and then return. This commute became a huge pressure in terms of both time and money. Returning to the campus from Dhaka around 11:00 PM or 11:30 PM in an exhausted state after a full day of classes was a regular experience. On top of that, as a woman, one has to go through various types of harassment and safety risks within the social context, which makes this journey even more difficult,” she adds.

Most active theatre practices in our country are totally centralised within the capital due to inadequate halls and the absence of commercial platforms, which makes the profession inaccessible to a large number of people.

Reflecting on her own homeland of Rangamati, Igimi noted that attempting to pursue theatre as a core profession there is a difficult prospect. The acute scarcity of performance stages, a total absence of proper rehearsal rooms, minimal facilities, and severely limited sponsorships collectively choke regional practice. Furthermore, outside the capital's cultural hubs, artists face a major deficit in audience cultivation, as a large portion of the local community has yet to understand, recognise, or properly value the profound artistic gravity of stage drama.

Despite all, young artists continue to battle between optimism and passion. Arpita, who is also an on-camera actress, says, “Financial constraints have always been there. A few theatre groups or companies have managed to sustain their practice by securing political, government, or private funding at various times. On the other hand, the groups that could not access these benefits are fading away. We tend to judge people entirely by the metrics of money and social status.”

Photo: Sheikh Mehedi Morshed

“An actor is an artist. If they want to survive by taking up acting as a profession, they must fight. In the context of Bangladesh, that battlefield is vast, yet the space to actually fight is extremely narrow. It often seems to me that compared to other countries in the world, being a Bangladeshi actor means that if you look from afar, it is a comedy, but if you look closely, it is the greatest tragedy,” she concludes with a sigh.

Theatre practice on the Bangladeshi stage is still primarily driven by the activities of group theatres. Outside of Dhaka, barring a few district towns, professionalism in theatre practice has not yet developed. In most cases, after graduation, students take up jobs in various production houses. Furthermore, there is a severe crisis in the institutional infrastructure of theatre. The remuneration that most artists receive is nowhere near adequate compared to the production costs and the intense labour required to create a play.

Despite these structural limitations, the passion for cultural preservation sparks visionary dreams among practitioners. As an indigenous artist, Igimi envisions building a dedicated platform that unites indigenous theatre students and artists from across Bangladesh to research, preserve and showcase their unique folklore, heritage and history to the world. She remains highly optimistic, believing that dramatising their traditional lifestyles can bridge generational gaps by bequeathing them to the next.

“My dream is that one day our theatre will reach a height where people will be inspired by our work and look at our culture and creativity with respect. There is a song in Chakma culture, ‘Nu-o dinor nu-o geet shunebong’, which translates to Bangla as ‘Notun diner notun gaan shunabo’ (I will sing the new song of a new day). Within these words, I see a new dream — to present our stories, our culture, and our art in a new light to the new generation in a new era.”

Titir is a contributor at The Daily Star. Contact her at [email protected].

title: The Grand Tour enters a promising new era
text:
The Grand Tour – a motoring television series on Amazon Prime – is back with a new season, but it is no longer hosted by its original legendary trio of hosts Jeremy Clarkson, Richard Hammond, and James May.

I went into this new season with a fair amount of scepticism. As someone who grew up watching the trio of Clarkson, Hammond, and May for years on BBC’s Top Gear, and later followed them to The Grand Tour, I was not convinced that the formula could work without them.

We have seen this before: the various attempts to carry on Top Gear after the trio left never quite captured what made the original so special. The problem was never really the cars. It was the chemistry between three very different personalities.

So, when Thomas Holland, James Engelsman, and Francis Bourgeois were announced as the new hosts, my expectations were fairly modest. I expected a competent car show; I did not expect to enjoy it nearly as much as I did. What gave me relief was that the new hosts brought their own personalities to the format without spending all their time and energy pretending to be the original trio.

Thomas and James already have a natural chemistry from their work on their YouTube channel Throttle House, which I highly recommend everyone check out, where they make some of the most entertaining car reviews on the platform. They bounce off each other comfortably, and their enthusiasm for cars feels genuine rather than manufactured.

Image

On the other hand, Francis, who became a TikTok sensation owing to his trainspotting obsession, is the wildcard inclusion. At first, I wondered whether his presence was simply a clever casting decision designed to bring some online attention to the reboot. It quickly became clear that he actually adds something to the show.

There is a slightly awkward, almost innocent quality to his enthusiasm that makes him surprisingly funny. His excitement can be wonderfully infectious. His quirkiness, with all his train trivia sprinkled in the episodes, also reflected the authenticity of his character without taking away anything from his petrolhead side. And, most importantly, he gels with the duo of Thomas and James brilliantly.

The show also handles its transition from the old trio better than I expected. The cameos of Clarkson, Hammond, and May act as an obvious nod to the past, but it does not feel like the entire season is built around nostalgia. This new season acknowledges its history without becoming a tribute show to the past.

Image

The format of the show ditches the audience segments of the early seasons of The Grand Tour and runs continuously as a series of documentaries akin to the latter seasons and the specials. Fast cars, slow cars, cheap and expensive cars all feature in magnificent shooting locations in each episode that represent unique car cultures across the world. There are also solo car reviews, road trips, comparisons, and the kind of unnecessarily elaborate challenges that have always been part of the show's DNA.

The production still looks as polished as ever. The show’s runtime is also well managed, packed full of content in only six episodes with negligible filler. But the direction feels noticeably less chaotic than the old one.

This tonal shift is probably the biggest difference between the old and the new. Clarkson, Hammond, and May had spent decades developing their particular rhythm. Their arguments, insults, and ridiculous decisions felt completely natural. Thomas, James, and Francis may still need some time to carve out their particular rhythm as a trio. Some jokes feel slightly forced, which had me searching for the punchline. Some sequences lack the wonderfully unpredictable feeling that the original trio could create without even trying. Nevertheless, the show never kept me yearning for more humour or pandemonium with its balancing act of the spectacle and the personalities.

However, those shortcomings became less of an issue when I decided to stop comparing the new hosts with the old ones and started watching them on their own terms. The new Grand Tour does not have the same magic as the Clarkson, Hammond, and May era with its safer setting and toned-down humour and chaos, but there are still moments when you can feel the shadow of the old Grand Tour. Most importantly, it introduces the new trio splendidly and establishes a great starting point for what could be a new winning formula for the years to come.

Image

After watching the disastrous attempts to simply replace the original Top Gear trio, I think Amazon has taken the more sensible approach here: give the format to people who genuinely love cars, let them be themselves, and see what happens. Perhaps the new hosts were due some credence from the fans as well, since they had been handpicked by Clarkson, Hammond, and May as their successors. And it has clearly worked. They are genuinely hilarious, energetic, and essentially sincere in their act, and together, they are surprisingly entertaining.

I would be lying if I said that I did not miss Clarkson's shouting, Hammond's spectacular mishaps, and May's increasingly exasperated explanations. But after completing the new season, my mind did not jump to the thought of wanting to see the original trio make a comeback. Rather, I was watching and wondering what Thomas, James, and Francis might do next. For a long-time fan of the original Top Gear and The Grand Tour, that is probably the strongest endorsement I could give this new season.

title: The Wonderfools: Messy at first, but surprisingly worth the ride
text:
I went into The Wonderfools with very low expectations. Superhero comedies aren't exactly a genre K-dramas have mastered, and the early promotional material did little to convince me otherwise. But the combination of Extreme Job writer Heo Da Joong and director Yoo In Sik, whose work includes Dr. Romantic and Extraordinary Attorney Woo, was enough to make me give it a chance. And I am glad I did.

That said, The Wonderfools doesn't make a strong first impression. The opening episodes are certainly messy. The humour feels aggressively chaotic and forced; the central trio, initially, comes across as very exhausting for the viewers, and the pacing felt so draggy that I myself contemplated dropping the series after only watching the first few episodes.

However, I persevered because I had faith in the talent behind the project even though I found the characters quite overwhelming. If you're someone who prefers your comedy subtle and your protagonists immediately likeable, there's a good chance you'll struggle to get into it.

Ironically, the person who kept me watching was Cha Eun Woo’s character Lee Woon-jung. His character's constant deadpan reactions and visible exasperation toward the trio mirrored exactly how I felt as a viewer. It wasn't until later that I realised the show was fully aware of how ridiculous and overwhelming these characters were meant to be.

Image

Looking back, those earlier episodes function as important groundwork to establish both the emotional stakes and the eccentric world these characters inhabit. And once the drama finds its footing around the end of the third episode, it becomes surprisingly difficult to stop watching.

What impressed me most was how confidently director Yoo In Sik eventually balances the show's wildly different tones. The Wonderfools swings between absurd comedy, mystery, action, family drama, and genuine emotional heartbreak, sometimes within the same episode. On paper, it shouldn't work, yet somehow it does.

As the relationships develop naturally, the trio that initially tested my patience slowly becomes oddly lovable. The drama never asks you to admire perfect heroes. Instead, it invites you to root for deeply flawed, chaotic people trying their best.

Park Eun Bin, playing Eun Chae-ni, unsurprisingly delivers another committed performance. I do think the writing initially does her character a disservice by pushing her eccentricity to almost cartoonish levels. However, once the drama starts rolling on its unique rhythm, her portrayal becomes incredibly charming. It's a performance that requires complete sincerity, and Park has always excelled at making unconventional characters feel emotionally grounded.

Image

The biggest surprise, however, was Cha Eun Woo. I have enjoyed several of his previous projects, but there was often a visible tension in his previous performances that prevented me from fully connecting with his characters. Here, that tension seems to disappear. He feels more relaxed, more natural, and significantly more confident.

What caught me off guard was how emotionally central his character becomes. By episodes five and six, his storyline evolves into one of the drama's strongest emotional pillars, and he rises to the occasion beautifully.

The casting is remarkably strong across the board. Veterans Kim Hae Sook and Son Hyun Joo also bring their A game to the series, but I couldn't help but feel that both were slightly underutilised. Additionally, the portrayal of the villain roles was commendable, as the antagonists did not feel generic or one-dimensional and were memorable and entertaining. As for standout moments, Choi Dae Hoon's The Shining parody and the giant inflatable onion mascot sequence nearly stole the entire show for me. His comedic timing is impeccable.

Ultimately, The Wonderfools is not a drama I would recommend to everyone. It demands patience, and its opening episodes may be enough to drive some viewers away. But if you're willing to embrace its chaotic energy and give it time to settle into its rhythm, you'll find a series that's funny, heartwarming, wonderfully eccentric, and unexpectedly moving.

title: The Odyssey: A poignant reframing of Homer’s epic, distinctly Nolan’s own
text:
Christopher Nolan’s decision to adapt The Odyssey after the monumental success of Oppenheimer immediately fascinated me. A director at the height of his powers tackling one of history’s most influential stories felt bold yet inevitable. But there was a tinge of anxiety as well. Could Nolan’s minimalist, almost dogmatically realist style meet the maximalist demands of a fantasy filled with gods, monsters, magic, and sweeping grandeur?

It’s a testament to Nolan’s strengths that they not only outweigh his limitations but also result in a bracingly cinematic adaptation that makes an ancient story feel urgent.

A man, a fleet, a war, a trick

Much has been said about Nolan’s nonlinear style, but its most vital extension is the fractal editing within individual scenes, where his surrealism truly emerges. Rapid bursts of imagery plant motifs and memories like seeds, letting Nolan juggle a vast cast while weaving thematic threads into a dreamlike tapestry that only clarifies at the end. It’s a perfect stylistic match for The Odyssey, a sprawling narrative spanning decades and multiple perspectives.

The film begins with two primary threads. In the first, King Odysseus’s absence has left son Telemachus and Queen Penelope struggling to control Ithaca against a horde of suitors who want the throne. It then branches into a coming-of-age arc for Telemachus, who learns bits and pieces of the father he never knew, including tales of his tactical genius behind the Trojan Horse.

The second thread finds Odysseus with a hazy memory, trapped with Calypso. As he attempts to remember the man he himself has forgotten, the film unleashes the spine of the narrative, the epic’s iconic set pieces.

Editor Jennifer Lame’s blistering cross-cutting gradually brings these threads together to ground themes of memory, guilt, nostalgia, and faith, condensing a dense material without losing depth.

“A time of apparent magic…”

The opening text perfectly captures Nolan’s approach to the fantastical. Unlike the poem, the gods never appear onscreen (yes, not even Athena), and Nolan plays coy about their existence. Like the characters, we wonder whether the crashing waves and frequent lightning are Poseidon’s wrath and Zeus’s signs. That ambiguity shifts the focus from how the Greeks told stories of gods—sitting atop Mount Olympus, bickering and meddling in human affairs—to how they felt their presence through thunder, fire, good harvests, and a child’s smile.

Magic, however, is never in doubt. The Cyclops sequence lets Nolan flex horror muscles like he’d never done before, only to outdo himself with the Circe scene. As she moulds Odysseus’s men into pigs like clay, the film suddenly shifts gears into pure body-horror grotesquerie. By never letting us hear the Sirens’ song, Nolan lets Damon’s performance, Ludwig Göransson’s haunting score, and a beautifully written monologue evoke what spectacle never could: our imagination of what we most desire yet cannot have.

Rendered largely with practical effects, Nolan’s restraint makes these classic sequences feel visceral, fresh, and unmistakably his own.

Trade-offs

Yet relentless pacing denies certain beats room to breathe. While we feel the hardship of Odysseus’s journey, we rarely feel the passage of time itself. When he crosses the ocean on his raft and finally returns home, the sequence lacks the emotional weight it deserves. Partly to blame is the underwritten Calypso, with whom Odysseus confronts his inner hurdle and one of the film’s major revelations: his repressed desire not to return home. Her motivations remain so thinly dramatised, along with Nolan’s aversion to sensuality, that even the Cyclops feels like a somewhat fuller character.

Cinematographer Hoyte van Hoytema can lend even mundane frames texture and gravitas, but Nolan’s long-standing disinterest in spatial blocking often underserves the film’s action, crowds, and elemental spectacle.

Odysseus’s homecoming is intentionally tense rather than triumphant, but it still needed a proper pause. Without it, the transition into the third act blurred, leaving little space to absorb a lifelong odyssey before the film begins laying the groundwork for its climax.

But once that final act takes shape, it becomes one of the most emotionally rousing and thematically satisfying Nolan has ever executed.

Destroyer of worlds

The film repeatedly emphasises “Zeus’s Law". Nolan’s simplified term for Xenia, a sacred tenet of hospitality that dictates that hosts must honour guests who might be gods in disguise. But we see it repeatedly violated. In Ithaca, it’s the suitors who throw lavish feasts and squander its wealth. In Odysseus’s journey, it’s when he’s trapped in the Cyclops's cave, or his men are transformed by Circe over a meal.

But as he enters his own palace posing as a beggar and confesses to Penelope, the film's central recontextualisation emerges: Odysseus’s great trick of the Trojan Horse was not a heroic triumph but the ultimate betrayal of Zeus’ Law, a sacrilege so profound that it broke human contracts and shattered their world.

The film flashes back to the sack of Troy, and this time, instead of a gripping action scene, it’s a hellish massacre of fire, pillage, and slaughter. There, Athena is revealed to bear the face of a priestess who was killed in front of him. The man who used to pluck his bow to warn prey before hunting only watched as his cunning resulted in the brutal beheading of an innocent girl. Is she the ghost of his greatest moral failure haunting his psyche, or is Athena taking the guise of the girl he couldn’t forget to guide him, or both? Nolan leaves it up to you. But as the fragmented motifs finally crystallise with this revelation, Nolan turns Homer’s adventures of wits, pride, and hubris into a manifestation of Odysseus’s guilt and an examination of the dark underbelly that exists in Homer’s myth and thus all of Western civilisation.

By turning the Trojan Horse into an original sin, he presents a vision of civilisational collapse driven by the collapse of hospitality and trust. He rejects the notion that the ruthless, stoic masculinity embodied by figures like Agamemnon sustains Western civilisation, presenting it instead as the very ideology that corrodes the human bonds on which it depends. Here, Nolan departs radically from Homer.

A song for a darkened world

Some will resist the use of one of Western literature’s foundational texts as a vessel for contemporary anxieties. But long before The Odyssey was written down, it survived as a living oral tradition, reshaped by every rhapsode who sang it. Historical fidelity is an odd standard to impose on a myth that itself blends centuries of history, memory, and imagination.

Nor do Nolan’s deviations betray a misunderstanding of Homer. On the contrary, the way he reconfigures very specific aspects to serve his vision reveals an intimate knowledge of the text. From the anachronistic aesthetic choices to incorporating elements outside of the poem, like the character of Sinon from Virgil’s Aeneid, who makes Odysseus confront the sins of his past, and the inclusion of “The Sea People”—a group of unidentified seafaring marauders from history who were largely thought to be responsible for the Late Bronze Age collapse, revealed in the film to be the Greeks themselves—every alteration feels deliberate, serving a thematic purpose rather than simply modernising the source. The result echoes concerns that have long run through his filmography. Here, those anxieties culminate in a homecoming that is less about reclaiming a kingdom than reckoning with the world one’s own victories helped destroy.

Such reframing inevitably sacrifices the experience of encountering a worldview profoundly unlike our own. But what is gained is an apocalyptic anti-war epic told by arguably the biggest filmmaker in the biggest format, a melancholic meditation on masculinity, conflict, and the price civilisations pay for mistaking conquest for greatness.

That is the beauty of myths. They can speak to the thoughts and fears of a different age and endure, not because they remain unchanged, but because every generation finds new questions to ask of them. The Odyssey succeeds because it is more than a faithful retelling; it is Nolan’s conversation with Homer. Those discovering the tale for the first time would be left eager to engage with the original, while long-time readers witness two storytellers, separated by nearly three millennia, speaking across time.

Miazee Abrar drowns in daydreams and writes stories for worms.

title: Backrooms is a liminal nightmare, until it isn’t
text:
For a while, everyone I knew seemed to have Backrooms on their watchlist. Whether they were a fan of the horror genre itself or familiar with earlier works of the director, it seemed to be a unanimous preconception that a movie about exploring yellow-tinted liminal spaces where unknown, incomprehensible horror awaits the adventurer was something worth watching. Thus, it's pretty redundant to talk about how anticipated it was among the viewer base.

Backrooms started becoming a popular internet phenomenon in 2019. The words "liminal spaces" and "backrooms" are often used interchangeably, although there’s a subtle difference in that the latter is more malicious than the former. Empty, abandoned locations, doorways, and staircases that trigger a sense of nostalgia and comfort mixed with the unsettling absence of people and noise—it's no wonder the internet lore became popular with a generation that survived through isolation during the pandemic. The director, Kane Parsons, had previously released his own web series on YouTube called The Backrooms (Found Footage) and made his film debut at the age of 20 with Backrooms (2026).

After what seemed like forever, Backrooms finally got its digital release, and yet, for some reason, it didn't seem to prompt as much discourse as another recently released film of the horror genre, Obsession. Of course, that isn't enough to immediately conclude the failure of the film, but that did sow the seeds of doubt in my mind and intrigued me to get started as soon as possible.

The premise is expected. A seemingly endless, apparently harmless physical space opens up below a furniture store, hiding in plain sight. It’s unsettling, resembling the set of every TV show taking place in an office during the 90s but with the saturation set to max and mundaneness cranked up so high it starts to feel like overcompensating – which it does. For a seemingly endless liminal space that shifts and moves, it's eerily stagnant and claustrophobic. The distorted, often muffled, fluctuating-in-volume audio does nothing to help settle the unease. It sets the scene perfectly, an immaculate representation of backrooms, the subconscious of the universe where everything and everyone is remembered, just incorrectly.

Without giving away the plot too much, it follows a furniture salesman, his employees, and his therapist as they discover and navigate this space. The film drops the viewer into the backrooms without any ado, letting you take a view of the place through grainy, shaky film as the cameraman unsteadily reports to someone and asks for help, struggling to find an exit in an ever-shifting dimension. We don’t find out what happens to him. We are not really supposed to. But it’s safe to assume he’s there, in the backrooms, whether it is in his original form or in the memory of the universe.

Of course, when liminal spaces become truly scary is when it forces you to face a physical manifestation of something you’re facing about yourself. You’re claustrophobic, rattled, and anticipating something sinister. Is there any better time for introspection? Backrooms taps into that throughout the movie, keeping the entities out of sight for the larger part of the movie.

The atmospheric, disconcerting nature of the film, unfortunately, stops somewhere around the first half for me. Despite the intense buildup of a mysterious nature, the film fails to sustain the same unsettling nature. The climax feels weak, and in spite of being the highest point of the movie that’s meant to truly knock you off your seats, it doesn’t. The last half of the movie was chaotic and a little listless. The falling action and resolution are similarly weak and somehow explain too much and too little at the same time.

This isn’t to say the movie was bad. I do think the movie has its merits; the atmosphere, the sound, and the setup were executed perfectly. It’s a movie venturing into the uncharted space (pun intended) of an internet creepypasta that has existed for a long time, and it isn’t easy to take such an abstract concept and give it a plot that works in its favour.

If you enjoy having to read in between the lines to understand what’s truly going on, this is a movie that should appeal to you. The direction of horror movies in recent times seems to have strayed from the usual supernatural haunted house or abandoned locations sheltering evil entities into something introspective, often incorporating social commentaries. Movies like The Substance, Obsession, and Heretic are a far cry from traditional horror, and Backrooms seems to bridge the gap between what horror is now and what horror used to be.

But if you’ve ever found those “your month, your liminal space” or “your month, your liminal space entity” and obsessively scrolled through each one only to find out your month has a zero percent survival rate, then you’d enjoy the movie. At least the first half of it.

title: Spider-Man: Brand New Day: A timeless hero’s confrontation with isolation
text:
*This review contains spoilers for the film.

Spider-Man: Brand New Day is a reminder as to why Spider-Man is such a multigenerational character that anyone can relate to. Tom Holland delivers his best performance as Peter Parker yet, bringing a much more mature and nuanced chapter in the character’s story that delivers on almost all the hype and expectations.

The movie's premise, in simpler terms, follows Peter Parker some years after Spider-Man: No Way Home. He's grappling with the absence of Aunt May and the fact that his friends, MJ and Ned, no longer remember anything about him. While he continues to focus on crime-fighting, he comes across a mysterious villain with the ability to control minds.

However, when you break it all down, the story really is about Peter’s severe grief and isolation. He tries to mask these issues (both metaphorically and literally) by focusing solely on being a hero, which in turn causes him to undergo physical distress as well, from headaches to rapid mutations in his powers. While this is told through a superhero context, the concept of drowning oneself in work as a coping mechanism instead of dealing with grief and trauma healthily is a very real experience many people go through. Peter’s own journey in the film teaches us that it’s important to confront that grief rather than avoid it, as that confrontation will ultimately guide us towards overcoming it.

Every supporting character in the story has a significant role that iterates on this theme. The Punisher (Frank Castle) and The Hulk (Bruce Banner) are the two other MCU heroes prominently featured, and they both mirror who Peter is now. Frank is a hero who has lost his entire family, and his war on crime is all he has left. Bruce, on the other hand, is a hero who has managed to control his monstrous mutations and powers.

Meanwhile, MJ and Ned remind Peter of who he used to be. Through these characters, we see Peter’s psychological struggle between forcing himself to embrace isolation and wanting to reconnect. The memory of Aunt May plays a crucial role in this dichotomy as well. It is ultimately both the catalyst and resolution of this core emotional conflict. This aspect is pivotal to how the villain is handled as well.

The villain of the film is rather unexpected, as rather than a typical member of Spider-Man’s rogues gallery, this time around it is Jean Grey (portrayed by Sadie Sink), a telepathic mutant who is a pivotal member of the X-Men. While her inclusion does feel like a setup for the inevitable MCU X-Men reboot, much like The Punisher and Hulk, her inclusion actually serves a narrative purpose rather than simply being there for a crossover’s sake. As such, her story also complements Peter’s as the climax of the film has them both simultaneously overcome their separate forms of trauma.

Both tonally and thematically, the movie feels more like a spiritual successor to the Tobey Maguire and Andrew Garfield Spider-Man films rather than a continuation of Tom Holland’s previous outings. It’s not just the plot; rather, Brand New Day is a significant step up from the previous MCU Spider-Man trilogy directed by Jon Watts.

The cinematography is the most evident upgrade – be it the lighting and composition of the slower and emotional scenes or the thrilling direction and pace of the faster parts of the film. Moreover, the action sequences and web-swinging scenes might be the best in any Spider-Man film to date, with both taking heavy inspiration from the recent Spider-Man video games. Besides the previous movies and video games, the movie features many references to the comic books as well. Director Destin Daniel Cretton took all the right ingredients and mixed them with his brilliant filmmaking skills to cook the perfect Spider-Man story.

Spider-Man: Brand New Day goes beyond the superhero spectacle to teach us important lessons through Peter Parker. Even if the world doesn’t see us, we should not lose sight of who we are. We should learn to reach out instead of suffering in isolation, and confront our grief rather than avoid it. This is what makes Spider-Man a character that continues to resonate with different generations, which is something the film exemplifies.

title: Obsession and the horror of a stolen self
text:
*This review contains spoilers

Curry Barker's low-budget horror Obsession gave the viewers one of the year's genuine box-office surprises, grossing well over a hundred times its production cost after breaking out of the Toronto festival circuit. Like many horror films in the contemporary scene, the premise is a folk-tale trick transmuted to fit modern times.

Bear, a shy and insecure music-shop worker, snaps a novelty charm called a “One Wish Willow” and wishes that his friend Nikki would love him more than anyone else in the world. She does exactly that. And the story takes off from that very point.

On the surface, this is The Monkey's Paw logic transplanted into a story about romantic longing, but Barker's script is interested in what happens to a person once it takes hold of them rather than the mechanics of it all.

Nikki's devotion presents itself as possession in the most literal sense: her body driven by something that has seized her from within. She screams in fear mid-embrace, catches herself, and smooths her expression back into calm, which is incredibly jarring to watch as a viewer.

It is horror built on the idea of watching someone lose command of themselves while some sliver of them remains awake inside, aware of what is happening and powerless to stop it. Her jolt of autonomy is suppressed by this “other Nikki”, who becomes someone Bear wants.

This is where the film's themes matter more than its plot mechanics. The scares are largely predictable, but they become terrifying when you take into account that they are about the terror of a self that can be overwritten, hijacked by a will other than one's own, with just enough consciousness left intact to be cognisant of the violation. Bear receives the devotion he asked for, but he never has to reckon with the cost until it is far too late, and that delay tells more about Bear’s moral construction.

Bear is a nice guy, only until niceness stops requiring sacrifice, which would entail killing himself. Once Nikki's love curdles into something monstrous, his instinct is to enjoy the spoils rather than undo the harm, and Barker lets that cowardice sit with the audience.

Inde Navarrette, who plays Nikki, carries the weight of this idea almost entirely through her physical performance, swinging between rictus grins and moments of genuine anguish that puncture the fantasy Bear has built for himself. It is a performance about the body being used as a vessel while the person trapped inside can do nothing except leak out in parts – a scream here, a flinch there – before the control resets almost too violently. That imbalance between awareness and agency is the beating heart of the horror. The animal violence and murders punctuate the back half of the story by building on the chaos that ensues right after Bear gets what he wanted.

Where the film falters slightly is in its comic tone, which sometimes undercuts the very dread it has worked to build, turning Nikki's suffering into a punchline more often than the material can comfortably support. Even so, Obsession has resonated with its gargantuan viewership because it understands that the most frightening loss of self is one furnished to look exactly like happiness.

title: Is the CFA worth it? Bangladeshi candidates weigh in
text:
A Chartered Financial Analyst (CFA) is a professional designation signifying advanced proficiency in investment management and financial analysis. It is offered by the CFA Institute, an organisation that measures and certifies the competence and integrity of financial analysts. Candidates must have a bachelor’s degree, pass three levels of exams covering topics such as accounting, economics, and ethics, and have three years of work experience to obtain the CFA charter.

A growing number of students and young professionals in Bangladesh are choosing to pursue the qualification, albeit for very different reasons.

For some, like Anik Mahmood, CFA, Deputy Head of Research at UCB Stock Brokerage Ltd., the CFA pathway felt like the natural extension of a finance degree. “I enjoyed studying finance,” says Anik. “Coursework on equity research, capital markets, and financial statement analysis and valuation greatly interested me, and with the CFA being the gold standard qualification, it naturally felt like the next step.”

On the other hand, Kashfia Binte Hassan, an analyst at Lion City Advisory Limited, embarked on the CFA journey to challenge herself and dismantle existing stereotypes against women. “Women are often not taken seriously in the workplace, and their competence is frequently scrutinised, particularly in a quantitative field like finance,” remarks Kashfia. “I want to push myself to achieve greater heights and gain the knowledge needed to successfully complete the tasks I am assigned. Thus, the CFA programme seems to be a stepping stone towards a smoother career path, as employers and people, in general, tend to take you more seriously once they see that you are dedicated enough to put in this much effort.”

For many at present, earning a CFA has become the ideal way to distinguish themselves in a competitive job market in the financial sector. Such was the case for Kazi Ajwad Ahmed, CFA, currently working as a financial planning and analysis (FP&A) manager. “I wanted to distinguish myself from the rest of the job seekers, which was the primary reason to pursue the CFA,” Ajwad notes. “Apart from that, the CFA seemed to offer employability both at home and abroad. It increased my options while still allowing me to stay in the country with my parents, which was a priority for me.”

Image

While individual motivations may differ, universities have also played an important role in encouraging students to consider the qualification. The CFA Institute, the global non-profit providing finance education to professionals across the globe, works closely with universities through its University Affiliation Program (UAP). The programme recognises academic institutions that broadly align one or more degree programmes with the CFA programme curriculum. The Institute assesses whether a university has a viable cohort of students currently enrolled in the academic degree programme and whether the curriculum contains the required minimum number of semester hours of coursework while demonstrating broad alignment with the CFA curriculum. Currently, six universities in Bangladesh are part of the UAP network. Selected students from these universities not only receive a discount on registration fees but also gain access to the CFA Program Learning Ecosystem, which offers students study plans, e-books, practice questions, mock exams, and a discussion forum.

Reflecting on the role his university played in reinforcing his interest in the qualification, Samin Al Fattah, a member of the champion team of the CFA Research Challenge 2026, said, “Back in 2023, when I was a first-year student, my university signed an MoU with the CFA Institute, which became my formal introduction to the programme. Although I already had a vague idea about it, that event played a key role in cementing my goal, as I hoped to secure a scholarship.”

While candidates pursue the CFA for different reasons, charter holders say that the certification’s greatest value lies in how they apply the knowledge in their everyday professional lives. Anik, for instance, notes how the CFA curriculum plays a central role in his daily responsibilities as a research professional. His work involves analysing macroeconomic and industry data, monitoring sector trends, building valuation models, and communicating investment insights. He also works with foreign investors, whose growing focus on environmental, social, and governance (ESG) considerations has made sustainable investing increasingly relevant, although ESG implementation in Bangladesh is still at an early stage. He further says that the CFA curriculum also provides a strong understanding of buy-side and sell-side research, enabling professionals to better serve clients and navigate different roles within the investment industry.

Echoing this sentiment, Ajwad says that the CFA curriculum has become an integral part of his daily work: “Whether I'm preparing forecasts, analysing financial statements, building valuation models, or evaluating capital investments, the concepts I learned through the CFA programme help me make more informed decisions and communicate financial insights more effectively.”

Even before earning the certification, many candidates say they begin to notice the practical value of the curriculum in both their studies and early careers. Regarding this, Samin says, “The concepts I had studied in my university coursework started making more sense after I began studying for the CFA. Since our courses have to be completed within six months, there is often limited time to explore topics in depth. Preparing for the CFA gave me a broader perspective on what I had already learned, and many of the concepts finally started to click. It also made me more attentive in my university classes.”

“One of the biggest realisations I had was that I genuinely enjoy building financial models from scratch,” Samin continues. “Every company is different, and there is no universal template that analysts can simply follow. Creating structure and meaning from that ambiguity is incredibly satisfying, and I enjoy the sense of autonomy that comes with it. Had I not pursued the CFA, I would not have been exposed to the wide range of career paths available to a finance graduate. Apart from that, passing CFA Level I also gave me an edge when applying for entry-level analyst roles focused on the capital market.”

Like Samin, Kashfia believes that pursuing the CFA gave her a competitive advantage when entering the job market: “So far, I have published two macroeconomic reports and recently carried out the equity valuation of an asset management company. Pursuing CFA Level I gave me the confidence to take on the daily responsibilities of my role as an analyst. The knowledge I gained through the programme helped me approach these tasks with greater confidence and a stronger analytical foundation.”

Beyond helping candidates in their professional lives, the CFA curriculum has also influenced the way they manage their own finances.

Image Illustration: Abir Hossain

“In many ways, I have become my own financial manager,” Kashfia remarks. “Compared to many of my peers, I have become more confident and disciplined in managing my finances. I apply the concepts I have learned to my own financial decisions. I actively invest in the stock market, save half of my monthly salary through a DPS, and maintain a fixed deposit account.”

Despite its many benefits, candidates unanimously agree on one thing: the CFA journey is far from easy. From dedicating more than 300 hours of study for each exam level to balancing preparation with a full-time job, the journey can be both isolating and mentally demanding.

“You could say that I lived like a monk during my preparation,” says Anik. “I would wake up early and dedicate one to two hours to studying before heading to work. I limited my time at social gatherings so that I could return home and continue from where I had left off in the morning. I also reserved my weekends for studying, leaving very little room for recreation.”

For some candidates, the demands of the programme extend beyond long study hours, requiring difficult compromises in their personal lives. Such was the case for Ajwad, who says, “I got married a few months before my Level III exam, and it was excruciating to spend my time studying instead of going out with my wife whenever I had the chance.”

Time, however, is not the only investment candidates have to make. CFA exam fees, which are charged in US dollars, can be quite expensive for aspirants in Bangladesh due to the exchange rate. Coupled with relatively low pass rates and the gruelling study hours required, the financial burden can discourage many students from taking the exams. As a result, candidates often feel immense pressure to pass each level on their first attempt, even though doing so is not always possible.

Samin puts the financial commitment into perspective: “A four-year Bachelor of Business Administration (BBA) degree at my university cost me around 1,20,000 taka, while registering for just the CFA Level I exam cost around 1,60,000 taka.”

To improve their chances of success, many candidates also invest in supplementary learning resources, which can make earning the certification more expensive.

Image

Ajwad says, “I focused on the video lectures provided by Mark Meldrum. It cost extra and made the whole thing even more expensive, but without it, I don't think I would have been able to pass.”

Ultimately, whether pursuing the CFA is worth it depends on an individual's career aspirations. Critics argue that the qualification may be more rigorous than what the Bangladeshi market currently demands, as the country has relatively limited use of complex financial instruments such as derivatives, and many organisations still view the finance function primarily as an accounting department rather than a strategic business partner.

Yet, for the candidates and charterholders we interviewed, the value of the CFA extended well beyond the designation itself. From improving technical competence to opening doors to new career opportunities, they viewed the journey as a worthwhile investment despite the sacrifices it demanded.

Tazrin is a finance major and a contributing writer at The Daily Star. You can reach out to her at [email protected].

title: The making of a doctor
text:
To obtain full registration from the Bangladesh Medical and Dental Council, Bachelor of Medicine and Bachelor of Surgery (MBBS) graduates in Bangladesh must complete a mandatory one-year rotatory internship. The 52-week-long internship programme consists of 19 weeks each in medicine and surgery, 12 weeks in obstetrics-gynaecology, and a mandatory two-week community placement at a thana or upazila health complex.

In practice, it is a year filled with long shifts, sleepless nights, steep learning curves, emotional highs and lows, and difficult conversations.

Dr Myesha Ahmed, an intern doctor at Sirajganj Medical College Hospital, describes the usual work schedule: “We have morning duty six days a week, typically from 8 AM to 2 PM. Some days we also have evening duty, which is six hours—from 2 PM to 8 PM—or night duty, which is 12 hours—from 8 PM to 8 AM the next day. The frequency varies depending on how busy a department is and how many interns are placed there. On some weeks we have Friday shifts, and on some we don’t.”

The very first thing Dr Ahmed has to do is take handover from the doctor of the previous shift.

“If there are critical patients, handover can take as long as half an hour. After that, I go and check on the critical patients again, observing their vitals and treatment. At the same time, if new patients arrive, we have to receive them as well,” Dr Ahmed shares. “Alongside all this, if there are any procedures left to do, such as inserting a nasogastric tube or a catheter, performing a pleural or ascitic fluid tap, or assisting with short surgical cases, those fall on me.”

Dr Md Aminul Islam, an intern doctor at Monno Medical College Hospital, breaks down how the whole day unfolds: “After the ward rounds, I monitor the condition of admitted patients, take histories of new arrivals, perform physical exams, write daily progress notes, and present patient conditions to senior doctors. I am also responsible for executing treatment plans, preparing patients for various tests, helping collect and analyse reports, and properly documenting all medical records.”

During their shifts, interns have little time to eat, sit, or even pray due to the heavy workload.

“If it’s a busy shift, I don’t get to sit at all. I barely manage to pray. As for eating, that’s not even an option. We’re constantly running around. Patients just keep coming, one after another,” Dr Ahmed says.

Photo: Orchid Chakma

The daily responsibilities that keep these interns busy vary from department to department. Dr Islam elaborates on the different day-to-day tasks he performed during his rotations: “In the emergency department, I had to rapidly assess patients’ conditions and begin initial treatment. I participated in managing trauma cases, severe respiratory distress, heart attacks, strokes, seizures, hypoglycaemic emergencies, and other critical conditions. Often, we had to make crucial decisions within minutes to save a patient’s life while working under the guidance of senior physicians.”

“In the surgery department, I had to prepare patients for the operating theatre, assist during operations, monitor patients after surgery, and dress wounds,” Dr Islam adds. “In medicine, I participated in the management of patients with chronic illnesses, infections, diabetes, hypertension, and kidney and liver diseases. During my gynaecology and obstetrics rotation, I helped with normal deliveries, caesarean sections, and pregnancy complications. In paediatrics, I helped care for newborns and took part in vaccination programmes.”

For Dr Ahmed, the tiny, precious patients of the paediatrics department are the bright spots amidst the heavy workload. “There was a neonate (newborn baby who is four weeks old or younger) whom I had to suction quite a few times and observe throughout the night. That little baby boy recovered, and I still remember his tiny fingers gripping my hand. There was another child named Taha in the paediatrics department. She was so fussy at the beginning, but later on, she used to smile whenever she saw me.”

While every departmental rotation comes with its own challenges, interns find some more demanding than others.

Dr Md Hasibuzzaman Hasib, another intern doctor from Monno Medical College Hospital, notes, “Although the workload was lighter in surgery, I found it more difficult because of the constant mental pressure. Gynaecology night shifts, however, are by far the toughest. It’s not unusual to have two or three emergency operations throughout the night while simultaneously admitting new patients. Then, instead of going home to rest, we continue working until 2 PM the next day. By the end of it, you’re completely drained both physically and mentally, but you still have to keep going.”

This is well reflected in the experience of Dr Fariba Binte Masud, an intern doctor at Sher-e-Bangla Medical College Hospital. Night shifts in the gynae ward, especially admission duty, are the most stressful for her.

“Patients who come in for admission late at night are almost always in serious condition,” says Dr Masud. “Someone may need emergency surgery, immediate blood transfusion, or urgent tests to assess their internal condition. Managing all of this is extremely difficult. Because at that time of night, a lot of things aren’t open anymore. Even the hospital does not have everything readily available. Many times, even after giving our absolute best, we still cannot save the patient.”

To cope with the sheer exhaustion and emotional toll, Dr Masud firmly keeps her eyes on the finish line: “I remind myself that I don’t intend on building a career in this department anyway. It is just a temporary phase, and it will be over before I know it. That thought alone keeps me going.”

On the other hand, Dr Ahmed found the medicine rotation to be the most physically demanding of all.

Photo: Orchid Chakma

“I became ill after my medicine placement. The workload was so intense that my body simply couldn’t take it. I was working continuously without eating or sleeping properly. The 24-hour shifts became a regular part of my routine. This may sound crazy, but at one point, I was on duty for almost 36 hours and once even for 50 hours. The 50-hour stretch happened because we were doing consecutive double shifts,” Dr Ahmed remarks.

Dr Masud feels that the biggest part of the internship is spent dealing with patient-related hassles.

“It’s not just deciding on a treatment plan and carrying it out. You also have to explain everything to the patient’s family and make sure they understand what’s happening. Even after explaining things thoroughly, they may still fail to understand and end up doing something wrong,” Dr Masud explains. “In most cases, the patient’s attendants are uncooperative. They assume that once they bring someone to the hospital, everything becomes the doctor’s responsibility.”

Due to the shortage of resources, Dr Masud often takes on responsibilities beyond her role. When the hospital’s supplies aren’t enough, she counsels patients’ families to buy what they need, shows them to the hospital’s poor fund when they cannot afford it, and even helps them financially herself.

“If a required procedure isn’t available here, we refer them to specialised institutions in Dhaka. But those hospitals are far away, and I often wonder whether our sickest patients are actually able to make it there,” Dr Masud states.

Dr Ahmed points out another challenge that interns face: inadequate workplace safety.

“Even though there are guards in the hospital, it doesn’t always make us feel safe,” says Dr Ahmed. “If our safety could be properly ensured, we’d be able to work with greater peace of mind. Some of my colleagues have been physically assaulted and harassed by patients’ attendants.”

Faced with circumstances outside their control, interns sometimes feel an acute sense of helplessness.

“One night, a patient cried out, ‘Save me, save me’. She had severe valvular heart disease but couldn’t afford the surgery she desperately needed. After giving her the available treatment, I went back to my room and cried on my prayer mat, asking Allah to help her. I will never forget her face or her cries,” Dr Ahmed recalls. “Another time, I felt like quitting when I had to tell a patient with urosepsis that we didn’t have an intensive care unit (ICU) facility.”

Repeated encounters with such situations have made Dr Masud question whether she belongs in the profession at all: “There are times when I feel this profession simply isn’t for me. To survive as a doctor in this country, you need immense mental resilience.”

Dr Masud still vividly remembers the first death she had to declare: “At the start of the internship, I had to declare the death of a young woman with dengue. She had two small children. My heart broke for her family.”

There is often no time to pause or mourn before moving on to the next patient, which leaves interns like Dr Ahmed feeling numb.

“Some moments were truly surreal,” Dr Ahmed recalls. “My first patient death was a child in the paediatric ward. After declaring the child dead, I went back to my room, cried, wiped away my tears, and then walked straight back out to receive another patient. One moment I was declaring a death and the next, I was calmly asking someone else, ‘What seems to be the problem?’ and checking their vitals.”

“I remember thinking, ‘What is happening?’ People say doctors are heartless or emotionless, but the reality is that we witness many patient deaths and face several traumatic experiences. We spend a lot of time explaining diseases and treatment plans and even dealing with misunderstandings and misbehaviour. After a point, we stop processing our emotions. We’re like, ‘It happened. Fine. Move on.' There were days when I wondered why I had chosen this profession,” Dr Ahmed shares.

The demands of the internship also leave little room for life outside the hospital, often straining relationships with family and friends.

“Internship kept me so busy and exhausted that I became the busy daughter, the distant sister, and the absent friend,” Dr Ahmed admits.

“It has affected my personal life a lot, to be honest. I only go home once every few months. In fact, there are many days when I can’t even find the energy to talk to my family over the phone,” adds Dr Masud.

Photo: Orchid Chakma

The long hours and sacrifices are not well reflected in the monthly stipend. “We receive a monthly stipend of BDT 20,000, which isn’t enough,” Dr Hasib comments.

Dr Ahmed tries to find joy in simple moments to keep herself sane: “Whenever we get a day off, we try to go outside or rest in our rooms. I love cooking with my roommates. Fridays are my favourite; we either follow our self-care routines or go out to refresh our minds. We don’t exactly study during the little free time we get; we use it to reboot ourselves.”

All four interns we talked to agree that those outside the medical field can never fully comprehend what they’re going through. When asked whether they would choose medicine again, knowing what they know now, their answers differed.

Dr Hasib responds with a firm “No, never”, while Dr Masud is more reflective: “Why would I? It’s so hard and painful, and there are many other options.”

Dr Ahmed, however, had a completely different answer to this question: “Despite the missed meals, sleepless nights, exhaustion, and the lives we sometimes lose, there is something extraordinary about seeing a patient smile again, heal again, and have hope again. In those moments, every hardship feels worthwhile. To be entrusted with the opportunity to ease someone’s pain and serve them in their time of need is, I believe, one of the greatest ways a person can serve humanity. So, I would choose this profession again and again, despite every hardship and sacrifice, because there is no greater privilege than helping another human being heal.”

title: What I learnt building a career at the intersection of compliance, AI, and research
text:
As a global financial compliance & crime associate at JPMorgan Chase, I investigate high-risk financial crime and file the reports that feed directly into federal law enforcement intelligence. It's demanding, detail-heavy work, and most days, it's invisible by design. A good investigation prevents a headline rather than making one.

Alongside that career, I have spent the last several years publishing peer-reviewed research applying artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning to financial crime detection, testing how far these methods can be pushed beyond what conventional rule-based compliance systems can see. Looking back, a few lessons stand out from that work, and I want to share them in case they're useful to anyone building a similar path.

Let AI-driven thinking guide your investigative work – and vice versa

Anti-money laundering (AML) compliance is fundamentally a pattern-recognition problem, and traditional AML systems are built on fixed rules: if a transaction matches a known pattern, it gets flagged. The limitation is obvious once you've worked in the field – rule-based systems only catch what they were already told to look for. That gap is what drove much of my research.

One study I am particularly proud of built an unsupervised machine learning ensemble to detect new money-laundering typologies within transaction graphs – patterns a system trained only on known, labelled laundering behaviour would never catch, because they don't resemble anything it has seen before. That's close to the exact problem I evaluate in live investigations, where the most dangerous cases are often the ones that don't fit any existing template.

I followed that work with related studies applying machine learning to credit card fraud detection and corporate bankruptcy prediction, and later to equity market forecasting using a hybrid ensemble model. In each case, I tested multiple algorithms – logistic regression, random forest, gradient boosting, XGBoost, and LightGBM – against real datasets rather than betting on one method. After all, in financial crime detection, a wrong model isn't an academic error; it's a missed case or a false accusation.

My advice: don't treat your AML expertise and your AI research as separate skill sets. The strongest financial crime research comes from investigators who understand both the criminal behaviour and the modelling well enough to know where each one breaks down.

Publish even when nobody is telling you to

Nobody required me to formalise my AML detection work into a peer-reviewed paper on emerging laundering typologies or to test ensemble AI models for fraud and market forecasting outside work hours. I did it because I wanted proof that the machine learning approach I trusted in live investigations would hold up to scrutiny from researchers with no stake in my day job. If you're wondering whether your AI-driven compliance work is "publication-worthy", my honest answer is you won't know until you write it up and submit it. Some of my early submissions were rejected. That's part of the process, not a sign to stop.

Practically, here's what worked for me in the AML and financial crime space specifically: start with a real detection problem you already understand from your job – laundering, fraud, or default risk. Then, find a dataset that reflects it realistically and run a rigorous, comparative test of several machine learning approaches rather than just one.

Reviewers in this field respond to honest, methodical model comparison far more than to a single flashy accuracy score.

Protect what you build

One thread of my AML and fraud-detection research eventually became a patent filing for a network security verification device, built on the same anomaly-detection logic I had already validated in my money-laundering typology research. The patent came from asking, after publishing, "Could this AI-driven detection logic be built into something deployable beyond a research paper?"

If you're doing applied AI research in fraud, risk, or security, ask that question of your own work. Not every paper needs to become a patent, but the strongest detection methods usually can.

Stay disciplined about your core field

It would have been easy to drift once I had a stable AML job, but I made a point of keeping my AI and machine learning research anchored to financial crime and financial risk – laundering typology detection, credit card fraud, bankruptcy prediction, and market forecasting. That focus meant each new paper built on the last, rather than starting from zero. My suggestion, especially for those early in a financial or compliance career: build depth with AI applied to your core field first. A stack of related, rigorous studies is worth more than a scattered handful of unrelated ones.

Build a body of work, not just a resume line

If I could go back and give my younger self one piece of advice, it would be to think in terms of a portfolio, not individual achievements.

A single AI-driven fraud-detection paper is a data point. A sequence of studies, like laundering typology detection, credit card fraud, bankruptcy prediction, etc., is a body of work. It compounds, and it becomes far more persuasive than any one credential on its own, whether you're applying for a job, a visa, or simply trying to convince yourself you're on the right track.

For anyone reading this and wondering where to start: pick one real detection or risk problem you already understand well from your job or your studies. Test more than one machine learning approach against it before you trust your conclusion, and write it up properly. Then ask what the next version of that idea could be – a related paper, a patent, an adjacent detection problem. Repeat that a few times, and a career takes shape that looks, in hindsight, a lot more deliberate than it ever felt while you were living it.

The author is a global financial compliance & crime associate at JPMorgan Chase. He holds an MS in Business Analytics from the University of North Texas, a BBA from American International University-Bangladesh, and completed a scholarly exchange as an Erasmus Scholar at Mykolas Romeris University in Lithuania.

title: Zero-cost Malaysia jobs for 10,000 workers
text:
Bangladesh is preparing to send 10,000 workers to Malaysia at zero migration cost, with recruitment to focus on skills, experience and employers’ requirements as the two countries move ahead with restarting labour migration.

Malaysian employers have started issuing demand letters, while a delegation from the country is expected to visit Bangladesh next week to discuss the types of workers, skills and experience required.

Labour and Employment Minister Ariful Haque Chowdhury, who is also the expatriates’ welfare and overseas employment minister, said Malaysia had agreed to receive 10,000 workers initially and that the process would begin with workers being sent free of migration costs.

Speaking to reporters at the labour and employment ministry’s conference room yesterday, he said workers would be trained according to employers’ requirements before selection and sent through Bangladesh Overseas Employment and Services Limited (BOESL) and other recruiting agencies.

Ariful said the Malaysian labour market had reopened following discussions between the two countries, but the government wanted to prevent a repeat of the problems workers had faced under syndicate-based recruitment.

“For a long time, people going abroad have faced different forms of harassment through syndicates,” he said, adding that the government has set conditions while discussing the reopening of the market.

According to officials from the expatriates’ welfare ministry and recruiting agency owners, Malaysian employers have begun issuing demand letters and enrolling workers in the Foreign Workers Centralised Management System (FWCMS) through levy payments.

The Bangladesh High Commission in Kuala Lumpur has also begun attesting to demand letters from Malaysian employers.

Last week, the high commission attested a demand for 28 Bangladeshi workers from the Malaysian supermarket chain NSK Trade City under Goodness Services Limited.

Officials said priority would be given to sending the 10,000 workers through BOESL at zero migration cost.

Mohammad Rashedul Haque, managing director of BOESL, told The Daily Star yesterday that workers with the required expertise, experience and fitness would be selected from among the 10,000.

“We want to leave the selection criteria entirely to the recruiter -- who they want, what kind of workers they need and what qualifications they are looking for,” he said.

Rashedul said a Malaysian delegation was expected to visit Bangladesh next week to discuss recruitment criteria.

He said a clearer timeframe would emerge after the delegation’s visit and once employers’ demand became known.

Before sending new workers, however, BOESL plans to complete the migration of workers who could not travel to Malaysia before the market was closed for Bangladesh on May 31, 2024.

That process is expected to be completed by October 16.

A BOESL official said around 120 to 150 of the previously stranded workers were still waiting to travel to Malaysia. The agency would write to their employers to complete the process.

Recruiting agencies, meanwhile, said they had yet to receive specific guidelines on when and how worker selection, medical examinations, training and other procedures would begin after receiving demand letters.

Ariful said the medical examination process had not yet been approved and the government would provide details once arrangements were finalised.

There are currently 17 approved medical centres for Bangladeshi workers.

On October 1, the authorities sealed Human Diagnostic and Medical Centre on Box Culvert Road in Paltan after finding that it had been conducting medical tests and issuing reports for Malaysia-bound workers without approval.

At yesterday’s briefing, Prime Minister’s Adviser and PMO spokesperson Mahdi Amin said the government was working to reopen the Malaysian labour market while giving Bangladesh’s interests the highest priority.

Without giving further details, he said the process was subject to certain conditions and that some complications remained because of the existing memorandum of understanding and the structure put in place under the previous government.

Mahdi said the expatriates’ welfare ministry was working on the issues and would brief the media once an effective decision was reached.

title: Navigating a career in public health
text:
Most of us enter medical school with a fairly uncomplicated idea of what comes next. You study, you graduate, you become a doctor, and somewhere along the way, you figure out which branch of medicine you want to call your own.

But healthcare is much larger than the hospital corridors. There are people who spend their careers asking why a disease spreads through one community and not another, why an intervention works in one population but fails in another, or what a country’s healthcare system needs before the next crisis arrives.

The variables surrounding these questions converge under the banner of public health. And for students trying to figure out what they want to do with their degrees, particularly those who know they want to work in healthcare but are not entirely sure that clinical practice is where they belong, public health is an option worth looking into. It is also a field that is often misunderstood.

Public health is not simply “community medicine”, nor is a Master of Public Health merely another degree to add to a CV. Instead, it brings together medicine, epidemiology, statistics, economics, sociology, policy, communication, and research to answer a deceptively simple question: how do we keep people healthy in the first place? For Bangladesh, that question is hardly theoretical.

Image Photo: Orchid Chakma
