title: The cost of our obsession with meritocracy
text:
Ask a student what their roll number is, and you might get a very different reaction depending on the number. A low number can come with praise, whereas a higher one can invite jokes, assumptions, and, sometimes, a shift in how people treat you. We laugh about it, but the joke points towards something more serious about the way we understand academic success.

In our culture, there is a certain obsession with meritocracy. We love the student who comes first: the perfect score, the name announced at the assembly, and the photograph posted after results. We celebrate the outcome so enthusiastically that we rarely stop to ask what happens before that moment. What does it actually take to create an environment where students can succeed?

A meritocracy only works if everyone starts from the same point, with the same resources, the same support, and the same room to fail and try again. In reality, only some students are at the starting line while others are already 10 metres ahead.

What we’ve built, instead, is a culture that expects everyone to run the same race, while quietly ignoring the fact that some students were given a head start. We celebrate it as if grades show who worked hardest but rarely admit the unequal circumstances, expectations, and treatment that surround those grades.

In Bangladesh, academic success is often compressed into a handful of numbers: marks, grades, GPA, and class rankings. Sometimes, roll numbers become convenient shorthand for a student’s ability. But a number can tell us what happened. It cannot always tell us why.

If we look at two students who scored 70 percent marks on a test, one of them could have spent months working their way up from 50, and the other may have just fallen from 90. Same score, different stories. Yet our culture is often more interested in the final destination than the journey it took to get there.

Take something as ordinary as seating arrangements. In many classrooms, students are segregated by their grades. The high scorers are seated up front, and everyone else is seated in the back rows, as if it were a gravitational pull. It may just seem like a simple seating arrangement, but it can often make students feel marginalised. Teachers call on them less, their questions start getting shorter answers, and, eventually, some students just stop asking.

This is the part of meritocracy nobody wants to talk about. It doesn't just reward the front row; it also penalises the rest. A student who is struggling isn't simply identified as needing help. Rather, they're sorted out of the spaces where help usually reaches. The system claims to measure ability, but what it's often measuring is who already had the advantage of stability at home, tutoring at home, or being able to join multiple coaching classes.

This shows up even in the simplest, mundane parts of school life in the form of how students get divided into different sections just because of contrasting grades or how friend groups drift apart after they are advised not to surround themselves with students with lower grades, as if academic performance is a personality trait.

The same fixation can extend beyond classrooms. Report card season isn't really about asking whether a child understood the material or grew as a learner. It ends up fixating on the number attached to their name and how it compares against a cousin's, a neighbour's, or a classmate's. "Did you improve?" quietly gets replaced by "Where did you rank?" And the two questions, despite sounding similar, lead students toward entirely different relationships with learning, where one builds curiosity and the other instils self-consciousness.

A student who moves from struggling with mathematics to confidently solving problems may have achieved something profound, even if their position barely changes. A student who learns to write independently, develops the courage to ask questions, or finally understands a concept they once feared may have made an achievement that cannot be captured by a rank sheet.

None of this means that grades are meaningless. They are useful indicators of hard work, and healthy competition itself is not harmful, so excellence should absolutely be encouraged. But if meritocracy is supposed to reward ability and effort, the culture surrounding it must also give students opportunities to develop both.

The real failure of our obsession with merit is not that we celebrate achievement too much, but that we, sometimes, celebrate the result while forgetting the conditions that make improvement possible.

A healthy academic culture should not only ask, “Who came first?” It should also ask, “What did we do to help them get there?” Otherwise, we are not cultivating merit. We are merely getting very good at counting it.

title: Can fluency in English be a measure of intelligence?
text:
"Wow! An IELTS band score of 8.5! Kiss your brains! You are a genius!"

This is a common line that IELTS high-achievers must have heard.

Often, a good command over the English language is considered a major sign of intelligence, especially in Bangladesh. English proficiency has always been admired, and why not? It is the primary global lingua franca. Roughly 1.5 billion people around the world speak English, with non-native speakers outnumbering native speakers by around three to one. There is no denying that English is an essential language, but there are some individuals who frequently mistake linguistic fluency for intellectual superiority.

Image

Apart from prodigies, the vast majority of the people who achieve a good band score in these standardised tests have secured that milestone owing to countless hours of practice and studying the various techniques. Simply masking the effort behind the term “intelligent” does not suffice, so simply stating it does not help.

The curling of lips and the stretching of the jaws to produce the correct phonic sound, along with adjustments in the pitch while maintaining voice intonations, is not a skill picked up overnight. Likewise, when the speaker appears to be a “walking dictionary”, they have already worked for hours on picking up every word they came across over the years. Diligence and perseverance were key here; hence, relating them to inherent ability is not very helpful.

Nonetheless, society has always inclined to equate the ability to speak fluent English with intelligence. But proficiency in English, or any language as a matter of fact, actually reflects consistent practice, exposure, learning, and constant corrections during communication. Innate intelligence can help you learn quicker or adapt swiftly, but the relentless perseverance to push forward gives you that edge.

Howard Gardner's theory of “Multiple Intelligences”, an educational perspective, highlights that linguistic skills can be defined as being equipped to understand, use, and communicate a language effectively: native or non-native, first or second language. Therefore, according to Gardner’s concept, a person considered excellent in English or any other language must have a well-wired brain to process literature and understand the nuances of the language; subsequently, having a strong foothold while using the language in its written or spoken form is important. Then perhaps that person speaking could be honoured with the epithet “intelligent”.

Furthermore, for these individuals, the use of these linguistic skills must not be limited to the classroom or conversations within friend circles. Students with strong linguistic intelligence will use their skills in domains beyond their surroundings, such as extempore speeches, public speaking, debates, critical analysis, creative writing, presenting monologues, and finally creating their individual piece of literary work. Thus, it is much more than speaking fluently in English.

It is important to acknowledge that a fluent speaker may not have the necessary writing proficiency; likewise, a person proficient in writing the language may not have exceptional speaking skills. Similarly, an 8.5 IELTS band or high PTE score may not mirror an individual’s linguistic potential, as known to all that these evaluation systems are strategic English language tests that do not focus on potential creativity.

To put it straight, English fluency is highly regarded, especially in the Bangladeshi context. Why so? Because a vast majority may not be able to confidently communicate with precise grammar, use, and application of phrases, idiomatic expressions, and figurative language, which are all forms of wordplay. English is a subject taught at school from nursery to higher secondary level, sometimes even in university as a fundamental course.

According to the 2022 Bangladesh Census, 6.10 percent of the population reported English as a second language. Importantly, this does not mean that 6.10 percent are fluent; it simply indicates that they reported English as a second language. Even within this domain of efficiency, ability is not uniform. Consequently, in a country where only a minority speaks English, the genuine ability to speak the Anglophone language could be considered a rare skill, but simply terming that person “intelligent” robs an individual of all the effort they poured into honing their skills in that particular language.

Reference:

Bangladesh Bureau of Statistics. (2024). Report on Socio-Economic and Demographic Survey 2023.

Salma, a contributing writer at Campus, is a teacher by profession but a student at heart: curious, questioning and always learning.

title: How performance enhancement classes put progress beyond marks
text:
Contrary to popular belief, a report card cannot always be the perfect measure of how a student is learning at school. It can tell us where a student understands a lesson, where they are performing well, or where they need more support. But as a teacher, I’ve learned that there are things a report cannot fully capture, including a student's hidden potential.

Every classroom has students who learn at different paces. Every term, some students lag in class assessments or hesitate to write answers on the board. In a classroom with a diverse group of students, identifying these students might seem daunting, but it is not impossible.

Our starting point is often assessment. Through formative and summative assessments, we can identify areas where students may need additional attention. Formative assessment monitors students' learning during instruction to provide ongoing feedback, helping teachers improve teaching and students fix gaps. Examples include short quizzes and class tests. Summative assessment evaluates student learning at the end of an instructional period to measure final achievement against set standards, such as final exams.

But assessment is not the end of the process; it is a starting point for understanding what a student needs next, which is where performance enhancement classes (PEC) come in.

For me, one of the most valuable things PEC provides is something very simple: having the time to notice. I remember a student who was particularly hesitant during mathematics lessons. He rarely volunteered answers, and when he did not understand a problem, he would often wait rather than ask for help. His assessments showed that he was struggling with certain concepts, but they did not tell the whole story.

During PEC, with more time to work through problems step by step, I began to see that the issue was not that he could not understand mathematics. He was not confident enough to make mistakes in front of others.

We started breaking problems into smaller steps and giving him time to work through them himself. One day, after practising a similar question, he volunteered to solve one on the board. He got part of it wrong, paused, and then corrected himself. It was a small moment, but as his teacher, I noticed the difference. The goal was no longer simply getting the answer right. He was beginning to trust his own ability to find the answer.

That is what I find most valuable about PEC. Integrated into the weekly timetable for core subjects, including mathematics, science, English, and Bangla, these sessions give students time to revisit difficult concepts and approach them through different learning methods, using worksheets, multimedia presentations, and learning from each other.

We sometimes use peer teaching as well, allowing students to review one another’s work and learn from different approaches. It gives students a chance to engage more actively with what they are learning while allowing teachers to observe how they think, explain, and solve problems.

Over time, I have seen students become more willing to attempt difficult questions, ask for clarification, and participate in class. Some eventually begin helping classmates with concepts they once found difficult themselves. These changes may not immediately show up in a report card, but they tell us something important about how a student is learning.

For me, that is why student progress is more than a mark. An assessment can tell us where a student stands today. A teacher gets to see the steps they take to move forward.

The author is the Dean of Academics, Lower Secondary (Grades 6-8) at Glenrich International School, Uttara.

title: Why Ducsu’s faculty evaluation move matters
text:
Three years ago, while pursuing my bachelor’s degree at Dhaka University (DU), I penned an article for this publication titled “Faculty evaluation should be a must in all universities” about faculty evaluation and included this line in it: “Dhaka University has recently implemented faculty evaluation, viewed as a significant step for its students’ benefit.” I have since finished my undergrad in 2025, and my master’s this year. Yet, this evaluation system still hasn't materialised.

In 2023, we were given tutorials on how we could evaluate the faculty members. A seminar was held, and a video was showcased on one of our student portals, so I thought faculty evaluations might actually be on the horizon. It’s been three years, and the horizon kept slipping away, but the administration kept assuring us that it was going to happen, although no one could say when. The process remained stalled in meetings and reviews, as many things do in this part of the city.

But on September 10, 2026, the Dhaka University Central Students' Union (Ducsu) launched a faculty evaluation website named “DU Evaluation” for students to rate their respective faculty members. Students can rate their teachers based on the course design, teaching method, engagement and support, assessment and feedback, professionalism, and overall satisfaction. At the time of writing, over 11,800 reviews have been submitted.

Many faculty members were less than thrilled about Ducsu’s decision to introduce the website. Dhaka University Pro Vice-Chancellor (Academic) Prof. Abdus Salam argued that the initiative was simply not within Ducsu’s purview. Pro Vice-Chancellor (Administration) Prof. Mohammed Almujaddade Alfasane also questioned the appropriateness of DUCSU taking up such an activity. According to him, however, DU students will be able to evaluate their teachers starting from the 2026-27 academic year. The same was voiced by the Vice-Chancellor, Prof. ABM Obaidul Islam.

The initiative was inspired by Rate My Professors, the website where students have long been able to say what they really think about their teachers. Ducsu’s platform aims to create a public record of students’ views on their teachers and, more broadly, on the academic environment at DU.

Action-reaction from both camps has its merit. The teachers feel as though the ratings may cultivate a culture of fear. The ratings may also be a source of public ridicule and harassment. They are not wrong in their thinking, because photocards of student reviews are circulating online to garner reactions. Such behaviour, by any means, is not constructive. If anything, it erodes the symbiotic relationship between teachers and students that must be nurtured to make an academically conducive environment.

As a student, I must also say that globally, faculty evaluation is a regular practice to ensure that students can provide feedback to their teachers so that they can better understand where they can improve in terms of pedagogy. Without it, the feedback system remains one-way, with only the teacher having the option of choosing whether to listen to students’ concerns.

Another important point to be noted is the length of time that has passed since students were given the assurance of a faculty evaluation system. It is, thus, not unnatural for students to develop a sense of frustration.

The result is a distrust between the teachers and the students; the teachers are wary of a parallel administrative system, and the students are channelling their internal grievances through a website after years of vapid promises.

Rate My Professors ratings are often taken with a grain of salt because the reviews can be constructive and destructive at the same time. Simply leaving a negative review because one didn’t score well on a test doesn’t help with the overall educational context because reviews should be detailed and helpful for students taking the class or for teachers who are receptive to feedback.

Acknowledging that students are free to have opinions about their teachers and that rating systems for professors exist in other countries, Pro VC Prof. Abdus Salam clarified that this is not an official form of evaluation. Such initiatives, he said, may exist informally. But ironically enough, a probe committee has been formed to investigate the matter and submit a report within seven working days.

The point I am hammering on is that the inception of such a drastic measure for students to give their two cents to faculty members indicates one thing that has been plaguing DU for far too long: promises that remain promises for years on end. Only when push comes to shove does the pressure unsettle the administration.

Of course, there should be a balance of responsibilities from both sides. The students have a major task of being objective in their judgements, and the university must facilitate a conversation where the students can remain anonymous so they can evaluate the quality of the education they are receiving without the fear of being singled out by teachers.

It’s been three years since the first time I heard “teachers’ evaluation”, and it still sounds elusive to me because of the lack of interest from the university’s end. Instead of seeing the ratings as a threat, the administration should view this as an opportunity to propel the central teachers’ evaluation process. The conversation about faculty evaluations should disperse to other public universities in Bangladesh. Public universities should also take this pertinent fact into consideration: student voices are integral when it comes to nurturing an equally beneficial relationship between students and teachers.

References:

1. The Daily Star (September 15, 2026). ‘No scope for a parallel administration’ at DU.

2. Prothom Alo (September 11, 2026). DUCSU launches teacher evaluation at Dhaka University, administration questions its legitimacy.

3. Dhaka Tribune (September 8, 2026). Ducsu member launches online platform to evaluate DU teachers.

4. New Age (September 12, 2026). DU teachers criticise DUCSU rating website, fear partisan misuse.

title: AI will, inevitably, raise the value of writers
text:
People put little effort into writing anymore. And why would they? Writing, once a laborious process, has become remarkably easy. Give AI a few basic instructions, and it can draft an email, polish an article, write a caption, or structure an essay within seconds.

The convenience is undeniable. But there is a paradox here: the easier writing becomes, the more valuable human-written articles may become.

Think about how people wrote centuries ago. Educated people had to write constantly, even if simply to communicate with friends, family, colleagues, and acquaintances. And these were not WhatsApp messages or two-line texts. A letter could easily run to several pages.

Even people who never considered themselves writers were, therefore, practising the craft regularly. They had to organise their thoughts, explain themselves, describe experiences, and express their emotions in words. Over time, they naturally became better at it.

Today, we are losing that habit.

People use AI even for the smallest acts of expression: a birthday wish, a condolence note, or a few words accompanying a photograph with someone they love.

But writing is not merely a way of communicating what we already think. Writing is also one of the ways we learn to think.

When we struggle to explain an idea, we are forced to understand it. When we search for the right word, we refine our thought. When we write something badly and rewrite it, we develop judgement. The difficulty is part of the process.

If we outsource that process completely, we may eventually lose more than our ability to write. We may lose our ability to think independently and articulate what is actually going on inside our heads.

And that is where I see an interesting future for writing.

As AI-generated text becomes ubiquitous, polished writing will become abundant. There will be no shortage of grammatically flawless articles, perfectly structured essays, and smoothly worded social-media posts.

What will become scarce is original thought.

There is a difference between writing that is technically good and writing that has something genuinely worth saying. AI can help with the first. The second still depends on a human being who has observed, experienced, and questioned something or connected ideas in a novel way.

If machines can produce polished prose instantly, being able to produce polished prose will no longer be a particularly rare skill.

Think about it this way: who gives you credit for pressing a button on a remote control to turn on the air conditioner or change the television channel? Nobody. The action is too effortless to be considered an achievement.

AI-generated writing could eventually be viewed in much the same way. When everyone can produce a polished article, essay, script, or caption within seconds, simply producing those words will no longer be impressive. A byline means little if the person behind it has contributed neither an original idea nor a distinctive voice.

What will matter is the person behind the prose: the journalist who notices what others missed, the essayist with an unusual argument, the novelist with a distinct voice, the screenwriter who sees a story differently.

And this may finally change how society values writers. Those with genuinely original voices across creative fields may begin to receive the recognition, respect, and reward their work deserves, precisely because their ability will have become rarer.

That is why aspiring writers should refrain from falling into the temporary convenience trap.

Why spend an hour struggling with a paragraph when AI can give you ten versions in seconds? Why sit with a blank page when a machine can tell you what to say?

Because the struggle is the training.

Every time you force yourself to find the right expression, you exercise your mind. Every time you reject a sentence and try again, you develop judgement.

I say this as someone who works in writing.

I use AI too. I use it all the time. I need references, information, and sometimes help processing large amounts of material. But I also try to think through and write an idea myself before bringing AI into the process.

At the same time, I have been trying to read more. Whenever I have time, I read news reports, Facebook posts, Messenger group chats, essays, long-form journalism and, of course, books. I also watch news packages, documentaries, and films while listening to audiobooks and podcasts.

All of these keep the brain active. They expose us to different ways of thinking, give us new material to work with and help us make connections that might otherwise never occur to us.

For me, that is the balance we need in the age of AI: use the machine, but do not surrender the mind.

Read. Listen. Watch. Think. Write. Not always in this order, but in whichever order works for you. Then use technology – not to replace the thinking that makes the work worth reading, but to make the work better.

title: How students can use their mistakes to learn better
text:
“You got this wrong again!”

Sounds familiar?

Once in your lifetime, you must have heard something like this. I heard something similar a while ago.

Just as I was penning this article, “A four-step module to never make mistakes”, a student of mine spoke out, “Make that: A guide to using mistakes.” That left me thinking: can teachers actually help students benefit from mistakes?

Mistake-making is nothing unusual, so treating it as an injury is not helpful. But how many students actually flip through pages to study their mistakes? For many, only marks matter.

Mistakes happen for many reasons: lack of content clarity, minimal practice, and the like. But one thing that is to be noted with urgency is that mistakes also happen because our minds think differently.

There goes a saying: “It’s good to learn from your mistakes. It’s better to learn from other people’s mistakes.” But would you agree if I said, “You can learn better from your mistakes"?

Let’s take penicillin, for example. Fleming left unwashed culture plates out on his bench before going on a two-week summer vacation. Upon his return, he noticed a fuzzy mould colony had grown on one dish. And the rest is history. Now, it is termed an accidental discovery.

In a classroom filled with a sea of students, how can we learn from others’ mistakes? Pinpointing a student’s mistake in front of the entire class would perhaps corner the student. In the modern-day classroom, there is little time to dwell on mistakes. We don’t like to sing our errors to others, so that leaves us with learning from our own failures.

Most importantly, this is where the teacher must walk in. They can be the inspiration for a child to turn mistakes into marvels. To begin with, they must set the mood for acceptance. A classroom culture which encourages mistake correction is more likely to thrive, for making mistakes shows attempt and initiative, and that must not go unnoticed.

Just like a connecting bridge, the teacher turns mistakes into methodology: a methodology to expedite learning. It also opens windows to understanding mindset.

Let’s consider this meme for a second. A question asks to "find x”. The student draws an arrow pointing directly to the letter “x” on a triangle and writes, “Here it is.” This has me rolling on the floor all the time. Tell me, is this thought wrong? There are times when the naive mind thinks differently, but we cannot single that out as wrong. Did you, for a second, ever think that this could be a possible answer for locating “x”, standing next to that isosceles triangle, who always finds a way to get lost?

Making students doubt their questions or question their own thoughts are two things a teacher mustn’t do. If your student says the sky is pink, let it be. Feedback always helps; correction may not.

Having said this, there exists the “protégé effect”. Psychological studies show that people learn information more deeply when they have to teach or correct someone else rather than simply consume it.

You may have experienced this at some time: a teacher intentionally or unintentionally makes strategic mistakes in class to pique students’ attention. Funnily enough, students just love finding their teacher’s errors. That should not be embarrassing; that should be liberating. This move encourages students to make mistakes because the teacher makes them too.

Now that the classroom culture has created space to breathe, let’s develop a four-step model that makes the best of mistakes.

First, sense it. Give your intuitions some credit. When things don’t seem to fit, or you think you are making a mistake, your senses are likely to kick in. Prioritise that. Revisit the question if you are in the hall, or reread the verse during practice time if a doubt settles in.

Next, retrace it. As you write the formula down or practise an experiment in the lab and make a blunder, note it down and recheck the step at home. Even though for students getting marks might be the most important aspect of learning owing to our marks-centric upbringing, we must keep in mind that you study to learn, not to score.

Then, chalk it up to experience. At least for five minutes every day, go back in time and think about how things could have been done better. Then, the next day, be the preacher—share what you have learnt.

Finally, find the other way. Have a plan B for how the situation could be dealt with differently. Parents have an important role to play here. They’ve seen you grow: the good and the bad. Allow them the space to help. Parents must also emphasise less on marks and more on understanding to create a more conducive environment for learning.

Now, if you are making mistakes, here is your chance to learn. Make the best of them.

Salma is a contributing writer at Campus. She is a teacher by profession but a student at heart: curious, questioning, and learning. Mail her at: [email protected].

title: The digitalised public court
text:
Before selecting a course, Sisyphus finds himself anxiously looking up the faculty initials to read the shared experiences of his fellow Sisyphuses to discover whether he might also have to carry the burden of the grades on a rocky hill or a smooth slate with rollerblades. The culture of Facebook groups for faculty reviews serves as a hideout for the students from the keen eyes of surveillance. Serving as a communal space, Facebook groups for faculty reviews informally assess faculty members, their desired courses, and assessment strategies.

In search of an easygoing section and faculty, the hunt for wishful thinking continues, as it is in human nature for us to find easier and shorter routes to decode the unknown for uncertainties.

10 years ago, I, too, stumbled upon a Facebook faculty review group, anxiously trying to decode my science electives as a humanities major. Being on the other side of the discourse, I find myself sympathetic to both parts of the academic ecosystem. Informal, student-friendly online spaces serve as an effective medium for first-year students to connect with students and the campus in a manner that seems more accessible to their “survival” throughout the semesters. While in the West, “Rate My Professor” is globally accessible, the practice of review groups in Bangladesh is more gatekept. Because universities carry an institutional hierarchy, students seek solace through these internet spaces in navigating this newfound individual agency.

The transitional evaluation cycle of each semester is almost loop-like. A teacher assesses students, and students later assess the faculty member in two ways: one in an official system organised by the university and another in social media groups. While it is a standard practice of confidentiality on university official portals, students tend to share their frustrations with the faculty members on online forums through anonymous posts. Most reviews entail a detailed list that can often come across “accusatory” without evidence and at times reads more personal than providing constructive criticism on pedagogical approaches.

With the lack of monitoring towards anonymous posts, this space creates an unsettling form of confirmation bias amongst the students. Reputation aside, such posts affect the grading and course design, along with the emotional anxieties that prevail for the faculty member. Between burnout followed by research deadlines and endless academic chores, an anonymous evaluation pining against a faculty member on social media inevitably impacts their teaching philosophy.

We must put into perspective how, amidst LLM-based writing and lack of enthusiasm towards literary discourses, the space for curiosity and open-ended conversations has been met with mostly symbolic cricket noises with occasional responses from the same set of one or two students, creating almost an unintentional echo chamber. Being viewed only in numbers and in the binary of “would and would not recommend", one can’t help but feel a strange empathy towards fast food joints on review groups oscillating between three and five stars.

Of course, actionable feedback increases academic rigour, but the lack of accountability on anonymous reviews only causes further anxieties for both parties. That being said, it is almost urgent for universities to hold mandatory departmental town hall meetings between the students and the department. A recurring debate amongst students is that university-based teacher and course evaluations are ineffective. At a time when there is a rise in the number of student intakes in private universities, it is, without a doubt, important to have a space for open dialogue between departments and their students. As most evaluations are conducted at the end of the semester, it is also necessary for faculty members to offer anonymous surveys mid-semester to improve and effectively incorporate honest feedback from their classrooms.

Under the constant need to improvise a certain CGPA, it has almost become an archaic culture to pursue the end goal without preparing oneself for challenges. The rising discourse on the effectiveness of higher education providing any value other than climbing the corporate ladder is yet another journey Sisyphus must dread. The tension between the facilitator and the student is not merely dependent on the teacher-student relationship but a larger cultural shift in philosophy surrounding education. Whether one needs to attribute it to lifelong learning is hardly a conversation when the number of graduates is known to be highly dissatisfied with their degrees and their job availability. As a result, the need for a commendable grade requires fast-paced gratification, and without one, the rise of apprehension becomes more targeted towards a person rather than the overall systemic change. Academic camaraderie affects the way we often find difficulties in sustaining a community of trust and effective communication.

The challenge is neither the Facebook groups nor the students, but rather the question of what and how we channel our voices via digitalism. While faculty should seriously reflect on the evaluation comments, it is equally important for the students to create a space to communicate through critical thinking with the determination to not only focus on the teaching skills but also to improvise in curating a better academic culture for the student community.

Regardless of what material the boulder is, Sisyphus must move forward.

Sumaiya Tasnim is a lecturer at the Department of English & Humanities, BRAC University.

title: Is it time to rethink our board exam schedules?
text:
My friend, whose sister is sitting for the Higher Secondary Certificate (HSC) exams in Lama Upazila, Bandarban this year, was growing increasingly anxious as the water from the nearby river reached the entrance of their house. Yet, she still had to think of ways to get to her examination centre while the roads remained submerged. Fortunately, the exam was postponed at the last minute because the situation had deteriorated beyond what could reasonably be managed.

I remember that in June 2024, HSC examinations in Sylhet had to be postponed due to flooding. Even before that, in 2023, the Chittagong Secondary and Higher Secondary Education Board (CSEB) postponed four HSC and equivalent examinations because of floods. There is a pattern here that is unmistakably clear: floods have altered the course of education for lakhs of students across Bangladesh.

The HSC is one of the most important public examinations a student has to sit for, serving as a crucial stepping stone towards their future aspirations. And yet, we seem to be overlooking that some students have to put up with hurdles that others do not, namely, those who simply have the geographical luck of not having their homes flooded.

The problem persists simply because of the time at which the HSC examinations have been scheduled. The schedule changes followed the Covid-19 pandemic and the earlier arrival of Ramadan in the calendar year. But now is the time to rethink the HSC schedule because of the ongoing disruption caused by the incessant rainfall over the past few days, which has triggered flooding in many parts of Bangladesh.

This forced examinees in Cumilla, Bogra, and Noakhali to wade through knee-deep to waist-deep water and take boats and vans to their centres. Students left home early yet struggled to arrive on time. Some were unable to obtain transportation, while others took a motorbike or rickshaw before walking through muddy water. The situation was severe at Comilla Government Women's College, where the entire campus was inundated. Water invaded the buildings, and the road in front was submerged in knee-to-waist-deep water.

The education minister calling the students "farm chickens" only added to their distress. The Inter-Education Board advised students to reach their examination centres well ahead of time, signalling a lack of recognition of those bearing the brunt of the crisis: the students whose futures depend on this examination. Here, the issue of privilege comes into focus because the further one is removed from the hardships of ordinary people, the less one understands their realities.

As this has become a recurring pattern in Bangladesh, with heavy rainfall affecting many key regions of the country every year, how can one of the most important examinations in the country be so casually scheduled during the flood season? Although the education minister has apologised for his remarks, that does not make the problem disappear. The scheduling of key board examinations must be reconsidered to make them more student-friendly.

If annual monsoon flooding continues to disrupt examinations, then the examination calendar must evolve accordingly. Education should not become another casualty of a predictable climate pattern, nor should a student's future depend on whether their home lies on higher ground. Rethinking the Secondary School Certificate (SSC) and HSC schedules is a necessary step towards ensuring equal opportunity for every examinee, regardless of where they live.
