2. The Daily Star (July 14, 2026), HSC examinees take to streets nationwide, demand education minister’s resignation.

3. The Daily Star (July 14, 2026), HSC exams likely to continue under all boards except Chattogram.

4. Dhaka Tribune (July 14, 2026), Education minister regrets remarks amid student protests.

5. Daily Ittefaq (July 14, 2026). The exams will be held as per the routine, Inter-School Education Board advises to reach the center with sufficient time.

6. Prothom Alo (August 13, 2023), Chittagong Board announces new schedule for four postponed HSC exams.

7. Prothom Alo (June 20, 2024), Sylhet division HSC exams postponed until July 8.

title: The privilege that goes into the ‘faaka’ Dhaka discourse
text:
Dhaka, the capital of our country, is the city of dreams for countless people. Yet, it stands on crumbling infrastructure, cramped so tightly you can feel it bursting at its seams. Ranked as the world’s second most populous city, it packs a staggering 36.6 million people into an area of roughly 1,500 square kilometres, according to the United Nations. While it remains a luminous city filled with most of the educational, professional, and career-driven opportunities our country has to offer, from a bird's-eye view, the twinkling lights of Dhaka's nightlife cannot drown out the frustrations of its residents.

Almost every problem of this city can ultimately be boiled down to overpopulation, in my opinion. As the mega-capital, it inevitably attracts people desperate to turn their lives around—whether they are graduates chasing high corporate ambitions or climate refugees seeking shelter in the sprawling slums. You can’t deny that Dhaka has a systematic problem. After all, trying to accommodate people well beyond what the land can offer is utter madness.

Therefore, during any major holiday—especially Eid, when a very big portion of Dhaka’s population leaves for their hometowns—the residents who stay back can’t help but sigh in relief. Suddenly, people are celebrating how nice it is to finally reach their destinations on time. The air feels cleaner as there aren’t many buses on the roads, street vendors aren’t blocking the sidewalks, and you can walk on the footpaths without constantly bumping into people. This is a natural human reaction to getting momentary relief from a constant problem, and it is a thought we have all had at least once in our lives.

Yet, some of us take this opportunity to mock the people who return to their hometowns – “migrants” who are just temporary residents of this city as a means to better their future, by sneering on social media, saying, “Please, don’t come back; Dhaka is finally tolerable.”

This casual cruelty is often targeted towards municipality workers, domestic workers, drivers, guards, rickshaw pullers, and garment workers – mostly people who live hand to mouth. These hard-working individuals are blamed for systemic problems that should instead be solved by urban infrastructure and the decentralisation of opportunities across the country. The distance between the workers leaving to celebrate Eid with their loved ones and a person who does not acknowledge their privilege can be attributed to geographical luck. The privilege of being able to tell someone not to come back, who has no other choice but to come to Dhaka for better opportunities, needs to be scrutinised.

They did not create this trap where you must come to Dhaka for a decent livelihood, only to be forced to leave when you are out of a job. They certainly did not take part in the climate crisis that is pushing rural families to move to the centre of the country. Yet, we often overlook our own privileges when judging others.

After all, when we are done with the festivities of Eid-ul-Adha, the very first thing most of us look for is the municipality workers to clean up the waste, the domestic workers to help with household chores, and the rickshaw pullers to take us to our relatives’ homes so that we can share the joy of Eid with our loved ones. People in Dhaka celebrating Eid depend on the labour (which is often underpaid) of those being ridiculed.

If there is still any doubt that the congestion isn’t solely the fault of the general population, think of the last time you went out with your family in Dhaka during Eid. While the roads are empty, recreational spaces become overcrowded. Because this city lacks sufficient public parks, the few that exist become overwhelmed by the families who stay behind. The city doesn't have the capacity to host its residents even when only half of them are present.

Despite the fact that these festivals fall under national holidays, a huge number of workers still don’t get any vacation days. So, they remain, serving people who are celebrating these meaningful days with their families, and they can’t help but watch on.

As we navigate the empty streets this Eid, smelling the bleach in the air and riding past lonely security guards, we must recognise our own privileges and become a bit kinder. Let us stop treating the workers who keep Dhaka running as background actors in our festive reels and start viewing them as the vital backbone of the metropolis.

Eid Mubarak.

Fabiha likes to yap about her favourite media with people. If you also like to be unhinged about anything, send her your unabridged thoughts at [email protected].

title: Stop taking health advice from AI-generated social media videos
text:
A cartoon garlic clove aggressively scrubbing toxins off of blood vessels. A bright yellow turmeric root polishing the liver. Spinach being dragged across the colon like a sponge wiping everything clean.

You’ve seen these short videos. Everyone has. These AI-generated videos are designed to be oddly satisfying. Clean visuals, simple ideas, and a reassuring sense that health is just a matter of “cleansing” the body the right way. One food, one organ, one problem solved.

But what makes them effective is exactly what makes them misleading. They take real human anatomy and turn it into a cartoon system of dirt and detergents. They replace medical complexity with visual certainty, where turmeric is not a spice with mild anti-inflammatory properties, but a liver “detox tool”, and garlic is not a food with limited cardiovascular associations, but a direct pipe-cleaner for arteries.

As a medical student, one of the lessons you learn in your early years is that the human body seldom behaves in simple, linear ways. There is no single food that “cleans” an organ, no universal detox pathway that can be activated through dietary hacks, and no shortcut that bypasses physiology. Yet, social media thrives on exactly the opposite idea: health is a puzzle with easy answers waiting to be unlocked. It is emotionally entrancing. It gives viewers a sense of control in a system that often feels overwhelming. This is where AI-generated content fits in. It does not just spread misinformation; it packages it in a format that feels intuitive and passively rewires how people understand their own bodies.

The danger today is not only that false health advice exists online, but that it is increasingly being generated at scale by systems that are not accountable to evidence. AI tools can replicate the tone of educational content while stripping away the safeguards of medical accuracy. Combined with animation tools and content templates, this results in a flood of videos that look like simplified medical education but are often detached from clinical reality.

In clinical practice, one pattern physicians notice is that people interpret symptoms through whatever information is most accessible to them at the time. Increasingly, today, that information is coming from short-form social media content rather than trained professionals. A persistent headache becomes “toxins”. Fatigue becomes “deficiency”. Digestive discomfort becomes a “colon cleanse issue”. By the time real medical attention is sought, the narrative has already been shaped, sometimes in ways that delay proper diagnosis. This does not happen because people are careless. It happens because the content is persuasive, visually clear, and emotionally reassuring. It offers certainty where medicine often cannot.

What makes AI-generated health content particularly difficult to challenge is its tone. It sounds confident, structured, and explanatory. In medicine, however, confidence is not the same as facticity. Real clinical guidance is always cautious, conditional, and inherently context-dependent. It does not promise universal fixes because it cannot. But caution does not perform well on social media; certainty does. And so, that certainty gets amplified, even when it is unsupported.

It would be easy to place all responsibility on viewers, but that would be incomplete. Platforms are designed to maximise engagement, not accuracy. AI-generated content is cheap, fast, and scalable. Medical correction is slow, nuanced, and often ignored in algorithmic systems. This creates a structural imbalance: evidence-based medicine competes with content optimised for attention. The result is not just about spreading misinformation but rather about misinformation outperforming information.

The solution is not to disconnect from digital platforms entirely. They are now part of how people learn and communicate. But there needs to be a stronger culture of scepticism when it comes to health content, especially content that feels too simple.

A useful question we can ask ourselves is, does this explanation acknowledge complexity, or does it discard it? Real medicine rarely fits into a single cause-and-effect story. When something claims to do so, it deserves scrutiny.

Equally important is where we choose to get medical understanding from. Not all information sources carry the same weight. Peer-reviewed literature, trained clinicians, and established medical institutions exist for a reason. They are built on systems of validation, emendation, and accountability.

There is an implicit risk in the way health information is evolving online. It is not just that false claims are circulating. It is that the boundary between education and entertainment is blurring. When a cartoon vegetable can convincingly “clean” your colon in 30 seconds, and when that feels more intuitive than actual physiology, we are no longer just dealing with misinformation. We are dealing with a shift in how people understand their own bodies.

Medicine is not a set of visual metaphors nor a collection of easy fixes. It is a discipline where patterns are interpreted through evidence, probability, and clinical judgment rather than certainty or shortcuts. And the more we replace that complexity with algorithm-friendly simplicity, the further we drift from what a genuine understanding of health is supposed to be.

Purna is a fourth-year medical student at Sirajganj Medical College. You can reach her at [email protected].

title: Kodom always reminded me of her
text:
It was raining when we met. Not the gentle rain where mothers worry about their cherished children catching a cold, nor the drizzle that encourages high school students to escape mundane classes to crowd the neighbourhood khichuri stalls.

Indeed, it was raining as if the sky had just lost its mother. The grief of the clouds had emptied the streets – no rickshaw-turned-half-coloured plastic carriage drifted by; no passerby rushed for sanctuary. There was only the pitch-black, uneven wet road.

Yet I sat, accompanied by a scrawny, scarred tomcat, nestled comfortably on the cold steel bench, under a bus stop, barely safe from the needles of water. I studied the dusty, oat-coloured furball. He bore a missing ear and two defining lacerations across his nose – an asymmetrical cross. If scars are the medals of the feline world, he was a decorated general, perhaps a veteran of the “Great Trash Bin Wars”, silently lecturing the youth on the art of survival. Maybe he nods with his whiskers and starts his sentence with “Back in my days…”

"BOOM!" A transformer nearby burst, showering orange-blue sparks. The veteran hissed, which sounded more like a curse, and bolted, leaving me alone with my thoughts.

That’s when she arrived under the bus stop, panting but not tired.

For a long time, I have wondered what she wore that day. Did she wear a short, block-printed kurti and flared jeans? Or was she draped in something more traditional? A vibrant salwar kameez or a navy-blue saree? The memory refuses to sharpen.

The only thing I remember is her vivacity – the way her face sparked with excitement and a hint of mischief, completely unbothered by the ruined kajal streaming down her cheeks like dark tears.

“Good heavens! What a treacherous downpour! And to think the weather report promised a gentle breeze and soft sun – perfect for an outing!”

With no one on the side, I came to the conclusion that, indeed, her rhetoric was directed towards me. Hence, I reluctantly replied, “Why not? You don’t like the rain?”

“Quite the contrary! I hate the Sun," she said, wiping the rain from her chin. "I hate how bright it is. I hate how it makes me feel like a drought, as if it is sucking the life essence out of me. Come now! Don’t laugh!"

I didn’t laugh. In fact, her words made perfect sense to me. I shifted on the bench to make room for her. She didn't hesitate. She took the spot where the scarred cat had been sitting moments ago.

The air around us shifted. The smell of ozone from the burnt transformer mingled with the scent of her – damp cotton, rain, and the faint, sweet trace of Arabian jasmine.

"I’m not laughing," I said. My voice was barely audible over the rain. "The sun can be... demanding."

She looked at me, surprised I agreed. She began to wring out water from the end of her orna.

"Exactly. It demands that you be happy. It demands that you be seen. The rain is different. It allows you to release emotions you’ve bottled up.”

"How so?" I asked.

"People like us," she said with a faint smile playing on her lips. "We can’t ever cry without scrutiny. But in the rain? In the rain, you can let the sky's tears mix with yours without judgment."

I had no reply to that.

"So, are you waiting for any bus? Or someone else?"

"I don't think either will arrive," I replied as I nodded toward the road, which had become a river of black oil. Truth is, I had forgotten why I was there. Perhaps I was merely a wanderer of my own thoughts, jumping from one lane of consciousness to another, waiting for the rain to wash away the solitude.

“And what brings you here?” I asked.

“I was supposed to meet two of my friends," she said, as I watched a droplet trace her jawline. “They cancelled at the last minute.”

“Do you know what their excuse was? Well, not that it matters anymore…” She paused before continuing again, “But I couldn't let my makeup go to waste. So, stubbornly, I came out, and gosh! What a rain!" She grinned, and for a heartbeat, the grey gloom of the shelter burned brighter than any noon sun.

However, something in her tone revealed that she was expecting her friends to leave her alone anyway, that she had prepared herself to be the only traveller in the rain, and that she was determined to find solace in solitude with a stranger.

That was when she proposed we go collect kodom. Having nothing to lose but the dull sanctuary we were perched under, I agreed.

Why kodom? I have revisited her reply a thousand times in the library of my memory.

“Because it represents the resilient soul that only reveals its true fragrance when the world is weeping.”

Her voice was the only competition against the roar of the wind.

We waded through the rising water, our footsteps heavy and rhythmic. We jumped over a widening puddle that had become a small lake, our laughter lost to the thunder. She slipped once, her hand clutching onto my arm for balance. And for a second, the world narrowed down to the scent of her glistening, wet hair and the shivering reality of another person.

We found a tree near the edge of a muddy park. Its branches were sagging under the weight of the monsoon.

When she reached for a low-hanging branch, her fingers trembled slightly from the cold. "Look at them," she whispered. They only bloom when the world is at its most violent, when the sky is breaking apart. They are the reward for enduring the storm."

I helped her steady the branch, my hand brushing against hers – a brief, electric contact that felt warmer than the July air. I pulled down a cluster of flowers. The rough, wet bark grazed my palm.

As we stood there, we were drenched to the bone, holding the heavy, spherical blooms.

She handed me a kodom. The kodom flowers had a hue ranging from the spectrum of yellow to orange, almost like nature's ping-pong ball, armoured with white filaments.

“There is only one thing I hate about kodom, though. Can you guess?” She asked and handed me a second kodom.

“How quickly it wilts and turns from a sweet scent to a pungent, earthy decay?”

“Bingo!” She handed me the third one as the pour thinned to a drizzle. The hum of the city began to bleed back in. A lone rickshaw bell tinkled in the distance, such a metallic, lonely sound!

“One for me, one for you.” Suddenly, her voice dropped to a conspiratorial whisper. She paused and peered at my palm. Maybe she foresaw the decay of the kodoms.

“The third is for the distance. The space that grows when the rain stops and we go back to being people who don't know each other.”

The temporary sanctuary of the bus stop was dissolving; the "Great Trash Bin Veteran" would soon return to claim his bench, and the world would forget we had ever met.

“I should go,” she said. She didn't offer a name, and I didn't ask for a promise.

And then she vanished into the grey concrete urban crowd, where she blurred and became nothing but the flicker of a damp candle.

Nostalgia is a strange rot. It doesn’t smell of decay at first; it smells of July rain and wet earth. But as the years pass, the sweetness turns heavier. It ferments into something that sits at the back of the throat.

I realise now that she was right to leave.

Had we stayed, we would have become the sun to each other: demanding, bright, and exhausting. Instead, we remained the kodom: a brief, moody bloom that only the storm was allowed to remember.

Mueen Walee Maheer is an aspiring polymath who is currently a master of none but a fan of many. Send him a new obsession at [email protected].

title: The piper’s solace
text:
On most evenings at our colony, we experienced an hour-long power cut. Like other city children in those days, we considered it a break rather than a hazard. We siblings, along with our parents and grandma, would sit on our big bed or on the floor of our wide inner balcony to talk and share our experiences of the day. Sometimes our elders would entertain us with interesting stories; sometimes my elder sisters would sing new songs which they had learnt from their music teacher that weekend.

Grandma mostly told us her childhood memories. The most interesting thing about her storytelling was that it was always in the present tense. But we enjoyed it anyway. She also told us stories from her little collection of storybooks. One such summer evening, I was lying down with grandma on the sheetol paati that was spread on our big bed. The sheetol paati was laid out on a bed or the floor to keep them cool in the summer. Other members of my family were sitting on the balcony and talking.

We all longed for it to rain. It was too hot. Grandma kept fanning me with her haatpakha and began preparing to open Thakurmar Jhuli (it was indeed a jhuli full of repeated stories) on request. Then a tune reached my ears, breaking the sultry darkness. It seemed to come from the other side of the wall, which separated our colony from a series of go-downs.

Someone was playing the bamboo flute. The melodious tune that emanated from the flute seemed so natural and lyrical. Even Grandma stopped fanning for some time and started to listen in silence. The flute threw off soft, sweet notes with a melancholy tune all over the place. I laid there, speechless, without any motion. The piper was playing with the tunes so effortlessly, pouring out all his emotions. It touched my little mind so deeply that I can still recall every detail of it.

Only a heart full of pain can play like that.

Each note floated in the air, as if to reach the passionate listener to share the story of his life. The life that he had left behind in a faraway village that was green and beautiful. There, he had a loving family, a group of caring and playful friends, or someone special. When I closed my eyes, I could imagine him running through the fields with a big bright kite with paper patches glued on to the torn parts, playing danguli with his dear friends, crossing the river, and sharing steaming hot rice with his siblings. In sickness and in happiness, his parents were his sanctuary.

On stormy nights, he perhaps filled up baskets with mangoes, the ones that came undone because of the storm, and it brought him incomparable joy. On bright sunny mornings, he might have sat on the edge of the canal with a makeshift fishing pole and it did the same.

All these vibrant memories were so fondly cherished in his heart. Each season in the village served him with its offering. Kobi gaan, paala gaan, nouka baich, and melas must have filled his young heart with the joy of belonging. It all moulded his life into a simple yet content one. Giving up these entities he was fond of, he left for the unseen and unknown to earn a living.

After a hard day at work, leaning against the concrete wall, he picked up his only precious possession – his flute, his solace. He tried to make peace with his city life in vain. He played it not to beg for those he longed for, but to impart to the listener the pain and emptiness he felt. When it ended, it was hard to get over that heart-touching, melancholic tune. The next morning, though I knew that it was sheer foolishness, I stood on the balcony looking for my bashiwala.

Monica Margaret Gomes is an English literature and language teacher.

title: Sweet in the palm of your hands
text:
There is a certain category of person I tend to dislike. I refer to individuals who possess a notable inability to exist in a state of rest. They are precisely incapable of lying still for over half a second without the thought of some form of routine hanging in the corners of their minds at all times. In general, these are also the types of people who enjoy being dictators in every situation, and will usually go out of their way to do so.

My acquaintance with Parveen Apa was initiated almost five years ago. I was appointed as a private-duty nurse at Mrs Aleya Khatun’s residence to look after her ill mother. She was a bedridden patient suffering from third-stage lung cancer and paralysis, and required 24-hour surveillance. There, I worked alongside Parveen Aktar, who was my rotational caregiver.

Back then, I was a third-year nursing student studying at a lesser-known private college in Dhaka. When financial constraints at home took a grotesque turn after the death of my father, the sole income source of the household, I was bound to survive on my own. Initially, I had considered working part-time shifts as a patient caregiver, along with a handful of tuitions I was already running, so a distant relative of mine put me in contact with a service-providing agency. But they told me that part-time duties were more demanding. More people want them. As such, I had to perform full-time shifts for a couple of months to start with, before they handed me part-time duties.

“How old are you? You look so young.”

“Twenty-two.”

“Ah! The age of my knee. How much are they paying you?”

“Twenty-one thousand. This is my first shift.”

“That much? And you are new? They didn’t pay us half that amount when we first started out,” she said in a complaining tone. “I have been doing this for six years in a row now.”

“Apa, my shift here is that of a junior nurse. I have almost completed my diploma. You are working as a general attendant. Payments are likewise.”

I think I almost caught her rolling her eyebrows before she turned away.

This was my first interaction with Parveen Aktar, and I wouldn’t necessarily say it had been the most pleasant of starters. Nevertheless, we settled our belongings in a fairly empty guest room beside the patient’s, where there were no beds, so both of us had to share a mattress on the floor. I remember the first two weeks had gone by more or less comfortably, and I was beginning to get a grasp of what I was doing rather well. Or so I had thought.

Perhaps it was on one of the weekends that the helping hand of the house, Laizu, was absent from work. I woke up slightly later than usual that morning, and as I came out of my room, Parveen Apa was already awake. In fact, she was mopping the dining area.

“What are you doing, Apa?” I asked in surprise.

“Oh, nothing. Laizu called a while ago and said she has a third-degree fever and cannot get out of bed. Meanwhile, this is the condition of the house. Look! Yesterday also, she left early with some excuse.”

It was quite strange to me that Laizu had Apa’s number, as she most certainly did not have mine. Frankly, that was the first time I had realised I hadn’t really had a conversation with any of the several people coming and going around the house every day. Most of my time I would spend caring for my patient, and any spare time I got, I would utilise it to study or nap. Parveen Apa, though, was the opposite.

As days passed, certain things in my sight started to shift. I began to notice how she had spent the greater fraction of her time working in the kitchen and attending to visitors while I nursed Aleya Khatun’s mother. Soon enough, major household decisions also fell under her authority. Matters such as what to serve for lunch, weekly grocery purchases, and even the allocation of household chores — responsibilities that had previously been overseen by the mistress of the house, who lived abroad and could only be reached by phone.

As I mentioned earlier, I was barely able to form a bond with anyone around, as I had thought it to be unnecessary. She, on the other hand, had sturdy relationships with everyone, starting from their driver Rafiq Uddin to the caretaker of the building. I think I even caught sight of her chatting with the gardener of one of the flat owners once or twice.

The cause of my annoyance was not solely directed by the fact that she was no longer attending to her patient as much, which meant that I had to do her part of the job on top of mine, but it was also because I repeatedly failed to make sense of the entire situation. My irritation grew to the point where I thought it would have been better if she had sat idle instead and not done anything at all. She had remained occupied with some chore or the other throughout the day, even beyond the ones assigned to her.

After a while, I resigned myself to the arrangement. By then, it became apparent that she had been successful in establishing herself as the indispensable intermediary of the household, and frequently positioned herself as the point of contact for various informal matters. Gradually, this resulted in a shift wherein others began to rely on her judgement or presence for major-to-minor decisions and assistance involving their personal lives.

Later, it became quite evident to me that she was getting tipped a greater amount outside of contract, which I was not. Surprisingly enough, I did not mind. Before the company had transferred me elsewhere, I often pondered whether she was previously involved in any form of managerial position, though I hadn’t had the chance to ask her that question. I never saw Parveen Aktar again.

title: Sins of the blameless
text:
Vile minds supporting the depraved souls

Suffering in a world where the victims get blamed, and the tainted hearts get praised

Exploitation of women's bodies rises like a growing monster,

Yet the demon is worshipped in the same land where girls are covered with the blanket of insults

Accusations arise for what they wear, where they go, to crumple our thoughts

But when a child is violated, why does society's verbose mouth stop?

Child marriages occur for the safety of girls instead of the blooming flowers of love

But when a married woman gets assaulted, what alibis are they going to shove?

In the name of protection, the female body and mind have been caged in the four walls of the house

But when the cage itself is filled with lustful creatures, how are they going to save us then?

title: Sorceress
text:
By the flickering stove,

blue potion jars

cradling in-between worn-out fingers

swivelling amidst cracks of skin

meld into warmth.

By the stirring ladle,

blue potion jars

tucked underneath hollow armpit spaces

slipping between stitches of a tattered blouse piece

stream into liquid.

By the brewing cauldron,

blue potion jars

spilled into spread mud vessels

scent of warm coconut

waft through the air.

By the old sorceress,

who plaits my hair

stretched fingers pressing against desert scalp

drenched roots untangled tufts

threaded back.

By the silence that moulds,

my drowsy head rested onto her laps

drift into time

until the snug melts away

like blue potion jars.

title: When time stands still
text:
At first glance, you would not notice that I live in a fragile prison, a home with two bulbs of glass pinched at the throat, sand forever descending. Inside, I walk on grains as fine as dust, pale gold that shifts beneath my weight. No matter how much I gather into my hands, the sand slips through my fingers, scattered by the smallest breath of movement.

I have always measured myself by time, not in the softness of moments but in the speed of them. I am the child who ran before she could walk, the student who devoured lessons meant for later years, the woman who leans into tomorrow before today has even finished. To be ahead of the curve is not just ambition; it has become my rhythm. My eyes are rarely fixed in the present; they are drawn instead to the narrow passage where sand rushes through, to what comes next, to what I must achieve sooner rather than later.

So, when he steps into my hourglass the very first time, the impossible occurs: the sand halts mid-air. The falling grains suspend themselves in light, glittering as though a thousand stars were scattered between us. Time, once relentless, stills in anticipation. The urgency I have always carried, the need to be faster, better, and further, dissolves into something weightless.

He is not a clock or the hand that turns it. He is the light that refracts through the glass, bending the hours into strange, beautiful shapes. Where once I saw nothing but a relentless funnel, I now see colours dancing on each grain, hues that only appear when illuminated by him. I was so busy counting the sand before it even fell that I never thought to just watch how it descends.

Inside the glass walls of my hourglass, I have always felt the inevitability of decline, yet I never realised that even falling is beautiful. The sand between my fingers has meaning as it slips through: each grain is precious because each grain can hold him. It would be easy to say that he stops the hourglass entirely, but it would not be true. Each grain lingers longer before falling, each second swells into a full breath, and the hourglass does not stop; it slows just enough for me to pause.

My home grows beyond the hourglass; time stops becoming my enemy; it is no longer a race. It is a companion, and like all companions, it requires attention. To love the present, to dream of the future without regretting the past. He exists in this very moment, and so, if I want to be with him, I must exist here too.

Your time is only well spent if it is traced to the feelings you share with the ones that make it meaningful. For the first time, I understand that it is not meant to be outrun; it is meant to be lived.

So, we remain here, where sand is suspended like stars around me, light refracting across the glass. I am alright with staying still. I do not always have to run to conquer or to achieve. The hourglass flips over and over. I do not notice. I am simply here.

Tinath Zaeba is an optimistic daydreamer, a cat mom of 5 and a student of Economics at North South University. Get in touch via mailing to [email protected]

title: Letter from my dead grandmother
text:
My grandma died an unnatural death at the age of seventy-five. During a certain period preceding her passing, she was seized by delirium, exhibiting delusions, agitation, and a persistent mistrust of her surroundings. She had likely succumbed to their effects. Collective effort was underway to convince her to seek treatment. Though it was quite a difficult task, as she had been ruthless. The following letter was composed during this interval and must therefore be read with utmost caution and is not to be taken seriously at all costs. I subsequently destroyed the original, as its continued existence would have invited misinterpretation and unnecessary familial discord at the time.

Rashamoni,

It is unfortunate that your foremost thought of me involves that of a rotten steel almirah, though I will not fabricate the fact that I am only somewhat disheartened. I can almost picture you rummaging through the corners of my jam-packed drawers stacked with worn-out property papers and copies of old passport-sized photographs; bear in mind, however, that the object of your search is not to be found here.

By virtue of my untimely demise, it appears that I have all of a sudden been promoted, quite without my consent, to somewhat the rank of a posthumous enigma. I could go on and on, shedding dust upon the hypocrisy that exists to favour the hospitality of the dead. But rest assured, dear daughter, as this letter is neither about me nor is it about my former legacy and what it may have translated to your father and his three brothers.

Throughout the entirety of my existence, I leave behind me, of value, two things: a waning passion for over-steeped tea and a reputation for saying all of the wrong things at the right time. You will hear many versions of me now.

Listen carefully, Rasha. The bundle of keys that hangs beneath the broken picture frame must be stashed aside before the disputes warm up, as they shall inevitably arise in a day or two. I assume you have already done so. Next, attend to the bedside table in front of the lamp shade. Dispose of the medicines that are no longer fit for use and retain the remainder in a single container (you may return them to the pharmacy for recompense, on the express condition that you make no inquiry into the prescriptions). All loose papers are to be destroyed, with the exception of those bearing signatures, which must be stapled together and filed away. These matters are strictly outside of your concern; hence, do as I say and refrain from further intervention.

Rasha! You shall not visit my grave, and you shall not mourn my death. Your uncle Subodh should arrive at any given moment, draped in a shawl of pretentious grief and smelling of cheap naphthalene. He will proceed to lament about what I was and what I had become for about a good hour. Poor child, let him have this one. I do have a somewhat wicked reputation after I told Subodh to his face that his freelancing ventures did not, in fact, constitute a real profession, and that he might as well consider attending to my weekly chores and groceries, and chasing after tenants for rent. I could even fire Sobuj, the poor boy runs to the bazar five times a day. Huh! He has been a victim of my malicious torment for long enough, I think.

And by the way, how is Sabuj now? Shed a tear or two, no? Oh, I’m sure he's thanking God plenty that he need not pay back the ten thousand I lent him months ago. I had almost turned it into a ritual to make sure to remind him of it once every two weeks; you should have seen the look on the boy’s face turn all red and bashful. Rasha, why do I enjoy the feeling of standing superior to others so much?

Anyway, Robin, how about him? Note down my words, he will end up marrying that office peon’s daughter, despite my forbiddance, and both of them would eventually hang upon your shoulders like haunting ghosts. Ah, the weight of inherited burden! Have a great time figuring out means to get rid of them, child (spoiler: you can’t).

Now, since all roads lead back to land and locks, let us return to the matter that first summoned you to my drawers like a pilgrim to a shrine. You may rest your clever head: the house, the accounts, the parcels of stubborn earth that have outlived three governments and five family feuds — they have not been left to chance. I am not so careless in death as I was accused of being in life.

Nearly everything that bears my name has already been loosened from it and stitched, quietly and without ceremony, into yours. This, however, is not knowledge you are to parade. You will keep it as one keeps contraband. For a time, you must play the fool and wear ignorance as though it were mourning. Let them quarrel over cupboards and speculate over deeds. Let them weigh my memory like meat in the market. You will say nothing.

For reasons beyond my understanding, Rasha, I do love you dearly, I always have, even after all that you have done. Do not mistake my love for generosity, however. Property is a form of revenge, and I have chosen its shape carefully.

Even as I write, I can imagine your fingers already blackened with dust, tugging at folders, hoping paper might confess what blood will not. You look for land before you look for me. You search for signatures before you search for sense. Do not pretend otherwise. You are no different from the rest of them. I spared you the noise of my contempt while I lived. Death, it seems, has freed my tongue.

Farewell,

Didamoni

Titir uses the art of storytelling as an excuse to give life to her fantasies in the form of hideous characters. Find her at [email protected].

title: Names written on lists
text:
My father used to tell me

Remember that you are human

Even as the world tries its best to erase you

With rote headlines, indifference, and silence



So, I write my name in fading ink

Everywhere I can reach

On cracked walls, broken doors, inside my wrists

If—no, when—I disappear

Someone would know I was here



My hands are busy counting the dead

Yet I still dream of a place

Where the sky is never angry

And bread is always soft

A world where names are not written on lists

Nor mispronounced in the news

title: AdBlitz Season 9 by Ingenious Marketing Club crowns its Champion
text:
The Ingenious Marketing Club (IMC) of the University of Asia Pacific (UAP) concluded the ninth edition of its flagship ad-making competition, AdBlitz Season 9, presented by YC Bangladesh, with the Grand Finale held on October 12 at the UAP Auditorium.

The competition offered a total prize pool of BDT 1,00,000, with the Champion receiving BDT 50,000, the 1st Runner-Up receiving BDT 30,000, and the 2nd Runner-Up receiving BDT 20,000.

This season saw an overwhelming response, with over 250 participants from about 27 universities competing in the first round. From this pool, 10 finalist teams were shortlisted to advance to the Grand Finale, where they presented their advertising concepts live before a panel of judges, followed by a Q&A session.

The event was judged by a distinguished panel comprising Shazneen Tabassum (Campaign Marketing Specialist, Optimizely); Md Jafar Imam (Managing Director and CEO, Union BD Consumer Limited); Mahmudul Hasan Zisha (Head of Marketing, PRAN-RFL Group); Turas Ayman (Director, Analyzen); and Salman Ahmed (Brand Custodian, Nextjobz).

The event was graced by Farzana Elahi, Head of the Department, School of Business, UAP, and Helal Uddin, COO of Union BD Consumer Limited, along with faculty members of UAP. Also present were the club's two advisors – Mily Akter, Lecturer, School of Business, UAP, and Dr GM Shafayet Ullah, Assistant Professor, School of Business, UAP, as well as Mohammed Rakiv, Acting Director of the Directorate of Students' Welfare (DSW), UAP.

Balushai Duo from Army IBA, Savar, was crowned the Champion. Charizard from East West University secured the 1st Runner-Up position, while A24Buddha, a joint team from UAP and BRAC University, secured the 2nd Runner-Up position.

Since its inception, AdBlitz has grown into one of the most anticipated marketing and advertising-focused events among university students in Bangladesh, offering a platform for young minds to showcase their creativity, strategic thinking, and marketing acumen through real-world ad-making challenges.

title: Fourth SQAT Bangladesh to be held on December 5
text:
The fourth SQAT Bangladesh, Symposium on “Software QA & Testing” to be held on December 5, 2026, at Sheraton Dhaka, bringing together professionals, industry leaders, academics, policymakers, and international experts from the Software Quality, QA & Testing ecosystem. This year’s theme is “Quality in the Age of AI”.

A key highlight of the symposium will be the participation of Dr Klaudia Dussa-Zieger, Global President of the International Software Testing Qualifications Board (ISTQB), and Mr Olivier Denoo, former Global President of ISTQB. They will be joined by leading software quality experts, engineering and quality leaders, Chief Information Officers (CIO)/Chief Technology Officers (CTO), technology professionals, policymakers, and academics.

The symposium is organised by the Bangladesh Software Testing Board (BSTB). Daffodil International University is the Academic Partner, while iSQI (International Software Quality Institute) is the Exam and WBT Partner.

The full-day programme will feature global experts’ masterclasses, keynotes, plenary sessions, AI testing, test automation, quality engineering, professional networking, certification, and career insights.

Dr M NuruzZaman, President of BSTB, said: “Software quality is becoming even more important in the age of AI. Our goal is to connect skills, certification, employment, and global market opportunities within one strong ecosystem.”

title: Roundtable at SMUCT calls for collective action on violence against women across borders
text:
Scholars and development practitioners from Bangladesh and abroad gathered at Shanto-Mariam University of Creative Technology (SMUCT) in Uttara on October 17, 2026, for an international roundtable discussion on “Violence Against Women & Transnational Feminism Across the Borders”, examining the many forms of violence women face at home and abroad, including technology-facilitated gender-based violence (TFGBV) in the context of the July Revolution. The event was organised by the Department of English of the university with support from Women Living Under Muslim Laws (WLUML), an international solidarity network of women’s rights advocates and researchers.

Vice-Chancellor Prof. Dr Sha-E-Alam attended as a guest and shared his views on the topic. He said universities must do more than produce knowledge and should work to create safe, respectful and inclusive spaces, both on campus and online. Prof. Dr Syed Azizul Huq, Dean of the Faculty of Humanities and Social Science, was also present.

Among the speakers were Homa Hoodfar, Prof. Emerita at Concordia University and founder of WLUML; Mona Tajali, Lecturer at Stanford University and executive board member of WLUML; Summer Forester, Associate Professor at Carleton College; and Afra Jalabi, Affiliate Assistant Professor at Concordia University. Md Shahrear Talukder, Associate Professor and Head of the Department of English, SMUCT, facilitated the discussion. Speakers from Khulna University, BRAC University, and East West University also took part. Faculty members and students from different departments of SMUCT attended and shared their views.

Speakers discussed violence in its many forms, including domestic abuse, sexual harassment, workplace discrimination, economic exclusion and political intimidation, and noted that stigma, weak enforcement of laws and limited access to justice leave many survivors without redress. They also examined why women lag behind in politics, business, education and public service, citing unpaid care work, safety concerns, unequal access to resources and deep-rooted stereotypes.

A major part of the discussion focused on the women who took to the streets during the July Revolution. Speakers said that many of them, after being celebrated as symbols of courage, are now facing online smear campaigns, doxxing, moral policing, threats and the circulation of manipulated images on social media. They said such attacks are meant to silence women, discourage others from joining public life, and erase their role in the movement. Summing up, Md Shahrear Talukder said the July Revolution showed both the strength of women’s participation and the vulnerability that follows it. He said academic forums can turn lived experience into research, and research into ideas that communities and institutions can act upon.

Participants called for stronger and survivor-centred legal and reporting mechanisms, responsible moderation by technology companies, gender-sensitive education from an early age, greater political representation for women, and the engagement of men and boys as allies. They also urged that cases be documented ethically, protecting the privacy and agency of survivors.

Panellists agreed that violence against women and the barriers to their advancement do not stop at national borders, so the response must also be transnational, while remaining grounded in local realities. The session ended with a question-and-answer round with students and researchers. As the discussion closed, speakers said true democracy and justice remain incomplete until women can walk the streets, enter parliament and speak online without fear, and the organisers expressed hope for continued collaboration with international partners towards that goal.

title: International Conference on Computing Advancement held at AIUB
text:
The fourth International Conference on Computing Advancement (ICCA 2026), organised by the Department of Computer Science, American International University-Bangladesh (AIUB), was held between October 15 and 16, 2026. The two-day international conference brought together researchers, scientists, academics, and technology experts from Bangladesh and abroad to exchange knowledge, discuss recent advancements in computing technologies, and explore emerging innovations. Participants also presented their research findings across a wide range of computing-related disciplines.

This year, ICCA 2026 received more than 900 research paper submissions from 17 countries, of which 214 papers were selected for presentation after rigorous review. The selected papers featured research contributions from Bangladesh and 17 other countries, including the United States, the United Kingdom, Australia, Japan, and Canada. The conference covered key areas of computing and technological innovation, including artificial intelligence (AI), machine learning, the Internet of Things (IoT), cybersecurity, data science, and blockchain technology.

The inaugural ceremony was attended by Ishtiaque Abedin, Founder Member and Vice Chairman of the Board of Trustees of AIUB and Secretary General of the Association of Private Universities of Bangladesh (APUB), as the chief guest. The event was also attended by Dr Carmen Z Lamagna, former Vice-Chancellor of AIUB and a member of the Board of Trustees; Prof. Dr Saiful Islam, Vice-Chancellor of AIUB; Prof. Dr Dip Nandi, Dean of the Faculty of Science and Technology (FST) and Programme Chair of the conference; Prof. Dr Khandaker Tabin Hasan, Associate Dean of FST and General Chair of the conference; and Prof. Dr Md Abdur Razzaque, Chairperson of the Department of Computer Science and Engineering (CSE) at Dhaka University.

The closing ceremony, held on October 16, was graced by Dr Hasanul A Hasan, Founder Member and Chairman of the Board of Trustees, AIUB, as the chief guest. Nadia Anwar, Founder Member, Board of Trustees of AIUB; Prof. Dr Md Abdur Rahman, Pro Vice-Chancellor of AIUB; Prof. Dr Manzur H Khan, Proctor of AIUB; deans; associate deans; and other senior university officials were also present at the ceremony.

During the closing ceremony, certificates and commemorative mementoes were presented to the organisers and participants in recognition of their contributions and participation in the conference.

ICCA 2026 provided a valuable platform for knowledge exchange, academic engagement, and international networking.

The conference is expected to strengthen international collaboration, encourage interdisciplinary research, and create new opportunities for joint research initiatives among academics, researchers, and technology professionals worldwide. Through this initiative, AIUB reaffirmed its commitment to promoting research excellence, fostering innovation, and expanding global collaboration in computing and technology.

title: Nine-member Bangladesh team to participate in international geography olympiad in Russia
text:
A nine-member delegation from Bangladesh is set to participate in the “Multinational Youth Geography Olympiad (MY-GEO) 2026”, scheduled to take place from October 24 to 31 in the Sirius Federal Territory, near Sochi, Russia.

Image

The Bangladesh team consists of five students: Minhajul Islam Tahmid of Birshreshtha Munshi Abdur Rouf Public College, Shahriar Noor of Government Science College, Md Tawsikul Islam of Agrani School and College in Rajshahi, Arifa Atiq Mim of Netrokona Government College, and Tanvir Sadat of Notre Dame College. Three team leaders—Md Ayman Mahmud and Taseen Mohammad from Dhaka the University, and Ferdous Ahmed from BRAC University—will be accompanying the students as team leaders. The delegation will also be joined by Ahnaf Tahmid Uddin of BRAC University as the team observer.

The team will join students from BRICS member states and other participating countries. The olympiad is designed for students aged 15 to 18 and covers a wide range of subjects, including physical and human geography, environmental management, climate change, natural resources, and sustainable regional development. It is an international competition focused on geographical knowledge, analytical thinking, and practical problem-solving.

Six students selected through team selection test

Zero Competitions announced the Bangladesh delegation on October 10, 2026. The students were selected through a Team Selection Test (TST) held at the Russian House in Dhaka. The assessment evaluated geographical knowledge, analytical reasoning, and the ability to approach and solve unfamiliar problems.

The delegation's participation is being coordinated by Zero Competitions Limited and the Sustainability and Life Sciences Network (SLSN), with cooperation from the Russian House and Dhaka University.

MY-GEO competition breakdown

MY-GEO 2026 will feature three main rounds: theoretical, multimedia, and practical. Each round will examine different aspects of geographical understanding and the ability to apply scientific knowledge.

The theoretical round will cover topics such as physical geography, human and economic geography, environmental systems, climate change, and regional development. Students will be required to analyse geographical situations and develop reasoned responses rather than simply reproduce memorised information.

In the multimedia round, participants will work with maps, satellite imagery, statistical datasets, and other geographical materials. They will be expected to interpret the information, identify geographical patterns, and draw conclusions from the evidence presented.

The practical round will involve field observations in and around Sirius and the Black Sea coast. Participating teams will collect geographical information, analyse their findings, prepare maps, and develop proposals addressing regional development challenges.

The competition will be conducted in English. Alongside individual knowledge and reasoning, teamwork and collaborative problem-solving will play an important role.

Educational activities alongside the competition

The event will be hosted in the Sirius Federal Territory, located along Russia's Black Sea coast near the Caucasus Mountains. Sirius is known for its educational and scientific institutions, including the Sirius Educational Center and Sirius University. The area has developed into a centre for academic, scientific, and technological activities.

In addition to the competition rounds, participants will have opportunities to attend educational sessions, scientific lectures, and workshops on topics such as Geographic Information Systems (GIS), remote sensing, environmental conservation, and regional development.

These activities will also allow students to interact with participants, researchers, and specialists from different countries. Accommodation and meals for participating students and eligible team leaders will be arranged by the host organisers, while international travel expenses will remain the responsibility of the sending side.

Bangladesh Geography Olympiad to be held annually

Alongside Bangladesh's participation in MY-GEO 2026, efforts are underway to establish a regular national platform for students interested in geography and geology.

The Bangladesh Geography Olympiad (BGeO) will be organised annually from now on, providing opportunities for school and college students to explore geography, geology, and related Earth sciences. The initiative aims to encourage greater student engagement with these subjects and expand opportunities for participation in international geography and Earth science competitions.

Information about future editions of BGeO, including registration details and announcements, will be available through the olympiad's official Facebook page and the communication channels of Zero Competitions and SLSN.

For the selected students, MY-GEO 2026 will provide an opportunity to test their knowledge alongside peers from other countries and experience different approaches to geographical problem-solving.

The field-based activities and analytical challenges are expected to offer practical exposure to geographical research, spatial analysis, and environmental studies.

The experience may also help participating students develop a broader understanding of how geography is studied and applied beyond the classroom.

With the competition approaching, the Bangladeshi delegation is preparing to represent the country in an international academic event that combines geographical knowledge, scientific investigation, and cultural exchange.

title: NSU celebrates 20 Years of pharmaceutical sciences with ICPS 2026 and Pharma Fest
text:
North South University (NSU) concluded the International Conference on Pharmaceutical Sciences (ICPS 2026) and the 13th season of City Bank Presents Pharma Fest 2026, co-powered by ZEEHO CFMOTO, on October 12, marking the 20th anniversary of NSU’s Department of Pharmaceutical Sciences. The three-day conference brought together academics and researchers from 11 countries, with 30 international speakers, researchers and investigators participating in discussions on pharmaceutical innovation and global health. The festival showcased students’ knowledge, creativity and engagement with sustainability through various academic and extracurricular competitions.

The closing ceremony featured Rabbur Reza, Chief Operating Officer of Beximco Pharmaceuticals PLC, as chief guest. Prof. Abdul Hannan Chowdhury, Vice-Chancellor of NSU, chaired the session. Other distinguished guests included Professor Mohammad Hossain Shariare, Chairman of the Department of Pharmaceutical Sciences and Conference Chair; Dr Nusaibah Abdul Rahim, Dean of the Faculty of Pharmacy, Universiti Malaya, Malaysia, and Conference Co-chair; Professor Dr Dipak Kumar Mitra, Dean of the School of Health and Life Sciences, NSU; and Professor Nasar U. Ahmed, Pro Vice-Chancellor of NSU.



In his address, Rabbur Reza emphasised that the value of pharmaceutical innovation lay in its ability to reach people and improve lives. He said, “The true measure of any innovation, discovery or research lies in three questions: Who can afford it? Who can access it? And whose life can it change? Medicine is not just about scientific sophistication; it is about how many lives we can improve and how many people we can reach.”

Professor Abdul Hannan Chowdhury expressed his gratitude to the participants and organisers, noting the conference's international reach. He said, “I sincerely thank all participants, organisers and contributors. The representation of 11 countries and participation of 30 international speakers, researchers and investigators have made ICPS 2026 a valuable platform for global academic collaboration and scientific exchange.”

The program also featured addresses by Conference Chair Professor Mohammad Hossain Shariare, Conference Co-chair Dr Nusaibah Abdul Rahim, and Special Guests Professor Dr Dipak Kumar Mitra and Professor Nasar U. Ahmed. Adit Muktadir Pavel, Faculty Advisor of the North South University Pharmaceutical Club (NSUPC), delivered the vote of thanks. The ceremony concluded with the distribution of awards to the winners of the conference and festival competitions, followed by a cultural program.

Organised by the North South University Pharmaceutical Club (NSUPC) in collaboration with the Department of Pharmaceutical Sciences, Pharma Fest 2026 featured inter-university debate and olympiad competitions, poster presentations, a stall exhibition, a Pharma Walk and cultural performances, including a concert by Pritom Hasan.

In the Pharma Debate 2026, BRAC University Team B emerged as champion. The winning team comprised Rubaba Hafiz Shoshi, Arsha Rashid and Fahmida Afsan Chowdhury. Arsha Rashid was named Debater of the Final. NSU Team A, represented by Lamisa Nusrat, Sarah Zubayer and Ahmed Ibrahim, secured first runner-up. At the same time, UIU Team A, comprising Yusuf Ibrahim Khan, Janita Islam Jarin and Sadia Jahan Tasmim, placed second runner-up.

In the Pharma Olympiad, NSU Team A became champion, with Fahim Bin Hamid Tamal and Nafisa Nawal representing the team. NSU Team B, comprising Sadia Ishrak Rida and Md. Asif Aktab Chowdhury, secured first runner-up. Noakhali Science and Technology University placed second runner-up, represented by Chayan Kur and Salma Jafrin.

The Pharma Fest Stall Exhibition 2026 recognised PharMatrix as champion, followed by AcuNova in second place, and The Carbon Cure in third place.

ICPS 2026 was organised by NSU’s Department of Pharmaceutical Sciences in collaboration with the Faculty of Pharmacy, Universiti Malaya, Malaysia, from 10 to 12 October under the theme “Innovations in Pharmaceutical Sciences for Global Health Advancement.” Pharma Fest 2026 followed the theme “Sustainability” and the tagline “Conserve Today, Thrive Tomorrow.”

The festival was supported by The City Bank PLC as Title Sponsor and ZEEHO CFMOTO as Co-Sponsor. Beximco Pharmaceuticals Limited was the Platinum Sponsor, while Everest Pharmaceuticals Ltd., Beacon Pharmaceuticals PLC and Incepta Pharmaceuticals Ltd. were Diamond Sponsors. Renata PLC sponsored the Olympiad; DBL Pharma supported the debate competition; UniMed UniHealth Pharmaceuticals and Study Net were Gold Sponsors; and Healthcare Pharmaceuticals Limited, Apex Pharma Ltd., Square Pharmaceuticals PLC, and Radiant Pharmaceuticals Limited were Silver Sponsors.

title: IUB wins six titles at MTB-IUB Inter University Table Tennis Tournament 2026
text:
Independent University, Bangladesh (IUB) secured six out of the seven titles at the MTB-IUB Inter-University Table Tennis Tournament 2026, which concluded at the IUB Table Tennis Arena on October 16.

Sponsored by Mutual Trust Bank PLC (MTB), the tournament brought together 71 players, including 60 men and 11 women, from nine universities. Both singles finals were held on the concluding day of the five-day tournament.

Rahmim, a third-semester student of Anthropology at IUB, is currently ranked second in Bangladesh and was the national champion in 2024. He is set to represent the Bangladesh national team at the Asian Table Tennis Championship in Tajikistan starting October 18.

In the mixed doubles final, an IUB pair defeated another pair from the same university 3-0.

Saidul Haque Sadi, Secretary of the Bangladesh Table Tennis Federation, attended the concluding day's program. Also present were IUB Trustee Md Tanveer Madar and Trustee Rashed Chowdhury; Vice-Chancellor Prof. M Tamim; and Pro Vice-Chancellor Prof. Daniel W Lund. title: Razid Season: A filmmaker moving between worlds
text:
I have seen only three of Razid Season's films: Maze, Kaddish and Elijah. He has made several others that I have not yet had the opportunity to watch, so this is not intended to be a comprehensive survey of his work. What struck me about these three films, however, is how effortlessly he seems to move between vastly different worlds. Watch them in one sitting, and you will find yourself having to readjust your mindset with each film.

Maze explores how a Muslim woman experiences the burden of wearing the hijab. At a bus stop, she sees a Western woman and imagines herself in her place. What makes the film particularly compelling is the way Razid approaches its subject. It is largely silent, yet conveys its message with remarkable clarity. He does not lecture, nor does he overemphasise the act of wearing the hijab or the burden associated with it. Instead, he allows us to immerse ourselves in the protagonist's mind and contemplate the meaning of freedom.

Image Razid Season

Once you have seen Maze, you would hardly imagine that Razid could make a film like Kaddish. Like all his work that I have seen, it is short yet deeply impactful. Kaddish is set in Nazi-occupied Poland in 1943. It follows a young Polish Jewish man, Akiva, during the Holocaust as he attempts to reach his mother's grave to observe the anniversary of her death.

Suddenly, you find yourself immersed in the cinematic world of Tarkovsky, with its stillness, monochrome imagery, deliberate pacing and poetic treatment of human experience. The black-and-grey forest, the silence and the languages he uses all reflect meticulous research and delicate artistic handling. Razid chose to have his Polish Jewish protagonist speak Yiddish rather than simply making the film in English. In this 15-minute film, there is even room for other languages, including German, Polish, Aramaic and Hebrew. The Nazis are hunting down and killing Jews. Amid these killings, the protagonist's silent search for his mother's grave is heart-piercing, yet Razid handles it with extraordinary restraint. He has made the film with a poet's touch, so delicate that even the slightest deviation, it seems, would have disrupted its emotional balance.

Image A scene from Kaddish, which follows a young Polish Jewish man during the Holocaust as he attempts to reach his mother's grave to observe the anniversary of her death.

When I first watched it, there were moments when I felt as though I were watching scenes from Schindler's List. For a Bengali filmmaker, Razid, in my view, surpasses every conventional expectation with Kaddish.

Razid then takes us back to the world of Bangladeshi immigrants in Elijah. The film tells the story of a Bengali Muslim taxi driver in New York whose child comes out as transgender. The traditional family is initially devastated by the revelation but gradually moves towards understanding and acceptance. Once again, Razid approaches the subject with care, sympathy and remarkable restraint.

Razid is a highly unusual filmmaker. Living in New York, he has managed to move beyond the familiar boundaries of the diaspora experience. I am astonished by how radically and confidently he moves from a Middle Eastern woman's private consciousness to Holocaust-era Poland, and then to the intimate struggles of a Bengali immigrant family in New York.

Image Poster for Elijah, Razid Season's film about a Bengali Muslim taxi driver in New York whose child comes out as transgender.

A few months ago, I was in New York, and Razid came to visit me. I was struck by his humility and unassuming demeanour. We discussed his films, and I was particularly interested in how he had made Kaddish. He described his adventures in upstate New York, searching for a location that resembled a Polish forest and a farmhouse that looked European, where the protagonist could seek refuge. He also spoke about making a gravestone and carefully carving the inscriptions onto it.

Here is a passionate director who remains deeply committed to his art. I am confident that his finest work is still to come. The Goethe-Institut in Dhaka will be screening Kaddish on October 24. I hope some of you will have the opportunity to see this remarkable film.

Dipen Bhattacharya is a California-based writer and retired professor of physics and astronomy. His work spans fiction as well as writing on Bangladesh's geological history and astronomy.
