title: Ami dombo na: I am more than the cancer I survived
text:
There is a precise moment in late Toronto summer when the air shifts. July’s humid weight breaks, the afternoons turn golden and crisp, and for a few weeks, the city seems to understand that winter will come soon enough, so it might as well be generous.

On one of those afternoons, I stepped out of a yoga class downtown. Streetcars scraped along their tracks. In my headphones, “Rastay” by Arnob and Friends was playing. I was 34, wearing a bright yellow denim jacket, and I felt a sudden lightness in my limbs.

So I danced.

Not well. Not for anyone. There was no stage, no wedding, no audience whose approval mattered. I swayed my shoulders, spun once under the late-afternoon sun and let my arms trace the music in the air.

Growing up in Dhaka, dancing had usually belonged somewhere: a cultural programme, a stage, a wedding, a room in which movement had context and witnesses. Toronto gave me something I had not known I needed: the anonymity to be ridiculous without explanation.

Image By March 2024, Nabeela had completed 12 of the 16 planned chemotherapy sessions before treatment was discontinued due to a low platelet count. Photos: Author





In that moment, my body was an instrument of pure joy. The music was loud, the sky was vast, and my body belonged entirely to me.

I did not know I would one day remember that afternoon as a border.

Two years later, I would return to that pavement with a rollator.

Between those two versions of me lies a story about cancer. But it is also a story about what happens when survival does not restore the life you had before; when the body that survives is not the body you remember; when gratitude and rage coexist so comfortably that they begin sharing a room.

People imagine a cancer diagnosis as a cinematic scene: a doctor, a sterile room, a grave voice, a sentence dividing life into before and after. That moment happened to me. But the diagnosis truly landed later, on an aggressively ordinary morning.

I was sitting at my desk with my coffee going cold beside the keyboard. The laptop timed out, and the screen went black. In its reflection, I saw myself.

Same mug. Same apartment. Same refrigerator hum.

The walls were the same. I was not.

In October 2023, I had been getting ready for a photo shoot when a sharp pain shot through my left breast. Instinctively, I reached up and felt a lump.

Part of the human brain is stubbornly committed to keeping the day normal. It says: You are making a fuss. You are overreacting. It is probably nothing.

Image Triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC) gets its name from the absence of three common treatment targets in cancer cells: oestrogen receptors (ER), progesterone receptors (PR) and human epidermal growth factor receptor 2 (HER2).



I took two Advils and told my husband I was fine.

Fortunately, another part was more annoying.

Get it checked.

So I did.

Urgent imaging and a biopsy followed. The diagnosis was triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC), a form of breast cancer that lacks three common treatment targets. Chemotherapy is central to treatment, and immunotherapy is used in some cases. Mine was Stage IIIC.

I did what many frightened people with internet access do: I searched for survival statistics.

This was a mistake.

Statistics are useful for public health, but less so at two in the morning when your brain turns a population into a prophecy about you. I read numbers as if one of them were secretly my expiry date. I forgot that statistics describe groups, not destinies.

Instead, I spent weeks mentally rehearsing my death.

The next part of illness is rarely shown in awareness campaigns.

Administration.

Your life becomes a badly managed office whose only employee is ill.

Insurance forms. Prescription refills. Blood tests. Calls. Appointments. Consent forms. A calendar that begins to look like it belongs to a small corporation.

And then there is the person beside the patient.

My husband became my medication manager, appointment keeper, note-taker, driver, memory and witness. We often speak of cancer as something one person “fights”. That language can make everyone around the patient disappear. But illness rearranges households. It changes work, money, intimacy, sleep and time.

It turns love into logistics.

People loved me and wanted to say the right thing. Serious illness makes people uncomfortable, though, and discomfort can turn kindness into a script.

“Everything happens for a reason.”

“Stay positive.”

“You’re a fighter.”

“You’re so strong.”

I understand the intention. But compulsory optimism becomes another task assigned to a sick person.

Image Nabeela Nushaira Rahman before her cancer diagnosis.



Some days I was not a warrior. I was a woman on a sofa trying not to vomit. Some days strength looked suspiciously like crying. Some days it looked like sleeping. Some days it looked like being furious that this was happening at all.

The people who helped most did not require a motivational speech. They said: I am here. Can I bring food? Do you want company? Do you want silence?

There is cruelty in telling people to find the gift inside catastrophe while they are still bleeding from it.

Once a week, for twelve weeks, I sat in a vinyl recliner under fluorescent lights. Hair had never been just hair to me. Before chemotherapy could take it on its own terms, I donated what I could while it was still mine to give. When the rest came out in quiet handfuls, my husband helped me shave it at the bathroom sink.

Then the eyebrows went. Then the eyelashes.

Neuropathy followed: numbness, pins and needles, my feet feeling as though they had been dropped into an anthill run by ants with a personal grievance.

Immunotherapy caused a severe skin reaction and was stopped. By March 2024, I had completed twelve of the sixteen chemotherapy sessions originally planned. My platelets were too low for the next one.

Then, one morning, I woke up and my left side was gone.

Left leg. Left arm.

Gone.

During a hospital admission, violent tremors began in my arms and legs. Eventually, I was diagnosed with Functional Neurological Disorder (FND), a real neurological disorder involving problems with how brain networks function rather than the kind of structural damage that might appear on a conventional scan.

I remember thinking: That is not the lottery I wanted to win.

But here we are.

I left hospital with a walker for home and a wheelchair for outside. Soon afterwards, my oncologist called: no more chemotherapy. Surgery would move forward urgently.

Reconstruction had been planned. I wanted it. Then my heart was found to be too weak for the longer surgery.

This is something I wish we discussed more honestly when we talk about medical “choices”. Sometimes a patient technically has preferences but no meaningful choice. Reconstruction was not a decision I thoughtfully made after considering a tasteful brochure of options.

It was a door that closed while I was dealing with everything on the other side of it.

On May 13, 2024, I had a left mastectomy. Nine lymph nodes were affected. Despite treatment ending early, the pathology showed that my cancer had responded far better than we had feared.

I looked at my body and said, out loud, to no one: “So... yay. Good job, body.”

I can be furious at my body and proud of it in the exact same breath.

I will not pretend that losing a breast did not alter something in how I understood my femininity.

It did.

I grew up Bengali. The female body is never simply a body in our culture. It can become family honour, modesty, beauty, fertility, desirability, motherhood, morality, sometimes all before a woman has had breakfast. Breasts carry an especially dense cultural weight, simultaneously sexualised, hidden, policed, celebrated and turned into symbols of motherhood.

Then medicine turns a breast into tissue.

A scan. A specimen. A margin. A pathology report.

I am grateful for the surgery that treated my cancer. I am also allowed to grieve the breast that is gone. Those sentences do not cancel each other out.

What I resist is the idea that gratitude should make grief impolite.

Image A study involving 355 women at two major cancer centres in Dhaka found that 55.7 per cent experienced a delay of more than four months between recognising their symptoms and beginning treatment.



After surgery came radiotherapy. Treatment ended, at least in the active sense.

This is where many cancer stories begin to hurry.

The bell rings. The music rises. The survivor walks into sunlight. The audience understands that the frightening part is over.

But I could not find enough stories about the middle, the territory where treatment has ended but your old life has not returned; where scans can be reassuring while the body remains unreliable; where survival is real and disability is also real.

I had survived cancer treatment and still could not simply get up and dance.

The body that had once belonged to me without negotiation now required negotiations for everything.

Can we stand today?

Can we walk?

How far?

Will the leg hold?

Will the tremor come?

My relationship with my body became diplomatic. Every ordinary movement required a summit.

That changed the way I hear the language of “beating” cancer. I understand the appeal. Fight. Beat. Win.

But if survival is victory, what does that make the person who dies? Did they fight less? Were they insufficiently positive?

Disease is not a character test.

Neither is disability.

I do not want to be called inspirational because I went outside with a rollator. Sometimes I am simply going outside. A disabled person buying coffee is not automatically performing courage for the public.

Pity can be just as flattening. I have seen the look in people’s eyes, the instant transformation from person to tragedy. It can erase humour, vanity, sexuality, ambition, irritation, silliness, intellect, appetite and contradiction.

I do not want my life reduced to cancer.

I also refuse to pretend cancer did not change it.

The work is holding both truths.

For readers in Bangladesh, there is another reason for this story.

Breast cancer is the most commonly diagnosed cancer among Bangladeshi women, according to GLOBOCAN 2022 estimates. A recent facility-based study of 355 women at two major cancer centres in Dhaka found that 55.7 per cent experienced a delay of more than four months between recognising symptoms and starting treatment. Nearly 80 per cent reported delaying medical attention because they believed their symptoms would resolve on their own; financial barriers were reported by 65.5 per cent.

These figures should not be mistaken for a portrait of every Bangladeshi woman. But the instinct behind such delays is familiar to me.

Do not be dramatic.

It is probably nothing.

Take an Advil.

Finish what you were doing.

Women are trained in astonishing ways to downgrade their own discomfort. Endurance is praised so often that it can become dangerous.

Early assessment is not hysteria.

It is information.

But awareness cannot end with a pink ribbon or an instruction to “check yourself”. A woman may notice a change and still face financial constraints, distance, fear, shame, family pressure, misinformation or a health system that is difficult to navigate.

Awareness without access can become another way of blaming patients.

And sometimes a person does everything “right” and still gets very sick.

Cancer does not require a moral explanation.

I wish we could change one more thing about how we speak of illness: our hunger for clean endings.

We like the survivor who returns stronger, wiser, grateful and preferably productive.

I am grateful to be alive.

I am also tired.

I love my life.

I also miss the life I had.

I am proud of my body.

I am also angry with it.

I can feel beautiful and mourn what has changed.

None of these are contradictions that need to be resolved.

The pressure to become a symbol can be exhausting. I do not want to spend the rest of my life demonstrating that suffering made me better. Perhaps it did in some ways. Perhaps in others, it simply hurt me.

I would rather be a person than a lesson.

This past summer, I took the yellow denim jacket out again.

It did not fit the body I have now.

For a moment, that fact carried more grief than a jacket had any right to carry. Clothes are sneaky archives. They remember versions of us we did not realise we were documenting.

So I tied it around my waist.

Then I returned to the same stretch of pavement in downtown Toronto with my rollator.

Image Nabeela adjusts to changes in her mobility following her diagnosis of functional neurological disorder (FND). After leaving hospital, she relied on a walker at home and a wheelchair outdoors.



The streetcars were still there. The glass buildings still caught the late-afternoon sun. The city had not been waiting for me.

I did not dance.

I walked.

Slowly. Deliberately.

There was grief in that walk. I will not edit it out for a satisfying ending.

But there was something else, too.

Recognition.

I am not the woman who danced down that pavement without wondering whether her legs would hold her.

That woman trusted her body completely. She did not know what was coming.

This body knows.

It carries a mastectomy scar. It carries the memory of chemotherapy, radiotherapy, neuropathy, tremors and paralysis. It has spent years teaching me the humiliating intimacy of dependence.

But it also carried me back to the pavement.

Not triumphantly. Not cured of every consequence. Not restored to a previous factory setting.

Just back.

For a long time, I thought recovery meant getting my old body back. I am beginning to understand that this may be the wrong question.

Perhaps the work is not to recover ownership of the body I had.

Perhaps it is to claim ownership of the body that is here.

There is a Bangla phrase I return to: Ami dombo na.

I won’t back down.

I do not mean that attitude defeats cancer. I do not mean that people who die have surrendered, or that disabled people must spend their lives overcoming disability for an audience.

I mean something smaller, more stubborn and more mine.

Cancer does not get sole authorship of me.

Disability does not get sole authorship of me.

Neither does pity.

Neither does the mythology of the brave survivor.

I am still allowed to be vain. Funny. Difficult. Loving. Bored. Ambitious. Frightened. Sarcastic. Sensual. Lazy. Curious. Angry. Hopeful.

I am still allowed to want more from life than survival.

If something in your body has changed, please listen to the quieter voice that says: get it checked.

And if you are beside someone who is ill, resist asking them to be brave for you. Sit with the complicated version. Bring dinner. Make the phone call. Let them complain without converting the complaint into a lesson about gratitude.

A person can love life fiercely and still hate what has happened to her.

I know because I do.

On that Toronto pavement years ago, my body belonged entirely to me because I never had to think about ownership.

Now ownership means something else.

It means looking at a body that has changed without my permission and saying: you are still mine.

It means taking the yellow jacket even when it does not fit.

It means returning to the pavement even when I cannot dance.

It is still my body.

It is still my pavement.

I am still becoming.

I am still here.

Ami dombo na.

Nabeela Nushaira Rahman is a Bangladeshi writer based in Toronto whose work explores identity, illness, disability, culture, humour and the strange business of being human.

title: If heaven has food, let it taste like my mother's
text:
Memories surrounding food have a peculiar way of staying with us. Perhaps it is because food speaks to so many of our senses at once: the aroma of spices rising from a pot, the warmth of a freshly cooked meal, the familiar clatter of plates at a family table, or the taste of something that takes us back to a time we can never quite return to. Inevitably, intertwined with the stories of our lives is the story of the food we have eaten. We eat when we gather, when we celebrate, when we grieve, and sometimes simply because it is time to eat. Recipes become family heirlooms, passed down through generations alongside stories, habits and traditions. Even the most ordinary moments around a dining table can remain imprinted upon our hearts long after the people who once sat beside us are gone.

Flavours from an ancestral palate

I have faint but fond memories of sitting at the breakfast table in our ancestral home in Begum Bazar, with my Dadi beside me, watching over me as I ate. I can still recall the crisp parathas, the eggs fried in ghee, and the simple sprinkling of salt and pepper that made those mornings so comforting. I remember the quiet tenderness of her presence, the sort of affection that needed neither explanation nor expression. Then, another memory comes rushing back: my childhood self sitting on my father's lap while he ate with one hand and held me close with the other. At that age, I knew nothing of how precious these moments were. I did not know that one day I would find myself searching for them in the smallest things, in a familiar aroma, a remembered taste, or a dish prepared just as it had always been.

Image Sindhi Biryani made by my mother

But today, I do not wish to write about my Dadi or my father, both of whom have departed from this world. Today, I want to write about my mother, Rahat Hussaini, and the extraordinary way she has made a home for us through her food.

It is nearly impossible for me to feel entirely satisfied when I eat at a restaurant. I find myself making mental notes of what is missing, whether a dish has the right balance of spices, whether its texture is as it should be, or whether its flavour has achieved that elusive perfection. I sometimes wonder if I have become too particular. But the truth is that I have spent a lifetime eating food prepared by my mother, and once you have grown accustomed to that kind of cooking, the standards by which you judge every other meal become rather difficult to meet.

My mother, Farzana Rayhan, known to us as Rahat, married Syed Faizul Hussaini, the eldest son of Manzur Sahab, at a very young age. Born into a Mirza family with roots in Bengal that, according to the documents I have been able to trace, extend back approximately two centuries, she spent the first sixteen years of her life under the loving care of her parents. Marriage brought her into a different household, with its own customs, expectations, tastes and ways of life. Over the thirty-two years of her marriage, she became an integral part of this family, learning its traditions from her in-laws and, in time, making them her own. After losing my father, she became the strongest thread holding our family together, ensuring that it continues to thrive, that its children continue to receive an education, and that we remain guided by her steady hand, like a compass pointing us in the right direction. As she has often told me, much of what she knows today, she learned from her in-laws. For thirty-eight years, she has been part of this family, carrying its traditions forward while adding her own warmth and wisdom to its legacy. She raised two children, my sister, Sarah, and me, and today, she is the doting grandmother of our little angel, Hamza!

Image Murgh Roast

When I think about this journey, I realise that there is something remarkable about the way my mother learned to cook for a family whose culinary traditions were not entirely her own. She had to familiarise herself with unfamiliar ingredients, understand the nuances of our family's dishes, and learn to navigate the markets for the right cuts of meat, the freshest produce and the spices that give each preparation its distinctive character. What began as a young bride's adjustment to a new household gradually became something much more intimate: a culinary language through which she would express her love for us.

And express it she does.

Heirlooms in jars

If I were to begin anywhere, I would begin with my mother’s achaar and murabba, for some of my fondest memories of her kitchen are preserved in glass jars. Her kuchla achaar carries a history of its own, travelling from Ghazipur, Uttar Pradesh, India, where my Dadi came from, into our home through a recipe inherited like a family heirloom. I can still picture my mother peeling raw mangoes into thin strips, tossing them with her secret blend of spices and kalonji, and carefully arranging them in transparent glass bottles, washed and dried with the utmost precision. She would place these bottles under the summer sun for days, allowing the mangoes to soften, absorb the spices and develop that extraordinary, sharp sourness that made the achaar so irresistible. Then there was her Kashmiri achaar, with its finely sliced mangoes immersed in a sugary syrup, punctuated by red chillies. Even recalling it now makes my mouth water beyond measure. And then came her anaras murabba: pineapple pieces steeped in sugar, simmered with whole cloves and infused with delicate strands of saffron until they turned translucent and golden, glistening like little jewels in their fragrant syrup. Each jar held more than a preserve; it held the patience of her hands, the inheritance of generations and the sweetness of a home I have known all my life.

Parchas and unwritten table laws

Then there is my mother’s handi kabab, a dish whose name might lead one to imagine meat threaded onto skewers and charred over glowing coals. Hers is something altogether different. She takes thin slices of beef, which she calls parchas, marinates them in yoghurt and her chosen spices, and cooks them slowly in a handi, allowing the meat to absorb the flavours until it becomes tender and deeply savoury. It can be eaten with parathas or rice, according to one’s preference, but in our household, there is one unwritten law that no amount of personal preference can overrule: every bite must be accompanied by a piece of raw onion. The sharp, crisp pungency of the onion somehow elevates the entire experience, cutting through the richness of the meat and making the next bite all the more irresistible. Some rules in a family are never written down; they are simply inherited at the dining table.

Image Kushla Achaar

Mint, steam and spiced rice

And then comes the crown jewel of my mother’s kitchen, her much-loved Sindhi biryani. I have eaten biryani elsewhere, but hers has never found a rival in my memory. Built around fragrant rice, chicken and potatoes, it brings together the warmth of ginger, garlic, red chilli, turmeric, tomatoes and onions fried to a deep golden brown, with the occasional sweet-tart surprise of aloo bukhara tucked between the layers. Yet the ingredient that transforms it, that gives it its unmistakable identity, is the pudina. My mother scatters fresh mint leaves through the layers of the biryani, and the moment the lid of the degh is lifted, the fragrance rises like a wave, filling the room with the freshness of mint mingled with the rich aroma of spiced rice. I can almost see the steam escaping as the lid comes off; I can almost smell that first breath of fragrance. And then there is the aloo bukhara. Every so often, in the middle of a mouthful, one finds a piece unexpectedly, its sweet and tangy flavour bursting through the spices. It is a little surprise I have always looked forward to, a pleasure so particular that I can hardly put it into words. Beside the biryani sits a bowl of cold raita, made with yoghurt, mint, coriander leaves, green chillies and generous amounts of garlic. Its coolness offers the perfect counterpoint to the warmth of the biryani, and together they create a combination that, to me, tastes like no other.

Image Hamza Hassan Khan

When my mother prepares her mutton rezala or her much-loved murgh roast with sada pulao, even the dining table seems to acquire a certain ceremony. There is an anticipation that begins long before the food is served, as the aromas travel from the kitchen and draw everyone closer. The murgh roast arrives with its rich, inviting colour, while the pulao offers a quiet elegance of its own, its delicate grains carrying the fragrance of the preparation without competing for attention. And then there is the rezala, with its velvety gravy and carefully balanced spices, commanding its place at the table. These are the meals around which a family gathers, conversations unfold and ordinary days become memories without anyone realising it at the time. Looking back, I wonder whether what I remember so vividly is only the taste of the food or the feeling of being home, knowing that my mother was in the kitchen, making something with her own hands that would bring us all together. Perhaps that is the secret ingredient I have spent my life trying to identify. It was never merely the spices, the ingredients or the recipes. It was my mother.

Image Mutton Rezala

These are not dishes one approaches casually. They demand attention, appetite and, if I may say so, a certain degree of reverence. Once the food is served, conversation often gives way to the more immediate business of eating. Everyone knows what awaits them, and nobody wishes to waste time.

The alchemy of instinct

There is, of course, a great deal of skill behind what might appear to be an effortless meal. Take the mutton rezala, for instance. The ingredients may sound simple enough: tender cuts of mutton, yoghurt, ghee, poppy seeds or posto, saffron and mace, known as jaitri. Yet the magic lies not merely in the ingredients themselves but in the proportions, the sequence and the patience with which they are brought together. Too much of one spice or too little of another, and the entire character of the dish can change.

It is tempting to believe that if one follows a recipe precisely, the result will be the same. But anyone who has tried to recreate a beloved family dish knows that recipes rarely tell the whole story. They cannot explain the instinct that tells a cook when the yoghurt has blended properly, when the spices have released their fragrance or when the meat has reached that perfect tenderness. They cannot measure the experience accumulated over years, nor can they account for the little adjustments made almost unconsciously by a practised hand.

And perhaps this is where the real secret lies, not in a single ingredient, but in the knowledge that has become second nature through years of cooking for the people one loves.

I am beginning to understand that the food I grew up eating was never simply about taste. It was also about continuity. Every meal carried traces of the generations before me, of the household my mother entered as a young bride, of the traditions she learned and of the family she gradually made her own. In her kitchen, unfamiliar recipes became familiar, unfamiliar ingredients became indispensable, and the expectations of a household became part of her own way of expressing affection.

As a child, I never thought about any of this. I did not wonder how much time a meal required, how many decisions went into getting the flavours right or how often a mother must have stood in the kitchen while the rest of the household carried on with its day. I simply sat down and ate. I assumed that the food would be there, that the familiar dishes would return to the table and that the tastes I loved would always be within reach.

Growing older has made me realise how little we understand the labour of love when we are its recipients. We recognise the meal, but not always the hands that prepared it. We remember the taste, but not the patience behind it. And we seldom realise that what feels ordinary to us may, in fact, be one of the most extraordinary gifts we have been given.

Image Shahi Tukra

The truest taste of home

Perhaps that is why restaurant food so often leaves me wanting. It may be excellent, even exquisite, but it does not carry the same history. It cannot remind me of the home in Begum Bazar, of the people who once gathered around our table or of the woman who spent years learning how to feed a family that became hers. It cannot reproduce the quiet comfort of knowing that someone has prepared a dish with you in mind, remembering precisely how you like it.

My mother’s cooking has become my measure of what food ought to be, not because every meal must be perfect, but because hers has always meant something beyond perfection. It is the taste of a life built around family, of traditions carried forward and of affection expressed without the need for grand declarations.

Image Rahat Hussaini with her grandchild, Hamza

One day, I hope to preserve more than the recipes themselves. I want to remember the stories behind them: where she learned each dish, how she came to understand its ingredients, which preparations belonged to our family's older generations and how her own touch transformed them. I want these memories to remain with us, so that Hamza, too, may one day know something of the love that has travelled through our family and found its way to the dining table. Because, in the end, the food we remember most fondly is rarely just food. It is the people who made it, the homes in which we ate it and the moments we did not know we would one day miss.

Image Memories surrounding food have a peculiar way of staying with us. Perhaps it is because food speaks to so many of our senses at once: the aroma of spices rising from a pot, the warmth of a freshly cooked meal, the familiar clatter of plates at a family table or the taste of something that takes us back to a time we can never quite return to.



And when I think of my mother, I think of all the meals she has prepared for us, all the flavours she has perfected over the years and all the love she has placed before us without ever asking for it to be acknowledged. I think of her standing in the kitchen, tending to a pot, adjusting the spices and waiting patiently for the food to reach its fullest flavour. I think of the table being laid, the dishes arriving one after another and the familiar comfort of everyone gathering to eat.

And I realise that perhaps the greatest inheritance a mother leaves her children is not a recipe written down on paper, nor even the taste of a dish that no restaurant can reproduce. It is the feeling of being home. For me, that feeling will always taste a little like my mother's achaars, murabba, Sindhi biryani, mutton rezala, her murgh roast and sada pulao, and the immeasurable love of Rahat Hussaini.

Syed Faizanul Hussaini spends his weekdays navigating the world of HR and talent acquisition and his spare time wandering through the lanes of history, heritage and Urdu literature.

title: What Bangladesh needs from COP31
text:
During the recent Pre-COP31 meetings in Fiji, I kept thinking about southwestern Bangladesh. The geography was different, but much of what I heard was familiar: concerns about saltwater intrusion, damaged livelihoods, the cost of rebuilding and the difficulty of securing financial support for communities before the next disaster strikes.

I joined the discussions in Nadi with colleagues from Monash University's Pacific Action for Climate Transitions (PACT). We discussed investment in nature and climate finance with Pacific leaders and other partners. Pacific representatives were clear on one point: countries that have contributed little to global warming should not have to take on more debt to cope with its consequences.

That argument is particularly relevant to Bangladesh. I grew up in Khulna, near the Sundarbans, and spent much of my childhood in villages whose residents would later endure Cyclone Sidr in 2007 and Cyclone Aila in 2009. Aila's effects persisted long after the storm, with damaged embankments and saltwater intrusion disrupting farming and drinking-water supplies. My subsequent research examined how households recovered from these devastating events.

Next month, I will travel to Antalya for COP31 with Monash University's delegation, alongside PACT colleagues. As a boy growing up near the Sundarbans, I could hardly have imagined attending these international climate negotiations. Yet the questions I take there remain close to home: how can families protect their livelihoods, and what support will actually reach them when disaster strikes?

A familiar struggle on a different shore

Pacific island countries and Bangladesh face different circumstances. Some island states face threats to their long-term habitability and the high cost of providing services to scattered populations. Bangladesh must protect a much larger population living in a densely settled delta. Yet both depend on vulnerable land and water resources: saltwater intrusion can change what farmers grow and where families obtain safe drinking water.

Bangladesh's exposure extends well beyond its coastal regions. Floods and river erosion displace households; drought threatens agricultural production; and extreme heat makes outdoor work increasingly dangerous. People may face several of these pressures within the same year. A household still paying off repairs from one disaster has less financial capacity to withstand another.



Image Fishing boats rest along a fragile riverbank beside makeshift settlements on Bangladesh's vulnerable coast, where river erosion and tidal surges threaten homes and livelihoods. Protecting these communities requires grant-based climate finance that supports coastal infrastructure, restores livelihoods and strengthens resilience against future disasters. Photo: Habibur Rahman





Not every cyclone or flood can be directly attributed to climate change. However, global warming is changing the conditions in which these hazards occur. The Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change projects heavier rainfall associated with tropical cyclones and an increase in the proportion of the most intense storms globally, although regional differences remain. Rising sea levels also increase the risks associated with storm surges. Poverty, meanwhile, determines how much capacity households have to withstand and recover from these pressures.

Recovery means restoring livelihoods and food security

Bangladesh's cyclone shelters, early warning systems and community volunteers demonstrate what sustained investment in disaster preparedness can achieve. The World Bank's 2022 climate and development report documented a hundredfold reduction in cyclone-related deaths since 1970. Yet a family can survive a disaster and still lose its livelihood. Mortality statistics cannot capture the months spent searching for work, rebuilding damaged homes or repaying emergency loans.

In our research on households affected by Cyclone Aila, we examined how relatives and neighbours shared resources during the recovery process. The study found that exposure to the disaster within a household's social network mattered for its subsequent income and investment decisions.

In another study, we found that disaster-affected participants were less likely to withdraw from experimental risk-sharing groups than those who had not been affected. This finding points to a capacity for mutual support that recovery programmes should recognise and strengthen. However, the willingness to help one another cannot replace resources lost across an entire community. Public assistance remains essential, particularly for families with limited social connections or support networks.

A farming household may lose both its harvest and its earnings. An agricultural labourer may lose employment without owning any damaged land and consequently be overlooked by compensation schemes based on property losses. Families who depend on purchasing food face additional pressure when disruptions to agricultural production and transport push up market prices.



The World Bank's 2022 assessment warned that climate variability and extreme weather events could cost Bangladesh one-third of its agricultural GDP by 2050. Food security depends not only on restoring agricultural production but also on wages, functioning markets and whether families can afford to plant crops again. A new crop variety may be suitable for saline soil but remain beyond the reach of a farmer who has exhausted their savings and cannot afford to risk another failed harvest. Similarly, training offers little protection if there is no market for the resulting product or demand for the skills acquired.

Support should connect immediate emergency assistance with preparations for the next farming season. Cash assistance arriving after a household has sold its tools or missed the planting window may prevent hunger but do much less to restore its earning capacity. For households unable to return to farming, assistance should help them identify and secure other viable sources of employment and income.

Recovery also requires access to safe drinking water, adequate nutrition, healthcare and schooling. Women caring for children or older relatives may struggle to travel for work or navigate the process of applying for assistance. Programme evaluations should therefore assess whether household earnings and food consumption have recovered, and whether poorer and more vulnerable families are actually benefiting from the support provided.



Image Women carry water pitchers in coastal Bangladesh, where saltwater intrusion has made access to safe drinking water an everyday struggle. Climate adaptation efforts must prioritise reliable freshwater supplies, particularly for vulnerable households. Photo: Habibur Rahman

Go to Antalya with proposals that can be funded

COP31 runs from 9 to 20 November, with Türkiye hosting the conference and Australia leading the negotiations. Bangladesh should pursue stronger international commitments while also advancing specific, actionable funding proposals. Its National Adaptation Plan provides an important starting point. The task is to identify priorities that clearly demonstrate who is at risk, what interventions are needed, how much they will cost and how they will be maintained over time.



A comprehensive coastal programme could combine embankment repairs with improved drainage, freshwater supplies and livelihood support. These investments need to work together: protecting land from tidal flooding will not restore agricultural production if drainage systems fail or usable freshwater remains scarce. Maintenance must have a dedicated budget from the outset. Elsewhere, priorities could include targeted support for flood-prone farming communities, improved urban drainage, heat protection measures and essential services in urban neighbourhoods receiving climate-displaced households.

Meaningful local consultation should shape the design and implementation of these proposals. Each proposal needs clearly designated responsible agencies and practical arrangements to ensure that assistance reaches tenants, landless workers and others who may lack formal ownership documents.



Bangladesh should also present climate risks honestly and accurately. The World Bank's 2022 assessment estimated average annual losses from cyclones at approximately US$1 billion and warned that climate impacts could generate 13.3 million internal migrants by 2050.

Bangladesh should also present climate risks honestly and accurately. The World Bank's 2022 assessment estimated average annual losses from cyclones at approximately US$1 billion and warned that climate impacts could generate 13.3 million internal migrants by 2050. These figures are estimates and projections, not a definitive count of future victims.

Funding decisions should recognise both vulnerability and the number of people exposed to climate risks. Small island states face exceptional costs and existential threats, while densely populated countries face enormous needs in absolute terms.

Make grants and predictable payments the priority

Grants should be central to financing adaptation measures that protect lives without generating direct income. Providing safe drinking water to poor households may produce benefits far exceeding its cost while generating too little revenue to repay a loan. Borrowing must be assessed against already stretched public budgets and the risks posed by future disasters. Commercial investment can support financially viable enterprises, including food processing and storage facilities, but it cannot finance every essential community service or post-disaster recovery programme.

Working with other climate-vulnerable countries, Bangladesh should press for a minimum grant share in adaptation finance for countries with the least capacity to pay, with that share publicly reported. It should also seek clarity on when payments will be made and whether the funding represents additional resources or merely the relabelling of existing development commitments.



Image Caption Homes, farmland and water bodies along Bangladesh's vulnerable coast. Protecting communities from cyclones, flooding and salinity intrusion requires sustained investment in embankments, drainage systems, freshwater supplies and livelihood support. Photo: Habibur Rahman

A COP declaration cannot guarantee Bangladesh a specific allocation from the Green Climate Fund (GCF). Under the GCF's approval process, Board approval is followed by legal agreements and conditions governing the disbursement of funds. A political pledge, therefore, is not equivalent to money immediately available for expenditure.

Bangladesh can nevertheless seek greater certainty through support for preparing priority funding proposals, agreed review milestones, clear explanations of outstanding requirements and predictable payment schedules once agreements are concluded. The delegation should leave each substantive meeting with a named counterpart, clearly defined responsibilities and a documented next step.

Bangladesh is not starting from zero. The GCF's country portfolio already includes projects involving national institutions such as PKSF and IDCOL, alongside international development partners. The GCF's contribution to PKSF's Resilient Homestead and Livelihood Support project includes a US$42.2 million grant, alongside other co-financing arrangements. It also supports adaptation to coastal salinity, particularly for women, through UNDP.

Policymakers should carefully examine these existing programmes before proposing additional initiatives: have they achieved their intended results, where has implementation slowed, and which interventions merit further expansion?

Bangladesh should seek published processing timelines, fewer duplicative administrative requirements and greater support for national institutions to prepare and manage funding proposals. Sound financial management and environmental and social safeguards remain essential, but requirements should be proportionate to the risks involved. Universities and local organisations can help strengthen the evidence base and develop lasting domestic expertise in climate finance and adaptation.

Make loss and damage a workable source of support

Adaptation reduces harm, but it cannot prevent every loss. Families can still lose their homes, livelihoods and places of cultural importance despite taking reasonable precautions. This is precisely why the Fund for Responding to Loss and Damage matters.

Its available resources remain far smaller than the demand for support. The fund's start-up phase reports US$342 million allocated. As of 29 June 2026, it had received 176 funding requests covering 119 countries, totalling US$2.8 billion. The first application window closed on 15 June 2026. Bangladesh needs to follow up on any requests already submitted and prepare thoroughly for subsequent funding opportunities.

The government should make its position clear: which requests, if any, it has submitted; what stage of consideration they have reached; and which institution is responsible for following them through to a decision. For future funding rounds, preparations should begin well before a call for applications opens.



Image Caption Saline water inundates agricultural land and shrimp enclosures along Bangladesh's southwestern coast. As climate variability threatens agricultural production and food security, adaptation programmes must connect immediate disaster assistance with long-term support for farming communities, including improved drainage, freshwater access and livelihood restoration. Photo: Habibur Rahman

Bangladesh should work with other climate-vulnerable countries to seek larger, more predictable financial contributions and practical arrangements for accessing the fund. The fund already covers losses associated with slow-onset events. Bangladesh should press for effective access to financial support for deteriorating freshwater supplies and livelihoods increasingly undermined by salinity intrusion.

At home, a consistent and comprehensive system for recording climate-related losses should connect data on natural hazards with the circumstances of affected households. A landowner's damaged crops are easier to value than an agricultural labourer's lost employment and earnings. Interrupted schooling and unpaid care responsibilities can also disappear from official assessments. Evidence-gathering systems should identify people without formal land titles and avoid double-counting losses. Monetary estimates, however, cannot fully capture the loss of a home community, cultural site or longstanding social connections.



Support for climate-related displacement must include access to adequate housing, employment, schooling and essential public services in receiving areas. Moving a household away from immediate danger without providing a viable future merely transfers hardship from one location to another.

The money must reach those entitled to it

In a separate study, we examined housing reconstruction grants distributed after Cyclone Aila. Political connections were associated with bribery and missing grant money. The fact that assistance reached an affected village did not necessarily ensure fair distribution among individual households. Climate programmes therefore need publicly available eligibility criteria, understandable application procedures and accessible appeals mechanisms that do not depend on political connections. Digital payments can improve financial traceability, but they cannot correct a beneficiary list that excludes deserving households. People without suitable bank accounts, mobile phones or digital access must also have alternative ways to receive assistance.

Every major climate programme should publish information on what funding was approved, how much was received, how it was spent and where the resources were allocated. Independent monitoring should examine who received support, who was excluded and whether services continue to function after construction or implementation. Public reporting must protect personal information while making the misuse of funds more difficult to conceal.

Local governments and community organisations need adequate resources and meaningful authority to help deliver programmes effectively. Women, landless households and people with disabilities must have a voice in project selection and accessible channels through which to report problems or grievances. Maintenance budgets and institutional responsibilities must be agreed upon before construction begins, rather than being treated as an afterthought.



The Sundarbans also belongs in this discussion. Coastal planning should protect mangrove ecosystems and the livelihoods of surrounding communities, alongside investments in engineering infrastructure and public services. Conservation finance must respect local access rights and livelihood needs; it should not force the people living closest to a protected ecosystem to bear the costs of conservation alone.

A shared voice and a clear measure of success

What I heard in Fiji reinforced the importance of cooperation between Bangladesh and Pacific island countries. Through their existing international negotiating groups, they can coordinate their positions on grant-based finance, simpler funding access and support for gradual, slow-onset climate losses. Bangladesh can contribute its experience in disaster preparedness and community-based resilience while learning from Pacific approaches to local stewardship and environmental protection.

Neither Bangladesh nor the Pacific countries should allow climate-finance discussions to overshadow the demand for meaningful emissions reductions. The ambition to limit global warming to 1.5°C matters because adaptation becomes increasingly difficult and climate-related losses grow as temperatures rise. Bangladesh should continue making that case internationally while pursuing its own cleaner development options and seeking the finance and technology needed to implement them effectively.



A meaningful outcome from Antalya would include tangible progress on priority funding proposals, clearer pathways to loss-and-damage support and financial commitments with identifiable amounts, terms and implementation timelines.

A meaningful outcome from Antalya would include tangible progress on priority funding proposals, clearer pathways to loss-and-damage support and financial commitments with identifiable amounts, terms and implementation timelines. Within three months of returning from the conference, the government should publish what was agreed, which commitments remain conditional and who is responsible for ensuring that promised support materialises.

As I prepare to travel to Antalya, I think of the villages of my childhood and the households whose recovery we studied after Cyclone Aila. Bangladesh should ultimately judge COP31 by whether its outcomes help such families secure safe drinking water, restore their livelihoods and face the next climate-related hazard with less fear of losing everything once again.

Asad Islam is Professor of Economics and a Professorial Fellow at Pacific Action for Climate Transitions (PACT), Monash University. He participated in the recent Pre-COP31 discussions in Fiji.

title: How AI is closing the door on Bangladesh's female freelancers
text:
When people talk about artificial intelligence taking over jobs, they usually picture sudden mass layoffs, with bosses replacing entire departments overnight. But real-world data show that the actual damage is much quieter. Companies are not rushing to fire their experienced, senior staff. Instead, they have simply stopped hiring beginners.

A study from Stanford University, led by economist Erik Brynjolfsson, tracked payroll records for millions of workers to examine who AI is actually hurting first. The researchers found that employment among young workers aged between 22 and 25 in jobs exposed to AI dropped by 11 per cent, falling 19 per cent behind employment in jobs where AI is rarely used. The most important finding of the study was that this gap was not caused by layoffs. Rather, it was driven by a collapse in new hiring.

The reason is straightforward. Entry-level jobs mostly involve following clear instructions, such as entering data, sorting through customer emails or writing basic product descriptions. AI can perform these rule-based tasks in seconds at next to no cost. Senior roles, on the other hand, require real-world judgement, negotiation and the ability to handle complex human problems that AI still struggles with. Instead of hiring three fresh graduates to support a senior manager, companies now provide that manager with an AI tool and allow them to handle the entire workload alone.

Image Female freelancers in Bangladesh often face additional barriers to adapting to AI, as childcare, cooking and other household responsibilities leave them with less time to learn new skills and technologies than their male counterparts. Photo: Pexels



The death of routine tasks

This silent hiring freeze is hitting hardest in precisely the areas that made remote freelancing so popular in countries like Bangladesh. Reports from the BBC and projections from the World Economic Forum reveal that routine office tasks are disappearing at a record pace.

Customer support is at the centre of this transformation, with up to 80 per cent of routine support tasks facing full automation as intelligent chatbots handle customer enquiries without human assistance. Data entry is in an equally precarious position, with roughly 7.5 million jobs involving routine data processing expected to disappear globally by 2027. Overall, about 41 per cent of employers worldwide plan to downsize their teams in areas where software can handle routine daily tasks.

For ordinary office workers, this means fewer graduate trainee opportunities. But on global freelance marketplaces such as Upwork and Fiverr, this shift is undermining the very system that beginners have traditionally relied upon to build their careers.

How the freelance ladder got broken

Explaining why these entry-level opportunities are vanishing, Syeda Sanjida Afrin, a former digital marketing manager at WPCenter, notes that in fields such as content creation, email campaigns and market trend research, AI tools have drastically reduced the time required to deliver finished work. By training an AI model on a specific product and providing clear prompts, tasks that once required an entire eight-hour working day can now be completed and polished in just a few hours. Activities that used to be assigned to junior assistants, such as researching competitors, building content banks and organising editorial calendars, can now be completed, with the results neatly formatted, by a single person in minutes.

Image AI is disrupting the traditional entry-level career pathway, leaving beginners with fewer opportunities to gain practical experience, develop their skills and establish themselves in the digital economy. Photo: Star



While this shift has unlocked substantial productivity gains for experienced marketers, it has also had a devastating effect on junior hiring. When a single professional can accomplish twice as much in half the time, companies no longer need as many junior assistants to conduct background research, compile spreadsheets or write first drafts.

Afrin notes that across the technology and digital marketing sectors, teams that once employed ten marketing staff members are frequently being reduced to five. Whether driven by AI adoption, falling revenues or corporate cost-cutting, the reality is that businesses simply need fewer people to produce the same volume of work. For beginners who previously gained experience by supporting senior managers with basic tasks, the door to entry has been firmly shut.

This corporate downsizing is not confined to businesses abroad; local business leaders in Bangladesh are adopting the same strategy.

According to PwC’s 29th CEO Survey (Bangladesh edition), more than a third of local chief executives expect AI to directly eliminate junior-level roles within their companies over the next three years, while three in ten CEOs anticipate cuts at the mid-level. The primary motivation is financial: more than a quarter of surveyed Bangladeshi executives reported that adopting AI had already reduced their operational costs.

When small and medium-sized business owners in North America and Europe apply this same cost-cutting approach to freelance platforms, junior workers in South Asia feel the pressure immediately. Instead of paying a beginner freelancer five or ten dollars an hour to format a database or crop an image, overseas clients can use their own software subscriptions to handle these tasks in-house.

The freelancer’s catch-22

To make a living as a freelancer, you face a classic catch-22: clients will not hire you unless you have good ratings on your profile, but you cannot get good ratings unless someone hires you first.

For years, beginners solved this problem through a simple strategy. They took on very easy, low-paying micro-tasks, such as managing data in an Excel spreadsheet or transcribing audio files. It was poorly paid work, but the purpose was never to make them rich. Instead, it was to earn ten or twenty quick five-star reviews. Once the platform’s algorithm recognised that a new profile was reliable, the freelancer could start bidding on better, higher-paying jobs.

Image As AI increasingly automates routine tasks, companies can assign work previously handled by several junior employees to a single experienced professional, reducing opportunities for fresh graduates. Photo: Collected



Today, that stepping stone is disappearing. When small business owners in the United States or Europe can paste a messy spreadsheet into ChatGPT or Claude and have it organised in thirty seconds, they are less likely to post those beginner-level gigs in the first place. To make matters worse, platforms such as Upwork require freelancers to spend real money on digital tokens called ‘Connects’ just to submit job applications. Because fewer simple tasks are available, hundreds of desperate beginners end up bidding on the same limited number of listings.

The irony of AI detectors

This corporate calculation hits fresh university graduates with immediate force. In a country where formal white-collar employment is scarce, freelance content writing and digital marketing have long served as important sources of income for students and recent graduates trying to support themselves.

Adiba Tuba, a graduate and freelance content writer, has witnessed this contraction first-hand. She points out that the fundamental staffing equation for entry-level work has changed. At the same time, beginners face another unfair technological hurdle: automated AI detection tools. Tuba explains that even when young writers compose entirely original articles based on their own ideas, imperfect algorithmic detectors frequently flag their work as AI-generated simply because of standard sentence structures or common vocabulary. Junior writers find themselves in an impossible position: clients demand that they use AI for efficiency, yet penalise them when automated checkers suspect algorithmic assistance.

Tuba emphasises that when corporate managers prioritise cost-effectiveness over creative nuance, beginners lose out entirely. Companies now seek human creativity at an automated pace, resulting in graduates being thrust into an increasingly aggressive competition over who can write the most effective prompts and manipulate AI models most successfully. In a developing economy already burdened by severe job scarcity, the loss of these flexible side gigs leaves students and fresh graduates without an important economic safety net.

The limits of prompts

Farjana Nupur, a third-year fashion design student at Shanto-Mariam University of Creative Technology and an apprentice pattern maker, sees this pressure first-hand. While early-career designers are increasingly expected to use AI to speed up their work, she warns that relying entirely on automation strips away genuine creativity and the human touch needed in both design and comfort. In fashion, thoughtful planning still demands manual drafting on paper and prototyping with test fabrics. A prompt cannot fully calculate how a garment moves on a real body, nor can it adequately account for fabric breathability, local humidity or the physical comfort experienced by a wearer.

Algorithms can generate designs by drawing on patterns and images found across the internet, but they may miss the emotional connection, cultural context and copyright considerations that authentic design requires. When designers rely on AI as a complete shortcut simply to deliver work faster, the result is often shallow and unoriginal. For young women trying to build lasting creative careers, being pushed to replace hands-on craftsmanship with algorithmic speed risks sacrificing the very human care and originality that make their work valuable in the first place.

Why upskilling isn’t enough

Industry observers and government agencies frequently offer a simple solution: freelancers must upskill and learn to work alongside AI. A study by Bangladesh’s National Skills Development Authority (NSDA) warned that the country's freelance workforce remains heavily concentrated in routine tasks while lagging far behind in advanced disciplines such as machine learning and programming. That deficit has reportedly contributed to Bangladesh slipping to 29th place in global freelancing rankings.

For many female freelancers in Bangladesh, however, keeping up with this technological race is an uphill struggle. Learning advanced AI workflows can require computers with high-end dedicated graphics cards, costing well over Tk 100,000, as well as monthly subscriptions paid in foreign currency. Many young women do not have access to dual-currency bank cards, and families are often hesitant to invest substantial household funds in a woman's home-based freelancing work. Afrin emphasises that staying relevant in today's market demands rapid adaptation, sophisticated prompt engineering and the financial ability to afford paid software tools. For her own work, she relies heavily on Claude, an advanced AI model that offers paid monthly subscriptions. The quality of the final output depends heavily on how well the user writes prompts and structures instructions. As Afrin warns, anyone who fails to keep pace with these rapidly changing tools risks being pushed out of the industry entirely.

Time is an equally difficult hurdle. While male freelancers may have greater opportunities to spend entire days uninterrupted in co-working spaces or private rooms learning to code and experimenting with new software, female freelancers often have to fit their professional work around cooking, childcare and other household responsibilities.

Image Protecting Bangladeshi women's participation in the digital economy requires an urgent overhaul of national skills development strategies, with greater attention to AI literacy, accessible training and the barriers faced by female workers.



The convergence of global hiring freezes, local corporate downsizing and the lived experiences of female freelancers reveals a growing crisis across Bangladesh's digital economy. The traditional apprenticeship model of freelancing, in which a novice could begin with simple, low-risk gigs and gradually build the experience needed for higher-paying work, has been undermined at its very foundation. Despite this shift, many public development initiatives and non-profit training programmes for women continue to teach increasingly outdated skills, such as basic typing, manual data entry and the creation of simple Canva templates.

If Bangladesh is to protect women's economic participation in the digital age, national skills development strategies must be overhauled immediately. Training programmes must move beyond basic computer literacy to include AI workflow integration, prompt design and practical software orchestration, while also recognising and valuing specialised, hands-on human craftsmanship that algorithms cannot easily replace.

title: The secret life of fungi and why Bangladesh should care
text:
When we hear the word fungus, two very different images often come to mind. One is that of a troublesome organism responsible for skin infections; the other is that of a remarkable group of organisms that have given humanity some of its most important medicines.

Fungi have given humanity penicillin, the pioneering antibiotic discovered in 1928. Although modern penicillin injections and tablets have been modified substantially over the decades to improve their effectiveness and combat resistance, penicillin remains an important weapon against infectious diseases. At the other end of the spectrum are familiar fungal infections such as pityriasis versicolor, known in Bangladesh by names such as Solong or Suli, and dermatophytosis, commonly called ringworm or Dad. Although generally not life-threatening, these conditions can cause considerable discomfort and cosmetic concern.

Image A colourful reishi mushroom, possibly a Ganoderma species, growing in the National Botanical Garden in Mirpur. Photo: Reza Khan

So, are fungi our friends or our foes? The answer is far more complex and intriguing than this simple distinction suggests.

From bang-er chhata to a kingdom of life

In Bangladesh, mushrooms are commonly known as ব্যাঙের ছাতা (bang-er chhata, or “frog's umbrella”) and fungi as ছত্রাক (chatrak). For generations, mushrooms have often been regarded as strange, umbrella-like growths that suddenly appear after rain on damp soil, decaying wood or even old food.

They are frequently associated with dirt, decay and disease and are therefore dismissed as useless or even harmful. But this familiar perception conceals an extraordinary world.

For a long time, fungi were grouped with plants in textbooks. We now know that they belong to neither the plant nor the animal kingdom. They constitute a separate kingdom of life, with a biology distinct from that of either.

Plants manufacture their own food through photosynthesis. Animals ingest food. Fungi do neither. Instead, they release enzymes into their surroundings and absorb nutrients from the organic material they break down.

This seemingly simple way of obtaining food gives fungi one of the most important jobs on Earth.

Image The hidden heroes of the soil: How fungi sustain life on Earth. AI-generated illustration.

Nature's great recyclers

Imagine a forest without fungi.

Leaves would accumulate on the ground. Fallen branches and dead trees would remain for years. Animal remains and crop residues would build up, while many of the nutrients locked inside this organic material would remain unavailable to plants. Fungi help prevent this.

They are among nature's greatest decomposers, breaking down dead leaves, fallen trees, animal remains and agricultural residues. As they digest this material, they release nutrients back into the soil, making them available to plants and other organisms. As such, fungi do more than simply remove nature's waste.

Their activity contributes to the formation and stabilisation of humus, the dark, carbon-rich component of healthy soil. Humus improves soil structure, helps retain moisture and stores nutrients. Fungal activity also helps bind soil particles into aggregates, creating spaces through which air and water can circulate. In simple terms, healthy fungi help build healthy soil, and healthy soil supports healthy forests, grasslands and agriculture.

Image One of the most common types of fungi in Bangladesh, bracket fungi of the genus Ganoderma, grow on dead trees or tree bark. Photo: Reza Khan

Bangladesh: A country made for fungi

Bangladesh provides exceptionally favourable conditions for fungal life. Its warm climate, high humidity and long monsoon season, combined with abundant vegetation and organic matter, create an environment where fungi can flourish.

They occur almost everywhere, including in forests, wetlands, agricultural fields, village homesteads and gardens. Even the mould growing on damp walls, leather items, bread or stored grains during the rainy season is a visible reminder that fungi are constantly around us. Yet people usually notice fungi only when they become troublesome.

Farmers contend with fungal diseases affecting rice, wheat, sugarcane, vegetables and fruits. People encounter ringworm, dandruff and other fungal conditions. These impacts are certainly real and, in some cases, economically important. However, they represent only a small fraction of the fungal world.

Judging all fungi by these examples would be like judging all birds by the birds that eat crops.

Image A type of toadstool, locally known as Banger Chhata, possibly a Lentinus species, at the National Botanical Garden in Mirpur. Photo: Reza Khan

The hidden partnership beneath our feet

Perhaps the most remarkable fungal story is not visible at all. Many fungi form intimate partnerships with plant roots, known as mycorrhizae, literally meaning “fungus-root”.

The main body of a fungus is usually not the mushroom that we see above the ground. It is a vast network of microscopic threads called hyphae. A mass of these threads forms a mycelium, which can spread through soil, leaf litter or moist wood.

In a mycorrhizal association, fungal hyphae extend far beyond the reach of ordinary plant roots. They explore tiny spaces in the soil and help plants obtain water and nutrients, particularly relatively immobile nutrients such as phosphorus, as well as nitrogen and other minerals. In return, the plant provides the fungus with carbon-rich compounds produced through photosynthesis.

It is a remarkable biological exchange: the plant provides carbon, while the fungus provides access to soil resources. The relationship is widespread. Estimates suggest that roughly 80 per cent of land plant species form mycorrhizal associations, although the precise proportion varies among plant groups and types of mycorrhizae.

What we see above ground, whether a forest, crop field, grassland or garden, is therefore only half the story. Beneath it lies a largely invisible fungal world intertwined with plant roots.

Image Possibly a mauve elfcup fungus, tentatively identified as a Sarcoscypha species, in the Hum Hum Waterfall area of Moulvibazar. Photo: Reza Khan

How much life is hidden in a handful of soil?

This raises an intriguing question: how much fungal life exists beneath our feet?

There is no single answer. Fungal abundance varies enormously between forests, grasslands, gardens and cultivated fields. It changes with soil depth, season, moisture, crop type and land management practices.

Scientific studies have measured fungal hyphal lengths ranging from only a few metres to hundreds of metres per gram of dry soil, depending on the ecosystem and the organisms being measured.

For example, one study of cultivated soils reported approximately 100–200 metres of fungal hyphae per gram of dry soil under conventional cultivation, compared with around 340–360 metres under organic cultivation.

This means that even a small handful of healthy soil can contain an astonishing length of microscopic fungal threads. Multiplied across thousands or millions of grams of soil, their combined length can become enormous, potentially reaching many kilometres within a cubic metre of soil, depending on the ecosystem and fungal density.

Claims of “millions of kilometres of fungal hyphae in a cubic metre of soil” should therefore not be presented as a universal measurement for Bangladesh unless supported by direct field research. Such figures are better regarded as illustrations of the potential scale of these hidden networks.

Image A fungus resembling the snow fungus (Tremella fuciformis) in Lawachhara Forest, Moulvibazar. Photo: Reza Khan

When we break the underground network

The fungal world beneath our feet is powerful, but it is also vulnerable to destruction.

Intensive land management can disrupt it. Repeated tillage physically breaks fungal networks, while changes in soil chemistry and excessive use of certain fertilisers or pesticides can alter fungal communities and mycorrhizal relationships.

The effects are not always the same. They depend on the chemical involved, its concentration, soil conditions, crop type, fungal species and management system. This is why protecting soil biodiversity means much more than protecting the visible organisms living in the soil. We must also protect the living infrastructure beneath it.

A field may appear quiet and lifeless, but beneath its surface, millions of microscopic threads may be recycling nutrients, exploring the soil and working in partnership with plants.

The fungal factory underground

The mushroom that suddenly appears after rain is only the visible part of a much larger organism. The mushroom is essentially the fruiting body, a temporary reproductive structure rather like the fruit of a tree. The main body of the fungus is usually the hidden mycelial network.

This underground fungal factory can spread through soil and wood, decompose organic material and interact intimately with plant roots using microscopic, thread-like hyphae.

Fungi therefore occupy a remarkable position in ecosystems. They are simultaneously decomposers, soil builders, plant partners and, in some circumstances, agents of disease.

They also play an important role in the global carbon cycle. By influencing the decomposition of organic matter, fungi help determine whether carbon remains stored in soil or is released back into the atmosphere. Their activities are consequently relevant to climate change and ecosystem stability.

Image Bracket or shelf fungi, possibly Microporus species, growing on a dead branch in the National Botanical Garden in Mirpur. Photo: Reza Khan

From forest floor to environmental clean-up

The usefulness of fungi does not stop at the soil. Some fungal species naturally suppress insect pests and may provide environmentally friendly alternatives to certain chemical pesticides. Other fungi can help break down pollutants, including petroleum products and toxic substances, offering promising possibilities for environmental clean-up.

Image Milky mushrooms cultivated in Bangladesh. AI-generated illustration.

Fungi as food

Many edible mushrooms contain protein, fibre, vitamins and antioxidants. Mushroom cultivation has expanded steadily in Bangladesh, creating opportunities for both nutrition and livelihoods.

For a country with a large population and limited agricultural land, mushrooms are particularly interesting because they can be cultivated in relatively small spaces using suitable organic materials. Thus, the humble mushroom that many people dismiss as “ব্যাঙের ছাতা” can be both a biological wonder and an economic resource.

The fungal contribution to medicine

Perhaps the most dramatic demonstration of the importance of fungi came from medicine. The discovery of penicillin transformed modern medicine. Since then, fungi have contributed to the development of numerous antibiotics and other biologically important compounds.

This is a striking reminder that organisms which may appear insignificant, unpleasant or even threatening can hold enormous value for humanity. The lesson extends far beyond medicine: we cannot know the value of a species until we understand it.

Bangladesh's forgotten fungal diversity

Here lies one of Bangladesh's greatest problems.

Despite the country's favourable climate and extraordinary biological richness, fungi remain among its least-studied groups of organisms. Compared with birds, mammals and flowering plants, our knowledge of fungal diversity is extremely limited. Large gaps remain in our understanding of forest fungi, soil fungi, mycorrhizal associations, medicinal species and the role of fungi in ecosystem and climate processes.

This scientific neglect matters. Bangladesh depends heavily on fertile soils, productive agriculture and functioning ecosystems. All of these are influenced by fungi.

Image A coprophilous (dung-loving) fungus growing on elephant dung in a degraded sal forest in Sherpur. Photo: Reza Khan

When nutrients remain locked in dead organic matter, fungi help release them. When soils need structure and organic matter, fungi contribute to their formation. When plants seek nutrients and water beyond the immediate reach of their roots, fungal partners may help them. When forests regenerate, fungal communities are part of the biological system supporting that process.

Fungi are therefore not optional accessories to nature. They are foundational components of it.

Image A fungus resembling a bonnet mushroom, growing on damp, decaying tree bark. Photo: Reza Khan

Time to look beneath our feet

Bangladesh should begin to give fungi the scientific attention they deserve. A national effort to document fungal diversity could be incorporated into biodiversity surveys, particularly in forests, wetlands, agricultural landscapes and other natural habitats. Research on soil fungi and mycorrhizal relationships could improve our understanding of soil health and sustainable agriculture.

Driven by rising demands for food production, many farmers apply chemical inputs, particularly fungicides, insecticides and unbalanced chemical fertilisers, at rates far exceeding recommended limits. This practice is severely disrupting the country's delicate agricultural ecosystems, highlighting an urgent need for sustainable alternatives to this destructive cycle.

Safe and scientifically guided mushroom cultivation should continue to be encouraged where appropriate, both as a source of food and as a livelihood opportunity.

At the same time, conservation policies should recognise the habitats that fungi depend upon. Leaf litter, fallen branches, dead wood and decaying organic matter are not simply signs of an untidy forest. They are essential components of fungal habitats and nutrient cycling.

Perhaps most importantly, fungi should become part of the way we think about biodiversity.

We have traditionally looked at forests from above: trees, birds, mammals, reptiles and insects. Nevertheless, a forest is also a world beneath our feet, a world of roots, microbes, hyphae and mycelia that keeps the visible ecosystem functioning.

The neglected villain is actually a silent hero

Fungi are far more than mould on bread or organisms that cause skin disease.

They are nature's recyclers, builders of soil, partners of plants, regulators of carbon, sources of food, potential tools for environmental restoration and producers of life-saving medicines. The mushroom is merely the part we see.

The real fungal world is largely hidden beneath the surface, quietly working day and night.

For generations, we have often regarded fungi as a nuisance or a sign of decay. It is time to look at them differently. The so-called neglected villain may, in fact, be one of Bangladesh's most important silent allies.

The sooner we begin to understand, study and protect this hidden kingdom of life, the stronger and more sustainable Bangladesh's environmental future can become.

Dr Reza Khan is a wildlife biologist and conservationist with over four decades of experience in wildlife research, zoo management and biodiversity conservation in Bangladesh and the United Arab Emirates. He has worked extensively in wildlife rescue, sanctuary management and community-based conservation initiatives.
