Durgabardi is derived from two words: Durga, the goddess, and bardi (or bari), meaning home or abode. Literally, therefore, it means "the abode of Durga." The name suggests that the village may once have had a substantial Hindu population. Indeed, my grandfather often spoke of Hindu families who left the area around the time of Partition in 1947 and continued to migrate throughout the 1950s and 1960s. By the time I was born, only a small Hindu community remained, but the village still carried traces of an older, more diverse social landscape.

The Ariyal Kha was immense in those days. Even now, when I revisit the village in memory, I see not a river but a presence, broad and commanding, flowing past our lives with quiet authority. Though Durgabardi stood only about ten kilometres from Madaripur town, it felt far more remote. Electricity belonged to another world, one that had not yet reached us.

Life followed the rhythms of daylight. Supper was usually eaten between Maghrib and Esha prayers. Soon afterwards, lamps were extinguished and conversations faded. By 8 o'clock, most villagers had surrendered to sleep. The darkness was almost complete, broken only by moonlight, starlight, and the occasional flicker of a hurricane lantern. Against such a backdrop, Durga Puja arrived like a small miracle.

For five days, the village stepped outside its ordinary routine. The Hindu community, perhaps ten or fifteen families in all, including two prosperous and respected households, organised the festival. Today, none of those families remains in the village. Time, migration, and history have erased their presence.

Yet, in those days, the Puja belonged to more than the Hindu community. The mandap was theirs, but the celebration belonged to everyone. Muslim families visited in large numbers. Elderly men spent long evenings in conversation there. Women arrived with children. Young boys and girls roamed freely in groups. Nobody spoke of communal harmony because such language seemed unnecessary. Participating in one another's festivals and sharing one another's joys were simply part of village life.

The mandap itself would seem modest by contemporary standards. There were no elaborate themes, artistic concepts, or competitions for grandeur. The idol stood beneath a simple structure decorated with restrained embellishments. Yet to my four-year-old eyes, it was magnificent. Its appeal lay not in spectacle but in the excitement, it generated in a village accustomed to darkness and routine.

At night, hajack lanterns illuminated the grounds with an almost magical brilliance. Even today, I can hear the cadenced pumping needed to keep them burning. Every so often someone would attend to a lantern, and its glow would flare again, pushing back the darkness gathering beyond the festival grounds. Beneath a samiyana, villagers sat on thick mattresses spread across the earth. Conversations drifted through the cool autumn air while children ran about tirelessly. The atmosphere was festive yet intimate, lively yet unpretentious.

The rituals were conducted by Bishu Kaka, a purohit brought from nearby Chandibardi, where there was a monastery. To me, he seemed an important and faintly mysterious figure. His chants, carried through the mandap's single loudspeaker, floated across the village night, mingling with the sounds of crickets, distant conversations, and the murmur of the river. Though I understood nothing of the rituals, I found the atmosphere captivating.

For us children, however, religion was never the main attraction.

We were far more interested in the prasad.

Beside the mandap, Kanu Dada, the village moira, worked tirelessly preparing sweets throughout the festival. The air around his workspace always seemed fragrant with sugar and milk, drawing us irresistibly towards it. Because my grandfather was one of the festival's patrons and a highly esteemed figure in the village, I enjoyed a small but meaningful privilege. I often received more prasad than I could possibly consume. Such abundance was never wasted. I happily shared it with my friends, who were always delighted to benefit from my good fortune.

Some memories survive through taste.

Others endure through sound.

The loudspeaker served many functions. When Bishu Kaka was not reciting mantras and stotras, it played songs. Most have disappeared from memory. One has remained.

Madhumalati dake aay.

Even today, merely hearing the title awakens a curious tenderness. At four, I knew nothing about music and certainly nothing about Sandhya Mukhopadhyay. Yet somehow the song lodged itself deep within me. Years later, when my father bought a National Panasonic cassette player, he also purchased a cassette that included the song. A lifelong lover of theatre who had once played the title role in village productions of Siraj-ud-Daulah that I was fortunate enough to watch, he listened to it often.

For children, though, the mela remained the true highlight of Puja.

Beginning around Maha Ashtami and continuing until Bijoya Dashami, it transformed an ordinary field into a kingdom of wonder. Vendors arrived in the afternoon and packed up before sunset, yet those few hours felt endless. Every stall promised discovery. There were clay toys, earthen pots, sweets, chanachur, and the iconic pink packets of Nabisco Glucose biscuits. Traders came from Madaripur town carrying spinning tops, tin cars, inexpensive plastic toys, household goods, and countless treasures that appeared priceless to a child.

Among all my childhood possessions, few brought me greater joy than the toy car I acquired from that mela. The purchasing process was wonderfully simple. During the afternoon, I would select what I wanted; later, my grandfather would settle the accounts with the vendors.

Then came Dashami.

What saddened us was not the departure of the goddess. We were sad because the fair would end, the lights would disappear, and village life would return to its familiar rhythm.

Nevertheless, we joined the immersion procession. Walking nearly four kilometres towards the Kumar River near Charmuguria, we followed the idol on its final journey. By evening, the goddess was consigned to the water, and the festival came to an end.

Today, Durga Puja is grander, brighter, and more spectacular than anything we could have imagined in 1970. Corporate sponsorship, artistic innovation, media attention, and modern technology have transformed it into a major cultural event. Such change is perhaps inevitable.

Yet what I miss is not the absence of grandeur.

It is the presence of simplicity.

I miss the lantern light, the single loudspeaker, the shared mattresses beneath the samiyana, and Kanu Dada preparing sweets beside the mandap. I miss a festival that seemed to grow naturally out of village life rather than one carefully staged for display.

Most of all, I miss the people.

Many are gone now. Some have passed away; others have left the village forever. The Hindu families who once organised the festival have disappeared from Durgabardi's landscape, leaving behind only memories and a village name that still recalls an earlier chapter of its history. The child who wandered through the mela with boundless excitement has vanished too.

And yet, every autumn, when the air carries the faint promise of festival season, I find myself returning to that village beside the Ariyal Kha. In memory, the hajack lanterns are still burning. The loudspeaker is still playing Madhumalati dake aay.

A forgotten door opens.

The lantern-lit mandap returns.

The aroma of sweets returns.

The mela returns.



And with them returns a village that exists now only in memory, yet whose light has never entirely gone out.



Ahmed Ahsanuzzaman is professor of English and Director, Kazi Nazrul Islam and Abbasuddin Ahmed Research and Study Centre (KNIAARSC) at Independent University, Bangladesh (IUB). He can be reached at: [email protected]

title: The beating heart of Durga Puja
text:
Inside the dimly lit courtyard of the ancient Ramna Kali Mandir, the scent of burning incense, its smoke curling through the air, and the rhythmic beating of the dhak lend an ethereal quality to the atmosphere. Dusk settles on Maha Shashthi, and the priest begins offering the first Sandhya Aarti to Goddess Durga.

The slow, heavy thuds of the dhak initially match the measured arcs of the priest’s panchapradip. Then the dhakis shift to mid-tempo patterns, alternating deep beats with sharp, wooden rim shots.

Image

Suddenly, the drums explode into a deafening crescendo, transforming the solemn ritual into an electric celebration.

There is a saying among Bangalee Hindu devotees: “Dhak chhara Durga Puja hoy na” -- Without the dhak, Durga Puja is incomplete.

A large, barrel-shaped wooden drum wrapped in animal hide, the dhak is the literal heartbeat of the ritual. When dhakis strike its hide, the sound is not just heard but felt, vibrating through the chest.

Image

From the delicate rhythms of Chakshudaan (when a priest paints the eyes onto the clay goddess) to the high-energy tempos fuelling the Dhunuchi Naach (dramatic dance where devotees balance smoking pots of burning incense in a trance-like state) and from the frenetic Sandhi Puja (the festival's holiest hour) to the melancholic Visarjan (when the idol is finally immersed into the river) -- the dhak remains the pulse beating across the sacred rituals integral to Durga Puja celebrations.

Yet, this centuries-old craft is sustained by a class of traditional musicians who are navigating a modern world where legacy is fighting a losing battle against the cost of living in a megacity.

Image Photo: Sazzad Ibne Sayed

For Binoy Das, 35, the five days of the festival offer a brief, transcendent escape from his everyday life. A garment factory worker in Gazipur, he travels to the capital every autumn to perform as a seasonal drummer at Ramna Kali Mandir, bringing with him a seven-member troupe that includes a sanai (traditional oboe) player, a flautist, and a bell player.

None of them are full-time musicians. They are salon owners and agricultural labourers who put down their scissors and sickles and pick up their instruments when the festival arrives.

Binoy has been a dhaki for 14 years. This year, he will receive Tk 18,000 for his performance, an amount he says isn’t enough for five days of intense physical labour in an inflation-weary economy.

Image Photo: Shahrear Kabir Heemel

“Considering the cost of living in Dhaka and the quality of my work, I expected more,” Binoy admits candidly. “I had a better offer in Cumilla, but I didn’t go out of loyalty to this mandir.”

“It’s devotion to my craft and to Goddess Durga that has kept me going for more than a decade,” Binoy says, his eyes lighting up as the evening prayers begin. “The feeling I get when I play in front of Durga is otherworldly.”

Across the city at the Dhakeshwari National Temple, the epicentre of the country’s celebrations, a different group of dhakis speak of similar devotion.

Leading the temple’s drummers is Shanti Ranjan Das, 70. He is the senior-most dhaki, having slung the heavy wooden instrument over his shoulder for 45 years. Alongside him are Tapan Chandra Das, 47, and Ripon Chandra Das, 42, both permanent employees at the temple.

Image

Ripon takes home a fixed monthly salary of Tk 8,000.

“I learned the craft from my father at the age of 17,” Ripon says.

To supplement his income, he manages a local “band party” that performs on demand at weddings and household pujas.

“My devotion to the craft and to Goddess Durga, and my wish to uphold my father’s legacy, have been my guiding forces all these years.”

But that legacy may stop with him. His 21-year-old son, Shaon Chandra Das, watched his father struggle and chose a different path. He now works as a journalist at a local newspaper.

Image

The younger generation’s reluctance to inherit the drumsticks is compounded by a shift in the seasonal migration of artists across the country. Historically, the capital has been the destination of choice for seasonal performers during Durga Puja.

“There was once a time when dhakis from all over the country would come to Dhaka during Durga Puja in search of work and stay until Kali Puja,” Ripon recalls. “There was better pay here than in the suburbs and villages.”

Now, a reverse seasonal migration is occurring as urban expenses rise. “Nowadays, they’re reluctant to come to Dhaka because the costs outweigh the pay,” Ripon explains. “There are better opportunities in suburban towns where puja organisers backed by wealthy donors offer better pay to employ local dhakis.”

The financial anxieties of the drummers stand in sharp contrast to the festival’s global profile.

Image Dancers portray the mythical battle between Goddess Durga and the demon Mahishasura at Dhakeshwari National Temple in the capital yesterday, marking Mahalaya, which heralds the arrival of Durga Puja -- one of the biggest religious festivals of the Hindu community. The performance depicts the goddess’s triumph over evil. Photos: Mehedi Hasan

In 2021, UNESCO inscribed Durga Puja on its Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity, recognising the festival’s extraordinary cultural value and the many traditional art forms that sustain it.

Heritage, however prestigious, cannot guarantee livelihoods.

As the nights of Durga Puja unfold across Dhaka, the city’s temples continue to pulse with the familiar rhythms of the dhak. Worshippers sway to its cadence. Priests move in step with its tempo. Children watch in fascination.

Few pause to consider the uncertain future of the men producing those sounds.

For now, the beat endures.

For five autumn days, the dhakis will breathe life into the festival, sustaining a tradition that has endured for generations, even as the heartbeat of their own profession grows fainter with each passing year.

title: A Goddess, a home, and a culture
text:
Every autumn, Durga arrives in Bengal with her children, weapons held across ten hands, and a lion crouched at her feet. To the wider scriptural world, she is Mahishasuramardini—the terrifying, ten-armed sovereign forged to crush cosmic chaos.

Yet within the Bengali imagination, her armour softens into something profoundly intimate: she is Uma, the child returning to her maternal hearth (bapbari) for a fleeting visit before her inevitable departure. This meeting of cosmic power and domestic kinship lies at the heart of Durga Puja, a festival where an unapproachable deity is received with the warmth of a family reunion.

Image

The first inception of the grand celebration of Durga Puja unfolded under distinct political and sociological limitations.

Raja Kangshanarayana of Rajshahi’s Tahirpur played a pivotal role in bringing Durga Puja to Bengal as it is known today. Living during the late 16th century, (It is to be noted that some historians dispute that the Durga Puja dates back to 1480), the feudal administrator and nobleman sought to perform a grand, sovereign-tier sacrifice—traditionally the Rajsuya or Ashwamedha Yagya. He was advised, however, that such royal Vedic horse or imperial sacrifices were impossible or forbidden in the modern iron age (Kali Yuga).

Image

To establish his supreme political authority and spiritual merit instead, he turned to the counsel of his court scholar Rameshwar Bhattacharya and chose the autumn worship of Goddess Durga as the ultimate, all-inclusive alternative for his worship. By orchestrating a magnificent, multi-lakh-rupee public spectacle that united scriptural grandeur with broad societal participation, Kangshanarayana created a monumental precedent that permanently reshaped the cultural and ritual landscape of the Bengali delta.

Image

Yet, whether Kangshanarayana’s celebration was truly the first remains a matter of historical debate, with alternative accounts pointing to figures like Bhabananda Mazumdar of Nadia in 1606 or regional landlords in Malda and Dinajpur.

What began as a grand, aristocratic enterprise resembling a Rajsuya or Ashwamedha Yagya—requiring mammoth wealth, resources, and manpower—gradually transitioned from elite zamindari courtyards into the collective, democratic, cultural, and communal fabric of the Bengali public sphere.

Image





Despite its democratisation into modern community-owned (Sarbajanin) celebrations, the underlying ritual grammar of Durga Puja retains an astonishingly complex, paradoxical materiality, remaining adaptive and always open to improvisations. Beyond the vast inventory required for the sacred Maha Snaan—such as waters from oceans and holy sites, precious metals, and specific soils like Varaha Danta Mrittika from a boar's teeth—the ritual demands Punya Mati, or sacred soil collected directly from the doorway of a sex worker.

Image

For rulers and landed families, an elaborate puja could display wealth, prestige and political authority. Raja Krishnachandra of Nadia became known for patronage of goddess worship. Later, Nabakrishna Deb’s puja in Calcutta after the East India Company’s victory at Plassey in 1757 entered popular history as the Company Puja. Such celebrations brought priests, artists, musicians, cooks and other specialists into the household courtyard, turning worship into a public spectacle even when the privilege of hosting it remained restricted.

Image

The festival’s social character changed as communities began pooling resources to organise worship. The barowari tradition and later sarbajanin pujas shifted the centre of celebration from the wealthy household towards the neighbourhood. This did not remove caste or class divisions, but it widened participation: the puja increasingly became something a community could organise and experience together. Its inclusiveness lay not in the disappearance of social boundaries, but in the many ways people could contribute to and gather around the festival.

Image

That capacity for adaptation remains visible in Bangladesh. Dhakeshwari National Temple, Ramna Kali Temple and Siddheshwari Kali Temple are among Dhaka’s important centres of goddess worship, while local temples, university halls and neighbourhood mandaps give the festival different expressions across the country.

Partition and migration changed the social landscape in which many pujas were organised. As old household and landed traditions weakened, community committees and collective contributions became increasingly important. Today, Bangladesh’s Durga Puja brings together established temple rituals and contemporary artistic interpretations.

Image

At the Gulshan–Banani Sarbajanin Puja Foundation in Dhaka, this year’s theme, Jalaj — born of water — places the goddess within the relationship between water and life. Theme artist Partho Protim Saha draws on water as a source of creation, linking the natural world to the goddess’s creative power. Such interpretations show how the festival can remain rooted in religious observance while responding to contemporary concerns. The mandap becomes a place where inherited beliefs and present-day ideas meet.

Image

That meeting begins long before the first day of worship. Bamboo and straw provide the structure of the image; clay gives it form, and the sculptor shapes the face that devotees will recognise as the Mother. Ritual traditions also prescribe particular materials and acts of preparation. In some parts of Bengal, punya mati — sacred earth associated with the threshold of a sex worker’s home — is included in the making of the image. The practice is not universal, and its use in Bangladesh should be confirmed locally, but its symbolism is significant: the sacred draws material from a social world that often excludes the people connected with it.

Image

When Mahalaya approaches, the painting of the goddess’s eyes, known as chokkhu daan, marks a particularly charged moment in the making of the image. The eyes give her a gaze; the figure that has taken shape through clay, paint and ornament is prepared for its ritual presence. Formal consecration follows its own rites, but the painting of the eyes has a powerful place in Bengali devotional imagination. The goddess is no longer simply being represented. She is being prepared to receive the attention, prayers and offerings of her devotees.

Image

For idol-maker Ratan Pal, who has worked in the tradition for more than 26 years, this work carries the weight of inheritance. Many image-makers, he says, enter the craft through their families and learn through knowledge passed from one generation to the next. “This is not a profession for us. We take it as a prayer,” he said, describing the process as one that continues to inspire new creative ideas. His words speak to a relationship between maker and deity that cannot be reduced to the construction of an image: the act of shaping Durga is itself part of the devotion.

Image

The completed goddess brings many traditions into one space. Priests recite Sanskrit verses; the dhak sounds; conch shells announce the rites; offerings, flowers, clothing and ornaments prepare her for worship. Around the central rituals, people gather to celebrate, and the festival’s cultural life cannot be separated from its religious meaning. It is through these practices that devotion becomes collective memory.

Image

In 2021, UNESCO inscribed Durga Puja in Kolkata on its Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity, recognising its public celebration and collaborative artistic traditions. The inscription applies to Kolkata, not Bangladesh, but the cultural practices it identifies — ritual, craftsmanship, performance and community participation — are also familiar across the border.

Image

In the end, the genius of the Bengali sensibility lies in its refusal to worship power from a distance. By weaving sacred earth, artistic expression, and domestic warmth into the fabric of absolute authority, the delta transformed a distant celestial warrior into an intimate mirror of human grief and joy. As the goddess’s eyes are painted at dawn, devotees do not merely gaze upon a deity; they see their own resilience, their shared history, and their eternal capacity for homecoming reflected back at them.

title: MT Hossain Institute: A fading chapter of Bangladesh’s cultural history
text:
A crumbling building on a sprawling railway compound along Fire Service Road in Lalmonirhat town stands as a fading reminder of the region’s rich cultural history. This is the historic MT Hossain Institute, once a major cultural hub of northern Bangladesh and home to one of the Indian subcontinent’s rare revolving theatre stages.

Established in 1905 as the Pierce Institute on around 2.73 acres of railway land, the institution was renamed in 1934 after railway ticket examiner MT Hossain, whose dedication and service earned him widespread respect among railway employees.

Naming such an institution after a local railway worker during British rule was considered highly unusual, as public institutions of the time were generally named after colonial officials.

The institute’s most remarkable feature is its revolving stage, built on a circular platform with an iron rail-and-wheel mechanism that allowed scenery to be changed without lowering the curtain.

During its heyday, the institute hosted theatre productions, musical performances, poetry recitals, literary gatherings and film screenings, attracting artists and cultural figures from across the country.

Veteran playwright Advocate Chittaranjan Roy, who performed there several times, said it was once considered a prestigious venue for cultural organisations.

Image Photo: S Dilip Roy /Star

“I acted here many times. Today, it breaks my heart to see this historic institution reduced to a skeleton,” he said.

Cultural activist Shamim Ahmed said, “It was simultaneously a theatre, cultural centre and cinema hall. It introduced modern entertainment to the people of Lalmonirhat," he recalled.

Researchers believe the institute also played an important social and cultural role before and after Bangladesh's 1971 Liberation War by fostering public awareness and strengthening community ties. However, from the 1980s onward, its activities gradually declined due to shrinking sponsored cultural programmes, the rise of television, declining public interest in theatre, inadequate funding and prolonged administrative neglect.

In 2017, a proposal to build an educational institution on the premises triggered protests from cultural activists and civil society members, eventually halting the plan. Heritage advocates have since demanded that the institute be declared a protected heritage site.

A theatre festival in 2019 and a folk festival in 2023 briefly revived activities there, but no comprehensive restoration has begun.

Architect Abeg Rahman completed an award-winning adaptive restoration proposal for the institute in 2024, documenting its historical significance and suggesting new cultural uses for the century-old building.

Image Photo: S Dilip Roy /Star

Sufi Mohammad, general secretary of the Sammilito Cultural Forum in Lalmonirhat, said they had been campaigning for years to revive the institute.

The Department of Archaeology says it is now working to bring the institute under its conservation programme.

As part of the initiative, the Ministry of Cultural Affairs has requested the Ministry of Railways to transfer ownership of the property before conservation work can begin, said Abu Sayeed Enam Tanvirul Islam, field officer of the department in the Rangpur Division.

Theatre historians consider the institute's revolving stage one of the last surviving historic revolving stages in South Asia, he said.

“The MT Hossain Institute was once the centre of cultural activities in northern Bangladesh. It possesses immense historical value and deserves preservation,” he added.

title: Panam city where history still whispers
text:
On the way to Sonargaon in Narayanganj, time seems to move backwards.

Leaving behind the bustle of the modern city, traffic congestion, and hurried lives, visitors suddenly find themselves in a quiet settlement where rows of old buildings, moss-covered walls, crumbling balconies, and shuttered windows make it feel as though history has stopped.

This is Panam City.

Once, horse-drawn carriages carrying wealthy merchants raced along its streets. Today, tourists walk those same roads through an abandoned town. The broken doors and windows of century-old buildings seem to wait for people who will never return.

Sonargaon was one of medieval Bengal’s most important commercial centres. Carrying that legacy, Panam City emerged during the 19th and early 20th centuries. Affluent Hindu merchants built their residences here, blending European colonial architecture with traditional Bangalee design.

Image

Elegant arches, intricate ornamentation, wrought-iron balconies, and decorative windows made every mansion a marker of prosperity.

Perhaps the most striking feature of Panam City is its silence. Standing here, it feels as though even the wind speaks. Sunlight filters through cracks in old walls, weeds grow on broken staircases, and birds perch along weathered cornices, as if narrating stories from another era.

Image

But Panam’s story is not only one of wealth. It is also a story of separation.

Following the Partition of India in 1947, residents gradually began leaving the town. After the Indo-Pakistan War of 1965, the migration of Hindu families left Panam largely deserted.

The houses that once echoed with celebrations, guests, and thriving business activities were abandoned. Over time, nature began to reclaim the city. Rainwater, tree roots, and decades of neglect have left visible scars on almost every structure.

Panam City’s main street is relatively short, yet the buildings lining both sides preserve centuries of architectural heritage. Each structure reflects a fusion of European colonial design, Mughal influences, and traditional Bengali craftsmanship.

According to Banglapedia, after the Mughals took control of Sonargaon in 1611, roads and bridges were built to connect the Panam area directly with the capital. Three brick bridges from the Mughal era still survive today: Panam Bridge, Dalalpur Bridge, and Panamnagar Bridge.

Image

Their locations, along with the canals surrounding Panam on three sides, suggest that the area once served as a suburb of a medieval city.

Modern Panam City developed largely through the commercial activities of the British East India Company and the Permanent Settlement introduced during British rule. Sonargaon became a major trading centre for cotton textiles, particularly English “thaan” cloth, giving rise to the new urban settlement of Panam.

During the 19th century, several wealthy Hindu landlords and merchants chose the area as their residence. The brick buildings that still stand today were their homes, with the earliest structures believed to have been built in the early 19th century and later ones in the late 19th and early 20th centuries.

Panam continued to expand and flourish until around the end of the Second World War.

Architecturally, the residential buildings in Panam can be classified into three main types: those centred on a grand hall, those built around an open courtyard, and hybrid designs.

Hall-centred houses featured lavish decorative elements, making the central hall the architectural focal point. Courtyard houses had rooms arranged around an open, paved courtyard surrounded by verandas with arched entrances. Most single-storey houses belonged to the third category, lacking both a central hall and a courtyard.

Today, the first thing visitors notice upon entering Panam City is its extraordinary tranquility. There is no urban noise, only birdsong and the gentle rustling of leaves. That silence has become Panam’s greatest charm.

Image

Last Friday, this correspondent spoke to a number of visitors at Panam City.

Md Anisuzzaman, a young visitor from Dhaka, said, “I’ve seen countless photographs of Panam City, but standing here is an entirely different experience. It feels like walking through history.”

Sushmita Roy, who travelled from Bandar in Narayanganj, said, “Many people don’t realise that Bangladesh has such magnificent historical sites. Coming here made me appreciate how rich our heritage truly is.”

Fazlur Rahman, who visited from Dhaka with his wife, said, “People travel abroad to explore historic cities, yet we have such an extraordinary place in our own country. If it were preserved more effectively, it could become a major attraction for international tourists.”

Local visitor Habibur Rahman, from Narayanganj, added, “I come here quite often, and every visit feels different. However, better cleanliness, more information boards, and trained guides would help visitors understand the site’s history much better.”

For many visitors, Panam City is more than a picturesque location for photography. It offers a rare chance to experience history firsthand. The weathered walls, broken wooden windows, and banyan trees growing from rooftops remind visitors that nature never leaves emptiness untouched.

Image

The Department of Archaeology is now responsible for preserving and maintaining Panam City. Still, many visitors believe restoring the buildings alone is not enough. They said regular maintenance, scientific conservation, wider research, and improved tourist-friendly infrastructure are equally essential.

Otherwise, they fear, this historic town may continue to deteriorate.

Amirul Islam Rajib, another visitor from Dhaka, said, “There are not enough resting areas, the number of guides is limited, and there is a lack of modern digital displays or audio guides explaining the site’s history. If Panam City could be integrated with local culture, traditional cuisine, and folk arts, it could become a complete tourism destination.”

Speaking to The Daily Star, Afroza Khan Mita, Regional Director of the Department of Archaeology, said, “We have undertaken a major project to make Panam City more visitor-friendly. Once the project receives approval, we expect to introduce a range of new facilities for tourists, which will significantly increase visitor numbers.”

As plans for the site’s future are discussed, the setting sun bathes the old buildings in golden light. In those final moments of the afternoon, Panam City becomes even more mysterious.

The warm glow on the weathered brickwork creates an unforgettable atmosphere. One cannot help but imagine that, a century ago, a merchant may have returned home under this very light, children may have played along these streets, or someone may have waited for a loved one from the balcony of one of these now-silent homes.

title: Old Dhaka’s Narinda wasn't always called Narinda!
text:
The Puran Dhaka locality of Narinda is no ordinary area. It is home to the oldest surviving mosque in the capital: Binat Bibi’s Mosque. Established in around 1456, it stands as a strong reminder that Dhaka is much older than just 400 years as some people think.

Our city dates back to pre-Mughal times; and Narinda, with this mosque, is a testament to that.

The area is historically important for commerce. To illustrate, the pages of history shows that the English had established a factory here in circa 1735.

But the twist is that the name Narinda is technically not original, even though we have heard our fathers and grandfathers call it Narinda.

Once upon a time, Narinda was called Narayandiah, meaning, island of the Narayan deity! Over time, this evolved into Narinda, sort of a distortion of the old name Narayandiah!

Sources- "Dacca: History and Romance in Place Names" by Azimusshan Haider; “Notes on the Antiquities of Dacca" by Sayid Aulad Hasan.

title: Farashganj: The testimony of French trade in Puran Dhaka
text:
What comes to mind when you think of Farashganj in Old Dhaka — chaos of the bazaars, loading and unloading of goods, or perhaps the elegant Northbrook Hall?

Or do you think of the French? Puran Dhaka is located thousands of kilometres away from France, but Farashganj brings it closer to us.

The word "Farash" means French and "ganj" means market, and hence, the name of the locality stands as a testimony of the French people and their businesses in Dhaka during the olden times.

In 1740, the French people had acquired permission to establish a "ganj" or market in Dhaka; the name "French Gunj" appears in a document from the year 1790.

In fact, before the famous Ahsan Manzil came into existence, the French used to have a factory in its place. Ahsan Manzil is quite near the Farashganj area.

The French had wrapped up those businesses and are long gone, but the presence they once had in our capital remains today through the name Farashganj!

Source- "Dacca: History and Romance in Place Names" by Azimusshan Haider

title: Ever wonder how the name Tikatuli came about?
text:
Tikatuli – have you ever stopped to ponder how this curious name came to be? Probably not, because the locality is all too familiar to even pause and think about.

But that’s exactly what this series intends to do! Welcome to “Naamer Araley Dhaka,” a project where each episode will explore the origin of a neighbourhood or street name in the capital.

For this first episode, our focus is on Tikatuli.

Once to upon a time, to meet the demand of hookah-manufacturing, there was a group of artisans who used to make “tikiya” (ember or charcoal tablets). And the place of these tikiya-makers eventually came to be known as Tikatuli!

These craftspeople took their artistry to a rather high level. The products were so light and exquisite that you could light up multiple embers with just one matchstick.

A curious detail regarding all this involves one tikiya-maker. He was mockingly nicknamed “Maharani ka Beta,” meaning Queen Victoria’s son!

Of course, Tikatuli is not the only area in Dhaka that gets its name from a trade or profession. What other names spring to mind?

Keep your eyes on The Daily Star’s Facebook page, and our website, for upcoming episodes!

Source: Kingbodontir Dhaka by Nazir Hossain

title: Punashcha Dhaka: Revisiting the city’s social and cultural past
text:
Dhaka has always been a city that returns to itself. Every alley, riverbank, and ruin seems to hold another story waiting to be rediscovered.

It is this endless wave of memories that Ridwan Akram’s book “Punashcha Dhaka: Charsha Bacharer Dhakar Samaj O Sanskriti” seeks to explore. Published by Kathaprokash, the book revisits more than 400 years of the capital’s social and cultural history, presenting Dhaka as a layered historical landscape.

The title “Punashcha Dhaka” itself announces a return. According to the author, writing about the city never truly concludes. The past often appears in small, overlooked details that have shaped Dhaka’s identity. Some stories remind us of the city’s golden past, while others trace its decline and transformation over time. Though they may sound like tales, they are rooted in history.

Akram structures the book thematically, allowing readers to explore Dhaka through different phases of its past. The chapters are arranged under sections such as Transport, Festivals, Administration, and Conflict. Through these categories, the author paints a mosaic of the city’s everyday life across centuries, its administrative structures, its cultural rhythms, and the professions and practices that once defined urban existence.

One of the book’s strengths is the historical anecdotes it brings to light. Dhaka became a Mughal provincial capital about 400 years ago, under Subahdar Islam Khan Chisti. The book revisits this period and raises curious questions about him, such as how he died in Dhaka and how his body was taken nearly 1,706 kilometres away to his final resting place.

The narrative also uncovers lesser-known chapters of the city’s history. According to the book, in 1790, foreign soldiers introduced horsecarriages for hire, marking an early chapter in public transportation in the city. The book also traces the origins of Ramna Park, which was first established during the Mughal era and has since witnessed many phases of the city’s historical transformation.

The book is complemented by historical photographs gathered from a variety of archival sources. Many come from the British Library’s collection, while others have been sourced from other repositories. These images add a visual dimension to the narratives, helping readers imagine the city’s transformations across time.

Speaking about the book, Akram emphasises the responsibility that comes with writing history. “Books live through detailed work, proper research and readers,” he explains. According to him, the task of a historical work is not only to document facts, but also to create a meaningful connection with its readers.

The author also notes that the history of Dhaka exists in pieces scattered across different sources. His effort, he says, was to gather those pieces together. “The history might be here and there, but I took the initiative to collect them,” he shares, adding that the work involved large-scale interviews and consultation with legitimate sources.

At the same time, Akram believes that historical writing must offer something fresh. “A book should give readers the taste of something new, something they may never have heard before.”

In fact, Punashcha Dhaka is not the result of a single period of writing. Rather, it is a compilation of his essays and research gathered over many years. “I did not write this in one sitting,” the author explains. “It is a collection that began many years ago, bringing together many of my writings about Dhaka’s history in one place.”

In that sense, Punashcha Dhaka works both as a collection of history and an invitation to rediscover the city. By bringing together archival sources, stories, and research, Ridwan Akram reminds readers that beneath Dhaka’s busy present lies a rich past that still echoes through its streets.

title: Rose Garden: a palace where legacy blooms
text:
Hidden within the bustling alleys in Old Dhaka’s Tikatuli lies a regal architectural gem -- the Rose Garden.

Built in the early 20th century, the palace that once reflected an elite lifestyle now carries the scent of history, the echoes of political discourse, and the essence of cultural heritage.

Image Photo: Sukanta Halder

Located on KM Das Lane, the Rose Garden now stands as a preserved heritage site and public entertainment centre.

The estate features an elegant white marble mansion exuding Greek architectural style, white marble sculptures, a field with an artificial fountain at the centre, a pond with a paved bank, and a lush green garden with rows of rose bushes, creating a mesmerising ambience of grandeur.

The ground floor of the palace consists of eight rooms, all currently closed. On the upper floor, four of the five rooms are open to visitors. Along the wooden staircase to the second floor, there are colourful glass designs that make the palace come alive in a play of light and shadow.

The palace features a large hall, which was once the ballroom, with every corner intricately adorned and the ceiling featuring chandeliers that are still ready to shine.

On one side of the palace is the Bengal Studio, where the Bangladeshi film “Harano Din” was shot.

Every day, a host of local and foreign visitors visit the Rose Garden.

Image Photo: Sukanta Halder

Shiuly Akter, a visitor, said, “The architecture of old houses and palaces always fascinates me. The Rose Garden is not just a palace. As I entered, I felt as if I were standing as a witness to time. Its serene beauty is enchanting. If anyone ever seeks tranquillity, history, and beauty, then an afternoon visit to the Rose Garden is highly recommended.”

Rajnin Farhana, another visitor, said, “I heard about the palace since it reopened. A number of my friends visited earlier and posted photos on social media. Now I came to visit the palace and take a lot of photos.”

Monowar Hossain, a local resident, said, “I was born and brought up in this area. The Rose Garden is the symbol of pride not only for our locality but for the whole country.”

The story of Rose Garden begins during the British era in 1931, when Rishikesh Das, a nouveau riche businessman, constructed the mansion.

Once, after being humiliated at a cultural gathering at Baldha Garden, Rishikesh decided to host his own events at a grand garden house. Due to the abundance of rose bushes, the estate was named “Rose Garden”.

However, before the decoration of the building could be completed, Rishikesh went bankrupt and had to sell the property in 1937 to Khan Bahadur Abdur Rashid. The mansion was then renamed “Rashid Manzil”.

Later, it came under the ownership of Kazi Mohammad Bashir (popularly known as Humayun Saheb) and subsequently to Kazi Abdur Rakib and his wife Laila Rakib.

The mansion is deeply entwined with Bangladesh’s political history. Following the Partition of India, many significant political meetings were held here, including the first informal meeting to establish the East Pakistan Awami Muslim League in 1949. Numerous renowned politicians and leaders from Bangladesh and India were hosted here.

In 1966, the property was leased to Bengal Studio. In 1993, the Rashid family regained ownership. In 2018, the Government of Bangladesh acquired the property for Tk 331 crore.

After 2022, the building was restored and reopened on July 30 last year. Now, visitors can enter the building from 11:00am till 6:00pm. It remains fully closed on Sundays. On Mondays, it remains open partially from 2:00pm to 6:00pm. Entry tickets are priced at Tk 30 for regular visitors and Tk 10 for students each.

Afroza Khan Mita, regional director of the Department of Archaeology, said the Rose Garden has seen a steady stream of local and foreign visitors since its reopening.

“In August and September last year alone, we earned a total of Tk 17 lakh from ticket sales. Clearly, there is immense public interest. The site offers Dhaka residents a peaceful retreat while also contributing to government revenue,” she said.

title: Decay threatens 250-yr-old Lalmonirhat mosque
text:
Worshippers at Nidaria Jame Mosque, a protected 18th-century monument in Lalmonirhat, are facing safety risks as parts of the boundary wall and a tin-shed veranda remain in a fragile condition due to a lack of renovation.

Declared a protected archaeological monument in 1994 by the Department of Archaeology, the over 250-year-old mosque at Kismat Nagarband village under Panchgram union has seen little visible repair work in recent years, locals and mosque authorities said.

They urged the immediate need for steps to ensure safe prayer facilities while preserving the historic structure.

Image

According to the Department of Archaeology, the three-domed mosque was built in 1762 by Mansur Khan, son of Masud Khan, as indicated by a Persian inscription engraved on a black stone on the front wall.

The rectangular structure features octagonal corner towers and three mihrabs on the western wall, reflecting Mughal-era architectural style.

Locals said the main structure has remained largely unchanged since its construction and has not undergone significant renovation for many years.

The boundary wall is now at risk of collapse, while a tin-shed veranda built beside the mosque is being supported with bamboo poles.

Due to limited space inside the mosque, many worshippers offer prayers on the veranda, which becomes unusable even during light rain, they said.

Hossain Ali, general secretary of the mosque committee, said the mosque cannot undertake any renovation work independently, as it is a protected monument.

“Since the mosque is under the Department of Archaeology, we cannot carry out development work on our own. We are communicating with the authorities concerned,” he said.

Imam Fazlul Karim said the mosque is architecturally significant, with thick walls and high domes giving it a distinctive character.

“Visitors from different parts of the country come here every day. Many of them offer prayers,” he said, adding that the committee has been urged repeatedly to improve facilities.

Abidur Rahman, a college teacher from Sirajganj who recently visited the site, said, “I have offered prayers in the historic mosque. The veranda and boundary wall require urgent renovation to ensure safety for worshippers.”

Contacted, Abu Sayeed Inam Tanvirul, field officer of the Rangpur divisional office of the Department of Archaeology, said any development work must follow the department’s guidelines to protect the monument’s original features.

“If the mosque committee wants to renovate the walls or veranda, they should contact us formally. We will provide the necessary guidance and assistance,” he said, adding that preservation of the heritage structure must remain the priority.

title: Your complete map to Bangladesh’s most iconic Mughal mosques
text:
Our country is blessed with beautiful mosques. Be it the Sultanate era mosques or the modern marvels, Bangladesh is dotted with these awe-inspiring places of worship that span many centuries. Among them, Mughal mosques are indeed an interesting chapter of our heritage.

In this holy month of Ramadan, Star Lifestyle presents to you a map of Bangladesh's prominent Mughal mosques — your essential list of mosques from this era that you should definitely visit.

We invite you to see this map, which took us about a month to create, and we invite you to visit these age-old buildings.

Along with the map, this article will give an idea about our research journey, providing you with more insights than just names and geography.

Image Illustration: Ashif Ahmed Rudro

Time capsule

Mughal mosques combine to form a rich time capsule, but which timeframe are we really looking into?

According to the book Mosque Architecture in Bangladesh, by Dr Abu Sayeed M Ahmed and Syed Zakir Hossain, Bengal was "conquered by Mughal rulers" in 1576. So, that is the beginning.

On the other hand, we can cut off the Mughal era at 1757 if we are very strict — an obvious year, due to the Empire's collapse surrounding the Battle of Palashi that was led by Nawab Sirajuddaula against the British.

Of course, the timeframe is up for debate. To exemplify, it can be stretched to 1857, and rightly so, because there was resistance to the "new" British East India Company regime. Nazly Chowdhury and Babu Ahmed wrote in Mughal Monuments of Bangladesh, "In 1857, the Sepoy Revolt broke out but was soon suppressed by iron hands... and the rule of the Mughals in India was finally ended."

Neither the beginning nor the end of the Mughal era happened overnight.

Given this context, even though we kept in mind the 1576-1757 time period, we prioritised those mosques that are the most Mughal-inclined in terms of architecture, reputation, etc., hence allowing flexibility for a few mosques that were likely established after the 1757 milestone.

Image Photo: Jawwad Sami Neogi

The splendour of Mughal mosques

We will spare you the technicalities and details, leaving them for architects and historians. It is best to visit the mosques in person to appreciate it. And now, you have the map to guide you there!

Three-domed structures are common, although variations regarding the number of domes can also be easily found. Facades are decorative. Four corner turrets (or small towers) reinforce elegance. Inside, cusped arches, floral motifs, and views of the domes above your head will strike a chord in your heart!

Image Photo: Shadab Shahrokh Hai

Mughal mosques stripped out of their Mughal vibe

However, it is saddening that many mosques of that era underwent mindless paintjobs, addition of tiles, extensions, etc. in modern times. Where such cases were severe, we dropped them out of our list.

In some cases, old structures have more or less been completely replaced by modern ones. For such mosques, the only major Mughal connection is in the collective memory of locals, history books, or the dates on the signboards. We have not included those buildings in our map as well.

Furthermore, there are several mosques that locals believe to be Mughal, but that fact cannot be ascertained from inscriptions (or lack thereof), architecture, or books of history. We have dropped most of those as well.

Therefore, this map indicates the most prominent ones that are worth visiting for the budding history buff.

Image Photo: Shadab Shahrokh Hai

The Dhaka dilemma

You may be furious to see that very few number of mosques from the Dhaka district have made it to our map. Well, control your rage, and look at the disclaimer at the bottom of the map: Old Dhaka is home to so many magnificent Mughal-era mosques that it was not possible for us to fit them all: Haji Khwaja Shahbaz Mosque, Khan Muhammad Mirdha Mosque, Khwaja Ambar Mosque, and Begum Bazar Mosque are some of the names that have every right to be included in the map, and being history buffs ourselves, our hearts ached for this compromise.

Dhaka division posed another head-scratcher. This one had to do with the Mymensingh division. Curiously enough, this division is empty in our map! After consulting credible sources, we believe that Mymensingh's prominent mosques that are irrefutably Mughal in style, architecture, date, etc. are from the so-called "Greater Mymensingh" region, which includes places like Kishoreganj and Tangail; but in present times, they officially fall under Dhaka division!

Overcoming the many challenges throughout this journey, we have finally come up with this map. We hope it encourages you to visit the mosques and stir up conversations about the rich heritage the Mughals have left us.

Sources: Mosque Architecture in Bangladesh by Dr Abu Sayeed M Ahmed and Syed Zakir Hossain; Mughal Monuments of Bangladesh by Nazly Chowdhury and Babu Ahmed; Mosques of Bangladesh by Nymphea Publication; Banglapedia; Bangladesh government websites; UNESCO's Tentative List of "Mughal Mosques in Bangladesh".

Special thanks to Sazzadur Rasheed, architect, academician, and admin of Save the Heritages of Bangladesh for providing valuable inputs to our project. We are also grateful to The Daily Star's Habiganj and Moulvibazar correspondent Mintu Deshwara, and Sheikh Nasir, Sylhet photographer for their help in our research.

title: Nawabganj: Where heritage meets harmony
text:
A crumbling mansion rises unexpectedly along the main road of Kolakopa Union in Nawabganj, Dhaka, its grand pillars still holding their ground against time. Just an hour and a half from the capital, the riverside estate on the banks of the Ichamati is more than a relic. It is a window into centuries of wealth, memory and local legend.

This is the Kokil Pyari Zamindar Bari, a neoclassical marvel now abandoned but impossible to ignore. Its towering pillars and intricate carvings still catch the eye, even as the building succumbs to neglect.

After the zamindari system ended in 1950, the mansion served as a residence for teachers of Kokil Pyari High School. Locals recall that six to seven families once lived there. On closer inspection, the walls reveal faint sculptures, including one of Venus, the Roman goddess of love, beauty and prosperity.

Yet the history of Kokil Pyari is as layered as the walls themselves.

Who was Kokil Pyari? Locals offer two accounts.

Braj Niketan, now known as Judge Bari. Photo: Star

According to one version, Kokil Pyari was a descendant of the Bhagya Kul Zamindars of Bikrampur, who founded this estate. Around 200 years ago, Yadunath Roy acquired the zamindari from the British. He was related by blood to Radharaman Roy, the mansion’s builder. Both Yadunath Roy and Radharaman Roy were merchants, trading areca nuts, salt and saris from Barishal to Kolkata and Murshidabad.

Another account says that in the 18th century, a wealthy businessman named Brajen Roy, also known as Sudarshan Roy, constructed the mansion. Surrounded by a garden, the mansion, built with brick, lime and rods, was originally called Braj Niketan. Over time, ownership changed hands, first to an oil trader and later to a judge, which led to the mansion also being referred to as the Telibari (Oil House) and the Judge’s House.

The 500-yard premises of Kokil Pyari Zamindarbari include a Buddhist temple, the house of Shriloknath Saha, Kolakopa Ansar Camp, Ukilbari, Dasbari, Adnan Palace and the Ichamati river. Many believe all these structures were once part of the original estate.

Unofficial sources suggest that Kokil Pyari had five sons. He left his main house to his youngest son and built four additional houses for the remaining sons.

Within the premises stand two memorial shrines. After Zamindar Kokil Pyari died, his son Radharaman Roy built a shrine in the Bangalee year 1334 in memory of his father. Later, he built another shrine in memory of his mother. Both shrines originally housed sculptures of his parents. Locals say that during the Liberation War, the mother’s sculpture disappeared and the head of the father’s statue was broken. The sculptures were reportedly imported from Europe.

Adjacent to Kokil Pyari Zamindarbari is Braj Niketan, now known as the Judge’s House. Locals say that around 200 years ago, in the 18th century, wealthy businessman Brajen Roy built it as his residence. Its five elaborately decorated pillars, adorned with pieces of precious glass, immediately draw attention. Eight large windows and a central grand veranda add to its imposing appearance. Surrounded by a garden of diverse trees, the Judge’s House still carries a sense of the world it once belonged to.

Moving along the narrow road to the right of Kokil Pyari Zamindarbari, one encounters Telibari, also called Mothbari, by the riverbank. It is currently used as an Ansar and VDP camp and houses 17 Ansar Battalion members. According to local lore, it was once owned by an oil trader named Loknath, hence the name Telibari.

Telibari now being used as an Ansar camp.

Next along the riverbank is a structure called Painna Bari, said to have belonged to Madhubabu, who became wealthy by selling toddy (palm wine). Its walls are adorned with intricate carvings, and the house sprawls across a large area.

Galib Rahman Khan, a banker with extensive knowledge of Nawabganj’s history, said, “The buildings in Kolakopa are all late-colonial, dating from the late 1800s to the early 1900s. None of them were zamindar houses. They belonged to prominent businessmen, some traded in oil, others in salt or betel leaves. Most of these houses were abandoned after the Partition of the country.”

To the right along the road lies a two-storey mansion on the edge of a large pond, believed to have been built in the late 19th century. The ground floor houses several dark rooms. The building features nine domes resembling granary roofs, with the central dome being the largest. Some locals refer to this as Khelaram’s Vigrah Mandir or Khelaram Datar Kotha.

According to Syed Nurul Islam, a septuagenarian who lives nearby, “Khelaram was called a donor because he supposedly robbed from the rich and distributed among the poor. There was an underground passage from the mansion to the Ichamati river, which he used.” Towards the end of his life, he reportedly became devout.

However, Galib said, “There are many stories and myths about Khelaram Dutta’s Kotha. Putting those aside, documented history shows that it is a late Mughal-era temple, built by Khelaram Dutta himself.”

Across Kolakopa village, other old structures remain, each carrying its own story. On entering, the Shri Shri Mahamaya Mandir, built in Bangalee year 1315, stands out, where rituals are still conducted. Nearby, an old house is now home to the Mitra family, whose forebear was once a timber trader. Legend says he struggled to unload a piece of timber from a boat and was guided in a dream to bring it home, leading to the start of a worship practice centred on the timber. Locals believe dreams about it still occur.

In Baktar Nagar, Shikaripara Union, another zamindar house, Ata Khan’s Zamindarbari, is visible from across the road. The second-storey building, though now ruined, still shows the outlines of its past. Plaster has fallen away, and large banyan trees grow through the brickwork. Doors and windows are missing, and the structure appears precarious. Locals call it Sab Bari or Shaheb Bari. A mosque stands nearby.

Based on the mosque’s construction style, Professor AKM Shahnawaz of the Department of Archaeology at Jahangirnagar University said the buildings likely date to the Mughal era, though exact dates remain uncertain.

Galib, however, said a stone inscription at the mosque’s main gate shows that a woman, Foyzunnesa, built it in 1870 after inheriting the zamindari from her aunt, Janab Hasina. This suggests the mansion was likely built around the same time.

On Nawabganj’s architectural history, archaeologist Dr Shahnawaz said these settlements were established in the late 18th century, primarily by Hindu merchants who built multiple palatial residences along the Ichamati for habitation and for trade convenience. “Kolakopa and Bandura in Nawabganj are highly traditional and historically significant areas. These landmarks are important archaeologically,” he said.

Nawabganj is not only known for old architecture, but also for a tradition of communal harmony. Alongside temples and mosques, the area has several historic churches. In Hasnabad village of Bandura stands one of the most striking, Our Lady of Holy Rosary Church.

Hubert Joseph Gomes, principal of St Joseph Tutorial in Hasnabad, said, “It is the fifth church in undivided Bengal, built in 1777 by priest Raphael Gomez. It was renovated first in 1888 and again in 2002.”

“Over 1,700 Christian families live in Nawabganj. People of all religions have lived here peacefully and harmoniously for generations,” he added.

title: Aamir Khan hints at progress on ‘3 Idiots’ sequel
text:
Bollywood star Aamir Khan has offered an update on the much-anticipated sequel to “3 Idiots”, revealing that director Rajkumar Hirani is working on the script and may soon share its latest version with him.

Speaking at the Singapore International Film Festival, Aamir said Hirani was developing the screenplay and hoped to narrate the final version to him within the next few weeks.

“I’m not allowed to say a lot. I think I can say this much, and yes, Raju is working on the script. In fact, hopefully, once I’m back in the next couple of weeks, he’s going to narrate the final version to me. So, fingers crossed,” the actor said.

The update has renewed interest in a possible follow-up to the 2009 comedy-drama, which was directed by Hirani and starred Aamir alongside R Madhavan, Sharman Joshi and Kareena Kapoor Khan.

In an earlier interview with The Hollywood Reporter India, Hirani confirmed that he was still developing the screenplay, while acknowledging that considerable work remained.

The filmmaker said the story would explore what happens to the central characters 15 to 20 years after the events of the original film. Rather than returning to their college days, the sequel would follow them into adulthood, as they navigate marriage, parenthood and the challenges of a midlife crisis.

Meanwhile, Aamir also spoke about another beloved Bollywood comedy, “Andaz Apna Apna”, at the festival, where audiences expressed their affection for the film.

Asked whether a second instalment was in the works, the actor revealed that filmmaker Rajkumar Santoshi was working on something related to the project. However, he stopped short of confirming whether it would be a sequel and offered no further details.

Although neither project has received a definitive confirmation of its release plans, Aamir’s remarks have fuelled speculation about the possible return of two popular films.

title: Pori Moni announces new film ‘Farzana’ on her birthday
text:
Bangladeshi actress Pori Moni has announced her upcoming film “Farzana” on her birthday, marking her return to hosting birthday celebrations after a two-year break following the death of her grandfather in 2023.

The poster for the film was unveiled at her birthday celebration last Saturday. Directed by Tarek Rahman, “Farzana” has largely been shot in secrecy, with much of the filming already completed.

Pori Moni revealed that the look for the film was finalised six months ago, but various complications delayed the production. She said the team had kept the project under wraps until they could make an official announcement.

“The look for the film was finalised six months ago, but due to various complications, it took time to move the project forward. That is why we did not announce it earlier. If everything goes according to plan, filming will wrap up soon. I felt there could be no better occasion than my birthday to announce a new film,” she said.

The screenplay centres on a woman’s struggles, motherhood and the harsh realities of life. Rahman has written the script alongside directing the film. Although he has previously made several television dramas and short films, “Farzana” will be his feature-film debut.

Describing the project, Rahman said it tells the story of a woman navigating life’s challenges alone, with each day bringing a new struggle. He expressed hope that the film would introduce audiences to a different side of Pori Moni as an actor.

A newcomer will play the male lead opposite Pori Moni, while Sushama Sarker is among the other cast members. According to the director, the team is planning to release the film during Eid-ul-Fitr next year, provided production is completed on schedule.

Pori Moni was last seen on the big screen in “Felubakshi”, which marked her Tollywood debut in January 2025. Her other upcoming projects include “Dodor Golpo”, directed by Reza Ghatak with government funding, as well as “Golap”, directed by Shamsul Huda, and “Shasti”, directed by Leesa Gazi.

Nirab Hossain will star opposite her in “Golap”, while Chanchal Chowdhury is her co-star in “Shasti”.

title: Why we keep recreating movie weddings
text:
I have recently spent an unreasonable amount of time looking at wedding references. A cousin is getting married, which means I have become familiar with the strange ecosystem of screenshots, mood boards, saved Instagram posts and photographs of weddings that have apparently set the standard for what a wedding should look like. The more I look, the more obvious it becomes that most of our references are borrowed. We have been watching fictional weddings for so long that cinema has quietly become part of the way we imagine the real thing.



Hollywood gave us the white wedding fantasy long before Instagram existed. “The Parent Trap” gave us the enormous, picturesque ceremony that looks like it belongs in a storybook. “Bride Wars” turned wedding planning itself into a competitive sport, complete with impossible venues and increasingly elaborate details. “27 Dresses” made us intimately familiar with the bridesmaid’s wardrobe, the wedding chaos and the strange emotional ecosystem surrounding a bride. “Mamma Mia!” gave an entire generation a Mediterranean wedding fantasy so effective that an island, a blue dress and a flower crown could suddenly qualify as a complete aesthetic.

Image



And then there are the weddings that became visual landmarks in themselves. Bella’s minimalist wedding in “Breaking Dawn – Part 1” made a generation of Twilight fans obsess over her Carolina Herrera dress. “Crazy Rich Asians” gave us the sort of wedding where even the aisle requires production design, with Araminta’s spectacular walk through water becoming one of the most instantly recognisable modern movie weddings. The scene was so carefully constructed that the wedding almost felt like a fashion editorial with a love story attached.



Bollywood has arguably done more than any other film industry to make the wedding a participatory art form. It did not merely show us weddings. It gave us songs to perform at them. “Mehndi Laga Ke Rakhna” from “Dilwale Dulhania Le Jayenge” has long since escaped its original film and become wedding vocabulary. “Bole Chudiyan” from “Kabhi Khushi Kabhie Gham” is practically a choreographic inheritance. “Didi Tera Devar Deewana” from “Hum Aapke Hain Koun..!” has survived decades of cousins who were not even alive when the film came out. “Maahi Ve” from “Kal Ho Naa Ho”, “London Thumakda”, “Gallan Goodiyaan” and “Kaala Chashma” followed the same path. These songs are particularly powerful because they were designed for exactly what weddings eventually became: large groups of people performing happiness together. A film choreographer creates the original routine. A wedding choreographer watches it. Someone learns the hook step. Someone changes the hook step. Ten years later, somebody’s aunt is doing a surprisingly accurate version of it at a reception. Cinema creates the template; weddings keep remixing it.

Image



Then there are the clothes. “Kabhi Khushi Kabhie Gham” gave us an entire wardrobe of wedding references. “Yeh Jawaani Hai Deewani” gave us Aditi’s wedding, with its destination setting, jewel-toned outfits and deliberately effortless extravagance. “Veere Di Wedding” offered a more contemporary, fashion-conscious wedding fantasy. “2 States” gave us a different pleasure altogether: the wedding as a collision of two cultural aesthetics. And sometimes one outfit becomes more memorable than the wedding itself, because cinema has spent decades making us pause the screen and think, I want that.



This is where Bangladeshi cinema and television become especially interesting. Our own screen culture has given us a different, more familiar collection of wedding images. Bangladeshi films and television dramas have repeatedly used weddings, engagements and family celebrations as spaces for romance, comedy and visual glamour. The appeal of these scenes is often less about extravagant production and more about recognition: the clothes look like clothes we might actually wear, the families resemble families we know, and the celebrations carry the slightly chaotic warmth of events we have attended ourselves. The romantic comedy “Jodi Kintu Tobuo”, for instance, literally begins around an engagement and was described at the time as a colourful take on the local rom-com, with a wedding functioning as the central spectacle. Bangladeshi television has also made the wedding such a familiar comic and romantic setting that there are entire Eid dramas built around it; “Wedding Diary” and “Happy Wedding” are only two recent examples.



And that is perhaps why our wedding references can feel so wonderfully mixed. One person wants something that looks like a Bollywood sangeet. Someone else wants the polished simplicity of a Hollywood wedding. Someone wants the flowers from a Bangladeshi drama they watched years ago. Someone has saved a bride’s jewellery from Instagram. Someone has found a song from a 1990s film. Someone else has a cousin who knows a choreographer who can teach everyone the steps. There is no single source any more. There is simply the enormous visual archive we have accumulated by watching things.



Image



Cinema has also taught us that every wedding needs a moment. The bride walked in. The friends surprised the couple. The groom’s entrance. The family dance. The dramatic reveal of the outfit. The song everyone knows. The photograph where everyone looks inexplicably perfect. These moments have become so familiar that we now plan them in advance. Weddings have trailers, teaser videos, pre-wedding shoots, choreographed entrances and carefully constructed photographs. We have essentially taken the grammar of cinema and applied it to real life. The pre-wedding shoot might be the funniest example. For decades, films showed couples running through fields, walking along beaches, staring at each other beside lakes and standing dramatically under conveniently cinematic sunsets. We have now turned those scenes into a professional service. Even the mood board itself is cinematic. We save frames instead of photographs. We refer to colour palettes. We identify lighting. We want “something like this” without always remembering where the “this” came from.



Of course, fictional weddings are much easier to admire because they have editors. Nobody in “Crazy Rich Asians” is checking whether the florist has arrived. Nobody in “Hum Aapke Hain Koun..!” appears to be worrying about the seating arrangement. Nobody in “Mamma Mia!” is calling someone because 14 guests have changed their dinner preferences. Real weddings contain logistics. Movies contain lighting. And perhaps that is why we keep borrowing from them. A real wedding is an event that happens once. A fictional wedding can be paused, replayed, screenshotted, copied and choreographed at someone else’s wedding twenty years later. That is the strange afterlife of an iconic wedding scene. It stops belonging to the movie. It becomes someone’s outfit reference. Someone’s first-dance song. Someone’s entrance idea. Someone’s décor inspiration. Someone’s cousin’s choreography. Which means that when we plan weddings today, we are rarely starting from scratch. We are pulling pieces from a shared pop-cultural memory: a hairstyle from an actress, a flower arrangement from Pinterest, a choreography from YouTube.



The final wedding may look completely original. It probably isn’t. It is a little bit of everything we have ever watched and thought we wanted exactly that. And honestly, that might be the most entertaining thing about wedding planning: somewhere between the spreadsheets and the screenshots, we realise we have been collecting wedding references our entire life.

title: Eric Bauza, voice of Bugs Bunny and Daffy Duck, dies at 46
text:
Emmy Award-winning voice actor Eric Bauza, best known for bringing Bugs Bunny, Daffy Duck and several other iconic Looney Tunes characters to life, has died at the age of 46.

His family confirmed the news in a statement shared on his Instagram account on Sunday. Describing him as the voice behind beloved cartoon icons and dozens of other popular animated characters, the family said Bauza had died unexpectedly. They added that further details would be shared at a later date.

The circumstances surrounding his death remain unclear. According to press materials, Bauza was scheduled to attend the Sunday afternoon premiere of Warner Bros. Pictures Animation's "The Cat in the Hat" to support "Daffy Season", a short film set to screen ahead of the feature.

Channing Dungey, chairman of Warner Bros. Television Group and US Networks, paid tribute to the actor, describing him as an exceptional voice artist whose performances brought joy and laughter to millions around the world.

Reflecting on his 15-year association with Warner Bros. Animation, Dungey highlighted Bauza's portrayal of iconic characters, including Bugs Bunny and Daffy Duck, following in the footsteps of legendary voice actor Mel Blanc. She said Bauza had regarded carrying forward the Looney Tunes legacy as one of the greatest honours of his life. Beyond his extraordinary talent, she added, he was a cherished member of the Warner Bros. animation family, extending her condolences to his loved ones.

In the Looney Tunes film "Coyote vs. Acme", released earlier this year, Bauza voiced several beloved characters, including Bugs Bunny, Daffy Duck, Tweety, Elmer Fudd, Foghorn Leghorn, Porky Pig, Road Runner and Charlie the Dog. Many of these characters were originally brought to life by the late Mel Blanc.

His other notable Looney Tunes performances included "Space Jam: A New Legacy", in which he voiced Daffy Duck, Porky Pig, Foghorn Leghorn, Elmer Fudd and Marvin the Martian. He also voiced Bugs Bunny and Daffy Duck in the animated series "Looney Tunes Cartoons".

Born on December 7, 1979, in Toronto, Canada, Bauza was later based in Los Angeles. Throughout his career, he established himself as one of the prominent contemporary voices in animation, earning nominations for Daytime Emmy, Children’s & Family Emmy and Annie Awards.

His award nominations recognised his performances as the title character in "The Adventures of Puss in Boots", Fozzie in "Muppet Babies", and Bugs Bunny and Daffy Duck in "Looney Tunes Cartoons".

More recently, he lent his voice to several characters in DreamWorks Animation's animated film "Forgotten Island".

Bauza's extensive television credits included "Unikitty", "Archibald’s Next Big Thing", "The Rocketeer", "Ballmastrz: 9009", "Rise of the Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles", "Star vs. The Forces of Evil", "Breadwinners", "Uncle Grandpa", "Atomic Puppet", "The Powerpuff Girls", "The Fairly OddParents", "Ultimate Spider-Man", "Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles", "Guardians of the Galaxy", "Transformers: Robots in Disguise", "Sanjay and Craig" and "Mighty Magiswords".

His film voice credits also included "The Book of Life" and "The SpongeBob Movie: Sponge Out of Water". He further voiced the titular character in Universal's animated film "Woody Woodpecker".

title: Farooki dismisses separation rumours, calls it ‘nonsense’
text:
Filmmaker Mostofa Sarwar Farooki has dismissed reports of a separation from his wife, actress Nusrat Imrose Tisha, calling the claims baseless and saying he has no interest in engaging with them.

Farooki, a former culture affairs adviser to the interim government, also said his Facebook account had been hacked on Saturday morning. He alleged that a Bangladeshi cybercrime group was celebrating the incident in online groups and called for law enforcement agencies to take action.

“I woke up in the morning and saw what had happened. They tried to hack my account and deactivated it. A Bangladeshi cybercrime group is celebrating this in different groups. I have screenshots,” he told bdnews24.com. “Law enforcement agencies need to be active on these matters. This is an issue of citizens’ safety.”

Asked about the separation reports circulating online and in some media outlets, Farooki said he had no time to respond.

“I have no time to talk about that news, and no interest. There is no basis to any of this. I have no time to listen to such nonsense,” he said.

He also described social media discussions about his alleged property ownership in Australia and Switzerland as amusing.

“The most amusing thing is the idea that someone owns a house in Australia or Switzerland. Anyone can find that with a search. This kind of propaganda about me has surfaced before,” he said. “Instead of getting caught up in these irrelevant controversies, write about my work.”

Farooki said he had completed two commercials, one for a software company and another for a building materials company. The shoots took place in Dhaka, Mymensingh and South Korea.

He is preparing to shoot a third commercial featuring a celebrity, whose identity he said he might reveal within a day.

The filmmaker is also developing scripts for two feature films. One is a love story, tentatively titled “To Hell, With Love”, which explores changing ideas of romance among younger people.

“It is a love story, not a thriller. The definition of love is changing for the new generation. I am trying to capture these new definitions of love and understand what love looks like for Gen Z,” he said. “The script is almost complete. For now, I have named it ‘To Hell, With Love’.”

The second film has a political backdrop and is also nearing completion. Farooki said he had yet to decide which project would go into production first.

Farooki and Tisha married on July 16, 2010. Their daughter, Ilham Nusrat Farooki, was born in 2022.

Tisha has appeared in television dramas and films including “Third Person Singular Number”, “Television”, “Ostitto”, “Doob”, “Halda”, “Mayaboti” and “Phagun Haway”. She won the National Film Award for Best Actress for her performances in “Halda”, directed by Tauquir Ahmed, and “Ostitto”, directed by Anonno Mamun.

Farooki began making films in 1999. Under the Chabial banner, he directed single-episode and serial dramas including “Spartacus ’71”, “Ekannoborti”, “69” and “420”. His feature films include “Bachelor”, “Made in Bangladesh”, “Third Person Singular Number”, “Television” and “Doob”.

His latest feature film, “840: Democracy Private Limited”, was released in 2024. He has not directed another feature film since.

title: ‘Ramayana’ crosses Rs 10 crore in advance bookings in India
text:
Ranbir Kapoor’s “Ramayana” has recorded Rs 10.5 crore in advance bookings in India, including blocked seats, ahead of its theatrical release on November 5.

According to box office tracker Sacnilk, the Nitesh Tiwari directorial had recorded bookings for around 1.89 lakh tickets across 4,439 shows as of Saturday. The figures include seats blocked by cinemas, with overall occupancy standing at 19 percent.

The Hindi version accounted for Rs 9.15 crore, followed by the Kannada version with Rs 1.03 crore and the Telugu version with Rs 31.25 lakh.

Standard 3D screenings contributed 64 percent of the total advance booking value, generating Rs 6.72 crore from around 1.42 lakh tickets across 3,883 shows.

IMAX 3D screenings accounted for Rs 2.5 crore, with 22,410 tickets booked across 149 shows and occupancy at 50 percent. Meanwhile, 4DX 3D screenings recorded Rs 42.43 lakh from 5,546 tickets across 132 shows, with occupancy at 41 percent.

Overseas advance bookings have also crossed US $1.1 million across all available screening dates, according to Sacnilk. Opening-day bookings exceeded US $600,000, including around US $475,000 from North America. Of the North American total, approximately US $350,000 came from premiere screenings.
