title: Dengue claims 11 more lives
text:
At least 11 people died of dengue, and 2,071 others were hospitalised in 24 hours till 8:00 am, marking the highest single-day death toll of the year, according to the Directorate General of Health Services (DGHS).

With the latest deaths and cases, the number of fatalities from the mosquito-borne disease has risen to 400, while the total number of cases has reached 1,28,237.

Currently, 6,415 dengue patients are undergoing treatment at hospitals across the country, while 1,21,422 have been discharged so far.

title: 6 more die of measles-like symptoms in last 24 hours
text:
Six more children died of measles-like symptoms across the country in the 24 hours till 8:00am today, bringing the country’s combined tally of confirmed and suspected measles-related deaths to 1,233 this year.

The Directorate General of Health Services (DGHS) classified the latest fatalities as suspected measles deaths.

With this, the total number of suspected measles deaths has reached 1,129, while confirmed deaths have remained the same at 104.

A total of 1,388 new suspected measles cases were reported during the 24-hour period, taking the cumulative number of suspected cases nationwide to 222,552

Meanwhile, 78 new confirmed measles cases were recorded, pushing laboratory-confirmed infections to 23,478.

Since March 15 this year, a total of 197,999 patients with suspected measles have been hospitalised across the country, of whom 190,036 have recovered, according to the DGHS.

title: Bangladesh measles crisis 'warning sign' of other outbreaks: Report
text:
Experts have warned Bangladesh that deadly outbreaks of diphtheria, whooping cough and polio could follow an ongoing measles epidemic that has already killed over 1,200 children, according to a report seen by AFP on Monday.

"The measles outbreak is a litmus test and a warning sign of a deteriorating immunisation system," said the report by an independent committee of national and international experts, which carried out its research earlier in October.

Bangladesh has struggled since March to contain the outbreak, which has killed more than 1,200 children and infected 220,000 people, making it the country's deadliest in decades, according to the Directorate General of Health Services (DGHS).

"If no urgent mitigation measures are taken, it is only a matter of time before there are large outbreaks of pertussis (whooping cough), diphtheria and even vaccine-derived poliovirus," added the report, which has been submitted to the government.

The health ministry pledged action on Monday.

"We are going to recruit vaccinators as quickly as possible as the first step towards implementing the recommendations," spokesman Zahid Raihan told AFP.

The government, supported by the World Health Organization (WHO), UNICEF, the Gavi vaccine alliance and other partners, deployed a 70-member team earlier this month to assess the country's immunisation programme.

The review found that just 82 percent of children were fully immunised, well below the national target of 95 percent. Around 40 percent of vaccinator posts remain vacant.

Bangladesh was long considered an immunisation success story. Since its programme began in 1979, the country has eliminated polio and neonatal tetanus and controlled rubella and hepatitis B.

A measles vaccination campaign planned for 2024 was delayed by the revolution that toppled former prime minister Sheikh Hasina, while strikes and political instability further disrupted a campaign in 2025.

Authorities have since launched a mass vaccination drive, but cases continue to climb.

Measles spreads easily through coughs and sneezes and has no specific treatment. Complications include brain swelling and severe breathing problems, with young children particularly vulnerable.

Whooping cough can cause severe illness and death in infants. Diphtheria can obstruct breathing and damage the heart and nerves, while vaccine-derived poliovirus can cause paralysis in under-immunised populations.

title: Why are more women dying of dengue despite fewer infections?
text:
As dengue cases rise in the country, men account for a larger share of patients hospitalised with the mosquito-borne disease, while women account for more deaths.

According to the Directorate General of Health Services (DGHS), men accounted for around 62.1 percent of dengue patients hospitalised between January 1 and October 23 this year, while women made up 37.9 percent. However, in terms of deaths, the number of women who died of dengue was higher than that of men.

Experts say that women face a higher risk of death due to their illnesses not receiving adequate attention, delays in seeking treatment, and financial and social barriers.

According to the DGHS, 119,801 people have been hospitalised with dengue across the country between January 1 and October 23. During this period, 371 people have died of the disease.

Among patients hospitalised with dengue this year, 74,201 were men and 45,355 were women, meaning the number of male patients was significantly higher than that of female patients.

However, according to gender-disaggregated data from the DGHS, of the 371 people who died of dengue this year, 193 were women and 173 were men. This means women accounted for 52 percent of the deaths, while men accounted for 46.6 percent.

An analysis of age-disaggregated data in the DGHS regular dengue bulletin shows a significant number of cases among people aged 26 to 50. The combined number of male and female patients across the five age groups within this range stands at 53,238, accounting for 44.4 percent of all cases.

Of the patients in this age range, 32,195 were men and 20,935 were women.

Women also account for a higher number of deaths in this age group. Among people aged 26 to 50, the death toll for men stands at 75 and which is 99 for women.

Deaths among people in this age group account for 46.9 percent (174) of the 371 fatalities recorded this year. Of those who died aged between 26 and 50, women accounted for 56.9 percent, while men made up 43.1 percent.

Renowned epidemiologist Professor Dr Mushtuq Husain believes social inequality plays a significant role in the higher number of dengue deaths among women.

According to him, women often give less importance to their own illnesses than their male counterparts. Other family members may also fail to give sufficient importance to women’s need for medical care.

He said women from poor families, in particular, may delay seeking medical care. The cost of treatment, household responsibilities and the need to meet the needs of other family members may influence their decisions. As a result, many women do not seek medical attention promptly even when they fall ill.

He said women undergo various physical changes during pregnancy and need special care during this period. Excessive bleeding during menstruation can also complicate their physical condition.

Dr Tahmina Afrin Daisy, associate professor at the Institute of Mother and Child Health in Matuail, Dhaka, said dengue during pregnancy poses a risk of serious complications for both the mother and the baby.

She said physical changes during pregnancy may delay the detection of dengue-related complications. If warning signs are not properly monitored and treatment is not provided as needed, the patient’s condition can deteriorate rapidly.

She said dengue during pregnancy can cause complications such as a drop in platelet count, bleeding and liver problems. It also increases the risk of miscarriage, premature birth, low birth weight and respiratory complications in the unborn baby. In rare cases, if the mother contracts dengue close to delivery, the infection may also be transmitted to the baby.

According to her, women’s illnesses often do not receive adequate attention even outside pregnancy. Many women neglect their own health, while their families and society also fail to provide them with the care they need. Although it is important to seek medical advice as soon as a fever develops, many women seek treatment only after their condition has deteriorated. This makes it difficult to diagnose dengue and begin treatment in time.

She also stressed the need to pay greater attention to nutritional deficiencies and anaemia among women.

Dr Mushtuq said access to medical care for poor and marginalised communities must be improved to reduce dengue deaths. He said it was essential to ensure dengue testing, proper care following diagnosis and necessary treatment for people living in densely populated areas and among mobile populations.

According to him, in addition to the cost of treatment, concerns about feeding and caring for children in the family may discourage many people from going to hospital. Therefore, alongside reducing treatment costs, social support should be provided to patients’ families. This would improve access to timely medical care for people of all ages, including women, men, children and the elderly.

Dr Tahmina said families must take the initiative to raise awareness among women about dengue. It is important to involve male family members alongside women in this effort.

She stressed the need to seek medical advice promptly when a fever develops, rather than neglecting it, and to be aware of the warning signs of dengue.

She said awareness campaigns could be conducted in neighbourhoods. Outpatient departments of hospital gynaecology and obstetrics units could also offer women advice on nutrition, personal hygiene and healthcare.

She also emphasised the need for government support for economically disadvantaged women. According to her, special assistance programmes could be introduced to reduce financial barriers to accessing healthcare.

The physician believes that if families and society take women’s illnesses seriously and ensure they receive timely treatment, it would help reduce dengue-related complications and deaths.

title: Work and Migration
text: Prospective workers hoping to go to Malaysia are still waiting to know when medical tests will begin, how much migration will cost and when they can leave, despite moves to resume recruitment to one of Bangladesh’s major labour markets.

title: 174 Bangladeshis return from Libya; 41 ill, 36 previously detained
text:
Forty-one of the 174 Bangladeshis repatriated from Libya early today were physically ill, while 36 had been held at a detention centre in Tripoli after being intercepted at sea, according to the Bangladesh embassy in Libya.

The returnees arrived in Dhaka at 5:40am via Buraq Air flight UZ-222, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs said in a statement.

Of the 174 returnees, 36 had been detained at the Tajoura detention centre in Tripoli after being intercepted at sea. The remaining 138 returned home voluntarily amid dangerous conditions in the Libyan capital, according to the embassy.

Most of the returnees had reportedly entered Libya with the help of human traffickers, intending to reach Europe across the Mediterranean Sea, the foreign ministry said. Some alleged that they had been abducted and tortured during their stay in Libya.

The repatriation comes amid widespread exploitation of Bangladeshis attempting to reach Europe through Libya.

Bangladesh Ambassador to Libya Major General Md Habib Ullah met the returnees at the embassy before their departure and warned them about the risks of irregular migration.

He said such journeys could expose migrants to physical, psychological and financial harm, affecting both them and their families.

The ambassador urged the returnees to rebuild their lives in Bangladesh, follow legal migration procedures in future and help raise awareness of the dangers of irregular migration. He also called on them to cooperate with the authorities in taking legal action against human traffickers and brokers.

Officials from the foreign ministry, other concerned agencies and the International Organization for Migration (IOM) received the returnees at the airport.

According to the ministry, IOM provided them with travel allowances, food supplies, primary medical assistance and temporary accommodation where necessary.

The repatriation was arranged through cooperation among the foreign ministry, the Bangladesh embassy in Libya, the Ministry of Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment, Libyan authorities and IOM.

The embassy is also working to repatriate another 175 Bangladeshis from Misrata, Libya, tomorrow. They have expressed their willingness to return voluntarily.

title: Imams urged to use Friday sermons to warn against human trafficking, unsafe migration
text:
Imams across the country have been urged to use Friday Juma sermons to warn people against human trafficking and dangerous journeys abroad, as religious leaders could play a crucial role in saving lives.

Islamic Foundation Director General Mufti Muhammad Muhibbullahil Baki made the call at a workshop at the foundation’s headquarters in Dhaka’s Sher-e-Bangla Nagar today.

He said raising awareness through Friday sermons and religious discussions could help protect people from falling victim to traffickers and the dangers of unsafe migration.

He stressed that protecting a person’s life also meant safeguarding their overall wellbeing.

“It is now necessary to include the risks of human trafficking and unsafe migration among the issues discussed in Friday sermons,” he said.

The workshop was organised by BRAC’s Migration Programme under the Australian government-funded project, “Mass Campaign to Combat Human Trafficking and People Smuggling”.

Presenting the keynote paper, BRAC Associate Director Shariful Hasan said it was painful to see Bangladeshis losing their lives while attempting to travel abroad by sea or becoming victims of fraud and abuse during their journeys.

He said awareness messages delivered through imams’ sermons at 49 mosques had already reached more than 23,000 people over the past few months.

“If imams and religious scholars across the country speak out against human trafficking, migrant smuggling and irregular migration, many lives can be saved,” he said.

Shariful said the joint awareness campaign against human trafficking would continue.

Islamic Foundation Directors Md Mohiuddin, Md Anisuzzaman Sikder, Md Abdul Hamid Khan and Waliur Rahman Khan, and Deputy Secretary Md Golam Kabir also spoke at the workshop.

National Imam Association Secretary General Maulana Shah Mohammad Nazrul Islam and BRAC Migration Programme Manager Shayla Sharmin were also present.

title: 35 Bangladeshis repatriated from Italy, Greece and Cyprus
text:
Thirty-five Bangladeshis returning from Italy, Greece and Cyprus arrived in Dhaka this morning on a special chartered flight, airport and immigration sources said.

Of them, 19 were from Italy, 10 from Greece and six from Cyprus. Flight PVG-9445 landed at Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport around 8:15am.

BRAC’s Migration Programme, with support from Civil Aviation Security and the Expatriates’ Welfare Desk, provided the returnees with emergency assistance, counselling and financial support to help them reach home. Representatives from the foreign ministry and the European Union were also present at the airport.

Shariful Hasan, associate director of BRAC’s Migration Programme and Youth Platform, said all 35 returnees received assistance under the Prottasha-2 project, jointly funded by BRAC and the EU. They will also receive training, counselling and financial aid to rebuild their livelihoods and reintegrate into society.

The latest repatriation follows two similar operations this year. On August 27, 40 undocumented Bangladeshis returned from Europe, including 24 from Cyprus, 15 from Greece and one from Bulgaria. Another 27 returned on a special flight on May 21.

Bangladesh and the EU signed standard operating procedures in 2017 to facilitate the return of Bangladeshis living in European countries without valid documents or authorisation to stay. Repatriation takes place after legal procedures are completed and the returnees’ Bangladeshi nationality is verified.

Around 5,000 Bangladeshis have returned under the arrangement so far, with Cyprus, Italy, Romania and France accounting for the largest numbers.

Shariful said BRAC had received the highest numbers of returnees from Italy, Greece and Germany in recent years. The organisation is also conducting awareness campaigns across Bangladesh to discourage people from taking dangerous, irregular routes to Europe.

title: Body of Bangladeshi killed in Houthi missile attack brought home from Saudi Arabia
text:
The body of a Bangladeshi national killed in a missile strike in Saudi Arabia was brought back to Bangladesh today.

Three Bangladeshis have been killed in missile attacks in Saudi Arabia over the past month, and the government is working to repatriate the bodies of the other two as well, State Minister for Foreign Affairs Shama Obaed Islam said while receiving the body of Shahed Ahmed at Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport in Dhaka this morning.

She said the Bangladesh embassy in Saudi Arabia and the Ministry of Expatriates’ Welfare and Overseas Employment had promptly contacted the Saudi authorities to bring his body home.

The state minister also handed over cheques for financial assistance to Shahed’s family. Through the Wage Earners’ Welfare Board under the Ministry of Expatriates’ Welfare and Overseas Employment, the family received Tk 35,000 for burial and transportation expenses and Tk 50,000 in special assistance following his death in the conflict.

Shahed, from Madla village in Shajahanpur upazila of Bogura, was among those killed in a Houthi missile attack on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh on October 10, according to the information provided.

His employer, Saad Al Eissa Contracting Company, has deposited 27,395.62 Saudi riyals, equivalent to around Tk 9 lakh, into the Bangladesh embassy’s account in Riyadh to cover his outstanding salary, allowances and service benefits.

The amount will soon be handed over to his family through the Wage Earners’ Welfare Board, Shama said.

Shahed’s family may receive an additional Tk 3 lakh, subject to verification of his BMET card or valid employment documents. They may also be entitled to Tk 10 lakh in insurance benefits, depending on his insurance coverage.

title: Transport
text: Thousands of people using the Pirojpur-Barguna road via Charkhali-Tushkhali-Mathbaria-Patharghata areas have been facing immense hassle with their commute as construction of 16 bridges and 29 culverts on the route has dragged on for years.

title: Dhaka metro rail expansion: Contracts signed for 11.5km of tracks, 8 stations
text:
Construction of around 11.5 kilometres of elevated metro rail tracks and eight stations under MRT Line-1 and MRT Line-5 (Northern Route) is set to begin following the signing of four construction contracts today.

The contracts, signed with three joint ventures, cover two packages under each project, according to a press release issued by the Road Transport and Highways Division.

The agreements were signed at Metro Rail Bhaban in Diabari, Uttara in Dhaka.

The contracts cover major depot facilities and elevated infrastructure for the two metro rail projects being implemented by Dhaka Mass Transit Company Limited (DMTCL) with joint financing from the government and the Japan International Cooperation Agency (JICA).

Under MRT Line-1, the CP-02 package involves the construction of 49 depot facilities, including workshops, stabling sheds and an operations management centre. The contract was awarded to SINOHYDRO-SEBCL JV.

The CP-07 package includes construction of a 5.007km elevated viaduct from the underground-to-elevated transition point to the beginning of the Balu River section. It also includes three elevated stations at Joar Sahara, Boalia and Mastul. The contract was awarded to CREC-MIL-MBEC JV.

Image Photo: Courtesy

For MRT Line-5 (Northern Route), the CP-02 package covers depot infrastructure, including administrative buildings, operation and depot control centres, stabling yards, warehouses and workshop sheds. The contract was signed with CPC-HANIL JV.

Another package, CP-03, involves construction of 6.5km of elevated railway tracks along the Hemayetpur-Amin Bazar and Natun Bazar-Vatara sections.

The package also includes five elevated stations at Hemayetpur, Baliapur, Bilamalia, Amin Bazar and Vatara. The contract was awarded to CREC-MIL-MBEC JV.

Speaking at the signing ceremony, Road Transport and Highways Division Secretary Mohammad Ziaul Haque said reducing traffic congestion and travel time remained a government priority.

He directed the implementing agencies and contractors to ensure construction quality and safety while completing the work within the stipulated deadlines.

The secretary also stressed the need to minimise public inconvenience and environmental impacts during construction, particularly for communities living near the project sites.

He called for closer coordination among implementing authorities, engineers and contractors to avoid delays.

DMTCL Managing Director Md Shawgatul Alam delivered the welcome address, while Planning Commission Member Kabir Ahmed attended as a special guest.

Representatives of the Japanese embassy, JICA, consulting firms and contracting companies were also present.

title: Traffic gridlock hits major Dhaka roads
text:
Severe traffic congestion around Zia Udyan in Sher-e-Bangla Nagar, Dhaka caused immense suffering for commuters today.

The congestion affected several major roads, including Bijoy Sarani, Manik Mia Avenue, Kazi Nazrul Islam Avenue, Begum Rokeya Sarani and Mirpur Road.

Since morning, leaders and activists of the BNP's youth wing, Jatiyatabadi Jubo Dal, marched towards Zia Udyan to attend their 48th founding anniversary programme.

Vehicles reportedly remained stuck in traffic for up to an hour in the morning, prompting many commuters to get out of their vehicles and walk to their destinations.

Md Swapan, an employee of a private firm, said he became stuck near the Jatiya Sangsad Bhaban while travelling to his office in Farmgate.

Image This photo was taken from Dhaka's Farmgate area on October 27. Photo: Prabir Das/Star

Fearing further delays, he asked his driver to make a U-turn and return home. He later walked to his office, he said.

Centring the programme marking the Jubo Dal's founding anniversary, leaders and activists began gathering with banners in areas near Zia Udyan. They later marched to the graves of former president Ziaur Rahman and former prime minister Khaleda Zia to pay floral tributes.

Visiting the area in the morning, this correspondent saw groups of Jubo Dal leaders and activists arriving in processions from Dhaka and neighbouring areas.

Omar Ali, assistant commissioner of the Dhaka Metropolitan Police's Tejgaon Traffic Division, said the programme had worsened the traffic situation.

“We were informed about the programme and took steps to ease public suffering. The situation started improving after 2:00pm,” he said.

title: Mahanagar express extended to Cox’s Bazar
text:
The Mahanagar Express has been extended to Cox’s Bazar from Dhaka, becoming the third pair of trains operating on the route, as the government plans a major overhaul of Bangladesh Railway’s services and infrastructure.

Road Transport and Bridges, Shipping, and Railways Minister Shaikh Rabiul Alam inaugurated the extended service at Kamalapur Railway Station on Monday night.

“I believe that within two to two-and-a-half years we will be able to bring about a fundamental change in Bangladesh Railway’s overall management and services,” he said.

Around 80 locomotives are in the procurement pipeline, while 200 new coaches are expected soon, the minister said. Tender approval is pending for another 200 coaches, and around 150 existing coaches will be rehabilitated.

A separate project is also being prepared to bring 50 to 70 idle locomotives back into service at a relatively low cost, he said.

Rabiul alleged that some locomotives purchased under previous administrations failed to meet technical specifications and became unusable prematurely.

Previously operating between Dhaka and Chattogram, the Mahanagar Express will now run to Cox’s Bazar alongside the Cox’s Bazar Express and Parjatak Express.

The extension adds capacity for 1,442 passengers per operating day, with 706 seats on the Dhaka to Cox’s Bazar journey and 736 on the return trip.

The train will leave Dhaka at 8:30pm and reach Cox’s Bazar at 6:00am the following day. It will depart Cox’s Bazar at 9:00am and arrive in Dhaka at 6:30pm. The train will not operate on Sundays.

Covering 467.83km, the route includes stops at Airport, Narsingdi, Bhairab Bazar, Ashuganj, Brahmanbaria, Akhaura, Kasba, Cumilla, Laksam, Nangalkot, Feni and Chattogram. The previous stop at Kumira has been withdrawn. Existing approved fares will remain unchanged.

Asked whether the extension would reduce seat availability between Dhaka and Chattogram, the minister said more coaches would be added to existing trains to accommodate passengers.

He also said the proposed Narayanganj-Joydebpur electric railway project had received policy approval. A train service between Dhaka and Pabna would be introduced once new coaches became available.

On ticket black markets, Rabiul said demand far exceeded supply, particularly during Eid, when around 32,000 tickets could be available daily while millions of people attempted to buy them. He acknowledged that some people resold tickets at higher prices and said software-based measures were being considered to prevent unauthorised ticket transfers.

The minister also expressed concern over stone-throwing at moving trains and inadequate access control at stations, calling for greater public cooperation to prevent attacks.

title: 3,025 acres of railway land under illegal occupation: ministry
text:
Nearly 3,025 acres of Bangladesh Railway land are under illegal occupation, the railways ministry told a parliamentary committee on Monday, presenting figures that differ from those published on its website.

The railway owns 63,072.909 acres, including 3,024.84 acres under illegal occupation, and earned Tk 87.72 crore by leasing out 25,083 acres last fiscal year.

However, the ministry's website, last updated on May 1, 2025, lists 61,860.28 acres of railway land, including 3,678.83 acres under illegal occupation and 14,473.24 acres leased out.

The reason for the discrepancies remains unclear.

The figures were presented at the second meeting of the parliamentary standing committee on the railways ministry, chaired by Mohammad Ali Asgar at the Jatiya Sangsad Bhaban.

The ministry said eviction drives were continuing, while special committees in Pakshi and Lalmonirhat would identify encroached land within three months and arrange the phased removal of illegal structures.

New estate management software has been introduced to monitor unused land and encroachments. Joint operations with district administrations and police are also planned to address drug-related offences on railway property.

On online ticketing, some committee members proposed releasing 10 percent of intercity train tickets daily instead of making the entire quota available 10 days before departure. They argued that staggered sales could reduce ticket scalping and benefit passengers planning journeys at shorter notice.

The ministry said preparations were complete to invite fresh tenders for an online ticketing operator before its contract with Shohoz expires early next year.

The railways ministry also told the committee that a shortage of metre-gauge locomotives had forced Bangladesh Railway to reduce freight train operations.

According to the progress report presented at the meeting, containers are still being transported regularly between Chattogram port and Dhaka, while fuel and food grains are being carried to other destinations. However, the locomotive shortage has reduced the number of freight trains.

To address the shortage, a development project proposal to procure 30 metre-gauge locomotives has recently been approved, while tenders have been invited for another 30 under an earlier approved project.

The ministry said acquiring all 60 locomotives by 2029 would allow the railway to increase freight services, including the transportation of containers, fuel and food grains, and generate additional revenue.

Procurement of another 20 metre-gauge locomotives under the World Bank's Green Railway project is also being processed.

The ministry further informed the committee that molasses was being transported on a limited scale from Mongla port to Soydabad in Tangail and Joypurhat. However, the railway had received no demand for transporting other goods from Mongla.

title: Mohakhali-Kishoreganj bus services resume after owners settle dispute
text:
Around 250 buses operated by four transport companies resumed services on the Kishoreganj-Mohakhali route via Gazipur this morning following a suspension over a dispute among transport owners.

Anannya Super, Anannya Classic, Jalsiri and Ujan-Bhati suspended their services on Saturday and Sunday. They resumed operations from Gaital Inter-District Bus Terminal in Kishoreganj today after the transport owners reached an agreement.

Babul Khan, managing director of Anannya Classic Transport, told The Daily Star that the services resumed following discussions among the owners, coordinated by the secretary general of the Dhaka Road Transport Owners Association.

“I was in serious trouble as the bus services were suspended without any prior announcement. All the counters for my 50 buses had been closed,” he said.

The suspension had caused suffering for passengers, with many facing difficulties returning to their workplaces and educational institutions after the Puja holidays.

Earlier, Anisuzzaman Babul, president of the Kishoreganj District Road Transport Owners Association, told The Daily Star that the association’s new committee had taken an initiative to replace old buses with new ones to improve passenger services.

He said the initiative had triggered a dispute among transport owners.

However, he did not respond to several phone calls today seeking his comment on the resumption of services.

A ticket seller at the Jalsiri Transport counter at Amraid Bazar said their bus services resumed early this morning.

The resumption brought relief to passengers.

title: Xbox’s first COO leaves after three months: report
text:
Helen Chiang, Xbox’s first chief operating officer, is leaving Microsoft just months after the role was created, according to an internal memo seen by The Verge.

Xbox chief executive Asha Sharma announced the exit in a short note to staff. “Helen Chiang is leaving Microsoft today,” she wrote, adding that she was grateful for Chiang’s years of service. Chiang’s immediate duties are being shared among other Xbox leaders for now, and Sharma said more would be shared on COO leadership “as plans are finalised”, the report states.

Chiang had spent 21 years at Microsoft and previously headed the Minecraft franchise. She was promoted to chief operating officer in July 2026. The Verge says no reason has been given for her departure.

When the role was announced during a major Xbox restructuring this summer, Sharma said it would have responsibility for profit and loss across content, hardware, platform, and services. She said it was needed because Xbox had grown and become more fragmented, according to the report. Chiang reported directly to Sharma.

The exit comes as Xbox continues its restructuring. Under the plan Sharma set out in July, up to 3,200 jobs are expected to go over the coming year, The Verge reports.

title: How smart technology can transform small business loans in Bangladesh
text:
Imagine a small grocery shop in Dhaka. The owner sells everyday essentials, orders stock regularly from wholesalers, and serves a loyal group of customers. Business is steady, but when the owner approaches a bank for a loan to expand, the application quickly runs into familiar obstacles: no formal financial statements, limited credit history, and no land or property to offer as security.

For many small business owners in Bangladesh, this is not an unusual experience. Their businesses may be active and profitable, but proving that to a bank can be harder than running the business itself.

Small and medium-sized enterprises are a vital part of Bangladesh’s economy, creating jobs, supporting families, and keeping local communities moving. Yet many remain outside the formal lending system. The financing gap is estimated at around $2.8 billion, leaving countless entrepreneurs without the funds they need to restock, hire workers, buy equipment, or expand. The problem is not that these businesses are too risky; often, banks simply lack enough information to understand how they operate.

When paperwork hides potential

Traditional lending depends heavily on credit histories, formal accounts, and physical collateral. These requirements help banks manage risk, but they can also exclude successful businesses that operate outside conventional systems. A woman running a home-based tailoring business may have regular customers and reliable income but no property in her name. A small retailer may sell goods every day but keep only informal records. Under conventional rules, these entrepreneurs can appear invisible.

Technology offers a different way to look at them. Instead of judging a business mainly by the documents its owner can provide, lenders can examine its actual activity. A shopkeeper who regularly purchases stock, maintains consistent sales, and pays suppliers on time demonstrates financial discipline without owning land or a commercial building. Digital records can help make that pattern visible.

A new way to measure creditworthiness

This approach is gaining ground globally. In Ethiopia, the technology company Kifiya has used artificial intelligence to help lenders assess small businesses through digital records rather than relying only on property and traditional paperwork. In India, the Unified Payments Interface (UPI) has made digital payments a part of everyday business, creating transaction records that can help lenders understand sales and cash flow. In Indonesia, where small enterprises drive the economy, digital platforms like Shopee and QR payment systems like QRIS are stepping in. For small businesses without formal credit histories or property to offer as collateral, these digital footprints could open doors to financing that have traditionally remained closed.

Bangladesh can develop similar pathways. Mobile financial services and digital wallets can track everyday transactions, utility payments, and savings behaviour to assess creditworthiness. Consider a small vendor who has never taken a formal bank loan but regularly receives digital payments and pays bills on time through a mobile wallet. Those actions reveal important evidence: the person handles cash responsibly.

While digital behaviour cannot completely replace proper lending checks, it can provide useful data where traditional credit histories do not exist. It can also make applications faster, reducing a process that once took weeks to minutes or seconds, while giving informal and women-led enterprises a fair chance to be assessed on their real economic activity.

Rethinking trust in banking

The shift will require banks to rethink what they mean by trust. Traditional models often treat collateral as the strongest proof that a borrower is safe, but collateral does not run a business or generate cash flow. A small entrepreneur’s daily performance may provide a more direct indication of whether a loan can be repaid.

Financial institutions can transition to AI-driven credit assessment by using more relevant information. A digital credit score should not replace human judgment, but it can help banks see patterns that paper-based systems miss. If an entrepreneur has steady sales and a reliable digital repayment record, those facts should matter even without land ownership. For banks, this creates a wider customer base and better risk assessment; for entrepreneurs, it means faster access to working capital and a fairer opportunity to grow.

Building trust before expanding

Technology alone is not a complete solution. AI can make lending faster, but it can also reproduce unfairness if data is incomplete. Bangladesh will need clear rules before alternative credit scoring expands widely.

First, central regulators can provide practical guidance on what digital records lenders may use and what standards credit-scoring systems must meet.

Second, customers must understand and control how their information is used through informed consent and strong data protection. Fairness also requires regular attention to ensure women entrepreneurs, rural businesses, and first-time borrowers are not unfairly disadvantaged.

Third, new lending models can be tested carefully through regulatory sandboxes to monitor success rates and ensure responsible lending.

Giving small businesses a fair chance

A loan can mean much more than extra money for a small business. It can help a retailer keep shelves stocked, allow a tailor to buy a better sewing machine, or give an online entrepreneur working capital to fulfil a larger order.

AI-powered credit scoring will not solve every financing problem, nor will it remove the need for careful lending and strong consumer protection. However, it can help banks recognise entrepreneurs who have been overlooked because they lack conventional paperwork or property.

The country’s small business owners are already working hard to support their families and drive economic growth. They deserve a financial system that looks beyond what they lack and pays closer attention to what they are already doing well.

Izlal Moin Husain is Senior Program Manager at The Asia Foundation, Bangladesh.

Views expressed in this article are of the author’s own and may not reflect the editorial stance of The Daily Star.

title: KineMaster free users can now export watermark-free videos in Bangladesh
text:
KineMaster, the mobile video-editing app, has introduced watermark-free video exports of up to 1080p for users in Bangladesh, Pakistan and Indonesia who do not subscribe to its Premium service.

The change comes with version 8.2 of the app and removes the subscription requirement for watermark-free exports in the selected markets, according to a press statement sent to The Daily Star.

“This reduces a key barrier to entry for video editors to create and showcase their work both for fun and professionally. Eliminating the subscription requirement for watermark-free content empowers editors to produce video stories that truly belong to only them,” KineMaster said in the statement.

KineMaster said most of its editing tools would remain free to use. Its Asset Store also offers free graphics, music, transitions and AI plugins, while Premium subscriptions provide access to the full asset library, remove in-app advertising and lift usage limits on certain tools.

Premium subscribers will continue to have access to features including 2K and 4K exports on compatible devices, as well as project backup and private sharing through the company’s KineCloud service.

The change could help students, aspiring content creators and journalists in Bangladesh who use mobile apps to edit videos for social media, news reports and other projects but cannot afford a Premium subscription.

“KineMaster has been popular since the early days of mobile video editing, and I have been training people to use it since 2016,” said Jamil Khan, associate professor and head of the department of journalism, media and communication at Daffodil International University (DIU).

“However, not everyone in Bangladesh can afford a premium subscription, leaving students looking for alternative ways to access its features. Making watermark-free editing more accessible could benefit journalism students, content creators and multimedia journalists across the country,” he said.

Khan added that the change could help people producing content for television, social media and other platforms, as competition from apps such as CapCut, InShot and Meta’s Edits grows.

KineMaster said Premium subscriptions help fund the development of new features, assets and AI-powered tools. The company also said its AI plugins process media on users’ devices rather than uploading it to its servers.

title: Chattogram administration says 1 lakh saplings planted in one day
text:
The Chattogram district administration today said it planted 100,000 saplings in a single day across the port city and 16 upazilas under the district. Around 15,000 people, including representatives of various government agencies, took part in the programme.

The programme, titled “100,000 Trees in One Day, Our Goal is a Green Environment”, was inaugurated in the morning at Jamiyatul Falah Jame Mosque in Chattogram Wasa where Md Ismail Zabiullah, adviser to the Ministry of Public Administration, was present as chief guest.

The programme was organised under the government’s priority initiative to plant 25 crore trees in five years.

Chattogram Divisional Commissioner Dr Ziauddin, CMP Commissioner Hasan Md Shaukat Ali, Range DIG Abdul Quddus Chowdhury and Chattogram Deputy Commissioner Zahidul Islam Mia, along with other senior officials, were present.

In the evening, the chief guest planted the 100,000th sapling at DC Park in Sitakunda upazila.

Addressing the final programme, the chief guest said, “What has been done in Chattogram to make Bangladesh greener is truly admirable. The project to plant 250 million trees in five years is not an overly ambitious initiative. It is necessary for our own benefit and to protect our existence.”

Highlighting the importance of ensuring the survival of the saplings, the deputy commissioner said, “The work does not end with planting trees. The saplings must also be properly maintained.”

Zahidul Islam said the programme was being implemented without spending any government funds. He thanked the 24 Infantry Division of the Bangladesh Army, the Forest Department, non-governmental organisations, and officials concerned from the district and upazila administration for helping collect the saplings.

He said committees had been formed at different levels to monitor the saplings and protect them with fencing. An additional 10,000 to 20,000 saplings have been kept in reserve to replace any that die or become weak.

The deputy commissioner said discussions had been held with upazila nirbahi officers (UNOs), village police, local government institutions and teachers regarding the maintenance and monitoring of the saplings. The Forest Department is providing technical assistance for the initiative.

title: 3 former Prabartak Sangha officials fined for hill cutting
text:
A Chattogram court fined three former office-bearers of Prabartak Sangha Tk 2 lakh each for illegally cutting a hill to construct structures in the city.

Judge Farzana Yasmin of the Chattogram Environment Court delivered the verdict on Monday.

Alauuddin, bench assistant of the court, and Muhit Mohammad Mohiuddin, lawyer for the convicts, confirmed the verdict to The Daily Star.

The convicts are Subhash Chandra Lala, former president of the organisation’s managing committee; Ranjit Kumar Dey, former vice-president; and Tinkari Chakrabortty, former general secretary.

According to court records, a hill belonging to Prabartak Sangha in the Prabartak intersection area of Panchlaish in Chattogram was cut for construction purposes. The Department of Environment (DoE) inspected the site and found preliminary evidence of hill cutting. It filed the case in 2016 through its then assistant director, Sanjukta Dasgupta.

Alauuddin said the court fined each of the three Tk 2 lakh for violating Section 6 (kha) of the Bangladesh Environment Conservation Act, 1995. They will each face one year in jail if they fail to pay the fine, he added.

The verdict was delivered after the court examined three witnesses, he said.

Mohiuddin said his clients would appeal against the verdict.

None of the three convicts was present in court when the verdict was announced.

Alauuddin said that, under the Environment Conservation Act, the convicts must pay their fines before filing appeals.

title: Cyclone Arnab forms over Bay, to cross India on Wednesday as very severe storm
text:
A deep depression over the Bay of Bengal has intensified into a cyclone named Arnab, which is forecast to strengthen further before crossing India's Andhra Pradesh coast as a very severe cyclonic storm on Wednesday.

At 6:00am today, the cyclone was located 820 kilometres southwest of Chattogram port, 745 kilometres southwest of Cox’s Bazar port, 785 kilometres south of Mongla port and 745 kilometres south of Payra port.

The maximum sustained wind speed within 54 kilometres of the cyclone’s centre is around 62 kilometres per hour, with gusts or squalls reaching up to 88 kilometres per hour.

The Bangladesh Meteorological Department has asked the maritime ports of Chattogram, Cox’s Bazar, Mongla and Payra to lower distant warning signal No 1 and hoist distant warning signal No 2.

Fishing boats and trawlers in the North Bay of Bengal have also been advised to remain close to the coast and navigate with caution.

According to the forecast, the cyclone is likely to move west-northwestwards and intensify into a severe cyclonic storm over the west-central Bay of Bengal by early Tuesday morning.

It is then expected to move northwestwards and cross the Andhra Pradesh coast of India on Wednesday as a very severe cyclonic storm.

Meteorologist Abdul Hamid Mia of the BMD told The Daily Star that Cyclone Arnab was not expected to have a significant impact on Bangladesh.

Coastal areas may experience light rain tomorrow and the following day, but the likelihood of heavy rainfall is low, he said.

After the cyclone makes landfall the day after tomorrow, Dhaka and Rajshahi divisions may also experience light rain, he added.

How cyclones are classified

Cyclones are classified into five categories according to their intensity: cyclonic storm, severe cyclonic storm, very severe cyclonic storm, extremely severe cyclonic storm and super cyclonic storm.

Their intensity is measured based on the average maximum sustained wind speed over a three-minute period.

A cyclonic storm has sustained wind speeds of 62 to 88 kilometres per hour. For a severe cyclonic storm, the speed ranges from 89 to 117 kilometres per hour, while a very severe cyclonic storm has winds of 118 to 165 kilometres per hour.

An extremely severe cyclonic storm has sustained winds of 166 to 221 kilometres per hour. A storm with sustained winds of 222 kilometres per hour or more is classified as a super cyclonic storm.

How Arnab got its name

Thirteen countries in the region jointly name cyclones that form over the Bay of Bengal and the Arabian Sea. They are Bangladesh, India, Iran, the Maldives, Myanmar, Oman, Pakistan, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, Sri Lanka, Thailand, the United Arab Emirates and Yemen.

The countries are members of the World Meteorological Organisation’s (WMO) regional panel on tropical cyclones. Storms are named sequentially from a list submitted by these countries.

“Arnab” was one of the names on the list that had not yet been used. Bangladesh proposed the name, which means “sea” or “ocean”.

The practice of naming cyclones began in 2000. According to the WMO, naming storms helps avoid confusion, particularly as more than one cyclone can develop in the same region at the same time.

title: 3 injured in suspected leopard attack along Lalmonirhat border
text:
A woman and two farmers were injured in a leopard attack along the border in Hatibandha upazila of Lalmonirhat today.

The injured are Sharifa Begum, 32, and Afsar Uddin, 42, and his brother Nazrul Islam, 45. They are residents of Amjhol village under Gotamari union in the upazila, said Lt Col Mehedi Imam, commanding officer of the Lalmonirhat 15 Border Guard Bangladesh (BGB) Battalion.

The incident took place at Amjhol border area around 4:00pm.

Members of BGB and police, along with local residents, surrounded the animal in a paddy field. The injured were rescued and admitted to Hatibandha Upazila Health Complex. It is suspected that the leopard crossed the border from a forest in neighbouring India and entered Bangladesh.

According to BGB and local sources, Sharifa went to look for her pet goat beside a paddy field near her home in the afternoon. As she approached the goat, the leopard, which had been lying in wait nearby, suddenly attacked her. Hearing her screams, as people from the surrounding area rushed to the site, two more farmers were injured in the animal's attack.

Locals later rescued the injured and rushed them to Hatibandha Upazila Health Complex.

Sharifa, who is receiving treatment at the hospital, said, “The leopard was preparing to take away my goat. At that moment, it attacked me.”

Afsar said he and his brother were working in a nearby field. Hearing the woman's screams, they rushed to help her, but the leopard pounced on them. Later, as a large crowd gathered at the site, the animal quickly fled and hid in the paddy field.

Abdul Jalil, 55, a resident of the area, said villagers had surrounded the paddy field from all sides with sticks, spears and other sharp weapons. BGB and police personnel were also there. Everyone was using torchlights to prevent the leopard from escaping.

“The leopard has entered Bangladesh from India. There is no forest in our area. We suspect it crossed into Bangladesh this afternoon,” he said.

Monabberul Haque Mona, chairman of Gotamari union parishad, said the leopard was still hiding in the paddy field.

“BGB and police personnel are on alert. Forest department officials are on their way to the site. All-out efforts are underway to capture the leopard,” he said.

Lt Col Mehedi said additional BGB personnel have been deployed at the site.

“People present at the site have been asked to remain cautious and not to approach the leopard individually,” he added.

title: Tk 87cr climate-smart urban project on cards
text:
The government has proposed a Tk 87.40 crore Germany-funded project to promote climate-resilient urban development in four municipalities, with most of the funds earmarked for consultancy services and management costs.

The project, titled “Innovation for Climate-smart Urban Development”, is set to be placed before the Executive Committee of the National Economic Council for approval tomorrow.

It will undertake 12 pilot initiatives in Chapainawabganj, Charghat, Gaibandha and Sirajganj municipalities to identify climate-related problems and strengthen local authorities' capacity to address them.

According to a Planning Commission proposal obtained by The Daily Star, national guidelines for climate-resilient urban development remain inadequately implemented at the local level because of limited capacity to identify problems and devise solutions.

Poor coordination, inadequate local planning and funding shortages have also hindered the development of affordable, climate-resilient infrastructure and basic urban services, particularly in small and medium-sized towns.

The proposal said Town Level Coordination Committees and Municipal Standing Committees remained largely ineffective and needed guidance on climate-resilient planning, public participation and addressing the needs of vulnerable communities.

The project aims to address these gaps through local initiatives, planning support and training for municipal officials and other stakeholders.

The four municipalities were selected based on socioeconomic conditions, climate vulnerability, economic potential and implementation capacity, following an assessment by the Centre for Environmental and Geographic Information Services (CEGIS).

The Local Government Engineering Department (LGED) will implement the project under the Local Government Division, with the entire Tk 87.40 crore coming as a grant from German development cooperation agency GIZ. The Bangladesh government will provide in-kind support.

Of the proposed cost, Tk 57.26 crore has been allocated for national and international consultancy services, Tk 6.10 crore for domestic and overseas training, and Tk 18.52 crore for GIZ management charges.

Bangladesh and GIZ signed a memorandum of understanding on April 10, 2025.

Originally proposed for January 2025 to December 2027, the project has been recommended by the Planning Commission for implementation from July 2026 to June 2029.

The commission expects it to contribute to Sustainable Development Goal 11 and support similar initiatives in other municipalities.

title: Low pressure over Bay may turn into cyclone; rain forecast from October 27
text:
A well-marked low-pressure system over the east-central and southeast Bay of Bengal may intensify into a cyclone and is likely to move towards India’s Andhra Pradesh coast, meteorologists said today.

At the beginning of October, the Bangladesh Meteorological Department (BMD) had forecast that two or three low-pressure systems could form over the Bay of Bengal this month, one of which could develop into a cyclone.

Talking to The Daily Star, BMD meteorologist AKM Nazmul Haque said the well-marked low could develop into a depression today.

“Although there is a possibility of it intensifying into a cyclone, the likelihood of it moving towards Bangladesh is very low. However, we cannot completely rule out the possibility,” he told The Daily Star.

Fishing boats and trawlers in the northern Bay have been advised to avoid venturing into deep waters, he added.

Under its influence, rainfall may increase in the coastal areas of Khulna, Barishal and Chattogram from October 27, while Khulna, Rajshahi and Rangpur may see rain from October 29, Nazmul said.

If the system develops into a cyclone, it will be named Arnab, a name proposed by Bangladesh, he said. However, if the low-pressure system currently active over the Arabian Sea develops into a cyclone first, it will receive the name Arnab.

The next name on the regional list is Murasu, proposed by India, the meteorologist said.

title: Lunch on the go
text:
A little spiderhunter hovers beside a cluster of pinkish-white flowers, its wings spread wide as its long, curved bill probes for nectar in Chattogram’s Fatikchhari. Native to South and Southeast Asia, including Bangladesh, this member of the sunbird family inhabits tropical forests, forest edges and plantations. Despite its name, it feeds not only on spiders but also on other insects and nectar. Its slender, downward-curved bill allows it to probe deep into flowers, pollinating them as it feeds. Classified as Least Concern on the IUCN Red List, the species remains widespread, although deforestation and habitat loss threaten its populations.

title: Kolkata Police parade accused shirtless days after two teenagers and a man allegedly forced to walk naked
text:
Kolkata Police today paraded three accused men shirtless through the streets of Sarsuna in Behala while reconstructing an incident on Sunday in which an 18-year-old, his 19-year-old friend and the younger man’s father were allegedly assaulted, threatened at gunpoint, stripped and forced to walk naked.

Videos circulating on social media showed the three accused walking barefoot, with ropes tied around their waists, as police personnel escorted them.

Kolkata police have not issued an official statement on the incident. However, a senior police officer said the accused were being taken to the area to reconstruct the crime scene, reports The Indian Express.

The reported incident took place on Sunday when a teenager was seen kissing a 13-year-old girl near Khalpar Math in the Khudiram Pally area. He was accompanied by his friend.

According to police, a friend of the girl's uncle saw the teenager kissing her and alerted her father and uncle. The girl's father then arrived at the spot, forcibly took the teenager and his friend to their home, assaulted them and forced the teenager to call his father.

The girl's relatives then gave the three a choice -- face a police case, be shot dead, or walk naked through the streets while the incident was recorded on video.

The teenager, his father and his friend were subsequently paraded naked for around 50 metres through the streets of Behala and held at gunpoint. People nearby intervened, gave them clothes and provided shelter.

The teenager's father later approached the police and filed a case. The charges include attempt to murder, voluntarily causing hurt, wrongful confinement, criminal intimidation and kidnapping.

Police arrested the girl's relatives yesterday.

Although the victims alleged that a firearm was used to threaten them, police had not recovered the weapon as of the latest reports.

The incident has triggered a blame game.

Altaf Ahmed, general secretary of the human rights organisation APDR, questioned the justification for marching the accused in a state of partial undress. Trinamool Congress legislator Shovandeb Chattopadhyay also criticised both incidents, questioning whether public exposure could constitute legitimate punishment.

The Calcutta High Court has previously observed that law enforcement agencies cannot deliberately humiliate an accused person under the guise of arrest.

title: Houthis say they launched an attack on Saudi Ras Tanura oil refinery
text:
Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis said on Tuesday they had launched an attack on Saudi Arabia's Ras Tanura oil refinery, the ⁠biggest in the kingdom, located on the Gulf west of the Strait of Hormuz.

The group's military spokesperson Yahya Saree said in a statement that the ballistic missile attack caused a fire at the site. The Saudi authorities have not confirmed the attack.

The Houthi militia have escalated their attacks on Saudi Arabia since September, opening another volatile front in the wider US-Israeli war on Iran.

Nearly all of Saudi Arabia's oil exports flow through two main ports: Ras Tanura in the Gulf and Yanbu on the Red Sea, which the Houthis have attacked in the past.

Bloomberg News reported on Tuesday, citing a person familiar with the matter, that Saudi Arabia had contained a fire near the oil terminal at Ras Tanura in the early hours of the day.

title: Tetsuya Chiba, Japan's manga legend, dies at 87
text:
Tetsuya Chiba, a titan of Japanese manga best known for the legendary boxing series "Ashita no Joe", has died at the age of 87, his publishers said today.

Chiba's works often told stories about the physical and mental growth of young athletes across various sports including golf, boxing and the martial art kendo, while also showing the poverty, despair, joy and optimism of ordinary life in postwar Japan.

"Ashita no Joe", published in the 1960s through the 1970s, featured a troubled young man who learns boxing in a juvenile detention centre and rises through the professional ranks to engage in epic rivalries.

The series became a cultural phenomenon.

Fans held a funeral after Joe's main rival died in the story. Older fans can casually recite lines from the work, which also spawned enormously popular anime series, movies, video games, television commercials and theatrical productions.

Chiba, with a seven-decade career, also taught at university level, led the Japan Cartoonists Association, and received a number of Japanese cultural accolades, including the enormously prestigious Order of Culture, given to people who have made a significant contribution to art, science and culture.

Major publisher Kodansha has honoured his legacy with the "Tetsuya Chiba Award" for young manga artists for the past 46 years.

"Countless rookie manga artists took master Chiba's words to heart as they embarked on the path to becoming professionals, and many of them are still active today," the firm said in a statement, adding that he died last Thursday.

"Master Chiba's tremendous contributions to the world of manga are truly irreplaceable."

Another publisher, Shogakukan, credited him with helping to shape Japan's manga culture and capturing the hearts of generations of fans.

"For seventy years, master Tetsuya Chiba has been at the forefront of the manga world. He created countless masterpieces," it said.

Chiba also often gave media interviews to talk about his commitment to peace and discussed memories of his childhood in China during World War II before returning to Japan after its defeat.

title: IDLC Finance’s profit rises 17% to Tk 200 crore in nine months
text:
IDLC Finance PLC reported a 17 percent year-on-year rise in net profit for the first nine months of 2026, supported by higher investment income and growth in operating revenue.

The non-bank financial institution posted a consolidated net profit of Tk 207 crore for January-September 2026, up from Tk 176 crore in the same period last year, according to its unaudited financial statements.

The company’s total operating income increased 12.5 percent year-on-year to Tk 697.78 crore in the first nine months of this year.

Investment income was a key contributor to the growth, climbing 36 percent to Tk 353 crore from Tk 260 crore a year earlier.

Commission, exchange and brokerage income also increased to Tk 39 crore from Tk 29 crore.

However, net interest income declined to Tk 263 crore from Tk 287 crore, despite an increase in interest income.

The third-quarter results presented a more mixed picture.

IDLC Finance’s consolidated net profit rose slightly to Tk 70 crore in July-September, compared with Tk 68 crore in the same quarter last year.

However, net interest income in the three-month period declined to Tk 93 crore from Tk 109 crore in the same period last year, while investment income increased to Tk 34 crore from Tk 28 crore.

Shares of IDLC Finance remained unchanged at Tk 41 on the Dhaka Stock Exchange today.

title: Gas shortage keeps Ashuganj fertiliser factory shut for 1.5 years
text:
The Ashuganj Fertiliser and Chemical Company Limited (AFCCL) in Brahmanbaria remains shut over 1.5 years, leaving the state-run plant unable to produce urea amid the country’s continued reliance on imports.

The factory, which has remained idle since March 1 last year, has missed out on nearly Tk 3,000 crore worth of production over the past 19 months, according to estimates based on its daily output value of around Tk 5 crore.

On April 23 this year, independent lawmaker Rumeen Farhana raised the issue in parliament, calling for the reopening of the factory in her constituency, Brahmanbaria-2.

In response, Power, Energy and Mineral Resources Minister Iqbal Hassan Mahmood assured lawmakers that gas supplies would resume from May 1, citing the need to protect the country’s agricultural sector.

However, the assurance has yet to materialise, with the authorities unable to provide a definite timeline for restarting operations.

The prolonged closure has also left the government incurring salary and other operating expenses while raising concerns over the condition of machinery that has remained idle for an extended period.

Tajul Islam Bhuiyan, deputy general manager (administration) of AFCCL, said officials had initially expected production to resume in June, but the plan did not materialise because of the gas shortage.

He said increased supplies of liquefied natural gas (LNG) could help restore gas availability at the plant.

Senior officials are also discussing with a foreign company the possibility of operating the factory with a reduced volume of gas, he added.

The plant, which began commercial production in 1983, currently has the capacity to produce around 1,150 tonnes of urea daily, down from its previous daily capacity of approximately 1,600 tonnes, according to factory sources.

It supplies prilled urea to seven neighbouring districts within its designated distribution area, making the suspension of production a concern for regional fertiliser supplies.

Meanwhile, Bangladesh Chemical Industries Corporation (BCIC) Chairman Md Babul Mia expressed hope that production could resume before the end of this year.

Speaking to journalists after visiting the factory last Thursday, he said efforts were underway to ensure adequate gas supplies to keep the country’s fertiliser factories operational.

Bangladesh currently imports around 26 lakh to 27 lakh tonnes of urea annually, he said.

According to the BCIC chairman, operating domestic fertiliser factories at full capacity could enable the country to meet its own demand and potentially export urea.

He said the government aimed to save around Tk 22,000 crore in import costs by bringing all fertiliser factories back into operation.

Factory officials and workers, however, said repeated interruptions in gas supplies over the years had disrupted production schedules and made it difficult for the BCIC to meet its output targets.

They said preparations to restart operations often began when gas became available, but prolonged inactivity frequently caused technical problems with machinery.

By the time repairs were completed, supplies were sometimes suspended again, preventing production from resuming, they alleged.

Abu Kawsar, general secretary of the Ashuganj Fertiliser Factory Workers and Employees Union, said the plant could become profitable if uninterrupted gas supplies were ensured.

He urged the government to take effective measures to protect the state-owned facility, saying repeated shutdowns were undermining its production capacity and making machinery maintenance increasingly difficult.

Meanwhile, Bakhrabad Gas Distribution Company Limited (BGDCL), which supplies gas to the Ashuganj area, said it was awaiting instructions from higher authorities to restore supplies to the factory.

Mohammad Bappi Shahriar, deputy general manager of BGDCL’s transmission department, said the plant required around 48 million cubic feet of gas a day to operate at full capacity.

“We are ready to resume gas supplies to the factory once we receive instructions,” he told The Daily Star.

The country currently has eight fertiliser factories, seven of which are state-owned. Of the eight, six produce urea fertiliser and two produce non-urea fertilisers.

title: Rangpur farmers turn to organic fertiliser to boost soil fertility
text:
Farmers across the Rangpur region are increasingly making and using organic fertiliser, finding it a practical way to improve soil fertility while reducing their dependence on chemical fertiliser.

The shift is particularly visible among farmers growing winter vegetables. Some are preparing organic fertiliser at home, while others are buying it from fellow farmers and local markets. The growing demand has also created a small but expanding market for farmers who produce and sell it.

Last year, Nagendra Nath Roy, 65, of Chandonerhat village in Rangpur's Gangachara upazila, relied mostly on chemical fertiliser for his 16 bighas of land. This year, he has changed his approach.

He is now using mostly organic fertiliser prepared at home or bought from other farmers.

"The fertility of the soil has declined, which is why I have had to use organic fertiliser. Besides, chemical fertiliser is not available in the market in the quantities we need," he said.

Nagendra is not alone.

Mozammel Haque, 70, of Tajpur village in Lalmonirhat Sadar upazila, is using twice as much organic fertiliser this year as he did last year.

"Crop yields are lower when organic fertiliser is used alone, but it improves soil fertility. We cannot collect enough to meet our needs, though, so we still rely considerably on chemical fertiliser," he said.

According to the Department of Agricultural Extension (DAE), farmers in Lalmonirhat, Kurigram, Rangpur, Gaibandha and Nilphamari are producing, using and selling organic fertiliser in growing numbers.

Around 16,000 farmers in the five districts benefit from commercial production of organic fertiliser, with each capable of producing up to 10 tonnes a year. They use part of what they make on their own fields and sell the surplus for additional income.

Vermicompost, made with earthworms that break down cow dung and other decomposable matter, is one of the most common forms. Farmers can produce it at home using materials that are readily available.

For Azaharul Islam, 55, of Chawratari village in Lalmonirhat Sadar upazila, it has become a source of income as well as fertiliser.

He has been producing organic fertiliser for six years, making around 10 tonnes annually. He uses about three tonnes himself and sells the rest.

Demand for the organic fertiliser has doubled this year, he said.

"It costs Tk 7–8 to produce per kg. Last year, I sold it for Tk 14–15 per kg. This year, the price has risen by Tk 4–5," he said.

Maneshwar Barman, 65, of Mahipur village in Gangachara upazila, has also been using vermicompost for four years while growing potatoes and winter vegetables.

"Producing organic fertiliser does not require much money or labour; we just need to be careful during the process," he said.

He said more farmers were showing interest in producing it this year.

"All farmers should learn to produce it themselves. That would cut their dependence on the market — buying it costs more than twice what producing it does."

But organic fertiliser is not being seen as a complete replacement for chemical fertiliser.

Dr Abu Bakar Saiful Islam, additional director of the DAE in Rangpur, said chemical fertiliser quickly supplies essential nutrients, while organic fertiliser improves soil structure, water-holding capacity and long-term fertility.

Farmers should apply 60–70 kg of organic fertiliser per bigha, he said, adding that chemical fertiliser was still necessary to achieve expected yields and should be used in appropriate quantities.

The department was working to increase local production, training and market access, he said. Crop-specific management, soil testing and balanced fertiliser use are key to controlling costs while preserving soil fertility, he added.

Safinur Rahman, a soil scientist at the Rangpur regional office of the Soil Resource Development Institute, said several areas in northern Bangladesh suffer from low soil organic matter, acidity and nutrient imbalances.

"Fertiliser must be applied according to soil test results and crop needs. Combined use of chemical and organic fertiliser can help maintain soil health and productivity," he said.

title: A low-cost fix to cut onion losses
text:
Researchers at Bangladesh Agricultural University (BAU) say Internet of Things (IoT) and sensor-based storage systems could reduce post-harvest losses of onions caused by inadequate storage facilities, which leave the country dependent on imports later in the year.

A team of researchers at BAU is developing an IoT-based, bin-shaped storage unit that can hold 500kg of onions and automatically monitor and control its internal environment.

The setup can be installed for around Tk 25,000 and used for at least 10 years.

Electricity costs are expected to be low and could be minimal if farmers use solar panels, said Prof Rostom Ali, professor at BAU’s Department of Farm Power and Machinery, who is leading the research.

The research began in March 2025 with funding from UGC.

Prof Ali said the objective is to develop a comparatively low-cost modern storage system that can regularly monitor and control temperature, humidity and other environmental conditions to preserve onion quality for longer.

Sensors will detect changes in the storage environment and trigger adjustments to the airflow system, including automatically regulating fan operation, he added.

Experimental results so far suggest that the technology could reduce onion storage losses by around 15-16 percent. However, the research has not yet reached its final stage.

The researchers are also monitoring weight loss, rotting, sprouting and quality changes. The findings so far have been encouraging.

If the results remain satisfactory and the necessary financial and technical support is available, the team plans to introduce the technology on a pilot basis. A model suitable for field-level use could be developed within one to two years, the researchers said.

According to the Department of Agricultural Extension (DAE), Bangladesh produces around 4.264 million tonnes of onions annually, against demand of approximately 3.50-3.60 million tonnes. Despite domestic production exceeding demand, the country imported around 86,000 tonnes of onions in the 2025-26 fiscal year.

title: Fisheries department proposes Tk 47cr project for 29 baors
text:
The Department of Fisheries (DoF) has proposed a Tk 47.55 crore project to develop fisheries resources in 29 baors across four south-western districts, increase fish production and improve the livelihoods of genuine fishers.

The five-year project, titled “Community-Based Fisheries Resource Management in Selected Baor Areas”, includes excavating baors, establishing fish sanctuaries, upgrading fingerling production facilities, and strengthening training and community-based management.

Baors are crescent-shaped water bodies formed when a river changes course, leaving behind an isolated section of its former channel.

A press release issued yesterday by the Ministry of Fisheries and Livestock said the project aims to increase fish production in the baors of Jashore, Jhenaidah, Chuadanga and Kushtia by at least 10 percent.

The project was initiated by the Jashore deputy commissioner last year. The proposal was subsequently forwarded to the Planning Commission after the government approved its staffing structure.

It is now awaiting an assessment of its costs and activities, according to the release.

Md Delwar Hossain, secretary of the Ministry of Fisheries and Livestock, said the project aims not only to increase fish production but also to establish an effective management system involving local fishers.

Plans include designating selected water bodies as fish sanctuaries, monitoring them to protect fish stocks, and providing training to local people, he said.

Md Khaled Kanak, director general of the DoF, described the initiative as a community-based fisheries development project.

He said projects aimed at improving the livelihoods of baor fishers had been lacking for a long time.

Many baors have become shallow due to siltation, damaging fish habitats and reducing productivity, he said. The project seeks to restore these water bodies and establish an effective community-based management system, he added.

title: Middle East conflict threatens vegetable exports
text:
Bangladesh’s fresh vegetable export earnings fell nearly 7 percent year-on-year in the July-September quarter of the current fiscal year as higher airfreight costs and food-safety concerns squeezed exporters.

Exporters fear that the situation could worsen in the current October-December quarter as flight disruptions involving Saudi Arabia, a major destination, threaten to further complicate the movement of perishable produce.

Following a series of reported Houthi attacks in early October, restrictions at the Saudi Arabian airports have affected 134 flights involving Bangladesh, according to the latest figures from the Civil Aviation Authority of Bangladesh (CAAB).

Bangladesh earned $24.01 million from vegetable exports in the first three months of FY2026-27, down from $25.79 million in the same period a year earlier, according to data from the Export Promotion Bureau (EPB).

Exporters said higher freight charges, flight disruptions, excessive pesticide residues in produce and inadequate cooling facilities at airports were making it harder for Bangladeshi vegetables to compete in overseas markets.

Chowdhury Anower, organising secretary of the Bangladesh Fruits, Vegetables and Allied Products Exporters’ Association, said Bangladesh’s vegetable exports primarily went to Saudi Arabia and other Middle Eastern countries, as well as Europe.

He said conflicts in the Middle East had disrupted shipments, leaving exporters struggling to divert produce to alternative destinations. Unpredictable airfreight rates, rising labour costs and higher carton prices were also putting pressure on exporters.

Airfreight spot rates from South Asia to the Middle East remained 91 percent above their late-February levels in the week of September 21-27, according to freight intelligence firm Xeneta.

In its October 1 market update, Xeneta said global air cargo spot rates averaged $3.10 per kilogram in September, up 27 percent year-on-year and 2 percent from August. Demand growth outpaced capacity expansion, while higher fuel costs added to pressure on rates.

Anower said freight rates in Bangladesh were higher than those in neighbouring countries, making it difficult for local exporters to compete in international markets, particularly in Europe and the Middle East.

Kawser Ahmed Rubel, chief executive officer of vegetable exporter Global Trade Link, also identified higher airfreight costs, excessive pesticide residues and inadequate cooling facilities at the airport as major obstacles to vegetable exports.

Airfreight rates had risen to more than Tk 550 per kg from around Tk 490 to Tk 500 last year, he said. The Daily Star could not independently verify the figures.

Rubel added that pesticide residues detected in exported vegetables had led to restrictions on country beans and Zara lemons in European markets, affecting export opportunities.

EU regulations now require enhanced border checks on certain Bangladeshi vegetables because of pesticide-residue concerns. The European Commission, under a new regulation issued in June, requires identity and physical checks on 30 percent of consignments of “seem beans” and “helmet beans” from Bangladesh and 20 percent of Zara lemon consignments because of pesticide-residue concerns.

Rubel also pointed to a lack of cooling chambers at the airport, saying perishable cargo often remained at ambient temperatures for three to four hours after security screening before being loaded onto aircraft, potentially compromising product quality.

Mobasserur Rahman, proprietor of BK Trade International, said high airfreight costs were the primary reason for the decline in vegetable exports.

Freight rates to Canada had risen to Tk 750 to Tk 800 per kg from Tk 300 to Tk 350 last year, while rates to London had increased to more than Tk 750 from Tk 250, he said. The Daily Star could not independently verify the figures.

Bangladesh produces more than 15 million tonnes of vegetables annually but exports less than 0.3 percent of that volume, according to a recent report.
