title: Rajshahi-6 BNP MP receives Tk 12,500 farming incentive cheque from PM; party says he is eligible
text:
Rajshahi-6 BNP lawmaker Abu Sayeed Chand was among 15 sugarcane farmers who received government incentive cheques from Prime Minister Tarique Rahman at a rally in Rajshahi on Tuesday afternoon. Chand received Tk 12,500.

The cheques were distributed at Haji Muhammad Mohsin Government High School Ground, where the prime minister launched a Tk 12 crore incentive programme for 38,970 sugarcane farmers.

Contacted, Syed Shaheen Shawkat, Rajshahi division organising secretary of BNP's National Executive Committee, told The Daily Star that Chand received the incentive in his capacity as a sugarcane farmer.

Shawkat said Chand was a registered sugarcane farmer alongside being an MP, adding that there was no reason to view his receiving the incentive negatively if he was considered an individual farmer rather than a lawmaker.

Farmers from all eligible categories have been brought under the scheme in line with its eligibility criteria and conditions, he said.

He added that the initiative was not about giving anyone undue or additional money, but about utilising fallow land between rows of sugarcane. Farmers are cultivating pulses, cabbage, potatoes and seasonal crops such as onions, ginger and garlic in these spaces as intercrops.

Across the country, the unused land between sugarcane rows could amount to several hundred thousand acres, and the government has taken the initiative to utilise this vast area, he said.

Sugarcane is a long-duration crop, and farmers can grow short-duration crops such as chickpeas and potatoes in the vacant spaces during its growing period. This makes it possible to produce at least two to three additional crops of vegetables and spices a year, benefiting farmers and increasing the supply of such produce, Shawkat said.

Following the inauguration of the digital disbursement process, 15 sugarcane farmers were invited to the stage, where the prime minister handed them cheques one by one. Abu Sayeed Chand, identified as a sugarcane farmer supplying Rajshahi Sugar Mills, was the first to be called to receive a cheque, he added.

The Daily Star could not reach MP Chand for comment despite repeated phone calls.

In a Facebook post, Chand wrote, “Sugarcane cultivation and supply have been a family tradition for generations, from my grandfather and father to myself. I also cultivate various other crops. I have personally supplied hundreds of truckloads of sugarcane to Rajshahi Sugar Mills and will continue to do so.”

The relevant information and documents are preserved by the mill authorities, and the facts can be verified by examining those records, the MP added.

title: Farmers eye handsome returns from chillies in Jamalpur's Madarganj
text:
A smile spreads across Haider Ali’s face as he looks forward to a handsome profit from his chilli field. From just one bigha of land in Jamalpur’s Madarganj upazila, he has already sold green chillies worth Tk 60,000, raising hopes of earning Tk 1 lakh to Tk 1.5 lakh from the plot this season.

With cultivation costs standing at around Tk 30,000 so far, Haider is optimistic about his earnings, provided market prices remain favourable.

Green chillies are selling for Tk 80-90 per kg in wholesale markets and Tk 120 per kg at retail, said Haider, a farmer from Fuljor in Jorkhali union.

Like Haider, farmers in the char areas of Madarganj are hoping for substantial profits from a good harvest and favourable market prices, with many already earning from early sales.

Favourable weather and suitable soil have encouraged farmers to cultivate chilli on more land than targeted this season.

According to the Upazila Agriculture Office, Madarganj , chilli has been planted on 1,050 hectares against a target of 750 hectares, exceeding it by 300 hectares. Of the total, 300 hectares are under early-season cultivation, while farmers have adopted plastic mulching on 25 hectares.

Several varieties, including Moynamoti, Green Super, Naga Fire, Bijli, Green Star, Super and Premium, are being cultivated in the upazila. The agriculture department expects the area under chilli cultivation to increase further this season.

Image Photo: Star

A recent visit to the char areas revealed extensive fields dotted with green chillies. Farmers were harvesting the crop, tending plants and spraying pesticides. Harvesting has already begun on the 300 hectares planted early, with women and children working alongside men to pick the chillies.

Abdul Khaleque Islam, a farmer from Kaizar Char, said he had cultivated the Moynamoti variety on three bighas using plastic mulching. The plants are now flowering.

However, he said cultivation costs had risen compared with last year, with higher expenses for land preparation, irrigation, seeds, fertiliser, pesticides, transport and labour. He also reported difficulties in obtaining fertiliser.

Ratan Mia, a farmer from Sukhnagari in Balijuri union, said he had planted an early-season chilli variety on 34 decimals of land and had begun harvesting after getting a good yield.

He sold a maund of chillies for Tk 3,200 in the wholesale market but had heard that prices were beginning to fall. He said farmers could still make a profit if their plants remained healthy, even if prices declined. However, sudden plant deaths in some fields could cause substantial losses.

Upazila Agriculture Officer Habibur Rahman said chilli production in Madarganj could exceed 42,000 tonnes this season as cultivation had surpassed the target.

After meeting local demand, chillies are being sent to Dhaka, Narayanganj and other districts across the country, bringing profits to farmers, he said.

He added that more than 200 farmers had received government incentives to encourage chilli cultivation. “We provide farmers with advice and assistance to the best of our ability whenever they approach us with a problem,” he said.

title: Govt to buy 70,000 tonnes of urea
text:
The government will procure 70,000 tonnes of urea fertiliser, keeping food security and farmers' demand in mind.

Some 30,000 tonnes will be procured from the local institution Karnaphuli Fertiliser Company Limited (KAFCO) and 40,000 tonnes from Saudi Arabia.

The Cabinet Committee on Government Purchase gave the go-ahead to the procurement proposal of the industries ministry at a meeting today.

Bagged granular urea fertiliser will be procured from KAFCO at a unit price of $408.375 per tonne, while bulk granular urea fertiliser will be procured from SABIC Agri-Nutrients Company of Saudi Arabia at a unit price of $431.67 per tonne.

The government will spend around Tk 364.55 crore to purchase the fertiliser under the two proposals.

The demand for urea in the current fiscal year is 30 lakh tonnes, of which contracts have been signed to import 5.5 lakh tonnes from KAFCO and 3.2 lakh tonnes from SABIC Agri-Nutrients Company.

title: Illegal hilsa fishing, sales continue in Barishal despite 22-day ban
text:
Illegal hilsa fishing and open sales of the fish have continued unabated along both banks of the Meghna River in Barishal’s Hizla and Mehendiganj upazilas, despite the ongoing 22-day ban imposed to protect mother hilsa during the breeding season.

According to local residents, hilsa caught illegally is being sold every day in at least 30 markets across the two upazilas, with an estimated 2,000-3,000 maunds being traded daily.

The Fisheries Department has sought the deployment of the army or Coast Guard to strengthen operations in four upazilas in the district and prevent further deterioration of the situation.

Fisheries officials said Hizla and Mehendiganj upazilas had no fisheries officers until shortly before the ban began, with officers posted just a day before the 22-day restriction came into effect on October 8.

Thousands of fishers from at least 10 unions on both banks of the Meghna reportedly take to the river during the ban.

Mahfuzur Rahman, fisheries officer of Mehendiganj upazila, said, “The river is vast, and there are syndicates operating here. We are trying as hard as we can. So far, 10 people have been detained, around five lakh cubic metres of fishing nets have been seized, and 30-35kg of hilsa have been recovered.”

He alleged that the fishers had become increasingly defiant and were attacking enforcement teams. Two days ago, members of the Coast Guard also fired shots, but the illegal fishing continued, he added.

Local fishers told this correspondent that markets in Kaliganj, Burir Pul and Hajir Hat in South Ulania union, Aliganj in Alimabad union, and markets in Char Gopalpur, Jangalia and Bhasanchar unions of Mehendiganj were flooded with small hilsa.

Hizla Upazila Nirbahi Officer (UNO) Md Ilias Shikder said, “We generally do not conduct operations at night by crossing the turbulent river. It also takes considerable time.”

The administration was conducting drives and had recovered hilsa, which was later donated to orphanages, he added.

Mehendiganj UNO Mohammad Riazur Rahman said, “We have held awareness meetings with fishers, but they have not produced any meaningful results.”

Md Hadiuzzaman, Barishal district fisheries officer, said, “The river becomes extremely dangerous after sunset, making it difficult even to reach some areas. We have virtually no budget this year, so the number of enforcement drives has declined compared with previous years.”

Deputy Commissioner Mohammad Mamun Khandaker said, “We are conducting drives in one area, but they may be catching fish elsewhere. We have decided to intensify our operations.”

The Fisheries Department said Barishal district has 422,275 registered fishers. Of them, 358,516 are being provided with 25kg of rice each as government assistance during the 22-day hilsa fishing ban.

title: Shareholding cap relaxed for investors of UCB
text:
Bangladesh Bank (BB) has relaxed the ceiling on shareholding in United Commercial Bank PLC (UCB), allowing a single investor or family to hold up to 30 percent of the lender’s paid-up capital.

In a circular issued today, the central bank said the shareholding restriction under Section 14Ka of the Bank Company Act, 1991, would not apply to UCB.

The exemption covers any person, institution, company or family members holding shares in the bank, directly or indirectly, individually or jointly with others.

The circular, issued under Section 121 of the Act, which empowers the central bank to grant such exemptions, said the step was taken “to strengthen the capital base” of the bank.

It does not name any prospective investor, state how much capital UCB is expected to raise, or explain the reasons for the decision.

A BB official, requesting anonymity, said a large portion of the bank’s shares had been blocked by a High Court order. Those shares are owned by Saifuzzaman, a former director of the bank and former land minister. The relaxation was meant to create an opportunity to raise the bank’s capital, the official said.

In a statement, UCB welcomed the move, saying it removed a significant legal barrier to large share investments and would widen the participation of strategic investors.

The bank said a capital shortage was a well-known problem in the country’s banking sector and that strengthening its capital base was a top priority in building UCB into a strong, transparent and trusted institution.

It has already taken two steps with the regulator’s approval: a Tk 775 crore rights share issue and a Tk 800 crore subordinated bond issue.

UCB’s next goal is to bring in reputable and financially capable strategic investors, both local and foreign. Shareholders approved the plan at the bank’s last annual general meeting.

The bank said it wanted more than capital from such investors and was looking for advanced technology, international experience, good governance and a long-term commitment to its development.

UCB expressed confidence that, with proper regulatory oversight and governance, such initiatives could attract long-term investment to the banking sector and help restore public trust.

It said its aim was to build a reliable, customer-friendly and modern bank founded on strong capital, transparency and good governance.

title: Apparel makers to showcase sustainability initiatives at BATEXPO 2026
text:
The Bangladesh Garment Manufacturers and Exporters Association (BGMEA) will showcase sustainability initiatives in the country's readymade garment sector at BATEXPO 2026, as global markets place greater emphasis on responsible manufacturing and supply-chain transparency.

Organised by the association, the expo will be held on November 18-19 at the Bangladesh-China Friendship Conference Centre in Dhaka, the BGMEA said in a press statement today.

At the event, the BGMEA will set up a dedicated area called the ‘Impact Zone’ to highlight initiatives in decarbonisation, renewable energy, recycling, circularity and resource efficiency, as well as gender equity, worker health and nutrition, childcare and maternal care.

The association will also demonstrate digital traceability solutions, including the Digital Product Passport (DPP), in response to evolving European Union regulations and global supply-chain requirements.

The initiative aims to highlight how Bangladesh's apparel industry is moving beyond conventional compliance to strengthen sustainability, transparency and global competitiveness.

Speaking about the initiative, BGMEA President Mahmud Hasan Khan said the Impact Zone would reflect the transformation taking place across the industry amid growing emphasis on climate action, resource efficiency and the circular economy.

“This is not merely a story of compliance; it is the story of a distinctive and responsible journey towards leadership in global markets,” he said.

BGMEA Vice-president Vidiya Amrit Khan said the country's apparel industry must be prepared not only to meet evolving global sustainability requirements but also to lead the transition towards responsible manufacturing.

She said the Impact Zone would showcase progress in decarbonisation, circularity, worker wellbeing and digital traceability, including the Digital Product Passport.

“Our ambition is to position Bangladesh as a trusted, forward-looking partner in the global shift towards sustainable apparel production,” she said.

title: RMG wage board to be formed soon: Minister
text:
The government will soon form the minimum wage board for garment workers, Labour and Employment Minister Ariful Haque Choudhury said today.

The list of representatives from the employers’ side has already been received, and the gazette notification for the formation of the wage board will be published as soon as the list from the workers’ side arrives, according to a statement from the labour ministry.

The six-member wage board for garment workers consists of employer, worker, government and independent representatives.

The minister shared the information at the 96th meeting of the Tripartite Consultative Council (TCC) and the 25th meeting of the RMG Tripartite Consultative Council (RMG TCC), organised by the ministry at the CIRDAP Conference Centre in Dhaka.

Regarding the ongoing labour unrest and protests, the minister said he had urged employers to clear workers’ outstanding wages by the seventh of every month.

“At the same time, I would tell protesting workers not to cause public suffering by blocking roads in the name of a movement.”

Any problem should be resolved internally through discussions between employers and workers within the factories, he said.

He further warned that if anyone tried to put the government in an embarrassing situation or pursued any other malicious intent, neither the government, nor the employers, nor the worker representatives would tolerate it.

Image

“I am directing law enforcement agencies and intelligence organisations to swiftly bring to justice those who are instigating unrest from outside the actual labour leadership and turning non-issues into issues. No third party will be allowed to create chaos in the industrial sector at any cost,” he added.

At the meeting, Nazma Akter, president of Sommilito Garments Sramik Federation, talked about recent incidents of labour unrest in various industrial areas, including Gazipur.

She stated that the government, employers and worker representatives were working jointly to clear outstanding wages quickly, and efforts were underway to resolve the issues with the help of the industrial police and local administration.

She noted that initiatives had been taken to complete the process of forming the wage board within the month.

Furthermore, discussions were ongoing with the government regarding increasing workers’ wages, controlling house rent, reducing the prices of daily essentials, and resolving gas and energy crises.

Razekuzzaman Ratan, assistant general secretary of Bangladesher Samajtantrik Dal, said that a policy decision on forming the wage board had been made at the TCC meeting, and he expressed optimism that it would be implemented swiftly.

Rezwan Selim, vice-president of the Bangladesh Garment Manufacturers and Exporters Association, expressed concern over the ongoing protests in Gazipur and Kaliakair and called for a quick and sustainable solution.

Mohammad Hatem, president of the Bangladesh Knitwear Manufacturers and Exporters Association (BKMEA), said the government was highly committed to increasing workers’ wages.

If employers and workers shared the same mindset, there would be no need for fresh protests, he said.

The BKMEA president urged workers not to damage industrial factories or embarrass the government.

Md Abdur Rahman Tarfder, secretary to the labour and employment ministry, also spoke.

title: Square Pharma recommends 130% cash dividend
text:
Square Pharmaceuticals has recommended a 130 percent cash dividend for the fiscal year 2025-26 (FY26), backed by higher sales and profits.

The company made the decision at a board meeting today.

Its sales rose around 13 percent to Tk 8,606 crore in FY26, while profit increased 18 percent to Tk 2,770 crore.

The company paid cash dividends of 120 percent, 110 percent and 105 percent in the previous three financial years. Before that, it paid 100 percent and 60 percent dividends.

Square Pharmaceuticals, the country’s largest pharmaceutical company, began its journey in 1958 under the leadership of the late Samson H Chowdhury.

It now exports to more than 40 countries and aims to boost overseas sales by making better use of its existing facilities.

Shares of the blue-chip company have remained relatively stable over the years. Over the past year, its share price ranged from Tk 198 to Tk 236. Yesterday, it traded at Tk 218.

title: Govt’s one-stop service portal myGov goes offline
text:
Bangladesh's one-stop government service portal, myGov, went offline today, leaving citizens and businesses unable to access a wide range of public services, as authorities announced "emergency maintenance" for security upgrades.

Visitors to mygov.bd this afternoon were met with a "Web server is down" message and Cloudflare error code 521, which indicates that the origin web server is not responding to connection requests.

The error page showed that the user's browser and Cloudflare's Dhaka node were working, while the host server for www.mygov.bd was in error.

Aspire to Innovate (a2i), which runs myGov, displayed an "emergency announcement" saying urgent maintenance was under way to improve security and service quality.

The notice said the work would continue until midnight on October 27 and that users might face temporary disruption.

"We are sincerely sorry for this," it said. The notice did not state the cause.

Speaking to The Daily Star, Muhammad Anwar Uddin, project director at a2i, which runs myGov, said the platform needed upgrades.

"We need some upgrades. That is why we want to carry out the updates," he said.

Asked whether the shutdown was linked to vulnerabilities in PHP, a programming language widely used to build websites, he said some such issues had emerged.

"Yes, there are some issues like that. Some issues have come up that are PHP-based, and some of our systems are outside PHP," he said.

He said the updates were being made for protection.

An official of the Bangladesh e-Government Computer Incident Response Team (BGD e-GOV CIRT), the government's cyber security agency, also said the agency had flagged PHP-related issues on some websites run by a2i.

"We have raised some issues regarding PHP in some websites run by a2i, and they are working on it," the CIRT official said.

CIRT issued an advisory on October 22 about PHP2Shell, a set of vulnerabilities that could allow attackers to run malicious code on servers remotely without logging in.

In a high-severity alert issued yesterday, it warned that several government and private organisations were still using outdated or unsupported PHP versions and urged them to apply verified patches or restrict public access.

The vulnerability has already disrupted digital services.

Bangladesh Bank restored its website at 8am yesterday after keeping it offline for two and a half days.

On Saturday, the websites of six banks, including Agrani, Janata and Bengal Commercial Bank, went offline, with some remaining down until Sunday. The land ministry also suspended services on land.gov.bd for about 36 hours from midnight on October 22.

CIRT has cautioned that running an outdated PHP version does not necessarily mean a system has been attacked, as the actual risk depends on the version in use, whether patches have been applied and how exposed the system is to the internet.

myGov brings government-to-citizen, government-to-business and government-to-government services together online. Users apply for services from different ministries, track applications in real time and pay fees. Services include certificate attestation, land-related applications, allowances, and business licences and permits.

A prolonged shutdown is therefore likely to affect people with pending applications, including those seeking attestation for study or travel abroad, and businesses waiting for licences or permits.

title: Dollar edges up as oil, gas import payments mount
text:
The US dollar rose slightly against the taka yesterday as banks faced mounting pressure to settle letters of credit (LCs) for oil and gas imports.

Eastern Bank PLC quoted the dollar at Tk 123.98 for spot selling and Tk 122.98 for spot buying, up from Tk 123.95 and Tk 122.95, respectively, a day earlier. The rates were considerably lower a week ago.

State-owned Sonali Bank quoted the dollar at Tk 123.90 for spot selling and between Tk 122.63 and Tk 122.90 for spot buying.

In the interbank market, the weighted average dollar rate rose to Tk 123.75 yesterday from Tk 123.73 a day earlier and Tk 123.45 a week ago, according to Bangladesh Bank (BB) data.

Bankers attributed the increase mainly to higher payment pressure for oil and gas imports.

A BB official said dollar inflows and outflows were roughly balanced, but payment pressure usually increases towards the end of a month

A treasury head of a state-owned bank, who wished to remain anonymous, told The Daily Star that government payments for oil and gas imports were putting heavy pressure on the market. His bank was also facing a slight dollar shortage, he said.

Import payments rose 12 percent year-on-year to $12.20 billion in July and August of the current fiscal year, according to BB data. Payments for petroleum products alone doubled to $2.49 billion.

Industry insiders said global fuel prices had risen amid tensions in the Middle East, increasing the country’s import bill.

A BB official said dollar inflows and outflows were roughly balanced, but payment pressure usually increased towards the end of the month, pushing up the exchange rate.

Remittance inflows also tended to slow towards the end of the month, creating a temporary mismatch in the market, the official added.

Expatriate Bangladeshis sent home $2.13 billion between October 1 and 24, up from $2 billion in the same period last year.

Despite some volatility in the foreign exchange market, the country’s reserves remained at a comfortable level. The central bank data showed that reserves stood at $31.54 billion under the BPM6 method on October 19, up from $26.34 billion a year earlier.

title: First round of FTA talks with Malaysia starts today
text:
Bangladesh and Malaysia will begin negotiations for a free trade agreement (FTA) in Dhaka today as Bangladesh seeks to secure preferential market access after its graduation from the least developed country (LDC) category.

The first round of talks aims to advance an agreement by next year, a commerce ministry official told The Daily Star, asking not to be named.

Additional Commerce Secretary Khadiza Nazneen will lead the Bangladesh delegation at the meeting at Hotel Pan Pacific Sonargaon Dhaka, the official said. A 30-member Malaysian delegation is in the capital for the negotiations.

The proposed FTA is part of Bangladesh’s efforts to expand trade agreements with potential partners ahead of LDC graduation, which will erode some of the trade preferences the country currently enjoys.

Bangladesh signed an economic partnership agreement (EPA) with Japan and a comprehensive economic partnership agreement (CEPA) with South Korea this year to secure preferential market access.

However, both agreements are yet to take effect as they require parliamentary ratification in the respective countries.

Bangladesh also signed a preferential trade agreement (PTA) with Bhutan in December 2020, covering 34 Bhutanese products and 100 Bangladeshi products. The agreement is now in operation.

‘INCLUDE MANPOWER EXPORTS IN NEGOTIATION’

Md Anwar Shahid, president of the Bangladesh Malaysia Chamber of Commerce and Industry (BMCCI), welcomed the initiative, saying Bangladesh should pursue FTAs with potential trading partners to prepare for the loss of preferential market access.

“Trade should be used as a tool for development, as many developed and developing countries have already demonstrated,” he said.

He noted that an FTA with Malaysia could reduce the National Board of Revenue’s tariff revenue but argued that the potential benefits of a trade agreement should not be overlooked.

Anwar also called for including manpower exports in the negotiations, saying Bangladesh’s economic ties with Malaysia remained limited in scope and that Bangladesh had yet to diversify its exports significantly beyond garment products.

Bangladesh exports textiles and apparel, leather and leather goods, jute and jute products, fish and seafood, and pharmaceuticals to Malaysia. Its imports from the country include electrical and electronic equipment, palm oil, machinery and mechanical appliances, rubber products and chemicals.

In fiscal year 2024-25, Bangladesh exported goods worth $282 million to Malaysia and imported goods worth $2.29 billion, according to data from the Export Promotion Bureau and Bangladesh Bank.

The trade gap partly reflects Bangladesh’s substantial imports of palm oil from Malaysia.

‘MALAYSIA COULD BE A GATEWAY TO ASEAN’

M Masrur Reaz, chairman and chief executive officer of Policy Exchange of Bangladesh, also stressed the importance of securing market access and diversifying export destinations ahead of LDC graduation.

He said 84 percent of Bangladesh’s exports were concentrated in the garment sector, while a similar proportion went to just three destinations — the United Kingdom, the United States and the European Union.

Masrur said Bangladesh’s export concentration had been supported by duty-free market access linked to its LDC status, making it important to pursue new trade arrangements as those preferences change.

Asian markets could play a greater role in expanding trade and business after graduation, he said, adding that agreements with Malaysia, Japan, South Korea and other countries would be important in that effort.

He also noted that Malaysia could potentially serve as a gateway for Bangladesh to access the wider Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) market.

Despite the region’s growth potential, Bangladesh’s exports to ASEAN remain low, he said.

The PEB chief also said major trading nations were increasingly focusing on regional markets, partly amid geopolitical uncertainties, making closer trade ties within Asia more important.

Like Anwar, he too suggested that Bangladesh include manpower exports in the FTA negotiations with Malaysia to broaden the scope of bilateral economic cooperation.

title: Haier launches Tigris water heaters, microwave ovens
text:
Haier Bangladesh Limited has launched its premium Tigris water heater series and its first-ever range of microwave ovens in the local market, stepping up efforts to tap into growing demand for modern household appliances.

Fan Jing, chief executive officer of Haier Bangladesh, inaugurated the products at the company’s outlet in Gulshan, Dhaka recently, according to a press release.

The Tigris water heater series features Haier’s “Shockproof Water Heater. Safe as Unplugged.” technology and a Super Titanium Enamel Tank designed to ensure stable heating and long-term durability.

The series comprises premium golden-finish horizontal models with capacities of 35 litres and 45 litres, alongside an innovative 30-litre vertical model featuring the “No Hanging, No Drilling” design.

The design eliminates the need for complicated wall installation, allowing flexible placement and greater convenience for households.

Haier has also introduced three microwave oven models to meet diverse local cooking needs: a 20-litre solo model, a 23-litre grill model and a multifunctional 30-litre convection model.

The 30-litre model combines microwave, grill, convection and air-fry functions, offering an all-in-one cooking solution amid growing demand for versatile kitchen appliances that support healthier cooking.

With the launch, Haier Bangladesh aims to strengthen its presence across multiple home appliance categories.

The company said it would continue to combine global technological innovation with local market insights, introduce more consumer-focused premium products and provide reliable after-sales services to improve the smart living experience of Bangladeshi households.

Ashraful Alam, sales and marketing director of Haier Bangladesh, along with other company officials, was also present at the launching ceremony.

title: Prime Bank signs payroll banking deal with Pharma Solutions
text:
Prime Bank PLC recently signed a payroll banking agreement with Pharma Solutions Bangladesh Limited, a pharmaceutical distribution, warehousing and healthcare supply chain services company operating across Bangladesh, to offer comprehensive payroll banking services.

Mamur Ahmed, senior executive vice-president and head of distribution network at the bank, and Pallab Chakravorty, chief executive officer of general administration at the pharmaceutical distribution company, signed the agreement at the bank’s head office in Gulshan, Dhaka, according to a press release.

Under the agreement, employees of Pharma Solutions Bangladesh Limited will enjoy payroll banking facilities, including salary accounts with competitive rates, dual-currency debit cards with fee waivers and lifestyle benefits, customised loan and credit card facilities, and a wide range of consumer banking products and services on preferential terms.

They will also have access to PrimePay, the bank’s omni-digital platform, which enables seamless and automated salary disbursements, along with convenient, round-the-clock corporate payment solutions.

Hasina Fardous, senior vice-president and head of payroll banking at the bank; Md Robiul Alam Iskandar, senior business development manager of payroll banking; Abu Saied Md Al Mamun, director of finance at the pharmaceutical distribution company; and Md Zahid Hossain, head of human resources, along with other senior officials from both organisations, were also present at the signing ceremony.

title: Modhumoti Bank reviews branch business performance
text:
Modhumoti Bank PLC held a two-day conference on Saturday and Sunday to review branch business performance and develop strategies to achieve business targets.

The conference, held at Sheraton Dhaka, was inaugurated by Salahuddin Alamgir, chairman of the bank’s board of directors, according to a press release.

The meeting reviewed each branch’s year-to-date business performance and progress. Participants also developed branch-specific strategies and future action plans, taking into account the country’s business environment, the banking sector and broader macroeconomic conditions.

The conference was attended by A Mannan Khan, chairman of the Risk Management Committee; Md Shafiqul Alam, chairman of the Audit Committee; Md Shafiul Azam, managing director; Shahnawaj Chowdhury, additional managing director; Arab Fazlur Rahman, deputy managing director and chief business officer; and Arif Hasan Khan, deputy managing director and chief risk officer.

Divisional heads from the head office and all branch managers also attended the event.

title: NRB Bank eases banking services for expatriates
text:
NRB Bank PLC has launched a Non-Resident Convertible Taka Account (NRCTA) for non-resident Bangladeshis, aiming to expand banking services for expatriates.

The bank is among the first in Bangladesh to introduce the product, according to a press release.

Tarek Reaz Khan, managing director and chief executive officer (CEO) of the bank, inaugurated the product at a ceremony held at the bank’s corporate head office in Dhaka on Sunday.

Anwar Uddin and Kimiwa Saddat, additional managing directors of the bank; M Rashidul Huda, deputy managing director; and Oli Ahad Chowdhury, senior executive vice-president and head of retail banking, were also present at the launching ceremony, along with other officials.

title: Janata, Agrani get new managing directors from private sector
text:
The government has appointed contractual managing directors to four state-run banks, two of whom came from the private sector.

Md Mahbub Alam, former additional managing director of Southeast Bank, has been appointed managing director of Janata Bank.

Noor Mohammed, former deputy managing director of Jamuna Bank, will serve as managing director of Agrani Bank for the next three years.

Meanwhile, Janata Bank’s former deputy managing director, Md Nurul Huda, has been appointed managing director of BASIC Bank.

Shawkat Ali Khan will continue serving as managing director of Sonali Bank after the government today withdrew the order, under which his appointment was cancelled earlier.

Khan, who was appointed in October 2024, will now serve the bank until the end of his three-year tenure.

Apart from Khan, the other three managing directors will serve for the next three years.

Last week, the government decided to cancel the remaining tenures of the contractual appointments of the managing directors and chief executive officers of three major state-owned commercial banks: Sonali, Janata and Rupali.

Last month, the appointments of the managing directors of Agrani Bank, Bangladesh Development Bank Limited and BASIC Bank were cancelled.

title: Palli Sanchay Bank deposits Tk 60 crore dividend in govt treasury
text:
Palli Sanchay Bank has deposited Tk 60 crore in dividends declared in favour of the government for the period up to the 2023-24 fiscal year into the government treasury.

The cheque was formally handed over to Finance Minister Amir Khosru Mahmud Chowdhury at his office at the Bangladesh Secretariat in Dhaka today.

AKM Jahangir, chairman of the bank’s board of directors, and Salma Banu, its managing director, handed over the cheque to the minister where Nazma Mobarek, secretary of the Financial Institutions Division, was present.

Palli Sanchay Bank works to improve the living standards of people in remote areas of the country, promote socioeconomic development, alleviate poverty and create employment.

title: BRAC Bank to issue country’s first Tk 1,000 crore green bond
text:
BRAC Bank is set to issue a Tk 1,000 crore green bond, the first in the country to align with Bangladesh Bank’s policy on green bond financing for banks and financial institutions, as the private lender seeks to channel long-term money into renewable energy and energy-efficient industry.

The three-year bond will be senior, unsecured, non-convertible, fully redeemable and zero-coupon, the bank said at a press conference in Dhaka today.

Each bond will carry a face value of Tk 10 lakh and will be offered to corporate institutions and individual investors. Eligible company provident and gratuity funds may also invest, subject to regulatory and investment requirements.

Proceeds will go to eligible green projects, including renewable energy, green buildings and industrial energy-efficiency initiatives.

The bank said the framework follows the International Capital Market Association’s Green Bond Principles and has received a second-party opinion from S&P Global Ratings.

It also said it expects the funds to contribute to four United Nations Sustainable Development Goals: affordable and clean energy (SDG 7), industry, innovation and infrastructure (SDG 9), sustainable cities and communities (SDG 11), and climate action (SDG 13).

Tareq Refat Ullah Khan, managing director and CEO of BRAC Bank, said many factories were turning to renewable energy amid the global energy crisis and rising fuel prices, but such projects needed affordable, long-term financing.

“This green bond marks an important milestone in BRAC Bank’s sustainable finance journey and represents a meaningful step towards deepening Bangladesh’s capital market,” he said.

He said the bank was targeting a return of 7.5 percent and that the tax treatment of zero-coupon bonds could make the paper attractive to investors.

He thanked the government and the Securities and Exchange Commission for their support for the tax benefits. To ensure transparency, he added, the bank would conduct annual audits to verify that proceeds were used only for eligible green projects.

A zero-coupon bond pays no periodic interest. Investors buy it at a discount and receive the full face value at maturity, with the difference being their return.

At a 7.5 percent yield, a Tk 10 lakh bond would be priced at roughly Tk 8.05 lakh at issue, assuming annual compounding.

For a banking sector that has struggled with a shortage of long-term funding, the issue is also a test of the domestic corporate bond market, which remains shallow, BRAC Bank officials said.

“Most bank lending to renewable energy and energy-efficiency projects is tied to tenors that are hard to match with short-term deposits, so a three-year instrument, though modest in length, could help ease that mismatch.”

BRAC Bank said sustainable finance accounts for more than 60 percent of its loan portfolio. It has been named among Bangladesh Bank’s top sustainable banks for five consecutive years and ranked first among Bangladeshi banks in Bloomberg’s ESG Rating. It previously issued a social bond.

The BRAC Bank managing director said the bank wanted to contribute to a financial ecosystem in which sustainability is embedded in investment decisions and that the bond would help create an alternative source of long-term financing for sustainable development.

title: Bangladesh Bank restores website after two-and-a-half-day shutdown over cyber alert
text:
Bangladesh Bank has restored its website at 8am today after keeping it offline for two-and-a-half days as a precaution against potential cyber threats following a global cybersecurity alert.

The website had been inaccessible since Thursday noon. Visitors were greeted with a notice stating that the service was undergoing scheduled maintenance and would be restored shortly.

Arief Hossain Khan, executive director and spokesperson of the central bank, confirmed that the website was back online at 8am on Sunday.

A day earlier, he had said the bank was monitoring the situation and had yet to restore the website to ensure its security.

He also said the connection between the central bank and commercial banks was operating smoothly.

“Our IT department is working on it,” he said at the time, without specifying when the website would be restored.

The central bank took the website offline on Thursday as a precaution after receiving the cybersecurity alert.

The move followed emergency measures taken worldwide after critical vulnerabilities were disclosed in PHP, a widely used programming language. Cybersecurity firms Calif and Wiz identified the flaws using artificial intelligence tools. Although patches were released, details of the vulnerabilities became public before the fixes could be fully applied.

Bangladesh Bank has faced major cybersecurity incidents in the past. In 2016, hackers diverted $101 million from its account with the Federal Reserve Bank of New York, prompting then governor Atiur Rahman to resign.

In 2023, the central bank shut down some internal web-based services for 36 hours as a precaution against a possible cyberattack.

title: Govt relaxes experience rules for state commercial bank CEOs
text:
The government has revised its policy on appointing chief executives of state-owned commercial banks, allowing the experience requirement to be relaxed in exceptional cases.

The amendment, issued on October 19 by the Financial Institutions Division (FID), applies to the appointment of managing directors (MDs) and CEOs at six banks: Sonali, Janata, Agrani, Rupali, BDBL and BASIC.

The change comes as the government has cancelled the remaining tenure of the contractual MDs and CEOs of three banks: Sonali, Janata and Rupali.

Under the earlier rule, a candidate had to be a serving or former bank officer with at least 20 years of experience. An amendment in July this year added a requirement of at least two years of experience in the post immediately below that of MD or CEO.

Both requirements remain, but the new provision allows the two-year condition to be waived for candidates with special skills, professional qualifications, leadership ability and a good reputation.

The age range of 45 to 65 years, the three-year contract term and the nomination process remain unchanged.

The new policy repeals the July 2026 version, though actions taken under that version remain valid.

This is the third time in nine months that the government has changed the policy. The previous version was issued in January 2023.

Under the policy, the government nominates MDs rather than appointing them directly, and the board finalises the appointment after receiving a no-objection from Bangladesh Bank.

The government retains the power to appoint the heads of the six specialised banks, as well as the Bangladesh House Building Finance Corporation and the Investment Corporation of Bangladesh.

Under the revised policy, promotions will prioritise performance, leadership ability, service record and experience in key bank departments. Seniority alone, therefore, will not determine promotions.

The scoring tables for promotions to deputy MD and general manager positions remain unchanged.

Candidates must hold at least a master's degree from a recognised university, with no third division or class at any stage of their education.

In addition to the selection committee's recommendation, the candidate's intelligence report and the Anti-Corruption Commission's report will be reviewed.

Fahmida Khatun, distinguished fellow at the Centre for Policy Dialogue (CPD), said that the importance of skilled and competent manpower in banks, especially state-owned banks, is immense.

On the one hand, these banks must be kept free from political influence; on the other, skilled personnel must be recruited, she added.

“State-owned banks can be turned around only if rules and policies are followed. The boards of banks must be kept free from political influence, and transparent and professional people must be appointed.”

“But I do not understand why this policy was amended at this particular moment,” she said.

title: 8 places in Bangladesh to visit this winter
text:
There’s only so much scorching heat, relentless humidity and sweating through your clothes that a person can tolerate. After spending most of the year complaining about the weather, it's no surprise that winter is the season Bangladeshis eagerly look forward to. Finally, you can step outside without feeling like you're being roasted alive.

And what better way to enjoy this short-lived relief than to travel? From mist-covered tea gardens and chilly northern towns to beaches and bird-filled wetlands, Bangladesh has plenty to offer during the colder months. Here are eight places worth visiting before the summer heat makes its inevitable return.

Image Photo: Firoz Al Sabah

Tetulia

If you want to experience some of Bangladesh's coldest winter mornings, Tetulia is the place to be. Located in the country's northernmost district, it is known for its tea gardens, thick morning fog and occasional views of the Himalayas.

The biggest attraction is the chance to see Kanchenjunga, the world's third-highest mountain. On clear mornings, its distant snow-covered peaks can be spotted from the banks of the Mahananda River, particularly around Tetulia Dak Bungalow. The view depends entirely on visibility, so consider yourself lucky if you catch it.

Image Photo: Sakib Ahmed

Hakaluki Haor

Winter brings thousands of migratory birds to Bangladesh, and Hakaluki Haor is among the best places to watch them. Located across parts of Moulvibazar and Sylhet, this enormous wetland becomes a seasonal home for numerous species of waterbirds.

Visitors may spot northern pintails, ruddy shelducks and other migratory ducks gathering around the remaining water bodies. Unlike the monsoon, when the entire area resembles a vast lake, winter reveals stretches of land between the wetlands.

Bring binoculars, visit early in the morning and enjoy the birds from a respectful distance.

Image Photo: Shahrear Kabir Heemel

Paharpur

For history lovers, Paharpur offers a different kind of winter getaway. The site is home to Somapura Mahavihara, an ancient Buddhist monastery dating back to the Pala dynasty and recognised as a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

Its enormous archaeological complex is best explored on foot, which makes the cooler winter weather particularly welcome. Visitors can walk around the remains of the monastery, admire its terracotta decorations and explore the nearby museum.

If you have extra time, consider visiting Mahasthangarh in neighbouring Bogura.

Image Photo: Collected / Mamun Srizon / Unsplash

Sundarbans

There are few places in Bangladesh quite like the Sundarbans. The world's largest mangrove forest is home to spotted deer, crocodiles, monkeys, numerous bird species and, of course, the Royal Bengal tiger.

Winter's cooler temperatures and generally drier weather make boat journeys through the forest's waterways more comfortable. Popular tourist stops include Karamjal and Kotka, where visitors can experience the forest from designated areas.

Choose an authorised tour operator, follow the Forest Department's instructions and don't expect a tiger sighting. Seeing one in the wild is extremely rare.

Image Photo: Collected / Tanvir Hassan / Unsplash

Kuakata

If your idea of a holiday involves long walks along the beach, Kuakata deserves consideration. Known for its views of both sunrise and sunset over the Bay of Bengal, the coastal town offers a welcome break from city life.

Winter is a particularly comfortable time to spend the day outdoors, whether you're walking along the shore, exploring nearby Rakhine cultural sites or enjoying freshly prepared seafood.

Try waking up early for the sunrise and returning to the beach in the evening. Both views depend on clear skies, but they're worth making time for.

Image Photo: Collected / Iftekhar Nibir / Unsplash

Kantajew Temple, Dinajpur

Dinajpur's Kantajew Temple is an excellent destination for anyone interested in architecture, history or photography. Built in the 18th century, the temple is famous for the detailed terracotta panels covering its exterior walls.

These panels depict scenes from Hindu epics alongside everyday life in Bengal, offering plenty to examine up close.

Winter makes walking around the temple grounds much more pleasant than during the hotter months. You can also explore other historical attractions in Dinajpur and turn the visit into a short weekend trip.

Image Photo: Collected / Faisal Photography / Unsplash

Bagerhat

For a winter trip that combines history and architecture, Bagerhat has plenty to offer. The district is home to the UNESCO-listed Historic Mosque City, including the famous Sixty Dome Mosque, built during the 15th century.

Visitors can explore the mosque's impressive brick architecture, visit the nearby museum and see other historic sites associated with Khan Jahan Ali.

Most attractions involve walking around outdoor complexes, making winter a comfortable time to explore. The peaceful surroundings and centuries-old structures are reason enough to spend a day here.

Image Photo: Collected / Muhammad Niloy / Unsplash

Sreemangal

Few places make a winter morning feel quite as inviting as Sreemangal. The town's tea gardens, often covered in mist during the early hours, are reason enough to visit.

Beyond the plantations, travellers can explore Madhabpur Lake and Lawachara National Park, where guided walks offer opportunities to observe wildlife and experience the forest.

After a day outdoors, settle down with a cup of tea at one of the town's tea stalls. For those looking to escape Dhaka's traffic and noise for a couple of days, Sreemangal is an easy choice.

title: Taste of the supernatural: A Halloween feast for the senses
text:
For me, this creation is my interpretation of Halloween: a celebration of imagination, atmosphere, and the art of turning a simple dining experience into a memorable sensory journey.

My inspiration stems from two different things I observed as a chef. One was the dominant colours of the occasion, and the second was the shapes of food. Together, these formed the base of my idea, which is to create food in the shapes and colours of Halloween! With these, we can tell a story, create an atmosphere, and evoke emotions. Naturally, the relevant themes provide a rich canvas full of dark, supernatural elements that were perfect for my ideas.

I envisioned an intimate, candlelit setting where shadows, warm golden light, pumpkins, and carefully curated food presentations would come together to create an experience that feels both haunting and elegant. I wanted to balance the eerie spirit of Halloween with a sense of sophistication, allowing the spread to reflect culinary creativity, with surprising flavours, visual presentation and storytelling. A world where darkness becomes beautiful and ordinary dining transforms into something extraordinary.

Image Photo: Silvia Mahjabin

SOFT BREAD

Ingredients

500 g all-purpose flour or bread flour

7 g instant yeast

30g sugar

Salt

280–300 ml lukewarm milk

1 egg

50g softened butter

Extra milk or egg wash for brushing

Method

Combine the flour, yeast, sugar, and salt in a mixing bowl. Add the lukewarm milk and egg, then mix until a dough forms. Knead for 8–10 minutes until smooth and elastic. Gradually incorporate the softened butter and continue kneading until the dough becomes soft and stretchy. Place the dough in a lightly greased bowl, cover, and leave in a warm place for approximately 60–90 minutes, or until doubled in size.

Gently deflate the dough and divide it into 8–10 equal portions. Shape each portion into a smooth ball and arrange on a lined baking tray. Cover and leave for 30–45 minutes, until the rolls look puffy. Brush with milk or egg wash. Bake in a preheated oven at 180°C for 20–25 minutes, until golden brown. Brush the hot rolls lightly with butter and cover with a clean cloth for a few minutes to keep the crust soft.

Image Photo: Silvia Mahjabin

GUACAMOLE

Ingredients

2 ripe avocados

2 tbsp finely chopped onion

1 small tomato, deseeded and diced

1 tbsp fresh lime juice

1 tbsp chopped coriander leaves

1 small green chilli, finely chopped (optional)

Salt and black pepper

Method

Cut the avocados in half, remove the stones, and scoop the flesh into a bowl. Mash with a fork until creamy but still slightly chunky. Add the onions, tomato, coriander, lime juice, and green chillies. Season with salt and black pepper. Mix gently and adjust the lime juice and seasoning to taste.

BROWNIES

Ingredients

150 g dark chocolate

120 g unsalted butter

180 g sugar

2 large eggs

1 tsp vanilla extract

75 g all-purpose flour

25 g unsweetened cocoa powder

¼ tsp salt

50 g chopped walnuts or chocolate chips (optional)

Method

Preheat the oven to 170°C. Line a 20 cm square baking tin with parchment paper. Melt the chocolate: Melt the dark chocolate and butter together over a bain-marie or in short microwave intervals. Stir until smooth and allow to cool slightly. Whisk the eggs and sugar for 1–2 minutes until combined and slightly thickened. Stir in the vanilla extract.

Gradually mix the melted chocolate mixture into the egg mixture. Sift in the flour, cocoa powder, and salt. Fold gently until just combined. Add walnuts or chocolate chips, if desired.

Pour the batter into the prepared tin and bake for 22–28 minutes. The edges should be set, and a skewer inserted in the centre comes out with a few moist crumbs. Allow the brownies to cool completely before cutting into squares.

Image Photo: Silvia Mahjabin

BEETROOT DRINK

Ingredients

1 beetroot

Mint

Orange

½ tsp salt

3 tbsp sugar

1.5 litres soda water

Method

Mix all together. Serve chilled.

title: The tragic fate of stray animals in Japan Garden City
text:
In a heart-breaking incident at Japan Garden City, Mohammadpur several stray dogs and cats lost their lives after consuming poisoned food. These animals, often left to survive independently, placed their trust in the hands of individuals who pretended to offer them kindness. Instead, the deceit led to their tragic deaths, leaving animal lovers and activists devastated.

Stray animals, especially in cities and towns, are vulnerable to hunger and rely heavily on the goodwill of humans for survival. The poisoned food they consumed likely seemed like a lifeline to them—an act of compassion that turned out to be a cruel betrayal. Reports from the area suggest that the animals ate the food without hesitation, unknowingly consuming their death.

This incident raises serious concerns about the safety and welfare of stray animals in Bangladesh. While some citizens and organisations work tirelessly to rescue and protect strays, there remain individuals who view these creatures as a nuisance rather than as beings deserving of care and respect.

The poisoning of these innocent animals is not just an act of cruelty; it is a stark reminder of the darker side of human behaviour. In a society where kindness is celebrated as a virtue, such acts of violence against helpless animals reflect the urgent need for awareness and stricter laws to protect animal rights.

Activists are calling for an investigation into the incident and urging the community to step forward to ensure that such tragedies do not occur again. Animal rights organisations emphasise that humane solutions, such as sterilisation and adoption programmes, are the ethical way to address the challenges posed by stray populations.

This incident serves as a wake-up call for all of us to reflect on how we treat the most vulnerable members of our society, be they human or animal. The loss of these innocent lives is a tragedy that should never be repeated. Let us hope that justice is served and that this becomes a turning point in how animals are treated in Bangladesh.

If you witness or suspect cruelty to animals, report it immediately to local authorities or animal welfare organisations.

title: Navigating Dhaka's Eid shopping scene on a budget
text:
By now, many have already spent a good chunk of their time shopping for friends and families. After all, can you put a price on the smile of your loved ones after gifting them their Eid dress? However, for people with a limited income, it is a struggle to shop to their heart's desire.

So, I have taken it upon myself to take up a challenge. I set out on a mission: to deck myself out for Eid without breaking the bank or losing my mind in Dhaka's maze of shopping options. My adventure took me from the bustling streets of Elephant Road to the vibrant corners of ODC (opposite Dhaka College), with a few unexpected stops along the way.

Photo: K Tanzeel Zaman

First up, the shoes and Elephant Road did not disappoint. Amidst the labyrinth of shops, I found a pair of shoes that screamed luxury but whispered the whopping price of only Tk 2,500. Even after much bickering and bargaining, the salesman did not budge. Given my weakness for shoes, I spent half of my budget not knowing how to complete the rest of the shopping. Walking out of there, I felt like I had flopped the worst bargain in history. If only I had better control!

Left with only Tk 2,500 taka, next on my list was the panjabi, an essential Eid attire. Science Lab was my destination, hoping for it to deliver. For Tk 1500 taka, I bagged a panjabi that could easily pass off as aesthetic wear at a good price. The bargaining skill bestowed upon me by Mum has finally paid off. Pairing it with a pyjama from a street vendor for a mere Tk 300, I was starting to feel like a fashion icon on a budget.

Photo: K Tanzeel Zaman

My next quest to complete my challenge led me to a street vendor who offered me three shirts for just Tk 600. That's less than the price of a movie ticket at some of Dhaka's high-end cinemas! I, of course, haggled him to lower the price even further but to no avail.

To complete the ensemble, I snagged two pairs of jeans for Tk 400 from ODC. However, there was a slight hiccup. The shirts, in their ambition to make me look more buff than I actually am, were three sizes too large. For Tk 200, a local tailor turned them into bespoke masterpieces.

Photo: K Tanzeel Zaman

So, there I was, with a complete Eid outfit from head to toe, all within the mythical budget of almost Tk 5,000 (Tk 5,500 to be exact!). Who knew that navigating Dhaka's shopping streets could turn one into a thrift king? Let's be honest, we might not all have the wallet to match our high fashion dreams, especially with the soaring prices but with a little bit of patience, a lot of haggling, and the heart of an explorer, Dhaka offers hidden gems that can make you the star of any Eid gathering.

Photo: K Tanzeel Zaman

title: Comrade, give me a cup!
text:
Yet, the tiny, yellow-walled tea stall attracts customers like bees to flowers. "Comrade, give me a cup," is how they ask for tea.

The man behind the counter is comrade Yeasin Swapan -- a tea vendor like no other. For his rebellious nature and left-wing political alignment, he has had a reasonable number of adventures and tragedies in his life.

Always optimistic and smiling, Swapan makes his tea with love.

"I sell only 300 cups a day and not a cup more. My customers need to be polite and respectful of my ideology and pay first for the tea. I boil 30 litres of milk every day and brew 10 cups with one litre of milk," he says.

"Biplobi der Cha" is Tk 20 a cup where a dollop of brewed frothy, thick milk, a spoon of sugar, and dark black tea, made by steeping the tea leaves, is stirred in. This divine tea is served in paper cups inscribed with the stall's name on it, which is an added attraction.

Swapan had a chequered life. He ran away from home for the lack of food and fear of starvation during the devastating famine of 1974 and never returned home to his loved ones till today. From pulling a rickshaw to visiting South America, he has done it all!

He spent his wayward youth, visiting Agartala, the capital of the Indian State of Tripura by the day and returning home by night in the mid-70s with his friends. There he met an old man, an expert teamaker, at the bus depot and learned the tricks of making a cup of milk tea, gourmet coffee, buttermilk like ghol or mattha, curds, etc from him, who was almost like his adopted father.

Swapan is a well-read man having read memoirs of Che Guevara, the Marxist revolutionary, physician, author, and guerrilla leader, and books by Karl Marx and other writers of that genre. He studied till Grade II only and was later self-taught. He did many odd jobs in life from pulling a rickshaw to being a driver at Transparency International Bangladesh.

In his later years, he joined an uncle of his, who was involved in the practice of bringing goods into the country and this business took him to Singapore for assignments. Following his uncle's ventures, Swapan landed in Peru working in his uncle's new snack bar as a tea barista. His cup of frothy milk tea won many hearts.

In his wild hay days, he rode the motorcycle to Brazil, Chile, and other exotic countries, but he fondly remembers his visits to Che's house in Argentina, which is open to the public in the form of a museum, housing a collection of his paraphernalia.

Luck was never on his side, however, and following his uncle's death in the late-70s he returned home and had gone through a series of ups and downs. Currently, he has let go of his high-octane adventurous life and is stationed for the moment in making tea at his stall for the last 15 to 17 years.

"I am active in politics and sometimes go to gatherings and talk about my ideology and the life of the underdogs. People always greet me with 'Comrade Lal Salam' or red salute, which is a greeting used by communists in South Asia. They even come to my tea stand to listen to my adventures," says Swapan, a lanky man now in his late fifties.

So, the next time you are in the vicinity of Shantinagar, look for the comrade who sells tea.

title: Shankha Dasgupta: Meet the genius behind Guti
text:
Shankha Dasgupta is the genius behind Guti, and anyone who has followed his work over the years knows precisely how exceptional he is. The much-anticipated show, Guti, came out on Chorki in January, leaving the viewers binging. There was a photoshoot where the lead characters paid homage to the award-winning show, Breaking Bad, which went viral. The seven-part series gives us insight into Dhaka's drug peddling/smuggling scene of Dhaka and tells the gritting tale of drug smuggler Sultana, played by the versatile actress Azmeri Haque Badhan.

Guti also features Shahriar Nazim Joy, Sharif Siraj, Moushumi Hamid, Nasir Uddin Khan, Arya Aritra, Tuntuni Sobhan, Arfan Mridha Shiblu, and Mahmudul among others.

While the cast certainly played a sizable role in all the praises the show is receiving from its audience, the director's immaculate storytelling abilities really make it stand out. Guti, which was meant to be a film, was deconstructed into several parts to form a web series, and the rest is history. Through his story, Shankha explores the nuances and grey that make up the world of drug smuggling and peddling.

Sultana, the protagonist, finds herself in the heart of a local drug smuggling network which requires one to be ruthless and chaotic. Still, Shankha highlights her warmer and softer side as Sultana is also portrayed as an affectionate mother who wants a better life for her daughter. The series was shot in Dhaka, Cumilla, and Chattogram and is currently streaming in Chorki.

Shankha Dasgupta, the talented director started his journey as a young prodigy in 2007, directing various television dramas and commercials for local and international clients. His talent was apparent right from the get-go, but Dasgupta really took off in 2012.

He directed the film Hello Amit and also directed a commercial for Robi Nobanno, which saw him bag the best director award from Srijon Shonman in Kolkata. He also started his own production house named Filmy Features, which also doubled down as a learning centre for aspiring film professionals around this time. Shankha then went on to direct the telefilm Taxi in 2014 and a commercial for Doze internet under this banner. He is also the co-founder of One Minute Film.

Guti, which was initially supposed to be a short film which, eventually could not materialise due to the pandemic. He later submitted the story to the minds of Chorki, who unsurprisingly loved it. You have to check it out if you haven't already!

title: Wasfia Nazreen: Don’t let ageism break your spirit
text:
Our culture has conditioned us to discussions like 'You are too old to be wearing this dress, to be dancing at clubs, climbing mountains, or even enjoying burnt marshmallows dipped in hot chocolate.' These seem like regular conversations with people who are looking out for us, but to be frank, when does the official age of 'too old' even start?

"I am surprised when people tell me that outdoor sports are only meant for younger people. With my feats, I have proved time and again that outdoor sports, including mountaineering, are meant for everyone, and at any age, as long as the person is mentally and physically fit for it," says Wasfia Nazreen, Bangladeshi mountaineer, activist, environmentalist, social worker, and writer.

Photo: Shahrear Kabir Heemel

The mere fact that Wasfia Nazreen, even with her extraordinary achievements and so many accolades to her name, has to face these needless validations should not come as a surprise to the world, because the reality is that 'below average mentality' strikes everywhere, is highly deep-rooted, and pays zero respect to any type of accomplishment.

This brings us to our next discussion; how trends in fashion, food, and even music these days seem to be mostly tilted towards the younger generation – perhaps people who are in their early twenties and maybe not surprising at all, even younger! And yet, the people who can actually afford indulgences regularly are those who have worked hard at least a decade after university and saved enough to be able to pamper themselves with non-essential delights.

Photo: Shahrear Kabir Heemel

"The fashion world is the most brutal of all. You cannot be 'walking the ramp' in your thirties. The ramp is only meant for young blood. And that's why most of us prefer to go backstage, once in our thirties, if we still want to remain connected to this hip-and-happening world," explains Sonia Yeasmin Isha, model, and choreographer.

In the 21st century, when we are fighting and almost winning against thousands of baseless and hurtful stereotypes, we need to include ageism in the conversation as well. Seeking validation from any generation to do something we like is unwarranted, especially when we claim to be free in this modern age and world.

Having said all that, to round it all up, we need to get back to one of the most clichéd lines in the world: Our age is just a number. For the wiser, it can mean much more. Age can be a thing of pride – where you can do whatever you wanted to do earlier and yet with more fulfilment and confidence.

In frame: Wasfia Nazreen
