title: Bhoot FM: Defining late-night Friday nostalgia for a generation
text:
Launched in 2010, the show brought alleged paranormal encounters from across the country to the airwaves, with Md Asraful Alam, better known as RJ Russell, lending his voice to stories that made listeners question what might be lurking just beyond the darkness.

Image Md Asraful Alam

An unusual idea at midnight

Bhoot FM began with a simple idea: radio did not always have to follow the usual format of short segments interrupted by advertisements and music. Alam and his colleagues wanted something that could run continuously, giving listeners time to settle into a story without interruption.

“We selected the time of Friday 11:59 pm, as there were no ads then, and we could hold it live for a long period of time,” Alam recalls.

The format was unusual, particularly for a horror show. Yet, the timing soon became part of the experience. With the show beginning just before midnight, listeners were already “experiencing the dark” when the stories began. And once an episode ended, the fear did not necessarily end with it.

“The same story might not have the same effect on you if you listen to it in daytime,” Alam says. “At night, you listen; after listening, you have to sleep alone, or you might have to go to the washroom alone. The fright kicks off at that time.”

What began as a practical decision about scheduling turned into a defining feature of the show. For many, Friday nights became synonymous with Bhoot FM, and the anticipation was as much a part of the experience as the stories themselves.

Image Representational image — AI generated

The stories, and the voice that told them

Alam admits that the team did not expect Bhoot FM to become as popular as it did. The format was new, and the response surprised them. Listeners began sending in their experiences, while others tuned in week after week to hear what would come next.

For Alam, the appeal went beyond the subject of ghosts. He had always been interested in storytelling and horror, and he believes that genuine enthusiasm made a difference in how the programme connected with its audience.

“People resonate with that kind of originality,” he says. “They sense when someone is doing it only for the profession and when someone is genuinely interested.”

Among the experiences he remembers, one stands out even after nearly a decade. A man once came to the studio before the show began to share his story. He claimed that after feeding a beggar on the street at night, he had developed an unusual ability to sense what other people were thinking and knew things about them without understanding how.

It was the sort of encounter that stayed with Alam long after the broadcast. “It's been almost a decade since that, and I still haven't forgotten it,” he says.

Stories like these gave Bhoot FM a steady stream of material, but the show’s appeal also depended on how they were presented. Alam was not simply reading accounts into a microphone. He was guiding listeners through them, building anticipation and allowing the details to do their work.

When a radio show became a cultural memory

The popularity of Bhoot FM eventually followed Alam beyond the studio. Yet, as he points out, radio presenters often work in the background, recognised by their voices rather than their faces. His experience with Bhoot FM was different.

One night, on his way to the studio, Alam stopped at a grocery shop. A man pushed past him and urged the shopkeeper to serve him first because he needed to get home quickly to listen to Bhoot FM.

The encounter stayed with Alam. It was an unexpected reminder that people were not merely familiar with the programme. They were organising parts of their lives around it.

Bhoot FM went off air in 2019, leaving behind years of stories and a loyal audience. Alam says he initially wondered what he would do next after such a large part of his life came to an end. He eventually decided to leave mainstream radio and begin a new chapter rather than return to the same platform.

Beyond Bhoot FM

The end of Bhoot FM did not mean the end of Alam's interest in horror storytelling. He now hosts Bhoot.com.bd, continuing to share stories through a different platform. He is also preparing to launch an app that will allow people from around the world to submit their experiences.

For Alam, the medium matters less than the person and the idea behind it. Asked whether a show like Bhoot FM could achieve similar popularity today, in an era of podcasts, YouTube and social media, he returns to the same principle that guided him from the beginning.

“No matter the platform, it needs to be original, and the person doing it needs to be passionate about it,” he says.

Perhaps that is part of what made Bhoot FM last in people's memories. The show gave listeners a reason to stay awake, a reason to be frightened and, often, a story to share the next morning. Alam supplied the voice that brought those experiences into their homes.

Years later, the show may no longer occupy the Friday midnight slot, but for those who grew up listening, the memory of that voice is still there.

title: Eternally in search of Banalata Sen: A tribute to Jibanananda Das
text:
There are very few lines in Bangla literature that are as iconic and as popular as this: “She gave me a moment's peace—Banalata Sen of Natore.”

Banalata Sen, the modest feminine image created by Jibanananda Das, is still present among us. Whether you appreciate literature or not, whether you wonder what Banalata Sen represents or just enjoy the poetic lines, she remains a legend.

Such was Jibanananda Das’s mastery of words.

Born on 7 February, 1899 in Barisal, Jibanananda Das had the privilege of having poet Kusumkumari Das as his mother. His father was a teacher, and the poet himself followed this career later in his life, since most of his life was spent teaching.

Fame did not find him during his lifetime. But later it became evident just how much influence he had had on literature. The fact that he is called one of the “Pancha Pandab” of Bangla literature should speak for itself.

Anyone who has read his poems would know that he would prefer to be called “Rupashi Banglar Kabi”, and it’s interwoven in every single one of his lines, as conspicuous as the hoot of an owl in the middle of the night.

All it takes is one look at his literary career to realise how much Jibanananda Das admired Bangla’s nature. However, it was not just nature. There was surrealism, and there was melancholia. There were philosophical questions that perhaps he was pondering himself. And all of it was reflected in his work, combining nature, time, desire and wonder through dense metaphors, drawing similes with nature’s smallest quirks and whims taking inspiration from such smallest details that one can only truly appreciate them once they are back in nature’s cradle.

However, it is important to note that it was not essentially a romantic depiction of nature like many earlier poets have done. Instead, he was using the beauty of nature to reflect his thoughts in a rather quiet and sometimes melancholic way focusing on spiritual thoughts.

On that note, even though ‘Banalata Sen’ is a name thrown around very casually to refer to an imaginary feminine figure, in the poem she promises tranquillity to the narrator who has been walking the earth for a thousand years. It is a beautiful metaphor to represent the quest of humankind for the eternal longing for peace.

Aside from Banalata Sen, everyone knows the “Abar Ashibo Phire”, which is a spectacularly simple poem, yet it has so much to say. The nature and the longing, the volatility of human existence and the spirituality of it all; one can almost feel the poet’s desire to go back to “Dhansiri”. Most of us can even relate to this exact feeling when we go home and feel that pluck on our heartstrings that only your hometown can bring.

But in the poem ‘In Camp ’, I found a more interesting work by Jibanananda Das. The poem triggered heavy criticism because of the imagery it presented, as many failed to grasp what the poet was trying to convey. In his own words: “the melody that pervades ‘In Camp’ is one of life's helplessness—for all life, that of man, of worm, of locust."

22 October, 1954 is marked as the day the poet died eight days after a tram accident. Whether it was an accident or a suicide is still debated to this day. But what’s not up for debate is that Jibanananda Das is one of the defining poets of Bangla literature that gave it its identity.

title: What Durga Puja means to different generations
text:
Nobody announces Durga Puja in Dhaka as it arrives quietly. The light softens, and one evening a dhak is tested somewhere in the neighbourhood, a few rough beats, then a silence. We asked four people what that sound means to them, and each described a different version of the same festival.

Image

Missing the sanctity of the past

Shalini Thakur, 78, is a retired schoolteacher who lives in Tejgaon, in the same lane where she has kept Durga Puja memories alive for more than six decades. She no longer quite recognises it, and she says so gently, like you would to an old friend who has moved away and changed.

Image

"When I was a girl, nobody treated puja as a pastime," she said. "You woke early, you bathed, and you fasted until the anjali was finished. Now people arrive, take photographs, and have a lovely time, and it feels more like a get-together than a prayer. I think the sanctity has gone out of it. I do not say that is wrong. I only say I miss the hush."

Ask her what she means by sanctity, and she does not reach for theology. She means how seriously the occasion was taken.

Image

In the house she grew up in, everybody was expected to join in, and nobody sat it out. She remembers crying at the immersion when the goddess was carried down to the water. Her grandchildren, she says, do not.

"I cried every single year," Thakur said. "My mother used to laugh and wipe my face. My grandchildren wave at the idol and ask where the sweets are."

Food matters to her too, as it does to her whole family.

"We are from Medinipur originally, and with us everything came back to the kitchen," she said. "I can still smell my grandmother's khichuri. Nobody has made it quite like that since, and I stopped asking them to try."

Shalini Thakur does not say that people have stopped coming. She says the festival used to ask something of everyone, and that it no longer does.

Image

When the neighbourhood built the festival

Keshab Chandra, 61, is a retired bank officer who grew up in Old Dhaka, where puja was something a neighbourhood built with its own hands. Where Shalini Thakur remembers the hush, he remembers the work, and he talks about it the way you might talk with more pride about a house you helped build.

"We made it ourselves," he said. "We hung the lights, dragged bamboo about for the pandal, and went door to door asking for donations."

Nobody was hired, and nobody was a guest, and a boy who turned up empty-handed was soon given a ladder to hold. He remembers the evenings fondly, when the lights were finally on, and the whole lane stood about admiring something it had constructed.

Image

His children, he says, have never had to build anything.

"My children think about what to wear, and then they think about sleeping," Chandra said, laughing. "I do not mean that unkindly. Times change, and so do the things that feel like puja."

His own festival has moved too. What he looks forward to now is his brother, who lives in Kushtia.

"One year I go to him, the next year he comes to me," Keshab said. "Puja is the excuse we need to meet. Without it, we would both say we were too busy."

He does not think the festival has got worse. It has changed, as most things do, and he has changed with it.

Image

A festival of friends, food and freedom

Parthiv Roy, 23, is a university student in Malaysia who grew up in Dhaka. Where the older two measure the festival against what it used to be, he does not believe it has lost anything, and he says so without hurry, as if he has made the case before.

"For my parents and grandparents, puja is about rituals and religious duties," he said. "For me and my cousins, it was and still is, about resting, meeting each other, and eating well. I think that is a real way of keeping it, not a lesser one."

In his telling, the second list is not a falling away from the first. It is simply what the festival is for his generation.

His favourite childhood memory is pandal-hopping, seeing as many mandaps as he could manage in a day, from Banani all the way to Shankhari Bazaar in Old Dhaka.

Image

"We started in the morning, and by evening my feet were useless," he said. "I would happily have gone on for another day."

Food was the reward at the end of it, and he does not pretend otherwise.

"The sweets and the new clothes were what I looked forward to most," he said. "There were sweets at nearly every stop, and I always had something new to show off. That was the whole point for me."

He does not care less about puja, only about different parts of it.

Image

When the whole city celebrated

Tabassum, 27, is a student in Dhaka who grew up in Rajshahi. She watched Durga Puja from the street rather than the mandap, so what she remembers is a city and not a ritual, something that happened to everyone at once.

"Puja brought excitement to me as the whole city turned festive and I went out with my friends," she said.

"In Dhaka it is much more confined, as the fun I had in Rajshahi is unmatched," she added.

Excitement, for her, has little to do with the rituals. It means the streets and the evenings when the roads filled up and the lights came on and nobody stopped to ask whose festival it was.

In Rajshahi, she says, she and her friends simply walked out of the house and joined the crowd. She has not found that kind of ease in Dhaka.

"Back home it felt like everyone was in it together," she said. "Here you have to know where the pandals are and go out of your way for them. It is not the same feeling."

She has no quarrel with Dhaka. The fun she had in Rajshahi as a child is simply what she measures everything against.

What stays

Today, Shalini Thakur misses the hush, Keshab Chandra recalls the making of the bamboo pandals, Parthiv Roy the sweets, and Tabassum the festive roads of Rajshahi. The dhak will sound again in the lanes this week, and while people will hear a prayer in it, others will find a sense of time for a reunion, and some a night out with friends. But each of them will await the arrival of the same goddess in their own special way.

title: The double standard behind how we view strong women today
text:
A poignant reflection on the societal paradox of worshipping Goddess Durga’s multi-faceted power during festive days, while policing, judging, and restricting the everyday authority and freedom of real women throughout the rest of the year.

Every autumn, we dress the streets in lights, put on new clothes, stand before elaborately decorated idols and celebrate a woman who is powerful, fearless and almost impossible to defeat. We call her Durga.

She is worshipped as the embodiment of Shakti, the divine feminine power. She rides a lion, carries weapons, defeats demons and stands at the centre of one of the most important festivals of our culture. And then, after the puja lights go out, we return to our ordinary lives.

There is something almost poetic about the contradiction. We have no problem with a woman holding ten weapons in her ten hands, but a woman holding a leadership position can still make people uncomfortable.

The different forms of Durga represent different dimensions of feminine strength. The forms offer a remarkably broad understanding of womanhood. She can be nurturing and fierce. Intellectual and emotional. Powerful and compassionate. A protector, provider, creator, leader, or fighter.

Yet, society often wants women to choose only one acceptable version. It seems we are comfortable with the goddess having multiple identities. We just struggle when an actual woman does.

Consider women in sports, the military, policing, firefighting, construction or other physically demanding professions. A woman serving in a physically demanding job is often expected to prove herself twice: first through her performance and then through her femininity. The question is not always, “Can she do the job?” Sometimes it becomes, “But does she still look feminine?”

Interestingly, nobody asks Durga whether defeating a demon will ruin her manicure! We admire physical strength when it is represented through mythology, but can become strangely uncomfortable when a real woman develops that strength herself.

The same contradiction appears in leadership. A decisive man is often described as confident. A decisive woman can be called arrogant. A man who speaks firmly is “assertive”; a woman who does the same may be “difficult.” The vocabulary changes, but the judgement remains.

There is a particular cultural irony here. Bengali society has long celebrated educated women, working women, and accomplished women. We proudly talk about daughters becoming doctors, engineers, journalists, athletes, entrepreneurs, and civil servants. That celebration, however, sometimes comes with invisible terms and conditions. Progress, yes. But not too much. Success, yes. But remember your responsibilities at home.

It is almost as if society has created an unofficial women’s handbook titled: “You May Succeed, Provided Nobody Feels Threatened by Your Success.”

And this is not uniquely a Hindu issue, or a Muslim issue, or a Christian issue. Misogyny does not usually check someone’s religious identity before entering the room. Women across communities experience different versions of the same social policing: how they dress, whom they marry, how late they stay outside, whether they have children, whether they work after marriage, how they speak and how much authority they are allowed to exercise.

Perhaps nowhere is the contradiction more painful than in the conversation about women’s safety. Women are repeatedly told to be careful. Do not come home late. Do not wear that. All of this may be practical advice in an unsafe environment. But when safety becomes a woman’s responsibility primarily, society quietly moves the burden from the person causing harm to the person trying to avoid it.

Durga, meanwhile, is celebrated precisely because she confronts danger rather than being instructed to organise her life around avoiding it. Her weapons are not symbols of helplessness. They represent power, protection, courage and the ability to confront injustice. Perhaps that symbolism deserves more attention.

At the end of the day, the uncomfortable question is: What do we actually worship when we worship Durga? Do we admire female power only when it is divine, distant and safely contained within mythology? Or can we recognise that same strength in the woman sitting across from us at work?

If Durga represents Shakti, perhaps Shakti should not become acceptable only when accompanied by incense, drums and an idol. Maybe the real test of our respect for feminine power is not how enthusiastically we celebrate a goddess for five days. It is how we treat women for the entire year. Because it is easy to worship a woman when she is a goddess. The harder thing is to respect her when she is simply a woman. And perhaps that is the demon worth defeating.

title: Dhaka's Best Bread launches at Crowne Plaza Dhaka Airport
text:
Crowne Plaza Dhaka Airport launched Dhaka's Best Bread, a range of artisanal sourdoughs and baguettes, at its Connexions venue on World Bread Day, 16 October.

James Goldman, deputy high commissioner and development director at the British High Commission, Dhaka, was chief guest. Sakib Ershad, the commission's director of trade and investment, was guest of honour.

Goldman said the UK is the largest source of foreign direct investment in Bangladesh, bringing expertise and creating vital jobs. "Prominent British brands like IHG are not simply taking a slice of the market, but forming long-term partnerships that contribute to Bangladesh's economic ambition," he said.

Ashwani Nayar, area general manager of IHG South West Asia and cluster general manager of Crowne Plaza Dhaka Airport, said the idea began earlier this year, during a bread tasting in the hotel's bakery. Chef Philip had brought out hot rolls straight from the oven.

That tasting settled it. "We really wanted to stake a claim to Dhaka's best bread," Nayar said. The aim, he added, was a bread that carries tradition and heritage and can stand beside any in the world.

Image

Romano Kreutz, the cluster director of culinary, said the loaves would be baked fresh each day and served throughout the day, not only at breakfast. Guests could eat them at the hotel or take them home.

Nayar traced bread from the flat, unleavened loaves of this region to the larger, leavened breads that arrived with European influence. "What could be better than bringing Dhaka's best bread to Dhaka?" he asked.

The project, he said, would not stop at a bread counter. "It's going to be the launch of a new era."

Philip Gomes, the cluster executive pastry chef, presented five signature breads, each pairing traditional baking with local ingredients. The Dhaka Sour Bread starts with a flour-and-water starter left for three to four days, which gives a chewy crumb and a crisp crust.

A multigrain loaf uses about eight grains and seeds, including millet, barley, sesame, sunflower, and pumpkin seeds, with local honey such as Sundarbans or mustard honey. A third contains quinoa, chia, and oats soaked overnight. A savoury loaf carries roasted garlic and provolone, and a soft bread is made with coconut milk, fresh turmeric, and ginger.

Image

Gomes said about 80 per cent of the bakery's products use the same mother dough. A sourdough takes roughly four days from starter to loaf, including a night proofing in the chiller.

A sixth option lets guests design their own loaf. They can tell the chef whether they want it nuttier, sweeter, or sourer, and the order stays on record. "Your bread, your way," Nayar said.

Custom orders need between 8 and 72 hours, depending on the bread. "If you want something that requires effort, then that effort requires time," he said. Gluten-free versions could follow, depending on how guests respond.

Kreutz said the team gave trial baskets to regular guests before the launch and took their feedback. That led to local accompaniments such as caramel, pineapple cinnamon marmalade and local honey.

The tasting at the event also included sandwiches and dips, among them tomato chutney and cream cheese.

Tastes, Kreutz said, had changed. Bread in Bangladesh once meant mostly milk bread and toast, but now "people are more open and enjoying the taste."

Nayar said IHG is a British company working with its local partner, United Group, which caught the interest of the British High Commission's trade office. Beyond RMG, he said, food is an important part of trade between the two countries.

He likened the idea to the corner bakeries of his childhood. Children carried dough from home, and the baker knew each family's taste on sight. "Bread as bonding," he said.

title: Why actors Toya and Shawon are fighting child marriage
text:
During a visit to Bagerhat, celebrity couple Toya and Shawon encountered a powerful shift among local mothers and matchmakers resisting underage proposals. Now, they are speaking out against legal loopholes that threaten to undermine years of hard-won progress for Bangladeshi girls.

"I realised I have rights, and I must speak up for my future" — A young girl said these words to celebrities, Mumtaheena Chowdhury Toya and Sayed Zaman Shawon, in July, at a Department of Women Affairs training room in Bagerhat.

When she was only in Class 11, the girl’s father initiated talks for her marriage. She was informed that her studies were becoming expensive and that he had other children to think of.

Determined not to get married at such an early age, the girl fought back. She learned a skill, started tutoring, and now pays for her own studies and her nursing college coaching. She wants to be a nurse, help her parents, and, in her words, "Be an example to others!"

As actors, both Toya and Shawon have spent years saying lines other people wrote. Nobody scripted what the girl had said. And it is the line that stayed with both the celebrities. They went to Bagerhat with UNFPA and the Department of Women Affairs to listen, and they went with their own lives in mind.



Toya started modelling at 19, after a television talent show. Shawon worked as cabin crew for Biman Bangladesh before he ever acted. They met on the set of a TV serial and married in 2020, when Toya was 28. Nobody settled their futures for them at 16. Every girl they met in Bagerhat deserves that same time to find out who she can be.

The Multiple Indicator Cluster Survey of 2025 revealed that 47.2 per cent of women aged 20 to 24 had been married before 18. Among girls aged 15 to 19, the share of those already married has risen since 2019, from 32.9 to 38.9 per cent. At this pace, ending child marriage in Bangladesh would take more than 200 years!

The conversation that moved the thespians most was with mothers and grandmothers who receive the Bangladesh government's Vulnerable Women Benefit and meet in group sessions through a programme called Shombhabona, which means "potential."

When Toya enquired what they do when neighbours or relatives push a family to marry off a young daughter, they replied that they make sincere efforts to explain to the family that the girl has to finish her education and stand on her own feet first.

If the family still does not listen, they go to the village chowkidar (village police) or the Union Parishad chairman. In one recent case, the chairman and police stepped in, and the wedding was put off until the girl reached the legal age.

"We suffered early marriage ourselves," one mother told them. "We are determined our children will not suffer the same fate." Her elder daughter is now studying for an Honours degree.

Mothers and grandmothers usually initiate the marriage conversation in a family. After the sessions, 89 per cent of participating mothers said they intend to delay their daughters' marriage.

At Rangdia School and College, Bagerhat, Shawon asked whether every girl who starts school makes it to college. In a dismal reply, the teachers said that ten to twelve in every hundred do not, and Classes 9 and 10 are the most vulnerable years.

While visiting the school, Toya asked students what they do when a friend is about to be married.

One girl explained, first they tell their friends, then a teacher, and then they all go to the family together. If the family does not listen, they call 109, the toll-free, 24/7 National Helpline Centre for Violence Against Women and Children.

The matchmakers Toya and Shaon met in Bagerhat ask for a birth certificate before they initiate a proposal for marriage. They turn away families looking for a bride under 18. Some mentioned that the families now ask for an educated daughter-in-law. The Kazis, too, now refuse to register a marriage when the bride is under 18. When Toya asked what happens then, they told them that some families get an affidavit from a notary instead, which, however, is not valid for a marriage.

So, when people like Toya and Shawon hear calls to lower the minimum age of marriage to 16 for girls, they think of the people they met.

Those who make this case say that underage marriages are happening anyway, through affidavits and without registration, and that girls in them have no legal protection. They are right about the affidavits, and notary affidavits should have no place in a marriage or a divorce. But lowering the age would not protect those girls. It would only make their marriages legal.

After seeing the situation at Bagerhat, as two citizens of the country, Mumtaheena Chowdhury Toya and Sayed Zaman Shawon make the following pleas.

To the government, and to every official: Keep the minimum age of marriage for girls at 18. Then make the enforcement of the law stronger. Close the Section 19 exception in the Child Marriage Restraint Act 2017, which still allows a marriage below the minimum age in a "special case" with a court's direction and parental consent.

They also demand that the Kazis be heard in their demand to make marriage registration digital and check it against birth registration and national ID records, so that an affidavit can never stand in for a girl's real age.

To fathers, brothers and husbands: A "good match" should never cost a girl her childhood. If your family is talking about marrying off a daughter who is under 18, be the one who says no.

To mothers and grandmothers: Be the voice in your own family like the women Toya and Shawon met in Bagerhat Sadar who speak against early marriage.

To teachers, Kazis, matchmakers, religious leaders and Union Parishad members: You already have the power to say no. Say it together, the way they do in Jatrapur, Bagerhat.

And to the young people: if you hear that a friend is about to be married, do what the students at Rangdia do — inform a teacher, try to convince the family, and if that fails, call 109, 1098, or 333.

Mumtaheena Chowdhury Toya and Sayed Zaman Shawon are actors and UNFPA high-profile supporters in Bangladesh.

title: Unseen struggle of caring for a family member fighting cancer
text:
When a severe diagnosis enters a home, the illness rarely stays confined to one bed. For family members thrust into caregiving overnight, the emotional and mental weight rewrites daily life entirely.

There are countless accounts of cancer survivors detailing their ordeals. What is far harder to find are the accounts of the people who fought alongside them: the loving husband who learned to cook for a wife who could not keep food down, the teenage daughter who quietly set aside her exam preparation, the brother who took the night shift at the bedside. Their struggles are no less than the patient’s. They are simply less visible.

In Dhaka, that invisibility has a particular texture. When someone falls ill, the household does not divide the work so much as absorb it. The daily routine of the whole house bends around one room, and that closeness is both the greatest comfort and the heaviest load.

The first price is financial

Mizanur Rahman, 41, lives in Mohammadpur. He ran a small pharmacy on the ground floor of their building. When he was diagnosed with prostate cancer, his wife, Rehana Rahman, took over the accounts.

“The first month, I thought we could manage with savings,” she says. “By the third month, I was selling my gold bangles to pay the hospital deposit. By the sixth, we had sold the car, and my brother-in-law had sold his share of our plot in Savar so we could continue.”

The plot was not a luxury. It was the family’s safety net, and it is gone.

When the routine changes

Mornings that once began with one parent leaving for work now begin with a whole new routine: who takes the patient to the oncology clinic, who queues at the diagnostic centre, and who stays overnight.

Evan Nazrul, 38, describes the time when his mother was being treated as a ‘devastating blur,’ saying, “Making breakfast for yourself and your parents, then leaving for work, dropping off the extra breakfast at the hospital for my father, doing your 9-5, which usually always stretches to something like 6 or 7, heading to the hospital, and then just sitting there, waiting for any change, any chance to speak to the doctor, any chance to see her, until it's past 12 AM, and you head home.

“You simply can’t do anything other than just pass out. And the same routine follows the next day. There may be off days at work, but not for this.”

This intense change in daily lifestyle comes with unspeakable stress. Some turn to religion to cope. Others seek social support. Some even seek some form of solace in harmful habits.

For many families, the person most visibly under strain is the husband, assuming he is not the patient himself.

Rafiq, 42, runs a consultancy firm in Mirpur. When his wife Nasrin was diagnosed with cancer, he became the person who knew where every prescription was kept, what time school ended, and how much cash was left in the drawer.

Image Representational image — AI generated

“People think the hard part is the hospital,” he says. “The hard part is coming home. Nasrin is trying to be brave for the children, and I am trying to be brave for her. Then the children look at me to see if the house is still safe. I cannot show them I am scared, so I go to the balcony and be scared there.”

For the children, the diagnosis brings a different kind of uncertainty.

Suraiya, now 17, was 13 when her mother began treatment. Nobody sat her down to explain what was happening. She pieced it together from overheard phone calls and the way the adults lowered their voices.

“What I wanted was a clear sentence,” she says. “Nobody gave me one, so my head filled the gaps with the worst possibilities. I stopped asking, because I could see it made my father sad when I did.”

Children in these situations often take on responsibilities beyond their age: managing their younger siblings, doing chores that were once never their concern, and a quiet pressure to stop being a problem. Many families do not talk openly about the possibility of death, which leaves children carrying that thought alone, which, in itself, gives rise to future mental health concerns.

Survival is not the end of the story

Even when treatment succeeds, the family’s story does not end at the discharge summary. Several families described new complications arriving years later, sometimes as side effects of the treatment itself. Some survivors go on to live full lives. Others face further illness, and some, unfortunately, do not even survive. For the family, each follow-up appointment can carry the old fear back into the house.

When a patient does pass away, the family is left with insurmountable grief, debt, and rearranged roles, often all at once. The household that spent every resource fighting for one person must decide how to recover, and that recovery is slow, rarely planned for by the health system, and rarely discussed in public.

A cancer diagnosis does not stay with one body. It moves through the household and settles on whoever is closest: the husband managing fear at the kitchen table, the child who learns the truth from a closed-door discussion, the parent whose savings and future are paused, and the relatives who sell land or move in to help.

Rehana Rahman puts the lesson plainly. “Cancer does not only come to the patient’s bed,” she says. “It comes to the kitchen, the school, the bank, and the bedroom. When you are the family, you do not get to leave the room. You just learn to stay.”

Any serious conversation about cancer care needs to count the people sitting beside the bed, because their endurance is doing work that the system has not yet found a way to count for.

title: Mental health matters to everyone—until your helper needs Thursday off
text:
When a Dhanmondi household’s domestic worker asks for time off to see a doctor, progressive awareness hits an abrupt wall. It turns out supporting mental health is infinitely easier when it doesn't disrupt the tea schedule.

At nine on Saturday morning, Dhaka was already having a collective nervous breakdown. A car horn had been blaring outside Runi’s Dhanmondi apartment for eleven consecutive minutes. The neighbouring building was being demolished, or constructed, or possibly both. A vegetable seller was shouting the price of potatoes with the urgency of a man announcing the end of civilisation. Inside, Farzana Aunty was watching the news over her third cup of tea. “The Prime Minister has announced plans to expand mental healthcare to the upazilas!” she declared. Runi looked up from her phone. “That’s wonderful. Mental healthcare should be accessible to everyone.”

“Apparently, doctors will be trained, referrals arranged, even counselling through technology. Very modern!” Shirin Bua entered carrying toast and eggs. “What is mental healthcare, Apa?” she asked. “It’s when you talk to someone about your worries, stress, sadness, things like that,” Runi explained. Shirin considered this. “Then I think I need it.” Aunty Farzana nearly dropped her toast. “You? Why? What happened?”

“Nothing, Apa. My husband hasn’t found regular work. My son’s school fees are due. My mother is sick. Sometimes, I cannot sleep because I keep thinking.” Aunty Farzana waved her hand. “That’s not mental illness. That’s life! Everyone has problems.” This was particularly interesting coming from a woman who had once required a week of emotional recovery after her favourite tailor misplaced a blouse. Runi intervened. “Aunty, that’s exactly the stigma we’re supposed to overcome.”

“Of course, of course. Mental health is very important. But Shirin should stop worrying so much.” A revolutionary medical breakthrough! Apparently, nobody had previously considered simply not worrying. Shirin smiled politely, and returned to the kitchen. Runi continued reading the announcement. The government wanted mental healthcare to reach rural communities through primary healthcare facilities, trained professionals, and referral services. She approved wholeheartedly. She had recently spent Tk 8,000 on a wellness workshop in Gulshan where a woman in beige linen had explained that inner peace began with setting boundaries. The workshop included complimentary matcha. Half an hour later, Shirin appeared again. “Apa, if they start these services in our upazila, could I see a doctor when I go home?”

“Of course!” Runi said enthusiastically. Shirin hesitated before asking, “Then could I take Thursday off?” Runi froze. “Thursday? But I have guests coming for dinner.”

“I can finish the cooking before I leave,” Shirin offered. “And the cleaning?” Runi asked. “Yes, Apa.”

“And the ironing?” Shirin lowered her eyes. “Perhaps I could do that on Friday.” Runi sighed. “Shirin, you really need to manage your time better.” From the sofa, Aunty Farzana nodded approvingly. “Exactly. These days, everyone wants special treatment.” Outside, a rickshaw puller argued over Tk 20, while an expensive SUV blocked the road. Somewhere in the city, another woman was probably paying a therapist to help her say no without feeling guilty. Shirin, meanwhile, was struggling to say yes to herself. After a moment's hesitation, she admitted, “Actually, Apa, I don’t know if I can go anyway. If people in my village see me asking for mental treatment, they’ll think I’ve gone mad.”

“That’s ridiculous,” Runi replied, dismissing the concern almost instinctively. Shirin nodded politely. “Yes, Apa. But people talk.” The remark stayed with Runi. She thought about the building WhatsApp group, where a woman visiting a psychiatrist had once been discussed with the enthusiasm usually reserved for a celebrity divorce. For all her progressive views, Runi had never challenged the conversation. Now, confronted with Shirin’s hesitation, she found herself with nothing to say.

By lunchtime, Aunty Farzana had forwarded the Prime Minister’s announcement to seventeen family groups, adding a message of her own: Mental health matters. We must all be compassionate. Runi glanced towards the kitchen, where Shirin was washing dishes with her sleeves rolled up, her phone tucked beside the sink in case her mother called. Feeling a twinge of discomfort, Runi walked over and told her, “Take Thursday off, Shirin. Your pay won’t be affected. And if the service isn’t available yet, we’ll find out what help you can access.” Shirin looked at her in surprise before quietly thanking her. It was a small gesture, Runi knew. One afternoon off could not repair years of financial insecurity, sleepless nights, or a healthcare system still trying to reach those who needed it.

But perhaps mental healthcare was not only about building services closer to people’s homes. It was also about making sure they could afford the journey, take the time and seek help without shame. That evening, Aunty Farzana called from the drawing room, sounding genuinely alarmed. “Runi! If Shirin takes Thursday off, who will make my tea?” Runi turned towards her aunt. “Aunty, perhaps you could practise some independence.”

Aunty Farzana gasped, visibly offended. “Are you suggesting I make my own tea? Do you know how much stress I’m under?” And just like that, the household discovered its first mental health emergency. Unfortunately, it was not the one that needed a doctor.

title: Joyeeta Trisha refused to let cancer steal her future
text:
When photographer Joyeeta Trisha was diagnosed with breast cancer at 36, her entire world came to a halt. As a single mother facing terrifying uncertainty, she held on to work, family, and hope to rebuild her life.

Trisha says the first signs did not look like what she might have imagined breast cancer would look like. She began experiencing unusual tiredness, nausea and changes in her bowel habits. Food no longer tasted the same, and before her periods, she experienced breast pain that felt different.

Initially, she attributed the symptoms to her busy lifestyle, stomach problems, migraine or sinus issues.

“I thought I was sick because I did a lot of work,” she recalls.

For three to four weeks, however, the symptoms continued. Then all of a sudden, she noticed something else: a lump near the side and lower part of her breast, extending towards the underarm area. Her instinct told her something was wrong.

“I never felt this before,” she says.

That feeling eventually prompted her to see a doctor.

“No one expects to have cancer”

The diagnosis came at an age when Trisha never imagined she would be dealing with such a serious illness.

“I was 36-37 years old. I didn’t expect to have cancer,” she says.

The financial burden was one of the first challenges she had to confront. As a middle-class family, she says, they did not have a large amount of savings readily available for prolonged cancer treatment. She had some gold jewellery that her mother had given her, which became part of the financial consideration during her treatment.

At one point, she thought of fundraising, but later decided against it. “I thought about fundraising first. But then I thought about my self-respect. I thought, I won’t do this. I will see how long I can continue.”

Her treatment expenses came gradually rather than all at once. With the support of her siblings and family, she continued. But money was only one part of the struggle.

Treatment, exhaustion, and a body that wanted to recover

Trisha’s treatment was particularly difficult because of how frequently she had to undergo chemotherapy. She explains that chemotherapy cycles are often spaced out so that the body has time to recover. In her case, however, she had chemotherapy at shorter intervals.

She would spend days recovering at home, only to face another cycle soon afterwards.

“I couldn’t leave my house for a week or ten days,” she says. “Then I would have another chemo cycle.”

The physical effects were difficult. Her appearance changed, and she lost her hair.

But she learned to separate the temporary effects of treatment from the disease itself.

She knew that chemotherapy, rather than cancer itself, was responsible for her hair loss. She reminded herself that once treatment was completed, her hair could grow back.

For Trisha, understanding what was happening to her body became an important part of coping with treatment.

The hardest part and the hidden cost of cancer

While the physical side of treatment was difficult, Trisha describes the emotional struggle as one of the hardest parts of her journey.

She was a single mother. Her son was around 10 or 11 when she was diagnosed. Trisha did not tell many people outside her family that she had cancer. There was a reason: she had seen how cancer is often viewed in Bangladesh.

For many people, a cancer diagnosis immediately creates an assumption that the person will die. She did not want that fear surrounding her while she was trying to survive.

“I don’t want to die before I actually die,” she says.

For the first few months, she cried frequently. She became deeply depressed and could not work. She also feared that she would die. Her son feared the same. Even her doctors could not promise her that treatment would definitely work. They could tell her that if the treatment worked, she could recover. But cancer does not respond identically in every person. That uncertainty was frightening.

She kept fighting

Despite the fear, Trisha decided to keep going. She also realised that she needed something beyond medical treatment to help her cope mentally. During one of her visits for an ultrasound, a doctor encouraged her to continue doing whatever activities she could manage and to keep herself occupied. Trisha followed that advice. Gradually, work became part of her recovery.

She began returning to professional activities whenever her physical condition allowed it.

“I believe that doing meaningful work helped me during my recovery,” she says.

For someone whose life had always revolved around photography and creative work, staying connected to that part of herself gave her something to focus on beyond cancer.

Nearly two years of treatment

Her treatment was not a short journey. She underwent eight chemotherapy sessions in total. She received chemotherapy before surgery, underwent surgery after the initial rounds, and later received further chemotherapy and radiotherapy. Targeted therapy and immunotherapy also formed part of her treatment. The exact combination and sequence of treatments, she emphasises, depended on her individual condition and response. The process continued for almost two years.

At the end of it, mammograms and blood tests showed that she was cancer-free.

But for Trisha, “cancer-free” did not mean that the journey was completely over. Regular follow-ups remained important because breast cancer can recur, particularly during the years following treatment.

Life after cancer

Today, Trisha is working almost fully again. She continues to work as a photographer, focusing on lifestyle and portrait photography. She travels whenever she can, taking her son with her. Recently, she travelled to Japan and South Korea with him.

The woman who once spent months wondering whether she would survive now speaks about cancer from the other side of a long and difficult treatment journey. But she does not describe herself simply as a survivor. Her story is also about paying attention, asking questions, understanding one’s own treatment and refusing to let fear dictate what happens next.

Her message to others is perhaps the simplest part of her story. If something feels different, get it checked. Because sometimes, the body speaks long before a diagnosis does. The important thing is to listen.

title: Weekly Horoscope: What the stars have in store for every sign
text:
Cosmic energy is constantly shifting, offering new opportunities for growth, alignment, and self-discovery. Your weekly horoscope breaks down the essential astrological trends affecting your relationships, personal goals, and emotional well-being. title: The rise of the passion economy: Turning hobbies into modern careers
text:
The line between pastime and profession is blurring as more creative minds find ways to monetise their interests. Explore the shifting mindset toward alternative careers and entrepreneurship.

Hobbies are the things we do after work, between classes or whenever we get a little time for ourselves. But the moment someone suggests turning one into a career, the questions begin. Is there enough money in it? Is it stable? What happens if it does not work out?

In Bangladesh, where career choices are often tied to financial security and conventional professions, choosing a less familiar path can take some courage. Yet, some people decide to take that chance. Their hobbies become businesses, their interests become professions, and something they once did simply because they enjoyed it starts paying the bills.

Their journeys are rarely straightforward. For some, the transition takes years. For others, it begins with a small business opportunity. And for some, the first sign that a hobby could become a career is simply getting paid for doing it.

Knowing when to take the leap

For Ashraf Shiddike Rizve, founder of Aquarium Park Dhaka, it was a process that stretched across decades. What began as keeping fish gradually grew into an interest in aquatic life, aquascaping and nature.

Image

Around 2011, he and other hobbyists started Bangladesh Aquarists, a Facebook community for people interested in fishkeeping. As the community grew, so did the demand for products and services, eventually leading to Nature Aquatics and, years later, Aquarium Park Dhaka.

“Eventually, however, I realised that this was something I genuinely wanted to build my life around,” Rizve said.

Image

His story shows that taking the leap does not always mean making one dramatic decision. Sometimes, it happens through a series of smaller ones.

Image

For comic book artist Fahim Anzoom Rumman, who has worked with Dhaka Comics and Prothom Alo, there was no fixed point either. His work with The Daily Star magazine Rising Stars helped push him towards digital art, but the real turning point came when his work started earning him money.

Image

“The turning point, I think, would be when I first started earning. This was around 12 years ago,” Rumman said.

And for Raihan Ahmad, founder of BanglaNumis Auction, the transition came from an opportunity hidden inside his existing hobby. As a banknote collector, he would sometimes buy multiple copies of an item, keeping the best one and selling the extras at a small profit.

Image

Over time, he realised that his knowledge and network could support something larger. That eventually became BanglaNumis Auction, a platform for collectable banknotes, coins and other numismatic items.

When the people around you don't quite get it

Taking an unconventional career path can be difficult even before the first business problem appears.

Rizve felt that pressure partly because of his education. After studying pharmacy, choosing to build a career around fish and nature naturally raised questions. His family eventually understood that this was not a sudden decision. His father, who kept birds, had actually encouraged his son's interest in fishkeeping.

Rumman's experience was similar. His parental support was limited at first, but changed after his work for Rising Stars began generating an income.

“When I started writing for Rising Stars and earning, they realised that it was something serious,” he said.

Ahmad, meanwhile, did not face the same family pressure. His family and friends supported his decision, although there was some uncertainty because numismatics remains a specialised field.

Sometimes, the challenge is not convincing people that you enjoy something. It is convincing them that something you enjoy can become a viable profession.

The hobby stops being just a hobby

Once money, customers, employees and deadlines enter the picture, the freedom of simply doing something for fun can disappear.

Rizve acknowledges that shift. There are days when his work feels more like a business than a passion, particularly when he has to think about investment, operations and customers.

For Rumman, the challenges changed as his career developed. He spent years building the skills required to work professionally and later joined another venture where he could not express his creativity in the way he wanted.

His experience has taught him that the obstacles do not necessarily become easier; they simply change.

“At every stage, my obstacles changed dynamically and if you want be successful you need to adapt to the unpredictable obstacles,” Rumman said.

For Ahmad, one of the greatest difficulties has been dealing with customs procedures when importing collectable items from international auctions and dealers. Delays, classification issues and shipping problems can make international trading difficult.

Rizve has faced a different set of problems. Building an aquarium business meant helping customers understand proper fishkeeping, filtration and water quality. As Aquarium Park Dhaka grew, the challenges expanded to large aquarium systems, landscaping, visitor management and maintenance.

So, do they regret it?

A hobby can look very different once it becomes the source of your income. That does not necessarily mean the decision was a mistake.

Neither Rizve nor Ahmad regrets making the change.

Rizve acknowledges that he would have approached some business and financial decisions differently. But the wider choice remains one he stands by.

For him, there is something satisfying about seeing a childhood interest become an experience shared by other people.

Ahmad has no regrets about turning collecting into his profession, particularly because he gets to work in a field he genuinely enjoys.

Rumman's regret is not about choosing art. Instead, he wishes his work could reach more people through translation.

“I'd like all my works to be translated into multiple languages,” he said, pointing out that something that works in English may not necessarily work in Bangla.

What you should know before you turn your hobby into your job

Their advice is similar in one important way: enjoying something is not enough to make it a business.

Rizve advises people to understand their market and customers before making a major investment. He also stresses learning first and building a community around the hobby.

“Don't confuse passion with a business model,” he said.

Ahmad also puts knowledge before business. He advises aspiring hobby-based entrepreneurs to develop expertise, understand their market, start small and build a reputation based on trust rather than chasing quick profits.

For Rumman, networking and collaboration matter. He advises artists to build trust within their community, reach out to other artists and understand their audience. In Bangladesh, he says, social media can be useful for making those connections.

All three point to the same uncomfortable truth: there is no guarantee that passion will pay.

Turning a hobby into a profession requires learning the business side, adapting when circumstances change and accepting that something once done purely for enjoyment may eventually come with pressure.

But perhaps that is the real leap of faith.

For Rizve, it took more than three decades. For Ahmad, a collection became a business. For Rumman, earning from his art showed him that it could be more than a hobby.

None of their journeys followed the same route. There is no fixed timeline for turning something you love into a living. Sometimes, you simply have to start and see where it takes you.

title: Why this guitar school from Bandarban is winning hearts everywhere
text:
A heart-warming online video of local children strumming guitars has captured nationwide attention. Their pure passion and dedication prove that simple acts of goodwill can inspire millions.

Recently, a Facebook video of children from Bandarban playing guitars and singing songs went viral on Facebook. I personally discovered them performing the “Bus Shohokari” song by the musical band Bagdhara. The children of Bandarban strumming the guitar strings in harmony captivated me instantly.

Image

Bawm Ram Tiam Amlai, the founder of Basic Guitar Learning School, mentions, “One cannot progress much in guitar without basics, so my aim was to teach basics of guitar to the children.” That is how the name came into place.

Amlai adds, “I have seen kids playing digital games from a very early age. Instead of getting into bad habits like online gambling, drugs, video games, I want them to be involved in playing guitar.” Hence started the journey of Basic Guitar Learning School.

The beginnings were small: 4 or 5 students came to a small room in the 2nd floor of a house in New Gulshan, Bandarban. Now, almost 50 students are playing guitar at Marma Artists Group Training Room in Bandarban town.

Image

What started as a journey in 2018 has now won the hearts of millions online and reached many popular bands. The first song cover that gained widespread popularity over the internet was “Asha” by the rock band Warfaze. “Later, during our performance day at Manik Mia Avenue, we met the band members in person and sang the same song in front of them in the green room,” mentions Amlai.

In these 8 years, Amlai did not stop his lessons even when the pandemic struck. Over WhatsApp calls with his students, he kept delivering guitar lessons.

Amlai mentions, “There are students who are even 10 years old learning guitar. Some of the students come from five to ten kilometres away.”

He did not think his videos would gain so much popularity; he just started posting to keep memories. In this regard, Amlai adds, “I wanted to keep these videos saved in my page so that the children can come and look back at these when they get older.”

Image

Till now, Basic Guitar Learning School has performed in four programs in Dhaka and had two performances in Bandarban. Last year, on occasion of Chaitra Sankranti, 8 of his students performed the song “Heal the World” along with the band Warfaze in tribute to Michael Jackson at BICC. Last year, they were invited to sing the National Anthem in a program at the National Parliament Complex.

He recalls one special moment from the performance at National Parliament Complex, “The school students who came as audience were taking autographs and clicking pictures with the children of Basic Guitar Learning School. We did not know any of them, even they did not know me, but they knew the children who performed in those Facebook videos.”

Basic Guitar Learning School also performed at the opening ceremony of Poh Chu Gro that took place this September in Bandarban, organized by Green Milieu and British Council Bangladesh.

The children can currently perform songs in five different languages: Chakma, Marma, Tripura, English, and Bengali. He believes that while preserving our own culture, we should also respect different cultures. Amlai mentions, “By performing songs from different languages and different cultures, we can make people from that culture feel happy and respected.”

He was inspired to playing guitar when he saw his seniors performing at school functions. And now, Amlai’s students are inspired by him. Some of his students even post videos of them playing guitar on their social media.

Amlai extends his gratitude to Chathui Pru Sir, who had encouraged him to play the guitar. He highlights in this regard, “If it was not for Chathui Pru Sir, I would not have been where I am today.”

With encouragement from him, Amlai joined the Chimbuk band, one of the earliest bands in Bandarban. Amlai dreams that in the future, some of his students would also be a part of that band.

Speaking of his aims, Amlai notes, “I would be more than happy if even one or two students can come up as a rising star.” Every year, as an end of year ritual, Amlai records his students’ yearly accomplishments and performances. He dreams to build a studio one day where students can play guitar, perform other artistic activities, and engage in meaningful conversations.

title: How childhood stories help raise empathetic sons
text:
Gender equality begins at home, often shaped by the media boys consume. Here is how simple childhood storytelling can instil lifelong values of fairness and respect in young men.

I have a younger sister, and I never understood why being the boy should make me more important. The older one, yes, although that is hardly an achievement on my part. But when it came to being loved, listened to or respected, I could not see a reason for there to be different rules for us. Looking back, I realise a little girl on television called Meena had quite a bit to do with that.

She was part of my childhood, along with Raju and Mithu, who could make life rather uncomfortable for anyone hoping to get away with social injustice. I watched their stories as a boy, without thinking about what I might carry away from them. Now, as a man, I find her influence in opinions I have held for years, sometimes without giving much thought to where they began.

Meena's work around the house was easy to take for granted until he had to do it himself. Watching that, I began to understand that unfairness could exist within a loving family, among people who did not necessarily think they were doing anything wrong. That was harder to dismiss than a story with an obviously wicked person in it.

At home, I was a brother. My sister being younger and a girl did not make her feelings any less important than mine. Meena helped me understand that loving someone meant taking them seriously. Respecting my sister as an equal required no generosity. She did not owe me gratitude for something that should have been hers anyway.

As I grew older, that understanding became part of how I thought about relationships beyond our own. I was strictly against dowry. Still am. Meena had shown me how a marriage could become an opportunity for a greedy family to keep asking for more, and how refusing them was possible. I carried that refusal with me well after the cartoon ended.

The older I got, the less patience I had for finding respectable explanations for it. Call it joutuk, call it a gift, say the parents are giving it willingly; I still want to know whether their daughter would receive the same treatment if they gave nothing. I am married now, and I cannot see why becoming someone's husband should entitle me to anything from her parents. Meena made that seem absurd when I was a boy. Adulthood has not improved the argument.

What I appreciated more gradually was her way of dealing with things. She questioned people, including adults, but she also tried to work out what could help. Denied a place in school, she sent Mithu to bring the lessons back to her. There was a resourcefulness there that I came to admire, particularly as life grew more complicated and having a strong opinion did not necessarily mean knowing what to do next.

She made me want to speak up against injustice, while paying attention to the person caught in it. It is easy to be offended by unfairness in the abstract. Empathy asks a little more of you. Someone's worry deserves consideration even when you do not share it, and being unable to solve everything does not excuse you from helping with anything.

Meena's concern for her village gave me a sense of community as well. Her family mattered, but so did the people beyond their home. I learnt to think of care as something that could extend further, without needing everyone to be related to me or to have something to offer in return.

I don't think I understood all of this while watching. Much of it became clearer later, as I grew into a brother, a husband, and a man with his own choices to make. But I still come back to that early feeling: my sister deserved the same love and respect I did. I haven't found a good reason to think otherwise.

title: Dhaka women are modern until Brown Aunty Syndrome kicks in
text:
The brown moms and aunties of Dhaka — which includes me — have been on my mind lately. As I flipped through old photographs of Dhaka’s socialites, I found myself comparing them.

The conclusion was simple: Dhaka ladies are cosmopolitan and plugged into global trends, yet still tethered to brown aunty syndrome. They meditate, sip organic teas, and quote Western magazines, but continue to gossip about weight gain and saree choices. It’s a culture of contradictions — progressive on the surface, but influenced by a brown script passed from mother to mother, judging every generation as it unfolds.

Brown aunty syndrome is a cultural shorthand in South Asia, especially Dhaka, for women who look cosmopolitan yet remain bound to inherited habits of gossip and judgement. Modern on the surface but conservative underneath, they pass down a script fuelled by the refrain “what will people say.”

I vividly remember our mothers having tea in the afternoon with a sister-in-law or at their mother’s house. Socialising also meant parties with husbands at office dinners, clubbing and weddings. Crisp, starched sarees, sleeveless blouses, and trips to Mayfair for shaggy or pageboy cuts embodied a sense of style and freedom.

Those old afternoon get-togethers had magic: cards, housie, knitting on lawns, sewing, learning shorthand or typing, even picking up a new language. Yet the black-and-white photographs expose a gaze quick to criticise anything that strays from its own codes. These women — modern, graceful, and daring in ways that sometimes outshine us — also revealed prejudice beneath the sophistication.

The list stretches to young, accomplished women who believe they’re modern and inclusive, yet still whisper about a friend’s witch vibes. This fashionable mysticism blends bohemian fashion, spirituality, gothic chic and global wellness trends. Others embrace slow living or belong to an artsy crowd draping cotton saris, critiquing films and literature, and quoting New Yorker essays.

I admit, despite being conscious of what is right and wrong, I am a brown aunty too. Anything that doesn’t sync with my way of living, the brown aunty instinct kicks in — gossiping, judging, prescribing — and I am not being sarcastic.

The black-and-white frames capture a daring modernity that isn’t linear. Those women created cultural scripts that still resonate, carrying a magic of belonging that today’s compartmentalised, digitalised socialising struggles to match. Yet they also share the brown aunty syndrome, creating societal pressures, giving in to comparison culture, and getting obsessed with “what will people say.”

But we do not recognise that we are those people, and it’s time to stop being them. The legacy of grace and elegance across generations of Dhaka ladies is undeniable — but so too is the condemnatory, ingrained reflex of disapproval.

title: Why Esha Rushdi prefers raw vulnerability over curated perfection
text:
In a digital world dominated by filters and polished highlights, creator Esha Rushdi offers a refreshing mirror. Discover how her commitment to unvarnished honesty is redefining what it means to build genuine connections online.

Her journey into the public eye did not follow a traditional script. Long before the term "content creator" became a household job description, Rushdi was already documenting her life. She was the person sharing cooking experiments and capturing unscripted, funny moments with her son. With a background in communication, she naturally gravitated toward editing and visual storytelling, driven by an innate desire to forge genuine bonds with an audience.

Image

That natural affinity for human connection traces back to her childhood. She was always the person others gravitated toward, someone who could make strangers feel comfortable enough to open up within minutes.

"Making people feel good about themselves and about life is a gift I was born with," she says, smiling.

It was this quiet, instinctive charm that laid the groundwork for everything she would build later on.

From a fashion house to a beauty venture

Esha Rushdi’s path to entrepreneurship was equally organic, shaped by life's shifting chapters. Having navigated roles as a student, a housewife, and a stay-at-home mother, she did not step into business until after her son was born. Rushdi started working with a local fashion house before eventually taking a leap of faith to build her own beauty venture, The Powder Room.

When she first started, success meant building a business people could trust. But as her platform grew, so did her vision.

"Now, with a growing platform, I can reach more people and create a bigger impact," Rushdi emphasises.

"For me, success is no longer just about what I build; it is about how many people I can connect with along the way," she adds. This evolution from a traditional entrepreneur to a community builder highlights a deep shift in her priorities. This explains how she is curating a space for shared experiences.

Image

That same hunger for deeper connection eventually birthed her podcast, The Other Side, by Esha Rushdi. Growing up watching legendary interviewers like Oprah Winfrey and later drawing inspiration from modern long-form shows like The Diary of a CEO, she wanted to create a space that moved beyond surface-level chatter. She wanted unvarnished, vulnerable stories.

“I wanted to create a space where guests could feel comfortable being honest and sharing the parts of their stories we don’t usually get to hear,” she shares.

The emotional resonance of the podcast has far exceeded anything she originally expected.

Finding balance in the chaos

Juggling entrepreneurship, a growing podcast, content creation, and family life is a constant tightrope walk. Yet, Rushdi refuses to subscribe to the toxic productivity culture that defines modern entrepreneurship. She does not keep a rigid routine. Instead, she takes each day as it comes, focusing on what matters most and making ample time for her family.

Image

When creative fatigue hits, she does not believe in forcing ideas. She steps away from work for a few days, rests, and resets through travel or a simple change of scenery.

On chaotic days, she reminds herself why she started. "I do all of this because I am passionate about it, and I should enjoy it too," she declares.

She chooses to take things one step at a time, keeping a healthy balance and protecting her mental peace.

Looking toward live horizons

Looking ahead, Rushdi is excited about the future of her brand and community. The love and respect she received from her audience mean everything to her, even if it is just someone watching for three seconds. She hopes to pass that inspiration on by giving people a space to feel heard.

Her next big dream involves taking those deep conversations beyond the digital screen. She envisions a large live talk show where people can gather in person, share their stories, and feel part of something tangible and meaningful.

Esha Rushdi proves that true influence is built on empathy, turning ordinary spaces into arenas of genuine human understanding.

title: Prof Nasir Ahmad appointed Jagannath University proctor
text:
Jagannath University has appointed Prof Dr Nasir Ahmad of the history department as its new proctor for the next two years.

The university administration announced the decision today in an office order signed by Acting Registrar Prof Dr Md Sheikh Gias Uddin. The appointment takes effect on October 28.

According to the office order, Prof Nasir will be entitled to specified allowances and other benefits in line with university rules.

Speaking to The Daily Star, the newly appointed proctor said, "I want to work with all Jagannath University students as a united JnU community, and I seek everyone's cooperation for this. The doors of the proctor's office will always remain open for students. The proctor's office will stand by them in all their needs."

title: Sajek road blockade enters sixth day as talks end without breakthrough
text:
Vehicular movement on the Sajek Valley tourist route remained suspended today as protesters enforced a road blockade in Rangamati's Baghaichhari upazila for the sixth consecutive day.

The indefinite blockade was called on October 22 by the Sajek Gano Odhikar Rokkha Committee and the Sajek Karbari Association.

A meeting between senior administrative officials from Rangamati and Khagrachhari and leaders of the two protesting organisations on Monday afternoon ended without a resolution.

At the meeting, representing the authorities were Abdul Wadud Bhuiyan, MP for Khagrachhari and chairman of the Parliamentary Standing Committee on the Ministry of Chittagong Hill Tracts Affairs; Rangamati MP Dipen Dewan; Rangamati Deputy Commissioner Nazma Ashrafi; Rangamati Superintendent of Police Muhammad Abdur Rokib; Khagrachhari Deputy Commissioner Anwar Sadat; Khagrachhari Superintendent of Police Mortoza Ali Khan; Baghaichhari Upazila Nirbahi Officer Amena Marjan; and Sajek Police Station Officer-in-Charge Tofazzal Hossain.

The protesters were represented by Babudhan Chakma, Sajek Karbari Association President Natun Joy Chakma and Chattra Janata Sangram Parishad President Ushatan Chakma.

According to protest leaders, the administration agreed to four of the five demands that were placed, but no agreement was reached on the demand for the withdrawal of armed JSS members from Sajek.

Later on Monday night, senior administrative officials returned to Khagrachhari and briefed journalists at the district circuit house.

At the briefing, Abdul Wadud Bhuiyan said the administration had agreed to four of the five demands raised by the protesters. He said further discussions would be held within the next few days regarding the withdrawal of armed JSS members from Sajek.

From 6:00am today, protesters staged demonstrations by burning tyres at Machalong 14 Kilo, Gangaram Bazar and Baghaihat Hazachhara 10 Number on the Sajek road. Vehicular movement on the route remained completely suspended.

Babudhan Chakma, convener of the Sajek Gano Odhikar Rokkha Committee, said, "While the administration agreed to four of our five demands, they sought time regarding one demand. We gave them five days, but the administration did not agree, resulting in an inconclusive meeting," he said.

"Our blockade programme will continue until our demands are met," he added.

Speaking about the situation, Sajek Police Station OC Tofazzal Hossain told The Daily Star, "No untoward incidents have been reported. Patrolling by law enforcement personnel has been intensified."
